14209320.label: Project Title(Chinese)
14209320.value: 多個FPGA上大型結構網絡的物理綜合

14209320.label: Project Objectives
14209320.value: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is developing rapidly in multiple areas, and is undoubtedly an important field in computing, with a lot of research being conducted to create useful and reliable AI techniques. Due to the complexity and the large amount of computations required, highly parallel hardware like GPUs have been deployed for training and making inference of AI systems. GPU systems however will consume large amount of energy and may be too big for some applications and scenarios. FPGA is a good choice for this challenge. The re-configurability and power efficiency of FPGAs make possible the generation of high-performance, low-power hardware solutions for AI systems to meet stringent requirements on throughput, delay, and power in diverse environments. However, we need an efficient flow to map large neural networks to FPGAs. Objective: In the past few years, there are works on high level synthesis (HLS) to map automatically neural network (NN) to hardware at the register-transfer level (RTL). The result will then be fed into some synthesizing tools to generate circuits (logic synthesis) and final placement and routing solutions on FPGAs (physical synthesis). Existing physical synthesizing tools rarely take into account the inherent structure of the application, resulting in much longer design space exploration time and less optimized solution. Neural networks have well-defined structures consisting of layers of processing units systematically and sometimes symmetrically connected. This nature of NN will help the synthesizing tools to obtain better optimized tailored solutions to AI applications, bringing further gain in circuit performance. The objective of this project is to study and develop a multi-FPGA placement tool for large and structural neural networks. Sub-objective #1: Network Structure and Data Flow Driven Placement A typical neural network is composed of a number of layers executed sequentially one after another. The most common types of layers are convolution layer, fully connected layer and pooling layer. There are also non-linear layers with activation functions like sigmoid, tanh or ReLU. Neural network applications have explicit and systematic geometrical structures which give the synthesizing tools much additional information to place and route the circuits with better quality. For example, logic elements on consecutive layers can be placed regularly with equal offset to favor data path flow, and repeated structures can be mapped similarly to save synthesizing time, etc. This structural information can be obtained by data flow analysis of the circuit or even more effectively by proper annotation of the processing units and wires during HLS. Most of the previous works on mapping NN on FPGA architecture focuses on HLS, but physical synthesis with awareness of neural network architecture is rarely done, which definitely will improve circuit performance. Thus, another key issue is an effective methodology for network structure-driven and data path-aware pack and place on FPGAs. Sub-objective #2: Timing-driven Network Partitioning In today’s AI systems, neural network models are huge with hundreds of millions of weights and tens of billions of operations. It is impossible to implement the whole network on one single FPGA board. In many cases, the problem is resolved by partitioning huge circuits into sub-circuits and map the sub-circuits into different FPGAs. It is a challenging task on how to partition a large network into sub-networks under multiple resource constraints on entities like lookup tables, memories and flip-flops, etc., while optimizing the performance under the time-multiplexing scheme of the inter-FPGA connections. Network partitioning with multiple resource constraints considering time-multiplexed connections to optimize timing and throughput is one key problem to resolve. Sub-objective #3: Time-Multiplexed Routing Neural networks today can be huge with billions of connections between processing units and partitioning is needed due to limited hardware resources. The connections between partitions are time-multiplexed to increase connectivity logically by having several nets sharing a single physical wire time-wise. For signals sharing physical wires with others (TDM nets), their time division multiplexing values need to be determined to minimize critical path delay and to maximize throughput. Other signals can then be routed considering the delays of the TDM nets. One of the key issues is thus to assign TDM values and to route the TDM nets effectively to optimize timing. Summary of Objectives: Our objective is to develop a physical synthesizing tool for mapping large structural networks on FPGAs: 1. Research on a timing-driven and multiple resource constrained partitioning method for large networks. 2. Research on a network structure-driven placer for FPGAs. 3. Research on the TDM assignment problem and the routing problem with TDM nets. 4. Develop a timing aware physical synthesizing tool for mapping large neural network models on multiple FPGAs.
rows: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is developing rapidly in multiple areas, and is undoubtedly an important field in computing, with a lot of research being conducted to create useful and reliable AI techniques. Due to the complexity and the large amount of computations required, highly parallel hardware like GPUs have been deployed for training and making inference of AI systems. GPU systems however will consume large amount of energy and may be too big for some applications and scenarios. FPGA is a good choice for this challenge. The re-configurability and power efficiency of FPGAs make possible the generation of high-performance, low-power hardware solutions for AI systems to meet stringent requirements on throughput, delay, and power in diverse environments. However, we need an efficient flow to map large neural networks to FPGAs.

Objective: In the past few years, there are works on high level synthesis (HLS) to map automatically neural network (NN) to hardware at the register-transfer level (RTL). The result will then be fed into some synthesizing tools to generate circuits (logic synthesis) and final placement and routing solutions on FPGAs (physical synthesis). Existing physical synthesizing tools rarely take into account the inherent structure of the application, resulting in much longer design space exploration time and less optimized solution. Neural networks have well-defined structures consisting of layers of processing units systematically and sometimes symmetrically connected. This nature of NN will help the synthesizing tools to obtain better optimized tailored solutions to AI applications, bringing further gain in circuit performance. The objective of this project is to study and develop a multi-FPGA placement tool for large and structural neural networks.

Sub-objective #1: Network Structure and Data Flow Driven Placement A typical neural network is composed of a number of layers executed sequentially one after another. The most common types of layers are convolution layer, fully connected layer and pooling layer. There are also non-linear layers with activation functions like sigmoid, tanh or ReLU. Neural network applications have explicit and systematic geometrical structures which give the synthesizing tools much additional information to place and route the circuits with better quality. For example, logic elements on consecutive layers can be placed regularly with equal offset to favor data path flow, and repeated structures can be mapped similarly to save synthesizing time, etc. This structural information can be obtained by data flow analysis of the circuit or even more effectively by proper annotation of the processing units and wires during HLS. Most of the previous works on mapping NN on FPGA architecture focuses on HLS, but physical synthesis with awareness of neural network architecture is rarely done, which definitely will improve circuit performance. Thus, another key issue is an effective methodology for network structure-driven and data path-aware pack and place on FPGAs.

Sub-objective #2: Timing-driven Network Partitioning In today’s AI systems, neural network models are huge with hundreds of millions of weights and tens of billions of operations. It is impossible to implement the whole network on one single FPGA board. In many cases, the problem is resolved by partitioning huge circuits into sub-circuits and map the sub-circuits into different FPGAs. It is a challenging task on how to partition a large network into sub-networks under multiple resource constraints on entities like lookup tables, memories and flip-flops, etc., while optimizing the performance under the time-multiplexing scheme of the inter-FPGA connections. Network partitioning with multiple resource constraints considering time-multiplexed connections to optimize timing and throughput is one key problem to resolve.

Sub-objective #3: Time-Multiplexed Routing Neural networks today can be huge with billions of connections between processing units and partitioning is needed due to limited hardware resources. The connections between partitions are time-multiplexed to increase connectivity logically by having several nets sharing a single physical wire time-wise. For signals sharing physical wires with others (TDM nets), their time division multiplexing values need to be determined to minimize critical path delay and to maximize throughput. Other signals can then be routed considering the delays of the TDM nets. One of the key issues is thus to assign TDM values and to route the TDM nets effectively to optimize timing.

Summary of Objectives: Our objective is to develop a physical synthesizing tool for mapping large structural networks on FPGAs: 1. Research on a timing-driven and multiple resource constrained partitioning method for large networks. 2. Research on a network structure-driven placer for FPGAs. 3. Research on the TDM assignment problem and the routing problem with TDM nets. 4. Develop a timing aware physical synthesizing tool for mapping large neural network models on multiple FPGAs.

14209320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14209320.value: Deep neural networks have shown remarkable performance in various tasks like computer vision, natural language processing and many other applications. However, the enormous amount of computation and storage requirements bring limits on power, throughput and delay. In many applications that require low-latency and low-power, like autonomous driving and drone navigation, FPGAs (Field Programmable Gate Arrays) provide a high-performance and low-power execution platform to be configured to meet performance. To map a neural network to FPGAs, one needs to go through logic synthesis and physical synthesis. There have been a lot of recent works on high level synthesis to convert a neural network computational model in high level programming languages like c++, python, java, etc. to a circuit at register-transfer level. The circuit will then be converted to one at gate level and mapped to the logic devices on FPGA by synthesizing tools. The physical synthesis process that maps a circuit onto FPGA plays an important role to optimize performance. However, there are not many works on this placement and routing problem of neural networks on FPGAs. In this project, we will consider this problem of physical mapping of very large structural networks on FPGAs. To deploy a very large system on FPGAs, we need to partition the circuit on multiple FPGAs. This partitioning problem is challenging since there are multiple resource constraints on lookup tables, memories, flip-flops, etc., and constraints on multiple clock domains, while the target is to minimize latency and throughput of the whole system. Since inter-FPGA delay will dominate total delay, it is essential to route and time multiplex inter-FPGA nets properly. This TDM (time division multiplex) assignment is a challenging problem to address in order to balance the routing resources between different FPGAs while optimizing timing. Finally, neural networks usually exhibit very regular structure, the placement of the partitioned circuit on each FPGA should be aware of the regular network structure and align data flow paths to bring further optimization. Being able to address all these problems in a complete flow will be a key to effectively synthesize very large neural networks on FPGAs. With the increasing importance of AI in today’s technology, the success of this project will contribute to both the AI and EDA communities in bringing advancement in technology. 現有的物理綜合工具很少考慮應用程序的固有結構，從而導致更長的設計空間，探索時間和更少的優化解決方案。神經網絡具有定義明確的結構，該結構由系統地，有時對稱地連接的處理單元層組成。神經網絡的這種性質將幫助綜合工具為AI應用獲得更好的優化定制解決方案，從而進一步提高電路性能。該項目的目的是研究和開發用於大型和結構化神經網絡的多FPGA放置工具。

14209320.label: Realisation of objectives
14209320.value: We have successfully achieved the ultimate goal of developing a timing aware physical synthesizing tool for mapping large networks on multiple FPGAs. This include solving the timing driven routing problem on multiple FPGA systems (MFS) with consideration of TDM and solving the placement problem of a network on multiple FPGAs. We propose a practical and scalable partitioning and routing framework, called SPARK, for a multi-FPGA system in a 2-dimensional near-square mesh shape and utilizing the minimum number of FPGAs. To make the most of the valuable FPGA resources, SPARK adopts the homogeneous mesh structures and tailors the mesh shape according to the resource demand of the input network. With a trade-off between inter-FPGA connections and the number of FPGAs, SPARK determines a near square mesh with the minimum number of FPGAs based on the resource supply of each basic FPGA and the resource demand of the network. We proposed a practical partitioning method with multi-resource awareness, where PaToH, an effective hyper-graph partitioner, is applied to conduct general circuit partitioning based on the most critical resource to reduce resource overflow. An efficient legalization algorithm is then applied to fix the overflow issues while reducing the increase in the number of cut nets. Next, each circuit partition is assigned to a unique FPGA in the system with a cut-driven mapping algorithm to reduce the minimum total cut size considering the routing distance in the multi-FPGA system. In the inter-FPGA routing stage, we proposed a novel maximum cut-driven maze routing on the routing grid derived directly from the multi-FPGA mesh to iteratively reduce the maximum cut between two connected FPGAs. At last, SPARK applies maximum hop-driven refinement to minimize the maximum number of routing hops, which can significantly affect the frequency of the multi-FPGA system.

14209320.label: Major findings and research outcome
14209320.value: For the routing problem on a multi-FPGA system (MFS), a system-level routing and TDM assignment algorithm is proposed to optimize timing, which considers both wirelength and TDM ratios. The method is multi-thread friendly, which can be parallelized with little or no quality loss. The routing algorithm will first generate the routing topology of each net, and then maze routing is applied to connect the nets that are timing critical. The remaining nets are routed by a fast minimum terminal spanning tree method in parallel. A fast and effective two-step algorithm is proposed to determine the TDM ratio of each inter-FPGA routing edge. A practical and scalable partitioning and routing framework, called SPARK, was developed based on the findings that resolves the tight constraints on multiple hardware resources by leveraging a general hypergraph partitioning tool and combining it with an efficient legalization algorithm to map a network on an MFS, minimizing cut size without resource overflow. A novel maximum cut-driven maze routing and a maximum hop-driven refinement algorithms are developed to improve the system frequency. Extensive experiments using the largest public benchmarks for FPGA demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of SPARK.

14209320.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14209320.value: To further improve on the current framework SPARK, we can perform GPU acceleration on the partitioning, placement and routing components so as to increase the efficiency of the compilation. On the other hand, a better timing model to capture the inter-FPGA and intra-FPGA delays will also be some good directions to pursuit to further improve the current framework.

14209320.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14209320.value: With the growing size of modern network designs, multi-FPGA systems have become a popular choice for various applications like circuit emulation and prototyping. Scalable MFS architectures with efficient design compilation framework are crucial. In this project, we propose and developed a practical and scalable partitioning and routing framework, named SPARK, for multi-FPGA systems with an adjustable near-square mesh shape and using the minimum number of FPGAs. Our design compilation flow will make full advantage of the limited FPGA resources and will partition, place and route in such a way to improve the system frequency. Extensive experiments using the largest public circuit benchmarks for FPGA demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of SPARK.

14209420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14209420.value: As the transistor feature size becoming smaller and smaller, the complexity of the circuit design flow increases significantly, which makes the next-generation design flow and design methodologies are of great importance. Recently, machine learning draws much attention in the area of EDA. Meanwhile, a set of graph-based machine learning models, called Graph convolutional network (GCN), has been widely used in graph-structured tasks. Traditional EDA problems are mostly graph-based problems, including circuit partitioning, logic synthesis, and physical synthesis. These problems are greatly challenged by both performance and scalability issues. In this project, we aim at developing next-generation algorithms for good performance and large scale graph applications in EDA. Although machine learning has been well studied in several EDA problems, learning-based graph applications are still under exploration. In particular, we will adopt and customize a graph convolutional network for a better understanding of circuit netlists. We will also dig into how to speed up the graph-based machine learning algorithms for a more efficient inference procedure. With all these graph-based learning models in the EDA area, we can develop a more complete framework for digital or analog design. We will partner with several leading semiconductor companies (nVIDIA, Cadence and Huawei HiSilicon) on this topic. The academia-industry collaboration promises innovative and high-risk academic research coupled with realistic industry data/benchmarks, and timely technology transfer through the companies can benefit the 300 billion semiconductors and equipment industry. The project will also contribute to the education plan, including curriculum development, undergraduate/graduate student training, and research mentoring. 隨著晶體管特徵尺寸的越來越小，電路設計流程的複雜性顯著增加，這使得下一代設計流程和設計方法變得非常重要。最近，機器學習在EDA領域引起了很多關注。同時，圖卷積網絡（GCN）的一組基於圖的機器學習模型已廣泛用於圖結構化任務。傳統的EDA問題主要是基於圖形的問題，包括電路劃分，邏輯綜合和物理綜合。這些問題同時受到性能和可伸縮性問題的挑戰。 在此項目中，我們旨在開發下一代算法，以在EDA中實現高性能和大規模圖形應用。儘管已經在幾個EDA問題中對機器學習進行了很好的研究，但基於學習的圖形應用仍在探索中。特別是，我們將採用和定製圖卷積網絡，以更好地了解電路網表。我們還將探討如何加快基於圖的機器學習算法的速度，以實現更高效的推理過程。借助EDA領域中所有基於圖的學習模型，我們可以為數字或模擬設計開發更完整的框架。 在這一主題上，我們將與多家領先的半導體公司（nVIDIA，Cadence和Huawei HiSilicon）合作。產學合作將承諾進行創新和高風險的學術研究，並提供切合實際的行業數據/基準，並且通過公司及時進行技術轉讓可以使3000億個半導體和設備行業受益。該項目還將為教育計劃做出貢獻，包括課程開發，本科生/研究生訓練以及研究指導。

14209420.label: Major findings and research outcome
14209420.value: In a recent DAC'2022 "Functionality Matters in Netlist Representation Learning", we proposed a novel netlist representation learning framework that utilizes a contrastive scheme to acquire generic functional knowledge from netlists effectively. We also propose a customized graph neural network (GNN) architecture that learns a set of independent aggregators to better cooperate with the above framework. In DATE'2022 work "FastGR : Global Routing on CPU-GPU with Heterogeneous Task Graph Scheduler", we proposed a global routing framework running on hybrid CPU-GPU platforms with a heterogeneous task scheduler and a GPU-accelerated pattern routing algorithm. We demonstrated that the task scheduler can lead to 2.307× speedup compared with the widely-adopted batch-based parallelization strategy on CPU and the GPU-accelerated pattern routing algorithm can contribute to 10.877× speedup over the sequential algorithm on CPU. In addition, in DATE'2021 work "Global Placement with Deep Learning-Enabled Explicit Routability Optimization", we proposed a fully convolutional network model to predict congestion hotspots and then incorporate this prediction model into a placement engine, DREAMPlace, to get a more route-friendly result. Also in DATE'2022 work "Mixed-Cell-Height Legalization on CPU-GPU Heterogeneous Systems", for the first time, we investigated dedicated legalization algorithms on heterogeneous platforms, which promises intelligent usage of CPU and GPU resources and hence provides new algorithm design methodologies for large-scale physical design problems. Moreover, in our ASPDAC'2021 work "TreeNet: Deep Point Cloud Embedding for Routing Tree Construction", we modeled the pins of a net as point cloud and formalize a set of special properties of such point cloud. Considering these properties, we propose a novel deep neural net architecture, to obtain the embedding of the point cloud. Based on the obtained cloud embedding, an adaptive workflow is designed for the routing tree construction. Experimental results show that the proposed model is superior to other mainstream models for the point cloud on classification tasks. This work is the winner of ASPDAC'2021 Best Paper Award.

14209420.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14209420.value: The developed framework can be further applied for some large industrial cases under collaboration with partner companies such as Cadence and Huawei. Such sophisticated and large-size tests can enhance the flexibility and robustness of our method. At the same time, the method may contribute to practical industrial solution by matching our methods with industrial requirements. For example, we plan to focus on very-large layout problem, whose problem size is thousands and even millions of times the original problem. Besides the industrial extension, we plan to explore more deep learning techniques that are specifically for the target problem such as full-scale layout timing prediction and congestion prediction.

14209420.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14209420.value: Electronic Design Automation (EDA) is a term for a category of software products and processes that help to design electronic systems with the aid of computers. With the advance of the integrated circuit, a chip design and manufacture without the assistance of EDA system is no longer possible. Our project mainly handles placement and routing, where both of them are two indispensable steps in EDA. Also, the two steps are two main challenges in the whole EDA workflow, therefore, our research project is able to contribute to the development of EDA.

14209620.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14209620.value: This project aims to generate the fundamental knowledge and technological know-hows to enable application of organic heterojunction phototransistors in ambulatory and wearable functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) systems. Brain monitoring in situ and with long duration is essential for cognitive psychology and brain diseases research. A promising technology to realize such monitoring capability is fNIRS, which exploits near-infrared wavelengths to noninvasively probe the hemodynamic responses associated with neural activities. Current fNIRS systems rely on either avalanche photodiodes that require large-sized high-voltage suppliers or silicon photodiodes that exhibit low light responsivity. A wearable (thus enabling brain monitoring during daily activities) and high sensitivity fNIRS system is yet to be developed. In this project, we propose to exploit the self-amplification mechanism of organic bulk heterojunction (BHJ) phototransistors to enhance the sensitivity of the fNIRS detection unit and meanwhile enable light-weight and flexible system configuration. Our pilot study has suggested that polymer/non-fullerene (NF) BHJ systems may offer unique advantages in realizing fNIRS applications. However, exisiting understandings on polymer/NF BHJs are developed almost exclusively for photovoltaic applications, and it remains unknown how the morphological and energetic properties of the material systems can be utilized to manipulate the photodetection characteristics (e.g., responisivity, noise and bandwidth) of the phototransistors. Furthermore, to realize the fNIRS function, specific design guidelines of device structures and systems should be generated to accommodate the measurement conditions. Accordingly, we propose four research tasks in this project. Firstly, we will use prototype polymer/NF systems to investigate how each performance parameters of organic BHJ phototransistors are affected by the morphological and compositional features of the heterojunctions. Secondly we will focus on studying the nonlinearity of photoresponse and noise generation under weak light bias, with the aim of exploring new mechanisms, enabled by energetic and morphological tuning, to enhance the photodetection performance at fNIRS settings. Thridly, we will extend the research to the entire phototransistor structure and establish material and device strategies to optimize the photodetection characteristics under fNIRS conditions and to improve operation stability. Lastly, we will perform simulations and phantom experiments to eluicidate the measurement conditions of fNIRS, based on which we will develop system design and signal acquisition methods that allow for optimized operation of the organic phototransistors during fNIRS measurements at human forehead sites. The science and technological findings generated in this project can be extended to enhance the performance of other optical brain monitoring platforms such as diffuse optical tomography. 該項目初期通過基礎研究與系統開發，開創有機異質結光電晶體管在動態和可穿戴功能性近紅外光譜（fNIRS）系統中的應用。 fNIRS是可實現這種監測功能的另一極有前途的技術。該技術利用近紅外波長以非侵入方式探測與神經活動相關。的血液動力學反應。當前的fNIRS系統依賴於需要高驅動電壓的雪崩光電二極管或呈現低光響應性的矽基光電二極管。而真正適用於可穿戴設備（因此可在日常活動中進行大腦監視）而同時具有高靈敏度的fNIRS系統尚未問世。 在本項目中，我們提出利用有機體異質結（BHJ）光電晶體管的自放大機制來增強fNIRS檢測單元的靈敏度，同時實現高集成度及輕巧的系統配置。我們的初步研究表明，聚合物/非富勒烯（NF）BHJ系統在實現fNIRS應用方面具有獨特的優勢。然而，關於聚合物/ NF BHJ的現有研究僅針對光伏應用。而對於如何利用材料系統的形貌和電子能態來替代其光電檢測特性（例如，響應度，噪聲和帶寬）的理解幾乎是空白的。以及，如何進一步將器件推向fNIRS系統還需要整體的系統設計創新。 因此，我們在該項目中提出了四個研究任務。首先，我們將使用典型聚合物/ NF系統研究有機BHJ光電晶體管的每個性能參數如何受到異質結的形貌和組份特徵的影響。二，我們將專注於研究弱光校正下光響應和噪聲的非線性特徵，以探索如何通過能級匹配和形貌調整增強fNIRS設置下的光檢測性能。第三，我們將把研究擴展到整個光電晶體管結構，並建立材料和器件策略，以優化fNIRS條件下的光電檢測特性並提高操作穩定性。最後，我們將進行仿真實驗，以消除fNIRS的測量條件，在此基礎上，我們將開發系統設計和信號採集方法，以在人體前額部位進行fNIRS測量期間優化有機光電晶體管的運行。該項目中產生的器件設計可以擴展到其他腦部光學監視平台（如漫射光學層析成像）達到性能提高。

14209620.label: Realisation of objectives
14209620.value: 1. We have carried out a systematic study to (1) characterize the different morphologies of organic heterojunctions formed by polymer/non-fullerene (NF) and polymer/fullerene blends and (2) understand how the morphological differences result in different charge separation, charge transport and charge trapping processes and how these processes affect the characteristics of the heterojunction-based phototransistors. (Objectives #1 and #2) 2. We discovered that the newly developed non-fullerene acceptors, such as Y6, outperform fullerene acceptors in phototransistors by creating a unique vertical phase distribution that reduces dark noise and enhances responsivity at low light intensity. This leads to a detectivity of 1.28×10¹⁵ Jones, driven by a float-gate effect and trap-assisted photoconductive gain. (Objective #3) 3. We have carefully analyzed the noise origins in organic phototransistors by comparing the effects of (i) operation mode (depletion vs accumulation), (ii) trapping processes at the semiconductor-dielectric interface and (iii) surface aggregations in the semiconductor heterojunctions. Based on the findings we optimized the device structure for fNIRS applications (Objective #4 and #5) 4. By developing ternary organic heterojunctions, we discovered that the photoresponse linearity can be tuned and optimized by carefully aligning the energy levels of the three organic components. (Objective #4) 5. We designed and realized a monolithically integrated photovoltaic transistor to solve the gain-bandwidth trade-off in common heterojunction phototransistors. In the new structure, the photovoltage generated by a superimposed solar cell, acting as a float-gate, is amplified by the underlying thin-film transistor. The new design has led to a record high gain-bandwidth product. (Objective #5); 6. We have designed and fabricated the customized circuit to realize the organic phototransistor-based wearable fNIRS system that allow for optimal operation of the organic photodetection unit for monitoring brain hemodynamics responses. The fNIRS sampling system is powered by 9 V batteries. It can provide up to 8 channels, 24 bits, and 250 Hz real-time sampling. With the system we have demonstrated high quality forehead-site fNIRS measurements with ≥ 3 cm source-detector distance (Objective #6).

14209620.label: Major findings and research outcome
14209620.value: 1. Structure-property-performance relations in organic phototransistors: Current organic phototransistors often use fullerene molecules as electron acceptors. However, we investigated non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs), which outperform fullerenes in detectivity and speed. NFAs, when mixed with semicrystalline polymers, exhibit a unique vertical phase distribution that reduces dark noise and enhances responsivity through a float-gate effect. This results in high detectivity (1.28×10¹⁵ Jones) at low light intensity. Our study links the energetic and morphological characteristics of organic heterojunctions to their electrical performance in phototransistors, demonstrating NFAs’ superior photodetection capabilities. (Work under journal revision) 2. New device design for performance enhancement: Conventional phototransistors face a gain-bandwidth trade-off, limiting performance at low light intensity. We developed a monolithically integrated photovoltaic transistor that overcomes this limitation by amplifying photovoltage through a thin-film transistor. Through processing optimization to eliminate deep-trap defects, we achieved a record gain-bandwidth product at a low 3 V driving voltage. The device can detect pulse waveforms beyond the capability of conventional phototransistors under weak illumination. (Published in Science Advances) 3. From broadband to spectral photodetection: Wearable devices benefit from integrating spectral analysis, but current miniaturized spectrometers typically have centimeter-scale sizes. We developed a microsized optical spectrometer using an optical-spacer-integrated organic heterojunction-based photodetector with a bias-tunable spectral response, allowing computational reconstruction of light spectra from photocurrents. The device has a 0.0004 cm² footprint, broadband operation across visible wavelengths, and sub-5-nm resolution. This enabled the creation of an 8 × 8 spectroscopic sensor array for hyperspectral imaging. (Published in Nature Electronics) 4. Implementation of fNIRS system: We developed a dual-channel fNIRS system using two probing wavelengths (780 nm and 830 nm) and a twin-phototransistor detection unit. To optimize the system, we performed Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate light intensity distribution during standard measurements. Based on these results, we designed a battery-powered, low-noise 24-bit, 8-channel sampling system with a 24-bit ADC to handle signal filtering, amplification, and conversion. We developed an algorithm for noise cancellation and real-time extraction of oxygenated hemoglobin concentration, based on the differing absorption of oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin at the two wavelengths. Our system successfully monitors dynamic hemoglobin concentration changes. Currently we are gathering more clinical data to further validate the methodology.

14209620.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14209620.value: Our newly developed photovoltaic transistor structure has demonstrated excellent responsivity and bandwidth simultaneously achieved under ultralow light conditions, opening the door to numerous potential applications. However, the devices currently exhibit relatively high noise levels, alongside baseline current drift during extended operation. Future research should focus on advanced interface engineering strategies aimed at mitigating these noise sources and eliminating defect states at the metal/semiconductor and semiconductor/dielectric interfaces. Such improvements will enhance the operational stability and signal-to-noise ratio of the devices.

14209620.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14209620.value: This project aims to advance the understanding and technological framework necessary to integrate organic heterojunction phototransistors into wearable functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) systems. Conventional organic phototransistors typically rely on fullerene molecules as electron acceptors. However, out study investigates the use of non-fullerene acceptors (NFAs), which have demonstrated superior detectivity and response speed. By correlating the structural and energetic properties of organic heterojunctions with their electrical performance, this research highlights the significant advantages of NFAs for photodetection applications. A dual-channel fNIRS system was constructed, capable of monitoring hemoglobin concentration changes. Ongoing clinical data collection will further validate the system’s efficacy. Beyond the two-component organic heterojunction and the conventional phototransistor structure, we further invented a monolithically integrated photovoltaic transistor to address the commonly seen trade-off between gain and bandwidth in low-light photodetection is. This design leverages a photovoltage generated by an embedded solar cell, which acts as a floating gate, amplifying the signal through the transistor. Optimizing the process to eliminate deep-trap defects enabled a record gain-bandwidth product. Finally, we developed a microsized optical spectrometer with bias-tunable spectral response, enabling broadband operation and sub-5-nm resolution, ideal for compact wearable systems due to its 0.0004 cm² footprint.

14209720.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14209720.value: 物聯網設備，尤其是“智能家居”正在逐漸普及，使得這些物聯網設備的安全性也日益重要。由於行業標準的缺乏、軟件和硬件平臺的多樣化等原因，目前我們仍缺乏有效地方法和工具去評估各種物聯網設備的安全性。 本項目將從物聯網設備中的“隱藏功能”角度入手，研究物聯網設備的安全性分析方法。所謂“隱藏功能”，是指那些在代碼中存在但是並沒有被顯式地出現在功能描述或者用戶接口中。隱藏功能的存在，其本質原因是上層代碼功能描述與底層實現代碼之間的不一致。本項目的主要目標是研究隱藏功能的搜尋方法，理解它們出現的具體原因，並調查它們潛在的安全隱患。我們將首先在現有工作基礎上尋找更多的實例，並手動分析每個收集到的實力，尤其是識別這些隱藏功能的特徵和模式。在此基礎上，將研究相應的算法，從給定的物聯網設備固件代碼中搜索新的隱藏功能實例。最後，我們創建一個物聯網固件代碼庫，並應用所研發的算法進行大規模測試與應用。 本項目將豐富目前物聯網安全性分析的方法，提升物聯網系統的安全性，除去研究價值之外，對於保護一般大衆的信息安全也大有裨益。

14209720.label: Realisation of objectives
14209720.value: The PI and his team had tried their best to achieve all of the research objectives defined in the research proposal. Below are some details. Objective 1: Find three or more real world cases which suffer from the problem of discrepancy between code and function specifications. We have investigate and identified three vulnerabilities in real-world devices. The first device is D-Link DIR-619L wireless N300 Cloud Router. We have analyzed the code inside the firmware and have found two hidden services. (1) The first risk is that: accessing “/common/info.cgi”, “/version.txt” and “DevInfo.txt” can lead to information disclosure, some of which are sensitive, like the WPS password of the current WiFi. After checking the function invocation trace, we find that this hidden service is of the type “persistent output” since a call to open with write capability(0x302) is captured by IoTBolt . (2) The second risk is that: IoTBolt had identified a function table structure at address 0x4f9014, and via symbolic analysis it further recovered 21 handlers from the function table. We then observed that this function table was looked up inside the form handler of url “formSetHNAP11”, which was not used by web interface files. However, with some manual code analysis, we found that such services can be utilized to set new passwords or DoS the device. The second device is D-Link DIR-823G Dual Band Smart Wireless Router. The firmware we use to evaluate IoTBolt is version A1 FW102B03, IoTBolt first recognizes a request-handler binder sub 40b1f4. Tracking the usage of that function, we find handlers of four types of urls – “/HNAP1/*”, “/goform/*”,“/cgi-bin/*”, “/EXCU SHELL”. Using the automatic triggering scripts, IoTBolt collects network requests generated by a normal user when accessing the web interface. After comparing against the services found by IoTBolt, we find “/EXCU SHELL” is a hidden service which can be utilized to remotely execute arbitrary Linux commands, which is very dangerous. The third device we have analyzed is D-Link 8010LH (a new Wi-Fi camera). Different from other two samples, IoTBolt does not find any web servers inside the firmware, however, there are three service binaries found - “Rtk MainProc”, “StreamProxy” and“TW Monitor”. All of them are recorded inside the system initialization configuration file “/init.d/rcS” to launch during the starting process. IoTBolt found one hidden service inside “Rtk MainProc”belonging to system command execution. Tracking the traces output by IoTBolt , we find that inside the “main” func- tion of “Rtk MainProc”, when the binary detects that file .tw enable telnet exists, telnet service will be enabled by system(“telnetd &”). We further try cracking the credentials of the root user and find the password can be cracked within two seconds. Besides, IoTBolt also finds another hidden service inside the service binary “StreamProxy” that creates new network activities. By tracing back from the call to “SSL connect”, IoTBolt finally recovers a HTTP packet that can establish an unauthenticated RTSP channel with a remote server. Objective 2: A set of algorithms and techniques to detect code and specification discrepancy, by leveraging information such as User Interface vs. code (UI), pairing between App and IoT device, listening port vs. device functions, and so on. We have also studied and developed several algorithms and techniques to detect the discrepancies between the code and the associated function specification. For example, we have developed a method to identify and locate the code of interest (like the document root, executable files and code blocks, etc.) For the special challenge caused by indirect calls based on function tables, we developed an algorithm to recognize and recover function tables inside executable code. Another important task is to recognize the code that handles the incoming network requests and extract the network services, so that we can identify the hidden services. Objective 3: A prototype that implements above algorithms to detect code and function specification discrepancies automatically for selected domains. We have built a prototype that implemented above algorithms and techniques on code analysis and hidden service identification. The prototype we developed is called IoTBolt which has been used to analyze real-world IoT devices. Currently, we are re-organize the code base of IoTBolt and plan to make it open source on github. Objective 4: Research paper(s) and/or report(s) on using the above prototype to perform large scale study on real world IoT devices and their paired mobile Apps. Based on the above works, including the algorithms, techniques, prototypes and case studies, we have completed a paper titled "Hunting the Ghost: towards automatic mining of IoT Hidden Services". Within this paper, we have introduced the design of IoTBolt and the techniques behind IoTBolt, as well as the evaluation results of IoTBolt over real world devices. The paper currently is in the status of pre-print and can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.06822 or PI’s homepage https://staff.ie.cuhk.edu.hk/~khzhang/my-papers/dsk-iot-hidden-service.pdf . We will continue to improve it and make it published formally as an either journal paper or conference paper. Objective 5: Possible defense techniques to prevent or mitigate threats caused by the problem of code and function specification discrepancies. To mitigate the problem of hidden services caused by the problem of discrepancies between code and function specifications, it is important to first find the possible hidden services and this requires tools and techniques to helper security analyzers to acquire better understanding about the functionalities of the code. Towards that goal, the PI has done two piece of works. In the first work (refer to Paper 1 in Section 8 of Part C with title “ARMED: Disassembling ARM Binaries by Knowledge-aware Transfer Learning”), where we have explored novel techniques to translate more accurate assembly code from the binary code. The ARMED employs a multi-level masking strategy, which not only integrates domain knowledge about ARM architecture into the model but also captures deeper connections among basic units, fields, and instructions. As the result, it can deliver better assembly code than existing tools, helping more accurate detection of hidden services. The other work towards objective 5 is about helping security experts better understand the functionality of binary code and enable them to find the hidden services more efficiently. This is to address the challenge when finding hidden services: currently it heavily relies on the manual code inspection in order to understand the functionality of the assembly code, which is error prone and time consuming. To help experts complete the jobs more efficiently, we have studied a technique called "Bin2Summary" that can generate human readable descriptions for binary code automatically. The core technique behind Bin2Summary is an auto-encoder based on the machine learning techniques. This work has led to a paper titled “Bin2Summary: Beyond Function Name Prediction in Stripped Binaries with Functionality-Specific Code Embeddings” published on the conference of FSE (The ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE) - 2024). Please refer to the paper 4 in Section 9, Part C of this paper.

14209720.label: Major findings and research outcome
14209720.value: 1. Brief summary of research outcome With support from this GRF project, we have completed 9 research papers in total, with 1 journal paper under preparation, 7 conference papers published on top tier international conferences in the area of system security and software engineering, and 1 pre-print paper published on arXiv.org. Please refer to Part C for more details. We will continue our effort and try to formally publish the pre-print paper and the paper under-preparation by the end of 2026. 2. We studied the techniques to recover data type information from binary code. During our studies on hidden services, we found that the data type information plays important roles for accurate results. However, such information was removed and stripped away after compilation process. To address that problem, we developed a method using few-shot learning. Evaluation results showed that our method can deliver better results than the state-of-the-art. This works was published in a paper titled "TypeFSL: Type Prediction from Binaries via Inter-procedural Data-flow Analysis and Few-shot Learning" on the top-tier international conference(the 39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering). Refer to paper 2 in Section 9 of Part C. 3. We have extended our study from IoT devices to Linux applications and Linux kernels. This work was motivated by the observation that: there are discrepancies between the required capabilities and the capabilities assigned to many Linux applications. This problem would cause either an unexpected crash of the program or an unnecessarily-large attacking surface. To address this problem, we developed a technique and a framework called LiCA that can automatically map from the arguments of system calls to the required capabilities of the system calls. Based on this information, we are able to assign the right capabilities to Linux applications. This work was published in a paper titled "LiCA: A Fine-grained and Path-sensitive Linux Capability Analysis Framework" at the conference of the 25th International Symposium on Research in Attacks, Intrusions and Defenses (RAID'22). Paper 5 in Section 9 of Part C. 4. We also explored the methods to detect the semantic discrepancies between the binary code and its lifted intermediate representation (IR). We found that existing binary code lifters would change the code semantics when translating binary code into IR code. We have used the techniques borrowed from Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate effective inputs for fuzzing the binary code lifters.

14209720.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14209720.value: The major part of this project can be further developed into a system that can evaluate the security of IoT firmware. Given the wide use of IoT devices in smart homes and modern factories, it has become a very important problem to perform security analysis over IoT firmware and check if there is any security vulnerability or malicious code. The techniques developed in this project will be useful in such IoT security evaluation systems. Based on the works already done in this project, there are several follow-up works that can be done. For example, based on the work of accurate data type recovery (the paper 2 in section 9, Part C), we can further explore the techniques of more accurate recovery of indirect calls, which is a very important but still an open problem faced by many program analysis tasks.

14209720.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14209720.value: In this project we have studied the problem of identifying hidden services inside IoT devices. Hidden services means the functionalities that could be invoked by incoming network packets but not defined in the documents. Normally, a hidden service could be either a security vulnerability (like an opened door accidentally left over and could be exploited by hackers) or malicious (like a secret back-door purposely created by hackers who may access the device stealthily without being noticed. With the techniques and tools developed in this project, we are able to find hidden services by analyzing the code of IoT devices, thus secure these devices and protect their owners by eliminating the security risks. With the support of this project, we have also explored some related problems in performing security analysis of IoT firmware, including the data type information recovery, automatic generation of code behavior, etc. Works from this project have lead to high quality publications with international impacts, as well as reports to the device vendors who would make their devices more secure by fixing problems identified by us.

14209920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14209920.value: Motivated by advances in neural networks, in recent years several results about the complexity of circuits computing over the real numbers have been obtained. We propose to examine these results from the viewpoint of natural proofs, a cornerstone of Boolean circuit complexity. As a first step, we identify the relevant properties of the existing neural network lower bounds and argue that they are natural. We argue that these properties are consistent with the intuition that high-dimensional data sets are harder to learn than low-dimensional ones. To argue hardness of learning, we ask which sets of data points can support low-complexity pseudorandom functions. On the positive side, we sketch how one PAC learning algorithm can be derived from lower bounds. Motivated by complexity-theoretic applications we also propose studying testing questions about functions with real domain and real range under product distributions. Many algebraic tests over discrete structures do not carry over readily to the real setting owing to the lack of a uniform measure, suggesting the need of new techniques. Moreover, we argue that natural constraints on functions over the reals, such as continuity or smoothness, may affect the complexity of the testers: Some hard instances in the discrete case are based on random boolean functions and thus have no continuous counterpart. We discuss potential extensions of these lower bounds to the continuous world. 受神經網絡技術進步的推動，近年學術界發表了不少關於實數演算的電路複雜度的結果。此研究的重點是以布林電路複雜度研究的基石－－自然証明的角度來看待這些成果。首先，我們確立了現有關於神經網絡下界的相關特點並證實它們是自然的，而且這些特點亦意味著高維度比低維度的數據集難學習，這點是與直覺一致的。我們用數據集能否支撐低複雜度的偽隨機函數這個基準來量度學習它們的難度，研究的一個正面結果是我們可以由下界得出一個PAC學習演算法。 我們還建議研究有關積分佈下具有真實域和真實範圍的函數的測試問題，此方面可以推動關於複雜度理論的應用。由於欠缺統一的測度，很多在離散結構下的代數測試並不能輕易延伸到實數範疇，這表明我們需要新的技術。我們亦指出一些對具有真實域函數的自然的約束－－例如是否連續或光滑－－可能會影響測試函數的複雜性：某些困難的數據集是由隨機布林函數產生，但現時未有類似後者的連續函數，因此我們會討論如何把這些下界延伸到連續的領域。

14209920.label: Realisation of objectives
14209920.value: This project aimed to investigate two complementary objectives in the context of real-valued models of computation: (1) To develop concepts analogous to pseudorandom functions and natural proofs for real-valued computational models, and (2) To study the algorithms and complexity of property testing problems for functions over real numbers. We are pleased to report that both objectives have been realized, yielding theoretical insights, practical algorithmic contributions, and publications in top-tier machine learning conferences. The research addressed challenges in bridging complexity theory and modern machine learning, with a particular focus on generative models and real-valued functions. Objective 1: Pseudorandomness and Natural Proofs for Real-Valued Computation We developed new theoretical tools that adapt the concepts of pseudorandomness and natural proofs to models operating on real-valued data. Traditionally, pseudorandom functions have been studied in Boolean settings. This project extended these ideas by analyzing whether high-dimensional geometric structures can support function families that appear “random” to a learning algorithm, despite being computationally simple. A contribution was our characterization of known lower bounds for neural networks through the lens of “natural properties.” We showed that several existing lower bounds in the literature implicitly exploit regularities in the input space that satisfy analogues of largeness and constructiveness in the Boolean natural proofs framework. These results suggest that real-valued models, particularly neural networks, may be subject to similar limitations on provable hardness as their Boolean counterparts. As a practical application of this insight, we used spectral methods inspired by pseudorandomness theory to guide the analysis and comparison of modern generative models. These methods form the theoretical backbone of our entropy-based evaluation framework, detailed below under Objective 2. Objective 2: Algorithms and Complexity of Property Testing for Real-Valued Functions The second core objective was to study property testing for real-valued functions, particularly under product distributions and natural function class constraints (e.g., smoothness, continuity). This line of inquiry required extending classical property testing techniques, which are predominantly discrete and combinatorial in nature, into the continuous domain. An insight from this work is that algebraic or combinatorial testers for Boolean functions do not readily translate to real-valued settings due to the absence of a uniform probability measure and the need to account for analytic properties like differentiability. To address this, we developed a formal property testing framework for real-valued functions that considers query complexity under smoothness constraints and product distributions. We analyzed the complexity of testing properties such as monotonicity, convexity, and bounded variation in real-valued functions. In particular, we established both lower and upper bounds for testing these properties when the functions are defined over bounded domains like [0,1]^d and satisfy Lipschitz or Hölder continuity. Our results show that while continuity can simplify some testing problems, it also introduces new structural constraints that affect hardness in subtle ways. Key Algorithmic Outcomes and Integration of Objectives The intersection of the two objectives, real-valued pseudorandomness and property testing, led us to propose a sequence of entropy-based metrics for evaluating generative models: • Rényi Kernel Entropy (RKE): A diversity score based on the eigenspectrum of a kernel matrix over generated samples. This score captures the number and spread of modes in the generated distribution and is supported by theoretical bounds on its estimation accuracy. • Fourier-based Kernel Entropy Approximation (FKEA): A scalable approximation method for computing entropy metrics using random Fourier features. This reduces the cost of eigenspectrum estimation while preserving theoretical guarantees. • Kernel-based Entropic Novelty (KEN): A spectral method for detecting novel modes introduced by a generative model relative to a reference dataset. This framework decomposes the difference between two kernel covariance matrices and interprets leading eigenvectors as indicators of novelty. • FINC (Fourier-based Identification of Novel Clusters): An extension of KEN for scalable, reference-free model comparison, particularly in settings involving high-dimensional data such as images or text embeddings. These methods, developed in the course of the project, were applied to evaluate and compare state-of-the-art generative models. The algorithms were tested on synthetic and real-world datasets and demonstrated strong performance in terms of interpretability, sensitivity to novelty, and scalability. Publications and Dissemination The outcomes of this project have been disseminated through the following publications: 1. An Information-Theoretic Evaluation of Generative Models in Learning Multi-modal Distributions, NeurIPS 2023 2. Towards a Scalable Reference-Free Evaluation of Generative Models, NeurIPS 2024 3. An Interpretable Evaluation of Entropy-based Novelty of Generative Models, ICML 2024 4. Unveiling Differences in Generative Models: A Scalable Differential Clustering Approach, CVPR 2025 These papers collectively illustrate how the theoretical objectives were translated into practical contributions to the machine learning research community. Challenges and Mitigation The main challenge encountered was the computational cost of spectral methods, particularly when working with large-scale generative models. To address this, we invested significant effort into developing randomized approximation techniques such as FKEA, which successfully enabled the application of our methods to real-world datasets. Another conceptual challenge was extending discrete notions of pseudorandomness to continuous domains. The lack of a canonical definition of randomness in real-valued function spaces required careful reformulation of complexity measures. We overcame this by grounding our analysis in kernel methods and spectral decompositions, which offer a natural analog of discrete structure in continuous settings. Conclusion In summary, this project successfully achieved both of its core objectives. It developed novel theoretical frameworks for pseudorandomness and natural proofs in real-valued computation, and it introduced new methods and complexity results in the testing of real-valued functions. The integration of these ideas into practical tools for evaluating generative AI models has resulted in both theoretical impact and concrete applications, fulfilling the promise of the proposed research agenda.

14209920.label: Major findings and research outcome
14209920.value: This project produced several theoretical and algorithmic advances at the intersection of pseudorandomness, property testing, and real-valued computation. A central contribution was the development of entropy-based evaluation frameworks for generative models that do not rely on reference datasets. These frameworks use spectral properties of kernel similarity matrices to quantify the diversity and novelty of generated samples, and they are supported by formal analysis linking entropy estimates to mode coverage and separation in the data distribution. To make these methods scalable to large datasets, we introduced a novel use of random Fourier features to approximate the eigenspectrum of kernel matrices. This approach significantly reduces the computational burden while preserving interpretability and accuracy. Theoretical guarantees were established for the approximation quality, and empirical validation on image and text datasets confirmed the practical effectiveness of the method. These results demonstrate how tools inspired by pseudorandomness and spectral analysis can be applied to real-world learning problems, particularly for monitoring and improving generative AI models. In addition, we proposed the Kernel-based Entropic Novelty (KEN) score, an interpretable metric that identifies modes in the generated distribution that are absent or underrepresented in the reference data. This score is computed using spectral decomposition of kernel covariance differences and was shown to effectively detect novel or shifted components in high-dimensional generative outputs. We extended this method further by developing scalable algorithms for identifying differential sample types between generative models, enabling fine-grained comparison and targeted model refinement. The research outcomes have been disseminated through peer-reviewed publications at top venues in machine learning, including NeurIPS, ICML, and CVPR. Together, these contributions advance the theoretical understanding of learning and testing over real domains, while also providing practical tools for evaluating and improving the behavior of complex models. The insights gained from this project are expected to influence future work on trustworthy AI, robust learning, and evaluation methodologies in high-dimensional settings.

14209920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14209920.value: The outcomes of this project open several promising directions for further research. One natural extension is to explore the cryptographic hardness of pseudorandom functions over real-valued domains, which could lead to new security frameworks for continuous data and function spaces. Additionally, the entropy-based evaluation metrics developed in this project can be adapted to inform the training and fine-tuning of generative models in an online or adaptive setting. Another avenue is to extend the property testing framework to more structured input domains, such as manifolds or graph-based data, where continuity and smoothness constraints interact in complex ways with the underlying geometry. This could broaden the impact of our methods in areas such as scientific machine learning and generative modeling for physical systems. We plan to consolidate the theoretical findings into a unified framework for real-valued function complexity, and to further validate the proposed algorithms in collaboration with researchers working on generative modeling, fairness, and robustness. These efforts will support the development of more interpretable, reliable, and generalizable learning systems grounded in principled theory.

14209920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14209920.value: This project studied how to better understand and evaluate modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems, especially those that generate data such as images or text. While today’s AI models are very powerful, it is often unclear how to measure what they have truly learned, or whether they produce reliable and diverse outputs. Our research applied mathematical tools from theoretical computer science, such as randomness, entropy, and function testing, to design new methods that can evaluate and improve these models in a more principled way. One key result was the development of efficient techniques for measuring how diverse or novel the outputs of a generative model are, even without needing a reference dataset. These methods can be used to detect when a model is generating new and meaningful content, or simply repeating known patterns. We also created tools to compare different AI models and identify where one outperforms another. Although theoretical in nature, this research lays important groundwork for making AI systems more trustworthy, interpretable, and useful across a wide range of real-world applications, from creative design to scientific discovery.

14210120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14210120.value: The subject of study proposed here is motivated by PIs prior work in several fundamental open problems in network information theory which has resulted in successfully resolving a number of them. While that study has been primarily inspired by improving the efficiency of the utilization of the wireless spectrum for communications, this particular study - driven by the observations from there - has a more fundamental aspect in that it should be interesting for researchers in many disciplines. The main objective of this study is motivated by the following observation: resolution of the optimality or the sub-optimality of certain achievable regions in network information theory has been shown (by the PI and others) to reduce to testing the sub-additivity of certain (non-convex) information-theoretic functionals that belong to a particular family. While the PI and collaborators has been able to resolve a few of them by specifically tailored arguments, it now appears that there may be a more general method to test the sub-additivity property, which in turn may greatly boost the study of certain families of non-convex problems. This new direction relies on studying the properties of maximizers of a family of information-theoretic functionals. The family of information-theoretic functionals whose maxima is the subject of the study for this proposal has already been shown (some by the PI and some by others) to capture functional inequalities such as hypercontractive (forward and reverse) inequalities, Brascamp-Lieb inequalities, and entropy-power inequalities. Indeed for some of these inequalities, the information theoretic characterizations have been shown to be particularly useful in deriving optimality of Gaussian distributions. Further, for Brascamp-Lieb inequalities, the properties of maxima were used to derive fast algorithms for approximating the optimal parameters. Thus the objectives of this study, which covers a more general family, ought to be interesting to a multitude of researchers in functional analysis and theoretical computer science, apart from the PIs home field of network information theory. In short, the proposal aims to investigate the properties of maximizers of a family of non-convex information theoretic functionals that are directly related to fundamental problems in network information theory and is also of interest in functional analysis and computer science. 本研究課題是項目負責人最近十年在網絡信息論領域幾個懸而未決的基礎問題上的工作成果的延續。這些成果已經成功解決了一大批這樣的問題。儘管該項研究最初是用於提高無線通信頻譜的使用效率，但是其中的觀察和結論對於其他許多領域的研究者有著更廣泛而基礎的意義。 本研究主要目的源自於以下的觀察：確定網絡信息論當中某些可達到的通信速率區域的最優性可以被（項目負責人和其他人）簡化為測試某一特定族裡面的信息論類型的（非凸）泛函的次可加性。迄今為止項目負責人和合作者能夠用特定的局限性較強的論據來證明其中一部分泛函的次可加性，但極有可能存在一種更泛用的方法來測試次可加性。這種方法一旦發現將會極大地促進特定非凸問題族的研究。該新方向需要研究某一族信息論類型泛函的最大值點的性質。 本研究計劃的研究對像是某一族信息論類型泛函的最大值點。而該族信息論類型的泛函已經能夠被用來證明某些泛函不等式（一部分由項目負責人證明，一部分由其他人證明），例如雙向的超收縮不等式，Brascamp-Lieb不等式，以及熵次方不等式。事實上，對於某些這樣的不等式，信息論表徵在推導高斯分佈的最優性的時候極其有用。此外，對於 Brascamp-Lieb不等式，最大值點的性質被用來推導出估算最優參數的高效算法。因此本研究計劃的目的涵蓋了以上泛函不等式，不僅能在項目負責人所在領域網絡信息論引發反響，還能引起大批泛函分析和理論計算機科學領域的研究者的興趣。 總之，本研究計劃目的在於探究某一族信息論類型的非凸泛函的最大值點的性質。這些性質不僅和網絡信息論裡的基礎問題直接相關，對於泛函分析和計算機科學領域也有著重要的意義。

14210120.label: Major findings and research outcome
14210120.value: A whole variety of instances relating to local tensorization have been explored. In every such case, the purported statement holds. In some cases, as stated in Objective 2, we could prove it. The case of k-receiver less-noisy broadcast channel has been established (in the doctoral work of my student Ken Lau), and we were able to develop new conjectures on Marton's inner bound based on this evidence. Bolstered by the evidence gathered, the meta conjecture has turned into a central driving force behind a lot of my research agenda. Further for the Gaussian broadcast channel and from Brascamp-Lieb parameters, we showed that there is an uniqueness of the maximizers (despite the functionals being non-convex, thus showing the equivalence between local and global tensorization. We have explored Onbjective 3 in the case of interference channels in particular and have observed that maximizers may not move smoothly in the underlying space. This forced us to use Fenchel duality and adopt a complete different approach to prove sub-additivity. One of the (hopeful) conjectures by the authors was refuted by other authors subsequently, but as acknowledged by them, the conjecture seems to hold for the parameters of the space that really matter. We have extended the study of Brascamp-Lieb type inequalities to finite Abelian groups, and this work received the Jack Wolf paper award at ISIT 2024.

14210120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
14210120.value: As stated in the earlier section, we are greatly driven by the conjecture that a set of parameters satisfies local tensorization if and only if it satisfies global tensorization. Tensorization and sb-additivity go hand in hand. To determine sub-additivity for interference channels, we realized that the additivity of the channel played an important role. This led us to study information inequalities involving additive structures. This has initiated a surprising interdisciplinary study linking additive combinatorics and multiuser information theory.

14210120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
14210120.value: To determine the fundamental limits of communication, one has to employ the tools of information theory and, in particular, employ information inequalities. As is often the case in fundamental research, one cannot use existing inequalities, but has to first conjecture and then establish them. This is a painstaking scientific process, and this project has provided lots of evidence to boost some observed conjectures and prove results that conform to this conjecture. It has been extremely useful to the PI to continue in his quest to seek answers to some of the most fundamental questions in the area.

14210320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
14210320.value: As more and more services (including computations and I/O workloads) are moving into the cloud, the multi-tenant system has gradually become a mainstream infrastructure. Meanwhile, the high-density flash memory (e.g., triple-level-cell (TLC) and quad-level-cell (QLC)) based solid-state-drives (SSDs) have become a vital option for high-performance data storage in the enterprise infrastructure. For the service provider/user, not only the tenancy fee but also the quality of service (QoS) are of most concern. Even though an SSD can demonstrate very low latency for most of I/O requests, the tail latency of an SSD can be very long due to the internal garbage collection. Moreover, in multi-tenant environment, the mixed workloads may further exacerbate the performance predictability (i.e., I/O determinism) of an SSD, since multiple tenants may interfere each other. To deliver predictable performance for SSDs, the performance isolation solution is introduced by serving I/O requests of each tenant in a dedicated, performance-isolated partitions (or sets) of the internal flash space. Nevertheless, based on our preliminary studies, although the existing performance isolation solution reduces the performance variations among tenants, the performance throughput of individual tenant may be inevitably constrained due to the reduced access parallelism of a partition. In addition, we further observe that the upcoming high-density flash memory brings not only the increasing in storage capacity at low cost but also the reduction in the overall access parallelism to a high-density SSD. Inevitably, the reduced access parallelism may further hinder the performance isolation solution from exhibiting high performance throughput. Thus, this research aims to deliver a higher degree of “Quality of Storage (QoS)”, in terms of both performance throughput and I/O determinism, for the multi-tenant environment with high-density SSDs. To achieve this goal, this research will first propose the brand new concept of “Time Isolation Parallelism Sharing (TIPS),” then further co-optimize the performance throughput and I/O determinism by utilizing the abundant multi-queue resources in high-speed host-device interface (e.g., Non-Volatile-Memory Express (NVMe)) and enriching the functionalities of SSD and flash die controllers. To realize the proposed designs, this research will also develop a vertical simulation framework that can co-ordinate the multi-queue resources of NVMe protocol, the SSD controller, and even the micro-controller(s) on flash dies. This project is particularly important for Hong Kong, since the success of this research will benefit all the possible service users/providers (ranging from end-user, enterprises, to government units) by presenting the low-cost yet high-quality data storage to multi-tenant environment. 伴隨著越來越多系統服務（包含資料運算及資料存取）的雲端化，多租戶系統已逐漸成為主流的系統建設。同時，基於高密度快閃記憶體（如：三層單元快閃記憶體及四層單元快閃記憶體）的固態硬碟也已經成為企業級系統建設中，不可或缺的高效能資料存儲設備。對於多租戶系統服務的提供者與使用者而言，除了租賃費外，存儲質量更是一個重要的考量。雖然目前商用的固態硬碟能對大部分的存取請求展現極低的存取延遲，固態硬碟的最差延遲卻可能因為其內部的垃圾回收而變得極為耗時。在多租戶系統中，由於來自不同租戶間交錯的存取請求可能相互干擾，固態硬碟的效能可預期性（或稱存取可決定性）更可能進一步劣化。因此，藉由將不同租戶的存取請求分配獨佔的存儲分區，現有的效能區隔技術能有效保證不同租戶在同一固態硬碟上的效能可預期性。 然而，基於我們初步的調查研究，雖然現有的效能區隔技術有效地降低了不同租戶間的效能變異，每個租戶其獨佔分區內有限的存取並行度，卻也衰退了對單一租戶的性能吞吐量。我們更觀察到，即將商用化的高密度固態硬碟雖然能降低存儲容量的成本，其內部的存取並行度卻也隨之降低；而此存取並行度的下降，更將會使得現有的效能區隔技術無法展現高的性能吞吐量。因此，此研究將基於高密度固態硬碟之多租戶系統，針對性能吞吐量及存取可決定性，致力於提供更佳的「存儲質量」。為了能達成此目標，此研究將提出一個全新的「時間區隔並行共享」技術，並透過善用主機與設備間高速傳輸接口（如：Non-Volatile-Memory Express）其內含的豐富佇列資源，及增進固態硬碟與快閃記憶體芯片控制器的功能等策略，來共同最佳化多租戶系統其性能吞吐量及存取可決定性。為了實現與驗證，此研究也將開發一個垂直整合的系統模擬框架，來協同傳輸接口的佇列資源、固態硬碟及快閃記憶體芯片的控制器。 此研究將能實現一個低成本但高質量的多租戶資料存儲系統，並有益於所有潛在的系統服務提供者與使用者（個人、企業至政府部門）。因此，此研究對香港的資訊科技發展極為重要。

14210320.label: Realisation of objectives
14210320.value: This project has been going very well. All the objectives stated in this project have been either completely achieved or exceedingly achieved. For Objective 1, we have proposed a dynamic hashing scheme to strike a good balance between performance throughput (i.e., efficiency) and performance isolation (i.e., predictability) for the multi-tenant system. One key design behind this scheme is a novel Level Segment (LS) structure that builds up a hash table with a unique and delicate indexing mechanism, mitigates the inefficiency in probing items randomly, and embraces the incremental resizing to prevent other concurrent threads from being blocked. Another key design is a low-overhead split operation that significantly suppresses the resizing-incurred performance unpredictability: it not only reduces the number of KV items to be rehashed to one-third of an LS but even avoids the pointer dereference required to rehash a KV item for most of the time. Moreover, a semi lock-free mechanism, which requires a nearly minimal amount of writes to handle an insertion, is devised to achieve ever-higher efficiency and scalability while ensuring correctness and crash consistency. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed scheme averagely achieves 2.12X higher throughput than extendible hashing-based hashing schemes and delivers 15.4X higher average throughput than level-based hashing schemes; also, it provides more reliable predictability by achieving 11.4X~19.3X lower tail latency. On the other hand, we have identified and resolved a performance issue of high-density NAND flash memory, which stems from the superpage organization in the modern SSD. Specifically, we observe that because of process variation (PV), each flash page may have its own read/write performance, and grouping a slow page with a fast page in a superpage unit will result in a poor performance result. To prove the existence and resolve this issue, we conduct a series of experiments on a real SSD platform and characterize 24 real NAND flash memory chips to derive hints for organizing super-fast superpages. Based on the derived insights, we introduce a PV check scheme that can group a superpage with an optimized performance at runtime with low overheads. According to the experiments, the PV Check scheme achieves encouraging results in performance improvement: it can decrease the extra program and erase latency by 16.61% and 34.55%, respectively, compared with a traditional method. For Objectives 2 and 3, we have developed several new solutions to maximize the access parallelism utilization of an SSD and to minimize the performance interference among multiple tenants. First, we have investigated eight directions, including one local-optimal solution, to organize superblocks and evaluate their capabilities on real flash memory chips and put forward a practical and near-optimal solution to organize superblocks on demand. This solution collaborates with three major components for gathering information, assembling superblocks, and allocating storage spaces for data in a performance-oriented manner. The experimental results show that this solution can shorten the extra program and erase latency by 16.61% and 34.55%, respectively, leading to better utilization of access parallelism and minimization of performance interference. Second, we have developed a self-governing block-interface all-flash array (AFA) based on zoned namespace (ZNS) SSDs. In particular, we design an innovative placement policy to explore the special zone random write area (ZRWA) feature, available in the emerging NVMe ZNS interface, to absorb data updates and reduce write amplification. Besides, we design a new I/O scheduler that enables concurrent writes on a zone to exhaust a zone's parallelism and arranges user writes and SSD-internal tasks (e.g., GC) to access the different I/O resources for tail latency reduction. To properly choose isolated zones for I/O serving, we propose a novel guess-and-verify mechanism that can confirm the zone-to-I/O-resources mappings online with low costs. The evaluation results show that this solution can reduce write amplification by 42.7% while achieving 93.2% higher throughput and 62.8% lower tail latency, compared to the state-of-the-art AFA solutions. Third, we have also proposed a novel erase suspension policy to maximally circumvent the observed issue of over-suspensions. The key idea is to only resume an erase command if we can push forward the erase progress very likely. Specifically, before resuming the suspended erases, our policy will scan the read transaction queue to avoid resuming the erases that hold the same die address as any of read transactions in the queue; otherwise, the resumed erase might be suspended right away by the read transactions. The results show that, when compared with an SSD without adopting any erase suspension policy, our policy is the only one that can bring a positive impact on the read tail latency (i.e., by more than 16%), while other existing erase suspension policies could unacceptably degrade the read tail latency by up to 50%. For Objective 4, we have developed a vertical simulation framework, based on the open-source SSD simulator MQSim, which can coordinate the multi-queue resources of NVMe protocol, SSD controller, and micro-controller of flash dies. Particularly, the original MQSim already comes with great support for NVMe protocol and SSD controller (i.e., the host-interface logic (HIL) and flash translation layer (FTL)). However, even in the latest version of MQSim, the support of program/erase suspension to micro-controller of flash dies is still incomplete. Thus, we have heavily modified MQSim to realize the fully functional erase suspension to the micro-controller of flash dies, which also enables us to evaluate the effectiveness of different existing erase suspension policies. Besides, we have built up evaluation platforms based on real NAND flash memory or SSD devices. Specifically, we have built up a real platform that is composed of four SMI SM2259XT SATA 3.0 controllers, 24 3D NAND flash memory chips, and a KSON chamber to facilitate our characterizations. Also, we have employed Western Digital SN640 4 TB SSD and Western Digital ZN540 4 TB SSD in a server equipped with a 26-core Intel Xeon 5320 CPU [32] and 512 GB DDR4 DRAM to facilitate our research study on AFA. For Objective 5, we have built up a multi-tenant testbed for evaluation using various representative benchmarks/traces. Specifically, we have studied on-line transaction processing (OLTP) benchmarks (i.e., TPC-C and TPC-E), Filebench and Postmark benchmarks, and the real-world workloads from the Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark (YCSB). Also, we have employed the open-source and flexible I/O tester (fio) to execute microbenchmarks and evaluated diverse I/O traces collected from productions, including FIU, Microsoft MSRC, Microsoft MSPC, SYSTOR, and Tencent Block Storage. These traces comprise different ratios of reads and writes with varied I/O sizes, making it possible to comprehensively examine different I/O patterns. Moreover, we have studied representative traces collected from 875 file system snapshots by Microsoft Research. For Objective 6, we have employed different QoS-related performance metrics for performance assessment. Specifically, apart from those common performance metrics such as the total execution time and overall throughput/latency, we have also implemented and examined several QoS-related performance metrics including tail latency at different percentiles and real-time throughput in the evaluation.
