15501720.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15501720.value: Conflicts among users of public recreational spaces are not uncommon, especially in urban areas with a high population density. While tourist-resident relationships and conflicts have been well researched, there is a third group of users of public spaces who are often neglected: foreign domestic helpers (FDH). In Hong Kong, FDHs are required by law to live with their employer, with one day off per week. Rain or shine, they seize the opportunity to relax and meet up with friends, and many public spaces, such as parks and footbridges in Central and Causeway Bay, become the hangouts of hundreds of thousands of FDHs on Sundays. Public recreation spaces are where complex negotiations of spatial and identity formations occur (Peters, 2010). On Sundays, many public facilities become unique social spaces shared by three groups of users. Regarding the gathering of FDHs, 40 complaints were received and 6,340 verbal warnings were issued by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department (LCSD) from 2015 to 2017 (Government of HKSAR, 2018). Although interactions between different groups may lead to conflicts, they are also opportunities for awareness and understanding. Some NGO groups organize tours and events on Sundays for FDHs to share their culture with the public (Zheng, 2018). This study aims to explore the use of public spaces by residents, tourists, and FDHs in Hong Kong from the perspectives of conflicts and social integration. Specifically, public leisure spaces in Central and Causeway Bay on Sundays, where all three user groups are co-present, will be the scope of investigation. Observations, structured interviews with residents and tourists, and in-depth interviews with FDHs will be conducted to explore each group’s leisure needs with regard to public spaces and their interactions with other users. Conflict theory will be used to identify the causes of conflicts and behavioral adjustments or negotiations in face of conflicts. Foucault’s (1986) theory of “heterotopia” and Oldenburg’s (1999) “third place” will guide the analysis of inter-group dynamics and untangle the complex issues of ownership, identity, status, and diversity in urban recreational settings. Findings will offer insights on the unique functions of public spaces to reflect social problems, contest utopian illusions, and build communities. Recommendations will be made to enhance urban planning and leisure services, provide alternative solutions to meet the leisure needs of diverse groups, and offer insights on the issues of public space, recreation, and well-being for all to achieve a more inclusive society. 公共娛樂場所使用者之間的衝突並不少見，特別是在人口密度高的城市地區。儘管已有許多關於遊客與居民之間的關係及衝突的研究，公共空間的使用者還有第三組，就是經常被忽視的外籍家庭傭工。在香港，法律要求外傭必須與雇主同住，每週只休息一天。因此，不論風雨，他們都會把握機會放鬆與朋友見面。每週日，許多公共場所成為數十萬外傭的聚會場所，例如中環和銅鑼灣的公園和行人天橋等。公共休閒空間是形成複雜的身分認同與空間協商的地方。在星期日，許多公共設施成為三組使用者共同享用的社會空間。針對外傭的聚會，康樂及文化事務署（康文署）於2015年至2017年接獲40宗投訴，並發出6,340項口頭警告（香港特別行政區政府，2018年）。儘管不同群體之間的互動可能導致衝突，也是增進彼此認識和理解的機會。例如一些非政府組織會在週日組織導覽和活動，以便外傭與大眾分享他們的文化。 本研究旨在從衝突和社會融合的角度探討香港居民、遊客和外籍家庭傭工對公共場所的使用。具體來說，研究範圍侷限在三組使用者同時存在並使用空間的情況，即每週日位於中環和銅鑼灣的公共休閒空間。本研究使用觀察法、對居民和遊客的結構式訪談以及對外傭的深入訪談，以探討每個群體在公共場所的休閒需求及與其他使用者的互動。衝突理論將用於識別衝突的原因以及面對衝突時的行為調整或協商。傅柯（1986）的“異托邦”理論和Oldenburg（1999）的“第三空間”理論將用於分析群體間的互動關係，並探討城市娛樂空間的所有權、身份認同、社會地位和多樣性等複雜問題。調查結果將揭示公共空間的社會功能，例如反映社會問題，抗拒烏托邦想像，以及建立社區共同體。並根據調查結果提出建議，以加強城市規劃和休閒服務，提供滿足不同群體休閒需求的替代解決方案。並就大眾的公共空間，娛樂和福祉問題提供見解，以實現更具包容性的社會。

15501720.label: Realisation of objectives
15501720.value: Project research activities consist of three stages: 1) Stage I: On-site observations in Central and Causeway Bay on Sundays, 2) Stage II: In-depth interviews with Foreign Domestic Helpers (FDHs), and 3) Stage III: Short structured interviews with Hong Kong residents and tourists. In Stage I, a total of seven on-site observation trips were conducted from January to June 2021, on the following dates: 17 Jan, 7 Feb, 7 Mar, 11 Apr, 2 May, 9 May, and 27 June. The observation locations include Central, Admiralty (Tamar Park), and Causeway Bay (Victoria Park). In Stage II, a total of 43 in-depth interviews with FDHs were conducted from April to September 2021. All interviews were conducted on-site and face-to-face. Interviewees include 20 Filipino domestic helpers, 19 Indonesian domestic helpers, and four staff or helpers affiliated with NGO groups related to domestic helpers. In Stage III, short, structured interviews were conducted with Hong Kong residents and international tourists in Hong Kong. A total of 72 interviews were conducted from November 2022 to June 2023, including 33 resident interviews and 39 tourist interviews. All tourist and resident interviews were also conducted on-site and face-to-face. Through on-site observations and interviews, all project objectives were realized. First, Objective #1 was achieved. In-depth interviews revealed the leisure needs of FDHs in public spaces on Sundays. In terms of location, due to the lack of their own private accommodation, FDHs cannot rest at (their employer’s) home. When choosing the location for their gatherings with friends, most people prefer spaces that are: open, large, outdoors, free, comfortable, relaxing, and safe. Most FDHs have their Sunday leisure activities in open, public spaces and spend several hours there. Moreover, the physical attributes they need in their leisure space are roof and storage. Some expressed the dream of having a building or shelter just for FDHs. Storage was also considered important because some of their leisure equipment (e.g., picnic mat, portable stove, karaoke machine) was vandalized by others. Accessibility was deemed important, as most FDHs have a limited budget for their Sunday leisure activities, ranging from HK$10 to $200, and cannot afford to spend too much on public transportation. Hong Kong residents and tourists have their need to use public leisure spaces as well. Downtown areas (e.g., Central and Causeway Bay) are popular for shopping, dining, and entertainment. Besides engaging in commercial activities, many residents and tourists would stroll around the area and need to find places to sit and rest. In urban parks (e.g., Tamar Park, Victoria Park), a lot of family and children activities, social gatherings, team sports, and exercise take place. Many residents and tourists also take walks in parks and harbourfront areas to enjoy pleasant weather, appreciate the scenery, and take photos. These open public spaces are utilized by FDHs, residents, and tourists simultaneously on Sundays, although residents and tourists generally spend shorter time in outdoor public spaces (e.g., footbridge, park benches) compared to the FDHs. Objective #2 was achieved. Overall, it was found that the level of cross-group social interactions among residents, tourists, and FDHs was not high. For all three groups, when asked about their interactions with other user groups within the same space, the most common response was “no interaction,” or polite greetings, such as eye contact, nodding, smiling, and saying “hi.” A few FDHs shared some friendly, positive interactions, such as when they were dancing, some local passersby would clap or give them a “thumb up” sign. Occasionally there were some deeper interactions. For example, some photographers would spend time talking to the FDHs and learning about their culture before seeking their permission to take photos. Many interviewees expressed hesitation with regard to interacting with other groups. For example, they would not take the initiative to start the conversation, but if the other party took the lead, they would respond. Some local and tourist interviewees also expressed that they might join the FDHs’ activities under certain conditions, such as “when I was young” or “if more people joined.” In terms of conflicts, most interviewees indicated that they did not experience conflicts themselves, but saw or heard examples of conflicts from friends or online. From all three groups’ perspectives, common types of conflicts include: local people scolding the FDHs (e.g., not wearing masks, blocking the way), or FDHs getting in trouble with the police for illegal street vending. Despite not being engaged in direct conflicts, local and tourist interviewees have expressed some complaints about the FDH activities, with the top two problems being noise (e.g., loud music, singing) and crowdedness (e.g., everywhere, full, overcrowded, occupy a lot of places). The causes of these conflicts could be identified as differences in activity style and resource specificity. Objective #3 was achieved. Although there were few direct conflicts between residents, tourists, and FDHs, many interviewees expressed that sometimes the public areas would be too crowded and uncomfortable. As a result, they would adjust their own behavior to avoid conflicts in numerous ways, such as walking very fast through the area, taking a detour, rescheduling their own activities, and sometimes canceling their activity plans. Moreover, it was found that a high sense of tolerance was expressed by resident and tourist interviewees. Although many of them did not like certain aspects of FDHs’ gatherings, they were willing to tolerate and would not resort to direct confrontations or calling the police, because: 1) they understood how important such social gatherings were for the FDHs’ well-being, 2) they realized that FDHs had no choice (e.g., no place to rest at home) but to congregate in outdoor public spaces, and 3) these gatherings only took place once a week, which was more acceptable. Objective #4 was achieved. Comparing the local and tourist interviewees, residents were more familiar with the FDHs’ situation, lifestyle, and Sunday leisure activities. Hence, they expressed lower interest in learning more about the FDHs’ culture. On the other hand, some tourist interviewees felt that they were able to increase their intercultural understanding. Through sharing the same public space and observing the FDHs’ activities, they learned more about the FDHs’ culture, such as their characteristics, language, and religion. Moreover, several interviewees stated that having the FDH gatherings enhanced the diversity and international image of Hong Kong. Compared to residents, tourists were more interested in the different activities of the FDHs, and some were willing to adjust their travel itinerary to see more. They were also more likely to take photos and videos and would want to post on social media to share with their friends and family. In the case of FDHs in Hong Kong, their low wage and difficult living and working conditions were recognized by residents and tourists. Hence, while some complaints were voiced (e.g., noise, crowdedness), most interviewees were very understanding. Specifically, a high degree of tolerance was revealed in light of the FDHs’ unique situation, and both residents and tourists were supportive of providing better rest spaces for FDHs.

15501720.label: Major findings and research outcome
15501720.value: On Sundays in Hong Kong, many public facilities become dynamic social spaces shared by residents, tourists, and Foreign Domestic Helpers (FDHs). This study investigated their interactions and conflicts in urban spaces, with a focus on open public spaces, such as parks, plazas, and pedestrian walkways. Sources of cross-group conflicts were identified and categorized into place, recreationist, and behavioral factors. Resource specificity was reflected in residents' and tourists' perceptions of different open spaces, such as parks vs. footbridges. This study contributes to urban tourism literature by expanding "the tourist city" users to include FDHs, as a unique form of temporary mobility. As consumption spaces received more attention in urban tourism, this study draws attention to the role of open public spaces and the interactions and conflicts in such unconventional leisure environments. Despite the causes of conflicts, a high degree of tolerance was revealed in light of FDHs' circumstances, which reduced the occurrence of confrontations and differed from tourist-resident conflicts in Hong Kong. The level of cross-group social interactions was not high, as people socialized more with their group and would not initiate social exchanges with strangers. The difference in activity style also reduced the opportunity for cross-group interactions. Nevertheless, the co-presence of different groups in public spaces was found to enhance tourists' understanding of diverse cultures, and transform their impression of Hong Kong from a rich, business city to a diverse and inclusive destination. The research outcomes are presented at the ISTTE Annual Conference (2022) and APTA Conference (2023), and published in Tourism Management (2024). 15501720.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15501720.value: This research examined residents, tourists, and FDHs' use of urban public space in popular downtown areas of Hong Kong (i.e., Central, Causeway Bay). In more peripheral districts, the experience and perceptions of different groups regarding public space usage may vary. As tourists to Hong Kong are becoming more experienced, some tourists also seek to explore local neighborhoods rather than simply visiting tourist zones. Hence, future research should expand the scope to other districts (e.g., New Territories) and examine the interaction dynamics among residents, tourists, and FDHs in public spaces in local neighborhoods, as opposed to downtown areas. Another area for further work is to take a deeper look at the specific events or tours related to FDH culture. There are many activities and events organized by migrant-related NGO groups that were not broadly promoted. This study revealed tourists' interest in FDHs' culture and found that, despite having interest, people were often hesitant to take the first step to initiate intercultural contact. Further research is needed to investigate how tourist and local participants, FDHs, and NGO groups behave and communicate during specific events, which may shed light on the barriers and identify better ways for co-presence to lead to actual interactions.

15501720.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15501720.value: Conflicts over the use of public resources are not uncommon in urban destinations. While tourist-resident conflicts have been well-researched, previous studies have not considered marginalized groups who cannot be categorized as tourists or locals, such as foreign domestic helpers (FDHs). This study explored the use of urban public spaces by residents, tourists, and FDHs in Hong Kong, and whether their co-presence led to more conflicts or intercultural understanding. By interviewing the three groups, the sources of conflicts were found, based on the varied experiences sought by users in different types of open spaces. Nevertheless, residents and tourists expressed a high level of tolerance and understanding of FDHs' circumstances, which prevented direct conflicts. Although sharing the same public space did not necessarily facilitate cross-group social interactions, both tourists and residents appreciated seeing the diversity in public spaces, which further improved the image of Hong Kong from "materialistic" to "inclusive." When examining the issues of public space and crowding in urban destinations, the opinions of FDHs, who are arguably the most forgotten and silent group in society, cannot be ignored. Study findings also highlight the urgency of improving FDHs' living conditions, which would reduce their need to occupy public spaces on Sundays.

15501820.label: Project Title(Chinese)
15501820.value: 企业社会责任对产品线决策的影响

15501820.label: Project Objectives
15501820.value: Analyze the firm's optimal product line and sourcing decisions in the presence of consumers' CSR concerns. We develop a game-theoretical model in which a monopoly firm can choose to sell one or two quality-differentiated products and needs to decide whether to source from socially responsible or irresponsible suppliers for its products. A fraction of consumers in the market have CSR concerns and would punish the firm's products via their purchase decisions if they find the firm's any contracted supplier violates social and environmental standards. By solving the proposed model, we can characterize the conditions under which the firm is optimal to sell two quality-differentiated products or a single high or low quality product. Moreover, we can also examine which type of supplier the firm should select for each product he sells. If the firm offers a single product, should he source from a socially responsible supplier or irresponsible supplier? If the firm offers two products, should he source from responsible suppliers for both products, only for the high-quality (or low-quality) product, or for none? Those are the questions we aim to answer in Objective 1. Examine the impacts of consumers' CSR concerns on the firm's product line and sourcing decisions and profit. After solving the base model, we will conduct comparative statics to examine the impacts of some key factors, including the fraction of consumers who have CSR concerns and their punishment for the firm's irresponsible sourcing behavior, on the firm's optimal decisions and profit. From the results of the above comparative statics, we could generate interesting managerial insights to address the following questions: As more consumers have concerns on CSR or their punishment becomes stronger, does the firm have more incentive to have a longer or shorter product line, or to source from responsible suppliers? Is the firm's profit always hurt by more CSR-concerns consumers or their stronger punishment? Study the impacts of consumers' CSR concerns on consumer total surplus and social welfare. Similar to Objective 2, we will conduct comparative statics to study the impacts of some key factors, including the fraction of consumers who have CSR concerns and their punishment for the firm's irresponsible sourcing behavior, on consumer total surplus and social welfare. To define the social welfare, we may consider that it includes both the economic and the non-economic measurements, in which the economic measurement is the sum of the firm's profit and consumer total surplus, and the non-economic measurement depends on the types of the firm's suppliers and production quantities. From the results of the above analysis, we could provide useful managerial implications from the perspective of consumers, government, and NGOs. Verify the robustness of our main results in different model settings and find additional interesting results. In our base model, we consider that a firm has two substitutable products and faces social responsibility risk, and the firm makes inventory decisions before the risk is resolved and the retail price decisions after the risk is resolved. We will study several possible model extensions: (1) The firm sells multiple independent products that do not cannibalize with each other; (2) the firm can postpone the inventory decisions after the risk is resolved to avoid the inventory risk; (3) the firm needs to decide the retail prices before the risk is resolved. By examining those model extensions, we can verify which results can hold qualitatively in different settings and which results may change, and further understand the roles of cannibalization effects, inventory risk, and pricing flexibility in this problem.

15501820.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15501820.value: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) has received extensive attention from both academia and industry in recent years. Consumer awareness of CSR across the globe also grows rapidly. Among all the issues related to CSR, sourcing from socially and environmentally responsible suppliers is one of the most critical concerns for global companies. It is common that a firm who sells a product line may adopt different sourcing strategies, and it may source from ethical suppliers for some products and unethical suppliers for the others to take advantage of the lower sourcing costs. Once a firm's certain products are discovered as sourcing from suppliers who violate social responsibility standards, the firm's reputation will be damaged and all of its products are negatively affected as consumers would boycott the brand rather than the individual products. Therefore, a critical question faced by a firm who sells a product line is how to construct its product line and make the corresponding sourcing decisions in the presence of consumers' CSR concerns. To answer this question, we develop a game-theoretical model in which a monopoly firm can choose to sell multiple quality-differentiated products and needs to decide whether to source from socially responsible or irresponsible suppliers for its products. A fraction of consumers in the market have CSR concerns and would punish the firm's products via their purchase decisions if they find any of the firm's contracted suppliers violates social and environmental standards. The purpose of this proposed project is to understand the interactions between a firm who sells a product line and consumers who have CSR concerns. We will first solve the firm's optimal decisions in the model and conduct comparative statistics to examine the impacts of consumers' CSR concerns on the firm's decisions and profit as well as consumer total surplus and social welfare. Finally, we will examine some possible model extensions to verify the robustness of our main results and generate additional interesting managerial insights. 近年来，企业社会责任受到学术界和行业的广泛关注。消费者对企业社会责任的意识也在迅速提高。在与企业社会责任相关的所有问题中，是否从有社会责任的供应商采购是公司最关注的问题之一。销售产品线的公司经常会对不同的产品采用不同的采购策略, 他们可能会从符合社会责任规范的供应商那里购买某些产品，而不符合社会责任规范的供应商那里购买其他产品以享受更低的价格。当公司的某些产品被发现采购于违反社会责任标准的供应商，该公司的声誉将受到损害，并且其所有产品均受到负面影响，因为消费者通常会抵制该公司品牌而不是仅仅是抵制单个产品。因此，销售产品线的公司面临的一个关键问题是，当消费者关注企业社会责任的情况下如何决定产品线的采购策略。为了回答这个问题，我们建立了博弈论模型，在模型中考虑一个垄断公司，该公司可以选择销售多种质量差异化的产品，并且需要决定是否从符合社会责任规范或者不符合规范的供应商那里采购产品。市场上有一部分消费者会关注企业社会责任，如果他们发现该公司的合同供应商违反了社会和环境标准，他们将通过购买行为来惩罚该公司的产品。这项研究的目的是了解销售产品系列的公司与关注企业社会责任的消费者之间的相互作用。我们将首先在模型中求解企业的最佳决策，并研究消费者的企业社会责任关注度对企业的产品线决策，采购决策，利润，消费者总盈余，以及社会福利的影响。最后，我们将研究一些模型扩展，以验证主要结果的稳健性。

15501820.label: Realisation of objectives
15501820.value: All the four objectives have been fully achieved. The main purpose of this project is to study firms’ optimal product line and sourcing decisions in the presence of consumers' corporate social responsibility (CSR) concerns. CSR has received extensive attention from both academia and industry in recent years. Consumer awareness of CSR across the globe also grows rapidly. Among all the issues related to CSR, sourcing from socially and environmentally responsible suppliers is one of the most critical concerns for global companies. It is common that a firm who sells a product line may adopt different sourcing strategies, and it may source from ethical suppliers for some products and unethical suppliers for the others for the purpose of reducing sourcing costs. Once a firm's certain products are discovered as sourcing from irresponsible suppliers, the firm’s reputation will be damaged, and all of its products are negatively affected. Therefore, a critical question faced by a firm who sells a product line is how to construct its product line and make the corresponding sourcing decisions in the presence of consumers' CSR concerns. This project targets to study the impacts of consumers’ CSR concerns on a firm’s product line and sourcing decisions. To this end, we have developed a game-theoretical model, in which a monopoly firm can choose to sell one or two quality-differentiated products and needs to decide whether to source from a socially responsible or irresponsible supplier for each product. The products are sold to consumers with CSR concerns who will punish the firm via their purchase decisions if they find any of the firm’s selected suppliers violates social and environmental standards. We have thoroughly analyzed the game model and achieved all four objectives. The main findings have been summarized in the paper titled “Product-Line Design and Sourcing with Consumer Awareness of Corporate Social Responsibility”, which will be submitted to the top-tier journal Production and Operations Management soon. Please see the attached paper in part C for details. In what follows, we will elaborate on how and to what extent the four project objectives have been achieved: 1. Objective 1: Through solving the model, we have derived the firm's optimal product line and sourcing decisions in equilibrium. Specifically, we have characterized the conditions under which the firm is optimal to sell two quality-differentiated products or a single product. Moreover, we have also examined which type of supplier the firm should select for each product, depending on the punishment level of consumers for the irresponsible product and the spillover effect within a product line. (Please see the paper “Product-Line Design and Sourcing with Consumer Awareness of Corporate Social Responsibility” attached in part C for details). 2. Objective 2: We have examined how consumers' CSR concerns affect the firm's product line and sourcing decisions as well as its profit. We focus on analyzing the impact of consumers' punishment level for the irresponsible product and the spillover effect within a product line. (Please see the paper “Product-Line Design and Sourcing with Consumer Awareness of Corporate Social Responsibility” attached in part C for details). 3. Objective 3: We have conducted comparative statics to study the impact of consumers' punishment level for the irresponsible product and the spillover effect on consumer surplus and social welfare. However, due to the page limit and based on feedback from experts in the field, we have decided to remove the results regarding consumer surplus and social welfare from the paper “Product-Line Design and Sourcing with Consumer Awareness of Corporate Social Responsibility” to ensure a clear focus on the firm’s product line and sourcing decisions. 4. Objective 4: We have conducted a related model extension to derive additional interesting results. Specifically, as an extension, we have developed a game-theoretical model to study firms’ sourcing strategy in an assembly setting when facing consumers with CSR concerns. We have completed the analysis and summarized the results in another paper titled “Sourcing Strategy for Assembly Systems with Corporate Social Responsibility Considerations”, which will be submitted to the top-tier journal Production and Operations Management soon. Please see the attached paper in part C for details. 5. Others: In addition to the above four objectives, we have developed further research ideas and extended our model to explore additional related questions during the course of the project. Specially, the focus of this project is on firms’ socially responsible practices, which fall under the broad area of sustainable operations management (OM). Sustainable OM encompasses a variety of challenges, one of which is managing inventory in the face of demand uncertainty. In practice, excess inventory often leads to significant waste, contributing to environmental harm. Inspired by this environmental issue and recent research on collaborative strategies in supply chains, we have conducted a study to examine how inventory sharing between competing retailers can mitigate inventory risks and reduce inventory waste. The findings are summarized in the paper titled “Inventory Sharing Under Service Competition”, which has been published in the journal Manufacturing and Service Operations Management. Please see the attached paper in Part C for details.

15501820.label: Major findings and research outcome
15501820.value: In this project, we have obtained fruitful results and managerial insights. To summarize those findings, we have published one paper tiltled “Inventory Sharing Under Service Competition” in the journal Manufacturing and Service Operations Management (MSOM), and completed two papers (“Product-Line Design and Sourcing with Consumer Awareness of Corporate Social Responsibility” and “Sourcing Strategy for Assembly Systems with Corporate Social Responsibility Considerations”), which will be submitted to the top-tier journal Production and Operations Management, respectively. We summarize the main findings below: 1.Objectives 1-3: We study the firm's optimal product line and sourcing decisions in the presence of consumers' CSR concerns. We find that consumers' punishment for irresponsible products and the spillover effect within a product line play critical but different roles in the firm's product line and sourcing decisions. Specifically, stronger punishment from consumers can motivate the firm to source from responsible suppliers, while a stronger spillover effect may or may not lead to this outcome. Moreover, from the perspective of product-line design, stronger spillover effect will drive the firm to shorten its product line, while the impact of consumers’ punishment is more complicated and non-monotone. Please see the details in the paper “Product-Line Design and Sourcing with Consumer Awareness of Corporate Social Responsibility” attached in Part C. 2.Objective 4: As an extension, we study a manufacturer’s sourcing strategy in an assembly setting when facing consumers with CSR concerns. We find that consumers' punishment for irresponsible products always hurts the manufacturer in a centralized system, but may benefit it in a decentralized system. Moreover, when making the sourcing decision for one component given the others are fixed, the manufacturer in a decentralized system may choose a supplier with a higher or lower responsibility level, compared to that in a centralized system. Please see the details in the paper “Sourcing Strategy for Assembly Systems with Corporate Social Responsibility Considerations” attached in Part C. 3.Others: Besides the above objectives, we have generated additional research ideas. Specifically, we investigate the tradeoffs of inventory sharing between competing retailers and find that inventory sharing may soften or intensify service competition. Moreover, the retailers’ inventory levels increase in the transfer price, and inventory sharing under the service competition cannot achieve full coordination. Please see the details in the paper “Inventory Sharing Under Service Competition” attached in Part C.

15501820.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15501820.value: For the future development of this research, we will further polish the two working papers and submit them to the top-tier academic journal Production and Operations Management. We will revise them based on the feedback from peer reviewers. Moreover, we will continue to develop additional research topics in this area. For example, collecting relevant data and conducting empirical analyses to validate our analytical results represents a promising direction for future work. In addition, there are numerous other issues related to corporate social responsibility that deserve further investigation. We believe that this research project can inspire more researchers and students to explore the related topics in the future.

15501920.label: Project Objectives
15501920.value: Study a system consisting of three players: (1) an AEV fleet operator that provides mobility-as-a-service to the public, (2) a smart grid operator that provides electricity with diverse sources including renewable energy, and (3) a policymaker that manages the vehicle-grid integration system. The AEVs can charge electricity from and discharge electricity back to the smart grid via V2G charging stations, indicating a vehicle-grid integration system. Investigate how the AEV fleet operator can achieve high profitability and service quality by creating a robust plan, which incorporates endogenous uncertainty in demand and vehicle failure despite limited available data, to deploy the AEVs and V2G charging stations. Investigate how the AEV fleet operator can continuously improve her decision-making, as additional data becomes available. Demonstrate the mutual benefits for the AEV fleet and the smart grid by building a synergistic vehicle-grid integration system, in which the smart grid operator can effectively optimize the electric generation portfolio while charging and discharging the AEVs. Explore how the policymaker should manage the AEV fleet and the smart grid via regulations (i.e., setting AEV and V2G charging station allocation limits and renewable energy utilization target) to establish a healthy ecosystem. Conduct case studies by using real data from the industry, particularly in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area and Singapore, to verify the effectiveness of our approaches.

15501920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15501920.value: This project is motivated by the emerging autonomous electric vehicle (AEV) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technologies, which, along with the smart grid, form the basis for so-called "vehicle-grid integration systems." Benefiting from the boom in artificial intelligence, wireless communication (e.g., 5G), and next-generation batteries, both traditional automakers and high-tech companies are racing to invest on and develop AEVs, while many nations are increasingly using green energy to generate electricity from the smart grid because of public interest in sustainability. Such new systems have two important features, namely, autonomy and electricity, which not only raise critical questions that are not adequately addressed but also possess substantial potential that is mostly overlooked. First, autonomy enables the AEVs to provide mobility-as-a-service (including shared mobility, taxi and bus services, trucking service) to the public. Nevertheless, it comes with high investment costs and operational risks (i.e., vehicle failure) at the current stage. These limitations pose great challenges to the AEV fleet operator who also faces demand uncertainty with initially limited data. Second, electricity establishes a synergistic bridge between the AEVs and the smart grid via the V2G technology, as AEVs can use V2G to return electricity back to the smart grid. Such synergy can boost the utilization of green energy and in turn improve the charging effectiveness of the AEVs, potentially leading to a smarter vehicle-grid integration system and obviously an urgent call for theoretical studies. To address the aforementioned challenges, we will tackle the following research questions: First, to realize the benefits of AEVs, how should an AEV fleet operator determine a robust plan, which considers the high investment cost, demand uncertainty, vehicle failure risk, and limited available data, to deploy the AEVs and V2G charging stations? Second, to unlock the synergy between the AEVs and the smart grid, can we develop an intelligent model for the smart grid operator to effectively optimize the electric generation portfolio while charging and discharging the AEVs? Third, given the social considerations (e.g., safety concerns) for the AEVs and the growing concerns about sustainability, how should a policymaker lead the fast-developing AEVs and the synergistic vehicle-grid integration system to create a healthy ecosystem? To answer these questions, we develop data-driven optimization and game-theoretic models. We obtain insights for managing vehicle-grid integration systems, ensuring effective business interactions among the policymaker, smart grid operator, and AEV fleet operator, and developing implementable solutions for their operations. Our results will eventually help support a smarter city. 受到無人駕駛電動汽車（AEV）和車輛到電網（V2G）技術所推動，該項目將研究一類 “車輛-電網集成系統”。一方面，受益於人工智能，無線通信（例如5G）和新一代電池的蓬勃發展，傳統汽車製造商和高科技公司都在競相投資和開發AEV。另一方面，鑑於社會對可再生能源的渴求，許多國家在智能電網中越來越多地使用綠色清潔能源來發電並滿足電力需求。 這樣的新興系統具有兩個重要特徵，即自主性和電力性。它們不僅帶來了被大多數人所忽視的巨大潛力，而且引出了眾多還沒充分解決的關鍵問題。首先，自主性使AEV能夠向公眾提供“出行即服務”（包括共享出行，出租車和公共汽車服務，卡車服務等）。然而，現階段AEV具有高投資成本和運營風險（比如車輛故障），從而給AEV車隊運營商帶來了巨大挑戰。同時，他們還面臨著運營初期有限數據情形下的需求不確定性。其次，電力通過V2G技術在AEV和智能電網之間建立起一座協同作用的橋樑。一方面，AEV需要從智能電網充電；另一方面，AEV可以通過V2G技術將剩餘電量送回到智能電網。這種協同作用可以促進清潔能源的利用，進而提高AEV的充電效率。綜合來看，我們有可能擁有一個非常智能的車輛-電網集成系統，但也迫切需要進行相應的關鍵理論研究。 為了解決上述挑戰，我們將研究以下問題。首先，AEV車隊運營商應如何制定一個考慮高投資成本、需求不確定性、車輛故障風險以及有限數據等情形的有效規劃，從而合理部署AEV和V2G充電站？其次，為了實現AEV和智能電網之間的協同作用，我們應如何為智能電網運營商設計智能模型來優化電網的調度決策以及AEV的充放電決策？第三，考慮到AEV的社會影響（比如顧客安全性考慮）以及社會對可再生能源的日益關注，政策決定者應如何領導快速發展的AEV和新興的車輛-電網集成系統來創建一個合理的生態系統？ 為了回答上述問題，我們將設計基於數據驅動的優化和博弈論模型。我們將獲得對於管理車輛-電網集成系統的有效建議，同時確保政策決定者、智能電網運營商和AEV車隊運營商之間有效業務互動。我們的結果最終將有助於建設更加智慧的城市。

15501920.label: Realisation of objectives
15501920.value: All six objectives of this project have been successfully achieved. The development of autonomous electric vehicles (AEVs) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technologies, along with advancements in smart grid systems, lays the foundation for what are known as “grid-vehicle integration systems.” A key challenge we face is the increasing integration of intermittent renewable energy sources into power grids, which poses significant operational hurdles. A promising solution lies in utilizing electric vehicles (EVs) equipped with V2G technology to both store and return electricity, thereby enhancing grid operations. This project focuses on integrating the power grid with an increasing number of AEVs to enhance the grid's flexibility and resilience while mitigating the limitations of traditional solutions. AEVs, which charge from the grid to fulfill mobility needs, can store excess electricity during periods of high generation and low demand. With V2G technology, AEVs can discharge electricity back to the grid during times of insufficient generation, providing valuable flexible regulation reserves. Significantly, unlike traditional power generators, which are often located far from urban centers, AEVs are situated closer to end-users, facilitating efficient power transfers without the constraints of the transmission network, thereby minimizing energy loss and congestion. This symbiotic relationship between AEVs and the grid represents a promising path toward enhancing flexibility and resilience without necessitating additional investments in power grid infrastructure. As AEVs gain global popularity, with numerous countries and major automotive manufacturers committing to phase out fossil fuel-powered vehicles by 2040, the integration of AEVs into the power grid is not only feasible but also increasingly urgent. We refer to this integration system as the “grid-vehicle integration (GVI) system.” Our primary focus is on the planning and operational dynamics of the GVI system across multiple periods under conditions of uncertainty. We aim to address several research questions that remain underexplored in the existing literature: (i) How can the power grid optimize its planning and operations when integrated with AEVs to robustly align power supply with demand, thereby minimizing the worst-case total cost amidst uncertainties in renewable generation, power load, and mobility trip demand? (ii) What impact does the adoption of V2G technology have on the grid's decisions regarding the initial startup of generators and subsequent power generation? (iii) How does the grid interact with the AEV fleet in terms of power transfer dynamics (i.e., charging and discharging interactions) under V2G technology? Are there significant temporal characteristics in these dynamics? (iv) How do system parameters, such as power load patterns, influence the overall performance of the GVI system, and to what extent can it contribute to carbon emission reduction? (v) What strategies should policymakers employ to promote the implementation of the GVI system? To address these questions, we examine a GVI system where the grid operates power generators to meet the power load, utilizing the support of AEVs over a multi-period operational horizon. Each period presents uncertainties related to renewable generation, power load, and AEV trip demand. At the beginning of the planning horizon, the grid operator decides whether to start up a dispatchable (i.e., thermal) power generator for each period, prior to the realization of these uncertainties. Once uncertainties unfold in each period, the grid determines the appropriate power generation levels and coordinates AEV charging and discharging to satisfy the power load. Simultaneously, the mobility operator manages the AEV fleet to meet charging and discharging interactions as well as trip demands. To ensure the economic viability of the AEVs, the grid guarantees that the AEV fleet reaches a specified service level after fulfilling the requested power interactions; if this is not achieved, the grid operator provides subsidies to the AEV fleet. The GVI system must demonstrate robustness against uncertainty to ensure that power generation aligns with demand while maintaining the reliability of both the grid and the AEV fleet. To achieve this, we have developed a novel two-stage robust mixed-integer programming (MIP) model for the decision-making process, enabling the grid operator to minimize the worst-case total cost across the entire operational horizon. In the first stage, we determine whether each thermal generator should start up; in the second stage, we establish the subsequent power generation levels, charging and discharging interactions, and AEV fleet operations throughout the horizon. It is important to note that solving a two-stage robust MIP model, which can be NP-hard, presents significant challenges. Given the large-scale power grid network and EV fleet involved in the GVI system, the operational details become complex due to the presence of integer variables, and the uncertainty space is high-dimensional. Consequently, we must incorporate numerous scenarios to effectively characterize the uncertainty, resulting in a computationally challenging, large-scale MIP model. To tackle this challenge, we have designed an innovative machine learning-driven optimization approach with theoretical guarantees, offering a practical solution to the computational difficulties posed by the extensive uncertainty set and integer variables. Our approach leverages machine learning techniques to identify a sufficient yet concise subset of scenarios from the uncertainty set, allowing us to generate optimal solutions without evaluating the entire set and thus reducing complexity. In addition, we decompose the two-stage MIP model: the first-stage integer program is solved as a linear program, while the second-stage problem is solved in parallel, further simplifying the computation. We also derive strong valid inequalities to enhance the linear relaxation of the two-stage MIP model, effectively addressing the complexity introduced by integer variables. Our method can quickly identify a lower bound using a single scenario learned from the training data, achieving an average optimality gap of less than 1.6%. Furthermore, by utilizing energy and transportation data from the real industry, we investigate the impact of V2G technology on the performance of the GVI system across various parameters. Initially, we solve our proposed two-stage problem to ascertain the online/offline status of thermal generators. Based on the first-stage solution, we then tackle the second-stage problem to determine out-of-sample operational decisions. Our findings offer valuable insights into GVI system operations and provide recommendations for enhancing sustainability. We also explore several variants of our proposed model to gain deeper insights into its functionality. (1) We analyze a power grid that operates without the support of an AEV fleet, examining how the grid operator manages the system under various uncertainties, such as fuel constraints and power flow instability. (2) We investigate an AEV fleet that is not integrated with the power grid, focusing on how the fleet operator plans infrastructure design and manages AEV operations amidst uncertainties like demand fluctuations and vehicle failures. (3) We simplify the operational details of both the power grid and the AEV fleet within the GVI system, exploring how they collaborate with policymakers to effectively reduce carbon emissions. These activities collectively contribute to achieving all six project objectives.

15501920.label: Major findings and research outcome
15501920.value: First, our analysis of the variant considering a power grid without AEV fleet support reveals that the grid faces significant challenges in operating under various supply and demand uncertainties (see Paper 2 and Paper 4 in Part C). Second, in the variant examining an AEV fleet not integrated with the power grid, we find that the fleet operator encounters difficulties in planning vehicle allocation and managing fleet operations amid market competition and demand uncertainty (see Paper 5 in Part C). Third, by employing the machine learning-driven optimization approach detailed in Paper 6 of Part C, alongside the robust optimization techniques developed in Paper 1 and Paper 3 of Part C, we successfully solve our proposed model for the grid-vehicle integration (GVI) system and derive several significant findings as follows. (i) V2G technology reduces the number of online generators and extends their operational periods, thereby enhancing grid stability and reliability. It stabilizes subsequent power generation through the valley-filling and peak-shaving effects, storing excess electricity in AEV batteries during low-trip-demand hours and returning it to the grid as needed. Moreover, V2G technology contributes to sustainability by lowering carbon emissions, particularly during moderate power loads. (ii) The power load pattern significantly influences the performance of the GVI system when V2G is adopted. Specifically, V2G technology reduces the number of online generators, decreases carbon emissions, and improves sustainability under a bimodal power load pattern compared to a unimodal pattern. (iii) An increased share of renewable energy or a larger AEV fleet enhances sustainability. We find that a sustainability score of 0.72 can be achieved when the AEV fleet size reaches 1,000,000 and the renewable energy share is 100% under a unimodal power load pattern (or 80% under a bimodal pattern). Furthermore, our analysis indicates that carbon neutrality can be attained when the renewable share exceeds 100% and the AEV fleet size is 1,000,000 under either power load pattern. Thus, while advocating for an increased share of renewable energy, policymakers are also encouraged to promote further integration between the power grid and the AEV fleet.

15501920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15501920.value: This project addresses a critical issue in the operations management of grid-vehicle integration (GVI) systems, and several promising directions for future research emerge from our findings. First, we can explore the integration of the GVI system with complementary systems, such as building systems and demand response programs, to further enhance grid flexibility and resilience. By leveraging synergies between these systems, we can create a more robust infrastructure that responds dynamically to fluctuating energy demands and supply conditions. Second, there is potential to incorporate additional ancillary services from the power grid into the GVI system. This could involve integrating services such as frequency regulation, voltage support, and spinning reserves, thereby enhancing the grid's operational capabilities and improving overall system reliability. Third, developing alternative machine learning techniques could significantly improve the optimization solving process. For instance, exploring advanced algorithms like reinforcement learning or deep learning could lead to more efficient scenario generation and decision-making strategies, allowing for real-time adjustments in response to evolving conditions. Fourth, it is interesting to study the socio-economic impacts of implementing GVI systems, examining aspects such as consumer acceptance and market dynamics. Understanding these factors will be essential for creating effective policies and strategies that promote widespread adoption.

15501920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15501920.value: As more renewable energy sources, like wind and solar, are added to our power grids, managing these energy supplies becomes increasingly challenging. A promising solution involves using autonomous electric vehicles (AEVs) equipped with vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology. This technology enables AEVs to store energy and return it to the grid when needed, thereby stabilizing operations. This project explores a grid-vehicle integration (GVI) system that utilizes V2G technology while addressing uncertainties in energy production, power demand, and AEV trip demand. We model the daily operations of this system as a two-stage process designed to minimize costs. In the first stage, the grid operator determines whether to start up power generators; in the second stage, decisions are made regarding the amount of power to generate and how to manage AEV charging and discharging to meet demand. To tackle the complexities involved, we propose a machine learning-driven optimization approach. It significantly speeds up calculations and improves the quality of solutions for large, real-world scenarios. Our findings indicate that utilizing V2G technology can reduce the number of generators required, stabilize power generation, and decrease carbon emissions, all while maintaining mobility services. This approach paves the way for achieving carbon neutrality without compromising mobility services.

15502120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15502120.value: Recent years have seen a surge of interest in the use of search query data to forecast tourism demand (Bangwayo-Skeete & Skeete, 2015; Li, Pan, Law & Huang, 2017; Wen, Liu & Song, 2019). Tourists often search for information when they plan their trips, and these search queries can serve as leading indicators that can be useful for forecasting tourism demand. As data on the frequency of search queries are often more readily available than data on tourism demand, mixed-frequency models such as mixed-data sampling (MIDAS) can be used to avoid the loss of information due to temporal aggregation that occurs when using traditional time series regressions (Bangwayo-Skeete & Skeete, 2015). However, MIDAS models assume that the parameters used remain constant over time. This assumption is restrictive and may not reflect reality, especially for newly emerging, fast-changing behaviours such as tourists’ online information searches. Therefore, this study will aim to develop a time-varying parameter MIDAS (TVP-MIDAS) model that can provide more consistently accurate estimates. As the standard Kalman filter can only be used to estimate linear TVP models, it is not applicable to estimate TVP-MIDAS due to the non-linearity of its weighting parameters. The particle filter (which is also known as the sequential Monte Carlo) can be used instead. Schumacher (2014) used a particle filtering method as proposed by Liu and West (2001) for estimating TVP-MIDAS models. However, this method involves only one iteration of the filtering procedure, and it has limitations in terms of its convergence property. In contrast, the iterated filtering method has been shown to have a theoretically justified claim to overcoming these limitations (Ionides, Bhadra, Atchadé & King, 2011; Ionides, Nguyen, Atchadé, Stoev & King, 2015). To the best of our knowledge, no study has yet used this method to estimate TVP-MIDAS models in either the tourism or the general econometric literature. A TVP-MIDAS model that is estimated by this method can provide more accurate estimates and better capture the time-varying properties of the underlying process. Therefore, this study will aim to bridge the research gap in this area, and will use a newly developed TVP-MIDAS model to forecast tourism demand in Hong Kong from its largest source market, mainland China. This new model will not only utilise the high-frequency information provided by search query data, but it will also accurately delineate how the relation between tourism demand and search-query frequency changes over time. 15502120.label: Major findings and research outcome
15502120.value: we find that the relationship between high-frequency data and the Factor MIDAS models with time-varying parameters is mutually reinforcing. In the absence of regularly updated high-frequency data, the Factor MIDAS models with time-varying parameters are unable to accurately capture the negative impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. Similarly, the Factor MIDAS model is unable to capitalise on the valuable information exhibited in high-frequency data without time-varying parameter specifications. This result validates the argument proposed by Foroni et al. (2022) that finding a reliable TVP model with changing explanatory variables over time is the best solution for improving the accuracy of forecasting and nowcasting during a crisis. The findings of this study have significant policy implications for the management and recovery of the tourism industry, particularly in times of crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The study highlights the importance of using reliable forecasting and nowcasting methods that can accurately capture the impact of the pandemic on tourism demand. It’s crucial to integrate a large amount of available data, particularly high-frequency data, to improve short-term forecasting accuracy. The use of Factor MIDAS models with time-varying parameters has been shown to accurately capture the impact of the pandemic on tourism demand. However, it is essential to update these models with real-time data to ensure their effectiveness. Additionally, the study highlights the limited usefulness of macroeconomic variables in improving nowcasting accuracy during crises compared to daily indexes. Therefore, policymakers should prioritize the integration of real-time data and adjust their forecasting and nowcasting approaches accordingly. The study also emphasizes the importance of using a TVP model with changing explanatory variables over time to enhance forecasting and nowcasting accuracy during crises. Overall, this study can serve as an alternative benchmark for tourism demand nowcasting during crises when baseline forecasts or nowcasts generated by traditional time-series or econometric models become rapidly outdated due to the outbreak of crises.

15502120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15502120.value: Nevertheless, our study has some limitations. The empirical results are generated using domestic tourism demand in a single destination in China. As most countries have lifted travel restrictions, the pattern of domestic and international tourism demand in these countries can differ greatly from the case of Hainan and the generalisability of the empirical results therefore needs to be investigated. In addition, the Baidu search engine is the sole source of high-frequency daily data in this study. Other types of high-frequency data, such as review data and hotel booking data, can be considered in future studies. Furthermore, only point forecasts and nowcasts are generated and evaluated in this study; interval and density forecasts can also provide valuable information, such as the uncertainties of the forecasts and nowcasts, to decision makers during crisis and post-crisis periods.

15502120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15502120.value: The uncertainties associated with the COVID-19 pandemic significantly reduce the accuracy of traditional econometric models in forecasting tourism demand, as the relationship between tourism demand and its determinants during the crisis changes over time. To address these inaccuracies, we apply three Factor MIxed DAta Sampling (MIDAS) models with different time-varying parameter (TVP) settings: Factor TVP-MIDAS, Factor MIDAS with stochastic volatility (Factor MIDAS-SV) and Factor TVP-MIDAS-SV. We explore the dynamic relationship between tourism demand and its influencing factors, capture the uncertainty and volatility in the data, and provide short-term forecasting and nowcasting. We subject the Factor MIDAS models with TVP specifications to different combinations of determinants to examine their performance. The empirical results demonstrate that the Factor MIDAS models with TVP settings show superior performance compared with the Factor MIDAS model in the short-term forecasting and nowcasting of tourism demand during COVID-19. The results also suggest that high-frequency data complement these Factor MIDAS models with TVP settings in improving the forecasting and nowcasting accuracy during crises.

15502420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15502420.value: Many sellers (e.g., the Hudson's Bay Company, Sears, and Wal-Mart) offer their customers full or partial refund for product returns or service cancellations. Much of the existing literature studies cash refund, where customers get their money back minus a fee upon a product return or service cancellation. A popular alternative to cash refund is store credit, which can be used for future purchases, possibly with an expiration date, after which the credit is forfeited. A prominent example is the airline industry, where customers who cancel nonrefundable fares are often issued a credit that is valid in a fixed time window. For instance, United Airline states that "the value of your nonrefundable ticket may be eligible to be applied toward the price of a new ticket, and tickets are valid one year from the date of ticket issuance." Compared with cash refunds, store credit have pros and cons that have not been carefully studied in the extant literature. Given the increasing prevalence of credit refund policy in practice, we study the optimal design of this policy in such settings and investigate whether the credit refund policy can outperform the cash refund policy. Different from models that consider cash refund, we explicitly model repeated interactions between the seller and customers over time. Specifically, we consider a monopolist selling a product to infinitesimal customers over an infinite time horizon. In each period, a customer shows up on the market with a given probability, and the customer's valuation is stochastic. There is an exogenously given probability that a customer returns the product after purchase. The firm chooses the pricing and refund policy to maximize its long run average revenue. A credit refund policy includes two elements: a credit refund and an expiration term. That is, the credit is only valid within a certain amount of time. We propose to use dynamic programming to analyze the customer's decision problem for a given credit refund policy, where the state is the number of periods left for the credit to expire. Based on the customer's optimal behavior, we plan to analyze the firm's optimal decisions on price, credit, and expiration term. Finally, we compare the optimal credit refund policy with the cash refund policy. To summarize, this research contributes to the literature of consumer returns by providing the optimal design of credit refund policy and an improved understanding of the rationale and effectiveness of this policy. 在消费者退货时，许多零售商（比如Hudson’s Bay，Sears，沃尔玛）会向消费者返还全部或者部分货款。目前的大部分文献研究的是现金退款，即消费者在退货时可以以现金的方式拿回之前支付的款项（可能会减去一些费用，比如邮递费、折旧费等）。除了现金退款，还有一种比较流行的退款方式是信用退款。这种信用可以用于未来的消费，但通常附带一个有效期，过了有效期之后，这个信用就会失效。一个典型的例子是航空公司，顾客在取消无法退款的机票时，航空公司通常会退给顾客一个信用，有效期通常为1年。比如，美国联合航空公司规定：这种通过退票获得的信用可以用来购买新的机票，有效期为1年，从获得该信用开始计算。与现金退款相比，信用退款既有优势，也有劣势，但是现有的文献却没有相关研究。 鉴于信用退款政策被越来越多的零售商采用，我们研究该如何设计最优的信用退款政策，以及与现金退款相比，信用退款政策能否给零售商带来更多的收益。与以往研究现金退款政策的模型不同，我们的模型刻画了零售商与消费者之间的长期的重复交易。特别地，我们考虑一个垄断零售商长期向消费者出售一种产品。每一期，消费者以一定的概率来到市场，以及消费者对该产品的估值是随机分布。消费者在购买产品之后，会有一定的概率选择退货，而这个概率是外生的。零售商通过给产品定价以及设计相应的退款政策来最大化自己的长期平均收益。信用退款政策包括：信用的大小，以及有效期的长短。换言之，该信用只能在有效期内使用。 对于给定的信用退款政策，我们提出用动态规划来分析消费者的决策问题，而动态规划的状态为该信用剩余的有效期。然后，基于消费者的最优行为，我们分析零售商的最优决策，包括产品定价，信用大小，以及有效期的长短。最终，我们会对信用退款政策和现金退款政策进行比较。总而言之，这项研究会向大家展示如何设计最优的信用退款政策，以及这项政策背后的逻辑和效果，从而为消费者退货这一领域做出相应的贡献。

15502420.label: Realisation of objectives
15502420.value: All four research objectives have been fully investigated. This research project focuses on studying the optimal design of credit refund policies and comparing them with cash refund policies to see whether and why credit refund policies can be more profitable. To achieve our research objectives, we assume that a monopolist sells a nondurable product to a population of infinitesimal consumers over an infinite time horizon. In each period, there is a fixed probability that each consumer shows up in the market. A consumer can be either a high-valuation consumer or a low-valuation consumer each time she arrives at the market, depending on the realization of the valuation. There is an exogenous probability that a consumer will return the product after purchase. The firm chooses its pricing and credit refund policy to maximize the long-run average revenue, where the credit refund policy includes a credit refund and an expiration term. Expired credit is forfeited. In what follows, I will elaborate how we achieve each objective and what are the findings. 1. Objective 1: The first objective is the most important and straightforward for this project, given that the project focuses on the design of the optimal credit refund policy. To derive the optimal price, credit refund amount, and expiration term, we need to first analyze consumers’ purchase decisions under any given price and credit refund policy. We formulate consumers’ decision problem as an infinite-horizon average reward dynamic program, where the state denotes the number of periods until the expiration of the credit. We then solve the dynamic programming equations and characterize the consumer’s optimal purchase decision under different prices. Intuitively, the consumer is less likely to purchase as the price increases, the refund amount decreases, or the expiration term increases. For example, when the price is relatively low, the consumer purchases in all states. When the price is in the middle, the consumer with a high-valuation realization (called a high-valuation consumer hereafter) purchases in all states, while the consumer with a low-valuation realization (called a low-valuation consumer hereafter) purchases only when she has a credit and the credit is close to expiration. When the price is relatively high, only the consumer with a high-valuation realization makes a purchase. Due to competitive pressure or industry norms, the expiration term is often exogenous in practice. Therefore, we first derive the optimal price and credit refund under an exogenous expiration term. To derive the firm’s optimal decisions, we formulate and solve the firm’s revenue maximization problem, taking into account consumers’ optimal responses. As shown above, consumer’s optimal responses can be divided into several cases. In our analysis, we first solve the firm’s problem for each of the cases. The overall optimal solution to the firm’s problem is obtained by comparing the optimal profits across different cases. We find that when the expiration term is relatively short, the optimal solution is the one associated with the consumer behavior that a low-valuation consumer always makes a purchase as long as she has a credit on hand. Intuitively, when the expiration term is short, consumers prefer to use the credit immediately, even if the realized valuation is low, given that the risk of losing the credit is high. Therefore, the optimal price and credit refund are set to induce the low-valuation consumer to purchase when she has a credit. While, when the expiration term is relatively large, the optimal solution is the one associated with the behavior that a low-valuation consumer only makes a purchase when her credit is close to expiration. Intuitively, when the expiration term is long, consumers face a low risk of losing the newly earned credit. Therefore, a low-valuation consumer would rather wait when her credit is far from expiration and only make a purchase when her credit is close to expiration. Hence, the optimal price and credit refund are set to induce the low-valuation consumer to behave in this way. Then, we investigate the optimal expiration term. We find that there exists an intermediate optimal expiration term under which a high-valuation consumer always makes a purchase, while a low-valuation consumer may only make a purchase when she has a credit on hand. The intuition for an intermediate optimal expiration term is as follows. A longer expiration term would incentivize low-valuation consumers to delay a purchase, while a shorter expiration term would make it more likely for the credit to expire unused, and thus make them less valuable to consumers. Hence, an intermediate expiration term that balances the two effects is optimal. 2. Objective 2: To compare the credit refund policy with the cash refund policy, in addition to analyzing the credit refund policy, we also formally introduce the model with the cash refund policy and derive the optimal price, cash refund, and expiration term. Then, we compare the optimal profits under credit and cash refund policies and find that credit refund policies are always more profitable than cash refund policies when consumers do not discount their future surplus. This result seems too strong and cannot explain the prevalence of cash refund policies in practice. To alleviate this concern, we consider an extension when consumers discount their future surplus and compare these two types of refund policy under this regime. 3. Objective 3: As stated in Objective 1, we first analyze consumers’ purchase decisions under any given price and credit refund policy, based on which we study the firm’s optimal decisions on price, credit refund, and expiration term. Then, we return to the consumer’s problem and find consumers’ corresponding behavior under the optimal price and credit refund policy. We find that a low-valuation consumer may be induced to make a purchase as the credit approaches expiration, which we call the demand induction effect. Specifically, there may exist a threshold τ on the expiration term such that a low-valuation consumer would not make a purchase when her credit is more than τ periods from expiration but would make a purchase otherwise. 4. Objective 4: Our numerical investigation shows that the optimal expiration term often takes the value T_0. Therefore, we discuss how T_0 changes with the parameters, such as the shopping frequency λ, the probability of being a high-valuation customer α, and return rate γ. We find that the optimal expiration term may decrease as the arrival rate increases, consumers' willingness to pay increases, or the return rate decreases. Intuitively, as the arrival rate increases, it is less likely for an earned credit to expire, and the firm should decrease the expiration term. A similar argument can be applied to consumer's willingness to pay and the return rate. We also conduct numerical experiments to investigate how the optimal price and credit refund changes with respect to the exogenous expiration term. The numerical result shows that the optimal price increases in the expiration term because a longer expiration term increases the value of a credit refund, and allows the firm to charge a higher price. A higher price is often paired with a higher credit, implying that the optimal credit increases in the expiration term as well.

15502420.label: Major findings and research outcome
15502420.value: First, a credit refund policy facilitates intra-consumer price discrimination for a single type of consumers with stochastic valuation. Specifically, the credit refund sustains consumers in the market when their valuation is low, given that a consumer with a low valuation never makes a purchase without the credit, whereas a consumer with a high valuation always makes a purchase without the credit. Consequently, in the long run, a consumer pays a higher price when her valuation is high. Second, an optimal policy often involves an intermediate credit expiration term, under which a consumer with a high product valuation always makes a purchase, while a consumer with a low product valuation may be induced to make a purchase as the credit approaches expiration, leading to a demand induction effect. As the credit approaches expiration, the consumer not only accelerates her purchase, but also gains more utility from a purchase. Moreover, this purchase acceleration in our model is purely driven by economic benefits, instead of psychological considerations. Third, credit refund policies are more profitable than cash refund policies when consumers do not discount their future surplus. A properly designed credit refund policy can collect the maximum revenue from high-valuation consumers. In the meantime, it can also lead low-valuation consumers to make a purchase when they have credits on hand. In contrast, under a cash refund policy, the firm either serves all consumers with a low effective price or only high-valuation consumers with a high effective price. However, when consumers discount their future surplus, credit refund policies can be less appealing than cash refund policies. This is because consumer discounting makes credits less valuable to consumers, leading to a lower consumer surplus that the firm can collect. Finally, adopting a credit refund policy instead of a cash refund policy can either help or hurt consumers. When the firm serves only high-valuation consumers under a cash refund policy, the aggregate consumer surplus is 0. Switching to a credit refund policy cannot hurt consumers and can lead to a win-win outcome for the firm and consumers. However, when the firm charges a low price and serves all consumers, switching to a credit refund policy can decrease both the consumer surplus and social welfare. These major findings are summarized in one paper that was eventually accepted for publication by Management Science in 2023.

15502420.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
15502420.value: There are several future research directions for this project. First, our analysis assumes that consumers are fully rational and forward-looking. As a result, they can strategically anticipate the value of the credit they earn. In practice, consumers may have bounded rationality; thus, it would be interesting to consider models where consumers are restricted to simpler strategies. Second, we assume that consumers' valuation uncertainty is fully resolved before making a purchase. In contrast, much of the existing literature on consumer returns hinges on the assumption that valuation uncertainty is only resolved after making a purchase. It would be worthwhile to investigate the efficacy of credit refund policies under such an assumption. Third, our consumer model assumes that the probability of product return is exogenous. Such an assumption is appropriate for some products but not for others. Investigating credit refund policies under alternative assumptions is a worthwhile topic for future research. All the above questions are not only relevant in practice but also not well investigated in the existing literature. Our current results lay a solid foundation for further exploring these questions.

15502420.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
15502420.value: This project considers the optimal design of credit refund policies in the presence of forward-looking consumers. We first analyze a consumer's decision problem under a given price and credit refund policy. We find that a consumer may be induced to make a purchase as the credit approaches expiration, which we call the demand induction effect. Note that this demand induction effect is purely driven by economic benefits instead of psychological considerations. We then characterize the firm's optimal pricing and credit refund policy with either exogenous or endogenous expiration terms. We show that there exists an intermediate optimal expiration term, under which a high-valuation consumer always makes a purchase, while a low-valuation consumer may make a purchase only when she has a credit on hand. Importantly, such consumer behavior facilitates intra-consumer price discrimination. Finally, we compare credit refund policies with cash refund policies, and conclude that credit refund policies can be more profitable. Moreover, the switch from cash refund policies to credit refund policies can lead to a win-win outcome for both the firm and consumers under certain conditions. Our work sheds light on the rationale of credit refund policies and provides guidance for the optimal design of such policies.

15502820.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
15502820.value: When service quality is unknown to some customers, they can sometimes infer quality through observing the length of queues. For example, tourists can infer that a restaurant's quality is good if they observe a long queue in front of the restaurant; patients can infer that a doctor's quality is high if the appointment takes a long time. Study on customers' queueing strategy with information updating based on queues has been conducted by many researchers. However, such literature ignores a key issue that the server's queue hiding /revealing action itself also serves as a device for conveying their quality. For example, for a low quality server, it may decide to hide its queue if the potential arrival rate is less than 5 and reveal it when it is larger than 5; and a high quality server may set such a threshold at 10. Then when the arrival rate falls into the range of 5 and 10, high- and low-quality servers have different incentives to reveal/hide the queue and customers can directly infer their quality by observing their action (hiding/revealing queue). Knowing customers' behavior, the low-quality server may try to mimic the high-quality server's behavior and the high-quality one may try to differentiate from the low-quality's behavior. Hence, this is a signalling game problem. This project aims to study such a signalling game between a server and customers. We plan to start with the simplest setting where customers are homogeneous on both service reward and delay sensitivity and they have no information on the service quality initially. The server can choose to reveal or conceal its queue length. We have conducted some initial studies with pure strategies of servers, and we show that there exist both separating equilibrium (high- and low-quality servers choose different signals) and pooling equilibrium (both high- and low-quality servers choose the same signal). We also identify some cases where no equilibrium exists for the signalling game. We plan to further investigate the signalling game along three dimensions. One, consider mixed strategy for servers where each type of server chooses to reveal/hide its queue in a probability. Two, consider more complex composition of customers with some being informed with the quality and some uninformed. Both the server's action and and the queue length convey quality information. Third, consider both selfish and collective customers, where collective customers make their queueing decision to maximize their overall utility. 在很多服务系统中， 服务质量对顾客而言是不清楚的。 对于新的顾客来讲， 他们有时候通过观察队列的长度来判断服务的质量。 比如， 如果观察到餐馆外的队列长度很长， 顾客就会判断食物不错。 已有的研究是集中在队列的长度和质量的关系上。 本研究从一个新的角度来研究这个问题。 服务台的开发与关闭队列本身的行为就已经表达了它的质量消息。 比如， 低质量服务台可能会努力遮掩它的队列长度。 因此， 本研究将服务台的队列可视性当作它的质量的信号。 本研究集中在研究服务台与顾客之间的信号博弈上。
