16102920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16102920.value: The brain and spinal cord together form the central nervous system which controls most of our bodily functions. Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating and largely irreversible neurological trauma and can result in lifelong disability and paralysis. To date, there is no cure for SCI. In the past, studies of axon damage and regeneration have been limited by a lack of in vivo imaging tools to visualize the spinal cord at the level of cellular processes. In the proposed research we will aim to develop a multimodal microscopy technology for in vivo imaging of important biological processes involved in the injury and repair of the spinal cord. The study could potentially reveal new biological insights leading to more efficient therapies for SCI. Although the primary injury causes functional impairment of the spinal cord, major damage termed secondary injury takes place after the initial trauma stemming from the inflammatory response of the immune system. Currently, most of the research being carried out focuses on exploring the mechanisms of secondary injury and trying to prevent it. A recent study showed that the myelin sheath that protects nerves and axons shatters into tiny pieces during primary injury. Macrophages, one major type of immune cell, migrate to the injured spinal cord and engulf myelin debris to form myelin-laden macrophages. These newly-formed abnormal immune cells secrete inflammatory substances and molecules which participate in tissue damage and contribute to secondary injury. In a preliminary study, we built a multimodal imaging system by integrating a two-photon excited fluorescence (TPEF) microscope with a stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscope for in vivo visualization of the microphages, axons and myelin debris in a spinal cord. We developed a surgical procedure to create an intervertebral window in a mouse model for in vivo imaging of the spinal cord. Our study confirmed that the procedure does not cause any inflammatory response and provides minimally invasive access for long-term optical imaging of the spinal cord. This is critical for the study of the inflammatory response of SCI. However, optical inhomogeneities in the window create aberration and impair the microscopes’ performance. We have now developed an adaptive optics (AO) technology to correct the aberration and demonstrated that it can significantly improve the performance of TPEF/SRS imaging of a spinal cord. 16102920.label: Realisation of objectives
16102920.value: The spinal cord serves as the primary communication pathway between the brain and the peripheral nervous system. Spinal cord injury is a devastating and largely irreversible neurological trauma, often resulting in lifelong disability and paralysis, with no available cure. In vivo spinal cord imaging in mouse models, without introducing immunological artifacts, is critical for understanding spinal cord pathology and discovering effective treatments. Over the course of the GRF project, we successfully achieved all the proposed goals and objectives, as detailed below: 1. Development of a Dual-Modal Imaging System Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy enables label-free imaging of biological tissues in their natural microenvironment by leveraging intrinsic molecular vibrations. By integrating two-photon excited fluorescence (TPEF) imaging into the SRS microscope, we developed a dual-modal in vivo imaging system capable of acquiring critical biochemical and biophysical information from multiple perspectives. This allows for a deeper understanding of dynamic processes such as cellular metabolism, immune responses, and tissue remodeling. The TPEF-SRS microscope system we developed enables in vivo imaging of the spinal cord in animal models, providing high-resolution visualization of myelin sheaths, axons, and glial cells. This capability is vital for studying the progression of neurodegenerative diseases and spinal cord injury. 2. Minimally Invasive Spinal Cord Imaging In vivo spinal cord imaging in mouse models, free from immunological artifacts, is essential for advancing our understanding of spinal cord pathology and developing effective treatments. To address this need, we developed a minimally invasive intervertebral window technique that retains the ligamentum flavum (LF) to protect the underlying spinal cord. By introducing an optical clearing method, we achieved repeated two-photon fluorescence and stimulated Raman scattering imaging at subcellular resolution, enabling up to 15 imaging sessions over a period of 6–167 days without inducing inflammatory responses. Specifically, to overcome scattering caused by the LF and improve spinal cord image quality, we employed a nontoxic chemical, Iodixanol, as an optical clearing agent. As an FDA-approved contrast agent for coronary angiography, Iodixanol enhances imaging performance by refractive index matching in live specimens. In this project, Iodixanol significantly improved the quality of spinal cord imaging during longitudinal imaging sessions and extended the number of repetitive imaging sessions. This minimally invasive approach enables long-term, repetitive, stable, high-resolution, and inflammation-free imaging of the mouse spinal cord, providing a reliable platform for studying spinal cord physiology and pathology. This portion of the study resulted in a publication in Nature Communications. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-29496-x). 3. Neuroprotective Role of Microglia in Axonal Injury Microglia, the primary immune cells of the central nervous system, play a critical role in regulating neuronal function and fate through their interactions with neurons. Despite extensive research, the mechanisms underlying microglia-neuron interactions remain incompletely understood. In this study, we demonstrated that microglia establish direct contact with myelinated axons at the Nodes of Ranvier in the spinal cord of mice. These contacts, associated with neuronal activity, occur in a random scanning pattern. Following axonal injury, microglia rapidly transform their contacts into robust wrapping formations, preventing acute axonal degeneration from extending beyond the nodes. This wrapping behavior is mediated by the function of microglial P2Y12 receptors, which are likely activated by ATP released through axonal volume-activated anion channels at the nodes. Additionally, voltage-gated sodium channels (NaV) and two-pore-domain potassium channels (K2P) contribute to the interaction between nodes and glial cells following injury, with NaV inhibition shown to delay axonal degeneration. Through in vivo imaging, our findings reveal a neuroprotective role of microglia during the acute phase of single spinal cord axon injury, achieved through neuron-glia interactions. This portion of the study resulted in a second publication in Nature Communications. (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-53218-0) In summary, the GRF project successfully developed innovative methodologies and provided novel insights into spinal cord imaging and pathology. These advancements, including the dual-modal imaging system, minimally invasive longitudinal imaging techniques, and the discovery of a neuroprotective role of microglia, represent significant progress toward understanding spinal cord physiology and pathology, as well as developing effective treatments for spinal cord injury.

16102920.label: Major findings and research outcome
16102920.value: The GRF project successfully achieved all proposed objectives, leading to significant advancements in spinal cord imaging and our understanding of spinal cord pathology. First, we developed a dual-modal imaging system that integrates Stimulated Raman Scattering (SRS) microscopy with two-photon excited fluorescence (TPEF) imaging. This innovative system enables high-resolution, label-free imaging of myelin sheaths, axons, and glial cells in their natural microenvironment. By capturing critical biochemical and biophysical information, this dual-modal system provides unique insights into dynamic processes, including cellular metabolism, immune responses, and tissue remodeling, making it an invaluable tool for investigating neurodegenerative diseases and spinal cord injury. Second, we established a minimally invasive intervertebral window technique for in vivo spinal cord imaging in mouse models. This method retains the ligamentum flavum (LF), a key protective structure, and incorporates an optical clearing technique using Iodixanol, a nontoxic, FDA-approved contrast agent. By reducing optical scattering and improving image clarity through refractive index matching, this technique achieved subcellular resolution imaging over 15 sessions spanning 6–167 days without inducing inflammatory responses. The ability to perform long-term, stable, and inflammation-free imaging of the spinal cord allows for detailed studies of spinal cord physiology and pathology. This portion of the study was published in Nature Communications, highlighting its importance and impact. Finally, the project uncovered the neuroprotective role of microglia in axonal injury through in vivo imaging. Under normal conditions, microglia establish contact with myelinated axons at the Nodes of Ranvier in a random scanning pattern. Following axonal injury, microglia rapidly transform their contacts into robust wrapping formations, halting acute axonal degeneration at the nodes. This behavior is mediated by microglial P2Y12 receptors, likely activated by ATP released from axonal volume-activated anion channels, and involves sodium (NaV) and two-pore-domain potassium (K2P) channels, with NaV inhibition shown to delay degeneration. These findings reveal a critical neuroprotective mechanism during the acute phase of spinal cord injury, achieved through neuron-glia interactions. This work resulted in a second publication in Nature Communications. In summary, the GRF project delivered groundbreaking methodologies and novel insights into spinal cord imaging and pathology. The dual-modal imaging system, minimally invasive imaging techniques, and discovery of microglia’s neuroprotective role represent major progress in understanding spinal cord physiology and developing effective treatments for spinal cord injury.

16102920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16102920.value: Building on the GRF findings, future developments could focus on therapies enhancing microglial activation and neuron-glia interactions for spinal cord repair. Strengthening microglial P2Y12 receptor activity or regulating sodium (NaV) and potassium (K2P) channels could prevent axonal degeneration after injury. The dual-modal TPEF-SRS imaging system and minimally invasive intervertebral window could facilitate high-throughput drug screening, enabling real-time evaluation of treatments. Additionally, this system could advance research on neurodegenerative diseases like multiple sclerosis. Refining the intervertebral window for clinical applications could enable minimally invasive imaging and real-time monitoring of therapies such as stem cell treatments or neural implants.

16102920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16102920.value: This research project focused on developing advanced tools and uncovering new insights to better understand and treat spinal cord injuries, which often lead to paralysis and have no cure. The spinal cord is the main communication pathway between the brain and the body, and damage to it is devastating. To study the spinal cord in detail, the team created an innovative imaging system that combines two techniques: one that detects natural molecules in tissues without the need for labels (SRS microscopy) and another that highlights specific structures like cells and fibers (TPEF imaging). This system provides high-resolution views of spinal cord structures like myelin, axons, and immune cells, helping researchers study how spinal cord injuries progress. The team also developed a minimally invasive technique for long-term spinal cord imaging in mice. By keeping a protective ligament intact and using a harmless clearing solution (Iodixanol), they achieved clear, inflammation-free imaging over multiple sessions spanning months. This method opens new possibilities for studying spinal cord diseases and testing treatments. Additionally, they discovered how microglia, the spinal cord’s immune cells, protect injured axons by wrapping around them to prevent further damage. These findings provide valuable insights that could lead to new therapies for spinal cord injuries and related conditions.

16103020.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103020.value: 細胞週期蛋白依賴性激酶（CDK）是細胞週期的重要調節器。儘管有著對不同CDK於正常細胞週期的調節機制之認識，在基因剔除小鼠研究還是顯示了不同CDK之間令人驚訝的遺傳冗餘性。然而，在人類細胞中的CDK是否具有相同的冗餘性仍未充分認識。此外，由於不同CDK的調節機制經常在癌細胞中重排，因此，其在癌細胞中的必需性或冗餘性仍然不太清楚。在欠缺適當的工具以及眾多CDK在細胞週期中多元化的功能，使解決這些長期存在的問題變得複雜。在利用新的基因組編輯和可誘導降解系統等工具，特定的CDK可以在特定的細胞週期時間點上被滅活。這將使我們能夠解決有關CDK在G1-S或G2-M功能上的多種問題。這些問題包括個別CDK在正常細胞和癌細胞中是否同等重要。基於我們的發現，在沒有CDK1的情況下CDK2是可以促進細胞進入有絲分裂期，但卻未能通過有絲分裂後期。我們計劃檢測CDK2的相對豐度是否促進有絲分裂的主要因素。以磷酸化蛋白質組學分析，我們還會考查CDK1或CDK2所促進的有絲分裂之間的差異。另一個研究方向是探討保有或缺乏pRb基因的癌細胞中對不同CDK需求的差別。最後，我們打算開發一種系統，可以在特定條件下以無活性或有其他突變的CDK取代原有的基因。利用這些工具，這個項目將擴大我們對這個重要的細胞週期調節機制的理解。由於CDK在不論正常或異常細胞分裂都起著根本作用，亦與許多抗癌療法有著複雜的聯繫，因此，破解其確切功能將對人類疾病和健康產生深遠的影響。

16103020.label: Realisation of objectives
16103020.value: Switching genes on and off on cue is a cornerstone for understanding gene functions. One contemporary approach for loss-of-function studies of essential genes involves CRISPR-mediated knockout of the endogenous locus in conjunction with the expression of a rescue construct, which can subsequently be turned off to produce a gene inactivation effect (achieved in Objectives 1–3). Expanding on this, we devised a strategy to concurrently activate a second gene construct to explore gene functions within a pathway (Objective 4). Our innovative gene switches, controlled by inducible promoters and degrons, enable efficient and tight regulation of gene expression with rapid on/off kinetics. Specifically, we designed an inducible gene-OFF switch utilizing TRE transcriptional control coupled with auxin-induced degron-mediated proteolysis via F-box protein AFB2. Furthermore, an independently controlled gene-ON switch was established using a modified ecdysone promoter and mutated FKBP12-derived destabilization domain (DD) degron for rapid and tuneable gene activation. This platform facilitates efficient generation of knockout-cell lines containing two gene-switches that are regulated tightly and can be flipped within a fraction of the time of a cell cycle. In our study, we replaced wild-type CDK2 with a kinase-inactive version in a CRISPR-mediated CDK2-knockout background, which has been detailed in our publication in the Journal of Cell Science (Yeung et al., 2023). Cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) orchestrate key events in the cell cycle. However, the uniqueness of individual mitotic cyclins and CDKs has been a long-standing puzzle. A cornerstone in cell cycle control is the highly conserved nature of CDKs in eukaryotic cells. However, one of the most interesting aspects is that while there are multiple CDKs in higher eukaryotes, a single CDK is responsible for both G1-S and G2-M in yeasts (by contrast, there are multiple cyclins in both yeast and human). Given that CDK1 is the only essential cell cycle CDK in mice, why metazoans contain multiple cell cycle CDKs is a long-standing puzzle. Although the conventional view is that the essential function of CDK1 in mitosis cannot be compensated by other CDKs, it is likely too simplistic a view for many cancer cells. We hypothesize that the presence of multiple CDKs and epigenetic rewiring may provide cancer cells the plasticity to use alternative CDKs to orchestrate the cell cycle. With the CRISPR-Cas9 and degron tools we developed, CDKs can be rapidly removed from human cell lines either individually or in combination (Objective 1). We confirmed that CDK1 assumes the role of G1-S CDK in the absence of CDK2. Unexpectedly, CDK1 deficiency does not prevent mitotic entry. Nonetheless, inadequate phosphorylation of mitotic substrates by noncanonical cyclin B-CDK2 complexes does not allow progression beyond metaphase and underscores deleterious late mitotic events including the uncoupling of anaphase A and B and cytokinesis. Elevation of CDK2 to a level similar to CDK1 overcomes the mitotic defects caused by CDK1 deficiency, indicating that the relatively low concentration of CDK2 accounts for the defective anaphase. Collectively, these results revealed that the difference between G2-M and G1-S CDKs in human cells is essentially quantitative. This work was published in Cell Reports (Lau et al., 2021). In addition to conditionally silencing the mitotic CDKs using degrons, we have also performed similar experiments targeting their cyclin partners. We discovered that depletion of cyclin A promoted an acute accumulation of CDC25A, a phosphatase of the inhibitory phosphorylation sites of the CDKs. This compensatory mechanism involving CDC25A was found to be transcriptionally regulated, underscoring its role in ensuring timely mitotic onset. These findings, detailed in the Journal of Biological Chemistry (Ng et al., 2023), shed light on the intricate regulatory network governing mitotic entry. Our studies also unveiled that deficiency of B-type cyclins attenuates mitotic onset and uncouples the G2-M kinase network from mitosis, resulting in sustained activation of PLK1 and cyclin A-CDK1. This culminates in mitotic slippage without completing nuclear envelope breakdown. Remarkably, elevation of cyclin A levels above endogenous levels could restore mitosis in the absence of B-type cyclins, emphasizing the plasticity and interplay among cyclins and CDKs in cell cycle progression. In contrast, cyclin A is rate-limiting but not essential for G2-M due to compensation by endogenous cyclin B1-CDK2, a non-canonical pair. These significant discoveries, published in the Journal of Cell Biology (Crncec et al., 2025), challenge conventional notions of cyclin indispensability and highlight their adaptive nature, particularly in cancer cells.

16103020.label: Major findings and research outcome
16103020.value: Our research has focused on the regulation of gene expression and the roles of different cyclins and CDKs for G2–M, leveraging advanced techniques including CRISPR and inducible gene switches that we specifically developed for these studies. 1. Gene regulation platforms: we developed a method for studying essential cell cycle genes through CRISPR-mediated knockout combined with a rescue AID construct that can conditionally inactivated This system allows for the concurrent activation of a second gene construct, enhancing our ability to explore gene functions within pathways. Our gene switches utilize inducible promoters and degrons for precise control of gene expression with rapid on/off kinetics. Notably, we established a gene-OFF switch using TRE transcriptional control and AID, alongside a gene-ON switch with a modified ecdysone promoter. This approach enables the rapid generation of knockout cell lines with tightly regulated gene switches, significantly improving experimental efficiency (Yeung et al., 2023). 2. Role of mitotic CDKs: our findings reveal that while multiple CDKs are present in higher eukaryotes, CDK1 can compensate for CDK2 deficiency during the G1-S transition. Surprisingly, CDK1 deficiency does not prevent entry into mitosis, but inadequate phosphorylation by noncanonical cyclin B-CDK2 complexes leads to multiple mitotic defects. This emphasizes the quantitative differences between G1-S and G2-M CDKs and suggests that cancer cells may exploit alternative CDKs for flexibility in cell cycle regulation (Lau et al., 2021). 3. Role of mitotic cyclins: we also investigated the roles of mitotic cyclins, discovering that depletion of cyclin A results in the accumulation of CDC25A, a phosphatase that regulates CDK phosphorylation. This mechanism is transcriptionally regulated and is crucial for timely mitotic onset. Furthermore, the absence of B-type cyclins disrupts the G2-M kinase network, leading to delayed mitotic onset and sustained activation of PLK1. Interestingly, elevating cyclin A levels can restore mitosis in the absence of B-type cyclins, highlighting the adaptive interplay among cyclins and CDKs (Ng et al., 2023; Crncec et al., 2025). Finally, our related publications included updated review articles in the field of mitotic control (Poon 2021; Poon 2023). Conclusion: These findings challenge traditional notions regarding the indispensability of cyclins and CDKs in human cells, highlighting their remarkable plasticity, especially in cancer cells. This research opens new avenues for future studies on cell cycle regulation and gene function.

16103020.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16103020.value: Our research on the roles of cyclins and CDKs has opened exciting avenues for exploration: 1. Expanded pathway analysis: We can leverage our gene-switch technology to investigate additional biological pathways, enhancing our understanding of complex networks involving essential genes. 2. Cancer cell adaptability: Given the plasticity of cyclins and CDKs in cancer cells, future studies could focus on specific cancer types to identify how alternative pathways are utilized, potentially revealing novel therapeutic targets. 3. Therapeutic applications: We propose to explore our gene-switch platform for developing targeted therapies by manipulating cyclin and CDK levels to disrupt cancer cell proliferation. Proposed course of action: • Conduct comprehensive studies of mitotic regulators: Identify additional gene interactions within mitotic regulators. • Targeted studies in cancer models: Develop specific cancer models to study CDK and cyclin mechanisms. • Collaborate on therapeutics: Work with pharmacologists to design drugs targeting identified cell cycle pathways.

16103020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16103020.value: Our research examines how genes are regulated during the cell cycle using advanced techniques like CRISPR and specially designed gene switches. We developed a method to study essential genes by knocking them out and then using a rescue system to reactivate them as needed, allowing us to investigate how different genes interact. We discovered that cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) in human cells exhibit remarkable plasticity. Specifically, overexpressing individual cyclins and CDKs can fully compensate for the functions of others that are typically active at specific points in the cell cycle. This challenges the conventional belief that certain cyclins and CDKs are absolutely necessary during the cell cycle. Overall, our findings provide insight into how cancer cells can adapt their regulatory mechanisms, opening new avenues for research into cell cycle regulation and gene function in the future.

16103120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103120.value: Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) have numerous applications for biological labeling, cancer treatment, biosensing, antibacterial activity, and antiviral activity. Their wide application increases the likelihood of AgNPs reaching the water systems, with the possibility of bioaccumulation in aquatic organisms, raising potential health and environmental concerns. A comprehensive understanding of the potential impacts of these nanoparticles on aquatic ecosystems is therefore required. In addition to direct bioaccumulation, these nanoparticles may be transferred up the food chains or maternally transferred to the next generation, but these aspects remain critically under-studied. Trophic and maternal transfers are important pathways for the movement of nanoparticles and have significant implications for the prediction of exposure and toxicity of nanomaterials in aquatic ecosystems. During complex trophic and maternal transfer, AgNPs and Ag+ can be redistributed and transformed biotically or abiotically, thus causing changes in the physical and chemical characteristics of the particles. Nevertheless, knowledge of the biodistribution patterns of AgNPs and Ag+ during trophic and maternal transfer is still very limited, mainly because of the lack of advanced technologies. In this project, I propose to employ novel fluorescent (aggregated-induced emission based) technology to address three exciting aspects of the toxicology of nanoparticles in aquatic environments, including transport and transformation, trophic transfer and maternal transfer, in two model aquatic organisms (Daphnia and Japanese medaka). We have successfully developed different Ag probes to visualize the distribution of both Ag+ and AgNPs directly in these organisms. Our primary objectives will be to 1) differentiate the distribution of Ag+ and AgNPs and their transport following bioaccumulation; 2) visualize the trophic transfer of Ag+ and AgNPs; 3) visualize the maternal transfer of Ag+ and AgNPs. We will perform various bioimaging analyses combined with the classic tracer labelling technique to visually and quantitatively evaluate the fate of both AgNPs and Ag+ during their trophic and maternal transfer. With the help of fluorescence techniques, it is now possible to observe the fate of AgNPs and Ag+ directly in the organisms. The application of novel bioimaging techniques allow us to address the most pressing questions such as whether these nanoparticles can be transferred further along aquatic food chains or maternally to the next generation of aquatic animals. We anticipate producing the first bioimaging data of NPs in aquatic animals following their trophic and maternal transfer, which are critical to any risk assessment of NPs in aquatic environments. 銀納米粒子(AgNPs)在生物標籤、癌症治療、生物檢測、抗菌活性和抗病毒活性方面有許多應用。 其廣泛應用增加了AgNPs進入水系統的可能性,增加了水生生物的生物累積的可能性,從而增加了潛在的健康和環境問題。 因此,需要全面瞭解這些納米粒子對水生生態系統的潛在影響。 除了直接的生物累積,這些納米粒子可以轉移到食物鏈上或母體轉移到下一代,但這些方面仍然嚴重研究不足。 營養和母體轉移是納米粒子運输的重要途徑,對預測水生生態系統中納米材料的暴露和毒性具有重大影響。 在複雜的營養和母體轉移過程中,AgNPs和Ag+可以生物或非生物性再分配和轉化,從而引起粒子的物理和化學特性的變化。 然而,在營養和母體轉移期間,對AgNPs和Ag+的生物分佈模式的瞭解仍然非常有限,主要原因是缺乏先進技術。 這個项目採用新型螢光(聚合誘導发光)技術, 解決水生環境中納米粒子毒理學的三個问题,包括運輸和轉化、營養轉移和母體轉移。 我們已經成功地開發了不同的Ag探針,以直接观测Ag+和AgNPs在生物體中的分佈。 我們的主要目標是 1) 區分 Ag+ 和 AgNPs 的分佈及其在生物累積後傳輸;2) 观测 Ag+ 和 AgNPs 的營養轉移;3)观测 Ag+ 和 AgNPs 的母體轉移。 我們將进行各種生物成像分析,結合传统的示蹤標記,直觀和定量地評估AgNPs和Ag+的營養和母體轉移過程。 新型生物成像技術的應用使我們能夠解決最緊迫的問題,例如這些納米粒子是否可以沿著水生食物鏈進一步轉移,還是母體轉移到下一代水生動物身上。

16103120.label: Realisation of objectives
16103120.value: There are 3 objectives in this project. Achievements of each objective are described below. Objective 1: To study the transport and transformation of AgNPs in aquatic animals. Phytoplankton: Here we made a major discovery that the cellular intake of nanoparticles was controlled by the cell cycle. Specifically, we found that the bioaccumulation of NPs was more favored in the G2/M stages, followed by the S and G0/G1 stages. Three key parameters (clathrin-mediated endocytosis capacity, algal membrane permeability, and exopolymer substance (EPS) thickness) were critical in the bioaccumulation of NPs during the cell cycling process. The cell cycle control of AgNPs internalization was further verified by exposing algae to different cell cycle stages. This study was published in the most prestigious journal in the field (Yan et al. 2021, ACS Nano, Research Item #8). Given the intracellular transport of AgNPs, Yan et al. (2021, Environ Sci: Nano, Item #5) quantitatively monitored AgNPs and Ag+ and identified the mitochondrial-specific toxic mechanisms caused by the Ag+ released from AgNPs. Bioimaging showed that more than 80% of Ag+ was concentrated in the mitochondria as a major storage site and potential acting target in the fish cells. Li and Wang (2021, Item #6) showed that the cellular uptake of Ag nanowires (AgNWs) occurred mainly via pathways of clathrin-dependent endocytosis and phagocytosis. For the first time, this study found that AgNW exposure inhibited the transmembrane ATP-binding cassette efflux transporter activity. Sun and Wang (2022, Item #13) then developed a novel technique to quantify the intracellular dissolution of ultra-small AgNPs based on the finding that dissolved Ag+ decreased the Zn2+-directed fluorescence increase of an adenine-deficient yeast [Ade(-) yeast]. Zooplankton: Li and Wang (2021, Item #3) examined the uptake and depuration kinetics of Ag nanowires in Daphnia magna. Compared with other Ag nanoparticles, Ag+ release from AgNWs contributed much less to the observed AgNW toxicity, and AgNWs were able to transport to inner parts of daphnids, including gills and hemolymph. The slow depuration of both AgNWs and Ag+ in D. magna may thus contribute to their combined chronic toxic effects. Oysters: In an exciting study, Shao et al. (2021, Item #2) achieved the first in situ subcellular imaging of Ag and determined the sites of AgNP interaction with organelles in the oysters. By coupling high-resolution NanoSIMS with SEM, we successfully visualized the subcellular localization and the potential toxicity effects of AgNPs in the oyster gill filaments. For the first time, we provided visualized evidence of AgNP-induced autophagy in the oyster gill cells. We further identified two categories of hemocytes (blood cells) and illustrated their roles in AgNP transport and sequestration. This study highlighted not only the intracellular but also the intercellular AgNP translocation and transformation, providing important subcellular imaging of silver and reliable methodology. Zhang and Wang (2023, Item #17) then examined the toxicity of AgNPs to the veliger larvae of the oyster Crassostrea angulata. Apart from the Ag released in the medium, the Ag dissolved from the ingested AgNPs may also greatly contribute to the toxicity of AgNPs. Based on the Shao et al. (2021) study, we then conducted a series of exciting investigations on the roles of oyster hemocytes in AgNPs. Hemocytes are the main immune cells in bivalves and consist of multiple functional heterogeneous cell types, but their different roles in the immune system against foreign particles remain largely unknown. Luo and Wang (2022, Item #14) clarified the different immune responses of oyster hemocyte subpopulations to silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) and Ag ions. Interestingly, AgNPs induced granule formation in semigranulocytes and further increased the proportion of granulocytes, whereas their ionic counterparts had no such effects on hemocyte composition. Luo et al. (2022, Item #16) then employed two AIE-based AgNPs and Ag+ to study the intracellular behavior of AgNPs in oyster hemocyte subpopulations. Dissolved Ag+ was mainly located in lysosomes of granulocytes. Finally, Luo and Wang (2023, Item #18) analyzed mitochondrial fragmentation induced by AgNPs by determining mitochondrial shape, size, and network connectivity. This study demonstrated that mitochondrial-lysosome networks (MLCs) exerted critical roles as upstream mediators of mitochondrial dynamics and functions. Objective 2: To study and map the trophic transfer of AgNPs in aquatic animals. Yan and Wang (2021, Item #9) demonstrated that AgNPs were internalized in a freshwater phytoplankton Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Citrate-coated AgNPs (Cit-AgNPs) and AIEgen-coated AgNPs were internalized by different mechanisms. The internalized AgNPs were dissolved intracellularly and the released Ag+ was distributed heterogeneously in the cytoplasm, in contrast to the directly accumulated Ag+. We then visualized and quantified the trophic transfer of AgNPs from the alga to the zooplankton. Both trophically transferred Ag+ and AgNPs were concentrated in the gut regions of D. magna as a result of direct ingestion of food particles. After ingestion, about 95% of the trophically transferred Ag+ was eliminated. The present study demonstrates that the trophically transferred AgNPs are related to the different surface coatings of NPs. Trophically transferred AgNPs may then produce different toxicity at the gut microbial levels. Li et al. (2022, Item #11) applied 16S rRNA sequencing, metatranscriptome sequencing and gut microbiota transplants (GMTs) to investigate the gut-microbial adaptation and transformation of different silver (Ag) forms over 4 generations of exposure of Daphnia magna. Our results demonstrated that the gut-accumulated Ag+ and AgNPs were transformed by gut microbial sulfidation, which subsequently affected the toxic symptoms of D. magna. Objective 3: To study and map the maternal transfer of AgNPs in aquatic animals. Yan et al. (2020, Item #1) visualized and quantified for the first time the maternal transfer of AgNPs in model zooplankton (Daphnia magna). We found that AgNPs were transferred from mother to offspring and mainly accumulated in the lipids due to the strong colocalization with lipid droplets, which were the major energy sources of Daphnia embryos. In contrast, Ag+ was irregularly distributed in different sites, probably due to the mobility and reactivity of Ag+. The maternal transfer efficiency was 2.37 ± 0.25 and 6.05 ± 0.89% for 110mAgNPs and 110mAg, respectively. Furthermore, AgNPs and Ag+ significantly inhibited the reproduction capability of F0 and F1 generations, but such maternal toxic effect inhibition was only found within the first two broods of F0 and F1 generations. Our bioimaging findings demonstrated that AgNPs could be maternally transferred to the next generation; thus it is critical to produce AgNPs with lower toxic effects, higher delivery efficacy, and more precise targeting. Yan and Wang (2022, Item #15) then examined the maternal transfer potentials and biodistribution of AgNPs. We performed a 100-day exposure of medaka fish to citrate-coated and luminogen-coated AgNPs and investigated long-term AgNPs exposure. AgNPs were mainly distributed in the liver, followed by the gills, intestine, and brain, but were also detected in the ovary and strongly colocalized with the dissolved Ag+. The quantified transfer efficiency of different Ag species was 1.56-5.07%. Long-term exposure of medaka to small size of AgNPs (20 nm) reduced the hatching rate attributable to the accumulation of AgNPs and their dissolved Ag+. During initial larval development, the maternally transferred AgNPs and their dissolved Ag+ were consistently concentrated in the intestine. Our results showed that long-term exposure to AgNPs caused distinct biodistribution in the next generation of medaka, and may have implications for assessing their potential adverse effects.

16103120.label: Major findings and research outcome
16103120.value: Over the 3-year project period, our research conducted under the constraints of the COVID-19 pandemic yielded numerous important discoveries across multiple areas. These studies resulted in 18 publications in top international environmental science journals, including ACS Nano, Environmental Science & Technology, Journal of Hazardous Materials, and Environmental Science: Nano, among others. Key findings include elucidating the intricate mechanisms governing nanoparticle (NP) bioaccumulation and internalization in cells. We found that the cell cycle stage exerts a critical control on NP uptake, with processes like clathrin-mediated endocytosis, variations in algal cell membrane permeability, and the dynamic thickness of exopolymer substances all playing important roles. We were able to quantitatively monitor the behavior of silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) and dissolved silver ions (Ag+), identifying the mitochondrial-specific toxic mechanisms caused by the Ag+ released from AgNPs in fish cells. AgNP toxicity was attributed to the accumulated Ag+, leading to the depletion of the cells' respiratory capacity and eventual cell death. We developed a novel technique to detect the dissolution of intracellular AgNPs, for which a U.S. patent has been filed. However, AgNWs were different from AgNPs. Ag+ release contributed less to AgNW toxicity compared to other forms of AgNPs. Using advanced Nano-SIMS imaging, we visualized for the first time the subcellular localization and toxicity effects of AgNPs in oyster gill filaments. Oysters have specialized endolysosomal and phagolysosomal systems for regulating cellular processes involving AgNPs, with dissolved Ag+ contributing significantly to the observed toxicity. Additionally, we found that different subpopulations of oyster hemocytes responded differently to AgNP exposure, with dissolved Ag+ primarily localized in the lysosomes of granulocytes. Our studies also revealed that the pathways of AgNP entrance into organisms varied depending on the surface coating of the NPs. Through trophic transfer, both Ag+ and AgNPs were concentrated in the gut regions of Daphnia magna, with the differences in toxicity between Ag+ and AgNPs related to the enriched organic matter in the gut, which facilitated sulfidation-based detoxification of Ag+ and inhibited Ag+ release from AgNPs. Lastly, we discovered that AgNPs were maternally transferred from mothers to offspring in both Daphnia and fish, with the AgNPs mainly accumulating in lipid droplets, which serve as the major energy sources for embryos. This maternal transfer of AgNPs and Ag+ was found to significantly inhibit the reproductive capability of the F0 and F1 generations, though the effects were limited to the first two broods.

16103120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16103120.value: Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) have been widely used in various sectors, but their toxicity remains controversial. This is largely due to the complexity of AgNP chemistry, which involves the dissolution of Ag ions under different conditions, and the diverse physiologies of animals and cells. This project has revealed numerous interesting results regarding the accumulation, transformation, trophic transfer, and maternal transfer of AgNPs. These aspects are the main concerns underlying AgNP toxicology, and numerous challenges still exist in this area. Two important areas for future development are: • Modeling of AgNPs in cellular and animal systems: Environmental systems are multi-compartmental, making it difficult to integrate all aspects into a single picture. Mathematical modeling is the only approach to integrate different systems and conduct quantitative analysis, which is critical for drug design. My lab has started developing models to simulate the complicated intracellular trafficking of AgNPs. • Resistance of cells/organisms to AgNPs: AgNPs have been used to kill bacteria, fungi, and other organisms. However, it is crucial to investigate whether organisms can develop tolerance to these nanoparticles, similar to the development of antibiotic-resistant genes. My laboratory's previous work on metal (e.g., Hg) tolerance suggests that animals can adapt to these substances, and this concept should be explored for nanoparticles as well.

16103120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16103120.value: Silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) have numerous applications for biological labeling, cancer treatment, biosensing, antibacterial activity, and antiviral activity. Their wide application increases the likelihood of AgNPs reaching the water systems, with the possibility of bioaccumulation in aquatic organisms, raising potential health and environmental concerns. A comprehensive understanding of the potential impacts of these nanoparticles on aquatic ecosystems is required. In addition to direct bioaccumulation, trophic and maternal transfers are important pathways for the movement of nanoparticles and have significant implications for the prediction of exposure and toxicity of nanomaterials in aquatic ecosystems. In this project, we employed novel fluorescent (aggregated-induced emission based) technology to address three exciting aspects of the toxicology of nanoparticles in aquatic environments, including transport and transformation, trophic transfer and maternal transfer, in different model organisms (phytoplankton, zooplankton, bivalves, and fish). We performed various bioimaging analyses combined with the classic tracer labelling technique to visually and quantitatively evaluate the fate of both AgNPs and Ag+ during their trophic and maternal transfer. We studies demonstrated the very different behavior of AgNPs and Ag+ in the biotic systems, and the importance of trophic transfer and maternal transfer of AgNPs. These data are critical to any risk assessment of NPs in aquatic environments.

16103220.label: Realisation of objectives
16103220.value: 1. Examination of changes in cell types in gastrocnemius muscles of mdx and Stat3/Dmd dKO mice of different ages by single-cell RNA-seq. Using the 10X Genomics scRNA-seq platform, we profiled 12,715 and 7293 cells from hindlimb muscles of two pairs of 5.5-month-old Stat3/Dmd double knockout (dKO) and mdx control mice respectively. Clustering analysis revealed pro-fibrotic changes in both fibro-adipogenic progenitors (FAP) and muscle-resident tenocytes. Briefly, Sub-clustering of tenocytes yielded 6 subclusters and the percentage of cluster 0 tenocytes increased by two-folds in Stat3-dKO mice (34.52%) than in mdx mice (15.84%). We found cluster 0 tenocytes are marked by high expression of extracellular matrix (ECM) genes especially those related to ECM organization and cellular adhesion such as Col8a1, Eln, Col3a1, Col14a1 and Lum. Sub-clustering of FAPs yields 11 subclusters and we immediately noticed a 2-fold increase in the cluster 3 FAP portion in Stat3-dKO mice. Gene expression analysis revealed Eln, Fmod, Thbs4 as marker genes of cluster 3 FAPs. Since tenocytes are known to express high level of Fmod and Thbs4, we named this subset of FAPs as tenocyte-like FAPs. Additionally, DEG analysis showed enriched transcripts of ECM genes (e.g., Col8a1, Col14a1, Col1a1, Col12a1, Eln) suggesting the heterogeneity of FAPs was altered and became more profibrotic in dKO mice. Using Monocle 3, cell state trajectory based on FAPs and tenocytes was inferred and we found FAPs from dKO mice acquired profibrotic features of tenocytes. NichenetR, an R-based package, was used to predict ligand-target paths based on integrated network of ligand-target regulatory potential. We found while ECM genes in FAPs are regulated by several cytokines whose expression increased in MuSCs of dKO mice such as Tgfb2, Vegfa and Ccn2, it seems that tendon gene expression is mainly driven by Tgfb2 signaling in the prediction model. 2. Examination of transcriptome profiles of bulk MuSC, macrophages, and FAPs from dKO mice and the mdx control of different ages. We performed bulk RNA-seq on freshly isolated CD31-/CD45-/Sca1-/Vcam1+ MuSCs from 5.5-month-old Stat3-dKO and mdx mice. In total, we discovered 974 differentially regulated genes (DEGs) among which 632 genes are upregulated and 342 genes are downregulated. Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed upregulated biological process (BP) terms including epithelial mesenchymal transition and Tgfbeta signaling in Stat3-dKO MuSCs. Importantly, we noted Tgfb2, Ccn2 and Mstn are upregulated in dKO MuSCs suggesting they could be potential profibrotic paracrine factors secreted by dKO MuSCs to influence FAPs. 3. Co-culture experiments to study mutual interaction among MuSC, FAP, and macrophages. To further strengthen the MuSC-FAP crosstalk model, we utilized a coculture system in which mdx FAPs (FACS sorting scheme: CD31-/CD45-/Sca1+) were placed in the bottom well and Stat3-dKO or mdx MuSCs were seeded in the upper transwell. In addition, an empty transwell was used as a negative control. In such co-culture experiments, we observed enhanced collagen production as well as proliferation of FAPs after coculturing madx-derived FAPs with Stat3-dKO-derived MuSCs for 48h. Similar co-culturing experiments were also carried out using mdx-derived FAPs and macrophages (FACS sorting scheme: CD45+/Ly6G-/CD11b+/F4/80+) derived from either mdx or Stat3/mdx dKO mice. Our results showed that macrophages isolated from Stat3/mdx-dKO mice were not more profibrotic than their mdx counterparts. 4. Testing whether IL-4/IL-13, CTGF, or other novel factors directly act on FAP to promote their conversion to SMA+ myofibroblasts. To test whether paracrine factors secreted by dKO MuSCs act on FAP to promote their fibrogenesis, we isolated CD31-/CD45-/Sca1+ FAPs from mdx mice by FACS and treated them with Ctgf, Myostatin or Tgfb2 at various concentrations for 32h followed by EdU treatment 4h before harvest. We found that FAPs from mdx mice treated with Tgfb2 and Myostatin were higher in collagen I protein level whereas Ctgf-treated FAPs have higher proliferation rate. However, only Tgfb2-treated FAPs produced significantly higher level of Elastin which is upregulated in cluster 3 FAPs to a larger extent than Col1a1. Moreover, we confirmed by RT-qPCR that the expression of selected cluster 3 FAP markers (i.e., Col8a1, Eln), tenocyte markers (i.e., Scx, Mkx) and Col1a1 were prominently upregulated only in Tgfb2-treated FAPs. Furthermore, Tgfb2 treatment specifically increased Scx and Tnmd protein level in cultured FAPs. These results suggest that Tgfb2, but not Ctgf or Myostatin, promotes the transition of FAPs to myofibroblast-like cells. We also detected increased protein level of both active and total Tgfb2 by ELISA in the muscle homogenate from Stat3-dKO mice. Activation of Tgfb signaling was further confirmed by increased Smad2/3 phosphorylation in FAPs isolated from Stat3-dKO mice. To further strengthen the MuSC-FAP crosstalk model, we utilized co-culturing system in which mdx FAPs were placed in the bottom wells and MuSCs from Stat3-dKO or mdx were seeded in the upper transwells. In addition, empty transwells were used as a negative control. We observed enhanced collagen production as well as proliferation of FAPs after coculturing with Stat3-dKO MuSCs for 48h. Importantly, the elevated collagen production, but not increased proliferation rate, was abolished by addition of a Tgfb2-neutralizing antibody at the beginning of coculture period which is consistent with recombinant Tgfb2’s effect on FAPs cultured in vitro.

16103220.label: Major findings and research outcome
16103220.value: In our previous work, we found that Stat3/Dmd double knockout (dKO) mice, a new mouse model generated in our group with the Stat3 gene specifically deleted in muscle stem cell (MuSCs) in mdx mice, exhibit severe muscle fibrosis, making the Stat3/Dmd dKO mouse strain a better animal model to study mechanisms underlying muscle fibrosis. By leveraging the Stat3/Dmd dKO mice, we first carried out bulk RNA-seq of MuSCs from Stat3/Dmd dKO mice and mdx mice, which revealed an increased expression of many profibrotic genes including Tgfb2. Furthermore, our new single-cell transcriptome analysis uncovered profibrotic changes in subpopulations of fibro-adipogenic progenitors (FAPs) and tenocytes, which implicates them as major contributors to aggravated muscle fibrosis in Stat3/Dmd-dKO mice. Both bioinformatic analysis and in vitro coculture assays confirmed that Tgfb2, which is secreted from MuSCs from Stat3/Dmd-dKO mice, enhances transition of muscle-resident FAPs and tenocytes to collagen-producing myofibroblasts. Our work demonstrates that impaired Stat3 functions in dystrophin-null MuSCs could promote conversion of FAPs and tenocytes to myofibroblasts, leading to enhanced muscle fibrosis. The findings from our work could lead to new therapeutic strategies to reduce muscle fibrosis in DMD patients.

16103220.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16103220.value: Our work is carried out in DMD mouse models. It remains to be established whether the STAT3 functions are also impaired in human DMD patients. Muscle biopsies may be obtained from DMD patients and age-matched healthy individuals and the levels of total STAT3 and p-STAT3 (Tyr705- or Ser727-phosphorylated STAT3) can be determined by western blot or immunostaining. Additionally, it will also be beneficial to determine which particular isoform of TGFb is elevated in human DMD patients. This can be done by both RT-qPCR and ELISA using muscle biopsies from DMD patients and age-matched healthy individuals.

16103220.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16103220.value: Muscle fibrosis is one of the pathogenic hallmarks of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), a fatal genetic disease (with a null mutation in the Dmd gene encoding dystrophin) impairing both cardiac and skeletal muscles. However, mdx mice (also having a null mutation in Dmd), a commonly-used mouse model for DMD, exhibit no or very little muscle fibrosis. In our previous work, we found that Stat3/Dmd double knockout (dKO) mice, a new mouse model generated in our group with the Stat3 gene specifically deleted in muscle stem cell (MuSCs) in mdx mice, exhibit severe muscle fibrosis, making the Stat3/Dmd dKO mouse strain a better animal model to study mechanisms underlying muscle fibrosis. We found that MuSCs from Stat3/Dmd dKO mice express higher levels of TGFb2, a profibrotic protein. Tgfb2 in turn acts on muscle-resident fibro-adipogenic progenitors (FAPs) and tenocytes and promotes their conversion to collagen-secreting myofibroblasts, a key cell type responsible for tissue fibrosis. Our work demonstrates that impaired Stat3 functions in dystrophin-null MuSCs could promote conversion of FAPs to myofibroblasts, leading to enhanced muscle fibrosis. The findings from our work could lead to new therapeutic strategies to reduce muscle fibrosis in DMD patients.

16103520.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103520.value: Human brain forms complexed neuronal network by connecting billion of neurons together. Neurons connect with each other via specialized structures termed synapses. There are two major types of synapses: the excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Abnormal formation of synapse is believed to contribute to a number of brain disorders, including autism, epilepsy and schizophrenia. The formation of synapses is tightly controlled and a large number of proteins participated in this process. Among them, neuroligins, a family of cell adhesion proteins, were found to be particular important for synapse formation. Neuroligins are transmembrane proteins that localized at the postsynaptic membranes. They bind to neurexins, which are transmembrane proteins localized at the presynaptic membranes and form trans-synaptic links that promote the formation of both pre- and post- synaptic terminals. The crucial roles of neuroligin and neurexin in synapse formation were also demonstrated by the facts that mutations of both neuroligins and neurexins cause autism and other brain disorders in human. There are four neuroligin family members in mammals, neuroligin-1 to 4. Among them, neuroligin-1 is mainly localized at excitatory synapses, while neuroligin-2 is mainly localized at inhibitory synapses. Neuronal activity has long been known to regulate the formation and plasticity of synapses. The molecular machinery underlining activity-depended synapse dynamics also involve neuroligins. In fact, neuroligin-1 has been implicated in the activity-dependent formation of excitatory synapses, although the precise roles remain to be further elucidated. Whether neuroligin-2 is involved in activity-regulated inhibitory synapse formation is not known. Since the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synapse formation is crucial for neuronal network function, and the imbalance of excitatory/inhibitory synapses is believed to contribute to brain disorders such as autism, it is crucial to understand the role of neuroligin-2 in activity-regulated inhibitory synapse formation. Here, we propose to investigate the role and mechanism of neuronal activity in controlling neuroligin-2 synaptic targeting and inhibitory synapse formation. Our preliminary results indicate that neuronal activity could indeed regulate neuroligin-2’s synaptic localization and surface expression. This is achieved by controlling the ubiquitination of neuroligin-2 at a critical lysine residue. We also identified an enzyme that specifically regulate the ubiquitination level of neuroligin-2 and plan to further investigate the enzyme’s function at inhibitory synapse formation. This study will eventually provide novel insights into how neuronal activity regulates inhibitory synapse formation and underscores the significance of neuroligin-2 ubiquitination in synapse formation. 人腦是由億萬個神經元鏈接起來的複雜神經網絡。神經元通過一個叫突觸的結構連接在一起。我們有兩類主要的突觸：興奮性突觸和抑制性突觸。不正常的突觸形成可以導致腦疾病，包括自閉症，癲癇和精神分裂症等。突觸的形成是由很多蛋白質來緊密控制的。細胞粘附蛋白Neuroligins是其中一個很重要的調節突觸形成的蛋白質家族。Neuroligins是定位於突觸後膜上的跨膜蛋白，他們跟突觸前膜上的跨膜蛋白neurexins結合並形成跨突觸的連接來促進突觸前和突觸後末梢的形成。Neuroligins 和neurexins 在突觸形成中的重要作用也體現在他們的突變可以導致自閉症和其他腦疾病。Neuroligins 家族在哺乳動物中有四個成員：Neuroligins-1 到 4。在他們當中，neuroligin-1 主要定位於興奮性突觸，neuroligin-2主要定位於抑制性突觸。 神經活動可以調節突觸可塑性和突觸形成。神經活動調節突觸的分子機器也有neuroligins參與。其中neuroligin-1被認為參與神經活動調節興奮性突觸形成，但是具體功能還有待澄清。而neuroligin-2是否參與神經活動調節抑制性突觸形成尚不明確。因為興奮性和抑制性突觸的平衡對神經網絡的功能很重要，失去此平衡可能導致自閉症等腦疾病，所以了解neuroligin-2在神經活動調節抑制性性突觸形成中的作用顯得非常重要。我們在此提議研究neuroligin-2在神經活動調節抑制性突觸形成中的作用和機制。我們的初步研究結果顯示，神經活動可以影響neuroligin-2在突觸的定位和表面表達。這是通過調控neuroligin-2的泛素化來實現的。我們也找到了調控neuroligin-2泛素化的關鍵酶並準備進一步研究這個酶在抑制性突觸形成中的作用。我們希望這一研究能給我們了解神經活動如何調節抑制性突觸的形成提供新的見解並突顯neuroligin-2泛素化在突觸形成中的意義。

16103520.label: Realisation of objectives
16103520.value: Objective 1: Determine whether neuronal activity regulates synaptic targeting of NL2 To address this objective, we have evaluated the impact of neuronal activity on NL2 in cultured hippocampal neurons using the sodium channel blocker TTX. When the activities of cultured neurons were blocked by TTX, immunostaining of the cultured neurons with NL2 antibodies revealed a significant reduction in both total NL2 and gephyrin-positive NL2 cluster densities, while gephyrin levels remained unchanged. In addition, GABAAR γ2 levels also decreased. To further assess neuronal activity's effects, neurons were treated with glutamate receptor antagonists APV and CNQX to inhibit synaptic activity, or a GABAAR antagonist bicuculline to increase neuronal activity. APV and CNQX reduced gephyrin-positive NL2 density by about ~50%, whereas bicuculline treatment significantly increased NL2 levels at these synapses. These results suggest that reduced neuronal activity leads to a loss of synaptic NL2, while increased activity enhances it. To further investigate if neuronal activity affects NL2's cell surface level, we conducted a cell surface biotinylation assay to label surface NL2. TTX and glutamate antagonists decreased the NL2 surface-to-total ratio, while bicuculline increased it, indicating that neuronal activity regulates NL2 localization at inhibitory synapses. Objective 2: Investigate the role of ubiquitination on neuronal activity mediated loss of NL2 at synapses. We measured the ubiquitination levels of NL2 by immunoprecipitating NL2 and then using ubiquitin antibody to detect NL2 level. We found that the ubiquitin level of NL2 is low in basal condition of neuronal culture. Interestingly, when the neuronal culture was treated with TTX, the ubiquitin level of NL2 is significantly increased. This indicates that NL2 is indeed ubiquitinated and its ubiquitination is regulated by neuronal activity. Objective 3: Identify and confirm USP8 as a NL2 deubiquitinating enzyme. Using immunoprecipitation of NL2 coupled with mass spectrometry, we identified USP8, a deubiquitinase, as a binding partner of NL2. The interaction of NL2 with USP8 was further confirmed using specific antibody to USP8 and also co-expressing of the two proteins in HEK293T cells. To confirm that USP8 could deubiquitinate NL2, we co-transfected NL2 with USP8 or USP8 catalytic inactive mutant and then examined the ubiquitination level of NL2. We found that USP8 significantly reduced the ubiquitination level of NL2, while USP8 catalytic inactive mutant failed to do so. This confirm that USP8 is indeed the deubiquitinating enzyme for NL2. Objective 4: Investigate whether USP8 regulates NL2 synaptic targeting and surface expression. To address this objective, we overexpressed wildtype (WT) and catalytic inactive mutant (CS) USP8 in cultured neurons and then immunostained for synaptic targeting and surface expression of NL2. Our data indicate that USP8-WT increased the number of NL2 at inhibitory synapses labelled with inhibitory synapse marker Gephyrin. On the other hand, the catalytic inactive mutant USP8-CS had no effect on NL2 synaptic localization. Furthermore, when we used an shRNAi to knockdown USP8, we found the number of synaptic NL2 was reduced. In addition, when we treated the cultured neurons with a USP8 inhibitor, the synaptic NL2 was also reduced. These data provided a coherent picture that USP8 activity positively promote synaptic targeting of NL2. Similarly, we analysed the surface expression of NL2 using biotinylation assay and found that USP8 increase the surface expression of NL2, while shRNAi of USP8 and USP8 inhibitor reduced NL2 surface expression. Objective 5: Study the role of USP8 in neuronal activity-regulated NL2 targeting and synapse formation We treated neurons with a USP8 inhibitor together with TTX to block neuronal activities. Our data found that while both TTX and a USP8 inhibitor reduced the synaptic targeting of NL2 and inhibitory synapses density, neuron treated with both TTX and USP8 inhibitor could not further reduce NL2 synaptic targeting or inhibitory synapses density. This indicates that neuronal activity-regulated NL2 targeting and synapse formation is likely mediated by the activation of USP8. Please note that Prof. Jun Xia, the original PI of this project, has relocated to HKUST (Guangzhou). Consequently, Prof. Yusong Guo has taken over as the PI, with Prof. Jun Xia now serving as the co-PI.

16103520.label: Major findings and research outcome
16103520.value: Neuroligin2 (NL2) has been shown to play a pivotal role in the regulation of inhibitory synapse formation and activity in murine models, with genetic modifications in NL2 being associated with severe cognitive impairments. In the present study, we reveal that NL2 undergoes activity-dependent ubiquitination both in vitro and in neuronal cultures, which serves to regulate its stability on the cellular surface and its targeting to inhibitory synapses. Utilizing immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS), we identified ubiquitin-specific protease 8 (USP8) as a binding partner of NL2. We subsequently examined the roles of USP8 in counteracting NL2 ubiquitination in vitro and in vivo, as well as a subset of protein-protein interaction determinants crucial for this function. The knockdown of USP8 resulted in increased NL2 ubiquitination and reduced inhibitory synapse density. Moreover, in vivo knockdown of USP8 in the dentate gyrus led to a decrease in NL2 cluster density within the granule cell layer and enhanced long-term contextual fear conditioning. Consequently, our findings provide the first evidence that USP8-dependent signaling constitutes a mechanism for modulating synapse density and long-term fear memory via the regulation of NL2 ubiquitination. For more detailed findings, please refer to section 5.3 “Realisation of objectives”. With the support of this project, we have published two papers, and another manuscript is under submission. One PhD student graduated, and another PhD student was under training with the support of this grant.

16103520.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16103520.value: Neuroligins are key molecules in synapse formation and their mutations were found in human diseases such as epilepsy, autism and schizophrenia. To further extend our study, we could use animal models, such as genetic modified mice, to validate our findings and explore the possibility of using our findings to provide mechanistic insights to related brain disorders and in the long run, found better diagnostic and treatment for these brain disorders.

16103520.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16103520.value: Human brain has billions of neurons that connected with synapses. The generation and withdrawal of synapse is a dynamic process that can be modulated by neuronal activity. However, the mechanism underlines the ever-changing synaptic network is still elusive. Neuroligin2 (NL2), a major inhibitory synapse protein, is crucial for inhibitory synapse formation and functions. Deletions or mutations in NL2 are associated with several brain disorders such epilepsy, autism and schizophrenia. In this project, we found that TTX-induced neuronal activity blockage cause a novel ubiquitination of NL2, leading to a decrease in inhibitory synapse density. To characterize the mechanism of NL2 ubiquitination, we performed an immunoprecipitation coupled mass spectrometry (IP-MS) experiment and identified ubiquitin specific protease 8 (USP8) served as a deubiquitinase for NL2 and controlled NL2 ubiquitination. By deubiquitinating NL2, USP8 can also regulate inhibitory synapse density. More importantly, we found TTX-induced neuronal activity blockage down-regulated USP8 expression level. USP8 inhibitor treatment displayed similar effects as TTX in reducing NL2 cell surface level. These results indicate that neuronal activity regulates inhibitory synapse density and stability by controlling NL2 ubiquitination and surface expression via deubiquitinase USP8. Together, these findings will help us better understand the mechanisms of brain disorders.

16103620.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16103620.value: The Scribble complex (Scribble/Scrib, Discs-Large/Dlg, and Lethal giant larvae/Lgl) is a highly conserved cell polarity complex important for maintaining epithelial tissue architecture in both Drosophila and mammals. These genes were originally discovered in Drosophila as “neoplastic tumor suppressor genes” (nTSGs) because fly larvae homozygous mutant for these genes grow malignant and immortal tumors. Studies using the Drosophila nTSG mutant tumor model have successfully provided many insights into human epithelial tumorigenesis processes over the past two decades. We have previously demonstrated that the scrib mutant tumors undergo a growth-arrest phase during the early tumorigenesis stage. In our preliminary studies we have found that the bidirectional signaling between the fat body and the nTSG mutant tumors is essential for suppressing the nTSG mutant tumor growth. Here we proposed to mechanistically decipher the signals between the fat body and the nTSG mutant tumors that mediate the tumor suppression function of the fat body. This study will likely uncover a novel role of adipose tissues in shaping a tumor-suppressive environment at the tumor initiation stage. 細胞極性復合物是進化高度保守的維持表皮細胞層結構的複合物。在果蠅和哺乳動物模型中，細胞極性複合物的失活和腫瘤的發生發展密切相關。我們在細胞極性複合物失活的果蠅成蟲盤腫瘤模型中發現，腫瘤周圍的脂肪組織具有先天免疫功能，對早期腫瘤生長具有抑制作用。本項目將解析腫瘤和脂肪組織之間複雜的信號通路，希望對早期腫瘤的發現和治療做出貢獻。

16103620.label: Realisation of objectives
16103620.value: 1. Investigating whether dILP6 or dILP8 expression from the nTSG mutant imaginal discs leads to insulin signaling activation in the fat body. We have previously found that the expression levels of two insulin-like peptide genes, dilp6 and dilp8, are significantly upregulated in the scrib mutant tumors. Dilp6 has been reported to be expressed in the larval ventral nerve cord (VNC) glial cells, muscle cells, and fat body to activate Insulin-Akt signaling in neighboring tissues, functioning as a short-range signaling ligand. Dilp8 was identified in injured or tumorous imaginal discs as a factor that delays development, allowing for tissue repair, likely functioning as a long-range signaling molecule. To test whether the high expression of dilp6 or dilp8 from the nTSG mutant tumors led to insulin signaling activation in the fat body, we knocked down dilp6 or dilp8 in the dlg and scrib mutant tumors and examined Insulin pathway activity in the fat body. The pAKT/total AKT level significantly decreased in the fat body when dilp6 was knocked down in the tumor, but not when dilp8 was depleted in the tumor. Moreover, when we knocked down dilp6 and dilp8 in the dlg mutant tumor, only the depletion of Dilp6 led to more aggressive tumor growth. These experiments indicate that Dilp6 derived from the dlg and scrib mutant tumors is responsible for insulin signaling activation in the fat body, which then sends a growth-inhibition signal back to the tumor at a distance. 2. Investigating whether InR/PI3K/Akt signaling functions upstream of Eiger activation and secretion in the fat body to repress nTSG tumor growth. We have examined Eiger transcript levels in the fat body with different insulin signaling levels and observed no significant differences between the groups. We generated a dlg; cgGal4 Egr-GFP transgenic line to examine the upstream signals in the fat body that affect Eiger cleavage and activation. When we varied the insulin signaling level through the expression of InR[CA] or InR[DN] in the fat body, we found that the Egr full-length protein level in the fat body and the secreted short-form Egr level in the blood were comparable to the control group. Together, these experiments suggest that insulin signaling activation in the fat body does not affect Eiger activation and secretion. 3. Investigating mechanisms of Eiger activation from the fat body in the presence of nTSG mutant tumors. We used the dlg; cgGal4 Egr-GFP transgenic line to perform further genetic screening and identified that Egr activation is downstream of Toll signaling, mediated by a previously uncharacterized peptidase. Specifically, when we repress Toll signaling activation in the fat body through Toll RNAi or Dif RNAi, we found that the active short-form Egr in the blood is significantly depleted compared to the control group. To identify the intermediate link between Toll signaling activation and Egr cleavage, we further examined TACE and Kuz, two enzymes proposed as potential candidates that cleave and activate Egr. Surprisingly, depletion of TACE or Kuz through RNAi in the fat body does not affect Egr cleavage. Therefore, we performed a genetic screening of all metalloproteases annotated in the fly genome and identified a previously uncharacterized enzyme, Ance-4, responsible for Egr cleavage and activation. We are currently delineating the molecular mechanism of how Toll signaling activation regulates Ance-4 activity. 4. Investigating additional downstream responses of insulin signaling activation in the fat body that potentially function to repress nTSG mutant tumor growth. In the previous objectives, we found that insulin signaling activation in the fat body suppresses distant tumor growth, but not through the Toll-Egr axis. We then performed proteomics and lipidomics analyses and identified that prolonged insulin signaling activation strongly alters the lipid metabolic status in the fat body. More importantly, genetic perturbations of lipid metabolism in the fat body, such as Gpat RNAi or Atgl OE, strongly affect tumor growth at a distance. These experiments indicate that lipid metabolism is the key link downstream of insulin signaling activation in the fat body that generates signals to regulate distant tumor growth. These results encouraged us to spend the past five years performing a large-scale genetic screening to identify the key metabolic messengers that carry signals between the fat body and distant tumors. We are currently preparing the first manuscript delineating an insulin-TAG metabolism-lipoprotein-mediated Wnt5 lipidation/transfer pathway that serves as a growth-regulating signal from the fat body to distant tumors. 5. Explore a potential tumor suppression role of mammalian adipocytes. Over the past five years, many studies in mammals have shown that systemic metabolism has a profound impact on cancer risk and growth outcomes. We find that it is no longer a good strategy to use co-culture systems of adipocytes and cancer cell lines to validate findings from flies. To understand whether the crosstalk between adipose tissue and growing tumors is conserved in higher organisms, we decided to adopt a computational approach to find the association between metabolic gene variants and cancer risk using data from the UK Biobank cohort of 502,154 people. This analysis will hopefully allow us to construct mammalian models with better precision.

Objective 3: Investigating mechanisms of Eiger activation from the fat body in the presence of the nTSG mutant tumors. We have identified that Eiger activation is mediated through Toll signaling activation in the fat body. In response to Toll signaling activation, Egr is cleaved and secreted to the blood. Objective 4: Investigating additional downstream responses of insulin signaling activation in the fat body that potentially function to repress the nTSG mutant tumor growth. We have found that insulin activation in the fat body affects tumor growth at a distance through regulating lipid metabolism and lipid modification/transport of a Wnt factor. Objective 5: Explore a potential tumor suppression role of mammalian adipocytes. We have identified lipid metabolism gene variants correlated with cancer risk from UK biobank. These findings are currently being prepared as two separate manuscripts for submission. We have trained two PhD students through this project with one PhD student successfully defended and graduated in 2021 and another PhD student expecting to defend and graduate in 2026. Meanwhile, the methods and tools developed for this project have yielded 5 publications in total listed in Part C. The findings were presented in the 6th Asia Pacific Drosophila Research Conference in Cairns Australia and in the 6th Annual Developmental Biology Society Conference in mainland China listed in Part C.

16103620.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16103620.value: Studies from this funded project have provided solid evidences that adipocytes function to regulate tumor growth at a distance through complex signals. We therefore performed large genetic screening to map the molecular network linking adipocytes function and tumorigenesis processes. Through this genetic screening, we have identified specific metabolic processes and molecular machineries in adipocytes that mediate the inter-organ crosstalk between adipocytes and remote tumors. In the next few years, we plan to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of these candidates from our screening and identify actionable drug targets for metabolic intervention and cancer risk control.

16103620.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16103620.value: Systemic metabolism is associated with complex diseases in humans like cancer. Numerous epidemiological studies from various populations have shown that obesity is associated with increased risks and mortality from different types of cancer. However, the molecular links between systemic metabolism and tumorigenesis processes remain largely unexplored. In this funded project, we have found that insulin signaling level in adipocytes regulate remote tumor growth outcome through modulating lipid metabolism and lipid modification of secreted cytokines. This study opened new venue to identify novel drug targets for metabolic intervention and cancer risk control.

16103920.label: Realisation of objectives
16103920.value: 1. Objective I: To define the cellular basis underlying the loss of pu.1-deficient microglia in pu.1cKO/Δ839 zebrafish To address this issue, we generated a knock-in zebrafish reporter line Tg(pu.1KI-eGFP), in which the eGFP is inserted into the pu.1 locus without interfering with the normal function of pu.1. We have shown that the eGFP expression recapitulates the pattern of endogenous pu.1 in the Tg(pu.1KI-eGFP) reporter line, which presumably labels microglia from early embryonic stage to adulthood. We the outcrossed the Tg(pu.1KI-eGFP) reporter line with Tg(coro1a:CreER) fish, which will enable us to inactivate the pu.1 in adulthood and test its role in microglia maintenance. We found that in the pu.1cKO/Δ839 mutant fish where both wild-type (WT) and pu.1-deficient microglia are present, the number and proportion of pu.1-deficient microglia remains normal within the first month of pu.1 inactivation. However, the number and proportion of pu.1-deficient microglia reduces dramatically 3 months after pu.1 inactivation. We further documented that the reduction of pu.1-deficient microglia in the pu.1cKO/Δ839 mutants is largely attributed to the cell competition from WT microglia. These results suggest that, although pu.1 is dispensable for the immediate survival of microglia, it is essential for the turnover and long-term maintenance of microglia in adult zebrafish. 2. Objective II: To identify Pu.1 downstream target genes essential for the long-term maintenance of microglia. To uncover the key downstream targets that mediate the chronic loss of pu.1-deficient microglia under mosaic condition, we isolated pu.1-deficient microglia and WT microglia from the 4-OHT-treated Tg(coro1a:CreER);pu.1KI/Δ839 fish at 3 mpi and performed transcriptomic analysis. Among the differential expressed genes, the tumor suppressor gene p53 was one of the top targeted genes robustly upregulated in pu.1-deficient microglia. We thus speculated that the chronic elimination of pu.1-deficient microglia is likely attributed to the elevation of p53. To support this hypothesis, we repeated the conditionally inactivation Pu.1 assay in the p53-deficient mutant background and asked if loss of p53 could rescue the microglia phenotype. Indeed, results showed that the number of pu.1-deficient microglia in the 4-OHT-treated Tg(coro1a:CreER);pu.1KI/Δ839 fish was significantly restored compared with the control fish. These results demonstrate that the chronic elimination of pu.1-deficient microglia under mosaic condition is mediated, at least in part, by the elevation of p53. 3. Objective III: To explore the molecular mechanism governing pu.1 expression in adult microglia. To explore the upstream regulation of pu.1, we first focused on the Csf1r-Il34 pathway, which we have shown that it is important for the turnover and maintenance of microglia. We examined the expression of pu.1 in il34-deficient and il34 overexpression zebrafish, and we found that the loss-of-function and gain-of-function of Il34 has little impact on the transcriptional regulation of pu.1 in microglia. Likewise, the loss of csf1r function also has minimal impact on the expression of pu.1. Based on these observations, we conclude that the transcriptional regulation of pu.1 in microglia appears to be independent of the Csf1r-Il34 pathway. To uncover the upstream regulator of the pu.1 in microglia, we examined several pathways known to be important for microglia development. We recently found that gain-of-function analysis suggests that activation of the Notch signaling pathway leads to the alternation of pu.1 expression in microglia. is a possible candidate. We hence speculate that Notch could be a potential upstream regulator modulating pu.1 expression in microglia. Publications: 1. 16103920.label: Major findings and research outcome
16103920.value: Microglia, the crucial immune cells residing in the central nervous system (CNS), have a profound impact on the development of central nervous system (CNS) and maintenance of CNS homeostasis. The dysfunction of microglia formation and function is often associated with the occurrence and progression of many neurodegenerative disorders. Thus, microglia have recently become a promising therapeutic target in the prevention and treatment of these neuronal diseases. It is generally well-accepted that under physiological condition microglia in mice are maintained locally by self-renewal throughout the lifespan. However, how microglia turnover and replenishment in the CNS under physiological condition remain largely unknown. In thus proposal, we utilize zebrafish, a model organism with the advantages of imaging, embryological analysis, and genetic manipulation, to study the mechanism controlling the turnover and maintenance of microglia in the CNS. We have first revealed two mechanisms, the Csf1r-Il34 pathway and the Pu.1-p53 axis, essential for the turnover and maintenance of microglia in adult zebrafish CNS. One piece of these works has recently been published in Science Advances, and another one is currently under review. In addition, we have performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis to decipher the heterogeneity of the tissue-resident macrophages and dendritic cells in adult zebrafish. We have identified various subsets of the tissue-resident macrophages and dendritic cells across organs, including the CNS. This work has been published in Cell Reports.

16103920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16103920.value: Given the important role of microglia in the onset and progression of various neuronal disorders, it would be interesting to search for chemical compounds that can regulate the turnover and maintenance of microglia. Our findings have provided potential targets for compound screening, and zebrafish certainly can serve as good model system for such study.

16103920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16103920.value: Microglia, the tissue-resident macrophages in the central nervous system (CNS), play important roles in the regulation of neural development and the maintenance of CNS homeostasis. The important functions of microglia are further supported by the observations that the onset and progression of various neuronal disorders, such as Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, Multiple Sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer’s disease, are often associated with the dysregulation of microglial development and their function. Hence, understanding the molecular mechanism governing the development and function of microglia may provide new strategies for therapeutic treatment of these neuronal disorders. One unique feature of microglia is their long-term self-renewal ability in adulthood without the contribution from peripheral macrophages/monocytes. However, the underlying mechanism controlling the turnover and long-term maintenance of microglia remain large unknown. In our proposed study, we have revealed the molecular mechanisms governing the turnover and long-term maintenance of microglia in adult zebrafish brain. We believe that the mechanism that we have uncovered in zebrafish can likely apply to humans. Hence, our findings may provide new potential targets for therapeutic treatment of various neuronal disorders.
