16500820.value: “All, None, or Some? Platform Information Sharing when Sellers Incur Nonlinear Production Costs” We study information dissemination of an online platform through which multiple sellers distribute their partially substitutable products. The platform takes a commission from each seller's revenue. The platform has superior information about the demand and determines whether, and with how many sellers, to share the information. An important feature of our study is that the sellers incur nonlinear production costs. We investigate the effect of and incentives for platform information sharing using a unified model that incorporates three types of nonlinear cost structure: constant marginal cost (linear), increasing marginal cost (diseconomies of scale), and decreasing marginal cost (economies of scale). There are four major findings: 1. The sellers' cost structure alone determines the direction of the impact of information sharing on revenue and cost, while the scope of information dissemination affects only the magnitude of that impact. 2. The platform's optimal scope of information sharing depends on how similar the sellers' products are, their cost structure, and the platform's commission rate. 3. The platform's optimal information provision is to offer just one, undiluted version, rather than differentiated multiple versions. 4. The platform's optimal information provision is to control the scope of information sharing rather than the accuracy of demand signal. Furthermore, when information is shared with some, but not with all sellers at once, we propose a self-realizing mechanism through which the information is distributed among the sellers fairly and equitably. This work is now under review at Production and Operations Management, a top-4 journal in my field. “Commissions and Profits on e-Tailing Platforms” An online marketplace is a platform that facilitates transactions by enabling sellers to sell directly to end customers. The platform earns a commission for its facilitating role on each transaction, equal to a fixed percentage of the seller’s revenue. This paper studies the commissions and profits on a platform where competing sellers sell partially differentiated products. We are motivated by a pattern of commission rates observed on platforms such as Tmall, Amazon, and eBay: the commission rate percentage is higher if the profit margin is higher or the products are more similar. Our simple model well explains this observed pattern. This work is nearly ready for submission.

16500820.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16500820.value: We have focused on incentives for ex ante information sharing, i.e., the platform offers long-term information sharing program with the sellers and the information sharing decisions are made before the market signal is observed. It would be interesting to explore the case where the platform can ex post decides whether to share information after the demand signal is observed. When sellers have private information of their own, information sharing/exchange between the platform and sellers having nonlinear cost structure would also be a worthwhile undertaking. Another case of interest is when the platform also functions as a retailer: the e-tailer earns commission from third-party sellers as a marketplace and also competes directly with these sellers for retailing profits as a reseller. Then, the e-tailer has an incentive to impose a relatively higher commission rate to ensure its advantage over third-party sellers.

16500820.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16500820.value: The online marketplace with a commission model brings about many changes in the way firms interact with one another to serve the retail market. The incentives in many activities like cooperative advertising, information sharing, and capacity buildup, which have been well studied for traditional supply chains, are very different in the context of the online marketplace and are worthy of reexamination to better our understanding of how firms interact with one another in the new economy. We have investigate two important issues. First, how the cost structure of sellers impacts the platform’s incentive to share information; and second, how the product differentiation among sellers and the nature of competition among them influence the platform’s commission rate.

16501020.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16501020.value: In this paper, we study how much construction has taken place on sea level rise (SLR) prone plains in the US in recent decades, in which locations, and why. Coastal areas offer many advantages and attract concentrations of economic activity, but some parts of the coast are particularly prone to flooding and other risks associated with SLR. As Kydland and Prescott (1977) discuss in their Nobel Prize winning contribution, this flood risk is partly borne by taxpayers. In recent years, the Federal government has paid tens of billions of dollars of subsidies, in the form of investment in flood defenses, subsidized insurance, and recovery assistance in the aftermath of floods. These costs are likely to increase further over time as the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts continue to experience fast rates of local sea level rise in the world since the 20th century. To make matters worse, the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) suffers from a number of deficiencies such as the underestimation of flood risks, which results in the accumulation of large debts. Another fundamental cause for construction in SLR risky areas is the path dependence of urban developments: coastal cities usually have their CBD located quite close to the coast, severely constraining urban expansion nearer the coast. In a monocentric city, land value decreases in distance from the CBD. A city with CBD close to the coast makes land exposed to higher SLR risks also more attractive to developers, which exacerbates the moral hazard and information problems described above. To study these issues, we use high-resolution data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). These include data on land cover change from 1996-2010, based on satellite imagery, combined with official maps of current flood risk and detailed maps showing areas expected to be inundated for various levels of future sea level rise. These allow us to study the rates of development in particularly risky parts of the US coast across time and space, and to investigate some of their causes. We then propose a conceptual framework that incorporates SLR risks into a monocentric urban model, which helps match key empirical patterns of coastal city development and simulate the effects of different policy interventions on the distribution of building activities near the coast and its welfare implications. 随着气候变化带来的海平面上升，沿海城市面临更大的洪涝风险。一个突出的矛盾是沿海城市的经济活动大多聚集在离海岸线很近的区域，一旦面临洪水的威胁将带来巨大的经济损失。我们的研究探讨了一下几个问题：（1）有多少经济活动聚集在受洪水威胁的地方？这个趋势在近几十年来是增强了还是减弱了；（2）经济活动聚集在受洪水威胁地方的原因以及政策建议

16501020.label: Realisation of objectives
16501020.value: Objective 1: Construct a comprehensive dataset on land cover, sea level rise risks, housing units and flood subsidies for the United States The project successfully constructed a comprehensive dataset that includes land cover, sea level rise (SLR) risks, housing units, and flood subsidies for the United States. This dataset was compiled from multiple sources, including satellite imagery and government databases. Objective 2: Document patterns of (1) Construction activities from 1960 to 2010 around coastal regions in the US; (2) Changes in housing prices in response to sea level rise (SLR) risks; (3) Responses in building activities to flood insurance, relief spending, and subsidies We have documented the patterns listed above following data construction. We find that from 1990 to 2010, new construction in coastal areas of the U.S. occurred equally in both sea level rise (SLR)-prone and safer locations, contrasting with historical trends where construction avoided high-risk areas. This pattern is specifically pronounced in dense areas, suggesting the important role of agglomeration economics. We also performed a preliminary analysis of the price and building activity responses to flood insurance; however, we decided not to include this in the final paper for two reasons: (1) it overlaps with existing literature and (2) it seems tangential to our main message and the model. Objective 3: Develop a conceptual framework that incorporates SLR risks into a monocentric urban model We have developed a monocentric city model that illustrates urban development centered around a Central Business District (CBD), highlighting the trade-off between coastal amenities and flood risks. As cities expand, new construction often occurs in sea level rise (SLR)-prone areas due to limited land and the appeal of urban agglomeration benefits. The model captures how rising sea levels may reshape urban boundaries, prompting dynamic adjustments in housing density and location choices. This framework underscores the need for informed policy interventions, such as stricter zoning and building regulations, to address the economic and environmental challenges posed by SLR in coastal cities.

16501020.label: Major findings and research outcome
16501020.value: We document the following findings regarding urban development in low-elevation coastal zones (LECZ) amid rising sea levels due to climate change. Analyzing spatially disaggregated data from the US Atlantic and Gulf coasts, we find that while the housing stock in 1990 largely avoided flood-prone areas, net new construction from 1990 to 2010 did not follow this trend; specifically, the share of housing units in sea level rise (SLR)-prone blocks increased from 12% to 14%, with 26% of new housing built in these risky locations. There is a critical distinction based on density: in sparsely built areas, new construction continued to avoid high-risk zones, whereas in densely populated regions, construction was positively correlated with SLR risk, suggesting that economic benefits from urban agglomerations outweigh the perceived risks. Additionally, we identify an asymmetry in coastal development, with central business districts (CBDs) located closer to the coast, a pattern more pronounced in larger urban areas. To explain these dynamics, we develop a monocentric city model that incorporates both the amenity value of coastal proximity and the disamenity of flooding risks, serving as a qualitative tool for evaluating future coastal development. The findings emphasize the need for informed urban planning and policy interventions to address the challenges posed by SLR, suggesting that government subsidies and land-use regulations may exacerbate risks rather than mitigate them.

16501020.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16501020.value: 1. We will broaden the research to include diverse international contexts vulnerable to sea level rise (SLR), such as Southeast Asia, the Caribbean, and Europe. By comparing urban development patterns across these regions, we aim to understand how socio-economic and environmental factors shape responses to SLR, informing localized policy interventions. 2. We are also considering to develop a structural econometric model to quantify the relationships between urban development decisions and SLR risks. By analyzing welfare implications of various policy scenarios—like zoning regulations and flood defenses—this research will identify strategies that balance economic growth with environmental sustainability, enhancing community resilience.

16501020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16501020.value: This research project explores how cities are developing in areas at risk of rising sea levels due to climate change. By looking at housing trends along the U.S. Atlantic and Gulf coasts, the study reveals that while older homes tended to avoid flood-prone areas, new constructions are increasingly being built in these risky zones. This is concerning because it puts more people and properties in danger as sea levels rise. The significance of this research lies in its potential to inform city planners and policymakers about the risks associated with coastal development. By understanding where and why new homes are being built, communities can make better decisions to protect themselves from flooding. The value of this project extends beyond the U.S.; it can guide similar studies in other countries facing the same challenges. Ultimately, the research aims to promote safer urban development, ensuring that cities can thrive while also being prepared for the impacts of climate change. This work is crucial for safeguarding lives, properties, and the environment for future generations.

16501220.label: Project Objectives
16501220.value: Objective 1. To theorize and test challenge construal (per control theory) and threat construal (per threat-rigidity theory) as two opposing mechanisms that explain the effect of a leader’s negative feedback on employee creativity. Objective 2. To theorize and test two sets of boundary conditions under which threat construal or challenge construal is more likely to hold. Objective 3. To provide a coherent and integrative theoretical account to reconcile the opposing predictions from control theory and threat-rigidity theory and to explain the mixed findings regarding the effect of a leader’s negative feedback.
rows: Objective 1. To theorize and test challenge construal (per control theory) and threat construal (per threat-rigidity theory) as two opposing mechanisms that explain the effect of a leader’s negative feedback on employee creativity.
Objective 2. To theorize and test two sets of boundary conditions under which threat construal or challenge construal is more likely to hold.

Objective 3. To provide a coherent and integrative theoretical account to reconcile the opposing predictions from control theory and threat-rigidity theory and to explain the mixed findings regarding the effect of a leader’s negative feedback.

16501220.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16501220.value: Negative feedback is widely practiced by corporate managers seeking to improve employees’ work performance. According to control theory (Carver & Scheier, 1982, 2012), an employee may construe a leader’s negative feedback as a challenge and be motivated to meet the challenge by identifying work-related problems and generating solutions and therefore achieving improvement. However, empirical findings are decidedly mixed: some found a negative effect of a leader’s negative feedback on employee creativity (Ilies & Judge, 2005; Zhou, 1998), while others found no significant effect (Gorge & Zhou, 2001; Hon, Chan, & Lu, 2013). These mixed findings suggest an intriguing possibility: that other theoretical mechanisms counteract or even reverse the positive effect via challenge construal. Building on threat-rigidity theory (Staw, Sandelands, & Dutton, 1981), we propose to consider threat construal as such a countervailing mechanism. A leader’s negative feedback can make an employee feel threatened, and such threat construal might engender anxiety and cognitive rigidity, thereby reducing creativity. To reconcile the two conflicting perspectives, we will seek to unpack in what situations the challenge or the threat construal mechanism is more likely to hold. Specifically, we propose to examine two sets of boundary conditions: (a) entity belief (i.e., the belief that one’s attributes are malleable) versus incremental belief (i.e., the belief that one’s attributes are fixed); and (b) narcissism (excessive interest in or admiration of oneself) and humility (which implies accepting negative feedback). Specifically, we will test the proposition that a leader’s negative feedback engenders threat construal, and therefore inhibits employee creativity when the employee is high in entity belief or narcissism. In contrast, such feedback engenders challenge construal, and therefore enhances creativity, when an employee is high in incremental belief or humility. We test these ideas using multi-source (i.e., leaders and members) and time-lagged data from 100 research and development teams in high-technology firms in China. The goal will be to contribute significantly to theory and research on leader’s negative feedback and employee creativity. The study will generate an integrated theoretical account which accommodates and reconciles control theory and threat-rigidity predictions. The practical implications should be significant as well. A leader’s negative feedback is neither invariably beneficial nor detrimental. Managers need to consider each employee’s individual characteristics in order to reap the most benefit from the negative feedback they give.

16501220.label: Realisation of objectives
16501220.value: We conducted the following research activities to achieve the project objectives: We obtained the agreement of a brand company to participate. The company operates 80 stores in Eastern and Southern China, primarily selling clothing, leather products, bags, and suitcases. We conducted focus group interviews with store managers and employees to develop specific dimensions of creativity for store employees. This work resulted in the identification of 7 items for measuring creativity. In our hypothesis testing study, we combined these items with the 3-item generic scale of creativity from Oldham and Cummings (1996) to measure creativity. To test the hypothesized relationships from the grant project, we then collected data at three different time points. In this company, store leaders evaluated and provided feedback to every employee on a quarterly basis (at the end of March, June, September, and December). During the second quarter, we collected data on employees' reactions (such as threat and challenge appraisal) to leaders' feedback provided at the end of the first quarter. Specifically, we collected data on leader's negative feedback and employee threat and challenge appraisals in early April. Then we collected data on employee approach and avoidance orientation, as well as threat and challenge appraisals in May. Finally, we collected data on employee threat and challenge appraisals along with store manager-rated employee creativity in June. We distributed surveys to all 204 store employees and obtained a final sample of 122 employees with supervisor-rated creativity. We collected an additional sample to validate the creativity scale developed through the focus group interview. The collected sample from the main study was used to conduct exploratory factor analysis, while the additional sample was used for confirmatory factor analysis. Using the main study data, we then tested the longitudinal measurement invariance of threat appraisal and challenge appraisal to ensure comparability across the different time points. Subsequently, we analyzed the data and tested the hypotheses using latent growth modelling. Most of the hypotheses proposed in the initial proposal were supported. Based on the results, we drafted a manuscript and submitted it to the 2022 Academy of Management Conference. We presented the paper at the conference in August 2022. Following the feedback received from conference participants, we revised the paper and finalized it. The next journal that we target would be the Journal of Applied Psychology. Overall, we have data and a paper and achieved the project objectives. The journal publication process is long and difficult. We will try hard to get the paper published in a respected if not a top journal.

16501220.label: Major findings and research outcome
16501220.value: We discovered that leader negative feedback not only triggered initial levels of threat and challenge appraisals but also influenced the magnitude of their growth over time. Threat appraisal exhibited a negative relationship with employee creativity, while challenge appraisal showed a positive relationship. After accounting for creativity stability, the growth in appraisal magnitudes independently impacted employee creativity, going beyond the initial levels of appraisals. Additionally, we observed that the negative indirect relationship between leader negative feedback and employee creativity, mediated by the initial level and growth of threat appraisal, was amplified by the focal employee's avoidance orientation. Likewise, the positive indirect relationship between leader negative feedback and employee creativity, mediated by the initial level and growth of challenge appraisal, was amplified by the focal employee's approach orientation. These findings were presented at the Academy of Management Conference in August 2022. This conference is competitive and peer reviewed.

16501220.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16501220.value: One potential avenue for further development is to conduct a lab experiment aimed at strengthening causal inference. In this experiment, participants can be randomly assigned to one of three conditions and given a task to perform: negative feedback, neutral feedback, or no feedback from a hypothetical leader. We would then assess their threat and challenge appraisals. Independent experts would evaluate their creativity in performing the task. This research design would enable us to examine the impact of leader negative feedback on creativity, mediated by threat or challenge appraisal. However, it would not allow us to examine the trajectory (e.g., the changes in threat or challenge appraisals and their impacts on creativity) because lab experiments have limited durations, typically lasting only a few hours at most.

16501220.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16501220.value: Providing negative feedback as a leader can simultaneously challenge and threaten the recipient, thereby both aiding and hindering recipient creativity. Organizations have the opportunity to tilt the impact towards a positive direction by directing such feedback towards individuals with an approach orientation. The significance and value of this finding lie in recognizing that giving negative feedback is a two-sided coin, and managers can leverage it more effectively for employees with an approach orientation.

16501320.label: Project Title(Chinese)
16501320.value: 網絡實驗網絡復原和團隊績效

16501320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16501320.value: Numerous studies have examined how variations in the structural properties and dynamics of global network structures as well as actors’ positions in those networks impact both individual and collective outcomes. In a temporally parallel set of inquiries under the rubric of network robustness, scholars of complex social systems have explored how the removal of actors or edges in the network affects the structural properties of networks. Building on both lines of inquiry, we aim to enrich studies of dynamic social systems with a systematic exploration of network experimentation and recovery. We investigate how organizations may maintain their level of performance following the unexpected departure of actors by adapting the network of interactions among their members. Specifically, we identify specific network configurations and dynamics that can help teams retain optimal levels of performance overall, while being prepared to manage the removal of actors. We propose professional ice hockey as the ideal empirical setting to test our theory and hypotheses. Due to the physical nature of the sport, injuries are inevitable and are a perennial challenge for managers. However, no one can predict when these injuries will occur or who exactly will be injured. As a result, teams need to prepare for scenarios where their players become unexpectedly unavailable, while not sacrificing team performance. Developments in network science provide us with tools to capture the structural and mathematical properties of complex, dynamic networks. Using these cutting-edge tools, we examine how changes in the network of on-the-ice interactions may help maintain or exceed the pre-injury levels of team performance following an injury. In particular, we conduct quasi-experiments of looking at different scenarios reflecting the coordination of individual skills and team dynamics and their resulting performance implications. We seek to make the following contributions. First, we contribute to studies of network dynamics by systematically exploring the dynamic pathways through which organizations reconstruct networks of interactions in response to sudden departures of organizational members. Second, we add to the research on the impact of employee departure on organizational performance. We contend that the consequences of employee turnover can be addressed more comprehensively by studying the interplay among the formal organizational structure, human capital, and networks of task-related interactions. Finally, this work can offer practical managerial implications by producing generalizable insights for teams regarding resilient design: the one that optimizes a team’s overall performance while equipping it to respond effectively to team member departures. 許多研究已探討全球網絡結構的結構特性、動態，以及行動者在結構中的位置變動如何影響個人與集體結果。在網絡強健性的評量指標下進行的調查中，學者曾探索在網絡中去除行動者或行動者之間的關係對結構特性的影響。建基於這方面的研究，我們旨在深入探索網絡實驗與網絡復原，為求增進動態社會系統的研究。我們通過調整成員之間的交互網絡來探討組織經歷行動者突然離職後應如何保持績效水平。具體來說，我們鑒定了可以幫助團隊保持最佳整體績效水平的網絡組態和動態，同時為團隊準備管理行動者的撤離。

16501420.label: Project Title(Chinese)
16501420.value: 不真實的自我：研究不真實消費行為的前因與後果

16501420.label: Project Objectives
16501420.value: This research introduces the idea that self-inauthenticity can have consequences for product disposal decisions (e.g., decisions to discard, donate, resell or swap one's possessions). It also offers a theoretical model for predicting the types of possessions consumers will dispose of (i.e., self-relevant possessions). This research is the first to consider the use of online avatars (e.g., in videogames and chat-rooms) as an antecedent to self-inauthenticity. It also offers a theoretical rationale for when this is more likely to occur (i.e., when avatars are highly discrepant from the self) and identifies the types of consumers who might be more likely to experience inauthenticity when using online avatars (e.g., consumers who are high in self-consciousness). This research introduces the theory that self-inauthenticity reduces consumers' sense of connection to aspects of the external world that have been incorporated into the self-concept, which can include objects, events, places and other people. It tests this model by examining its implications for consumers' feelings of connection to, and willingness to dispose of, self-relevant possessions. It also proposes how this effect can generalize to other external aspects of the self (e.g. self-relevant places).

16501420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16501420.value: 不真實的自我：研究不真實消費行為的前因與後果 研究摘要 “很明顯，當一個人說 我 和我的 的時候，這兩者之間的界限是很難劃清的。對某些我們擁有的東西，我們的感覺和行為往往跟我們對自己的感覺和行為是一致的” –William James (1890, p. 291) 真實性是指實在的，非僞造的或真實的。它可用來描述體驗，物件，或人物(Newman and Smith 2016)。市場學之前的研究大多著集中在消費體驗的真實性上（例如，一道墨西哥菜是否正宗）。本計劃則著重消費者的真實性或真實自我。引用Sheldon et al. (1997) “人們在能夠充分自由地選擇和表達自我的情況下會感到最真實。相反，如一個人的思想或行為出賣了自我時，他們會感到不真實。其中的特徵是，人們與真實的自我脫節(Hepner et al. 2008)或感到真實的自我很遙遠(Lenton et al. 2013a) 。我們的研究計劃通過整合人格心理學，社會心理學和消費者心理學的文獻，探索自我不真實性與消費行為之間的相互作用。我們將此項研究分為兩個主要目標，以了解由於不真實的自我而導致的消費者行為以及不真實的自我先決條件。 我們的首要目標是研究在決定棄置自己的物品的時候（包括丟棄，捐贈，轉售或替換財產的決策)，不真實的自我對這些決定的影響。我們將研究這些影響的邊界條件（例如，產品類別的自我相關性），該影響的潛在心理機制（例如，自我與產品之間的聯繫）以及該影響的下游後果（例如，對後續購買的影響力）。我們的研究項目會以實驗室為基礎，並設計相關的行為測試（例如，參與在線服裝交換平台）。 我們的第二個目標是研究什麼前提因素導致消費者充當不真實性的自我。我們將研究消費者使用化身的行為（例如在電子遊戲中的角色扮演）如何觸發自我不真實性。這項研究將研究化身如何影響角色扮演者（例如，扮演者的自我意識），這些影響的下游後果（例如，如何影響自我和自己擁有的物品之間的連接），以及這些後果的概括性（例如，是否會影響到自我與某些地點，事件，和重要人物之間的連接）。

16501420.label: Realisation of objectives
16501420.value: Broadly speaking, pursuing objectives 1-3 involved both theory development and theory testing. We conducted multiple empirical studies that involved both experimental data and correlational data, and were collected using both online participant panels and laboratory participants. To overview, our research pertains to the relationship between self-inauthenticity and consumer behavior. Objective (1) examined the consequences of self-inauthenticity for product disposal decisions. Objective (3) examined why self-inauthenticity has consequences for product disposal decisions. And Objective (2) examined the antecedents of self-inauthenticity. Below, we describe in detail how each of the three project objectives was pursued and achieved. Objectives (1) and (3): Consequences of self-inauthenticity and why they occur Objective (1) and objective (3) were pursued in tandem. Across multiple studies, consistent with our predictions, we found that self-inauthenticity can have consequences for product disposal decisions (i.e., exacerbating consumers’ decisions to discard, donate, resell or swap their possessions), and that such consequences emerge because, also consistent with our predictions, self-inauthenticity reduces consumers' sense of connection to their possessions. In addition to predicting a main effect of self-inauthenticity on product disposal, objectives (1) and (3) also layered in a moderating factor: self-relevance, or the strength of connection between a consumer’s self-concept and an aspect of the external world, such as a possession. We predicted, and found, that the effect of self-inauthenticity on product disposal decisions can depend on the self-relevance of the possession. However, when the manuscript was in the review process, reviewers felt that the moderator was unnecessary and requested that we focus the manuscript on the main effect and mediator – i.e., the effect of self-inauthenticity on disposal and why it occurs – and drop the studies pertaining to the moderator – i.e., evidence that the effect is enhanced when self-relevance is enhanced. Meanwhile, we were also invited to contribute a chapter to a book that described our research on self-authenticity and possession disposal. The invitation came from the book editors, two highly respected colleagues who specializes in self-possession connections, Ayalla Ruvio (‪Ayalla Ruvio‬ - ‪Google Scholar‬‬‬‬‬) and Russell Belk (‪Russell Belk‬ - ‪Google Scholar‬). Writing this chapter afforded us the opportunity to detail our full theoretical model, which is based in the premise that self-inauthenticity reduces consumers' sense of connection to aspects of the external world that have been incorporated into the self-concept, and its implications both for predicting the types of possessions consumers will dispose of (i.e., self-relevant possessions) and for predicting the generalizability of the effect to other external aspects of the self (e.g. self-relevant places).‬‬‬‬ In sum, the output of objectives (1) and (3) entails one empirically based, peer-reviewed journal publication (published in 2024), and one theory-based, invited book chapter (forthcoming 2025). Objective (2): Antecedents to self-inauthenticity Regarding objective (2) of this research, we sought to examine real-world antecedents to self-inauthenticity. As described in our original grant proposal, we had data in hand that showed a correlation between online avatars and self-inauthenticity that was directionally consistent with our theory, i.e., it showed that higher levels of videogame playing correlate with lower levels of chronic self-inauthenticity. Based on this correlational data, we proposed objective (2) and designed a series of experiments to test objective 2’s prediction that using video game avatars heightens self-inauthenticity. Importantly, self-authenticity is measured by asking people to report the extent to which they feel “in touch with their true self”. Unfortunately, by 2020 we were observing in our other research projects effects of Covid-19 on measures of self-authenticity. Essentially, the Covid-19 pandemic meant that people could not live their lives in an authentic way, and this was influencing participants’ responses to this measure. Nevertheless, in 2021 we conducted studies examining the role of online avatars on self-authenticity. We decided to ask participants to report the extent to which Covid-19 was influencing their lives, and planned to use this measure as a covariate in our analyses. It immediately became clear that the influence of Covid-19 on self-authenticity far outsized the effect of online avatar use. Rather than finding effects of online avatar use, we found a highly reliable and significant effect of Covid-19-related disruptions on self-authenticity, such that people felt more inauthentically themselves the more they felt Covid was disrupting their lives. We hoped that Covid-19 would pass but instead it remained an issue throughout 2021 and 2022 (for those of us in Hong Kong). Consequently, the results across studies were highly unreliable despite numerous attempts to correct for the impact of Covid-19 on our findings. We therefore were unable to fully complete objective (2) due to the Covid-19 pandemic’s influence on our research, as reported in the midterm progress report. (Objectives (1) and (3) were less influenced by Covid-19 because self-authenticity was manipulated, rather than measured, in those studies.) Fortunately, we were still able to study the antecedents of self-inauthenticity and publish a paper on this topic. Rather than examining the use of online avatars as a specific antecedent to self-inauthenticity, we instead pursued Covid-19-related disruptions as a more general antecedent to self-inauthenticity. Additionally, the manuscript not only establishes the relationship between Covid-19 and self-inauthenticity, it also compares several different types of coping mechanisms that people were using during the pandemic and comparing the effectiveness of these different coping mechanisms for preserving self-authenticity. We felt that this manuscript needed to be published quickly given the potential importance of the work during the pandemic and the potentially time-sensitive nature of publishing research related to COVID-19, so we prioritized the collection of those data and were able to publish in a peer-reviewed journal by September 2021. Lastly, we would like to address the specific written comments received on our mid-term progress report, as there seems to have been a critical misunderstanding: “The Panel... maintains the position that outputs reported from RGCfunded proposals should be directly related to work conducted during the reporting period and that is directly aligned with the approved and funded proposal. This is noted as the currently reported output does not appear to be consistent with this directive (e.g., Study 4 noted in the output was clearly conducted in 2019, well before the start date of the funded proposal [1-1-2021]).” Respectfully, study 4 was not conducted in 2019. Participants were recruited based on questionnaires they completed in 2019. We could not have foreseen Covid-19 and were fortunate to have pre-Covid data to draw on. We made a good faith effort to understand Covid-19’s impact on our ability to pursue our research objectives before our funding period began because we were working on interrelated projects. Correlational data collected in 2020 became highly informative and strengthened our manuscript considerably, so that bit of correlational data were included in the manuscript in 2021. In no way were we trying to violate RGC requirements, we simply wanted to publish the best manuscript we could. We apologize for the misunderstanding created by this decision and do hope the panel can sympathize with our position and recognize that we were simply trying to do our best in light of the Covid-19 pandemic.

16501420.label: Major findings and research outcome
16501420.value: Objectives (1) and (3): Consequences of self-inauthenticity and why they occur In this research, we propose that self-inauthenticity causes consumers to also feel out-of-touch with objects that are extensions of the self—namely, their material possessions. We find that chronic self-inauthenticity leads consumers to dispose of everyday products (e.g., apparel and electronics) at higher frequencies. Additionally, situational triggers of self-inauthenticity (e.g., using counterfeits or out-group-related brands) cause possession alienation and disposal. Self-inauthenticity thereby increases consumer intention to declutter at home, increases consumer preference to replace, rather than repair, broken electronics, and increases consumer participation in C2C product exchanges. Effects of self-inauthenticity on disposal can, however, be mitigated. Marketing interventions (e.g., advertisements) that reinforce consumers’ psychological connection to material possessions, compared to interventions that promote product functionality, encourage inauthentic consumers to retain possessions. Objective (2): Antecedents to self-inauthenticity In this research, we examine self-authenticity, the sense one is their “true self.” We find that COVID-19-related role disruptions lead to self-inauthenticity, such that people feel alienated from their true selves. This effect manifests when people are reminded of changes in their social roles and inauthenticity is measured as a state variable (studies 1-2). It also manifests as a chronic change in inauthenticity over time, absent reminder cues about role change (study 3). Moreover, this effect occurs when (and therefore because) the social roles undergoing change are central to individuals’ sense of self. Importantly, self-authenticity is safeguarded when the discontinuity in people’s lives is less salient. This is achieved by people attending to the here-and-now, rather than the past (pre-COVID-19) or future (post-COVID-19). Lastly, effects on inauthenticity occur independent of the valence of role change. That is, whether individuals perceive role changes positively or negatively, they nevertheless feel inauthentic. Three studies conducted with American and Asian participants demonstrate these effects.

16501420.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16501420.value: Given the difficulties we experienced studying our key construct, self-authenticity and its corollary, self-inauthenticity, during and immediately after the Covid-19 pandemic, we were unable to actively pursue this particular research project. We do, however, remain interested in conducting research at the intersection of authenticity and consumer behavior, and thus may pursue related topics in the future.

16501420.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16501420.value: The present research explores self-authenticity—or, more precisely, self-inauthenticity. While consumers often make disposal decisions by considering a possession’s functional value—“Is this clothing ill-fitting? Is this electronic device obsolete?”—consumers also may ask, “Is this possession still me?” when deciding whether to dispose of it. Consumers base the disposal decision on the strength of their psychological connection to a possession and might discard a perfectly functional product if they feel out-of-touch with it. Consumers’ psychological connection to a possession could wane for various reasons, such as evolving consumer tastes or market trends. Here, we show that self-inauthenticity offers one explanation for why consumers can feel out-of-touch with possessions and, in turn, dispose of them. In addition to examining self-inauthenticity’s consequences, we examine its antecedents. The COVID-19 pandemic posed a global threat. Our collective response to combat the virus entailed parents homeschooling children, friends socializing online, and employees working from home. While these collective efforts served the greater good, they took a toll at the individual level, particularly among people who coped in suboptimal ways. The present research identifies self-inauthenticity as one effect of social role disruption under COVID-19 and demonstrates how best to cope with it.

16501820.value: 自二十世紀末以來，嚴重的環境問題開始出現，其中包括全球暖化、城市空氣污染、食水短缺和生物多樣性的喪失 (Dresner 2008)，可持續發展的概念已成為環境討論的中心話題。根據世界環境與發展委員會 (1987) 的說法，可持續發展是指在不損害後代滿足其自身需求的能力的前提下，滿足當前需求的發展。截至2015年，世界各國政府每年在可持續發展相關的行業 (如農業、基礎設施、自然保育) 上花費約21萬億美元 (Kharas and McArthur 2019)。香港環境局 (2013) 還制定了一個藍圖，並分享了一個願景，就是通過在香港灌輸一個環境可持續發展的文化，來減少地球資源的使用和浪費。 隨著對促進可持續發展行為的日益重視，與可持續發展相關的促進因素在我們的環境中變得越來越普遍，例如香港政府計劃將回收箱的數量增加45% (Kao 2017)。公司和品牌也把市場營銷活動塑造成強調可持續發展：Frito-Lay最受歡迎的零食Sun Chips的最新廣告強調其100%可堆肥包裝；同樣地，可口可樂公司推出了「植物性塑料瓶」活動，宣傳其可完全回收的塑料瓶，部分由植物製成；國泰航空在航機上推廣「飛向更藍天」計劃，該計劃讓乘客通過捐贈碳減排項目來抵銷因飛行旅程而產生的碳排放。 過去的市場營銷研究都集中在促進可持續發展的消費者行為上，與可持續發展相關的促進因素和提示如何影響消費者行為這問題則尚未得到廣泛探討。在這項研究中，我們建議通過研究與可持續發展相關的提示如何影響各種消費者行為，來填補這一空白處。具體來說，我們將探討 (1) 與可持續發展相關的提示如何在一個等待的體驗中，影響消費者對時間的感知和耐性；(2) 這些提示如何影響消費者在時間和金錢之間的分配；以及 (3) 這些提示如何影響消費者在涉及一個短期而較小的收益和一個長期但較大的收益之間的取捨 (跨期選擇)。我們提出，與可持續發展相關的提示會把消費者的時間範圍延伸，使他們在等待體驗時更加有耐性；這些提示會提高消費者對時間可用性的感知，並讓他們偏愛需要更多時間的選擇；在跨期選擇時，這些提示會促使消費者偏愛那些提供長期收益的選擇。

16501820.label: Realisation of objectives
16501820.value: Across both working papers, the project has realized the originally proposed objectives. The findings lay a strong foundation for continued work in the area of sustainability cues and consumer psychology. Objective 1: This objective has been fully achieved. The working paper Going Green, Staying Calm systematically investigates how both recycling behaviors and exposure to recycling-related cues (e.g., signage, bins) affect consumers’ willingness to wait. Across nine studies—including laboratory experiments, a field study, and an archival data analysis—the research demonstrates that recycling activates the concept of an extended product lifespan, which increases perceived time availability. This shift in perception enhances consumers’ patience, willingness to wait, and likely satisfaction in various consumption contexts. Furthermore, the studies explore boundary conditions (e.g., when recycling is framed as decomposition or when consumers are dissatisfied with the product), contributing to a more nuanced understanding of the emotional and attitudinal aspects of the waiting experience. Collectively, these findings offer new theoretical insights and practical implications for managing consumer expectations and satisfaction. Objective 2: This objective has been fully achieved at the conceptual level. The research in Going Green, Staying Calm demonstrates that sustainability cues (both through being exposed to recycling-related information and through engaging in recycling behaviors) increase consumers’ perceived abundance of time availability, which in turn leads to greater willingness to wait in various consumption settings. This reflects a meaningful shift in how consumers allocate their time under the influence of sustainability cues. Although the original proposal mentioned time-versus-money tradeoffs explicitly, our conceptual focus was on how sustainability cues shape consumers’ resource allocation decisions. As the research progressed, we prioritized willingness to wait—an ecologically valid and psychologically meaningful measure of time allocation—over direct monetary tradeoffs. This approach avoided confounds related to individual financial variability and allowed for cleaner interpretation of sustainability’s impact on behavioral outcomes. In doing so, the project met the theoretical aims of this objective while offering greater practical and empirical clarity. Objective 3: This objective has been fully achieved. The working paper The Effect of Recycling on Sensation Seeking shows that engaging in recycling behavior enhances consumers’ sense of vitality, which in turn increases their tendency to seek novel and intense sensory experiences. These findings are directly relevant to intertemporal choice: sensation seeking and vitality are well-documented predictors of preferences for immediate versus delayed rewards. By identifying vitality as a mediator, the research uncovers a novel psychological mechanism through which sustainability cues can influence intertemporal orientation. This extends existing literature on time-related decision-making and opens new avenues for future research into sustainable consumption and behavioral self-regulation. Objective 4: This objective has been successfully met. Both of the working papers produced out of this project offer clear and actionable insights. For marketers, the findings suggest that placing recycling cues in consumption environments can enhance consumer patience and increase preference for stimulating products, thereby informing retail design and product positioning strategies. For government agencies and NGOs, our research reveals unexpected downstream psychological benefits of recycling, such as increased vitality and patience. These insights allow for more compelling narratives in sustainability campaigns that extend beyond environmental outcomes to include consumer wellbeing. Furthermore, the studies identify boundary conditions under which these psychological benefits may be reduced, helping practitioners design more effective and targeted interventions.

16501820.label: Major findings and research outcome
16501820.value: This project set out to explore how sustainability cues, specifically recycling behaviors and related environmental signals, affect consumers’ psychological experiences and decision-making. Drawing from two working papers, this research makes significant theoretical and practical contributions to the literature on consumer behavior, sustainability, and time perception. The first working paper, Going Green, Staying Calm: The Effect of Recycling on Consumers’ Willingness to Wait (under preparation), demonstrates that engaging in recycling behaviors or being exposed to recycling-related cues increases perceived time availability, which subsequently enhances consumers’ willingness to wait for products and services. Across nine studies—including laboratory experiments, a field experiment, and archival analysis—this research identifies perceived time abundance as a novel psychological mechanism linking sustainability behaviors to consumer patience. These findings offer actionable implications for service design and sustainability messaging. This paper was presented at the ISMS Marketing Science Conference 2023 (Miami, June 2023) and the Association for Consumer Research Annual Conference 2023 (Seattle, October 2023). The second working paper, The Effect of Recycling on Sensation Seeking (also under preparation), explores how recycling behaviors influence consumers’ motivational states. Specifically, the research finds that recycling enhances consumers’ subjective vitality, which in turn increases their tendency to seek novel and intense sensory experiences. This finding reveals an overlooked psychological benefit of sustainable behavior and contributes to the understanding of how sustainability cues can shape intertemporal preferences and product choices. Together, these findings advance theory by identifying previously undocumented downstream consequences of recycling—vitality, patience, and sensation seeking—and provide marketers and policymakers with new strategies to encourage sustainable engagement while enhancing consumer experience. Both papers acknowledge the support of the RGC (HKUST 16501820) and are targeted for submission to top-tier journals in marketing and consumer psychology. They are expected to be accessible upon publication via institutional repositories. Additionally, this project contributed to doctoral training: Lulu Shi, a PhD student whose thesis work was supported by this grant, graduated in August 2024 and obtained a job as an Assistant Professor in Paris School of Business. Together, the outputs of this project fulfill and in some cases exceed the original objectives. The findings contribute meaningfully to sustainability and marketing scholarship and have been disseminated at major international conferences, ensuring impact across academic and applied domains.

16501820.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16501820.value: The findings of this research open several promising avenues for future exploration and application. First, future studies can further examine the boundary conditions of the recycling–waiting relationship. For example, researchers could investigate whether the effect of recycling cues on willingness to wait varies across different types of waiting contexts (e.g., hedonic vs. utilitarian services), consumer segments (e.g., high vs. low environmental consciousness), or cultural settings. Additionally, longitudinal studies could assess whether repeated exposure to recycling cues can lead to more sustained changes in perceived time availability and patience over time. Understanding these moderating factors can help businesses fine-tune the placement and messaging of recycling prompts in service environments. Second, the observed link between recycling, vitality, and sensation seeking suggests that sustainable behaviors may have broader psychological and behavioral spillover effects than previously understood. Future research could explore whether recycling influences other downstream behaviors beyond sensation seeking—such as creativity, openness to experience, or risk-taking in decision-making. This opens a new direction for investigating how sustainability-based interventions can be used not only to encourage ethical consumption but also to enhance consumer engagement, experiential value, and emotional well-being.

16501820.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16501820.value: This research examines how everyday recycling behaviors—such as discarding a bottle in a recycling bin—can shape people’s psychological states and everyday decision-making. We found that recycling, or simply encountering recycling-related cues (e.g., posters, signage), increases individuals’ perceived time availability. This subtle shift leads to greater patience and a higher willingness to wait in common consumption settings, such as checkout lines or service queues. Furthermore, engaging in recycling also enhanced individuals’ sense of vitality, which in turn increased their desire for novel and stimulating experiences. These findings are significant because they reveal that recycling has psychological and behavioral consequences beyond its environmental benefits. It can influence how people feel, what they choose, and how they respond to everyday consumer experiences. Businesses and policymakers can leverage these insights by strategically placing recycling cues in environments where greater patience or engagement is desirable. By demonstrating that sustainability-related actions can influence core perceptions like time and energy, this research adds a novel dimension to our understanding of consumer psychology. It suggests that even small sustainable behaviors may have broad spillover effects on well-being, attention, and behavioral tendencies.

16501920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16501920.value: 從巴士上的咳嗽聲、親人的病徵、再到媒體對最新流感流行的報導──關於疾病的提醒無處不在。然而，這些無處不在的提示對消費者行為構成的影響力卻被市場營銷學學者忽略。本研究旨在利用社會心理學的最新觀點去探討其影響力，並對疾病威脅提供革新的看法。 心理學文獻認為，由於傳染病存在數千年並對人類構成潛在威脅，因此人類已經發展了一套適應性心理免疫系統以抵禦此類潛在威脅，包括對疾病相關線索的過度反應(Murray and Schaller 2012) 。另外，人們亦會迴避參與人際交往──這些都是具體的防禦趨勢(Sacco, Young, and Hugenberg 2014) 。 我們將以這種面對疾病威脅的進化觀點為基礎，概述並研究環境線索如何影響消費者行為。研究項目將涉及兩個不同層面，分別在單獨的研究項目中進行。第一項研究項目將疾病威脅的進化觀點與社會和經濟資源可互換的普遍觀點互相融合(Lasaleta et al. 2014) 。 因此，我們認為，由疾病威脅造成的缺乏其他聯繫將致增加對經濟資源的需求。實際上，我們認為疾病威脅（相對於其他危害威脅）會引發人們對財產的渴望，即增強物質主義。此證明將有利於營銷人員和決策者如何處理全球日益增加的物質主義。 第二個研究項目將調查與疾病相關線索如何影響對擬人化產品（即包含人樣特徵的產品）的反應。由於產品擬人化會令消費者對該產品產生喜好，所以是一種廣泛使用的營銷策略(Aggarwal and McGill 2007; Chandler and Schwarz 2010)。相反，我們認為，由疾病相關線索引起的人際迴避傾向將降低消費者對擬人化產品的喜好，尤其對於那些描述成擁有“熱情友好”性格的產品，因為這種性格傾向於積極地參與人際交往。 這兩項研究項目不但能有助加深我們對重要(及被低估影響力)環境線索的認識，更能將其影響力告知各持份者，包括營銷者，消費者及公共行政外判商。

16501920.label: Realisation of objectives
16501920.value: Regarding objective 1, a comprehensive literature review has been undertaken to arrive at a state-of-the-art understanding of how exposure to disease cues affects consumer behavior. This review provided the conceptual underpinnings for pursuing objectives 2 and 3 below. Regarding objective 2, it was almost fully met. We have obtained good evidence for the premise that exposure to disease cues increases desire for material possessions, as manifested in indicators such as a positive correlation with materialism scales, and wishing to upgrade current products. We are in the process of writing up these findings prior to journal submission. Regarding objective 3, it was partially met. We have obtained empirical evidence that exposure to disease cues lowers liking for anthropomorphized products -- which aligns with the basic premise that disease exposure leads to "people avoidance". In addition, our focus on anthropomorphism has led to an investigation on consumer responses to anthropomorphized products, in which we find that consumers tend to speak more favorably of the same product when it is anthropomorphized vs. not. The impression-management reason that underlies this finding also suggests that the effect is more likely to be obtained when speaking about the product to a distant vs. close other -- as we also empirically demonstrate. Findings from this research have been published in the premier journal in our field, Journal of Consumer Research (Chen, Sengupta and Zheng 2023). While the first objective has been fully met, and objectives 2 and 3 were met to a large extent, one important barrier that we had to deal with was the ongoing pandemic over the last few years. The pandemic ironically curtailed our investigation of the effects of disease cues on consumer behavior in two important ways. First, most of the studies in our investigation require creating different levels of disease salience (experimental vs. control conditions). However, because the thought of infection and disease is now so salient across the population, it has been very difficult to create variations experimentally. Second, conducting face to face studies -- something that was also vital for several of our studies -- became very difficult because of the prevailing restrictions. It is because of these barriers that objectives 2 and 3 could not be accomplished fully. Even so, we are happy that we were able to adapt to these barriers to a large extent. For instance, by broadening the scope of objective 3 to encompass consumer reactions to anthropomorphized products in general, we were able to conduct a very successful investigation into how anthropomorphism affects word of mouth, an investigation published recently in the Journal of Consumer Research. It is also because of the difficulties caused by the pandemic that expenditure in the General Expenses category was higher than initially estimated. Because, as mentioned above, the pandemic made infection cues extraordinarily salient, we had to try many different variations of stimuli and manipulations in order to arrive at appropriate levels of calibration for our studies. This necessarily increased expenditure to a considerable extent. In addition, expenditure also increased as our investigation broadened to include a systematic examination of how anthropomorphism affects word of mouth (as noted above), for which many studies were conducted.

16501920.label: Major findings and research outcome
16501920.value: The following major findings emerged from this research: 1. Exposure to disease cues induces individuals to stay away from others -- because of the risk of contagion. Because of increased social loneliness, this then increases the propensity towards materialism as a way of compensating for loneliness, as manifested in indicators such as a positive correlation with materialism scales, and wishing to upgrade current products. Studies testifying to this finding are now being written up. 2. Similarly, exposure to disease cues was found to reduce liking for anthropomorphized products. Finally, our investigation of this issue led to a related investigation on consumer responses to anthropomorphized products, in which we find that consumers tend to speak more favorably of the same product when it is anthropomorphized vs. not. The impression-management reason that underlies this finding also suggests that the effect is more likely to be obtained when speaking about the product to a distant vs. close other -- as we also empirically demonstrate. Findings from this research have been published in the premier journal in our field, Journal of Consumer Research (Chen, Sengupta and Zheng 2023).

16501920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
16501920.value: There are several directions in which we hope to take this research forward. First, we plan to distinguish between disease cues of greater magnitude (e.g., the pandemic) vs. lower magnitude (the flu season). One interesting possibility is that the former, because it enforces compulsory isolation -- as was the case in the "lockdowns" imposed in many countries during the peak of the pandemic -- actually creates a wish for more social connection. If this is the case, we should expect a reversal of several of our current findings -- e.g., a wish for greater social connection should yield a heightened liking for anthropomorphized products. Second and relatedly, the effects of disease cues might be quite different when the product usage context relates to infections (e.g., using dishes for dinnerware) versus when it does not (using dishes as wall decorations). In the former case, the wish to avoid infection should manifest the kind of social avoidance effects that we report. In the latter case, however, infection fears are unlikely to be salient when considering product usage. Rather, it seems likely that a conformity effect should be obtained, with consumers seeking products that are also endorsed by others. Third, while our work on product anthropomorphism emerging from this proposal (Chen et al. 2022) finds that anthropomorphism causes people to speak more highly of products in order to be deemed likable (a form of impression management), it is intriguing to explore other forms of impression management. For example, separate from likability, people sometimes wish to appear experts -- and such perceptions of expertise are more likely to be fostered by being negative and critical. It would be interesting, therefore, to explore whether the findings of Chen et al. 2022 can be reversed when an expertise impression-motive is salient (rather than a likability motive).

16501920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16501920.value: The inter-related projects that comprise this research provide several interesting conclusions, namely: a) Exposure to disease cues (e.g., public service announcements about the flu season, getting exposed to a coughing person on the bus, walking past a hospital, etc.) increases the tendency to avoid people. b) In turn, this people-avoidance tendency increases our propensity towards materialism, since products and possessions partly compensate for a lack of social connection. c) People-avoidance also translates to a lower liking of products that have humanlike elements -- again, because of the wish to avoid humans. d) Finally, our focus on products with humanlike elements (anthropomorphized products) shows that because of impression-management reasons, consumers tend to speak more positively of such products than their non-humanized equivalents.

16502020.label: Project Objectives
16502020.value: Study the equity investment dynamics of duration-sensitive long-term investors, e.g., pensions and life insurers. What is the optimal equity investment of these long-term investors? Investigate their exposure to duration risk. Pensions and life insurers have long durations for assets and liabilities alike, which expose them to duration risk. The duration of liabilities largely depends on the longevity risk, which is exogenous. How do they adjust their portfolio duration, i.e., duration hedging, when facing exogenous longevity shocks? Examine the equity portfolio rebalancing of pensions and life insurers. Stocks are often used as long-term investment instruments by long-term investors. To meet the duration-hedging demand, how do pensions and insurers adjust their equity holdings? The portfolio rebalancing of pensions and life insurers creates price pressure on stocks. How do duration-driven trades affect stock returns, in particular, cross-sectional return variations? When lots of pensions and life insurers adjust their equity portfolios in the same direction, their trades generate herding. How does such herding behavior relate to return momentum and reversals? How do individuals and households respond to longevity shocks? How do their flows to pensions and life insurance affect the equity holdings of these long-term investors? From the social welfare perspective, how would equity investment help financially address the longevity risk?

16502020.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16502020.value: This project studies the equity investment of two types of long-term investors, e.g., pensions and life insurers. Pensions and life insurance provide long-term financial solutions related to longevity shocks, which is vital for addressing the longevity risk accompanied by an aging population. These long-term investors have long durations for assets and liabilities alike. That is, they are duration-sensitive investors. To minimize potential shortfalls in the future, pensions and life insurers strive to match the duration of assets with that of liabilities. Pensions and life insurers rely heavily on stocks as long-term financial instruments in their strategic asset allocation. As the duration of liabilities largely depends on the longevity risk, they dynamically adjust their portfolios, especially stock holdings, in the presence of exogenous longevity shocks. Demand of duration-hedging drives their strategic asset allocation and trading activities. First, this project investigates how pensions and life insurers adjust their equity portfolios to change their portfolio durations when facing longevity shocks. Second, this project explores the impacts of their portfolio rebalancing on stock prices. Do these long-term investors herd and trade in the same direction? Do they trade in momentum or contrarian ways? Third, this project studies the implementable trading strategies for these long-term investors. Fourth, this project examines how individuals and households respond to the longevity shocks by changing their investment in pensions and life insurance, which affects flows to these long-term investors and their equity holdings. Finally, this project evaluates the effectiveness of equity investment by pensions and life insurers to address the longevity risk financially. 本项目研究两类长期投资者（包括养老与寿险基金）的股权投资。这两类投资者致力于提供与人寿风险相关的财务解决方案。这在目前日趋老龄化的社会具有重大意义。因为他们的资产与负债端均具有长期性，这些投资者是久期敏感型投资者。为预防长期的现金流短缺问题，这些投资者需要匹配资产与负债端的久期。他们的负债端久期取决于人寿风险。 当人寿风险变化时，他们需要相应地动态调整资产端的久期。因为他们使用股票作为长期投资，这意味着他们需要动态调整股票投资组合。本项目研究他们久期驱动的股票投资与交易行为。首先，本项目研究这些投资者在人寿风险变化时如何调整他们的股票组合。其次，本项目研究他们的交易对股票价格的影响。例如，是否造成股票价格的动量或反转效应？第三，本项目针对这些投资者提出一些可行的投资策略建议。第四，本项目研究个人与家庭是如何应对人寿风险变化。最后，本项目评估目前养老与人寿基金的股权投资效率。

16502020.label: Realisation of objectives
16502020.value: This project studies equity investment of duration-sensitive long-term investors, e.g., pensions and life insurers, in particular, from the longevity perspective. 1. Research Objectives 1-4 First, this project studies how to measure stock duration. The duration measure is useful for portfolio-choice or risk-management purposes (see, e.g., Hasler, Khapko, and Marfè (2019)). Following the literature, the first measure I used is the Macaulay duration. This measure relies on the assumptions of fundamental cash-flow and discount. Prior papers typically use some statistical models to estimate future cash flows, together with actual earnings/dividend data or analyst forecasts. For example, Dechow et al. (2004) and Weber (2018) assume the first-order autoregressive processes of book equity growth and return on equity (similar procedures are used in Gonçalves (2021) and Gormsen and Lazarus (2023)). In addition, researchers often assume exogenously specified discount rates or even a common discount rate for all stocks (see, e.g., Dechow et al. (2004) and Weber (2018)), which makes it less desirable to study cross-sectional return variations. The Macaulay duration is an appropriate measure if one cares only about the timing of future cash flow or for assets with fixed future cash flow. However, for stocks, the expected future cash-flow growth often increases with the discount rate (see, e.g., Menzly, Santos, and Veronesi (2004), Lettau and Ludvigson (2005), and Binsbergen and Koijen (2010)). This requires a new duration measure to capture the overall effects, including both direct and indirect effects. I propose a second duration measure: the effective equity duration, which is defined as the negative ratio of the percentage change in stock prices to changes in the discount rate. I also propose an event-based estimation that uses price information. I first use policy surprises regarding the federal funds rate set by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) as the events (see, e.g., Bernanke and Kuttner (2005), Neuhierl and Weber (2019), and Ozdagli and Velikov (2020)). I also use the Federal Funds futures traded at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange to measure the federal funds rate expected by the markets and to detect the policy surprises after FOMC announcements. I choose an event window of 60 minutes before and 5 minutes after the FOMC announcements. Next, I use NYSE TAQ data to compute the stock price reactions around the events. Then, I use a vector autoregressive model to compute changes in the expected returns of the market portfolio and apply CAPM to compute the changes in the discount rates for individual stocks (see, e.g., Campbell and Vuolteenaho (2004), Campbell, Polk, and Vuolteenaho (2010), Campbell, Giglio, Polk and Turley (2018), and Savor and Wilson (2014)). Finally, the effective equity duration can be computed as the negative ratio of the percentage change in the stock prices to the changes in the discount rate. I apply both Macaulay duration and my new duration measure in the subsequent studies. The main results are published in the Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis in 2022. Second, I study how pensions and life insurers adjust their stock portfolios when they face duration risks, including their equity holdings and trading strategies. Their liabilities are often long term and their assets appear to be long term, too. Given the regulatory constraints, to minimize long-term shortfalls, pensions and life insurers strive to match asset duration with liability duration, e.g., duration hedging (see, e.g., Greenwood and Vayanos (2010), Klinger and Sundaresan (2019)). The asset duration depends on the assets they invest in and is driven by market prices. However, the liabilities of pensions and life insurers largely depend on the life expectancy of participants, i.e., the longevity risk, which is an exogenous shock. Following the actuarial science literature, I use the Human Mortality Database (HMD) to estimate longevity risk in a population. Longevity shocks are measured as the innovations of the weighted average period life expectancy in the U.S. population. Life expectancy in the U.S. increased from 73.27 years in 1951 to 81.93 years in 2018, an average increase of 0.14 years per year, which is substantial. I use the Thomson-Reuters Institutional Holdings (TR-13F) Database to identify pensions over 1981-2017. I also use the life insurers’ data from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners over 2005-2017. I compute durations of their stock portfolios. I find that pensions and life insurers are sensitive to longevity shocks, i.e., they adjust their portfolio duration according to longevity shocks. For a one-standard-deviation increase in longevity, their stock portfolio duration increases by 0.5 years. Their portfolio choices show a strong duration-hedging motivation. For example, their portfolio-rebalancing flows to long-duration stocks closely follow longevity shocks (a correlation coefficient of 0.26), while portfolio-rebalancing flows to short-duration stocks move in the opposite direction of longevity shocks (a correlation coefficient of -0.16). These address Research Objectives 1 and 2. Next, we study the trading activities of pensions and life insurers, including their impacts on cross-sectional stock returns. We show that pensions and life insurers are momentum or contrarian traders because losers have longer duration than winners in three steps. First, we confirm the momentum effects among stocks held by pensions and life insurers. We show that a momentum strategy strengthens during periods of low longevity shocks but it becomes insignificant during periods of high longevity shocks. Second, conditioning on the longevity status, we identify winner and loser stocks from the holdings of pensions and life insurers, based on the stock durations, the changes of stock durations over a quarter, and the trade size, without reference to historical stock returns. We find stronger momentum (reversal) among these identified stocks than over the entire universe of stocks. For example, the momentum strategy has an alpha from the Fama-French five-factor model (α_FF5) of 2.43% per month (t-statistic = 3.37) when the longevity shock is low. When the longevity shock is high, the contrarian strategy generates an α_FF5 of 1.11% per month (t-statistic = 2.09). Third, we exclude these identified stocks from the entire stock universe and we find that momentum is no longer significant among the remaining stocks. It confirms that pensions and life insurers behave like momentum (contrarian) traders during periods of low (high) longevity shocks. The main results are provided in a working paper which is currently under revision. These address Research Objectives 3 and 4. 2. Research Objective 5 I study how individuals and households respond to longevity shocks. To this end, I examine the net capital flows to pensions and explore how pensions adjust their stock portfolios. I find that long-duration stocks attract more capital flows than short-duration stocks when the longevity shock is high. That is, when longevity shock is high, households do allocate more to pensions which drives pension funds to invest more in long-duration stocks. 3. Research Objective 6 Last, I quantitatively evaluate how equity investment helps to address the longevity risk, e.g., the social welfare costs. The sizable longevity shock (0.13 years per year) implies that the claim period of annuity holders increases by 13%, which significantly increases the liabilities of pensions. I estimate that in US markets, pensions need to trade more than 400 billion dollars in stocks each year due to longevity shocks. This demonstrates the important role of stock markets in managing longevity risks.

16502020.label: Major findings and research outcome
16502020.value: 1. Longevity improves over time (life expectancy increases by about 0.14 years per year), with a large volatility (the annual standard deviation is 0.14 years). 2. Pensions and life insurers are significantly exposed to longevity shocks. A one-standard-deviation increase of longevity causes an increase of the claim period of annuity holders by 13%. 3. To minimize the duration risk and satisfy the regulatory constraints, pensions and life insurers strive to match asset duration with liability duration, e.g., duration hedging. 4. Pensions and life insurers adjust durations of their stock portfolios. For example, their portfolio-rebalancing flows to long-duration stocks closely follow longevity shocks. 5. Because losers have longer durations than winners, pensions and life insurers behave like momentum (contrarian) traders during periods of low (high) longevity shocks. 6. Households respond to positive longevity shocks by allocating more capital to pensions and annuities. Such funds are subsequently invested long-duration stocks. That is, long-duration stocks attract more capital flows than short-duration stocks when the longevity shock is high. 7. Stocks are long-term assets, which play an important role in managing duration risk and dampening longevity shocks to pensions. In the US markets, pensions need to trade more than 400 billion dollars in stocks each year due to longevity shocks. Such trades affect cross-sectional stock returns.

16502020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
16502020.value: This project studies equity investment of pensions and life insurers, which are exposed to longevity risks because their liabilities depend on the life expectancy of participants. In the US, the annual longevity increase is 0.14 years per year and it is volatile. On average, this increases the claim period of annuity holders by 13%, significantly increasing the cost of annuity products. To minimize the long-term underfunding issue, they need to manage the duration risk by matching their asset duration with the liability duration, i.e., adjusting holdings of stocks with various durations. This project applies various duration measures and finds that pensions and life insurers adjust durations according to longevity shocks. For example, they invest more in long-duration stocks when longevity increases unexpectedly. Because loser stocks have longer durations than winner stocks, pensions and life insurers behave like momentum (contrarian) traders during periods of low (high) longevity shocks. Also, this project finds that households respond to positive longevity shocks by allocating more capital to pensions and annuities. Such funds are subsequently invested in long-duration stocks. Overall, in US markets, pensions trade more than 400 billion dollars in stocks each year to manage the longevity risks.

16502520.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
16502520.value: The peer-to-peer-based activities of obtaining, giving, or sharing access to goods and services via community-based online platforms, termed as the sharing or gig economy, have gained tremendous popularity in the past decade. Not only are these markets growing rapidly, they are also disrupting long-standing industries and displacing their incumbents. Despite their prominence, there is a marked shortage of studies that consider the supply side of the sharing economy. An important, but understudied aspect of the supply side of the sharing economy pertains to the intrinsic motivations of the providers in these markets. This work aims to address three inter-connected questions: 1) does the intrinsic interest of providers influence their market entry time?; 2) how do intrinsically motivated providers position themselves in the sharing economy market?; and 3) what are the subsequent revenue impacts of these actions? Leveraging a proprietary dataset provided by a sharing economy platform that specializes in home-cooked food, we investigate whether having cooking as a personal interest affects the entry decisions and positioning strategies of providers, and the consequences of the adopted positioning strategies on providers’ sales performance. This research will make several important contributions to the literature. First, it can provide answers to the question related to the nature of collaborative consumption markets by investigating the role of intrinsic motives on providers’ actions. Second, it can give an understanding of the downstream economic outcomes of the strategies of these providers by quantifying the revenue impacts. Third, this work bears policy implications for platform owners and government agencies. 通过基于社区的在线平台实现对商品和服务的使用权限的获取、给予或共享这些对等活动，称为共享或零工经济，在过去的十年中获得了极大的欢迎。这些市场不仅迅速增长，也在颠覆长期存在的行业并取代他们的位置。尽管共享经济表现突出，但是关于它的供应方面的研究文章仍然明显不足。其中一个重要但尚未研究的方面就和这些市场中供应者的内在动机有关。 这项工作旨在解决三个相互关联的问题：1）是否供应者的内在兴趣会影响其进入市场的时间？ 2）具有内在动机的供应者如何在共享经济市场中定位自己？3）这些行动对之后的收入有何影响？利用来自于一个家庭厨房的共享经济平台的专有数据，我们研究把烹饪作为一个兴趣是怎么影响供应者的进入决定和定位策略，以及供应者采用的定位策略对其销售业绩的影响。 这项研究将对现有文献做出重要贡献。首先，它可以通过研究内在动机对供应者行为的影响来帮助回答有关合作消费性质的问题。第二，它可以通过量化对收入的影响来帮助大家了解这些供应者所采取策略的下游经济结果。第三，这项工作可以对平台所有者和政府机构提供政策性指导。

16502520.label: Realisation of objectives
16502520.value: All the research objectives listed above have been successfully achieved: Objective 1: We analyzed providers motivated by personal passions for cooking (self-driven interests) and those motivated by the social aspects of meeting new people (social-driven motivations). Utilizing techniques such as discrete-time survival analysis and copula estimation, our findings indicate that providers with self-driven interests tend to enter the market earlier but do not sustain long-term activity. In contrast, those with social-driven motivations generally enter the market later but demonstrate greater longevity. Objective 2: Our research uncovered that providers' motivations significantly affect their market orientation. Providers with self-driven interests mainly focus on competitors, engaging in social learning and strategic imitation. On the other hand, providers driven by social motivations show a strong customer orientation, dedicating more efforts to meet consumer needs and maintain relationships. Objective 3: We found that providers driven by self-interests typically attract a larger customer base and experience higher order volumes. Conversely, those motivated by social interests tend to achieve higher customer satisfaction and experience fewer service failures, which contributes to increased effective income. Objective 4: We discussed the implications of our findings for platform managers, government agencies, and providers within the sharing economy.
