17106820.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17106820.value: Following the successful development of our proposed 3D dMRI technique with high scan acceleration and motion compensation, we plan to test it on a higher-performance MRI scanner and seek collaborations to conduct a cohort study. Our future plans are summarized below. 1. We will test the developed 3D dMRI technique on a higher-field-strength MRI scanner (e.g., 3.0T) and a higher-channel-count head coil. This is expected to demonstrate its benefits for achieving high-resolution submillimeter dMRI and improved performance at higher acceleration factors. 2. We will seek collaboration with clinical sites to acquire 3D dMRI data from challenging patient cohorts. This will allow us to thoroughly assess the applicability and performance of the technique in a clinical setting.

17106820.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17106820.value: This research project makes brain imaging faster and more reliable, especially for populations who cannot stay still, such as children or those with neurological conditions. It focuses on improving a specific type of brain scan called 3D diffusion MRI (dMRI), which maps the neural fibers in the brain with high image resolution but is currently slow and sensitive to head movement. Our solution involves three key innovations: a new method to collect scan data more efficiently, reducing scan time to just one minute per image; a tiny, lightweight wireless marker to track head movements with high precision; and a real-time correction system that instantly adjusts the scanner to compensate for any motion. The significance of this work is that it makes advanced brain imaging more practical and accessible for neuroscience research. By overcoming the challenges of long scan times and motion artifacts for high-resolution mapping of neural fibers, this technology may improve the diagnosis of brain disorders and enable high-quality research in populations that were previously difficult to scan.

17107020.label: Realisation of objectives
17107020.value: Study 1 (Objective 1): To identify an optimum concentration of synbiotic-fluoride therapy for dental caries prevention. Investigation completed and Objective 1 fully achieved. Results: The study showed that 2% Arginine (Arg) with 0.2% sodium fluoride (NaF) enhanced the growth of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LRG). The combination of 2% Arg, 2000-ppm NaF and LRG provided optimum synbiotic-fluoride (SF) synergism for restoring oral ecological homeostasis. Publication: Bijle MN, Ekambaram M, Lo ECM, Yiu CKY. Combined effect of arginine and fluoride on the growth of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG. Scientific Reports 2021; 11: 973. Study 2 (Objective 2): To identify the effects of synbiotic-fluoride therapy on multispecies biofilm. Investigation completed and Objective 2 fully achieved. Results: SF therapy effectuates multi-fold changes in the multi-species biofilm matrix and cellular components, leading to superior ecological homeostasis than its individual contents, prebiotics (arginine), probiotic (LRG), and fluorides (NaF). The ecological-based SF caries-preventive therapy aids in maintaining biofilm homeostasis to preempt/restore dysbiosis, thereby sustaining dynamic-diverse health-associated microbial stability significant as a preventive regimen for high caries-risk patients. Publication: Bijle MN, Abdalla MM, Hung IFN, Yiu CKY. The effect of synbiotic-fluoride therapy on multi-species biofilm. Journal of Dentistry 2023b; 133: 104523. Conference Abstract: Bijle NM, Abdalla MM, Hung IFN, Yiu CKY. Synbiotic-fluoride therapy for multi-species biofilm ecological homeostasis. IADR United Arab Emirates Section. Study 3 (Objective 3): To determine the remineralization effect of synbiotic-fluoride therapy using a multi-species bacterial pH-cycling model. Investigation completed and Objective 3 fully achieved. Results: The study showed that SF therapy demonstrated enhanced enamel remineralization effect compared to its individual/combined components. Publication: Bijle MN, Abdalla MM, Chu CH, Yiu CKY. Synbiotic -fluoride synergism on enamel remineralization, cytotoxicity and genotoxicity. Journal of Dentistry 2023a; 128: 104356. Conference Abstract: Bijle MN, Abdalla M, Chu CH, Yiu CKY. The enamel remineralization potential of synbiotic-fluoride therapy. Journal of Dental Research 2022; 101 (Special Issue A): Abstract #248 Study 4 (Objective 4): To examine the biocompatibility of synbiotic-fluoride therapy through cytotoxic and genotoxic assessment. Investigation completed and Objective 4 fully achieved. Results: The study showed that SF therapy did not exhibit any potential cytotoxic and genotoxic effects on HGF-1 and Chinese hamster fibroblasts V79, thereby ruling out its biocompatibility concerns. 17107020.label: Major findings and research outcome
17107020.value: The findings of this project showed that 2% Arg with 0.2% NaF enhanced the growth of LRG. The combination of 2% Arg, 2000-ppm NaF and LRG provided optimum SF synergism for restoring oral ecological homeostasis (Bijle et al 2021). Further investigation of the enamel remineralization potential of SF therapy revealed that the combined therapy demonstrated enhanced enamel remineralization effect when compared to its individual/combined components (Bijle et al 2023a). Moreover, the SF therapy had the potential to modulate extra-cellular matrix components, exhibiting antimicrobial effect. It inhibited the growth of cariogenic pathogen S. mutans and enhanced the growth of LRG. Furthermore, the SF therapy downregulated the genes responsible for extra-cellular insoluble glucan synthesis, while upregulated the ADS-positive genes conducing to Arg biosynthesis cycle of LRG (Bijle et al 2023b). In conclusion, the ecological-based SF therapy aids in maintaining biofilm homeostasis to preempt/restore dysbiosis, thereby sustaining dynamic-diverse health-associated microbial stability significant as a preventive regimen for high caries-risk patients with negligible cytotoxicity (Bijle et al 2021).

17107020.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17107020.value: Based on the promising results of our in vitro studies, there is potential for further development of this research. The proposed course of action is as follows: 1. Exploring alternative probiotic strains: Other strains of probiotic bacteria could be investigated for their potential synergistic effects with L-arginine and fluoride. This may lead to the development of more effective SF therapy that target patients with high caries risk. 2. Developing SF-containing dental care products: Based on the findings of our research, there is potential to develop toothpaste, mouthwash, or other dental care products containing the SF combination for daily use by patients with high caries risk. 3. Conducting clinical trials: To better understand the clinical effectiveness of SF therapy, long-term clinical trials should be conducted on high caries-risk children using SF-containing toothpaste or mouthwash. This will help to evaluate the long-term benefits and potential side effects of the therapy in caries prevention.

17107020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17107020.value: This study found that the combination of a prebiotic (L-arginine), fluoride, and a specific type of probiotic bacteria (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG), leading to the development of synbiotic-fluoride therapy which improved oral health. The combined therapy helps to restore balance in the mouth by promoting the growth of good bacteria and strengthening tooth enamel, making it an effective way to prevent tooth decay, especially for people with high caries risk. Furthermore, this treatment is not toxic and can be used safely in patients as a caries-preventive measure.

17107520.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17107520.value: The most common matrix monomer used for dental composites is based on bis-phenol A which is a known oestrogen analogue. ‘Plastic’ food containers are tight restrictions of use and baby products have BPA containing materials banned. Yet this monomer is still very widely used in dentistry. Therefore, it is timely to consider the introduction of new monomers which are BPA-free, one such is a fluorinated version of urethane dimetharcrylate. The novel FUDMA monomers were developed by Dr J He at SCUT. Collaborative work is being undertaken between the HKU Dental Faculty and SCUT to more fully characterize the monomer. The research is now at the point where the development of a filled resin composites for use as dental restorations can be considered. Different filler systems will be considered to also impart some form of bioactivity into the filling materials. The bioactive composites can have the ability to remineralise or prevent demineralization around restoration margins from dental decay, modify the adhesion and growth of oral biofilms to slow biofilm dysbiosis and therefore slow initation of dental caries and periodontal diseases. The significant outcomes of this work are to create resin composite materials that can be used commercially that are BPA free and can be applied widely in restorative dentistry worldwide. 用于牙科复合材料的最常见单体基质是双酚A（BPA）, 这也是一种已知的雌激素类似物。 在“塑料”制成 的食品容器已经有了严格的限制，尤其是在婴儿使用的产品中， 基于BPA单体的任何材料都是被禁止使用的。但是这种单体仍然在牙科领域非常广泛。因此，是时候考虑引入一个不含BPA的新单体，比如氟化的氨基甲酸酯二甲基丙烯酸酯（FUDMA）。这种新型单体由华南理工大学的的何教授研制并与香港大学牙科学院共同合作研发。现阶段研究考虑将其研发成为树脂填充复合材料并用作牙体修复。不同的填充剂系统将会进行实验测试，并加入一些具有生物活性的填充材料。这些具有生物活性的复合材料可以使牙齿具有矿化或重新矿化的能力，防止由于龋齿而导致修复边缘周围的脱矿质, 同时可以减缓口腔生物膜的粘附和生长从而使生物膜生态失调，并因此减缓引发龋齿和牙周疾病。 这项工作的重要成果是创造可以全球商业化的不含BPA的新型复合树脂并可以广泛的用于牙科修复。

17107520.label: Realisation of objectives
17107520.value: The first two aims have been completed which is the bulk of the project. The project commencement was impeded by COVID-19 pandemic which led to a late start as it took a very long time to find a RA who had the capabilities to conduct the experimental work. Objective 1: Nine groups of resins and composites were prepared. The degree of conversion, flexural strength and modulus of 3 different combinations of FUDMA/TEGDMA (60/40, 70/30, 80/20 wt%) resins were investigated and compared with Bis-GMA/TEGDMA and UDMA/TEGDMA control groups using the same ratios. FUDMA resin (70/30 wt%) showed a 17.5% increase in Degree of Cure (62.9 %), compared to the Bis-GMA base resin with the same ratio. FUDMA resin system (80/20 wt%) presented the highest FS (114.5 ± 4.8 MPa) and FM (2.8 ± 0.1 GPa), whereas Bis-GMA resin (60/40 wt%) showed the lowest FS (79.2 ± 2.9 MPa) and FM (1.9 ± 0.1 GPa). This demonstrated the viability of this new monomer combination as an alternative to currently used base mononers. Objective 2: Composites were prepared by mixing the base monomers and TEGDMA in a ratio of 70/30 wt% to which were added silanized glass particles (mean diameter: 0.7 µm) in 3 different volume fractions (40, 45, 50 vol%). Various properties including degree of conversion (DC), flexural strength (FS) and flexural modulus (FM), water sorption (WS), solubility (SL), surface hardness and roughness, and initial of the bacteria S. mutans adhesion were investigated. This latter part of the experiment was not originally planned, but is an important part of evaluating the initial composite resin. Hence this portion is a new addition that was able to be easily incorporated into the project to expand the outcomes. A significant difference in FS between FUDMA-based composite with 40 vol% filler (120.3 ± 10.4 MPa) and Bis-GMA-based composite with the same filler (105.8 ± 10.0 MPa) was observed. The UDMA based group exhibited the highest WS (1.3 ± 0.3 %) amongst the experimental composite groups. The SL was positive for Bis-GMA-based composite (0.1 ± 0.1 %) and was negative for FUDMA and UDMA-based composite groups (-0.2 ± 0.2 and -0.4 ± 0.2 %, respectively). For bacterial adhesion of S. mutans on the composite surfaces, Bis-GMA showed greater initial adhesion after 6 hours incubation but was not statistically significant different from the other groups (p =0.082). Due to late start, it was not possible to commence. Objective 3 could not be commenced to the limited time of the project. Objective 4 : this part still needed more work on the initial combinations of fillers to be able to proceed. As the RA has now continued as a PhD student, this objective will be investigated. Objective 5 was also not completed due to the time limitations. Again the PhD student will investigate this in the overall PhD project. Early work investigating flexural strength provides the baseline for this work.

17107520.value: FUDMA-based resin composites exhibit comparable if not improved mechanical and antibacterial adhesion properties compared with Bis-GMA and UDMA-based composites. The FUDMA composites show positive outcomes indicating they could be used as substitute composites to Bis-GMA-based composites. 17107520.value: The uncompleted work has been taken on by a PhD student. The composite material shows excellent potential to be used as an alternative to currently used materials. Should further outcomes prove successful, there is good commercial potential for this resin based material for use clinically.

17107520.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17107520.value: One of the commonly used resins for dental filling materials has been implicated in releasing the oestrogen analogue Bisphenol-A. There is therefore the need to create new resin-based tooth coloured filling materials to replace currently used materials. The current project aimed to develop a BPA-free resin based tooth coloured filling material. A fluorinated form of urethane dimethacrylate (FUDMA) was used to make a new filling material. The resin was combined with filler particles to formulate a new filling resin composite material. Tests were conducted to investigate whether this new filling material is the same as, or better than, currently used materials. The results of the study showed the new FUDMA-based material was comparable and slightly better for strength, water sorption, solubility, and preventing the adhesion of a bacteria known associated wirh causing tooth decay. It was concluded this new material shows excellent potential to become an alternative BPA-free filling material. Further testing is needed however.

17108620.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17108620.value: Time is running out for corals and the reef ecosystems they form. Climate change is accelerating the loss of coral reefs globally.Yet, we have a very poor ability to predict the corals that will survive in the future ocean owing to a lack of research on the hundreds of species of extant corals and their diverse endosymbionts, the symbiodinians. Therefore, we aim to apply a novel method for assessing the strength of symbiosis in the sea, using geochemical measurements of stable isotope ratios in corals and their symbionts. This new method allows for a rapid understanding of the 'strength' of the symbiosis by defining the host and symbiont trophic niche and whether those niche areas overlap (resource sharing = mutualism), partially overlap (= mixotrophy) or are independent (=heterotrophy). Our prior work has demonstrated this is a robust method that correlates with bleaching resistance and polyp morphology, suggesting that nutrient cycling within the symbiosis is a major driver of scleractinian evolution. Here, we aim to expand this work through a collaborative expedition in a species rich area - the Philippines. This environment affords the ability to map geochemical attributes and morphological characters to a phylogenetic tree to determine which factors co-vary with patterns of speciation. We will refine our observations with in vitro studies of symbiosis within two model cnidarians to assess 1) the propensity for symbiont competition in hospite and 2) to assess the impacts of symbiont competition on host fitness. By doing so we will highlight the costs of associating with certain symbiont types, which may explain the rarity of mixed symbiont assemblages in nature and identify highly productive symbioses which may be an 'Achilles' heel' in a warming world. 氣候變化正在加速全球珊瑚礁的流失，珊瑚及其形成的珊瑚礁生態系統的所剩的時間已不多了。然而，由於缺乏對數百種珊瑚品種及其多樣的共生體（共生藻）的研究，我們很難預測哪些珊瑚能存活於未來海洋環境。因此，我們項目的目的是通過對珊瑚及其共生藻中穩定同位素比的地球化學測量，來評估海洋中的「共生強度」。通過定義宿主和共生藻的生態位以及這些生態位區域重疊（資源共享=共生），部分重疊（=混合營養）還是獨立（=異養）。我們先前的研究成果表明此方法可靠，其結果與珊瑚白化抗性以及珊瑚蟲的形態具關聯性，表明珊瑚與共生藻之間的養分交換驅動其生態演化。 我們希望透過與菲律賓的合作考察擴展這項研究。菲律賓的物種豐富，能提供一個理想的實驗場所。我們將探討該地區的地球化學屬性和形態特徵結合系統發生樹的演化進程，從而確定哪些因素決定物種的形成模式。我們將利用在兩種刺胞模式生物進行共生的體外研究以完善我們的觀察，以評估1）共生藻在細胞內競爭的傾向和2）評估共生藻的競爭對宿主適應性的影響。通過此方法，我們將揭示宿主與不同共生藻共生的成本，這可能有助解釋自然界中混合的共生藻組合的稀有性，並篩選高產的共生藻，這可能是在全球暖化的大環境世界中的“致命弱點”。

17108720.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17108720.value: 肝細胞癌 (Hepatocellular Carcinoma, HCC) 是主要的原發性肝癌，是發病率全球第五、致死率全球第二的癌症。在亞洲地區，肝細胞癌的主要成因是HBV以及HCV的病毒感染。在香港和中國大陸，超過80％的肝細胞癌病例都與慢性HBV感染有關。儘管我們已經明確了解肝癌的病因，但對肝癌發生的分子機制仍知之甚少。 HCC是每年導致700,000例死亡的致命癌症。手術切除和肝移植是治療肝癌的有效方法。但是，由於症狀出現較晚，大多數HCC患者被診斷時已為癌症晚期，不適合進行手術切除。目前，索拉非尼和樂伐替尼是唯一的FDA批准的晚期肝細胞癌一線治療藥物。然而，索拉非尼和樂伐替尼的臨床治療效果並不理想。因此，病人迫切需要一種新的治療手段來提高HCC患者的存活率。為此，我們需要對肝細胞發生的分子機制有更好的了解。 在人體細胞中，長達2米的DNA被組裝形成染色質儲存在直徑只有5微米的細胞核內。而染色質的有序結構決定了各個基因的表達水平和基因組的穩定性。所有有關DNA的生命活動，包括基因複制、轉錄、損傷修復等都是在這個基礎上進行的。而染色質結構的基本單位就是核小體。核小體由146 個DNA鹼基對和8 個組白 (H2A、H2B、H3和H4各兩個) 組成，組蛋白伴侶負責核小體的組裝及解聚是調控染色質結構的核心元件。因此組蛋白伴侶在DNA複製、DNA損傷修復以及基因轉錄中具有不可替代的作用。在這項研究中，我們發現FACT (facilitates chromatin transcription)複合體在HCC樣本中表達水平顯著上調並且與HCC的細胞生長與擴散轉移有關。為了進一步探索組蛋白伴侶FACT複合體在肝癌發生過程中的作用，我們利用CRISPR/Cas9基因編輯系統和小分子抑製劑Curaxin來抑制FACT複合體的表達。結果發現，抑制FACT複合體的表達有效地抑制了肝癌的發生以及HCC細胞的生長和轉移。有趣的是，我們最近的研究報導了FACT複合體通過促進NRF2的轉錄，來調節肝癌細胞的氧化應激反應。基於這項發現，我們猜想FACT複合體可能是癌細胞應激反應的關鍵調節因子。 低氧是癌細胞的常見特徵。低氧環境可以穩定HIF-1的蛋白表達，並可迅速激活兩類基因的轉錄。一類是使癌細胞能夠在低氧條件下存活的基因（代謝重整），另一類是能進一步賦予癌細胞的侵襲性的基因（自我更新，擴散轉移，血管生成和治療抗性）。在過去的幾十年中，大多數研究集中在HIF-1的調節機制，HIF-1的靶基因以及HIF-1的致癌功能上。在低氧環境下，HIF-1所介導的轉錄必須迅速進行，因為氧氣的即時消耗是細胞存活的關鍵。因此，幫助HIF-1迅速激活靶基因轉錄的分子機制至關重要。然而，現有的研究尚未明確的解決這個問題。我們的初步數據表明，當FACT複合體在HCC細胞中被抑制時，會同時阻礙HIF-1所介導的基因轉錄。我們由此推論，FACT複合體控制的核小體重組可能在HIF-1誘導的快速轉錄中起著重要作用。在這個項目中，我們將徹底研究FACT複合物在癌細胞低氧反應中的機制，以及FACT複合物抑製劑Curaxin在低氧肝細胞癌中的臨床意義。

17108720.label: Realisation of objectives
17108720.value: 1. The FACT complex is responsible for transcription elongation of hypoxic cancer cells The role of the FACT complex in regulating HIF target gene expression during hypoxic adaptation in cancer was investigated by stably knocking out its subunits, SSRP1 and SUPT16H, in MHCC97L HCC cell line. The inactivation of the FACT complex or treatment with curaxin significantly reduced cancer cell viability and mobility in hypoxia. It also repressed 68.4% of hypoxia-induced genes, including well-known HIF transcriptional targets such as VEGFA, ANGPTL4, LOX, NDUFA4L2, and CA9. As a histone chaperone, the FACT complex likely regulates transcription elongation of HIF targets by enabling rapid RNA polymerase II passage through chromatin. This was supported by findings from a 4sU-DRB assay showing decreased transcription elongation rates in FACT complex KO cells, particularly in 1% O2. These results suggest that while HIF-1 controls initiation, the FACT complex aids elongation of transcription during hypoxic adaptation in cancer cells. 2. Hydroxylation, ubiquitination, and protein degradation of the FACT complex through PHD/VHL axis Cancer cells use post-translational mechanisms to handle hypoxic stress. Normally, HIF-1/2α is hydroxylated by PHDs, allowing VHL binding and subsequent protein degradation. In hypoxia, the PHD/VHL axis is inactivated, stabilizing HIF-1/2α. Prior research indicated a protein-protein interaction between SUPT16H and VHL. We hypothesized that the FACT complex's stability is regulated by the PHD/VHL axis and hypoxic stress. Experiments with MHCC97L cells showed that SSRP1 and SUPT16H degraded rapidly compared to β-actin, but their expressions were restored by a proteasomal inhibitor, hypoxic stress, a PHD competitive inhibitor, a VHL inhibitor, and direct KO of VHL. This suggests that FACT complex stability, like HIF-1/2α, is likely regulated by PHD-mediated hydroxylation, VHL-mediated ubiquitination, and proteasome-mediated degradation. Further testing revealed that SSRP1 and SUPT16H are hydroxylated at proline residues by PHDs, with the FACT complex's hydroxylated prolines being identified through immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry. Hence, like HIF-1/2α, the FACT complex is likely prolyl-hydroxylated by PHDs, leading to VHL recognition, poly-ubiquitination, and proteasomal degradation. 3. The implications of FACT complex in HCC hypoxic adaptation Hypoxia is common in malignant tumors. In the TCGA cohort, expressions of SSRP1 and SUPT16H, components of the FACT complex, correlated with hypoxia signatures in various solid cancers, particularly liver cancer. FACT complex was upregulated in about half of 100 HCC samples and was essential for cancer cell proliferation in various cancer types. Its suppression alongside HIF1A completely inhibited cancer cell growth in hypoxia, underscoring FACT's significance. Upregulation of the FACT complex was linked with TP53 mutations. Using hydrodynamic tail-vein injection, we induced Tp53KO; c-MycOE mouse HCC and observed Ssrp1 and Supt16h overexpression, suggesting a relationship with TP53 mutation status. Notably, hepatic artery ligation, a common HCC treatment, induces hypoxia in the liver and inadvertently promotes HCC aggressiveness. However, knocking out Supt16h or SSRP1 or using the FACT complex inhibitor curaxin significantly inhibited tumorigenesis and lung metastasis in the hypoxic liver environment created by hepatic artery ligation. This suggests potential clinical benefits of targeting the FACT complex in HCC treatment. 4. The FACT complex facilitates metabolically reprograming in cancer cells and prevents intracellular acidification Under low oxygen conditions, HIF-1 activates genes to increase glycolysis and decrease pyruvate conversion into acetyl-coenzyme A, which enters the TCA cycle. Our analysis showed that glycolysis is the main pathway affected by the FACT complex in hypoxia. The upregulation of all hypoxia-induced glycolytic enzymes was repressed upon KO of SSRP1 and SUPT16H. Experiments with fluorescence-labeled 2-NBDG, a glucose analog, confirmed the FACT complex's role in regulating glucose uptake under hypoxia. Hypoxia-induced glucose uptake was abolished when either the FACT complex or HIF-1α was silenced. 13C [U-13C] glucose experiments showed hypoxia increased all 13C-labeled glycolytic intermediates, which was prevented when SSRP1 or SUPT16H was knocked out. Hypoxia-induced LDHA and MCT4 expression and extracellular lactate accumulation were also prevented upon SSRP1/SUPT16H KO or curaxin treatment. Intriguingly, intracellular lactate accumulation and acidification increased in SSRP1 or SUPT16H KO cancer cells in hypoxia, leading to extensive apoptosis. In summary, blocking the FACT complex disrupts glycolysis and lactate production/extrusion, causing hypoxic cancer cells to undergo acidification and apoptosis. 5. Targeting the FACT complex as therapy for advanced cancers FDA-approved targeted therapies in HCC, such as bevacizumab, sorafenib, lenvatinib, and cabozantinib, inhibit VEGF signaling. As VEGF induces angiogenesis, anti-VEGF therapies result in intratumoral hypoxia and activation of HIFs. We investigated whether inhibiting the FACT complex with curaxin could further hinder HCC growth by blocking hypoxic gene transcription. Curaxin and bevacizumab co-treatment exhibited a more potent effect in suppressing HCC tumor growth and lung metastasis in an orthotopic implantation model. Co-treatment with both drugs showed a synergistic effect on inhibiting proliferation (KI67) and angiogenesis (CD31). Curaxin also sensitized anti-tumor effects of first-line HCC drugs sorafenib, lenvatinib, and cabozantinib. Treatment with these drugs induced hypoxia response genes in in vivo implanted tumors, while co-treatment with curaxin significantly abolished their expressions. Thus, inhibiting the FACT complex created a vulnerability toward hypoxic stress, amplifying the anti-cancer effect of anti-angiogenetic therapies. Our findings suggest the FACT complex mediates metabolic adaptation to hypoxic stress in cancer, and targeting it may provide an effective therapeutic approach for cancer patients.

17108720.label: Major findings and research outcome
17108720.value: 1. FACT complex is responsible for transcription elongation of hypoxic cancer cells, aiding HIF-1 in regulating HIF target gene expression during hypoxic adaptation. 2. FACT complex's stability is regulated by the PHD/VHL axis and hypoxic stress, involving hydroxylation, ubiquitination, and proteasomal degradation of SSRP1 and SUPT16H. 3. FACT complex is implicated in HCC hypoxic adaptation, and its inhibition via KO or curaxin treatment significantly hinders HCC growth and metastasis in hypoxic liver environments. 4. FACT complex facilitates metabolic reprogramming in cancer cells, regulating glycolysis and lactate production/extrusion under hypoxia. Blocking FACT complex causes hypoxic cancer cells to undergo acidification and apoptosis. 5. Targeting the FACT complex, in combination with anti-angiogenetic therapies, provides a potential effective therapeutic approach for advanced cancers, as it amplifies the anti-cancer effect of these treatments.

17108720.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17108720.value: 1. **Drug Development:** The FACT complex could be a novel target for drug development. New drugs could be designed to inhibit the FACT complex, and these could be tested in pre-clinical models and eventually in clinical trials. 2. **Combination Therapies:** Given the synergistic effect observed when FACT complex inhibition was combined with existing anti-cancer treatments, further research could explore the efficacy of such combination therapies in various types of cancer. 3. **Understanding Resistance Mechanisms:** It would be beneficial to investigate whether cancer cells can develop resistance to FACT complex inhibitors, and if so, what mechanisms they use. This could guide the development of second-line treatments or combination therapies to overcome resistance.

17108720.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17108720.value: In this study, we investigated the role of a protein complex called FACT in the growth and survival of cancer cells under low oxygen conditions, or hypoxia. Hypoxia is common in solid tumors, including liver cancer (HCC), and cancer cells adapt to this environment by changing their gene expression and metabolism. The FACT complex was found to be crucial for these adaptations, helping cancer cells to survive and grow. Importantly, blocking the FACT complex led to a reduction in cancer cell growth and spread, especially when combined with existing anti-cancer treatments. These findings suggest that targeting the FACT complex could be a promising new approach for treating advanced cancers, particularly in combination with other therapies.

17109920.value: We have completed Objectives 1, 3 and 4 and Objective 2 will be completed in the upcoming 6 months. Cluster of differentiation-14 (CD14) is a GPI-anchored membrane protein (mCD14) predominantly expressed on monocytes and macrophages, and to a less extent on non-immune cells such as epithelial cells. It is best known as a pattern recognition receptor that transfers lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from LPS binding protein (LBP) to TLR-4/MD-2 complex to initiate signal transduction and cytokine release. To date, much of the studies that have investigated the role of CD14 in pathological conditions have been in the context of sepsis. Increased serum or plasma sCD14 levels have been observed in various non-sepsis, inflammatory disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis. In the context of renal injury, studies have shown that renal tubular epithelial cells constitutively express low level of CD14 mRNA and its expression is markedly increased in a murine model of unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO). The functional role of extra-myeloid CD14 in non-sepsis renal injury remains to be fully elucidated. Objectives 1 to 3: CKD was induced in wild-type (WT) and CD14 knockout (KO) mice using adenine-induced nephropathy, where excess adenine accumulates in the kidney and is converted to insoluble 8-dihydroxyadenine and 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which crystalizes in renal tubules causing injury. Kidney inflammation was observed in WT mice after 4 to 8 weeks, whereas kidney fibrosis was detected after 8 to 12 weeks following CKD induction. Using a combination of molecular, biochemical, flow cytometry and transcriptomics studies, we demonstrated that CD14 expression was increased in the kidney and localized predominantly in proximal tubular epithelial cells (PTEC) after 4 weeks of adenine-feeding compared to non-CKD WT mice, and its expression increased with severity of CKD, accompanied by increased serum and urinary sCD14 levels. Infiltration of CD45+/F4/80-/CD11c+ cells and CD45+/F4/80-/CD19-/CD3+ cells and a reduction in CD45+/CD11c-/F4/80+/CD86-/CD206+ M2 reparative macrophages were observed in the kidneys of WT CKD mice compared to non-CKD WT mice. Histopathological changes in the kidney included tubular dilation and atrophy, protein cast formation and interstitial fibrosis attributed at least in part to increased accumulation of fibronectin, collagen I, III and IV, alpha-smooth muscle actin and vimentin. Mediators of inflammation comprising MCP-1, RANTES, IL-1beta, IL-6 and TNF-alpha were also increased in the kidneys of WT CKD mice. Kidney injury was noted by an increase in KIM-1 and NGAL expression, and proteinuria, the latter an indication of kidney function deterioration. Kidney function decline was significantly reduced in CD14 KO CKD mice compared to WT CKD mice, and this was accompanied by an increase in Ki67-positive PTEC and infiltration of reparative M2 macrophages into the kidney, reduced influx of dendritic and T cells, preservation of kidney structure and a decrease in kidney injury markers and mediators of inflammation and fibrosis. Transcriptomics analysis of the kidney revealed a significant increase in genes related to cell cycle in CD14 KO CKD mice compared to WT CKD mice, which together with increased Ki67-positive PTEC and reduced cell atrophy and dilation would suggest increased cell proliferation and regeneration in PTEC in CD14 KO mice. KEGG and GO enriched pathways showed increased chemokine and cytokine-cytokine interaction, cell activation and fatty acid metabolism in WT CKD mice compared to CD14 KO mice, which all contributed to kidney inflammation and fibrosis. Pathways enriched in CD14 KO CKD mice included defence response and negative regulation of cell activation. Improvement of kidney function, histology and pathways related to kidney inflammation and fibrosis was also observed in CD14 KO mice in two other murine models of kidney injury comprising folic acid-induced nephropathy and UUO when compared to WT mice. Increased CD14 expression in PTEC was regulated by TNF-alpha and to a lesser extent by TGF-beta1 and IL-6. Overexpression of CD14 in PTEC in a microenvironment free of endotoxins revealed a novel mechanism through which CD14 alone, could induce inflammatory and fibrotic processes independent of LPS or TLR-4 signaling, mediated in part, through upregulation of PI3K and p38 MAPK signaling and increased IL-6, IL-8 and MCP-1 secretion. Although these cytokines are pro-inflammatory mediators, long-term exposure (up to 72 h) of PTEC to IL-6, IL-8 and MCP-1 induced PI3K, ERK and NFKB signaling, which mediated downstream fibronectin, vimentin, alpha-smooth muscle actin and collagen I expression. Inhibition of PI3K, ERK and NFKB signaling in CD14 overexpressing PTEC using specific inhibitors significantly reduced IL-6, IL-8 and MCP-1 secretion and expression of fibronectin, vimentin, alpha-smooth muscle actin and collagen I. Exposure of CD14 overexpressing PTEC to TGF-beta1, a key pro-fibrotic mediator in kidney fibrosis, synergistically increased inflammatory and fibrotic processes in PTEC, underscoring the importance of CD14 in mediating kidney injury and fibrosis. The pathogenic role of CD14 in mediating inflammatory and fibrotic processes was confirmed using CD14-deficient PTEC, which showed a reduction in secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines and reduced fibronectin in the extracellular milieu, mediated through decreased PI3K and p38 MAPK phosphorylation. Objective 4: CD14 expression was negligible in normal adult kidney specimens (n=10). In kidney biopsies from CKD patients (n=70) comprising diabetic nephropathy, IgA nephropathy, membranous nephropathy, hypertension-induced nephropathy and lupus nephritis, increased CD14 expression was localized to PTEC and was also detected in areas of interstitial fibrosis. Tubulo-interstitial CD14 expression correlated with serum creatinine level and proteinuria, and inversely correlated with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Since our murine and in vitro studies showed that CD14 expression induced inflammatory and fibrotic processes in PTEC, we further extended our studies to investigate the association of CD14 expression with mediators of inflammation and fibrosis. In transcriptomic datasets obtained from the public domain, tubulo-interstitial CD14 expression correlated with kidney function decline (positive corelation with proteinuria and serum creatine level, and inversely correlated with eGFR) and mediators of inflammation (IL-1beta, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha, MCP-1, RANTES) and fibrosis (vimentin, alpha-smooth muscle actin, fibronectin, collagen I, collagen III, laminin, matrix metalloproteinase-2 (MMP-2) and MMP-9, in addition to overall interstitial fibrosis score. Taken together, our findings revealed a novel role of CD14 in mediating kidney inflammation and fibrosis, through increased PI3K and p38 MAPK signaling that was independent of LPS or TLR-4 signaling. CD14 may be a novel target for therapeutic intervention in CKD patients although further studies are warranted to confirm this. Problems encountered Not long after the start of this study, we were informed that mouse hepatitis was detected in the animal facilities at the University of Hong Kong and all our breeders had to be culled and rederived. It took over 10 months to rederive breeders and re-establish breeding colonies for this study, which severely delayed part of our animal studies. The remaining studies will be completed in the next 6 months.

17109920.label: Major findings and research outcome
17109920.value: In this study, mCD14 expression was significantly increased in the tubulo-interstitium of renal biopsies from CKD patients, whereas serum sCD14 level was comparable between healthy subjects and CKD patients. Similarly, mCD14 expression was increased in PTEC in murine models of CKD or tubulo-interstitial fibrosis compared to normal kidney specimens, Our findings revealed a novel mechanism through which increased CD14 expression contributed to kidney inflammation and fibrosis independent of LPS and TLR-4 signaling. CD14 overexpression in PTEC induced pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion, cell cycle arrest and accumulation of extracellular matrix components resulting in tubular dilation and atrophy, kidney fibrosis and kidney function decline, whereas CKD induced in CD14 KO mice showed better preservation of kidney function and structure, mediated in part through reduction in PI3K and p38 MAPK signaling, reduced cytokine-cytokine interaction and improved fatty acid metabolism. Studies have reported that CKD is associated with impaired fatty acid oxidation. It is possible that CD14 overexpression may contribute to impairment of fatty acid oxidation although further studies are warranted to confirm this. Infiltration of macrophages into the kidney has also been shown to contribute to CKD through release of pro-inflammatory mediators. CD14 deficiency reduced inflammatory M1 macrophages and increased subpopulation of reparative M2 macrophages, which may contribute to the repair and regeneration of PTEC. CD14 overexpression in PTEC increased PI3K and p38 MAPK signaling, which mediated downstream inflammatory and fibrotic processes, and were further exacerbated in the presence of TGF-beta1 or pro-inflammatory cytokines. TNF-alpha and TGF-beta1 and IL-6, to a lesser extent, regulated CD14 expression suggesting a putative amplification loop through which increased CD14 expression regulates downstream inflammatory and fibrotic processes, which in turn, exacerbates CD14 expression in PTEC. In clinical studies, tubulo-interstitial CD14 expression correlated with kidney function decline, mediators of inflammation and fibrosis, and interstitial fibrosis score highlighting its pathogenic role in CKD. In summary, our findings suggest that CD14 directly contributes to tubulo-interstitial inflammation and fibrosis in CKD progression through increased PI3K and p38 MAPK phosphorylation and chemokine and cytokine secretion, promoting infiltration of inflammatory macrophages and deposition of matrix proteins in the interstitium. This project provided training for a PhD student. Part of these findings have been presented at international conferences such as the American Society of Nephrology Kidney Week 2022, 2024 and 2025 (top-ranked nephrology conferences), and two manuscripts are currently in preparation, with one to be submitted to Kidney International within the next month or so.

17109920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17109920.value: In this study, we made the novel discovery that CD14 overexpression in PTEC contributed to tubulo-interstitial fibrosis in CKD. Although global CD14 KO mice were used in this study, further development of this project would include PTEC-specific CD14 KO mice to validate our current findings. We have also extended our studies to investigate the role of CD14 and gut dysbiosis in lupus nephritis (a murine model of acute kidney injury and CKD) and demonstrated that CD14 expression is cell-type specific. During active lupus nephritis, CD14 expression was reduced in colon epithelial cells and increased in PTEC, leading to the inability of CD14 to retain LPS in the gastrointestinal tract, resulting in LPS to enter the circulation and bind to CD14 in the kidney to mediate kidney inflammation and fibrosis. Treatment of lupus-prone mice with antibiotics reduced gut dysbiosis with a concomitant reduction in CD14 expression in the kidney and subsequent improvement in kidney structure, suggesting an interaction or association between CD14 and gut dysbiosis. Due to our encouraging preliminary findings, we have submitted a grant application to the RGC GRF 2026/27 round for consideration of funding. The result is pending.

17109920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17109920.value: CKD is an escalating global health problem that affects more than 500 million adults. Irrespective of the primary aetiology, tubulo-interstitial fibrosis is considered the common pathway that drives CKD to end-stage renal failure. There is currently no effective treatment for kidney fibrosis. A greater understanding in the mechanisms that mediate tubulo-interstitial fibrosis in CKD will allow researchers to identify specific and novel targets for therapeutic intervention. In this study, we demonstrated that CD14, commonly expressed on macrophages, was increased in PTEC in patients and mice with CKD and its expression correlated with the severity of kidney function decline such as proteinuria and loss of glomerular filtration rate, and histopathological changes such as tubular dilation and atrophy. CD14 overexpression in PTEC induced PI3K and p38 MAPK phosphorylation, which triggered secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, deposition of fibronectin and collagen I in the extracellular milieu and recruitment of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages. In CD14 KO mice with CKD or tubulo-interstitial fibrosis, kidney structure and function were significantly improved, highlighting a previously unknown mechanism through which CD14 contributes to CKD, and which may serve as a novel target for therapeutic intervention.

17110020.label: Project Objectives
17110020.value: To develop a novel statistical method based on “back-calculation” techniques to estimate the epidemic size of an ongoing cluster outbreak similar to SARS/MERS clusters observed in healthcare settings To validate the statistical method with both simulated data and observed SARS/MERS cluster outbreaks, such as SARS clusters in Beijing and Singapore in 2003 and MERS clusters in South Korea in 2015 To evaluate how the real-time estimation of epidemic size will improve the understanding of coronavirus cluster outbreaks to provide valuable information for rapid mitigation responses in real-time

17110020.label: Realisation of objectives
17110020.value: Objective 1 We developed a framework based on the “back-calculation” method to estimate the final cluster size of symptomatic or laboratory-confirmed cases at the early stage of coronavirus super-spreading events (SSEs) when there is limited onward secondary transmission. Asymptomatic cases are not included if they are not reported. We assumed that (i) all cases in a given cluster were infected at around the same time (e.g. infected by the same index case or environmental exposure within a short period of time), (ii) all cases follow the same probability distribution function (pdf) of the incubation period and the onset-to-confirmation delay period; and (iii) the outbreaks are under control with sufficient contact tracing (such that secondary transmission is limited). For SARS and MERS outbreaks with relatively low transmissibility, we assumed that the effective reproductive number Rt after the primary exposure within the cluster was 0 and there is no secondary infection. Additionally, for COVID-19 outbreaks with much higher transmissibility due to significant pre-symptomatic transmission, where the infections happen before the symptom onset of the infectors, we assumed that Rt after the primary exposure can be greater than 1 within one disease generation before the outbreak was controlled by intensive contact tracing. Objective 2 To validate the statistical framework, four scenarios were simulated to mimic the stochastic cluster outbreaks of SARS, MERS, and COVID-19. For SARS and MERS outbreaks under control, we assumed that there was a single exposure and no secondary transmission. For COVID-19, we assumed that 60% of the transmission occurs during the pre-symptomatic phase. For example, we simulated a single-exposure COVID-19 SSE with 10 cases, among which 6 second-generation (60%) cases would be infected by the other 4 first-generation cases in the cluster during the pre-symptomatic phase. However, the 6 second-generation cases would be taken as first-generation infections directly linked to the index case if the pre-symptomatic transmission chains were undetected. With limited onward secondary transmission, we assumed that the transmission would be within one disease generation at Rt = 6/4 = 1.5 under intense contact tracing. We drew random samples of the parameters of incubation period, onset-to-confirmation delay, and generation time from the ranges observed from major outbreaks of SARS, MERS and COVID-19 using Latin-hypercube sampling. As outbreak sizes of 10 to 300 cases were reported in the past coronavirus SSEs, we simulated 1,000 stochastic cluster outbreaks of 30, 50, 100, and 200 infections with and without onset-to-confirmation delay (i.e., 8,000 outbreak scenarios). Prior information of the distributions of the incubation period and the onset-to-confirmation delay period were estimated by bootstrapping from either 50 or 100 simulated cases. From simulated scenarios, we found that the accuracy and precision of our estimates improve with longer observation time, larger cluster size, less uncertainty in onset-to-confirmation delay, and more accurate prior information on the incubation period distribution. As case studies, we applied our model to the Amoy Gardens cluster for the SARS outbreak in Hong Kong, nosocomial clusters for the MERS outbreak in South Korea, and two clusters for the COVID-19 outbreak in Hong Kong. The performance of our framework is satisfactory: the 95% credible interval (CrI) of the estimates contained the true cluster size after 37% of cases were reported in the Amoy Garden SARS outbreak in Hong Kong, 41-62% of cases were observed in the three nosocomial MERS outbreaks in South Korea and 76-86% of cases were confirmed in the two COVID-19 cluster outbreaks in Hong Kong. Objective 3 We found that the precision and accuracy of the cluster size estimation increase with more observed cases: large SSEs can be spotted earlier such that immediate responses can be taken. The estimation performs better with the absence of onset-to-confirmation delay but eventually converges with longer observed time, suggesting that timely reporting and responses benefit the control of SSEs. Further, prior information on parameters improves the performance of the model. In the case studies, we used data from previous outbreaks in the Middle East to inform the size estimation of South Korea MERS clusters. The estimation converges sooner for Cluster 2 and Cluster 3 with more accurate information about the incubation period and the onset-to-confirmation delay period obtained after fitting the model to Cluster 1. We showed that the final size of coronavirus outbreaks can be accurately estimated before 50% of the cases are reported in advance when there is no undetected secondary transmission (or it is accounted for). In the retrospective study on Amoy Gardens SARS Cluster, we got a robust estimation as early as only 37% of all the cases were identified. In practice, hospitals can plan for and prepare resources beforehand for such a large SSE. We also showed that estimates of SARS and MERS cluster sizes were more accurate compared with that of COVID-19, because symptomatic infections would be reported more accurately than the pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic infections of COVID-19 which are sometimes hard to detect and trace. In the case study of Amoy Gardens, it was suspected that SAR-CoV-1 was excreted in the stools when the index case had diarrhea and was transmitted through sewerage, as around 41% of Amoy Gardens cases came from the block where the index case stayed. With exclusive isolation and tracing within the building, the estimation converged soon. However, our method tends to overestimate the cluster size early in simulated SARS and MERS outbreaks when the observed case number is low. For simulated COVID-19 outbreaks if the pre-symptomatic transmission cannot be accounted for, our method always underestimates the cluster size as the secondary infection is not detected and is not observed till later in the outbreak. The real-time daily estimates can be unstable, especially when few cases are reported, and little is known about the distribution of the incubation period and reporting delays. In the Amoy Gardens SARS outbreak, the time of exposure of some cases could be later than the common exposure time that we assumed (May 19, 2003), depending on the time they contacted the contaminated areas. The virus could also transmit via person-to-person contact or contamination on communal facilities such as lifts and doors other than sewage. Nonetheless, it is hard to identify the exact exposure of each case. We adjusted the window of the time of exposure for the MERS outbreak in South Korea by breaking it into three clusters according to the major contact points (i.e., the hospitals) where the cases were from. The subjective reporting of symptom onset can be another source of errors, especially for COVID-19 infections where the symptoms are relatively mild. In summary, our framework can be applied to coronavirus SSEs with no or limited pre-symptomatic transmission and asymptomatic transmission. If SSE is alerted in time and compulsory testing is conducted, the model can be used to improve the projection of the final cluster size. Currently, with the COVID-19 pandemic transiting to the endemic phase and society gradually reopened, our method can be integrated into coronavirus surveillance systems to monitor potential SSEs in large social gatherings.

17110020.label: Major findings and research outcome
17110020.value: We developed a statistical framework based on “back calculation” to estimate the epidemic size of ongoing cluster outbreaks. We first validated the framework in simulated scenarios with the characteristics of SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 superspreading events (SSEs). We retrospectively applied the method to the Amoy Gardens SARS outbreak in Hong Kong in 2003, three nosocomial MERS outbreaks in South Korea in 2015, and two COVID-19 outbreaks in restaurants in Hong Kong in 2020 as case studies. We found that the accuracy and precision of our estimates improve with longer observation time, larger cluster size, less uncertainty in onset-to-confirmation delay, and more accurate prior information on the incubation period distribution. The 95% credible interval (CrI) of the estimates contained the true cluster size after 37% of cases were reported in the Amoy Garden SARS outbreak in Hong Kong, 41-62% of cases were observed in the three nosocomial MERS outbreaks in South Korea and 76-86% of cases were confirmed in the two COVID-19 cluster outbreaks in Hong Kong. We showed that the final size of coronavirus outbreaks can be accurately estimated before 50% of the cases are reported in advance when there is no undetected secondary transmission (or it is accounted for). In the retrospective study on Amoy Gardens SARS Cluster, we got a robust estimation as early as only 37% of all the cases were identified. In practice, hospitals can plan for and prepare resources beforehand for such a large SSE. We also showed that estimates of SARS and MERS cluster sizes were more accurate compared with that of COVID-19, because symptomatic infections would be reported more accurately than the pre-symptomatic and asymptomatic infections of COVID-19 which are sometimes hard to detect and trace. Our framework can be readily integrated into coronavirus surveillance systems to estimate the cluster sizes of SSEs in real-time. With intensive contact tracing to bring SSEs under control, it is possible to predict the epidemic size of SSEs before 50% of the cases are observed. If SSE is alerted in time and compulsory testing is conducted, the model can be used to improve the projection of the final cluster size. Currently, with the COVID-19 pandemic transiting to the endemic phase and society gradually reopened, our method can be integrated into coronavirus surveillance systems to monitor potential SSEs in large social gatherings.

17110020.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17110020.value: COVID-19 is more contagious with a substantial proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission and the emerging variants of concern are estimated to be much more transmissible than the ancestral strain. The model can further develop according to the characteristics of new coronaviruses to predict the community outbreaks that sustain with more disease generations and higher Rt.

17110020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17110020.value: Coronaviruses, including severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 1 (SARS-CoV-1), Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV), and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), are marked by their potential transmission threat of disproportionally large clusters from super-spreading events (SSEs). Real-time assessment of the size of SSEs is required for rapid surveillance and mitigation responses. We developed a statistical framework based on “back calculation” to estimate the epidemic size of ongoing cluster outbreaks. We first validated the framework in simulated scenarios with the characteristics of SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 SSEs. We then retrospectively applied the method to the Amoy Gardens SARS outbreak in Hong Kong in 2003, three nosocomial MERS outbreaks in South Korea in 2015, and two COVID-19 outbreaks in restaurants in Hong Kong in 2020 as case studies. The accuracy and precision of our estimates improve with longer observation time, larger cluster size, less uncertainty in onset-to-confirmation delay, and more accurate prior information on the incubation period distribution. With intensive contact tracing to bring cluster outbreaks under control, it is possible to predict the epidemic size before 50% of the cases are observed. Our framework can be integrated into coronavirus surveillance systems to inform situational awareness of SSEs.

17110220.label: Realisation of objectives
17110220.value: 1. To study the clinical significance of ADK and ENT in human HCC We showed that ADK downregulation and ENT4 upregulation were observed in human HCC patients in both TCGA database and our QMH-HKU cohort. HCC patients with low ADK expression or high ENT4 expression had shorter overall and disease-free survival, which was not observed in other ENT family members. ENT4 overexpression was also significantly associated with larger tumor size in OMH-HKU cohort. Together, we revealed that ADK suppression and ENT4 overexpression were associated with unpromising clinicopathological features. 2. To investigate the hypoxia-mediated regulation of ADK and ENT in human HCC We demonstrated that hypoxia suppressed ADK expression in multiple HCC cell lines and it was rescued by HIF-1 knockdown. Direct binding of HIF to gene promoter regions usually results in transcriptional activation of gene targets, therefore the suppression of ADK under hypoxia may be regulated indirectly. MXI1 is a transcription repressor that has been reported to be induced by hypoxia. It competed with C-MYC to dimerize with MAX protein and thus inhibiting C-MYC activities. We showed that MXI1 was induced in HCC cells under hypoxia and the effect was reversed by knockdown of HIF-1. In silico analysis identified putative E-box element (5’-CACGTG-3’), the binding site of MAX/MYC or MAX/MXI1 dimers, at ADK promoter region. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assay validated that there was a significant enrichment of MXI1 binding to ADK promoter region under hypoxia at the expense of MYC enrichment at the site. On the other hand, we showed that hypoxia upregulated ENT4 in multiple HCC cell lines and its expression could be rescued by HIF-1 knockdown. In silico analysis identified putative hypoxia response element (HRE) at ENT4 promoter region. ChIP assay demonstrated that there was a significant enrichment of HIF-1 binding to ENT4 promoter region under hypoxia. Luciferase reporter assay further confirmed the HRE identified at ENT4 promoter region to be functional. Luciferase signal was only induced by hypoxia in HCC cells expressing wild-type HRE but not the mutant one. With the above experiments, we illustrated that ADK was suppressed by hypoxia via HIF / MXI1 axis while ENT4 was a direct transcriptional target of HIF. 3. To reveal the functional implications of ADK/ENT in HCC development To study the functional role of ADK and ENT4, we have established Adk knockout (Adk-KO) and Ent4 overexpression (Ent4-OE) mouse HCC cell lines. Using mass spectrometry, we showed that Adk knockout and Ent4 overexpression led to accumulation of adenosine extracellularly under hypoxia. Adenosine is an immunosuppressive metabolite. Using NECA, a stable adenosine analog, we studied the effect of adenosine on different immune cells. We demonstrated that adenosine suppressed T cell proliferation and cytotoxicity (IFN-γ and granzyme B). Meanwhile, it induced T cell apoptosis and promoted differentiation to regulatory T cells. Bulk RNA sequencing analysis on NECA-treated T cells revealed the upregulation of regulatory T cell related genes and downregulation of cytotoxic genes. Moreover, we also revealed that adenosine induced myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSC) accumulation while suppressed differentiation to dendritic cells. Adenosine also suppressed MHCII expression but induced CD206 immunosuppressive marker on macrophages. Transcriptome analysis in NECA-treated myeloid cells showed that adenosine increased expression of multiple chemokines that were known to recruit immunosuppressive immune cells. To demonstrate the direct immunosuppressive effect of ADK and ENT4, we performed co-culture experiments of Adk-KO or Ent4-OE mouse HCC cells with T cells. We showed that Adk knockout and Ent4 overexpression further suppressed T cell proliferation. Using an orthotopic implantation model, we showed that Ent4 overexpression promoted HCC tumor growth in immunocompetent mice. We also used a hydrodynamic tail vein injection (HDTVi)-induced HCC model. We simultaneously knocked out Trp53 and Adk while overexpressed c-Myc in liver to induce HCC tumors in immunocompetent mice. Adk deficiency dramatically enhanced HCC growth. We further studied the tumor-infiltrating immune cells to understand how ADK ablation altered the immune composition in HCC. Consistent with what we observed in in vitro studies, we observed a reduction of CD8+ T cells with more exhausted phenotypes. There were also decreases of CD4+ T cells and dendritic cells, suggesting ADK ablation suppressed multiple types of immune cells in the tumor microenvironment. 4. To study the therapeutic effects of ENT inhibitors in HCC We have tried using ENT inhibitors in HCC-bearing mice but ENT inhibitors demonstrated moderate effects in tumor reduction and ENT4-specific inhibitor is currently unavailable. As we demonstrated that ADK and ENT4 promoted adenosine accumulation in the tumor microenvironment, we explored the therapeutic potential of adenosine receptors blockade. We showed that the promoting effect of adenosine on differentiation to regulatory T cells could be reversed by the addition of adenosine 2A receptor (A2AR) antagonist but not adenosine 2B receptor (A2BR) antagonist. On the other hand, the effects of adenosine on myeloid cells (MDSC accumulation and suppression of dendritic cell differentiation) were mainly mediated by A2BR due to the rescuing effect of A2BR antagonist. We then administered adenosine receptor antagonists in vivo together with anti-PD-1, a current second line treatment for HCC patients, to explore study whether the co-blockade of both adenosine receptors can overcome anti-PD-1 resistance. We induced anti-PD-1 resistant Trp53KO / c-MycOE HCC tumors by HDTVi and treat the mice using adenosine receptor antagonists in combination with anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody. The A2AR antagonist used is CPI-444, which is currently used in clinical trials in other cancer types (NCT04280328, NCT02655822). The A2BR antagonist used, PSB1115, reduced tumor growth and MDSC accumulation in a melanoma mice model. We showed that single treatment of anti-PD-1 or the co-treatment of adenosine receptor antagonists did not improve the survival rate of HCC-bearing mice when compared to vehicle group. Excitingly, we demonstrated that combination treatment of anti-PD-1 and co-treatment of A2AR and A2BR antagonists was able to bring survival benefit to HCC-bearing mice. This was accompanied by increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells and DCs into the tumors. This illustrated the potential of blocking adenosine receptors as a combination therapeutic option for HCC patients to improve anti-PD-1 efficacy.

17110220.label: Major findings and research outcome
17110220.value: We found that HIF-1 orchestrates adenosine efflux through two steps in HCC involving ADK and ENT4. First, HIF-1 activates transcriptional repressor MXI1, which inhibits ADK, the key enzyme that mediates adenosine phosphorylation to adenosine monophosphate. This leads to adenosine accumulation in hypoxic cancer cells. Second, HIF-1 transcriptionally activates ENT4, pumping adenosine into the interstitial space of HCC, elevating extracellular adenosine levels. Importantly, both ADK suppression and ENT4 overexpression were associated with poor prognosis in HCC patients. Multiple in vitro assays demonstrated the immunosuppressive role of adenosine on T cells and myeloid cells. Knockout of ADK in vivo skewed intra-tumoral immune cells to pro-tumorigenic and promoted tumor progression. Therapeutically, combination treatment of adenosine receptor antagonists and anti-PD-1 prolonged survival of HCC-bearing mice. We illustrated the dual role of hypoxia in establishing an adenosine-mediated immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and offered a potential therapeutic approach that synergizes with immune checkpoint inhibitors in HCC. The findings in this project were published in a manuscript titled as “Hypoxia-inducible factor orchestrates adenosine metabolism to promote liver cancer development” in the journal Science Advances in 2023.

17110220.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17110220.value: Therapeutic potential of targeting adenosine accumulation and signaling pathway could be further explored. Extracellular adenosine accumulation is well-known to be contributed by CD73/CD39 axis, which are two ectoenzymes that convert ATP to AMP to adenosine. We demonstrated that CD73/CD39 is not the only axis contributing to extracellular adenosine accumulation, adenosine will be pumped out of cancer cells to the surroundings via ADK/ENT4 axis. Therefore, to reduce extracellular adenosine levels, we could potentially target both axes simultaneously. On one hand, there are available CD73 and CD39 targeting antibodies. Ongoing clinical trials aim to study the efficacy of monoclonal antibodies targeting CD39 and CD73 in combination with ICIs (NCT02503774 and NCT04261075). On the other hand, with the advanced platforms of drug screening and protein degrader synthesis, we can identify and produce novel compounds that target ENT4, blocking the efflux of adenosine to the tumor environment.

17110220.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17110220.value: We showed that hypoxia, oxygen deprivation, in the tumor microenvironment led to the accumulation of an immunosuppressive metabolite, adenosine. While adenosine accumulation is well-known to be contributed by CD73 and CD39, we identified another source of adenosine in the cancer cells. In the situation of hypoxia, ADK, an enzyme that gets rid of adenosine, is suppressed. This results in adenosine accumulation in the cancer cells. At the same time, hypoxia also induces ENT4, an adenosine transporter, that pumps adenosine out to the tumor microenvironment. Adenosine suppressed anti-tumorigenic immune cells but promoted pro-tumorigenic immune cells, contributing to tumor progression. Importantly, we showed that blocking the adenosine receptors on immune cells can overcome anti-PD-1 resistance, which is a current FDA-approved treatment for multiple cancer types.

17110420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17110420.value: 非酒精性脂肪肝是一種盛行率達２５％的全球大流行病，其包括單純脂肪變性、非酒精性脂性肝炎、肝纖維化及肝硬化，隨之而患上的肝功能失代償及肝癌的風險亦會增加，為世界各地的社經環境帶來沉重負擔。 現時對於患上非酒精性脂肪肝的非糖尿病患者的療法有限，並會帶來不少負作用。第二型鈉-葡萄糖協同轉運蛋白（ＳＧＬＴ２）抑制劑是可以降低糖尿病患者肝脂肪的抗糖尿病藥物。但是，抑制劑對於患上非酒精性脂肪肝的非糖尿病患者的作用並未得到檢驗。利用磁力共振掃描以顯示質子密度脂肪分數是一種非侵入性手法，並較肝組織學檢查更易量化肝脂肪的變化。而以肝臟纖維掃描儀作肝硬度測量來診斷肝纖維化或肝硬化，亦是高度精準的非侵入性手法。 「老藥新用」概念的新穎性在於把本來用於治療糖尿病患者的第二型鈉-葡萄糖協同轉運蛋白抑制劑轉用以治療非糖尿病。我們以雙盲、隨機、安慰劑的對照試驗來檢視恩格列淨（一種第ＳＧＬＴ２抑制劑）對照安慰劑（比例為１：１）在降低患上非酒精性脂肪肝的非糖尿病患者的肝脂肪的功效，並以磁力共振掃描質子密度脂肪分數作量度。我們過往的研究已從肝臟健康普查的病人庫中確認出患上非酒精性脂肪肝的患者（ｎ＝１０５４），這次隨機抽樣９８位成人患者作研究。療程組將被給予每日１０亳克的恩格列淨。安慰劑藥丸會被製作至與恩格列淨藥丸外觀一致。符合資格的對象會被跟進至第５２週，並會在基準日、第６週、第１２週、第２６週、第４０週及第５２週對其進行臨床、體測及實驗室測試。肝硬度測量會在基準日、第２６週及第５２週進行，利用磁力共振掃描以顯示質子密度脂肪分數會在基準日及第５２週進行。主要結局將會是兩組患者在第５２週相對於基準日的肝脂肪的不同變化（利用磁力共振掃描以顯示質子密度脂肪分數）。次要結局將包括脂肪變性在第５２週的緩解（利用磁力共振掃描以顯示質子密度脂肪分數低於５％）、肝纖維化在第２６週及第５２週的降低（以肝硬度測量）、實驗室結果的改善（如肝轉氨酶、導管酶、鐵蛋白、空腹血糖、糖化血色素、脂肪組合）、各類體測的改善、心血管及腦血管事件。 我們的研究成果將判斷ＳＧＬＴ２抑制劑可以減低患上非酒精性脂肪肝的非糖尿病患者的脂肪變性和肝纖維化。

17110420.label: Major findings and research outcome
17110420.value: Empagliflozin use for 52 weeks significantly reduced liver fat content in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) patients without diabetes mellitus, which was associated with reduction in serum ferritin, fasting glucose and anthropometric parameters (body weight, BMI and waist circumference) and good safety profile.

17110420.value: Further large-scale, multicenter RCTs in diverse populations are needed to verify our results which could potentially extend the role of empagliflozin in treating non-diabetic MASLD, in particular those with steatohepatitis and advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis.

17110520.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17110520.value: 脊髓損傷後的中樞神經疼痛是一種嚴重的神經性疾病，病人長期遭受痛覺過敏和異常性疼痛，嚴重影響患者的生活質量。迄今為止，沒有一種有效的方法可以治愈中樞神經疼痛。多種藥物和物理治療已經被研發並用於神經疼痛治療，但這些方法往往伴隨著耐藥性和耐受性，大大降低了治療效率。脊柱背部的GABAergic神經元為抑制痛覺和感覺過敏的主要調控中樞，而脊髓受損後往往導致背部GABAergic神經元大量損失，為神經痛的主要誘因。鑑於成人脊髓損傷後，神經元不具有再生性，因此幹細胞治療為補充損失的神經元提供了良好前景。先前的研究已經證明移植由多能幹細胞衍生的前腦中間神經元於脊柱背部，可降低神經損傷導致的疼痛。然而這些方法同時伴有風險：多功能幹細胞的致癌性，移植的細胞含多種不同細胞類型以及移植的細胞與接受這脊柱微環境難以融合，由此限制了臨床應用和治療功效。綜上所述，利用譜系重編程方式將病人的體細胞直接誘導分化成為脊柱背部的GABAergic神經元具有重要的研究意義。 我們前期研究通過利用小分子化合物將多能幹細胞分化成為脊柱背部GABAergic神經元，同時鑑定了四個潛在的界定轉錄因子並進一步證明他們可誘導多功能幹細胞分化成為GABAergic神經元。與此同時，我們以非侵入的方式獲取病人尿液培養建立體細胞系，並進一步證明利用已知的界定轉錄因子可將體細胞轉化成為脊柱神經乾細胞。基於這些前期工作，我們旨在利用譜系重編程方式將病人的體細胞直接誘導分化成為脊柱背部的GABAergic神經元並治療脊髓損傷的神經痛。我們的研究目標為：1）建立人體GABAergic神經元報導細胞系用於實時監控其誘導分化的進程，並譜寫GABAergic神經元種基因表達情況；2）利用界定的轉錄因子將人體尿細胞轉化成為脊柱背部GABAergic神經元：3）將分化的GABAergic神經元移植於脊髓損傷神經痛大鼠模型中並評估其治療潛能。此研究將為獲取病人背部脊柱GABAergic神經元治療神經疼痛提供一個更安全，更有效率以及更便宜的策略，促進未來幹細胞移植，治療神經性疾病的臨床應用。

17110920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17110920.value: The segmented nature of the influenza A viral genome allows virus reassortment. Host determinants that can influence reassortment are relatively better studied. However, our understanding of viral factors, in particular at RNA level, controlling this event are limited. Recent studies have suggested that influenza viral RNA (vRNA) segments can interact with each other by forming base-parings. These results have triggered us to conduct a bioinformatics study to look for potential long-range RNA-RNA interactions between vRNA segments. Interestingly, excluding UTR sequences, we have identified 91 well-conserved potential vRNA-vRNA interactions in influenza viruses of diverse backgrounds. Strikingly, about one-third of these predicted interactions have been recently experimentally shown to exist in a few laboratory strains, but whether the other predicted interactions can be identified in other influenza viruses need further investigations. With these results, we have created a panel of isogenic viruses that have silent mutations to disrupt the potential Segment 1-Segment 3 vRNA-vRNA interactions. Recombinant viruses that only have mutations in either of these segments can achieve robust replication. However, when some of these PB2 and PA mutations are used in specific combinations, the resultant viruses are non-viable or highly attenuated. Our follow-up work further suggests that some of these silent mutations can create reassortment biases in co-infection events. The above data prompt us to hypothesize that a viral genome can potentially form multiple RNA-RNA interaction networks. A vRNA segment can use different interaction modes to interact with other viral segments for packaging. Disrupting a few of these critical interacting sites can still allow vRNA segments to adopt alternative RNA-RNA interaction networks for efficient virus production. However, when a significant number of these critical interactions are disrupted, there are very limited options for vRNA segments to build an effective interaction network, thereby resulting in non-replicating or attenuated phenotype. Here, we propose to use isogenic mutants and field isolates to study this topic. We will use a newly developed sequencing technique (SPLASH) to map vRNA-vRNA interactions in these viral genomes. We will identify vRNA-vRNA interactions that are commonly found in different strains and rank their relative importance in the interaction network. Silent mutations will be systematically introduced into representative sites and tested for their impacts on reassortment. Our work will help to explain influenza reassortment and vRNA packaging. It will also allow better understanding on the formation of highly stable internal gene constellations that are frequently found in some lineages (e.g. H9N2 and H5N1). 甲型流感病毒基因組的分段性質允許病毒重組。宿主可影響重組的結果。但是，我們對控制這事的理解是有限。最近的研究表明，流感病毒RNA（vRNA）可以通過形成鹼基配對而產生相互作用。這結果促使我們進行了生物信息學研究，以尋找vRNA片段之間潛在的長距離RNA-RNA相互作用。我們發現除UTR序列外，不同流感病毒中亦發現了91個相同的潛在vRNA-vRNA相互作用。最近亦有實驗證明了這些預測的相互作用中約有三分之一存在於一些病毒株中，但是是否可以在其他流感病毒中鑑定出其他預測的相互作用還需要進一步的研究。根據這些結果，我們創建了一組等基因病毒，這些病毒具有無表型突變，可破壞潛在的第1段3段vRNA-vRNA相互作用。僅在這兩個片段之一中具有突變的重組病毒可以良好複製制能力。但是，當這些PB2和PA突變中的某些突變以特定組合使用時，所得病毒將無法存活或高度減毒。我們的後續工作進一步表明，這些無表型突變可控制病毒基因重組。 以上數據從而令我們假設病毒基因組可能形成多個RNA-RNA相互作用網絡。 vRNA片段可以使用不同的相互作用模式與其他病毒片段相互作用而影響病毒包裝。破壞其中一些關鍵的相互作用位點仍然可以使vRNA片段採用替代的RNA-RNA相互作用網絡來生產病毒。但是，當大量此類關鍵相互作用被破壞時，vRNA片段可建立有效相互作用網絡的選擇變得非常有限，從而導致病毒變成非複制型或減毒表型。 在此研究建議中，我們會使用同基因突變體和其他病毒分離株來研究這一主題。我們將使用新開發的測序技術（SPLASH）來繪製這些病毒基因組中vRNA-vRNA相互作用的圖。我們將鑑定在不同病毒株中常見的vRNA-vRNA相互作用，並對它們在相互作用網絡中的重要性進行估計。我們的工作將有助於解釋流感病毒的基因重組和病毒包裝。

17110920.label: Realisation of objectives
17110920.value: i) Setup of influenza virus genome dataset for in-silicon analysis 17 viral genomes with different HA and NA subtypes were aligned (avian H1, human H1 (2016), pandemic H1N1/2019, swine H1, human H2, avian H3, human H3, H4, H5, H6, H7, H8, H9, H10, H11, H13 and H16; N=15 per group) were download from Influenza Research Database. Viral sequences were aligned and concatenated. Concatenated viral genomic sequences, with 5’ and 3’ UTRs being deleted, of each group are aligned and analysed by a program designed for detecting long range RNA-RNA interactions (LRIscan). Several potential RNA-RNA interactions that are conserved in each group are identified (Average base-paring region: 5-20 bp). Ninety-one of these interactions can be found in at least 15 out of 17 studied groups. Among the 91 interactions, we then focused on the interactions between PB2 and PA segments, two of the longest polymerase genes which are often co-packaged in pandemic strains (e.g. H2N2/1957, H3N2/1968 and H1N1/2009). ii) Development of bioinformatics pipeline to design viral mutants to study viral RNA interaction. We developed a bioinformatics platform design synthetic viral RNA sequences. Silent mutations with different sequence features (e.g. CG content, and codon bias) of our targeted sequences can be automatically generated via this in-house platform. Mutated PB2 (N=4) and PB1 (N==4) gene segments with silent mutations at the targeted sites were generated. These mutants all targeted to the PB2-PA RNA-RNA interacting sites (N=16) revealed about the above bioinformatics analyses. iii) Rescue of recombinant viruses with silent mutations All wild type (WT) and mutated viral RNAs from the background of A/Brisbane/57/2007 were tested in various combinations, with the aim of rescuing recombinants using reverse genetics techniques. No recombinants could be rescued when all designed mutations in both PB2 and PA segments were present. In contrast, when different combinations of PB2 and PA mutations were applied, recombinant viruses could be successfully rescued. Many of these mutant versions yielded progeny virus titres which were comparable to the WT level. Notably, two specific mutants: PB2-1M/PA-3M and PB1-2M/PA-3M (where 1M represents mutations at the 5’ end of vRNA, 3M represents mutations at the 3’ end of vRNA, and 2M represents mutations in region excluding the 5’ and 3’ ends) demonstrated attenuated phenotypes, evidenced by a greater than tenfold reduction in progeny virus titres and decreased plaque size in MDCK cells. iv) Application of SPLASH technology We successfully cultured and purified virions in quantities sufficient for subsequent RNA chemical modifications. Early attempts yielded low quantities of chemically-modified viral RNA, but this issue was addressed by sending a postgraduate student to an overseas laboratory for hands-on training. In light of our observations from the rescued viruses, we selected the WT, PB2-1M/PA-3M, and PB1-2M/PA-3M for further characterization. Progeny viruses were purified and subjected to SPLASH analysis using previously published protocols. The treated RNA molecules were then examined via next-generation sequencing (NGS) (NovaSeq, PE100). v) Development of an in-house pipeline to study results from SPLASH analyses and identify critical region for viral RNA interactions We developed an in-house program to study the deduced NGS data to revealing viral RNA interaction between PB2, PA and other viral segments. Deduced viral RNA interactions could be presented by either heat maps or chord diagrams. The viral RNA interactions disrupted by the mutations in the mutants, but not in the wild-type viruses, were identified. vi) Development of droplet-based RT-PCR assays To facilitate accuracy quantification of viral RNA in samples, we developed droplet-based RT-PCR assays to facility our work (M gene). We further converted these assays as multiplex assays to study other respiratory viruses. vii) Analysing influenza virus reassortment pattern using single cells In order to better understand viral reassortment at the single-cell level, we utilized our previously established microfluidic system to cultivate and capture individual infected cells. We successfully managed to extract infectious virus particles from a single cell co-infected with various influenza virus strains. Additionally, we were able to integrate the use of the microfluidic system with the above mentioned droplet-based RT-PCR platform to carry out single virion RNA sequencing. Partial viral RNA (vRNA) segments could be deciphered using this pipeline, allowing the study of viral reassortment patterns in progeny viruses produced from co-infected cells. viii) Study of viral reassortment patterns in nature influenza viruses We also applied our established bioinformatics pipelines to study virus reassortment patterns in isolates detected in our routine virus surveillance work. Major hurdles: The COVID-19 pandemic severely affected the progress of this project. A substantial number of experiments were unexpectedly interrupted due to unforeseeable COVID outbreaks in our laboratory settings or the governmental public health policy in 2021 and 2022 (e.g. Omicron wave). These caused unnecessary expenditure and manpower for unforeseeable events. A PhD student (Lai) was originally scheduled to receive on-site training for SPLASH at UK in 2021 (David Bauer’s Lab, Francis Crick Institute), but has to be cancelled due to the travel restriction in Hong Kong. As both my collaborator was heavily involved in COVID programs in UK, we could only manage to send another PhD student (Pavithra) to receive such laboratory training in 2023. Nonetheless, the SPLASH technique has been successful established in my lab at HKU. Attempt to overcome problems (Objective 5): Due to the delay in sending a postgraduate for an overseas training, we then explore the use of digital RT-PCR to study viral reassortment pattern at a single virion level. Highly diluted virus culture from co-infection experiments was used to generate single-virion droplets for viral genome amplification, followed by single virion sequencing. Virus segments that are frequently co-packaged together are considered to a highly stable internal gene cassette that have a strong linkage disequilibrium.
