17117020.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17117020.value: 生物入侵除了在全球物种灭绝过程中扮演了重要角色外，还造成了重大的经济损失，并且对人类健康产生严重威胁。外来物种的本地性以及全球性的引入速率均在增加且未见减缓趋势，导致外来物种的持续性大量积累。在亚洲，外来物种的本地性以及全球性的引入速率均在增加且未见减缓趋势，导致外来物种的持续性大量积累。在这一背景下，了解入侵物种对于物种群落和生态系统过程的影响，将对建立有效的生物保护计划和管理策略产生至关重要的作用。传统的研究方法往往只关注单个入侵/外来种的影响。然而，在目前的趋势下，我们亟需研究多个共存的入侵/外来种是如何共同影响本地物种群落和生态系统的稳定的。 在本研究中，申请人拟利用四种在香港和澳门广泛分布入侵蚂蚁，探讨其对本地自然群落以及生态系统过程产生的影响。首先，研究将会评估这些入侵物种对于本地自然分布的蚂蚁物种丰富度、个体丰度及群落物种组成产生的单一和累加效应。然后，通过利用功能多样性研究方法，本研究将会探究每个入侵物种对于本地群落的影响是随机性的还是有针对性的只对某些特定物种产生影响；同时利用生态、形态和生理性状检验Gause竞争排斥假说：最相似的物种间往往竞争最激烈。 在基于对蚂蚁群落物种构成的认识基础上，本研究拟通过三个实验来验证以下三种假说，深入了解其这四种入侵物种对生态系统功能如分解作用、种子扩散及对于脊椎动物的资源可用性上产生的影响。假说一：分解作用假说，入侵物种在增加分解速率的同时也会减少分解者的多样性。假说二：种子扩散假说，入侵种的存在会导致自然群落中某个特定子集蚂蚁的灭绝，从而将直接影响种子，特别是较大的种子的散布过程，并增加脊椎动物对种子取食。假说三：资源可用性假说，由于入侵种而导致的本地蚂蚁群落组成的变化将改变食虫脊椎动物的捕食模式。由于避免取食入侵蚂蚁，食虫动物可能增加对本地蚂蚁物种的捕食率。 总而言之，本项目将全面了解入侵物种的生态影响及其潜在机制。此外，当前以及未来全球化的趋势势不可挡。在此背景下生物入侵将成为一个重大挑战。 本研究将全面了解入侵物种的生态学影响以及其潜在机制，同时掌握入侵物种对本地群里以及生态系统的单一、累积以及级联效应之间的差别。其结果将使我们深入了解生物入侵的影响。

17117020.label: Realisation of objectives
17117020.value: In a first part, we confirmed that invasive ant species disrupt native communities. This was first shown in the sole case of the fire ants, Solenopsis invicta, which impacts competitive interactions and alter functional diversity of invaded communities (Wong et al. 2022). In a second time, we show that the magnitudes of invasive ant effects were, however, species specific, dependent on the density of the invasive species, and ultimately that the presence of multiple invasive species may mitigate some of these impacts (Hu et al. 2025). The invasion intensity of three invasive species, A. gracilipes, P. longicornis, and S. invicta, had significantly negative effects on functional diversity indices, while in areas invaded by P. megacephala, the near absence of native species (present in ~4% of the pitfall traps) prevented functional diversity analyses but indicated very strong impacts on local species richness. Comparisons across non-invaded, single invasion, and co-invasion scenarios revealed distinct patterns: single invasions caused pronounced reductions in both functional and taxonomic diversity, whereas co-invasion scenarios exhibited more limited changes. Further analyses demonstrated that antagonistic interactions between co-invasive species could mitigate the negative effects on α-diversity and preserve ecosystem functions through functional substitution. Using distinct sites and methodological approaches, results in Rocha et al. (to be submitted) reached similar conclusions on the impacts of A. gracilipes and S. invicta. In a second set of experiments, we were interested in studying the combined effects of competition and temperature on species performance to identify mechanisms of dominance by invasive species and exclusion for native ant species. To do so, we developed a new equipment and software allowing us to accurately quantify the foraging and recruitment behaviours of ants in situ (Hu et al. 2024). With this new approach, hundreds of individuals can be tracked to monitor their abundance, speed and direction of foraging individuals allowing to measure their activity on baits. Using this methodology, we then investigated the foraging behaviour and performance of eleven ant species (six native and five exotic) in response to temperature to evaluate how their thermal performance varied and could represent a significant trait in competition (Hu et al. submitted to the Proceedings of the Royal Society B). In total, we collected 846 hours of field behavioral recordings and simultaneously recorded substrate temperature data. Additionally, we measured the CTmax of 748 individual foraging workers corresponding to five exotic (420 individuals) and six native ant species (328 individuals). We constructed the thermal performance curves (TPC) of these eleven species to assess their responses to temperature. Finally, to compare thermal adaptability between exotic and native species, we integrated historical ant foraging activity data (10,023 records) and critical thermal limit data for local species (50 native species, 2,218 data points). Our results indicate that while CTmax values of exotic and native species are rather similar, all exotic ant species exhibit generally lower temperature sensitivity (lower Q10) and used different strategies to dominate baits. Overall, these results also suggests that increased temperatures could be more beneficial for exotic species survival. Finally, we investigated the roles of invasive species on several ecosystem functions. While the initial plan was to use four invasive species, we focused on three of them, A. gracilipes, P. longicornis and S. invicta, due to the limited number of sites invaded by P. megacephala. For each of the species studied, we used a split-plot design with replications conducted in both invaded and non-invaded areas, thus not only accounting for the effects of each individual invasive ant species, but also to those of particular field conditions in which those species are encountered. In a first experiment, we focused on the effects of invasive ants on carrion decomposition and on other non-ant decomposer insects (Rocha et al. In prep.). Ants accelerated decomposition, but the presence of invasive ants had mixed effects depending on their identity. Paratrechina longicornis and A. gracilipes had little effect on the carrion or were displaced by some native species. In contrast, S. invicta impacted the decomposition rate and was never displaced. Maggots were still the primary decomposers, but their contribution varied due to predation by ants and competition. Species like P. longicornis and A. gracilipes may not directly impact the process but could indirectly affect it by altering the ant community structure. In contrast, S. invicta impacts the decomposition process both directly and indirectly. We also focused on three specific ecosystem function performed by ants: scavenging, carbohydrate removal and predation efficiency and how the presence or absence of S. invicta affect the performance of these functions by ant community. By examining ecologically relevant morphological traits of ant assemblages across invasion density gradients, we expected to find traits that act as both response (traits that respond to invasion) and effect (traits that mediate ecosystem function efficiency) traits. Our findings highlight S. invicta invasion as a significant biotic filter, particularly impacting the body length and head shape of species in invaded communities. Moreover, we found that these traits not only serve as response traits but also influence both scavenging and carbohydrate removal efficiency. Interestingly, while S. invicta is responsible for trait abundance shifts in the resident assemblage, it appears that it provides compensatory effects that maintain or even increase function efficiency. It should be noted that while we initially proposed to study seed dispersal as an ecosystem function, we modified our plans for logistical reasons as the obtention of viables seeds accepted by ant species present in invaded and non-invaded areas was not possible. Instead, we focused on vertebrate carrion decomposition, scavenging (insects), carbohydrate removal and predation which represent ecological and ecosystem functions commonly performed by ants, and that are efficiently measured. In a last experiment, we evaluated how the presence of multiple invasive ant species belonging to different taxa and size-groups impacted local communities or limited the impacts of each other. For this experiment, we used the invasive frog, Eleutherodactylus planirostris, and two invasive ant species A. gracilipes and S. invicta. Here, we hypothesize that the two invasive ants will be avoided (low electivity) by the frog; and thus consequently, we hypothesize that the frog’s diet in invaded communities will have a higher percentage of non-Formicidae taxa in terms of abundance and volume than uninvaded communities, because of the joint effect of competitive exclusion of the native ants and the learned avoidance of the invasive ants by the frog. Finally, we hypothesize that the native ants will be more limited by the competition pressure of the invasive ant species than by the predation pressure of the frogs, considering the generalist nature of the invasive frog. Our results demonstrate that the invasive generalist predator frog can have deleterious effects on the native ant community, which can are additive to the deleterious competitive interactions caused by co-invaded invasive ant species. These combined effects, however, are ant species-specific and are still unfolding. The combined impact of these three species, particularly the invasive frog and the invasive ant, S. invicta, is expected to increase as they spread China and as the frog predator learns to avoid them. Finally, as several of the students working on these projects learnt more about ecosystem functions and services, we used this knowledge to publish an article of review (Rocha et al. 2024).

17117020.label: Major findings and research outcome
17117020.value: In a first study (Wong et al. 2022), we used morphological, dietary, physiological and behavioural traits to test whether environmental filtering, limiting-similarity competition or hierarchical competition explain invasions by Solenopsis invicta on ant assemblages. We detect both competition mechanisms; with invasion success not only explained by limiting similarity in body size and thermal tolerance but also by the invader's superior position in trait hierarchies reflecting competition for common trophic resources. In a follow-up study using four invasive ant species, however, we found that these mechanisms are both invasive species and density dependent (Hu et al., in prep.). In Hu et al. 2025, our results demonstrated that four invasive ants had profound impacts on the taxonomic, compositional and functional diversity of ants. The magnitude of these impacts, however, were highly dependent of the invasive species considered as well as their density. Surprisingly, single invasions caused more pronounced reductions in both functional and taxonomic diversity, than co-invasion scenarios with more limited changes. Antagonistic interactions between co-invasive species may mitigate the negative effects on species diversity and preserve ecosystem functions through functional substitution. Thanks to a new device and software allowing to track the abundance, speed, direction and behaviours of ants during foraging activities (Hu et al. 2024) as well as the use of traditional methods assessing ant thermal tolerance and foraging activities, we found that most invasive ants presented broader thermal niches than native ants, but all showed distinct competitive strategies, including higher activity levels. This suggests that environments with increased temperature favour the foraging strategies and dominance of invasive species over native species (Hu et al., submitted). Finally, we studied the impacts of ants on various ecosystem functions and how invasive species potentially altered those. Thanks to the development of a new apparatus (Bogar et al. 2024), we show the importance of body size in the functions played by ant communities. Then we found that invasive species roles in ecosystems were species dependent but could impact ecosystems functions through direct effects (e.g. S. invicta, Bogar et al. submitted) or indirect effects through the modification of native communities (Rocha et al. in prep). The presence of an invasive frog within ant-invaded areas, increased the predation pressure on ant communities and other insects, while invasive ants were largely avoided. This shows that additional invasions from distinct taxonomic groups could increase the risks of extinctions for native species (Rocha et al. in prep).

17117020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17117020.value: Biological invasions are well-known for their impacts on biodiversity. Several questions remain, however, on how the presence of multiple invasive species in a given environment may act on local communities and ecosystems. Based on the study of four invasive ant species present in Hong Kong, our results show widespread negative impacts of all invasive species on the species richness and morphological diversity of local ant communities, but the magnitude of these impacts varied in function of the identity of the invasive species and of their invasion density. When multiple invasive ant species co-existed, however, their impacts on local ant communities were mitigated, with antagonistic interactions between co-invasive species potentially limiting their negative effects. Co-invasions, however, may represent unstable state over longer periods of time. In distinct experiments, we show that ant invasions also altered key ecological processes such as carrion decomposition and the associated guild of decomposers (e.g. maggots) through the direct actions of invasive species (direct effects) or through the changes of native species composition (indirect effects). Furthermore, when invaders belonging to different taxonomic groups (e.g. ants and frogs) co-existed, their impacts can be additive, increasing local extinction risks for native species, and ultimately increasing weakening ecosystems.

17117120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17117120.value: Talaromyces marneffei (previously known as Penicillium marneffei) is the aetiological agent of a wide spectrum of potentially fatal infections in human, especially immunocompromised patients such as HIV-positive patients and transplant recipients. It is regarded as one of the world’s top ten most feared fungi. Talaromycosis (formerly penicilliosis) is endemic in Southeast Asian region but imported cases are also encountered in other countries. Infections are often severe and difficult to treat, requiring prolonged antifungal therapy. We have recently discovered and characterised the first mycovirus, Talaromyces marneffei partitivirus-1 (TmPV1), in T. marneffei. Using isogenic virus-infected and virus-free T. marneffei isolates, we showed that TmPV1 enhanced the virulence of T. marneffei in infected mice. Our previous study pioneered a new arena in the mycovirology field of thermal dimorphic fungi. However, we do not understand the molecular pathogenesis and mechanisms regarding the hypervirulence phenomenon of virus-infected T. marneffei. In this proposed study, we aim to investigate 1) the interaction between mycovirus-infected T. marneffei and the host, 2) the functional roles of secreted TmPV1-elements in TmPV1-infected T. marneffei. The gene changes of both host and pathogen, including isogenic virus-free and TmPV1-infected T. marneffei upon infection, both in in vitro and in vivo model, will be examined. Our preliminary results demonstrated that large number of TmPV1-like particles are released from virus-infected T. marneffei. Moreover, pilot RNA-Seq data showed that virus-infected T. marneffei suppress more immune genes, which are responsible for recruitment and activation of T-cells and phagocytes etc., than isogenic virus-free T. marneffei-infected human peripheral blood mononuclear cell-derived macrophages (hPBDMs). It is possible that TmPV1-infected T. marneffei hide inside macrophages by suppressing immune responses, inhibiting the recruitment of other immune cells. Our pilot studies further showed that the TmPV1-infected T. marneffei secretions, are immunomodulatory on host cells. Together these preliminary results suggested that likely virus-infected T. marneffei secretes immunomodulatory factors to suppress host immune responses, causing hypervirulence effect in virus-infected T. marneffei. 17117120.label: Realisation of objectives
17117120.value: Objective 1: Scope of investigation undertaken hPBMC derived marcophages were treated with virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei and then subjected to transcriptomic analysis for differentially expressed genes. Results achieved Transcriptomic analysis of the hPBMC treated with virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei 24 h.p.i obtained from RNA-sequencing suggests that virus-infected T. marneffei suppressed more immune genes than virus-free T. marneffei. 82 of them could be successfully mapped against the human reference genome, UCSC hg19, as identifiable genes. Majority of the DEGs that were downregulated in virus-infected T. marneffei treatment group played roles in the immune system such as defense response, response to cytokine, cytokine-mediated pathways, and immune system processes. Objective 2: Scope of investigation undertaken Isolated extracellular vesicles derived from virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei were characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and proteomic analysis. Additionally, virus-free T. marneffei and Aspergillus fumigatus were co- incubated with EVs of virus-infected T. marneffei to determine the role of EVs in the transmission of TmPV-1 elements. Results achieved TEM images revealed that EVs derived from virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei to be round and cup-shaped. EVs of virus-free T. marneffei were mostly concentrated in fraction 5 of an iodixanol density gradient, while EVs of virus-infected T. marneffei were mostly located in fraction 4 of an iodixanol density gradient. The EVs of virus-free T. marneffei ranged from 169.8 nm to 205.6 nm in diameter, while those of virus-infected T. marneffei ranged from 161.2 nm to 196 nm in diameter. A total of 1832 proteins were shared between the EVs of virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei, but only 184 of the proteins were found differentially expressed, in EVs of virus-infected T. marneffei in comparison to EVs of virus-free T. marneffei. Among these differentially expressed proteins, 45 of the upregulated proteins, played roles in cellular processing, while 37 downregulated proteins, took part in localization. Downregulated proteins were shown to be most prominent in multiple transporter activity and some threonine-type endopeptidase activity in the GO classification for molecular function, but none of the upregulated proteins were found under the same GO classification. Lastly, most of the upregulated proteins constituted to cellular anatomical entity of the yeast cell, and most of the downregulated proteins were components of the membrane. Mutually exclusive proteins, Thioredoxin and FMP32, were found in virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei, respectively. PCR amplification of the capsid gene of TmPV-1 revealed that TmPV-1 viral particles were not detected in both the pellet nor supernatant of virus-free T. marneffei and A. fumigatus after co-incubation with EVs of virus-infected T. marneffei in the culture broth. Objective 3: Scope of investigation undertaken Murine macrophage cells were subjected to virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei infection to determine the recovery rate of each fungal strain by CFU count and to examine the inflammatory response of the murine macrophage cells by RT-qPCR. Results achieved No significant difference was found between the recovery rates of virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei in J774 at 24 h.p.i and 48 h.p.i. The mRNA expressions of the pro-inflammatory cytokines, tumour necrosis factor, interleukin 5, and interleukin 6, anti-inflammatory cytokines, interleukin 1 receptor antagonist (IL-1RA), interleukin 10 (IL-10) and interleukin 13 (IL-13), and iNOS expression between virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei infection in J774 at 24 h.p.i and 48 h.p.i demonstrated no statistical differences. Objective 4: Scope of Investigation Undertaken The role of the secretions, EV, from T. marneffei in mice model were investigated by exploring the use of T. marneffei secretions, EVs, as a novel vaccine candidate. T. marneffei is a pathogenic fungus causing severe infections in immunocompromised individuals. We aimed to address the lack of existing vaccines for fungal pathogens by evaluating the immunogenicity and protective capabilities of these EVs in a controlled setting. We used a murine model to test the efficacy of these EVs in inducing immune responses that could protect against T. marneffei infection. The study specifically looked at the types of immune cells activated and the overall survival rate of the mice after exposure to the fungus. Results Achieved BALB/c mice were vaccinated with different doses of T. marneffei EVs (0, 2.5, 5, 10, 25, 50 ug) via i.p. administration thrice with 2 weeks interval each before challenging against lethal dose of T. marneffei conidia (8×106 conidia). Groups of 5 mice were included in each experimental group and their conditions were recorded daily. The Kaplan-Meier method and the log-rank test were performed for statistical analysis. The results demonstrated that EVs from T. marneffei with doses from 10ug to 50ug in terms of protein amount successfully induced protective immunity in mice. Mice vaccinated with these EVs doses showed enhanced survival rates when challenged with lethal doses of T. marneffei conidia, and the mice vaccinated with the highest 50ug EV dose even shown 100% survival. On the other hand, the lower doses of 5ug and below didn’t show any protective effect when challenged with lethal doses of T. marneffei. ELISA of mice sera against antigens of T. marneffei EV proteins and yeast proteins collected one week before conidia challenging. It is shown that the 25 and 50ug dose of EV vaccination were highly antigenic. Percentage of CD4+ T cell, CD8+ T cell and CD4+/CD8+ T cell ratio in PBS or EVs vaccinated mouse spleens at day 4, 7 and 10 after challenged with lethal dose of T. marneffei conidia were analysed by flow cytometry. The results suggested that T. marneffei EVs protected mice against T. marneffei infection by enhancing Th2 CD4+ and cytotoxic CD8+ Tcl cells response, which all together orchestrated the production and release of IL4, and interferon-gamma. These immune responses are critical for effectively targeting and eliminating the fungal pathogen. The study confirmed that the EVs could stimulate both antibody production and T-cell responses, providing a comprehensive defense mechanism. As a result, this suggested the potential of T. marneffei EVs as a foundation for developing vaccines against fungal diseases, demonstrating their capability to induce strong and protective immune responses in animal models. Scope of Investigation Undertaken The immunogenic properties of T. marneffei EVs were evaluated with talaromycosis patients’ samples. The goal was to determine if these EVs could trigger immune responses in hosts, particularly focusing on their interaction with antibodies from talaromycosis patients. Results Achieved The immunogenicity was confirmed through immunoblotting, where serum samples from patients showed strong reactivity against EV proteins. This suggested that the EVs contained multiple antigens that are targets of the immune system during infection. The presence of these antigens on the EV surface makes them accessible to the host's immune system, enhancing their potential as vaccine components. As a result, this demonstrated that T. marneffei EVs are not only capable of inducing specific immune responses in experimental models but are also recognized by the immune systems of infected individuals. This finding supports the potential use of these EVs in vaccine development, as they contain naturally immunogenic components that could provide effective protection against fungal infections.

17117120.label: Major findings and research outcome
17117120.value: T. marneffei causes a disease known as talaromycosis. Immunocompromised individuals especially HIV/AIDS patients are more susceptible to T. marneffei infection than immunocompetent individuals. Therefore, talaromycosis poses considerable health risk to HIV/AIDS patients. T. marneffei strains that harbours TmPV-1 depicted hypervirulent pathogenicity increasing the health concerns in infected individuals. Understanding the mechanism underpinning the hypervirulence phenotype of virus-infected T. marneffei that involves EVs in the process helps improve treatments against hypervirulent T. marneffei infection and offers insights into understanding the potential role of EVs as a virulent factor. The current study successfully isolated and characterized EVs of isogenic virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei to be round and cup-shaped. The EVs of virus-free T. marneffei ranged from 169.8 nm to 205.6 nm in diameter, while those of virus-infected T. marneffei ranged from 161.2 nm to 196 nm in diameter. Despite the diverse functions of EVs, their function as cargo transporter to deliver TmPV-1 from virus-infected T. marneffei to virus-free T. marneffei and A. fumigatus was unsuccessful. This reinforces the fact that transmission of TmPV-1 occurs through horizontal and vertical transmission of vegetatively compatible fungi and does not get transmitted through EVs. Additionally, mutually exclusive proteins, thioredoxin and FMP32, that were found in EVs of virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei, respectively, may a play a critical role in the virulence of each strain. Transcriptomic analysis suggested that there was an enhanced immunosuppression in hPBMC exerted by virus-infected T. marneffei than by virus-free T. marneffei. However, the results from reverse transcription coupled with Sybr Green qPCR showed no statistical differences in the mRNA expression of inflammatory cytokines of murine macrophage cells infected with virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei. The recovery rate of virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei in murine macrophage cells also did not reveal statistical significance. 17117120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17117120.value: The current study successfully isolated and characterized EVs of virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei. In future studies, macrophage cells can be treated directly with EVs derived from virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei to further understand their roles during infection. Additionally, the mutually exclusive proteins, thioredoxin and FMP32, that were found in virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei, respectively, may be involved in the virulence of the pathogens. Therefore, mutagenesis studies can be performed to verify their roles as potential virulence factors. Besides using isogenic fungal lines constructed through protoplast transformation, including an isogenic fungal line constructed through drug treatment can provide additional insight simultaneously in future comparative studies.

17117120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17117120.value: Talaromyces marneffei is an infectious fungus that causes a disease named talaromycosis. T. marneffei infection is common in immunocompromised individuals such as HIV/AIDS patients. A study previously found that the hypervirulent strain of this pathogen harboured a fungal virus, TmPV-1, but the mechanism underpinning the hypervirulent characteristic of the hypervirulent strain of T. marneffei is not fully understood. The current study found that both infected and uninfected T. marneffei strains secrete extracellular vesicles, which are recognized to exhibit diverse functions including immunomodulation. However, no significant difference was found in the mRNA expression of inflammatory cytokines between macrophage cells infected with virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei by Sybr Green qPCR. The recovery rates of virus-free and virus-infected T. marneffei from macrophage cells were also statistically insignificant. Therefore, further studies are required to verify whether the hypervirulent characteristic of the infected T. marneffei strain is due to immunosuppression of the host genes during infection.

17117320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17117320.value: Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are multipotent stromal cells that can be differentiated into various cell types, including osteoblasts (bone cells) and adipocytes (fat cells). In health, the lineage commitment of MSCs to osteoblasts and adipocytes is well balanced for the maintenance of bone density and metabolic homeostasis. Disruption of this fine balance due to ageing, obesity and/or diabetes often leads to increased bone marrow adiposity and osteoporosis, which is the most common metabolic bone disease characterized by reduced bone mass and density. However, the molecular machineries controlling MSCs fate and the pathophysiological roles of bone marrow adipocytes remain poorly understood. Piezo1 is a mechano-sensitive non-selective cationic channel transducing mechanical stimuli (including shear stress, compression and membrane stretch) into electrical and intracellular biochemical signals. Our preliminary findings indicate that Piezo1, unlike its homolog Piezo2, is highly expressed in bone marrow MSCs. Moreover, in a mouse model in which the Piezo1 gene is selectively deleted in platelet growth factor receptor-α-expressing progenitor cells (notably MSCs), we observed a markedly-reduced bone density and mass, accompanied with increased accumulation of bone marrow adipocytes. In the same line, bone marrow MSCs isolated from the Piezo1 knockout mice exhibit increased potential to differentiate into adipocytes, but decreased lineage commitment to osteoblasts. Altogether, our initial findings suggest that Piezo1 at the plasma membrane of bone marrow MSCs senses mechanical stimuli and regulates cell fate decision, thereby leading to increased bone formation and reduced bone marrow adiposity, which may in turn improves systemic insulin sensitivity. To further test this hypothesis, we will perform bone marrow transplantation experiments in mice to verify the MSCs cell autonomous function of Piezo1 and will evaluate whether or not exercise-induced increase in bone formation, reduction in bone marrow adiposity and improvements in systemic insulin sensitivity is dependent on Piezo1 activation in MSCs (presumably associated with shear stress). Furthermore, we will take advantage of our unique animal model to define the metabolic roles of bone marrow adipocytes, and will use both hypothesis-driven and unbiased omics approaches to comprehensively delineate Piezo1-evoked intracellular signaling pathways and transcription factors, and to identify Piezo1-dependent secretory factors involved in MSCs cell fate decision. These findings will deepen our understanding of MSCs mechanobiology, and will contribute to develop novel stem cell-based therapies for the treatment of osteoporosis, diabetes and other aging-related disorders. It will also provide a rationale to promote exercise in prevention of these chronic diseases. 骨髓间充质干细胞是一种多能基质细胞。它可以分化成多种不同类型的细胞，包括成骨细胞和骨髓脂肪细胞等。在健康的状态下，间充质干细胞向成骨细胞和脂肪细胞两个方向的分化形成一种良好的平衡，从而维持骨密度和代谢稳态。衰老、肥胖、糖尿病等因素会破坏这种平衡，并引发骨质疏松和骨髓脂肪增加，这是最常见的以骨量和骨密度降低为特征的代谢性骨病。然而，对于调控间充质干细胞分化命运的分子机制以及骨髓脂肪细胞的病理生理作用仍然知之甚少。 Piezo1是机械敏感的非选择性阳离子通道，它可以将机械刺激（如剪切应力、压缩和膜拉伸等）转化为电信号和细胞内的生化信号。我们的初步发现表明，与其同源物Piezo2不同，Piezo1在骨髓间充质干细胞中大量表达。此外，我们观察到在表达血小板生长因子受体α（PDGFRα）的间充质干细胞中特异性敲除Piezo1的小鼠表现出骨量和骨密度显著下降，并伴随着骨髓脂肪的增加。同时，我们发现从Piezo1基因敲除小鼠的骨髓中分离出的间充质干细胞分化为脂肪细胞的能力增强，但分化为成骨细胞的能力减弱。总的来说，我们的前期研究表明骨髓间充质干细胞膜上的Piezo1通道可以感知机械刺激并调控间充质干细胞的分化方向，从而导致骨形成增加和骨髓脂肪减少，并可能进一步改善全身胰岛素敏感性。为了进一步验证这一假说，我们将在小鼠中进行骨髓移植实验以验证Piezo1在间充质干细胞中的自主功能，并将评估运动诱导的骨形成、骨髓脂肪减少和全身胰岛素敏感性增强是否依赖于间充质干细胞中Piezo1的激活。此外，我们还将利用这一独特的动物模型来研究骨髓脂肪细胞的代谢作用，并将同时采用基于假说和组学的方法来全面阐释Piezo1激活的细胞内信号通路和转录因子，以及鉴定出调控间充质干细胞分化命运的依赖于Piezo1的分泌因子。这些发现将加深我们对间充质干细胞力学生物学的理解，并将有助于开发新的基于干细胞的疗法，以用于治疗骨质疏松症、糖尿病和其他与衰老有关的疾病。它还将为推广以运动预防慢性疾病提供理论依据。

17117720.label: Realisation of objectives
17117720.value: Objective 1: For this objective, we investigate whether G3BP1 regulates dendritic protein synthesis and dendritic spine morphogenesis in hippocampal neurons. We set up the metabolic labelling assay through puromycin labeling to visualize newly synthesized proteins in neuronal dendrites in situ. Primary hippocampal neurons at 16 days in vitro (DIV) were incubated with low dose of puromycin for 10 minutes followed by staining with anti-puromycin antibody. Strong fluorescence signal of puromycin was observed in both the soma and dendrites. Treatment with the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin significantly reduced the puromycin signal, thereby validating the specificity in monitoring protein synthesis. Using this approach, we found that co-transfection of G3BP1 and GFP by calcium-phosphate precipitation led to significantly lower dendritic puromycin signal intensity, as compared to the neighboring un-transfected (GFP-negative) neurons. The reduction in protein synthesis was not a non-specific consequence of over-expressing a protein, since parallel control with either over-expression of GFP alone or GFP together with the arginine methylation-deficient G3BP1 (Arg-433 and Arg-445 being substituted to His) did not change the puromycin signals in the transfected neurons. To further verify the role of G3BP1 in regulating dendritic protein synthesis, immunostaining and confocal microscopy was performed to demonstrate the co-localization of exogenous Tdtomato-G3BP1 with the endogenous translation initiation factor eIF4E in the dendrites of dissociated hippocampal neurons. Using two different eIF4E antibodies, we further demonstrated that G3BP1 was co-immunoprecipitated with eIF4E in the mouse brain. These findings support our notion that G3BP1 is localized near the translation initiation sites in neuronal dendrites to negatively regulate protein synthesis. Our hypothesis is that uncontrolled protein synthesis will give rise to overproduction to the immature filopodia. To test this idea, we examined the effect of over-expressing G3BP1 on the density of filopodia. Consistent with our hypothesis, G3BP1 over-expression, which suppresses protein synthesis based on our metabolic labeling assay, significantly reduced the number of filopodia, while the mature mushroom spines are not affected. These findings together suggest that G3BP1 serves to regulate protein synthesis in the dendrite to prevent the over-production of filopodia, possibly through its effect on the translation initiation complex. Objective 2 In this objective, we determine how arginine methylation regulates the function of G3BP1 in protein synthesis and dendritic spine development. We hypothesize that the translation initiation eIF4E is the downstream target of G3BP1. We found that purified GST-eIF4E was able to pull down recombinant G3BP1 in cell-free conditions, suggesting that the two proteins directly interact with each other. Importantly, the presence of recombinant protein arginine methyltransferase PRMT1 and the methyl donor AdoMet significantly increases the binding of G3BP1 to eIF4E, suggesting that their binding is promoted through arginine methylation. To address whether G3BP1 function in neurons indeed depends on its methylation, we investigate whether a methylation-mimetic G3BP1 (Arg-433 and Arg-445 being substituted to Phe) could rescue the neuronal deficits caused by the depletion of PRMT8, a neuron-specific arginine methyltransferase which we have identified to act upstream of G3BP1 in dendritic spine morphogenesis and the regulation of actin cytoskeleton (Lo et al., 2020). Firstly, we show that in metabolic labeling, the knockdown of PRMT8 by shRNA significantly increased puromycin signals in the dendrites, but this increase is reversed by the co-expression of methylation-mimetic G3BP1. Importantly, co-expression of wild-type or methylation-deficient G3BP1 cannot reverse the elevated protein synthesis, indicating that the methylation by PRMT8 is essential for the suppressed translation by G3BP1. Secondly, the knockdown and rescue experiments were performed to study dendritic spine morphogenesis. Consistent with our previous study, introduction of PRMT8-shRNA impairs dendritic spine maturation by significantly reducing the density of mushroom spines and increasing the abundance of filopodia. Similar to the metabolic labeling, co-expression of the methylation-mimetic G3BP1, but not the wild-type or methylation-deficient counterpart, can significantly reverse the spine phenotypes. These findings together indicate that G3BP1 is the major downstream target of PRMT8 to promote dendritic spine maturation of hippocampal neurons through the suppression of protein synthesis. In addition, the biochemical experiments suggest that the methylation acts on G3BP1 by enhancing its interaction with the translation initiation complex. Objective 3 This objective investigates how G3BP1 is mechanistically linked to the regulation of protein synthesis and dendritic spine maturation. Since we identified eIF4E, which has been previously characterized to directly link mRNA translation to actin organization, as the novel interacting partner of G3BP1, we determine whether eIF4E is essential for G3BP1 function in spine morphogenesis. We first map the domain on G3BP1 that interacts with eIF4E. Through the construction of various truncated mutants followed by co-immunoprecipitation, we identify the N-terminal NTF2-like domain on G3BP1 that mediates the binding to eIF4E. We reason that over-expressing the NTF-2 like domain would interfere with the interaction between endogenous G3BP1 and eIF4E. If this interaction is essential for dendritic spine development, the exogenous expression of NTF2-like domain should disrupt dendritic spine morphogenesis. Indeed, over-expression of the NTF2-like domain of G3BP1 significantly reduced the density of mushroom spines. However, the filopodia are not affected, suggesting that distinct domains of G3BP1 are responsible for the control of different spine types. If the negative regulation of mRNA translation by G3BP1 is required for proper dendritic spine maturation, we argue that the suppression of translation initiation should reverse the spine deficits caused by G3BP1 deficiency. Towards this end, we employ the small molecule inhibitor 4EGI-1, which specifically blocks the interaction between eIF4E and eIF4G during the translation initiation complex formation, to attenuate protein synthesis. We found that 4EGI-1 treatment (50 uM for 4 hours) has no effect on the dendritic spines of hippocampal neurons transfected with control-shRNA. However, the presence of 4EGI-1 completely abolished the over-production of filopodia in neurons transfected with shRNA against G3BP1. Moreover, the loss of mushroom spines upon G3BP1 depletion is partially reversed by the suppression of mRNA translation. Taken together, our findings collectively provide compelling evidence that eIF4E and mRNA translation are the major downstream targets of PRMT8 and G3BP1, and their interplay is essential for dendritic spine maturation in neurons.

17117720.label: Major findings and research outcome
17117720.value: Excitatory synapses of neurons are located primarily on dendritic spines which possess diverse morphologies, ranging from the elongated filopodia to the mushroom-shaped spines. The molecular mechanism that controls the balance between filopodia and mushroom spines is not well defined. G3BP1 is a key RNA-binding protein (RBP) that assembles stress granules in non-neuronal cells to adapt to cellular stresses by transiently blocking protein synthesis. The cellular functions of G3BP1 in neurons and how the protein is regulated remain poorly understood. We show that in the absence of exogenous stress, G3BP1 suppresses protein synthesis in hippocampal neurons and binds to the translation initiation factor eIF4E via its NTF2-like domain. G3BP1 depletion causes over-production of filopodia, which can be alleviated by a small-molecule inhibitor that blocks the formation of translation initiation complex. The interaction of G3BP1 with eIF4E is regulated by arginine methylation. Knockdown of the protein arginine methyltransferase PRMT8 by shRNA leads to elevated protein synthesis and filopodia production, which is reversed specifically by the expression of methylation-mimetic G3BP1. These findings, published in Journal of Biological Chemistry (Dong et al. 2023), reveals arginine methylation as a key regulatory mechanism in dendritic spine morphogenesis. It identifies G3BP1 and eIF4E as novel downstream targets of this post-translational modification during neuronal development and provides new insights on G3BP1 function by demonstrating its importance other than stress response. G3BP1 is dendritically localized in rodent neurons. Related to this project, we study the trafficking of RBP and mRNAs to synapse: one paper (Fok et al. 2024 Cell Reports) on the synaptic localization of the RBP FMRP in neurons of the cerebral cortex in awake mice and the changes after fear learning; another on the specific synaptic localization of different mRNAs (Fan et al., in preparation). Two review articles on methylation (Dong et al., 2021) and RNA transport (Fan and Lai, 2022) are also published. Aberrant stress granules contribute to neurodegeneration such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). We created human induced stem cell (hiPSC)-derived cortical neurons carrying an ALS- mutation on the FUS gene. Contrary to general belief, G3BP1 and the mutant FUS protein do not form aggregates in cultured hiPSC-derived neurons, but dendritic arborization and synapse formation are impaired. However, the mutant FUS form cytoplasmic aggregates containing G3BP1 in vivo after the hiPSC-neurons are transplanted into mouse brain (Wang et al., in preparation.), hence reporting a new ALS hiPSC model that better mimics the patient pathology.

17117720.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17117720.value: Arginine methylation often takes place at the RGG motif, which is present in many dendritic RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) besides G3BP1. Indeed, a recent article demonstrates a crosstalk between arginine methylation and phosphorylation in regulating the activity of FMRP, one of the key RBPs that carries mRNA to dendrites and control their local translation (Tsang et al., 2019). It is therefore of great interest to investigate in the future whether the similar regulatory mechanism that we have elucidated in this study can be applied to other dendritic RBPs and therefore represents a general mechanism in the control of RNA granule formation and mRNA translation. Moreover, aberrant arginine methylation is linked to neurodegeneration. Given the importance of G3BP1 in stress granule formation, it is imperative to study the potential link between dysregulated G3BP1 methylation and diseases in the nervous system. In particular, our pilot studies on the genome editing of hiPSC-derived neurons followed by xenotransplantation into mouse brain to study dendritic spines would be a useful approach to investigate the impact of G3BP1 methylation on the synaptic function in human neurons.

17117720.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17117720.value: Cells can adapt to various types of stresses by transiently suppressing their protein synthesis. This can be accomplished through the formation of a special type of RNA granules called stress granules. Selective RNA-binding proteins are recruited to protect the mRNAs in these granules from degradation, therefore protein synthesis can be resumed after the stress is gone. One key RNA-binding protein that assembles stress granules is G3BP1. This protein is also expressed in neurons, where it is present not only in the cell body but also in extensions (axons and dendrites). However, the function of G3BP1 in neurons is not clear. Our study reveals that G3BP1 can suppress protein synthesis in neurons in the absence of exogenous stress. We further identify EIF4E, a key translation factor for the initiation of protein synthesis, as a binding partner of G3BP1, and their interaction is promoted by G3BP1 methylation. Through methylation and binding to EIF4E, G3BP1 helps to prevent the over-production of immature neuronal connections during neuronal development. Our findings identify a new mechanism for the control of neural development through a RNA-binding protein involved in stress response, underscoring the versatility of RNA-binding proteins in participating various biological processes.

17118120.label: Realisation of objectives
17118120.value: To identify the deubiquitinases (DUBs) involved in regulating Vangl proteins, we employed a systematic screening approach using the Sanger CRISPR library, targeting approximately 100 known DUBs. Specific sgRNAs were transfected into HEK293T cells, and endogenous levels of Vangl1 and Vangl2 were assessed by immunoblot analysis. Through a few rounds of screening, we successfully identified two highly related ubiquitin-specific peptidases (USP), USP6 and USP32, for further investigation. To validate the deubiquitinating activity of USP6 and USP32, we demonstrated their role in stabilizing Vangl proteins and reducing Vangl polyubiquitination levels. Notably, catalytic mutants of USP6 and USP32 lacked these activities, confirming the enzymatic specificity of their DUB function. Further analysis revealed direct protein-protein interactions between USP6/32 and Vangl, with specific interaction domains mapped for each enzyme. Interestingly, USP6 and USP32 displayed distinct subcellular localization patterns. USP6 primarily localized to the plasma membrane, where it regulated plasma membrane-bound Vangl proteins, while USP32 accumulated in the Golgi apparatus, participating in the Golgi protein quality control (PQC) pathway to regulate Golgi-associated Vangl proteins. Moreover, we found that Wnt-induced Vangl phosphorylation significantly reduced Vangl ubiquitination levels via USP6/32. A phospho-mutant Vangl2 exhibited increased ubiquitination, whereas a phospho-mimetic Vangl2 showed decreased ubiquitination, further emphasizing the regulatory interplay between Wnt signaling and USP6/32-mediated deubiquitination. These findings elucidate a novel, multilayered mechanism by which USP6 and USP32 regulate Vangl proteins, providing new insights into their roles in Wnt/PCP signaling. Since USP6 is hominoid-specific and absent in most other mammals, we further investigated the function of USP32 in animal models. In zebrafish, knockdown of Usp32 using morpholino led to a significant reduction in Vangl protein levels and resulted in convergent extension defects, a hallmark defect of impaired Wnt/PCP signaling. To extend these findings to mammals, we generated USP32 mutant mice. These mice exhibited embryonic lethality, with no viable newborns observed. Our analysis suggested that the mutant embryos died around E16.5. We then investigated the genetic interaction between USP32 and Vangl genes, focusing on phenotypes associated with PCP-related abnormalities, such as neural tube defects, the loop tail phenotype, and misorientation of cochlear hair cells. Reducing the gene dosage of USP32 in Vangl1/2 mutant mice significantly increased the penetrance of these defects. Specifically, we observed a higher frequency of neural tube defects, the characteristic loop tail phenotype, and the misorientation of cochlear hair cells. These findings provide strong evidence that USP32 plays a critical role in Vangl-mediated developmental processes, further underscoring its importance in regulating Wnt/PCP signaling. Interestingly, we identified previously unknown functions of USP32 and Vangl in pancreatic duct development. Protein analysis showed significantly reduced Vangl levels in USP32 mutant mice compared to wild-type controls. During pancreatic ductal morphogenesis, a critical process occurring between E14.5 and E16.5, epithelial cells undergo elongation and extension to establish a hierarchical, arborized structure. Whole-mount immunostaining of E15.5 pancreatic tissue revealed that terminal ducts in USP32-/- mice exhibited an abnormally open lumen, indicating defective remodeling. This phenotype was similar to that observed in Vangl1-/-; Vangl2-/- mice, further supporting a functional link between USP32 and Vangl in pancreatic ductal remodeling. We extended our studies to pathological conditions using pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) as a model. Tumor tissues showed significant upregulation of both USP32 and Vangl1 compared to adjacent normal tissues. Elevated expression of these proteins positively correlated with cancer cell migration capacity and inversely with patient prognosis and survival. Functional assays demonstrated that USP32 stabilized Vangl1 and regulated its subcellular distribution, which in turn enhanced pancreatic cancer cell migration and invasion. Notably, overexpression of Vangl1 rescued the reduced metastatic potential caused by USP32 depletion, underscoring their interdependence. Importantly, neither USP32 nor Vangl1 affected pancreatic cancer cell proliferation, highlighting their specific roles in regulating cancer metastasis. These findings reveal that USP32 and Vangl collaboratively regulate pancreatic ductal morphogenesis under physiological conditions and contribute to tumor progression under pathological conditions, providing insights into both developmental biology and cancer metastasis.

17118120.label: Major findings and research outcome
17118120.value: Our research unveiled critical roles for USP6/32 in regulating Vangl proteins and their involvement in Wnt/PCP signaling under both physiological and pathological conditions. We identified USP6 and USP32 as deubiquitinases that stabilize Vangl1 and Vangl2 by reducing their polyubiquitination. These enzymes exhibited distinct subcellular localizations: USP6 at the plasma membrane and USP32 in the Golgi, each regulating specific pools of Vangl proteins. Furthermore, Wnt signaling-induced Vangl phosphorylation reduced ubiquitination via USP6/32, highlighting a novel regulatory mechanism linking Wnt signaling and protein stability. In developmental contexts, USP32 was essential for normal pancreatic duct morphogenesis and overall embryonic viability. Loss of USP32 resulted in defective ductal remodeling and exacerbated PCP-related abnormalities. In pathological conditions, such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, both USP32 and Vangl1 were upregulated, promoting cancer cell migration and invasion while correlating with poor patient outcomes. These findings establish USP6/32-mediated regulation of Vangl proteins as pivotal for Wnt/PCP signaling, with implications for both development and cancer metastasis, and identify USP32 as a potential therapeutic target in PDAC. With the support of this grant, our work has contributed to several research outputs. These include the publication of a review chapter discussing potential therapeutic agents targeting Wnt/PCP signaling (Research Output 1), a protocol paper detailing methods to analyze Vangl ubiquitination and phosphorylation (Research Output 2), and a study on the functional implications of Vangl mutations identified in a human disease (Research Output 3). While the main findings of the project remain unpublished, this is because we expanded our studies significantly beyond the original objectives to provide a more comprehensive understanding. Initially, the proposal focused on USP32 function in zebrafish; however, we extended our investigations to its role in mammals, examining USP32's relationship with Vangl in both developmental processes and pancreatic cancer in mouse models. These new studies, which involved time-consuming in vivo experiments, have yielded crucial insights. The delay of the publication is also partially due to the move of my lab from HKU to CUHK. A PhD student dedicated to this project has graduated and continues as a postdoctoral fellow, contributing further to this research. We have presented our findings at scientific meetings, including a poster at the EMBO Wnt Meeting and an oral presentation at the Gordon Research Conference, receiving valuable feedback from the research community. We are now preparing to consolidate all our data for a comprehensive publication, which will detail the significant outcomes of this work.

17118120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17118120.value: Wnt/Planar Cell Polarity (Wnt/PCP) signaling is a fundamental, evolutionarily conserved molecular mechanism essential for proper tissue organization. Perturbations of Wnt/PCP signaling can lead to developmental disorders like neural tube defects and skeletal malformations, whereas its aberrant activation has been implicated in cancer malignancy. We found that the core Wnt/PCP components, Vangl1 and Vangl2, are tightly regulated through post-translational modifications (PTMs), particularly via phosphorylation and ubiquitination. In this study, we identified and characterized two deubiquitinases, USP6 and USP32, that play a critical role in stabilizing Vangl proteins. In development, USP32 deficiency resulted in enhanced penetrance of the PCP phenotype in Vangl mutant mice. Interestingly, both USP32-knockout and Vangl-mutant mice exhibited similar defects in pancreatic ductal morphogenesis. The expression levels of USP32 and VANGL1 are highly correlated with pancreatic cancer progression and our studies indicate that USP32 and VANGL1 significantly impact pancreatic cancer metastasis. Our findings uncover a previously unknown mechanism in Wnt/PCP signaling that is essential for normal development and has potential implications for understanding and treating diseases like cancer.

17118620.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17118620.value: Cells can migrate, communicate, and are the fundamental building block of the living organism. Cell membrane, a lipid bilayer, is the frontier of signal transduction between extracellular space and intracellular cytoplasm. Phosphatidylinositol (PI) are rare lipid species in the cell membrane and play important roles in a wide variety of cellular events, such as cell migration and malignant cancer spread. Invadosome, the key invasive adhesion structure of cancer cells, is enriched in PI(3,4)P2 lipids. To facilitate cell migration, aged adhesion sites must be disassembled, and new adhesion sites need to be reborn toward the direction of migration. It is known that fast turnover and disassembly of integrin-mediated adhesion can promote invasive migration of cancer cells. Our pilot studies have suggested that the generation of PI(3,4)P2 lipids is highly corelated with the disassembly and endocytosis of adhesion receptor integrin-beta3. In this proposal, we aim to investigate the regulation of PI(3,4)P2-mediated membrane invagination and integrin endocytosis. We will focus on the upstream elements that cause the local production of PI(3,4)P2 at the invadosome, as well as the downstream effectors on sharping membrane and cytoskeleton organization. We will determine the factors that connect lipid signaling to membrane tubulation (BAR-domain proteins) and microtubule targeting (minus-end motors). With the combined approaches in molecular biology, mutagenesis, and fluorescence imaging, we will carry out the scientific investigation and identify key molecules along the signal axis of PI(3,4)P2-mediated integrin endocytosis and cell migration. Moreover, we aim to suppress these key molecules identified and examine their inhibitory effect on cancer invasive migration. Our finding will provide a better understanding of the mechanism how lipid signals reshape the cell membrane, capture microtubule, and facilitate cell migration via integrin endocytosis. Pharmaceutical and biotech industries will be potentially interested in applying our findings to develop new compounds and technologies to suppress malignant cancer spread. 磷脂酰肌醇在細胞遷移與惡性腫瘤侵襲中，扮演及其重要的角色。侵襲性偽足是整合素介導的胞膜突起結構，並富含一種特別的磷脂酰肌醇PI(3,4)P2。本研究旨在深入探討PI(3,4)P2在整合素內吞中的調節作用，重點研究PI(3,4)P2生成的信號通路，以及PI(3,4)P2膜內陷對於細胞骨架重整與囊泡運輸的下游效應，並進一步檢測這些關鍵分子蛋白對癌症細胞侵襲性遷移的影響。我們的研究將有助於製藥與生物技術行業，開發新的化合物與技術來抑制惡性腫瘤的侵襲。

17118620.label: Realisation of objectives
17118620.value: Summary of the investigation: To facilitate cell migration, aged adhesion sites must be disassembled, and new adhesion sites need to be reborn toward the direction of migration. While invasive cancer cells utilize integrin to form the invadopodium as the adhesion and migration apparatus, the endocytosis and recycling mechanism of integrin receptor at caner invadopodia are largely unknown. Phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate [PI(3,4)P2] is a key lipid messenger in endocytosis and locally concentrated in invadopodia. In this investigation, we find that the PI(3,4)P2 biogenesis regulates the integrin endocytosis at invadopodia. PI(3,4)P2 is locally produced by PIK3CA and SHIP2 and is asymmetrically concentrated at the trailing edge of the invadopodium arc. The PI(3,4)P2-rich compartment locally forms small puncta (membrane buds) in a SNX9-dependent manner, recruits dynein activator Hook1 through AKTIP, and rearranges into micrometer-long tubular invaginations (membrane tubes). The uncurving membrane tube extends rapidly, follows the retrograde movement of dynein along microtubule tracks, and disconnects from the plasma membrane. Activated integrin-beta3 is locally internalized through the pathway of PI(3,4)P2-mediated membrane invagination and is then actively recycled. Blockages of PI3K, SHIP2, and SNX9 suppress integrin-beta3 endocytosis, delay adhesion turnover, and impede transwell invasion of MEF-Src and MDA-MB-231 cells. Overall, our finding will offer new insights into integrin trafficking and membrane-microtubule interaction. In particular, the production of PI(3,4)P2 at the invadopodium promotes invasive cell migration by stimulating the trafficking of integrin receptor. Percentage of completion: 100%. We find that PI(3,4)P2-rich compartment in the plasma membrane contains integrin-beta3. The invagination and endocytosis of PI(3,4)P2 membrane compartment are specifically controlled by BAR-domain protein SNX9 and dynamin2. PX-BAR domain of SNX9 interacts with PI(3,4)P2 and locally deform the plasma membrane at the inner part of the invadopodium arc. Dynamin2 is subsequently recruited to the invaginated membrane by SNX9 and triggers the membrane fission and integrin beta3 endocytosis. Endocytosed integrin receptors are resided in Rab5-positive endosomes. Knockdown of SNX9 suppresses the number of membrane invagination sites, impedes the recruitment of dynamin2, the reduces the level of endocytosed integrin. It appears that the BAR domain protein SNX9 binds to PI(3,4)P2 lipid and is responsible for the recruitment of dynamin2. Therefore, we have achieved the investigation of Objective 1. [Objective 2] Determine molecular linkers of microtubule-induced membrane tubulation. Percentage of completion: 100%. The inward membrane tubulation (membrane tube) follows the direction of microtubule tracks in proximity to the invadopodium. When examining the spatiotemporal dynamics of microtubule retrograde motors, we find that dynein, monitored by dynein subunit Arp1, stays at the tip of the elongating membrane tube. We further find that dynein adapters Hook1 and AKTIP specifically concentrate at the elongating membrane tube. Knockdown of ATKIP results in the dissociation of Hook1 from the membrane tube and the increase of stationary PI(3,4)P2-positive endosomes behind the invadopodium arc. The wildtype AKTIP, rather than the PI(3,4)P2-binding mutant AKTIP 2RA (R168A and R169A), rescues the membrane tubulation. Thus, AKTIP and Hook1 are the functional linkers to connect the PI(3,4)P2 membrane compartment to dynein. Therefore, we have achieved the investigation of Objective 2. [Objective 3] Investigate the impact of PI(3,4)P2-mediated membrane invagination in invasive migration and integrin trafficking. Percentage of completion: 100%. The functional roles of PI(3,4)P2-mediated membrane invagination are examined in both MEF-Src and MD-MBA231 cells. When the production of PI(3,4)P2 by PI3K and SHIP2 is blocked, the level of endocytosed integrin is significantly reduced, and invasive cell migration across Matrigel-coated chamber is suppressed. Likewise, knockdown of SNX9, the key factor to trigger membrane invagination, also suppresses integrin endocytosis and invasive cell migration. In summary, we find that PI(3,4)P2-mediated membrane invagination accelerates integrin endocytosis, promotes adhesion turnover, and supports invasive cell migration. Therefore, we have achieved the investigation of Objective 3.

17118620.label: Major findings and research outcome
17118620.value: Phosphoinositide lipids are important signaling messengers to facilitate membrane compartmentalization and trigger a wide variety of cellular events. Here, we dissect the molecular pathway and examine the impact of PI(3,4)P2 biogenesis on membrane trafficking, integrin receptor endocytosis, and invasive cell migration. We find that PI(3,4)P2, unlike other phosphoinositide lipids, is asymmetrically concentrated at the trailing edge of the invadopodium. The PI(3,4)P2-rich compartment is actively reshaped and forms the invaginated membrane bud and tube in a SNX9- and microtubule-dependent manner, respectively. We further identify regulatory components of membrane tubulation, including AKTIP, Hook1, and microtubule retrograde motor dynein. Functionally, blocking the PI(3,4)P2-mediated endocytosis pathway impedes integrin endocytosis, prevents the adhesion disassembly, and suppresses the invasive cell migration. These results have been published in PNAS in 2021 (PMID 33947811), and here are the major findings. 1) Asymmetrical distribution of PI(3,4)P2 across the invadopodium arc 2) Knockdown of PIK3CA suppresses the production of PI(3,4)P2 3) SHIP2 is the major phosphoinositide 5-phosphatase to produce PI(3,4)P2 at the invadopodium 4) PI(3,4)P2-rich compartment actively develops into invaginated membrane tubes and endocytic vesicles 5) Microtubule and dynein complex control the growth of membrane tubes 6) SNX9 Is a PI(3,4)P2 effector and promotes the membrane invagination 7) Invadopodia stimulate the trafficking of integrin-beta3 receptor 8) PI(3,4)P2-mediated membrane invagination promotes the internalization of integrin-beta3 and the adhesion turnover 9) Suppression of PI(3,4)P2-mediated integrin endocytosis impedes the invasive migration of MEF-Src and MDA-MB-231 cells

17118620.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17118620.value: The dynamic distribution of phosphoinositide lipids orchestrates intracellular compartmentalization and receptor trafficking. Here, we report the PI(3,4)P2-dependent endocytosis of adhesion receptor integrin-beta3 at the invadopodium and its implication in promoting invasive cell migration. Accelerated integrin endocytosis promotes adhesion turnover, and subsequent integrin exocytosis further supports cell migration. The functional link between PI(3,4)P2 biogenesis and membrane internalization can be applicable to other membrane molecules at the invadopodium and provide insights into the regulation of cell migration. Other membrane receptors, such as CD44 and discoidin domain receptor, and other integrin coreceptors, are likely to be regulated in the SNX9- and PI(3,4)P2-dependent endocytosis pathway. Therefore, future work will be needed to examine and validate their impact on cell migration and cancer invasion. In general, factors that impede the PI(3,4)P2 signaling and the membrane invagination may offer new opportunities to inhibit the invasive migration of cancer cell.

17118620.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17118620.value: Cells synthesise various lipids and protein receptors on the cell membrane, in order to maintain the functional organisation of the tissue. For example, integrins are protein receptors on the cell membrane that provide the physical anchorage between the cell and surrounding tissue. Malignant cancer cells often utilise the invadopodium, a subtype of integrin-mediated adhesion with abundant PI(3,4)P2 lipids, to break the tissue barrier and facilitate cancer metastasis. This investigation has uncovered the molecular mechanism in which PI(3,4)P2 lipids weaken the stability of cell adhesion, accelerate the redistribution of integrins, and pave the path for the malignant cell invasion. By inhibiting PI(3,4)P2 synthesis, invasive cell migrations are effectively suppressed in various models, including in the triple-negative breast cancer cell line. In addition, this study has revealed several new druggable targets to suppress the malignant spread of cancer cells. Biotech and pharmaceutical industries may potentially benefit from these findings and be interested in developing new compounds and technologies to address the issues associated with cancer metastasis.

17118720.label: Realisation of objectives
17118720.value: In this project, we have successfully achieved our research objectives, demonstrating a novel role for PAR-1 activation in the AKI-to-CKD transition through vascular injury, inflammation, and fibrosis. First, we successfully established a mouse model of AKI-to-CKD transition following unilateral ischemia-reperfusion injury (UIRI). On day 7 after UIRI, mice exhibited kidney damage, inflammation, endothelial injury and fibrosis. Treatment of PAR-1 antagonist, vorapaxar, can effectively reduce kidney damage, inflammation, and fibrosis (completion of Aim 1). Notably, we demonstrated that vorapaxar administration after the onset of AKI could prevent long-term kidney fibrosis. These findings provide strong evidence that pharmacological inhibition targeting PAR-1 offers a promising therapeutic strategy for managing AKI and prevents its progression in the clinical settings. Second, we have elucidated the molecular mechanisms by which PAR-1 inhibition prevents the progression to CKD (completion of Aim 2). Using different cell culture models of tubular epithelial cells and endothelial cells, we found that PAR-1 promoted inflammatory pathways under hypoxic conditions in both cell types. Importantly, PAR-1 deficiency in tubular epithelial cells led to the stabilization of HIF-α, the critical protective player during hypoxia, and induction of the key angiogenic factor VEGFA, which supports vascular regeneration and improves endothelial integrity following AKI. These findings demonstrate that PAR-1 plays a critical role in tubulovascular crosstalk during AKI-to-CKD transition.

17118720.label: Major findings and research outcome
17118720.value: 1. PAR-1 Activation Contributes to AKI-Induced CKD PAR-1 activation significantly contributes acute kidney injury (AKI) using a transgenic PAR-1 knockout model. Wild-type mice subjected to unilateral ischemia-reperfusion injury (UIRI) exhibited severe renal tubular vacuolation, loss of nuclei, and inflammation and kidney dysfunction at day 3 after UIRI. These changes were markedly reduced in PAR-1-deficient mice. Due to the maladaptive repair, progressive kidney fibrosis developed in wild-type mice starting from day 7, which was significantly ameliorated in PAR-1-deficient mice, highlighting the importance of PAR-1-targeting for therapeutic intervention. 2. Vorapaxar Treatment Offers Therapeutic Potential Against AKI-Induced CKD The therapeutic potential of PAR-1 inhibition was assessed by 3 different protocols of vorapaxar administration; 1) full treatment from day 0 to day 7 after AKI; 2) pre-treatment from 24 h before AKI to day 3 after AKI and 3) post-treatment from day 3 to day 7 after AKI. In all protocols, vorapaxar effectively reduced renal tubular injury (KIM-1 expression and structural abnormalities), improved kidney function, reduced kidney inflammatory and profibotic phenotypes, and enhanced vascular regenerative capacity (increased VEGFA and VEGFR2 levels). 3. PAR-1 Inhibition Stabilized Nuclear HIF-α Expression in Tubular Epithelial Cells (TECs) Silencing of PAR-1 stabilized HIF-1α in TEC nuclei under hypoxic condition via activating Akt/GSK-3β signaling. HIF-1α plays a protective role during the repair phase of AKI. We confirmed that nuclear HIF-1α expression was diminished in mice at day 14 after UIRI which was induced in PAR-1-deficient mice. These results demonstrated a protective role of PAR-1 inhibition in TECs via HIF-α stabilization. 4. PAR-1 Inhibition Preserved Vascular Function via Tubulovascular Crosstalk Absence of PAR-1 enhanced hypoxia-induced VEGFA expression from TECs, indicating a protective effect on angiogenesis. Activation of PAR-1 by thrombin upregulated the expression of inflammatory molecules in cultured endothelial cells via activation of NFκB and ERK1/2 signaling. Although knockdown of PAR-1 reduced VEGFA expression in endothelial cells, enhanced secretion of VEGFA from hypoxic TECs with PAR-1 knockdown could increase cell proliferation (CCK-8 assay) and angiogenesis capacity (tube formation assay) of endothelial cells, supporting a role of PAR-1 in paracrine VEGF signaling for endothelial integrity via tubulovascular crosstalk. Mice with PAR-1 deficiency exhibited preserved endothelial integrity (increased CD31 level) and reduced vascular leakage (Evan’s blue extravasation) at day 14 after UIRI.

17118720.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17118720.value: This study demonstrates, for the first time, PAR-1 inhibition offers tubulovascular protection by reducing capillary loss and leukocyte adhesion in the early stage of AKI and alleviates the progression to CKD through anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects. Interestingly, we uncovered novel roles of PAR-1 in the regulation of hypoxia-induced tubular injury through modulation of HIF-1α stabilization and vascular injury via paracrine VEGFA signaling. Our findings not only align with the beneficial effect of HIF-1α stabilization in slowing CKD progression but extend our interest to further investigate the protective effect of PAR-1 inhibition on vascular complication in other forms of CKD such as diabetic kidney disease (DKD). Given that patients with DKD are at high risk for vascular complications, we are currently investigating the role of PAR-1 in vascular injury using an animal model of diabetic nephropathy. Preliminary results indicate that PAR-1 contributes to vascular damage in the kidneys of diabetic db/db mice, and further studies are underwent to dissect the underlying mechanisms.

17118720.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17118720.value: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is frequently associated with an increased risk of blood clotting, also known as a hypercoagulable state, primarily due to excessive thrombin production. This observation suggests that anticoagulant therapies may slow CKD progression and prevent kidney fibrosis. In our study, we demonstrated that pharmacological inhibition of protease-activated receptor-1 (PAR-1), a key receptor in the coagulation system, reduced the severity of acute kidney injury (AKI) in mice and prevented its progression to CKD. This protective effect was accomplished by preventing vascular damage in the kidneys, alleviating inflammation, and stabilizing nuclear hypoxia-inducible factor-1α which facilitates cellular adaptation to low oxygen condition. Importantly, inhibition of PAR-1 also inhibited the development of kidney fibrosis, thereby preserving kidney function and structure. Our findings support the therapeutic potential of targeting PAR-1 with the FDA-approved drug vorapaxar, to treat AKI and potentially improve outcomes for patients with acute kidney injury and the long-term complications.

17119120.label: Realisation of objectives
17119120.value: 1. To delineate the mechanism of how EV-NID1 induces TNFR1 secretion by the activated pulmonary fibroblasts in pre-metastatic niche formation NID1 delivered by EV has been shown to promote HCC tumorigenesis, metastasis and pre-metastatic niche formation. In order to identify the crucial functional domain of NID1, we made use of XPack engineering technology to express full-length and deletion mutants of NID1 in EVs of NID1 knockout (KO) cells established in metastatic HCC cell line MHCC97L. EVs that express full-length and deletion mutants of NID1 were used in various functional assays. EVs of KO-NID1 cells showed compromised effect in promoting colony formation and motility of cells compared to EVs of non-target KO-CTL cells. It was found that restoration of full-length NID1 in EVs rescued oncogenic ability of EVs. In addition, EVs with restoration of NID1 C-terminus exerted promoting effect, implying that the C-terminus domain (N670-N1247) is critical for EV-NID1 oncogenic capacity. The oncogenic ability of NID1 C-terminus was further validated in mouse experimentation. EVs with induced expression of NID1 C-terminus promoted lung colonization of murine hepatoblasts. Furthermore, EV-NID1 was found to elevate expression of TNFR1 at the transcriptional and translational level in MRC-5 fibroblasts. Two putative NF-κB binding sites were located in the promoter of TNFR1. We questioned whether TNFR1 induced by EV-NID1 was mediated by NF-κB. The results showed that the nuclear p-p65 level in MRC-5 fibroblasts was elevated by treating with EVs expressing full-length NID1 or only C-terminus of NID1. The C-terminus region of NID1 was shown to be crucial to the oncogenic ability of NID1, we identified the interacting partners of NID1 via the C-terminus using mass spectrometry and identified transglutaminase 3 (TGM3) as a critical binding partner of full-length NID1. Coimmunoprecipitation confirmed the interaction between TGM3 and NID1via the C-terminus. In EV-NID1-treated cells, we also observed an elevation in TGM3 expression. To investigate the functional role of TMG3 in HCC, TGM3 stable knockdown (TGM3-KD) clones were established in HCC recipient cells (HLE and PLC/PRF/5), and knockdown of TGM3 significantly hampered the oncogenic promoting effect of EV-NID1. We further extended our study in vivo and demonstrated orthotopic injection of TGM3-KD cells resulted in smaller tumor growth. Pathway analysis of NID1 co-IP MS revealed that proteins related to ECM-receptor interactions was prominently affected. The TGM family members have been found to interact with integrin family to promote YAP1 nuclear translocation. Therefore, we explored the effect of TGM3 on integrin expression and immunoblotting results showed that loss of TGM3 resulted in loss of multiple integrin members, including α4, β1, β4 and β5. We further assessed whether TGM3 was involved in the integrin-YAP/TAZ cascade, and revealed that loss of TGM3 resulted in suppression of the Hippo pathway. Clinically, TCGA dataset showed that TGM3 mRNA level was significant higher in HCC tumor tissues as compared to normal tissues, and the high TGM3 expression is correlated with poorer overall survival (Manuscript in preparation). Previous studies have demonstrated that EV secreted from cells cultured on a stiffer matrix contained a significantly higher protein level. To study whether high NID1 expression in EV of metastatic HCC cells was related to the effect of matrix stiffness, HCC cells (HLE and Huh7) were cultured with soft (0.5 kPa) and stiff (8 kPa) collagen-coated matrix. EV isolated from cells conditioned medium of both cultures, as determined by total protein amount, diameter and morphology, showed no obvious difference. However, the concentration (particle/ml) of EV was slightly higher in EV obtained from cells cultured in higher stiffness. To identify the regulatory mechanism of higher NID1 expression in stiff-EV, we performed mRNA sequencing on cells cultured in both matrix and detected an increase in the amount of NID1 mRNA in cells cultured on 8 kPa matrix than 0.5 kPa. Interestingly, the proteomic expression of these cells showed no obvious elevation, signifying the upregulation of NID1 was mainly sorted to EV instead of cellular level. To determine whether the high expression of NID1 in 8 kPa-EV may contribute to tumor promotive effect, we examined whether treatment of these EV would also result in tumor aggressiveness. Treatment of 8 kPa EV significantly augmented the tumor promoting effect, as indicated by the migration, invasion and colony formation ability. We further demonstrated in vivo that co-treatment of EV derived from HLE cells cultured on 8 kPa matrix resulted in larger tumor growth as compared to EV isolated from 0.5 kPa cells (Manuscript in preparation). 2. To characterize the functional effect of TNFR1-upregulated OXCT2 in enhancing ketolysis in HCC cells The expression of OXCT2 in PLC/PRF/5 cells was upregulated by TNFR1 as revealed by qPCR and immunoblotting. In mice injected with mouse p53-/-; Myc hepatoblasts and EV derived from MHCC97L cells, OXCT2 level in lung metastatic lesions was enhanced as shown by immunohistochemistry. Such increase in OXCT2 was abolished in mice administered with anti-TNFR1 antibody. Knockdown of OXCT2 in mouse p53-/-; Myc hepatoblasts reduced the ability of cells to migrate and invade. Cellular ATP level was found to be reduced in OXCT2 knockdown cells compared to non-target control cells. Co-injection of non-target control cells with EV of MHCC97L cells significantly enhanced the colonization of cells to the lungs. However, such enhancement was largely reduced in mice injected with mouse p53-/-; Myc hepatoblasts with OXCT2 knockdown. 3. To evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of anti-NID1 antibody in the blockage of EV signaling as a therapeutic strategy in HCC metastasis Various mouse models of liver cancer were used to test the therapeutic efficacy of anti-NID1 antibody. Orthotopic liver implantation model involves the use of nude mice implanted with tumor seed derived from luciferase-labeled metastatic MHCC97L cells in liver. Administration of anti-NID1 antibody was able to reduce liver tumor formation and incidence of lung metastasis compared to mice treated with control IgG antibody. Consistently, in mice with liver tumors induced by hydrodynamic injection of plasmids expressing sleeping beauty, myr-AKT and NRasV12 and by injection of plasmids expressing sleeping beauty, myr-AKT and N90-β-catenin, anti-NID1 antibody inhibited liver tumor formation and lung metastasis. EV education model was employed to assess the effect of anti-NID1 antibody in blocking EV-induced pre-metastatic niche formation. Mice were repeatedly injected with NID-enriched EV derived from MHCC97L cells prior to orthotopic liver implantation of tumor seed. The liver tumor development was monitored by bioluminescence imaging. The luciferase signal was highest in mice educated with MHCC97L-EV and injected with control IgG. The signal intensity was significantly compromised in mice treated with anti-NID1 antibody. In accordance with the luciferase signal intensity, mice treated with anti-NID1 antibody resulted in smaller liver tumor and lung metastasis compared to mice treated with control IgG. Lastly, in a physiologically relevant mouse model of HCC patient-derived xenograft (PDX), the circulating EV-NID1 level of mice implanted with subcutaneous PDX was found to be significantly higher than mice without PDX. In addition, the findings showed that either anti-NID1 antibody or sorafenib significantly suppressed tumor formation. Combined treatment of anti-NID1 antibody and sorafenib exhibited the most potent anti-tumorigenic effect, as revealed by most significant downregulation of tumor volume, weight and dimension. In all mouse models testing the effect of anti-NID1 antibody, no observable signs of distress or prominent change in body weight were observed among all experimental groups.
