17300020.label: Realisation of objectives
17300020.value: All four objectives had been addressed with 8 papers published, one under review, and two papers and one patent in preparation. Additionally, the PI had given 9 invited/oral presentations relevant to the project in international conferences. Below, we summarize the achievements made, challenges encountered, and our attempts to overcome such challenges. First, in the objective 1, we proposed to realize an ultra-narrow graphene p-n-p (or n-p-n) junction and study ballistic interference effects that may persist at high temperatures in such a short distance. The key idea is to use the graphene edge as a one-atom-wide gate electrode by attaching another graphene on the side of the hBN/graphene/hBN stack separated by a dielectric insulating layer. Thus, the graphene stacked between the hBN acts as an atomically thin gate electrode (referred to as a gate graphene) and the graphene attached to its side acts as a channel. By doing so, we expect to form only a few nanometers wide p-n-p junction in the channel graphene where strong ballistic interference effects may occur at high temperatures. Despite the simple device structure, we have encountered few challenges and the most significant one was to find a proper dielectric material between the gate and channel graphene. Through systematic COMSOL Multiphysics simulation, we found that to have a few nanometers wide p-n-p junction, the dielectric material must be as thin as 1-2 nm with a dielectric constant of over 40. We have tried different dielectric materials such as thin hBN and HfOx, but they showed problems such as a poor adhesion to the hBN/graphene/hBN stack or a large leakage current. Only very recently, through collaboration with a group in mainland China, we found a new material with a dielectric constant of over 1000 at only a few nanometer thickness. Thanks to this, we were finally able to build the working device and measure the signature of the quantum oscillations due to ballistic transport across an ultra-narrow p-n-p junction. Currently, we are preparing a paper and a patent simultaneously. In the objective 2, we proposed building 1D superlattice structures and study their effects. Since the graphene-gated device (the objective 1) had only been realized recently, we have explored and developed new ways to build 1D superlattices at different length scales and study their effects on electron transport in graphene. First, we developed a facile technique to build van der Waals stacks using a microneedle probe, published in AIP Advances 14, 015333 (2024) as an Editor's Pick. In this work, we demonstrated that the microneedle probe can be used as a high-precision cutter, rotator, or wire bonder for 2D materials. Using this method, we can reliably cut graphene/hBN stacks and reassemble them vertically to create a periodic hBN/graphene/hBN/.../graphene/hBN heterostructure to create a nanometer-scale 1D superlattice along the side wall. Moreover, the method also enables the precise alignment between graphene and hBN in hBN/graphene/hBN/graphene/hBN stack to investigate Coulomb drag between moire and graphene bands, published in Physical Review Letters 133, 186301 (2024). In addition, to control the periodicity of the hBN/graphene/hBN/.../graphene/hBN superlattice, it is important to determine the thickness of the hBN used accurately with a monolayer precision. For this, we have carried out statistical optical analysis of many hBN flakes exfoliated on 90-nm-thick SiO2/Si substrate and found that the red-filtered image exhibits the strongest optical contrast and the second harmonic generation signal must be measured to finally confirm the exact number of layers down to monolayer. The work is not only useful for this project but also for many other studies that use the hBN as an atomic spacer or to build twisted hBN ferroelectric interface. This work was published in Nano Letters 24, 14774 (2024). In addition, we have collaborated with a group in Mechanical Engineering to use a nano-imprinting technique to create 1D superlattice structure directly on SiO2/Si wafer with a periodicity of a few hundred nanometers. By placing graphene on top and using thin hBN as a dielectric material, we have found that the quantum-Hall plateaus in graphene vary with the number of p-n junctions between the Hall probes systematically. In addition, we had collaborated with another group to build small-scale junctions using a 3D printing technique and successfully demonstrated that we can make an array of Pt-Ag thermocouple in a micrometer size, published in Advanced Materials 35, 2301704 (2023) and featured in a frontispiece. This 3D printing technique can be used to create a micrometer scale gate array for this study. Apart from the fundamental study, we have also explored the possibility for practical applications in the objective 3. About a year after the project begun, we found a report in Nature that used a very similar structure to create ultrashort MoS2 field-effect-transistor (FET) devices [Nature 603, 259 (2022)]. This clearly shows that the graphene-gated device proposed in this project has a potential for device application. However, the work in Nature only uses a single gate to demonstrate the FET behavior while in this project, we make p-n junctions. Our device scheme has therefore unique advantages because it enables a precise control of charge density in an ultranarrow region. As we wrote above, we are already preparing one patent. In addition, we have also collaborated with a material synthesis/growth group to realize large-size semiconducting 2D materials [Natural Sciences 3, 20220059 (2023); under review in 2D Materials] to use them as a channel in our device. Moreover, we have proposed theoretically that the focusing of an electric field at the sharp metallic edge can create a fractional potential barrier in field-emission devices which can greatly enhance the emission efficiency. The work was published in Applied Physics Letters 123, 243503 (2023) and we are currently working to use the edge of the gate graphene in our device as the metallic edge to focus an electric field to realize our theoretical proposal experimentally. Lastly, we have been working with a theorist to explore new transport phenomena that may occur in ultrashort p-n junctions (the objective 4). We found that in a nanometer-scale 1D superlattice, the effect of the superlattice potential is greatly enhanced and in the extreme limit, it might even be possible to significantly quench the Fermi velocity along one direction. In addition, due to such a small periodicity, we may find the dependence of the effect on whether the superlattice potential is formed along the zigzag or armchair direction of graphene like in carbon nanotube, different from the other existing studies on graphene 1D superlattices. In summary, by finding a new dielectric material, we have finally resolved the most critical challenge in the project and have successfully demonstrated ballistic transport in a single-graphene-gated device (Objective 1; one paper and patent in preparation). In parallel, we have developed various new methods to build 1D superlattice structures [Objective 2; AIP Advances 14, 015333 (2024); Nano Letters 24, 14774 (2024); Advanced Materials 35, 2301704 (2023)] and explored the potential applications of this project [Objective 3; Natural Sciences 3, 20220059 (2023); under review in 2D Materials; Applied Physics Letters 123, 243503 (2023)]. Lastly, we have theoretically found that making few nanometer scale 1D superlattice can exhibit new transport phenomena (Objective 4). Therefore, we have addressed all four objectives.

17300020.label: Major findings and research outcome
17300020.value: During the project, we have published 8 peer-reviewed papers in international journals like PRL, Advanced Materials and Nano Letters, submitted one paper, and given 9 invited/oral presentations in international conferences (Graphene2024, RPGR2024, APS March Meeting, etc.). In addition to these papers and conferences listed in Part C, we are also preparing two papers and one patent. Below, I summarize the major findings. First, we have found new insulating material with high dielectric constant and used it to create an ultranarrow graphene p-n-p junction. Through simulation, we found that it is critical to have such a high dielectric constant material to create ultranarrow p-n junctions and by systematically testing various materials, we found that one of the water-soluble compounds has a large dielectric constant and nearly no pinholes even at few nanometer thickness. We used it to build graphene-gated device and observed the signature of the ballistic transport effect at high temperatures. We are preparing one paper and a patent. Second, we developed/demonstrated various new techniques to build 1D superlattice structure. Published in AIP Advances (publication no. 5 in Part C), we demonstrated a facile technique to use a microneedle probe as a high-precision cutter and rotator for 2D materials, and through systematic optical analysis, we established the way to determine the thickness of hBN precisely [Nano Lett. (2024); no. 7 in Part C]. Both works can be applied to build a hBN/graphene/hBN/.../graphene/hBN stack with a precise alignment and periodicity. Using these techniques, we have indeed made hBN/graphene/hBN/graphene/hBN stack with one of the graphene layers aligned with hBN and investigated Coulomb drag between the graphene layers [PRL (2024); no. 6 in Part C]. In addition, we have collaborated with other groups to apply new techniques, nanoimprinting and 3D printing, to create various types of 1D and 2D superlattice structures [Adv. Mater. (2023); no. 2 in Part C and one paper in preparation]. Lastly, we have explored the application potential of the proposed device architecture. Working with a material synthesis/growth group, we made large-scale 2D semiconductors [Nat. Sci. (2023); no. 1 in Part C; 2D Mater. under review], and with a group in mainland China, we proposed a field-emission device with high efficiency by utilizing the electric field focusing at the sharp metallic edges [APL (2023); no. 8 in Part C]. Currently, we are working to use the graphene edge as the metallic edge to realize the proposed device application.

17300020.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17300020.value: During the project, we have demonstrated that the ultranarrow p-n junctions can be formed and strong ballistic interference effect appears at high temperatures in such a short junction. This provides an opportunity to investigate the effect of 1D superlattice in a nanometer scale that had not been realized so far. According to our calculation, such a 1D superlattice can give rise to strong band renormalization that can reduce the Fermi velocity significantly in one direction. We will continue to realize such a narrow 1D superlattice experimentally and test the theoretical calculations. Apart from the fundamental study, the new high-dielectric constant material we found during this project has great potential in various fundamental studies and applications. First, it can certainly be used as a gate dielectric for high-performance and energy-efficient FET devices. For this, we have already worked with material synthesis/growth group to use large size 2D semiconductors as a channel material in our device structure. Second, one can use the material to induce large hole doping in various 2D materials to examine if the materials become superconducting as demonstrated on the electron side using an ionic liquid gating. We will constantly explore these new directions both experimentally and theoretically.

17300020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17300020.value: The project aimed to realize ultranarrow junctions between electron (n) and hole (p) doped graphene using the graphene edge as an atomically thin gate electrode. By finding new high-quality dielectric material with high dielectric constant, we have successfully demonstrated that such an ultranarrow p-n junction can be formed and exhibit strong ballistic transport phenomena at high temperatures. We have further investigated the possibility to create 1D superlattice structure using different techniques, such as van der Waals stacking, nanoimprinting, and 3D printing techniques, and showed that each technique has unique advantages in tunability of the structure and technical feasibility. In addition, we have also collaborated with different groups to explore the possibility of the proposed device architecture for potential applications such as high-performance and energy efficient FET and highly efficient field-emission devices. As a result, the project had led not only to the discovery of new physical phenomena and materials but also to the development of new techniques that can be used to explore new physics as well as to develop electronic devices with new functionalities originating from quantum interference or superlattice potential effects.

17300220.label: Project Objectives
17300220.value: We will perform a theoretical study on topology-enforced symmetry breaking in invertible topological phases of fermions with internal symmetries of finite groups. We aim to find the simplest symmetry group that is enforced to be broken for every 2D invertible topological phase, and ultimately derive a criterion or a practical algorithm that can determine if topology-enforced symmetry breaking occurs for a general finite group. We will derive the classification and physical properties of 2D fermionic symmetry-protected topological phases with mixed crystalline and internal symmetries, and derive a precise crystalline equivalence principle for fermions. We will study topology-enforced symmetry breaking and crystalline equivalence in fermionic invertible topological phases with crystalline symmetries, derive related Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorems, and seek for potential applications to experimental systems such as higher-order topological insulators.

We will derive the classification and physical properties of 2D fermionic symmetry-protected topological phases with mixed crystalline and internal symmetries, and derive a precise crystalline equivalence principle for fermions.

We will study topology-enforced symmetry breaking and crystalline equivalence in fermionic invertible topological phases with crystalline symmetries, derive related Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorems, and seek for potential applications to experimental systems such as higher-order topological insulators.

17300220.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17300220.value: Recently we have seen great advances in topological phases of quantum matter. Lying in the heart of the theoretical developments is the understanding of deep interplay between symmetry and topology. Such interplay occurs at least in two levels: (i) compatibility between symmetry and topology, and (ii) symmetry-refined classification and characterization of topological phases if compatible. Most of the previous works have focused on the latter, i.e., refined topology by symmetry, including symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases (e.g., topological insulators) and symmetry-enriched topological phases (e.g., fractional quantum Hall liquids). The latter hosts excitations that obey fractional braiding statistics and has potential application in topological quantum computing. In this proposed research, we aim to study the first level of interplay in a special class of topological phases, namely 2D invertible topological phases of fermion systems. In particular, we will study the phenomenon which we name topology-enforced symmetry breaking. That is, when equipped with certain topological properties, the system is enforced to break some symmetries. We will study topology-enforced symmetry breaking for both internal and crystalline symmetries. Crystalline symmetries are among the most widely found symmetries in the nature. Recently we have seen many experimental systems where crystalline symmetries play important roles, such as the so-called higher-order topological insulators. For crystalline systems, we will study the so-called crystalline equivalence principle, which states that the classification of SPT/invertible phases only depend on the group structure, but not on whether it is realized by internal or crystalline symmetries. Our objectives are as follows: (1) study topology-enforced symmetry breaking in 2D invertible topological phases with internal symmetry; (2) derive the classification of SPT phases with mixed crystalline and internal symmetries, and the precise form of crystalline equivalence for fermion systems; (3) extend the study to invertible topological phases, study related Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorems, and seek for potential applications to higher-order topological insulators/superconductors. 近年來量子物質的拓撲相研究取得了巨大進展。在理論上，核心發展是人們意識到對稱性與拓撲之間的深刻糾纏。這種糾纏至少體現在兩個層次上：（i）對稱性和拓撲之間的兼容性，（ii）如果兼容，由對稱性細化後的拓撲相分類和刻畫。目前的大多數工作都集中在後者，具體包括對稱保護拓撲相（即SPT相，如拓撲絕緣體）和對稱富化拓撲相（如分數量子霍爾態）。對稱富化拓撲系統中存在服從分數編織統計的元激發，具有應用在拓撲量子計算上的潛力。 本項目旨在壹類特殊的拓撲相中，費米子系統的二維可逆拓撲相，研究對稱性和拓撲在第壹個層次的糾纏。尤其，我們將研究由拓撲性質強制發生的對稱破缺現象。也就是說，當具備某些拓撲屬性時，系統的壹些對稱性將被強制破缺。我們會同時研究拓撲強制破缺的內稟和晶體對稱性。晶體對稱性是自然界中最廣泛的對稱性之壹。最近，許多晶體對稱性起著重要作用的實驗體系被發現，例如高階拓撲絕緣體。對於晶體系統，我們將研究所謂的晶體等效原理。該原理指出，SPT /可逆拓撲相的分類僅取決於對稱性的群結構，而不取決於是內稟對稱性還是晶體對稱性。 本項目的研究目標如下：（1）研究具有內稟對稱性的二維可逆拓撲相中的拓撲強制對稱性破缺現象；（2）得到同時具有晶體和內稟對稱性的SPT相分類，以及費米子系統的晶體等效形式。 （3）將(2)中的研究擴展至可逆拓撲相，研究相關的Lieb-Schultz-Mattis定理，並尋求在高階拓撲絕緣體/超導體中的潛在應用。

17300220.label: Realisation of objectives
17300220.value: This project aims to study the compatibility/incompatibility between topology and symmetry in quantum phases of matter. One of the questions that we look deep into is how a given topological order can enforce a symmetry to break, namely enforced symmetry breaking. We also study how certain symmetries (especially rotational crystalline symmetry) protect and enforce certain topological phases to occur. Overall, the objectives are achieved with satisfactory results. 1) For objective 1, we thoroughly studied the phenomena of Enforced Symmetry Breaking (ESB) for 0D, 1D and 2D fermionic invertible topological orders and extended the study to 3D topological orders with time-reversal symmetry. For 2D fermionic invertible topological orders, we obtained a series of criteria on the existence or non-existence of ESB. Using these criteria, we discovered many novel ESB examples. The results are published in Paper 4 of Part C. For 3D topological orders, we considered the compatibility between certain types of three-loop braiding statistics (resulting from Majorana-chain decorated 3D fermionic symmetry-protected topological phases) and the time-reversal symmetry. We found that these three-loop statistics were compatible with T^2=-1 time-reversal symmetry but incompatible with T^2=1 under certain circumstances. These results are still in preparation. A preliminary preprint can be found in Paper 5 of Part C. 2) For objective 2, we studied 2D and 3D symmetry-protected topological phases of fermions with rotation and internal symmetries and the so-called crystalline equivalence principle. We successfully obtained the stacking groups that classify 3D rotation SPT phases with additional internal symmetry. The classifications agree with the counterparts of SPT phases with internal symmetry only, justifying the extension of crystalline equivalence principle to fermionic systems. These results are published in Paper 2 of Part C. 3) For objective 3, we studied non-interacting higher-order topological phases with crystalline symmetry and discovered a new kind of three-dimensional topological phases, which we called intertwined Weyl phases. It is a phase that intertwines the existing topological gapped and gapless phases protected by the same crystalline symmetry. This work was published in Paper 1 of Part C. We also studied crystalline topological phases in non-Hermitian systems and discovered a new kind of exceptional semimetals that can only be stabilized by non-Hermitian crystalline symmetries. This work was published in Paper 3 of Part C.

17300220.label: Major findings and research outcome
17300220.value: 1. We obtained a series of criteria on the existence or non-existence of Enforced Symmetry Breaking for 2D fermionic invertible topological orders and discovered many novel examples via these criteria [Phys. Rev. Research 5, 023153, (2023)]. The phenomena of enforced symmetry breaking in 3D was also studied by considering the compatibility between three-loop braiding statistics and T^2=1 or T^2=-1 time time-reversal symmetries (manuscript in preparation). These results reveal intrinsic incompatibilities between topology and symmetry occur ubiquitously. 2. We obtained the stacking group of the classification of 2D and 3D symmetry-protected topological phases of fermions with rotation and internal symmetries, and verified the so-called crystalline equivalence principle for fermionic systems [Phys. Rev. B 105, 195154 (2022)]. In this work, we also constructed the so-called Majorana-type 3D SPT phases by using lower-dimensional blocks. 3. We discovered a new type of non-interacting higher-order topological phases protected by rotational crystalline symmetry, which we called intertwined Weyl phases [npj Quantum Materials 7, 15 (2022)]. We also found that non-Hermitian rotation symmetries can stabilize topological semimetals in a way that does not exist for the Hermitian counterparts. This shows that the interplay between topology and symmetry in non-Hermitian systems could be very different from Hermitian counterparts, in particular in gapless systems [Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 226401 (2022)].

17300220.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17300220.value: Many questions remain open in the study of interplay between topology and symmetry in correlated systems. Following the lines of this project, one of the questions is to obtain general criteria on enforced symmetry breaking for topological orders. We only studied a few examples for 3D systems and considered 2D invertible topological orders in this project. Obtaining general criteria boils down to derive various obstruction functions related to the quantum anomaly of symmetries. A challenging yet more interesting question is to study how symmetry stabilizes gapless phases of matter in correlated systems, including non-Hermitian systems. In this perspective, we would like to explore the so-called generalized symmetry described by category theory. In this way, we hope that by including more symmetries, we can move towards a better understanding of gapless phases of matter in the presence of strong interaction and explore the role of topology there.

17300220.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17300220.value: The interplay between symmetry and topology has played a central role in the recent study of topological phases of quantum matter. Many novel quantum phases are discovered, e.g., topological insulators and Weyl semimetals. Nevertheless, topology and symmetry do not always live in harmony. Incompatible situations do exist. We theoretically studied an interesting phenomenon as a consequence of such incompatibility, which we call enforced-symmetry breaking by topological order. General criteria are obtained and various examples are worked out. In the case when the symmetry and topology are compatible, we studied various quantum phases of matters protected by the crystalline rotation symmetry, including symmetry-protected fermionic topological phases, topological semimetals and their non-Hermitian versions. Our study deepens the theoretical understanding of role of symmetry in topological phases of matter.

17300320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17300320.value: The Triassic (252-201 Ma) was a time of transition, as life recovered from the Earth’s most devastating mass extinction, the Permo-Triassic event at 252 million years ago. Although the pattern and tempo of this recovery has not yet been strictly established, researchers generally agree that marine predators had emerged and already established dominant morphologies and lifestyles by this period. Triassic marine invertebrates are well understood, but marine vertebrates remain criptic due to the lack of well-preserved fossils. Fish and reptile fossils discovered over the last two decades in Triassic marine strata of South China are advancing understanding however. The new fossils have provided unique evidence of marine biological recovery and further indicate that marine reptiles thrived in considerable diversity during the early Mesozoic. In addition to their scientific significance, these discoveries have captivated the public. Volcanic units interbedded within Triassic marine strata can provide precise age constraints for the exact timing and duration for this, the largest marine reptile radiation in Earth history. Here we propose research that will establish a high-precision radiometric age framework for fossil-bearing units in Guizhou, Yunnan, Anhui and Hubei Provinces. Resultant chronostratigraphic constraints will enable correlation of these Triassic units with other marine successions elsewhere and help advance understanding of marine reptile radiation in the Mesozoic. 17300320.label: Realisation of objectives
17300320.value: 1. Throughout our funding period, we conducted two field trips to investigate the Triassic strata in South China. These trips involved the collection of 14 tuff samples from six well-known marine outcrops, resulting in the discovery of marine reptile fossils in Guizhou, Yunnan, Anhui, and Hubei Provinces. Through meticulous examination of the stratigraphic columns and analysis of the samples, we obtained valuable insights into the depositional environments that contributed to the formation of these fossil-rich strata. 2. Regrettably, our initial plan to utilize two distinct zircon U/Pb dating methodologies had to be modified due to unforeseen circumstances. Equipment malfunctions at HKU since late 2019, along with intermittent laboratory closures at MIT resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, necessitated a change in our approach. Consequently, the ICP-MS dating analysis was carried out in Wuhan, while U/Pb TIMS dating was conducted at the University of Toronto. However, the experiments in Wuhan and Toronto were delayed due to the Covid-19 lockdown. It wasn't until August 2023, just two months prior to the conclusion of the project's funding period, that we obtained the high-precision U/Pb TIMS results. Nonetheless, the U/Pb TIMS ages are notably precise. For instance, one sample from Yingou, Yunnan, dated at 247.96 +/-0.15 Ma, indicates that the marine reptile's recovery occurred much earlier than previously presumed. This represents the oldest-known evidence supporting the rapid recovery of marine reptiles following the end-Permian mass extinction event. 3. Despite the challenges posed by the COVID lockdown in China and Canada, our team successfully conducted an analysis of the biological recovery of the Triassic marine ecosystems. This involved the acquisition of highly precise U/Pb TIMS ages from the University of Toronto in August 2023, two months prior to the conclusion of the project. Our research findings have been presented at conferences, and we are currently in the process of preparing a manuscript for submission to Nature Communications by the end of 2024. 4. In a proactive initiative, we have initiated a new project that focuses on Triassic terrestrial ecosystems, expanding upon the funded project centered on Triassic marine ecosystems. This endeavor involves the active participation of Yangyang Xia, a dedicated HKU PhD student who specializes in the study of Triassic plants in NW and NE China. Furthermore, the research outcomes have been seamlessly integrated into two prominent HKU courses: "EASC3417-Earth Through Time" for undergraduate students majoring in Geology, Geology (Intensive), and Earth System Science, and "EASC6007-Mass Extinctions" for PhD students at HKU. 5. Due to the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, the Stephen Hui Geological Museum faced intermittent closures, which postponed our highly anticipated exhibition. A special dinosaur exhibition, including marine reptiles, will kick off in early 2025. Additionally, PI Chang demonstrated remarkable dedication by actively participating in various public outreach activities. This included delivering engaging and insightful talks to primary and high school students and participating in the HKU Information Day to effectively promote and share our groundbreaking findings with a wider audience.

17300320.label: Major findings and research outcome
17300320.value: Multiple studies have suggested that a significant mass extinction event led to a shift in marine predator communities, promoting the emergence of air-breathing top predators, such as large marine reptiles. Throughout the Mesozoic era, various lineages of reptiles expanded into marine environments, giving rise to approximately twelve thriving groups in marine habitats. The longest-lived lineage endured for over 180 million years, while the shortest-lived lineage ceased to exist after only a few million years. Fossil records from the Triassic period demonstrate a rich diversity of physically sizable marine reptile specimens. However, the precise timing and duration of the marine reptile radiation remain uncertain. The prevailing belief is that marine reptiles progressively increased their diversity around the middle of the Middle Triassic period (approximately 240 million years ago) in conjunction with the perceived pace of "delayed recovery." The Permo-Triassic mass extinction event, which resulted in the demise of over 90% of marine animal species and 70% of terrestrial vertebrate species, has prompted considerable interest in the timing of marine environmental recovery. Although different taxa exhibited varying recovery rates, it is generally accepted that complete marine ecosystem recovery occurred 7-10 million years after the mass extinction. The event itself is believed to have stemmed from a combination of external factors and intrinsic causes, including the eruptions of the Siberian Traps, methane clathrate gasification, oceanic anoxia event, and the configuration of continental crust into Pangea. Our high-precision U/Pb TIMS ages of 237.75+/-0.13 Ma and 247.93+/-0.15 Ma obtained from prominent outcrops in Yunnan and Hubei have enabled the assessment of evolutionary rates of marine reptiles and the speed of biodiversity recovery following the most severe mass extinction event. These findings align with recent discoveries from multiple outcrops in South China, challenging the delayed recovery hypothesis and providing evidence of the rapid diversification of Triassic marine reptiles. (Please refer to our published paper and the manuscript under preparation) (Project number 17505919 is not mentioned in the acknowledgment of paper 1, "Chapter 13," because the editor thought it was a book chapter, so the project number was deleted from our original manuscript by the editor.)

17300320.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17300320.value: Based on our enhanced comprehension of the recovery pattern and pace of marine reptiles, numerous questions remain unresolved. Specifically, did marine reptiles recuperate more rapidly than other marine animals, and if so, what were the underlying reasons? Additionally, what were the implications for terrestrial animals and plants following the most severe extinction event approximately 252 million years ago? A comprehensive understanding of the Triassic ecosystems is imperative to address these inquiries. To facilitate this, we have initiated a new research direction focusing on the terrestrial ecosystem of the Triassic period, commencing with the study of plant fossils (Yangyang Xia's probationary seminar). Our field studies have commenced in the Triassic outcrops of Xinjiang of NW China and Liaoning of NE China. This newly formulated project serves as an extension of the existing funded project, with the intention of submitting a proposal to the General Research Fund (GRF) in 2025.

17300320.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17300320.value: The deposits in South China contain a wide variety of Triassic marine reptiles, suggesting that this area may have been a central point of radiation. Abundant fossils, for example, Chaohusaurus, a small ichthyosaur found in Anhui Province, most likely used an eel-like swimming mode and could catch and consume invertebrates or fish with a quick attack. Fossils from this area also provide evidence of reproductive mode and sexual dimorphism in sauropterygians. Additionally, fossils from other areas in South China indicate primitive skeletons, possible amphibious lifestyles, and the oldest record of amniotes with reduced visual capacity. Establishing high-precision ages for these outcrops is the key to understanding the recovery pattern and ecosystems after the most severe extinction event at 252 Ma. Our research on the age of fossil-rich deposits clarifies regional correlations and chronostratigraphy of marine strata in South China, shedding light on fundamental large-scale questions regarding Triassic biodiversity and ecology.

17300520.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17300520.value: Stacking two atomically thin 2 dimensional (2D) materials could lead to a Van deer Waals 2D heterostructure. Depending on the lattice mismatch and the align angle, the stacking could generate various 2D periodical patterns, so called moiré patterns at nanometer scale without introducing any interfacial defect, forming perfect 2D complex crystals beyond individual atomically thin layers. This artificial 2D superlattice offers a great flexibility to tune electronic states for some exotic features. It opens a new route towards realizing quantum manipulation of electronic states in 2D systems. In this application we propose to study Van deer Waals stacked homo- and hetero-structures of 2D semiconductors including but not limited to monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) and III-VI monochalcogenides M-X with semiconductor optical spectroscopy. We are going to focus on the band modification and nonlinear optical properties arising from interlayer coupling and moiré superlattices. 17300520.label: Major findings and research outcome
17300520.value: We successfully fabricated twisted bilayer homo and heterostructure TMD (WSe2/WS2, MoSe2/MoSe2, etc) and investigated the interlayer coupling on electronic and optical properties. The direct outcomes from the project: 1. Near-field coupling of interlayer excitons in MoSe2/WSe2 heterobilayers to surface plasmon polaritons. We demonstrate the successful coupling of surface plamonic polaritons (SPPs) with interlayer excitons in molybdenum diselenide/tungsten diselenide heterobilayers. Our results indicate that the valley polarization can be efficiently transferred to SPPs, enabling preservation of polarization information even after propagating tens of micrometers. This work is published in J. Chem. Phys. 160, 141103 (2024)。 2. Moire exciton dynamic study: We carried out a time resolved pump-probe reflectance spectroscopic study on moire excitons in a twisted monolayer WS2/WSe2 heterostructure. By probing at the resonant energies of intralayer excitons, we observed distinct temporal tracks and attributes the different tracks to the evolution of electron and hole components of the interlayer moire excitons. We concluded that the interlayer moire excitons are formed within a few picoseconds and the lifetime of moire excitons ranges from a few hundreds of picoseconds to a few nanoseconds. Our results provide insights into the nature of moire excitons and their behavior in twisted heterostructures, which could have important implications for the development of novel optoelectronic devices. The work is under review at Physical Review. 3. We also develop a scanning probe microscopic method to detect the electric gap for 2D semiconductors including heterostructures. The work is published in Nature communications.

17300520.value: We are continuing our research on moire excitons on twisted bilayer TMDs and are making good progress on exciton dynamics. We expect one or two journal articles in 2025.

17300520.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17300520.value: We fabricated twisted bilayer 2D semiconductors and investigated the electronic and optical properties of the 2D semiconductors under the unique lateral moire potential induced by the moire pattern by the twisted structure. We developed methods of scanning probe microscopy and the device structure coupled with surface plasmon polariton to study the 2D bilayer structures. We also use ultrafast pump-probe spectroscopy to investigate the interlayer exciton dynamics of the interlayter excitons.

17300620.label: Project Objectives
17300620.value: Physical Conditions for the Formation of Infant Globular Clusters in NGC 1275. We plan to make a complete search for regions currently engaged in vigorous star formation throughout the gaseous nebula of NGC 1275, the giant elliptical galaxy at the center of the Perseus cluster. Identifying such star-forming regions is a necessary first step towards elucidating physical conditions in the nebula that lead to formation of infant globular clusters. To make this search, we have successfully proposed and recently acquired an image of the entire nebula in [OIII]λ5007 Å. This line is typically the brightest emission line from HII regions, but is undetectable from the characteristic nebular gas. In the meantime, we plan to search for dense molecular gas − a necessary condition for star formation − in two filaments previously identified to contain giant HII regions at their innermost tips. We have shown that the molecular gas in these filaments is infalling ballistically under the gravitational potential of NGC 1275: does dense molecular gas become increasingly abundant along the direction of gas infall, owing perhaps to ram pressure, thus explaining vigorous star formation at the innermost tips of these filaments? Finally, we plan to search for massive yet compact molecular clouds that presumably comprise the nurseries of progenitor globular clusters; where detected, we plan follow-up observations to search for dense molecular gas in these clouds. Formation History of Young Stellar Populations in Giant Elliptical Galaxies. Is star formation that is sustained over time characteristic of cluster central giant elliptical galaxies that exhibit young stellar populations? If so, what are the star-formation rates of these galaxies at earlier epochs, when they are still rapidly growing in, especially, size? Giant elliptical galaxies at the centers of galaxy clusters observed in the CLASH program span epochs dating back to nearly half the age of the Universe. Many of these galaxies exhibit spatially extended young stellar populations. By subtracting out light from a dominant old stellar population (formed in the early Universe), we fit stellar population synthesis models to the spatially-resolved spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the remaining young stellar population. In this way, we are able to infer the ages and masses of the young stellar population throughout space, and by integrating over space derive their star-formation rate over time. We find that the young stellar population in the giant elliptical galaxy at the center of MACS J0329.7-0211, which at z = 0.45 corresponds to a look-back time of nearly 5 Gyr, has formed over the past ~100 Myr at a rate that is ~100 times higher than that in NGC 1275. We plan to extend our study of other cluster central giant elliptical galaxies in the CLASH program that also exhibit spatially extended young stellar populations. Nature of Compact Circumnuclear UV continuum in Giant Elliptical Galaxies. Rather than a spatially extended young stellar population, over half of the cluster central giant elliptical galaxies in the CLASH program exhibit compact UV continuum from around the nucleus. We have started and plan to complete our work to address whether this continuum light originates from a young stellar population. Nature of Cool Gas in Cluster Central Giant Elliptical Galaxies. The manner in which their relatively cool gas is energized, and consequently also their physical properties and whether the ionized, atomic, and molecular components largely exist in different phases or co-exist in the same volume, remain poorly understood. We are addressing these questions by comparing the line profiles and measuring the line ratios of the atomic and molecular components in the complex filamentary nebula of NGC 5044, the giant elliptical galaxy at the center of the NGC 5044 galaxy group. We also plan to search for continuum light and measure the line to continuum ratio of the nebula in NGC 1275, and thus address whether and how much of the nebular emission lines is produced by recombination of ionized gas. A Spatially Diffuse, Intermediate-Age Stellar Population in Cluster Central Giant Elliptical Galaxies? The central giant elliptical galaxy of the Perseus cluster is much bluer compared with normal elliptical galaxies. We suspect that this bluish color traces a spatially diffuse stellar population spanning a broad range of ages perhaps of order 1 Gyr, presumably comprising the remnants of disrupted star clusters born from the cooler intracluster gas. Recently, we have discovered a radial gradient in the near-IR colors of the central giant elliptical galaxy of the NGC 5044 group. This color gradient also may trace a spatially diffuse stellar population with an age of order 1 Gyr. We plan to better understand the nature and physical properties of the stellar population traced by the aforementioned colors.

rows: Physical Conditions for the Formation of Infant Globular Clusters in NGC 1275. We plan to make a complete search for regions currently engaged in vigorous star formation throughout the gaseous nebula of NGC 1275, the giant elliptical galaxy at the center of the Perseus cluster. Identifying such star-forming regions is a necessary first step towards elucidating physical conditions in the nebula that lead to formation of infant globular clusters. To make this search, we have successfully proposed and recently acquired an image of the entire nebula in [OIII]λ5007 Å. This line is typically the brightest emission line from HII regions, but is undetectable from the characteristic nebular gas. In the meantime, we plan to search for dense molecular gas − a necessary condition for star formation − in two filaments previously identified to contain giant HII regions at their innermost tips.

Is star formation that is sustained over time characteristic of cluster central giant elliptical galaxies that exhibit young stellar populations? If so, what are the star-formation rates of these galaxies at earlier epochs, when they are still rapidly growing in, especially, size? Giant elliptical galaxies at the centers of galaxy clusters observed in the CLASH program span epochs dating back to nearly half the age of the Universe. By subtracting out light from a dominant old stellar population, we fit stellar population synthesis models to the spatially-resolved spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the remaining young stellar population. We plan to extend our study of other cluster central giant elliptical galaxies in the CLASH program that also exhibit spatially extended young stellar populations.

Nature of Compact Circumnuclear UV continuum in Giant Elliptical Galaxies. Rather than a spatially extended young stellar population, over half of the cluster central giant elliptical galaxies in the CLASH program exhibit compact UV continuum from around the nucleus. We have started and plan to complete our work to address whether this continuum light originates from a young stellar population.

Nature of Cool Gas in Cluster Central Giant Elliptical Galaxies. The manner in which their relatively cool gas is energized, and consequently also their physical properties and whether the ionized, atomic, and molecular components largely exist in different phases or co-exist in the same volume, remain poorly understood. We are addressing these questions by comparing the line profiles and measuring the line ratios of the atomic and molecular components in the complex filamentary nebula of NGC 5044, the giant elliptical galaxy at the center of the NGC 5044 galaxy group. We also plan to search for continuum light and measure the line to continuum ratio of the nebula in NGC 1275, and thus address whether and how much of the nebular emission lines is produced by recombination of ionized gas.

A Spatially Diffuse, Intermediate-Age Stellar Population in Cluster Central Giant Elliptical Galaxies? The central giant elliptical galaxy of the Perseus cluster is much bluer compared with normal elliptical galaxies. We suspect that this bluish color traces a spatially diffuse stellar population spanning a broad range of ages perhaps of order 1 Gyr, presumably comprising the remnants of disrupted star clusters born from the cooler intracluster gas. Recently, we have discovered a radial gradient in the near-IR colors of the central giant elliptical galaxy of the NGC 5044 group. This color gradient also may trace a spatially diffuse stellar population with an age of order 1 Gyr. We plan to better understand the nature and physical properties of the stellar population traced by the aforementioned colors.

17300620.label: Major findings and research outcome
17300620.value: NGC 1275, the giant elliptical galaxy at the center of the Perseus cluster, is the prototypical example of a Brightest Cluster Galaxy (BCG) exhibiting copious cool gas, extensive star formation, and an active galactic nucleus (AGN). Over a central radius of ~5 kpc, we showed that NGC 1275 formed a population of especially massive progenitor globular clusters (GCs) about 500 Myr ago (Lim et al. 2022), followed apparently by the formation of a rotating disk hosting spiral arms about 150 Myr ago (Yeung et al. 2022). Outwards to a radius of ~15 kpc, we showed that the many arc-like and diffuse stellar features in this galaxy have the same age as stars in the central spiral disk (Levitskiy et al. 2024, in preparation). We suggest that an episode of enhanced AGN activity in NGC 1275 began ~500 Myr ago, triggering an episode of enhanced ICM cooling - as we inferred, in a separate study, to explain the spatial-kinematic morphology of the cool gas (Vigneron et al. 2024). A population of progenitor GCs formed from the cooled gas, only the most massive of which survived to the present today; the remainder being disrupted by the strong tidal field at the inner region of NGC 1275, thus forming the stellar features seen around, and contributing in part or entirely to, the central spiral disk. Our work helps explain the enormous population of GCs around BCGs and suggests an additional pathway for their stellar growth to become the largest and most massive galaxies in the universe. Extending our study of NGC 1275 to the twenty-five BCGs in the CLASH program, we carefully established which of these BCGs exhibit star formation, cool gas, and AGNs (Levitisky et al. 2024). We also showed that only those clusters having the most steeply decreasing ICM entropies inward host BCGs exhibiting cool gas and star formation, as well as those having the most powerful AGNs. In a follow-up work (Lim et al., in preparation), we show that the different ICM entropy profiles of these clusters are related to how much they are dynamically relaxed: suggesting that their ICM thermodynamics are set by global (dynamical relaxation following a cluster merger) rather than local (a fine balance between ICM cooling and AGN reheating) processes. This discovery calls into question our most cherished example of AGN feedback in astrophysics, necessary in cosmological simulations to regulate star formation in galaxies.

17300620.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17300620.value: Motivated by our study of the CLASH clusters, we have embarked on a program to determine whether the ICM thermodynamics of other clusters also are largely determined by the degree to which they have dynamically relaxed following a cluster merger. Requiring us to learn how to infer the ICM thermodynamics from X-ray maps of galaxy clusters, we have successfully applied for a Germany-Hong Kong Joint Research Scheme to collaborate with Dr. Jeremy Sanders of the Max Planck Institute of Extraterrestrial Physics to work on this aspect of the project. Dr. Sanders has developed to most sophisticated algorithm available for deriving the ICM parameters from X-ray maps of galaxy clusters. In this way, we plan to confirm or refute - as well as probe for greater complexity - the relationship between ICM thermodynamics and cluster dynamical state.

17300620.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17300620.value: The formation and growth of galaxies - requiring feedback from an accreting central supermassive black hole to regulate the formation of stars from gas - is one of the outstanding problems in astrophysics. Galaxy clusters, which can comprise over a thousand galaxies bound together by gravity, for which the space between galaxies is filled with hot gas, provide a laboratory for studying the formation of the largest and most massive galaxies in the universe: their central giant elliptical galaxies. In some galaxy clusters, the hot gas around the cluster center is inferred to cool and fuel star formation in their central galaxies; at the same time, by helping fuel their central supermassive black holes, these galaxies generate powerful jets to reheat the cool gas thus regulating star formation. In this project, we showed that the powerful jets generated by accreting supermassive black holes in the cluster central galaxies may promote, rather than hinder, gas cooling and star formation. Furthermore, the gas thermodynamics in galaxy clusters, even at their centers, is determined by the degree to which galaxy clusters have dynamically relaxed following a cluster merger. Our work calls for a revision to our most cherished example of feedback in astrophysics.

17300720.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17300720.value: Tropical shallow-marine ecosystems foster a dazzling array of biodiversity which is facing critical threats from human-induced climate and environmental change. To confront these challenges, it is essential that paleontologists reconstruct the past history of tropical environments, ecosystems, and biodiversity to place present-day changes in context and uncover processes that can help predict the future. The Caribbean region is a prime example and arguably the best investigated tropical region on historical changes in shallow-marine ecosystem over the past 10 million years. Extensive and intensive paleontological, geological, geochemical data indicate that the isolation of the Caribbean Sea from the Tropical Eastern Pacific (TEP) by the formation of Isthmus of Panama caused a massive collapse in productivity in the Caribbean that has been implicated in a major regional extinction of marine taxa, which we call the Caribbean Extinction Event (CEE). However, the fossil record shows that the timing of the CEE is asynchronous with oceanographic change, questioning the role of Isthmus formation. In this project, we will reconstruct macroevolutionry patterns of Ostracods through the CEE to resolve the timing of macroevolutionary and ecological turnover in the Caribbean. Ostracoda is an ideal group to explore this critical question; they are a diverse group of shallow-marine Crustacea with an exceptional fossil record and are highly sensitive to environmental change. Analyses on preliminary ostracod data through the CEE are promising as (1) the results show distinct pre- and post-extinction assemblages with a transitional fauna during the CEE, and (2) we observe heightened extinction at ~3.45–2.5 Ma. Major new collections of samples, both modern and fossil with wide geographic and temporal scope, are already in hand, making this ambitious project feasible. Detailed analyses of new comprehensive ostracod dataset will allow us to better reconstruct and deconstruct detailed process of the CEE. More specifically to specify the extinction timing and to evaluate productivity collapse as the cause of the extinction. 热带浅海生态系统孕育了极丰富的生物多样性，但它们正面临人类活动导致的气候环境变化的威胁。为了应对这些挑战，古生物学家必须要重建热带环境、生态系统以及生物多样性的历史，在此背景下理解当下的生态变化并且预测那些因素会影响未来。加勒比地区是最好的例子，它的热带浅海生态系统在过去一千万年间的历史也是最广为研究的。广泛而深入的古生物学、地质学、地球化学数据显示巴拿马地峡的形成将加勒比海从热带东太平洋分隔出来，这个过程造成了生态系统生产力的显著下降；而生产力下降可能影响了区域生物多样性的锐减，即所谓的加勒比灭绝事件。然而化石记录显示加勒比灭绝事件的时间与海洋地质运动的时间不一致，这引起科学家怀疑加勒比地峡的形成在这次灭绝事件中起到怎样的作用。在这个项目中，我们将用介形虫来重建加勒比灭绝事件的宏观进化历史，以此揭示宏观进化与生态衍化的发生时间。介形虫是探索这个关键问题的理想生物。它是浅海甲壳类中非常多样的一类，有极好的化石保存，并且对环境变化极其敏感。对加勒比灭绝时期的介形虫数据初步分析得到了有价值的结果：（1）灭绝事件之前与之后的介形虫族群有明显区别，灭绝事件期间发现了介于两者间的过渡族群； （2）我们观察到在灭绝事件在3.45-2.5 百万年前加强。我们已经取得了来自广大时间地理区域的大量新样本，包括化石和现代样本，这保证了这个宏大的项目是可行的。对完整介形虫数据库的详细分析将会让我们更好地分解并重建加勒比灭绝事件的具体过程。我们将详细研究灭绝事件的时间和评估生产力崩溃作为灭绝原因的可能性。

17300720.label: Realisation of objectives
17300720.value: To achieve objectives 1-3, 18 samples dated between 9.6 – 1.4 Ma were retrieved from the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute as part of the Panama Palaeontology Project (PPP). The samples were picked for ostracods, and each sample was counted to create census data. Objective 1: To better constrict the timing of the Caribbean Sea extinction This objective was achieved by indicating which species are absent or present in the ancient PPP samples by comparison of species in the modern-day Panama surface samples and then exploring the timing of the extinction and origination rates by using PyRate in a Bayesian framework and running the BDCS and RJMCMC model. The point of complete closure of the Central American Seaway and shortly thereafter should correlate with the highest peak of extinction from the abolition of nutrient-rich waters into the Caribbean Sea. Results are indicated in 6.1 Objective 2: To better specify the cause of the Caribbean Sea extinction This objective was achieved by specifying the MART C (Mean annual range of temperature – a lower temperature indicates lower upwelling) , δO18 in mollusc, and (%) CaCO3 in sediment from the Caribbean since 10 Ma, taken from Jackson & O’Dea (2023) and correlating it with the rate of extinction, origination, diversity and abundance of ostracods. The project objectives have been achieved. Objective 3: To reconstruct the faunal compositional shift during the formation of the Isthmus of Panama This objective was achieved by transforming the census data into a non-metric multidimensional scaling based on three similarity indices. We will be able to see in two-dimensional space how the faunal composition of the 18 sample assemblages (separated into periods consisting of pre-, during, and post-closure of the Isthmus of Panama) behave/change with regards to the increasing sensitivity of rare species in the sample matrix, and how similar or dissimilar they are relative to each other. Results are indicated in 6.1 Objective 4: To better understand tropical shallow-marine biodiversity for the last 10 million years We have obtained many Cenozoic samples and ostracod data, and we published 12 papers as seen in the Part C, resulting in a better understanding of marine biodiversity for the past 10 million years. We also conducted a comprehensive review of the Cenozoic history of the tropical biodiversity hotspots (Yasuhara et al. 2022), including the Caribbean Sea using corals, benthic foraminifera, and ostracods. The project objectives have been achieved.

17300720.label: Major findings and research outcome
17300720.value: From the NMDS results supported by the Sørensen, Horn, and Morisita-Horn index, there is the greatest faunal turnover between the pre-closure of the Isthmus of Panama before 4 Ma and during the closure of the Isthmus of Panama which reflects a change in ostracod communities as productivity declines drastically. Both closure and post-closure assemblages overlap, indicating a partial recovery of the ostracod community. However, results between the similarity indices don’t imply a major change in the NMDS space, indicating rare abundances have little effect on ostracod assemblages. We used a Bayesian birth-death model to understand rates of extinction, speciation, origination, and diversification. Results reveal ostracod extinctions in the Caribbean between 4 - 2 Ma, confirming Isthmus closure periods from the literature between 4 – 2.5 Ma, as well as similar/same extinction periods from other taxonomic groups including corals, molluscs and bryozoans. Speciation rates decreased dramatically from 3 - 2 Ma, but species diversity escalated more than two-fold between 5 – 3 Ma, with certain species such as Hemicytherura cranekeyensis and Palmoconcha marginolaeva going extinct, and other species like Costa variabilocostata recticostata,, Bradleya pseudonormani, and Pellucistoma magniventra dominating the closure and post-closure phases. This echoes changes in habitat associations as oligotrophic conditions drove the proliferation of reefal-associated communities (in particular the ecological dominance of coral Acropora) and other various seagrass environments. Despite the closure of the Central American Seaway, the results imply some straits could have bounced between closure and re-emergence, allowing for sufficient planktonic productivity for ostracod species to survive.

17300720.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17300720.value: Further work can include how the productivity collapse in the Caribbean Sea impacted on the ecological behaviour of ostracod communities. For example, we can explore how the decline in productivity shaped the abundance and diversity of epifaunal and infaunal ostracods as well as ostracods that have affinities to certain environments such as coral reefs, algae, lagoons, and mangroves. Moreover, previous works have been published regarding a platycopid signal hypothesis, which highlights ostracods with certain feeding modes like suspension feeders, are better able to tolerate environments under oligotrophic or deoxygenated conditions. Interestingly, we have seen this with ostracods, yet other taxonomic groups, such as suspension-feeding bivalves, show a decline at the Isthmus closure. Thus, we can explore this hypothesis by demonstrating the abundance and diversity of ostracods with various feeding modes before and after the closure of the Isthmus of Panama.

17300720.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17300720.value: Around 3-4 million years ago, America underwent a complete transformation influenced by major tectonic and geological processes. This led to the simultaneous closure of the Central American Seaway and the formation of the modern land bridge of Panama. Such a closure ceased the exchange of productive waters coming from the Tropical Eastern Pacific into the Caribbean Sea, driving marine species extinction in the Caribbean. We used ostracods as a model system due to their extensive fossil record and high preservation status to understand community change before, during, and after the closure of the Isthmus of Panama. It is important to establish the exact cause of the extinction event, whether productivity collapse produced a negative impact, and to assess the community dynamics and morphological variability on records of tropical biodiversity. As a result, we will be able to better understand and predict how the biodiversity of modern tropical shallow marine ecosystems will be influenced by relative productivity changes under current and future scenarios. This will be critical for better conservation of tropical environments, particularly with high biodiversity ecosystems in the future.

17301220.label: Project Objectives
17301220.value: In the topological materials, it is believed that some peculiar transport properties are attributed to the multiple band structures instead of the behaviours of charge carriers near the Fermi surface. In the quantum diffusive regime, a set of quantum diffusive equations have been established with the help of Green’s function technique at magnetic field. These coupled equations reflect the strong interplay of the charge, spin and valley degrees of freedom. In this project it is planned to develop the quantum diffusive theory further to study the magnetotransport properties in three-dimensional topological materials and 2D materials. It is expected to explore the difference of magnetotransport properties of the topological trivial and non-trivial bands by tuning the band gaps between the conduction and valence bands. We can expect that the magnetotransport properties of the bulk states will also show distinct differences between different topological phases. The Berry curvature plays an important role in electric transport in the multiband structures according to the semiclassical transport theory, which is usually limited to the non-degenerated band system, i.e. the Abelian case. The effect of non-Abelian Berry curvature on the magnetotransport properties is rarely studied. It is expected to investigate the transport properties in topological materials with Abelian and non- Abelian Berry curvature at finite magnetic fields, and to explore possible relations to between the relevant properties and the non-Abelian Berry curvature. The temperature dependence of quantum correction to conductivity from the quantum interference effect will be examined in either two dimensions or three dimensions.

17301220.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17301220.value: Topological materials are topological phases of matter with topologically nontrivial band structures that are protected by the topology and symmetry. The key feature of these materials is the emergence of surface electrons covering around the materials due to the bulk-boundary correspondence. Topologically non-trivial band structure may host novel Dirac, Weyl and Majorana fermions in the bulk as well as the edge or surface of materials and can further lead to novel responses to external electric and magnetic fields. Some peculiar magnetotransport properties have been measured in topological materials. The primary objectives of this proposal are to develop the quantum interference and quantum diffusive theory for magnetotransport and to explore novel mechanisms and effects for unconventional magnetotransport properties in topological materials including topological insulators, topological Dirac and Weyl semimetals and narrow band insulators. We shall focus on transport properties of the topological bulk bands instead of the edge and surface states in the topological materials in quantum interference and diffusive regimes. Meanwhile the band gap opening indicates that the topological band structure become non-Abelian, and conventional Abelian semiclassical theories fail to describe the dynamical behaviors of the system. Materials with the Abelian and non- Abelian Berry curvature will be investigated comparably to clarify the role of Berry curvature in the quantum spin-related transport. This project will help us to understand interplay of the topology of band structure and quantum interference and diffusive transport of relativistic quasiparticles in topological quantum materials, to enrich the knowledge of condensed matter physics, and explore possible applications of topological materials in spintronics and quantum information industry. 拓撲材料是具有拓撲非平庸的能帶結構的拓撲物項，它們的能帶結構受到拓撲和對稱性的保護。這些材料的關鍵特徵是由於體態-邊界對應而出現覆蓋材料周圍的表面電子。拓撲非平庸的能帶結構可以在體態或材料的邊緣或表面中具有新穎的狄拉克（Dirac），外爾（Weyl）和馬約拉納（Majorana）費米子，並可以進一步導致對外部電磁場的新穎反應。目前在一系列拓撲材料中已經測量到了一些特殊的磁性輸運特性。 該項目的主要目的是發展一套用於磁性傳輸的量子相干和量子擴散理論，並探索包括拓撲絕緣體，拓撲狄拉克和韋爾半金屬和窄帶絕緣體在內的拓撲材料中非常規磁性輸運性質。在量子相干和擴散區域，我們將集中於拓撲體帶，而不是拓撲材料中的邊緣和表面狀態的輸運特性。同時能隙的出現表明拓撲帶結構成為非阿貝爾的，傳統的阿貝爾半經典理論無法描述該系統的動力學行為。我們將對具有阿貝爾和非阿貝爾曲率的材料進行比較研究，以闡明貝里曲率在量子自旋相關輸運中的作用。該項目將幫助我們了解能帶結構拓撲性質與量子乾涉的相互作用以及相對論性的準粒子在拓撲量子材料中的擴散傳輸，豐富凝聚態物理知識，並探索拓撲材料在自旋電子學和量子信息產業中的可能應用。

17301220.label: Realisation of objectives
17301220.value: In this project, there are three objectives: 1) In this project it is planned to develop the quantum diffusive theory further to study the magnetotransport properties in three-dimensional topological materials and 2D materials. 2) It is expected to investigate the transport properties in topological materials with Abelian and non- Abelian Berry curvature at finite magnetic fields, and to explore possible relations to between the relevant properties and the non-Abelian Berry curvature. 3). The temperature dependence of quantum correction to conductivity from the quantum interference effect will be examined in either two dimensions or three dimensions. In completion of the project, 12 papers are published, 2 in Physical Review Letters, 9 on Physical Review B and 1 in Physical Review Research. The major findings of this project are 1) to develop a theory of half-quantized Hall effect and to explore its physical realization in semimagnetic topological insulators; 2) to predict a novel type of metallic quantized anomalous Hall effect without chiral edge states, distinct from the quantum anomalous Hall effect; 3) to resolve a forty-year puzzle of experimentally observed resistivity anomaly in ZrTe5 and HfTe5; 4). to study topological phase transition and propose a new topological index in disordered electric quadrupole insulators; 5). To investigate helical symmetry breaking and its relation to quantum anomaly in massive Dirac fermions; and 6). to identify the anomalous behaviours of the coherent lengths of Majorana zero modes at vortices in superconducting topological insulators. Here we select several major research outcomes. Half-quantized Hall effect [Physical Review B 107, 125153 (2023); 105, L201106 (2022)]: Condensed matter realization of a single Dirac cone of fermions in two dimensions is a long-standing issue. Here we report the discovery of a single gapless Dirac cone of half-quantized Hall conductance in a magnetically doped topological insulator heterostructure. It demonstrates that the Hall conductance is half-quantized in the unit e2/h when the parity symmetry is preserved near the Fermi surface. The gapless Dirac point is stable and protected by the local parity symmetry and the topologically nontrivial band structure of the topological insulator. The one-half Hall conductance observed in a recent experiment [M. Mogi et al., Nat. Phys. 18, 390 (2022)] is attributed to the existence of the gapless Dirac cone and the parity invariance of the Fermi surface. The results suggest a condensed matter realization of a topological phase with a one-half topological invariant. Dirac polarons and resistivity anomaly in ZrTe5 and HfTe5 [Physical Review Letters 125, 256601 (2020)]: Resistivity anomaly, a sharp peak of resistivity at finite temperatures, in the transition-metal pentatellurides ZrTe5 and HfTe5 was observed four decades ago, and more exotic and anomalous behaviors of electric and thermoelectric transport were revealed in recent years. Here, we present a theory of Dirac polarons, composed by massive Dirac electrons and holes in an encircling cloud of lattice displacements or phonons at finite temperatures. The chemical potential of Dirac polarons sweeps the band gap of the topological band structure by increasing the temperature, leading to the resistivity anomaly. Formation of a nearly neutral state of Dirac polarons accounts for the anomalous behaviors of the electric and thermoelectric resistivity around the peak of resistivity. Topological phase transition in disordered electric quadrupole insulators [Physics Review Letters 125, 166801 (2020)]: We investigate disorder-driven topological phase transitions in quantized electric quadrupole insulators in two dimensions. We show that chiral symmetry can protect the quantization of the quadrupole moment qxy, such that the higher-order topological invariant is well defined even when disorder has broken all crystalline symmetries. Moreover, nonvanishing qxy and consequent corner modes can be induced from a trivial insulating phase by disorder that preserves chiral symmetry. The critical points of such topological phase transitions are marked by the occurrence of extended boundary states even in the presence of strong disorder. We provide a systematic characterization of these disorder-driven topological phase transitions from both bulk and boundary descriptions. Helical symmetry breaking and quantum anomaly in massive Dirac fermions [ Physical Review B 104, L241111 (2021)]: Helical symmetry of massive Dirac fermions is broken explicitly in the presence of electric and magnetic fields. Here we present two equations for the divergence of helical and axial vector currents following the Jackiw-Johnson approach to the anomaly of the neutral axial vector current. We discover the contribution from the helical symmetry breaking is attributed to the occupancy of the two states at the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band. The explicit symmetry breaking fully cancels the anomalous correction from quantum fluctuation in the band gap. The chiral anomaly can be derived from the helical symmetry breaking. It provides an alternative route to understanding the chiral anomaly from the point of view of the helical symmetry breaking. The pertinent physical consequences in condensed matter are the helical magnetic effect, which means a charge current circulating at the direction of the magnetic field, and the mass dependent positive longitudinal magnetoconductivity as a transport signature. Anomalous coherent length of Majorana zero modes at vortices in superconducting topological insulators [Physical Review B 107, 184517 (2023)]: The coherence length of two Majorana zero-energy modes in a p-wave topological superconductor is inversely proportional to the superconducting order parameter. We studied the finite size effect of the Majorana zero modes at vortices in a topological insulator/superconductor heterostructure in the presence of a vortex and found that the coherence length of the two zero-energy modes at the terminals of a vortex line is independent of the superconducting order parameter and determined by the intrinsic properties of the topological insulator. This anomalous property illustrates that the superconducting topological insulator is topologically distinct, contrary to a p-wave topological superconductor. In short, the three objectives of the project have been fully achieved.

17301220.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17301220.value: One of the striking research outcomes is the discovery of half-quantized Hall effect in a gapless Dirac cone of fermions. This result has impact to the study of transport properties of surface states of topological insulators and our understanding of quantum anomaly in quantum field theory. The robustness of the half-quantized Hall effect against the disorders and interaction will be one of the focuses in the future research. PI will seek the continuous support from RGC in this direction.

17301320.label: Project Objectives
17301320.value: Proxy Validation Part I: Produce a high-resolution record of trace metals (e.g., Mg/Ca) in benthic foraminifera from the bottom of the Laurentian Channel for the past century. This record will be compared to instrumental temperature data to calibrate the relationship between Mg/Ca and temperature in this region. This objective will be performed using sediments recovered with a box-core from high sedimentation site CR02-23. Proxy Validation Part II: Use existing δ18O record from the same species of benthic foraminifera analysed in Part I to remove the theoretical effect of temperature. This record will be compared to salinity instrumental data to calibrate the relationship between δ18O and salinity in this region. This objective will be performed using the high sedimentation box-core CR02-23. Proxy Validation Part II: Use existing δ18O record from the same species of benthic foraminifera analysed in Part I to remove the theoretical effect of temperature. This record will be compared to salinity instrumental data to calibrate the relationship between δ18O and salinity in this region. This objective will be performed using the high sedimentation box-core CR02-23. Synthesis: Develop a general conceptual model for the evolution of the western North Atlantic subsurface oceanography over past 7 ka.

17301320.value: 這項目旨於重建北大西洋西部於過去7,000年間的中層水水溫及鹽度。此項目的重要性在於過去一個世紀以來，北大西洋環流因全球暖化和受格陵蘭冰原融化影響的高緯度地區淡水增加而被削弱。這意味著赤道和兩極之間的水循環放緩，相應地影響著熱傳輸及海面溫度，從而改變北大西洋一帶海洋與大氣之間的熱交換作用，而這些變化可能對全球氣候以及北大西洋上空的極端氣候事件的出現和強度產生重要影響。 具體上，我們將會： (一) 根據於20世紀收集的儀器數據，驗證以聯合使用微量金屬及氧同位素重建箱形沉積物樣本的鹽度和溫度的方法 (二) 利用這些代用指標來重建過去7,000年間的海洋溫度及鹽度，從而推斷環流變化 以上數據將有助我們解答兩個問題： (一) 北大西洋環流是否於小冰河時期減弱了？ (二) 自從勞倫斯冰蓋完全倒塌以來，北大西洋環流有何變化？ 通過解答以上問題，我們將能更了解不同潛在驅動因素在北大西洋環流變化中的角色作用。 鑑於對北大西洋環流的連續定量觀測始於2004年，因此要基於年代際振盪和多年代際週期的背景而詮釋這相對較短的採樣期有一定難度。這記錄的時間長度不足以讓我們從自然變化中辨別出人為影響的信號，因而限制了我們識別和量化驅使近期循環減弱的主要機制。由此可見，如這裏所建議的長期環流記錄對於我們了解近期環流翻轉減弱的驅動因素而言至關重要。

17301420.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17301420.value: 可解释人工智能的量子多体计算研究

17301420.label: Project Objectives
17301420.value: The first objective is to employ explainable-AI techniques, such as explainable neural networks and quantum machine learning, to derive numerically-accurate models directly from experiments. These models gives rise to effective quantum many-body Hamiltonians, which unreveal the nature of exotic phenomena such as topological ordered systems and twisted bilayer graphene. The second objective is to employ large-scale AI-accelerated computation with convolutional/spiking neural networks and neuromorphic computation to formulate enhanced quantum Monte Carlo and tensor network renormalization group update schemes. The aim is to reduce drastically the computational complexity of conventional algorithms to the extent so that realistic quantum simulations of larger system sizes and lower temperatures can be achieved to compare and guide further experimental efforts. The third objective is to address the critical situation of missing team efforts into large-scale computational physics within Hong Kong and the extended Greater Bay area. Leveraging on current robust development in artificial intelligence and quantum computation in the region, i.e. through collaboration with National supercomputer centers in Guangzhou/Shenzhen, we boost related developments into quantum material research. Collaborations include the Songshan Lake Materials Laboratory and the China Spallation Neutron Source in Dongguan.

17301420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17301420.value: 在本项目中，我们将会运用可解释神经网络和量子机器学习等方法，更加准确地从量子多体实验材料中提取有效模型，然后运用大规模数值计算研究以拓扑序和石墨烯层状结构为代表的新型关联电子体系。同时我们将会使用卷积神经网络和脉冲神经网络等人工智能方法，克服现有的量子蒙特卡洛和张量网络重整化群的计算复杂度，使得大规模量子多体系统的数值计算可以推进到之前没有的物理尺度。这些努力，将会有力地改变香港地区和粤港澳大湾区在大规模量子多体材料计算方面的短板，并且通过与区域内诸多量子材料研究机构的深入合作，如东莞松山湖材料实验室、中国散裂中子源，全面推动量子材料的理论、数值和实验进展。

17301420.label: Realisation of objectives
17301420.value: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Quantum Computing have seen significant growth, providing new opportunities for Computational Physics. This report describes a strategy to enhance quantum material research in Hong Kong and the Greater Bay area. The project has already produced several high-impact publications, including 5 Nature Communications, 8 Physical Review Letters, and 2 npj Quantum Materials publications. The first objective involves using explainable-AI techniques, such as explainable neural networks and quantum machine learning, to create accurate models from experiments. These models help us understand complex phenomena and measure quantum entanglement. The second goal is to use AI-accelerated computation to improve quantum Monte Carlo and tensor network update schemes. This will simplify conventional algorithms, enabling more advanced quantum simulations and providing insights for future experiments. The third aim addresses the lack of team efforts in computational physics in the Greater Bay area. Plans are underway to collaborate with National supercomputer centers in Guangzhou/Shenzhen to stimulate quantum material research. The integration of advanced AI techniques, AI-accelerated computations, and collaborative efforts is expected to revolutionize computational physics in the region and pave the way for future breakthroughs.
