17301420.label: Major findings and research outcome
17301420.value: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Quantum Computing have experienced unprecedented growth in recent years, opening up vast avenues for research and development in various domains. One such domain is Computational Physics, which has the potential to be revolutionized through the integration of AI and Quantum Computing. This report outlines a three-pronged approach aimed at employing AI techniques, large-scale AI-accelerated computation, and fostering team efforts to improve quantum material research within Hong Kong and the Greater Bay area. During the course of this project, several impactful works have been completed, including 5 Nature Communications, 8 Physical Review Letters, and 2 npj Quantum Materials publications. The first objective revolves around the utilization of explainable-AI techniques. These techniques include explainable neural networks and quantum machine learning, which are used to derive numerically accurate models directly from experiments. These models consequently yield effective quantum many-body Hamiltonians, uncovering the nature of exotic phenomena such as topological ordered systems and twisted bilayer graphene. With this objective, we have designed a series of methods to measure quantum entanglement, which leads us to the nature of quantum physics. The second objective involves large-scale AI-accelerated computation with convolutional/spiking neural networks and neuromorphic computation. The aim here is to formulate enhanced quantum Monte Carlo and tensor network renormalization group update schemes. This strategy aims to drastically reduce the computational complexity of conventional algorithms, thereby allowing for more realistic quantum simulations of larger system sizes and lower temperatures. This, in turn, will provide valuable insight to guide further experimental efforts. The third objective addresses the current critical situation of missing team efforts in large-scale computational physics within Hong Kong and the extended Greater Bay area. Capitalizing on the robust development in AI and quantum computation in the region, collaborations with National supercomputer centers in Guangzhou/Shenzhen are being planned. The goal is to boost developments in quantum material research, with partnerships including the Songshan Lake Materials Laboratory and the China Spallation Neutron Source in Dongguan. Through the integration of advanced AI techniques, AI-accelerated computations, and collaborative efforts, the aim is to revolutionize computational physics, specifically quantum material research in the Greater Bay area. The results of this project are expected to yield significant advancements in the field, leading to a better understanding of complex quantum systems and paving the way for future breakthroughs.

17301420.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17301420.value: The outcomes of this project are expected to contribute profoundly to the field, instigating substantial advancements and fostering a more comprehensive understanding of complex quantum systems. This will indeed lay the groundwork for future breakthroughs in the realm of quantum physics. These anticipated results will not only have a substantial impact on current research paradigms but also open up new, unexplored avenues. They are set to illuminate the path towards the further integration of Artificial Intelligence technology and condensed physics. This combination presents an exciting frontier in the field of Computational Physics, with the potential to revolutionize our approach to problem-solving. By effectively merging these two areas, we can tap into a powerful toolset that will help us delve deeper into the quantum many-body system. This integrated approach could help uncover previously unknown aspects, yielding insights that could be instrumental in shaping the future of quantum research

17301520.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17301520.value: 鈣鈦礦發光二極管（LED）因其低成本及廣色域在顯示技術應用領域受到廣泛關注。自2014年首次報導室溫下的電致發光以來，金屬鹵化鈣鈦礦LED的相關研究已取得巨大進展，其中綠光、紅光LED效率均超過20%。儘管如此，藍光LED的效率仍不足10%，且基於混合鹵素鈣鈦礦的LED通常因鹵素相分離現象致使發光光譜不穩定。鈣鈦礦LED最為顯著的問題是器件穩定性較差，這是由鈣鈦礦材料固有穩定性缺陷，以及外界偏壓引發鈣鈦礦材料中的離子遷移現象共同導致。上述穩定性缺陷導致目前報導的鈣鈦礦LED通常具有數秒至數分鐘的工作壽命，最長工作壽命也僅有幾百小時。降低鈣鈦礦缺陷及離子遷移可以有效提高鈣鈦礦LED器件穩定性。與常用的三維鈣鈦礦相比，準二維鈣鈦礦材料具有較好的光譜穩定性和環境穩定性。除了目前主要用於LED發光材料的準二維Ruddlesden-Popper（RP）鈣鈦礦，另一種準二維Dion-Jacobson （DJ）鈣鈦礦雖然在太陽能電池應用方面已展現出明顯的穩定性優勢，但至今僅有一篇關於DJ鈣鈦礦應用於近紅外LED器件的報導。儘管如此，基於DJ鈣鈦礦LED器件穩定性的大幅提升，表明了深入研究可見光譜範圍DJ鈣鈦礦發光材料的必要性。 我們提出研發基於含溴DJ鈣鈦礦的藍光及綠光LED。初步研究已表明這些含溴DJ鈣鈦礦發光材料具有優異的環境穩定性，使得LED發光層可以在一般環境中製備，無需惰性氣體保護，並且在一般環境中製備的DJ鈣鈦礦發光材料具有出色的發光性能。我們將研究DJ鈣鈦礦材料組分對其發光性能及環境穩定性的影響，優化藍光及綠光發光材料的形貌和光學性質，並應用於LED。我們還將引入能夠抑制鈣鈦礦離子遷移的阻擋層，以及具有離子捕獲能力的間隔層，從而進一步提升LED器件穩定性。同時利用多層結構實現高效荷注入，最終實現高效率高穩定性鈣鈦礦LED。

17301520.label: Realisation of objectives
17301520.value: 5.3 Realisation of objectives Objective 1: Synthesis and characterization of novel Dion-Jacobson (DJ) perovskite materials with improved ambient stability As described in mid-term progress report, we have investigated a large number of possible diammonium spacers and their ability to form 2D and quasi-2D DJ perovskites. DJ perovskites are known for their exceptional stability (Commun. Mater. 3, 63, 2022). The characterization of the prepared materials was performed (X-Ray diffraction, UV-Vis spectroscopy, photoluminescence). We have also studied the ambient stability of different DJ bromide perovskite materials. We have found that DJ perovskites are generally very stable in ambient, and that stability extends even to DJ perovskites with Sn2+ as a metal cation (Adv. Funct. Mater. 31, 2102182, 2021). However, the number of diammonium spacers which form DJ perovskites is rather limited. Furthermore, the films generally display low crystallinity and low luminescence due to inefficient energy funneling. Commonly observed phenomenon in the absorption spectra of DJ perovskites with formula CAn-1PbnBr3n+1 , where C is diammonium spacer cation, A is small cation, and n is the number of perovskite octahedral layers, is the presence of multiple phases including undesirable n=1 phase. The difficulties in achieving good crystallinity and low defect density in DJ perovskites could be due to the spacer cations forming bonds to perovskite octahedral layers on both sides, which could result in increased strain. This hypothesis is consistent with observations of improved properties of films with very long alkyl chain spacer cations, as well as mixed spacer cations. Thus, we achieved improved film quality by utilizing mixing of the spacer cations, which enabled increased photoluminescence and higher efficiency devices. For the green emitting film, the optimal film composition was DDA0.75HDA0.25Csn-1PbnBr3n+1, where DDA stands for 1,10-decanediammonium and HDA denotes 1,6-hexanediammonium (J. Mater. Chem. C, 2022, 10, 108–114). PLQY increased dramatically from 1.4% for pure HDA films to 20% for DDA0.75HDA0.25 films (J. Mater. Chem. C, 2022, 10, 108–114). The achievement of efficient blue emission is even more hampered by difficulty in controlling the film crystallization to achieve favorable distribution of different n phases. The emission commonly occurs either from a small content of 3D phase in the green spectral range, or there is weak multipeak emission due to inefficient funneling. Furthermore, while quasi-2D films do not decompose under illumination or heating based on the absorption spectra (Figure 3 in mid-term progress report) they exhibit phase transformations when highly mobile MA cations are used as evidenced from changes in the PL spectra. Thus, we investigated formamidinium (FA) and Cs containing DJ perovskites. The inclusion of FA has failed to improve control over layer crystallization, and the PL spectra showed weak multipeak emission even in the cases where one phase was dominant in the absorption spectra. Thus, we mainly focused on Cs containing films, and we achieved sky-blue emission by optimizing the ratio of DDA and methylenediammonium (MDA) spacer cations (Figure 1 in J. Mater. Chem. C, 2023, 11, 14207–14216). Objective 2: The optimization of the Dion-Jacobson perovskite film deposition As described in the mid-term progress report, different methods were investigated to improve the film quality and light emission intensity of the DJ perovskites with spacer cations and small cations identified as promising in the work on Objective 1. Different additives have been attempted for blue- and green-emitting DJ perovskites, including KBr, NH4SCN, RbBr, YCl3, dimethylpropyleneurea, Crown 18, GABr (GA=guanidinium), polyethylene oxide (PEO), and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP). Among these, only KBr and PVP exhibited some promise for green emission, but the effect of KBr was not significant if solvent vapor annealing was used. Solvent vapor treatment (J. Mater. Chem. C 10, 108–114, 2022) resulted in significant luminescence enhancement, which was attributed to the recrystallization of perovskite film. Objective 3: The investigation of the effect of interfacial layers on ion migration, charge balance, and device stability The use of polymer interlayers, such as PMMA, have not resulted in a significant increase of device performance parameters. However, we found that the insertion of (TSPO1), which is an electron transport material, between the hole transport layer and the perovskite layer resulted in an improved charge balance and higher efficiency (Figure 2 in J. Mater. Chem. C, 2023, 11, 14207). We have also investigated the effects of different phosphine oxide based passivating molecules for the top passivation of perovskite layer in green emitting devices, and we found that the molecule used significantly affected the performance. However, in this case observed differences were attributed to a large degree to recrystallization of the perovskite layer when triphenylphosphine oxide (TPPO) passivation is used (ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2023, 15, 30083−30092). Objective 4: The development of efficient perovskite LEDs with high operational stability We have developed both green (J. Mater. Chem. C, 2022, 10, 108–114, ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2023, 15, 30083−30092) and sky blue (J. Mater. Chem. C, 2023, 11, 14207) LEDs based on Dion-Jacobson perovskite emitting layers. In both cases, we have used spacer cation mixing to optimize the emitter layer composition, combined with post-deposition treatments and/or device archi-tecture optimization. The significant improvement in device stability is obtained, with T50 lifetime increased more than 3 times for TSPO1 passivated devices compared to control devices (ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2023, 15, 30083−30092). Problems encountered: The following problems were encountered as described in detail in mid-term progress report. During the project, there were renovation works conducted in the building which resulted in closure of the lab during the work. Lab operation was also negatively affected by pandemic control measures due to reduced occupancy in the lab based on working guidelines at the time, difficulties in equipment maintenance since engineers were not coming to Hong Kong, delays in chemical and lab consumables deliveries, etc. Due to pandemic conditions, travel was also affected, as Covid-related restrictions were only lifted in the first quarter of 2023, hence the findings from the project were reported in journal articles rather than presented at conferences.

17301520.label: Major findings and research outcome
17301520.value: Different diammonium spacer cations were investigated for the preparation of 2D and quasi-2D Dion-Jacobson Perovskites, and the properties of the prepared films were characterized. We found that Dion-Jacobson perovskite materials exhibit high environmental stability, including stability under heating and illumination. High stability is observed even in the case of Sn-containing perovskites which generally have significantly lower stability compared to the lead-containing perovskites (Adv. Funct. Mater. 2021, 31, 2102182). However, for several different diammonium cations, 2D perovskites did not form , while for others films with low crystal quality were obtained. Alkyl chain based diammonium spacer cations, such as 1,6-hexanediammonium (HDA) and 1,8 octanediammonium (ODA), exhibited the best ability to form films with good crystallinity. However, all of the films exhibited relatively low intensity of light emission as for this type of materials it is relatively difficult to control crystallization to achieve low defect density and efficient funneling. The deposition conditions optimization and the use of various additives has resulted in improvements in photoluminescence intensity of the Dion-Jacobson films based on the most stable spacer cation (HDA), but further improvements were necessary to obtain efficient devices. Therefore, film composition optimization using different spacer cations was implemented to improve the film properties, and solvent vapor annealing process was developed in order to achieve further improvement in light emission for green emitting materials. The exposure to dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO) vapor for optimal time (90 s), followed by annealing to remove solvent residue, enabled fabrication of efficient green light emitting diodes with Dion-Jacobson perovskite emitting layer (J. Mater. Chem. C, 2022, 10, 108–114). These devices exhibited strong dependence of device performance on both the antisolvent and passivating molecule used (ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2023, 15, 30083−30092). In contrast, for sky blue emitters only composition optimization was used to control film crystallization to achieve sky blue emission and avoid either multiple emission peaks due to inefficient funneling or green emission due to presence of higher n phases (J. Mater. Chem. C, 2023, 11, 14207–14216). Compared to blue emitting devices, green emitting perovskite LEDs exhibited both higher efficiency and higher stability, in agreement with the expectations from the published literature as blue perovskite LEDs are lagging behind those in other spectral regions.

17301520.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17301520.value: Dion-Jacobson perovskite materials are highly promising for halide perovskite device applications due to their significantly higher stability compared to other types of perovskite materials. However, the light emission intensity is commonly not very high. Further development of the research can involve studying the nature of nonradiative defects in these materials, and developing different methods to improve their crystallinity and photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQY). Currently, the biggest limitation to broad applications of this class of materials in light emitting devices are difficulties in achieving high quality films with low nonradiative defect densities and favorable energy landscape for efficient funneling, which can enable high performance devices in particular in the green spectral region. We expected that improvements in crystallinity and reduction in nonradiative recombination would result in higher brightness at lower current densities, which is expected to further improve both the efficiency as well as stability of light emitting diodes using Dion-Jacobson perovskite emitters. Possible approaches to achieve this would involve composition optimization to minimize strain and thus reduce defect concentrations in the film, as well as the development of novel passivating agents which could reduce nonradiative recombination.

17301520.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17301520.value: Lead halide perovskite materials are highly promising for applications in light emitting diodes. However, these materials are generally sensitive to exposure to moisture, oxygen, illumination, elevated temperature, and electrical bias, which has detrimental effects on device stability. Dion-Jacobson perovskite materials exhibit improved stability compared to other types of perovskite materials, but they have been less commonly studied, in particular for light emitting applications. Here we investigated the synthesis of different Dion-Jacobson perovskites and performed a comprehensive characterization of the prepared films. All films studied exhibited good stability, but unfortunately they also commonly exhibited low crystallinity and/or weak light emission. Optimized film composition and post-deposition treatment have resulted in improved crystallinity and optical properties of the films. This enabled preparation of sky blue and green Dion-Jacobson perovskite light emitting diodes with the best efficiencies of 4.1 % for sky blue and 14.4% for green perovskite light emitting diodes, respectively. The investigation of the relationships between film composition, its optical properties and device applications for different Dion-Jacobson perovskites will enable further improvements of the devices based on these materials, which is expected to lead to significant stability improvements.

17301620.label: Project Objectives
17301620.value: To develop computationally efficient and theoretically supported strategies under the framework of factor model for large tensor time series without side information. Compared with the tensor factorization community, the key novelty is the removal of the negligible idiosyncratic noise by taking advantage of the autocorrelation. Compared with the existing literature which does not require negligibility, the key innovation is the marriage of high order orthogonal iteration and autocorrelation. Furthermore, theoretical justification will be provided. To develop the general statistical framework of dynamic tensor factor models with side information. The majority of the existing literature on tensor decomposition with side information in computer science, engineering, or statistics is either model-free or based on two kinds of modeling assumptions: mean plus iid noise or iid observations. Dynamic tensor factor models strive to treat the temporal dimension in the tensor differently from the other dimensions. Given the nature of side information, innovative coupling generative model will be constructed together with the dynamic tensor factor model, whose estimation will be achieved simultaneously and more efficiently. To extend the linear relation between the target tensor and the auxiliary covariates in Objective 2 to a nonlinear relation. To the best of our knowledge, the relationship between the target tensor and auxiliary variables is usually linear in the literature. Extension to nonlinearity will be considered. To perform variable selection for dynamic tensor decomposition. When the variables are high-dimensional, due to computational concerns, variable selection under the framework is often adhocly performed in the past. We will investigate the selection procedure systematically. To verify the efficacy of the new statistical tools using simulated and real data in various important applications, including economics, finance, social science, business, and more. To develop a companion software for all the statistical tools studied in this project.

17301620.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17301620.value: With the rapid advancement of modern technology, large tensors, or multi-dimensional arrays, are ubiquitous nowadays. Oftentimes, such data with tensor structure are observed over time, forming tensor time series naturally. The goals in time series analysis mainly lie in the decipherment of the dynamic system, the discovery of interconnection, and the accuracy of the forecast of potential outcomes. For scalar or vector time series, these goals are usually achieved by a traditional time series factor model through the combination of dimension reduction and time series forecasting strategies, which has been proven a powerful analytical tool in many areas. But for tensor time series, there is scarce literature. In addition to the target tensor time series, additional covariates that have explanatory powers sometimes exist and need to be fused properly. The proposed research is to respond to the pressing challenges posed by the large and complex tensor time series, including the investigation of appropriate statistical factor models for dynamic tensors, construction of computationally efficient algorithms and software, derivation of the associated theoretical and empirical properties, and development of a wide range of applications in multiple fields of enormous data sets. The research is divided into two scenarios: dynamic tensor factor models without or with side information, where under the latter scenario the quality of the resulting procedure is expected to be boosted. Due to the temporal correlation in the time series, traditional tensor factorizations without or with auxiliary information are not directly applicable and innovative methods based on autocorrelation tensors and orthogonal projection will be developed. Moreover, nonlinear or selective dependence of the target tensor on the auxiliary covariates will also be studied. In the presence of widely encountered and highly important tensor time series, the proposed project will have broad, immediate, and far-reaching beneficial impacts in many fields, such as economics, finance, social media, business, biomedical studies, and healthcare analytics. 隨著現代技術的迅速發展，如今大張量或多維陣列無處不在。通常，隨著時間的推移會觀察到這種具有張量結構的數據，自然形成張量時間序列。時間序列分析的目標主要在於動態系統的解密，互連的發現以及潛在結果的預測準確性。對於標量或矢量時間序列，這些目標通常是通過結合降維和時間序列預測策略的傳統時間序列因子模型來實現的，該模型已在許多領域被證明是功能強大的分析工具。但是對於張量時間序列，文獻很少。除了目標張量時間序列以外，有時還存在具有解釋能力的其他協變量，需要適當融合。 擬議的研究旨在應對龐大而復雜的張量時間序列所面臨的緊迫挑戰，包括研究動態張量的適當統計因子模型，構建計算效率高的算法和軟件，推導相關的理論和實踐特性，以及在巨大數據集的多個領域中開發廣泛的應用程序。這項研究分為兩種情況：沒有或帶有輔助信息的動態張量因子模型，在後一種情況下，預測的質量有望得到提高。由於時間序列中的時間相關性，沒有或帶有輔助信息的傳統張量分解不能直接應用，因此將開發基於自相關張量和正交投影的創新方法。由於張量時間序列無處不在且非常重要，擬議的項目將在許多領域產生廣泛，直接和深遠的有益影響，例如經濟學，金融，社交媒體，商業，生物醫學研究和醫療保健分析。

17301620.label: Realisation of objectives
17301620.value: We are pleased to report that we have fully achieved all six original objectives. Below, we summarize the key results corresponding to each objective. Objective 1: Tensor Factor Models for Time Series – We published three papers in Part C that together provide a comprehensive treatment of tensor factor models for time series data. • Paper 1 develops the Tucker decomposition for tensor time series. • Paper 4 builds on Paper 1 and derives an optimal solution under the same framework. • Paper 6 studies the CP decomposition for tensor time series. All three methods are computationally efficient and provably statistically optimal. Objective 2: Supervised Tensor Decomposition – Paper 3 (under moderate revision) introduces side information to guide tensor decomposition, substantially improving decomposition accuracy. – We establish the statistical optimality of our approach and demonstrate its computational efficiency through simulation studies. – A real‐data application on predicting currency risk premiums using the global trade network confirms the practical benefits of the proposed method. Objective 3: Functional Tensor Prediction in RKHS – Paper 7 develops a framework for functional tensor prediction within a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space. – We propose an innovative penalty structure and a novel procedure for selecting tuning parameters. – The methodology is shown to be statistically optimal and is validated on applications involving weather forecasting and biomedical time-series data. Objective 4: Sparse Tensor Modeling – Paper 8 (currently under review) addresses sparsity in tensor models for variable selection, introducing bias-corrected estimators. – The resulting model offers new insights into global economic dynamics and maintains both interpretability and statistical rigor. Objective 5: Diverse Empirical Applications – Across Part C (with the exception of Paper 4), we apply our methods to a wide range of real-world datasets from business, economics, and finance— including taxi flows, currency premiums, global trade networks, equity markets, macroeconomic indicators, weather records, and biomedical measurements—demonstrating broad applicability. Objective 6: Software Development – To facilitate adoption of our methods, we have developed an R package, tensorTS, accompanied by Paper 5 (under review) which provides detailed usage examples for all core functions. – The package is fully functional and available to the research community. In summary, we have not only met our primary research objectives but also produced a suite of theoretically sound, computationally efficient tools and applied them to diverse, real-world challenges. We are confident that these contributions will have lasting impact in both methodological development and practical data analysis.

Compared with the tensor factorization community, the key novelty is the removal of the negligible idiosyncratic noise by taking advantage of the autocorrelation. Compared with the existing literature which does not require negligibility, the key innovation is the marriage of high order orthogonal iteration and autocorrelation. Furthermore, theoretical justification will be provided.

To develop the general statistical framework of dynamic tensor factor models with side information. The majority of the existing literature on tensor decomposition with side information in computer science, engineering, or statistics is either model-free or based on two kinds of modeling assumptions: mean plus iid noise or iid observations. Dynamic tensor factor models strive to treat the temporal dimension in the tensor differently from the other dimensions. Given the nature of side information, innovative coupling generative model will be constructed together with the dynamic tensor factor model, whose estimation will be achieved simultaneously and more efficiently.

To extend the linear relation between the target tensor and the auxiliary covariates in Objective 2 to a nonlinear relation. To the best of our knowledge, the relationship between the target tensor and auxiliary variables is usually linear in the literature. Extension to nonlinearity will be considered.

To perform variable selection for dynamic tensor decomposition. When the variables are high-dimensional, due to computational concerns, variable selection under the framework is often adhocly performed in the past. We will investigate the selection procedure systematically.
To verify the efficacy of the new statistical tools using simulated and real data in various important applications, including economics, finance, social science, business, and more.

17301620.label: Major findings and research outcome
17301620.value: Over the course of this project, we have developed a unified suite of tensor‐based methodologies that push forward both the theory and practice of high‐dimensional time‐series analysis. At the core of our contributions lies a comprehensive framework for factorizing tensor time series: by formulating both Tucker and CP decompositions within a statistically rigorous setting, we established minimax‐rate guarantees and devised computationally efficient algorithms that scale smoothly with dimension. Building upon this foundation, we demonstrated that incorporating auxiliary side information—such as network features or economic covariates—yields substantial gains in estimation accuracy. Through rigorous analysis and extensive simulations, we proved that these supervised decompositions remain statistically optimal, and we validated their real‐world impact by predicting currency risk premiums from global trade‐network data, where our approach outperformed unsupervised baselines by a wide margin. Recognizing that many modern applications involve functional measurements, we further extended our tensor framework into a reproducing‐kernel Hilbert space setting. Here, we introduced a novel penalty structure that enforces smoothness both across tensor modes and over time, along with a tuning‐parameter selection procedure that attains optimal convergence rates. Empirical studies on regional weather forecasting and longitudinal biomedical signals confirm the flexibility and robustness of our RKHS‐based approach, providing accurate predictions even under complex spatio‐temporal dependencies. To address the need for interpretable factor selection in large‐scale systems, we also designed bias‐corrected sparse estimators that automatically identify the most relevant tensor modes while preserving statistical rigor. Applied to global economic data, these sparse tensor models reveal meaningful drivers of macroeconomic fluctuations and variable interactions that were previously obscured in high‐dimensional settings. Across all methodological advances, we tested our tools on a broad spectrum of real‐world datasets—including taxi‐flow records, equity and macroeconomic indices, weather observations, and biomedical time series—thereby demonstrating both broad applicability and robust performance under diverse error structures and sampling schemes. Finally, to ensure that our contributions are accessible to the research community, we packaged every algorithm into an R library, tensorTS, complete with a companion manuscript offering in‐depth tutorials and usage examples. This software suite brings cutting‐edge tensor methods into the hands of practitioners, enabling seamless adoption and fostering further innovation in multidimensional data analysis.

17301620.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17301620.value: Building on our foundational tensor‐time‐series framework, we see three promising avenues for future work. First, we will extend our models to accommodate non‐Gaussian and heavy‐tailed noise, missing entries, and dynamic covariates, developing robust estimators with accompanying minimax guarantees. Second, we plan to integrate online and streaming algorithms—leveraging sketching and randomized updates—to enable real‐time analysis of massive tensor streams, such as high‐frequency sensor or financial data. Third, we aim to fuse our statistical decompositions with deep‐learning architectures (e.g., tensorized neural networks) to capture highly nonlinear interactions while retaining interpretability. To realize these goals, we propose the following course of action: Theoretical Development: Formulate robust loss functions and derive convergence rates under weak moment and dependence assumptions. Algorithm Design: Implement scalable, parallelizable solvers for streaming updates, and prototype hybrid tensor‐neural modules. Software Enhancement: Expand tensorTS with C++ back ends, GPU support, and interfaces for Python and TensorFlow. Empirical Validation: Partner with domain experts in climate science and high‐frequency trading to benchmark our methods on real‐world tasks. Dissemination: Host workshops and tutorials to promote adoption and gather user feedback for continual refinement.

17301620.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17301620.value: In today’s world, data often come in many dimensions—think of tracking weather measurements across regions and time, monitoring financial transactions among global markets, or recording multiple health signals in patients. Our research created new “tensor” methods that treat such multi-way data as multidimensional arrays, uncovering patterns that simpler tools miss. We also showed how to feed in extra clues—like economic indicators or network links—to sharpen predictions. Tested on real cases, from forecasting regional weather and predicting currency risks from trade networks to analyzing biomedical time series, our approaches proved both faster and more accurate than existing techniques. To bring these advances to everyday users, we packaged them into an easy-to-install R library called tensorTS, complete with step-by-step examples. By combining solid mathematical guarantees with practical software, our work helps scientists, analysts, and decision-makers draw deeper insights from complex time-series data—supporting better strategies in finance, climate science, healthcare, and beyond.

17302020.label: Project Objectives
17302020.value: The general objective is to uncover the bonding, electronic structures and reactivities of novel and/or underexplored metal-carbene complexes/intermediates and study their impacts on selective metal-catalyzed C-H functionalization and/or C-C bond formation reactions. Since most of these reaction intermediates are too short-lived or too unstable for direct detection/isolation, we plan to stabilize such elusive species through appropriate design of carbene ligands and/or macrocyclic supporting ligands, which is beneficial to their spectroscopic and structural characterizations and structure-reactivity relationship establishment. These investigations provide a straightforward way to elucidate, or shed light on, the reaction mechanisms and to gain useful insight for improving the current synthetic methodologies for related environmentally benign organic transformation reactions. Particular efforts will be focused on the structural-reactivity relationships of metal-alkylcarbene, -quinoid carbene and -perfluoroalkylcarbene complexes. The objectives stated in this proposal are as follow: First, we plan to synthesize and characterize isolable group 8-10 metal complexes of the dialkylcarbene 2-adamantylidene (Ad), and study their competences in transferring Ad group under electro- and photochemical conditions. In the literature, many different metal catalysts were used for various carbene transfer reactions; however, direct and systematic comparisons between different metal catalysts are sparse, and the carbene transfer reactivity of an isolated metal Ad complex remains unexplored. In view of this existing research gap, we plan to study the electronic structures and reactivities of group 8-10 metal Ad complexes in a systematic way. Our preliminary studies showed that these species are stable and isolable. Second, we aim to employ homo- and/or heterogeneous Fe, Ru, Co, Rh, Ir salen/porphyrin complexes with axial Ad ligand as robust or selective catalysts for alkylcarbene and/or arylcarbene transfer reactions such as alkene cyclopropanation and C-H insertion reactions, including asymmetric catalysis. In view of our initial success in metal-catalyzed alkylcarbene transfer reactions, we will continue to expand the substrate scope, improve stereoselectivities, increase catalytic turnover number, and even replace noble metal catalysts with those based on inexpensive metal, with special emphasis on iron complexes (which are Earth-abundant with high biocompatibility). We plan to develop efficient protocol in generating metal alkylcarbene species under ambient conditions, which is essential for highly enantio- and diastereoselective alkylcarbene transfer reactions using the novel chiral porphyrin recently designed and prepared by our group. We will also use chiral metallosalen complexes for enantioselective carbene C-H insertion. Moreover, heterogeneous catalysts, such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) containing M-Ad (M = Fe, Ru) porphyrins or Ir porphyrins, will be developed as recyclable catalysts for carbene C-H insertion reactions. Third, we will develop dirhodium phthalocyanine (Pc) catalysts for site-selective acceptor-type carbene or diaryl carbene C-H insertion reactions with high regioselectivity. We found that, using typical dirhodium paddlewheel complexes as the catalysts, the corresponding dirhodium carbene species underwent side reactions and did not lead to the desired C-H insertion products. In view of this, we propose to use Rh-Pc complexes designed by our group for such reactions, and our preliminary studies revealed promising results using a dirhodium phthalocyanine complex as catalyst. Another advantage of our Rh-Pc system lies in the differences from the existing systems in trapping and characterizing highly reactive rhodium carbene intermediates using spectroscopies with high sensitivities, such as ESI-MS, EPR and UV-vis. Through these studies, we envision to uncover the essential and key features of effective catalysts for metal-catalyzed carbene C-H insertion reactions. Finally, we will develop metal-catalyzed C-H functionalization or C-C bond formation reactions involving transfer of relatively small carbene groups such as the perfluoroalkylcarbene CHCF3. In view of the high tendency for such light species to dimerize and/or to undergo oxidation, we plan to use metal complexes supported by sterically-encumbered ligands for stabilizing the carbene intermediates. The stabilized carbene intermediates are also important for uncovering the bonding information and structural-reactivity relationship for further improvement of these carbene C-H insertion reactions.

17302020.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17302020.value: 碳原子之间的成键（常见的碳碳键的解离能约为350-380千焦/摩尔）反应在药物化学和材料化学中应用十分广泛。然而使用各种常见的原料直接进行碳碳键生成反应，特别是直接对sp3碳氢键（键解离能为370-440千焦/摩尔）进行碳碳键生成反应极具挑战性。其难点在于：a）反应要从键能较强的碳氢键生成键能较弱的碳碳键，从热力学角度缺乏驱动力；b）相对于反应体系中存在的其它官能团，sp3碳氢键一般更为惰性而难以发生反应；c）不同碳氢键反应的选择性控制，特别是如何实现优先活化一级碳氢键而不是二级或三级碳氢键发生反应十分困难。因此，利用构效关系明确，可以分离且高活性的金属卡宾化合物对于发展高效高选择性的金属催化sp3碳氢键官能化反应来说十分重要。此外，卡宾中的两个取代基可以根据不同的合成需求进行调整，由此可以实现卡宾物种的多样化利于在有机合成中应用。尽管在过去几十年间已经有大量金属催化的卡宾转移反应报道，化学家们至今仍在寻找更加广谱和高效的卡宾转移和插入反应催化剂。我们长期以来的工作主要集中于研究不同的金属与各种独特配体形成的络合物在催化卡宾转移和插入反应中的应用。尽管我们最近报道了金属催化的烷基卡宾sp3碳氢键的插入反应，但这方面的研究仍然需要进一步深入，尤其反应的机理研究，特别是对活性金属-烷基卡宾中间体的检测和分离是巨大的挑战。在本项目中，我们致力于通过以下方式改良当前的方法学研究：a）设计合成高活性的铁、钌与卟啉，西弗碱、O^N^C^N四齿配体、钳形配体、咔咯等配体形成的络合物，并引入2-金刚烷卡宾作为碳给体配位；b）制备并分离钴、铑、铱等金属的金刚烷基络合物并研究它们在电化学条件下的金刚烷转移反应；c）以第十族金属烷基卡宾络合物作为催化剂及模型研究其卡宾转移和插入反应的机理。在基础实验和理论研究的基础之上，我们预期在以下的几种条件下实现选择性的碳氢键官能化反应：a）金属卟啉的醌型卡宾（撅氢诱导的碳氢键氟化或芳基化反应）；b）铑酞菁二聚体、铑卟啉形成的单或双芳基卡宾（区域和对映选择性的碳氢键官能化反应）；c）光驱动的卟啉-金刚烷络合物的均相和非均相催化（对映选择性和立体选择性碳氢键官能化反应）。

17302020.label: Realisation of objectives
17302020.value: The objectives of this project were achieved, and some important findings are described in 4 PhD thesis completed by my students. My PhD student, Yan Sijia, discovered exciting results on the anti-Markovnikov hydroazoation of unactivated alkenes with diazo quinones and is preparing a manuscript to Nature Synthesis/Chem (see output 9). I aim to publish my PhD’s research in top journals, but have been delayed by the requested theoretical calculations. My previous PDF who helped with DFT calculations of reaction mechanisms has left. With the help of colleagues in computational chemistry in the Mainland, these unpublished results will be submitted for publication within this year. Nonetheless, we have published 1 paper in ACIE and 2 book chapters. 3 Manuscripts have just been submitted, one to Chem, one to ACIE and one to Organic Chemistry Frontiers. We have acknowledged this grant in all publications. Objectives 1, 2 and 3: We developed an axially arylated chiral [Ir(D4-Por)(diClPh)] complex supported by D4 Halterman porphyrin ligand. This complex shows unprecedented efficiency in the insertion of donor-acceptor carbene into N-adjacent primary C(sp3)–H bonds, affording the corresponding product in up to 94% yield with up to 99% ee. A record-high turnover number (TON) of 1,380,000 was achieved. Scaling up this reaction to 100-gram scale did not affect product yield and selectivity. We also present the first example of utilizing this catalytic carbene transfer reaction to prepare poly-β-aminoester. This work has been submitted to Chem. (Output 4). We prepared three [IrIII(Por)Ad]+ with Ir–Ccarbene distances of 1.854(8)–1.908(6) Å. The bond angle sum around the Ccarbene atom indicates that the Catom is sp2 hybridized. [IrIII(TMP)Ad]+ is an active catalyst for intramolecular alkylcarbene C(sp3)–H insertion, intermolecular cyclopropanations and X–H (X = C, S, O, N) insertion, resulting in good to excellent product yields. A manuscript is in preparation (Output 11). Chiral [RuII((+)D4-Por)Ad] and [FeII((+)D4-Por)Ad] complexes were synthesized and well-characterized. X-ray crystal structure of [RuII((+)D4-Por)Ad] reveals a 5-coordinated structure with Ru–CAd bond of 1.892 Å. [RuII((+)D4-Por)Ad] can catalyze intramolecular alkylcarbene C(sp3)–H insertion of 1,3,4-oxadiazolines under UV irradiation (365 nm) to obtain substituted tetrahydrofuran (30 examples) and pyrrolidine (3 examples) with product yields up to 92%, dr up to >99:1 and er up to 95:5. Notably, substrates derived from Piperonyl alcohol, Adapalene, and Probenecid are also compatible, providing the corresponding derivatives in good yields and ee. [RuII((+)D4-Por)Ad] shows high stability and can be recovered quantitatively, providing a TON up to 820. These findings are described in Chapter 5 of Ms. Tingjie You’s PhD thesis. Objectives 1 and 3: Chiral [(S,R)-cmcporFe]Cl can catalyze carbene cyclopropanation of aryl alkenes with diazo compounds (70 examples), affording the desired products in excellent yields (up to 99%), diastereoselectivity (up to >99:1 dr) and enantioselectivity (up to 99% ee). In the presence of 0.002 mol% [(+)-(D4-Por)Fe]Cl, 3,4-difluorostyrene and α-diazoacetonitrile reacted on a gram-scale to obtain the desired product, with TONs as high as 31000 and 88% ee. The versatile cyclopropyl nitrile can be converted into cyclopropyl carboxylic acids, cyclopropylamines, and cyclopropylmethanamines, which are key intermediates for bioactive or drug-like molecules. This work has been submitted to ACIE. (Output 5). We prepared [(S,R)-cmcporRuCO] for the catalytic enantioselective cyclopropanation of 1,3-dienes, using tert-butyl 2-cyano-2-diazoacetate as carbene source, to obtain substituted vinylcyclopropanes (30 examples, including modification of 8 natural products) with product yields up to 96% and ee up to 95% . Monitoring the reaction progress via 1H NMR spectroscopy revealed the formation of Ru-carbene intermediate followed by a slow transfer of the carbene moiety to the diene substrate. The Ru-carbene intermediate was identified by HR-MS. This work has been submitted to Organic Chemistry Frontiers. (Output 6). Chiral [FeIII(salen)]BPh4 complexes could catalyze the intramolecular alkylcarbene C(sp3)–H insertion reaction of 1,3,4-oxadiazoline under UV irradiation (365 nm) to produce disubstituted tetrahydrofuran, with yields up to 85%, good diastereoselectivity (trans:cis ratio up to >99:1) and moderate enantioselectivity (up to 86:14 er). The effect of noncovalent interactions between borate anion, substrate, and iron complex on the induction of diastereoselectivity and reactivity was investigated. We prepared and characterized FeII-alkylcarbene complex [FeIIsalen=Ad], providing insights into reaction intermediates. We developed a novel water-soluble iridium porphyrin catalyst for carbene transfer reactions in aqueous medium, such as the modification of cystein-containing peptides and proteins with donor-acceptor diazo reagents. We extended this reaction to membrane protein modifications in HepG2 cells in vivo. These findings are described in Chapter 3 of Dr. Un-I Ng’s PhD thesis and a manuscript is in preparation. (Output 7). Objectives 1 and 4: [Rh2(tBuPC)2] can efficiently catalyze various intermolecular carbene C–H insertion reactions, affording corresponding products with up to 97% yield and >99% site-selectivity. Based on experimental/spectroscopic/computational mechanistic studies, RhIII-carbene radical anion species was proposed as the intermediate. These findings are described in Chapter 4 of Dr. Long-Hay Au’s PhD theses. Objectives 1 and 5: [Ir(TTP)Me] can catalyze highly site- and diastereoselective intramolecular α-CF3-α-alkylcarbene insertion into aliphatic C–H bonds to afford multi-substituted CF3-bearing cyclopentanes (50 examples). Unprecedented TONs of up to 82,000,000 and TOFs of up to 2,000 s-1 were recorded. This reaction could be performed on a gram scale using 0.25 ppm of catalyst. Modifications of natural products, pharmaceuticals, sugars and peptides are also shown (Output 8). Using [IrIII(D4-Por)Me] as catalyst, intramolecular asymmetric α-CF3-α-alkylcarbene insertion into O-adjacent C–H bonds can be achieved, with TON of up to 10,000,000, up to > 99:1 rr, >99:1 dr, and >99% ee. A manuscript is in preparation (Output 8). We prepared [Fe(F8-TPFPP)Cl] (iron(III) β-octafluoro-5,10,15,20-tetrakis(pentafluorophenyl)porphyrin) chloride) catalyst. Late-stage synthesis of trifluoromethyl-substituted cyclopropanes was achieved by cyclopropanation of unactivated alkenes using [Fe(F8-TPFPP)Cl] catalyst and N2CHCF3 (in-situ generated) [Fe(F8-TPFPP)Cl] exhibits excellent reactivity even at room temperature. Terpenes, steroids, hormones, and drug-like substrates (20 examples) are compatible with this reaction, producing the desired product in up to 99% yield and with diastereoselectivities up to 10:1. The catalyst loading can be reduced to 0.03 mol%, and the TON for simple olefin substrates reaches 3000. We captured the Fe(II)-α-CF3-carbene reaction intermediate using F8-D4-Por ligand and characterized it by 1H and 19F NMR and MS. Stoichiometric reaction of alkenes with this iron-carbene intermediate yields the cyclopropane product with moderate enantioselectivity (20% ee), providing evidence for the involvement of Fe-α-CF3-carbene species. We developed a mild method for anti-Markovnikov hydroazoation of unactivated alkenes with diazo quinones. Its broad versatility was tested extensively using multi-substituted unactivated alkene substrates and through late-stage functionalization of medicinal scaﬀolds, providing N-alkylated o-azophenol products in good yields. Modular synthesis of 6 types of fluorescently-labeled natural products was achieved. Mechanistic studies revealed a radical chain pathway (Output 9). Objective 3. We prepared and characterized the Ru(II) porphyrin-based MOFs Ru-MOF-Zr, which is an effective heterogeneous catalyst for inter- and intramolecular carbene cyclopropanations of alkenes. Compared with its homogeneous counterpart, heterogeneous Ru-MOF-Zr exhibits: (1) easy separation from the reaction mixture; (2) recyclability of the catalyst; (3) size selectivity of substrate through finite-sized pores of Ru-MOF-Zr. Ru-MOF-Zr could efficiently catalyze carbene transfer reactions in environmentally-friendly solvent 95% EtOH, providing the desired products in up to 82% yield. A manuscript is in preparation. First, we plan to synthesize and characterize isolable group 8-10 metal complexes of the dialkylcarbene 2-adamantylidene (Ad), and study their competences in transferring Ad group under electro- and photochemical conditions.

Second, we aim to employ homo- and/or heterogeneous Fe, Ru, Co, Rh, Ir salen/porphyrin complexes with axial Ad ligand as robust or selective catalysts for alkylcarbene and/or arylcarbene transfer reactions such as alkene cyclopropanation and C-H insertion reactions, including asymmetric catalysis.
Third, we will develop dirhodium phthalocyanine (Pc) catalysts for site-selective acceptor-type carbene or diaryl carbene C-H insertion reactions with high regioselectivity.
Finally, we will develop metal-catalyzed C-H functionalization or C-C bond formation reactions involving transfer of relatively small carbene groups such as the perfluoroalkylcarbene CHCF3.

17302020.label: Major findings and research outcome
17302020.value: [1] We have published 3 papers (two are book chapters). We have just submitted 3 manuscripts, one to Chem, one to ACIE, and the other to Organic Chemistry Frontiers. [2] We developed axially-arylated chiral [Ir(D4-Por)(diClPh)] catalyst for asymmetric carbene insertion into primary N-adjacent C(sp3)–H bond. This catalyst showed a record-high TON (> 1,000,000) in asymmetric C–H functionalization. We also applied this catalytic reaction to synthesize poly-β-aminoester through stepwise carbene insertion into primary C(sp3)–H bonds. This work has been submitted to Chem. [3] We prepared a series of metalloporphyrin complexes containing axially-coordinated adamantane carbene ligand. We use these complexes for catalytic carbene transfer using N-tosylhydrazones, 1,3,4-oxdiazoline or diazo compounds as carbene source. We achieve asymmetric carbene transfer/insertion reactions with excellent enantioselectivity using chiral D4 Haltermann porphyrin ligands. [4] Chiral Fe-based catalysts were used in asymmetric carbene cyclopropanation/C–H insertion reactions with high stereoselectivity. With 0.002 mol% [(+)-(D4-Por)FeCl], 3,4-difluorostyrene and α-diazoacetonitrile were reacted on a gram scale to obtain the desired product with TON of up to 31000 and ee ratio of 88%. [FeIII(salen)]BPh4 catalyzes asymmetric intramolecular alkylcarbene C–H insertion of 1,3,4-oxadiazoline under UV irradiation, exhibiting good product yield and stereoselectivity. [5] We have developed [Rh2(tBuPC)2] catalyst for various intermolecular carbene C–H insertion reactions, affording corresponding products with up to 97% yield and >99% site-selectivities. Based on experimental/spectroscopic/computational mechanistic studies, the active intermediate is believed to be the RhIII-carbene radical anion species. [6] [Ir(TTP)Me] could catalyze intramolecular α-CF3-α-alkyl carbene aliphatic C–H insertion to afford CF3-bearing cyclopentanes (50 examples) with high site- and diastereoselectivities. In particular, accessing to trisubstituted CF3-containing cyclopentanes has led to unprecedentedly high catalyst efficiencies (up to 82,000,000 TON and up to 2,000 s-1 TOF). Chiral [IrIII(D4-Por)Me] allows asymmetric α-CF3-α-alkyl carbene O-adjacent C–H insertion reactions to give triﬂuoromethyl-bearing tetrahydrofurans with up to 10,000,000 TON, and excellent regio-, diastereo-, and enantioselectivity. [7] Fe(F8-TPFPP)Cl can catalyze the cyclopropanation reaction of unactivated alkenes with in-situ-generated N2CHCF3 to produce drug-like products with yields up to 99%, and diastereoselectivities up to 10:1 (20 examples). [8] A water-soluble iridium porphyrin catalyst was developed for carbene transfer reactions in aqueous media. Using this catalyst, various peptides and proteins are modified at cysteine sites using donor-acceptor diazo reagent. We also demonstrated modification of membrane proteins in HepG2 cells.

17302020.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17302020.value: Based on the results of this project, we significantly improved the catalytic activity of metalloporphyrin complexes for carbene transfer/insertion reactions by introducing axial carbon-based adamantane carbene or aryl ligands. These catalysts exhibit unprecedented multi-million TONs in catalyzing carbene C–H insertion reactions while retaining their high diastereoselectivity and/or enantioselectivity, representing record-high TONs for asymmetric C–H functionalization. These results further confirm our hypothesis that the catalytic activity of metalloporphyrin complexes towards atom and/or group transfer reactions can be modulated and fine-tuned through the rational selection of axial ligands. The high TON exhibited by our metalloporphyrin catalysts can greatly facilitate the Practical synthesis of natural products, pharmaceuticals and/or fine chemicals. The application of these catalyzed carbene transfer/insertion reactions to construct libraries of bioactive or drug-like molecular compounds will be further explored.

17302020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17302020.value: Transferring substituted carbene motif to an inert saturated hydrocarbon through the formation of carbon-carbon bonds simplifies the syntheses of bio-active molecules and pharmaceuticals and minimize the use of protecting/deprotecting reagents and the generation of by-products. However, direct C-H functionalization often requires harsh reaction conditions and uses toxic reagents (e.g. halogen-containing compounds). One of the key elements to develop efficient, green synthetic methods for organic transformations is the discovery of novel metal catalysts whose catalytic performance can be fine-tuned through carefully designed auxiliary ligands. In this project, we are convinced that the axial ligands of metalloporphyrin complexes play an important role in modulating the catalytic activity of these complexes. The catalysts developed in this project have extremely high catalytic activity, allowing the use of very small amounts of metal catalysts for the synthesis of drug-molecules without affecting the yield and selectivity of the product. These findings have been submitted to leading international chemistry journals including Cell Chemistry and Angewandte Chemie International Edition. From a sustainable development perspective, the aforementioned achievements expedite the development of metal-catalyzed C-H functionalization for the pharmaceutical industry in the coming decades.

17302820.label: Project Objectives
17302820.value: Objective 1: To introduce selective and directional bonding to active colloids. Active colloids are microscopic particles that autonomously propels and assemble with external energy input. They are promising candidates for making microscopic machinery where both motion and the coordination of moving parts are necessary. While the ability of particle propulsion has been significantly enhanced and their motion trajectories can be controlled, it remains a key issue to tune their assembly. One reason is that the interactions between active particles are highly dynamic and complex, which often result in particle swarms, schools, aggregates, close-packed clusters/crystals. These structures are indeed dynamic and intriguing, yet their kinds are much limited leaving little space for further adjustment. Unlike active colloids, the self-assembly of passive colloidal particles have been significantly improved over the last several years, where, by modifying particle shapes and surface chemistry, the interactions between particles are “programmable”. In particular, the introduction of specific and directional bonding has enabled numerous new structures for colloids in a way like how atoms and molecules assemble with fidelity and diversity. Inspired by what has been achieved for passive systems, the objective of this proposal is to introduce “selective” and “directional” colloidal bonds to the community of active colloids, anticipating that these would dramatically expand the scope and complexity of colloidal structures by dynamic self-assembly. Objective 2. To create active colloidal clusters/molecules by selective and directional bonds. The propulsion of active particles is driven by constant energy input, so do their assemblies. Regardless of the origin, the energy injected into the system often produces localized, imbalanced cloud of chemicals or charges surrounding individual particles, which impose phoretic, dipolar, osmotic, and other forces to nearby colloids. As these forces are complex and dynamic—and yet their interplay determines the assembly behavior of active particles—it remains an important issue how to orchestrate the forces to favor colloidal bonding with selectivity and directionality. In this project, anisotropic patchy particles with various sizes, shapes and compositions will be synthesized and utilized under AC electric field, which serves as a powerful way to tune the colloidal interactions and thereby control the colloidal bonds. To demonstrate, we aim to assemble active colloidal molecules comprising two or multiple particles that possessing distinct bond properties: different bond angles, selectivity, orientations, etc. We envisage that the new bonding scheme enabled may in future be used for the assembly of not only discrete structures like clusters but also extended structures like 2D and 3D crystals. Objective 3. To investigate the dynamics of assembled structures. The selective and directional bonds introduced in the project will help create various structures assembled by active particles. As the individual particle is now part of an assembly, they are expected to show collective dynamics rather different from that of a single particle. Traditionally, a major research focus for active particles (also known as micromotors) is to precisely control their motion and trajectory. Here, motions can be achieved through an “assembly first” approach, in which multiple parts coordinate to perform the designate tasks such as translation, steering, spinning, etc. In response to the changes of the external field, the structures may reconfigure thus resulting in evolving dynamics. In this project, we will study in detail how colloidal bonds, assembled structures, and dynamics are related. In such assembled system, the flexibility of modulating dynamics and complexity of active colloids is tremendous; it could be a critical step toward “programmable” active matter. Objective 4. To integrate selective and directional assembly with biological entities. An essential motivation for developing active material is to perform microscopic tasks in small length scales not easily accessible by traditional means. A mounting interest is to interface with biological system: to conduct microsurgeries or simply to deliver a drug/medical device. With the working principle of dynamic assemblies, we will explore the integration of active colloidal molecules with biological entities such as bacterial and living cells, creating synthetic-biological hybrid structures. This will bring synthetic materials in contact with cells in a predetermined manner, i.e., with selectivity and directionality. This could lead to, for example, precision in delivering drugs with high efficiency and accuracy to location of interest. On the other hand, the shapes of biological entities are quite different (for example they are deformable), which can be utilized to further increase the diversity of structures and dynamics we can obtain. We expect that such exploration would help us identify new pathways and strategies for therapy as well as fabricating new materials.

17302820.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17302820.value: Self-assembly is a powerful tool nature uses to create materials in which small components (e.g., atoms, molecules, and nanoparticles, etc.) are autonomously combined into complex patterns or structures. From the energy perspective, self-assembly is “static” when the final structures are the thermodynamic ground states; materials at equilibrium such as woods and crystals are of this kind. Alternatively, the process is “dynamic” when the assemblies are out of equilibrium and maintained by external energy. Notable examples are from biological systems such as living cells and tissues etc., where energy (food and nutrition) is consumed to preserve the structural ordering, functions, and activities. While the principles of static self-assembly has been widely exploited to make synthetic materials with many structures and phases, it remains a formidable challenge to control dynamic self-assembly due to the high complexity and far-from-equilibrium nature. The incapability has imposed great limitation for creating smart and active matter that emulates their biological counterpart. The aim of this project is to explore strategies to tune dynamic self-assembly, as an effort to expand the scope of structures and dynamics one can realize for active materials. In an analogy to static assembly where precisely engineered interactions between components is the key, regulating the interactions in dynamic systems is considered crucial, yet the pathway to do so is largely undetermined. In particular, “selective/specific” and “directional” interactions, the seminal ingredients that has led to the structural fidelity, diversity and tunability of static assembly, are still missing. To tackle this challenge, we propose to introduce selective and directional bonds in dynamic assembly. Specifically, we will focus on active colloids—microscopic particles capable of self-propulsion with external energy—and investigate how they come together, combine and integrate with high selectivity and directionality resulting in various structures and dynamics. To reach our goal, we will take the advantage of the team’s expertise in synthesizing anisotropic particles with tunable sizes, shapes and compositions and drive them in an AC electric field, whose parameters are also widely adjustable. Preliminary results based on our approach reveals a diverse range of surprising structures that steer, move, evolve and reconfigure, formed by both synthetic particles and biological entities (living bacterial and cells). As interactions determines structures, success of this project may be a critical step toward “programmable” active matter. 自組裝是自然界用來創建材料的強大工具，其中小成分（例如原子，分子和納米粒子等）自動組合成複雜的結構。從能量的角度來看，當最終結構是熱力學基態時，自組裝是“靜態的”。處於平衡狀態的材料（例如木材和晶體）屬於此類。而當組裝是由外部能量維持時，該過程是“動態的”。例如活細胞和組織等，在其中消耗能量（食物和營養）以保持結構有序，功能和活性。儘管靜態自組裝原理已被廣泛用於製造具有許多結構和相的合成材料，但由於其高度複雜性和非平衡態的性質，控制動態自組裝仍然是一項艱鉅的挑戰，以至不足以創造出模仿其生物學對應物的智能和活性物質。 該項目的目的是探索調整動態自組裝的策略，以擴大活性材料可以實現的結構和動力學的範圍。與靜態裝配的類比，精確設計和調節組成單元在動態系統中的相互作用力被認為是至關重要的，但是如何實現確並不確定。特別是，“選擇性/特定”和“方向”相互作用是導致靜態裝配的結構準確性，多樣性和可調性的重要因素，目前在動態體系中仍然缺失。 為了應對這一挑戰，我們提議在動態組裝中引入選擇性和定向性鍵合。具體來說，我們將研究能夠通過外部能量自我推進的微觀顆粒，即活性膠體，並研究它們如何以高選擇性和方向性結合在一起，從而產生各種結構和動力學。為了實現我們的目標，我們將利用團隊的專業知識來合成尺寸，形狀和組成可調的各向異性粒子，並利用交流電廠驅動粒子。根據我們的方法得出的初步結果表明，由合成顆粒和生物實體（細菌和細胞）形成的各種令人驚訝的結構都可以操縱，移動，進化和重新配置。當相互作用決定結構時，該項目的成功可能是邁向“可編程”活性物質的關鍵一步。

17302820.label: Realisation of objectives
17302820.value: Objective 1. To introduce selective and directional bonding to active colloids. Activity 1: Literature review on selective and directional bonding for passive colloidal systems. The concept of selective and directional bonding, as proposed, is prevailing in equilibrium colloidal system for designing materials by self-assembly. Our literature review indicates that the feasibility of such bonding schemes is attributed to the utilization of anisotropic particles and heterogeneous surface chemistries. As illustrated by the renowned DNA-coated patchy particle system, the positioning of surface patches dictates the direction of colloidal interaction, while the surface tethers (DNA) confer bond selectivity and specificity. Activity 2: Comparing passive and active systems. In passive systems, short-range attractive interactions are employed to ensure that the directionality of the colloidal bond by particle anisotropy is effective. In contrast, dynamic systems are characterized by long-range interactions, including dipolar, phoretic, and osmotic interactions. The difference in length scale of interaction plays a significant role in determining the realization of selective bonding. In both cases, the non-spherical shape and heterogeneous surface of the particle can influence their interaction and the resulting assemblies. Activity 3: Refining research hypothesis. By the above research activities, we have refined our hypothesis for introducing selective and directional bonding in active systems. Our exploration focuses on fabricating various non-spherical particles, such as Janus, ellipsoidal, and polyhedral shapes, as well as heterogeneous materials, including dielectric, metallic, and magnetic components (see Objective 2 below). The use of an AC electric field and co-assembly with passive particles can enhance the diversity of the assembly scheme. (Related research Output: Curr. Opin. Colloid Interface Sci. 2022) Objective 2. To create active colloidal clusters/molecules by selective and directional bonds. Activity 1: Spherical dielectric particles of different sizes. We have investigated the simplest case, where all particles are spherical but vary in size. When subjected to an AC electric field, the particles assemble into colloidal clusters/molecules with size selectivity, driven by the size-dependent dielectrophoretic forces between the particles. Activity 2: Synthesis and propulsion of polyhedral particles. Microcrystals of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) with various polyhedral shapes are synthesized and propelled under an AC electric field. In these cases, symmetry breaking is realized by orienting the polyhedral particles in a unique direction to generate uneven electrohydrodynamic flow. Furthermore, by leveraging the MOF types and shapes, or surface properties, the propulsion of MOF motors can be tuned or reversed. Activity 3: Metallodielectric Janus particles. To introduce material heterogeneity, Janus/patchy particles with distinct dielectric and metallic lobes were prepared. The size and distance between the distinct lobes can be fine-tuned by our scheme. We conducted an investigation on the propulsion of these particles and their subsequent co-assembly with dielectric particles. The structures of the assemblies are further modulated by field parameters, such as electric field intensity and frequency. Activity 4: Metallodielectric ellipsoidal two-patch particles. Additionally, ellipsoidal particles with dual metallic patches were synthesized, incorporating both shape and surface/material heterogeneity, and their assembly behaviors were also explored. Activity 5: Colloidal clusters. By fusing spheres of varied numbers and sizes, a range of clusters spanning from dimers to hexamers has been created. Asymmetric clusters can be obtained by selectively modifying magnetic nanoparticles. Furthermore, these clusters can be used as templates to direct the dynamic assembly of active particles. (Related research output: J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2021; ACS Nano 2021; Nature Communications 2020.) Objective 3. To investigate the dynamics of assembled structures. Activity 1: Cooperation in motion. The dynamics of active particles and assemblies can be significantly adjusted by the collective organization of the constituent particles. Initially, we observed a variety of intriguing phenomena where multiple particles collaborated in propulsion or assembly. Subsequently, we have investigated the dynamic assembly of particle into clusters and 1D chains under and AC electric field, where directional bonding is realized by the symmetry of the patches. Further investigation will focus on the creation of 2D and 3D structures. Activity 2: Structural reconfiguration. The collective assembly of particles demonstrates reconfigurability attributed to their dynamic behavior under field-driven interactions. We have analyzed the reconfiguration of, for example, colloidal molecules assembled with spheres, ellipsoidal, and Janus particles, as well as 1D reconfigurable chains by two-patch ellipsoidal particles. Notably, the chain comprising patchy ellipsoidal particles can transition from a rigid to a flexible curved conformation by adjusting the ionic strength of the system. Activity 3: Soft and stretchable microgears. Colloidal clusters serve as templates to guide the dynamic assembly of self-propelled Janus particles under an AC electric field, forming the multi-level gear assemblies. By adjusting the shape of the bridging clusters, we can regulate the architecture of assemblies and their synchronization behaviors, including both physical meshing and hydrodynamic coupling. Physically meshed gears rotate in opposite directions without any overall motion, exhibiting a soft and stretchable nature, with each tooth having a different angular velocity. Hydrodynamically coupled gears rotate either in the same or opposite direction, resulting in global rotation or translation, respectively. (Related research output: ACS Nano 2021; Paper under preparation.) Objective 4. To integrate selective and directional assembly with biological entities. Activity 1: Selection of biological entities. The objective of integrating synthetic particles with biological entities is two-folded. One is to consider living cells as particle to provide extra properties such as soft surfaces and unique shapes. The other is to use synthetic particles to manipulate cells. Our investigation focuses on E. coli and yeast cells, both ranging in size from several hundred nanometers to several micrometers. We have collaborated with Dr. Ying Li in the department to obtain these biological materials. Activity 2: Co-assembly of biological entities with synthetic particles. We have primarily explored the assembly of bacteria and cells with synthetic spherical and Janus particles to form active colloidal clusters. We have found that the inner workings of assembly can be applied to these biological entities, which has led to the formation of hybrid assemblies and dynamics. Future study will focus on analysing the dynamics and expanding the scope of particles and cells. In summary, by synthesizing colloidal particles with varied shapes, surface characteristics, and compositions, and exposing them to an AC electric field, we have created various systems that demonstrate controlled colloidal interactions with directionality and selectivity. These systems have displayed fascinating dynamic organization behaviors. Moving forward, these systems will undergo thorough assessment to leverage their distinctive attributes for a range of applications.

17302820.label: Major findings and research outcome
17302820.value: The key discoveries of the project involve introducing selective and directional colloidal bonds to the community of active colloids, significantly broadening the range of colloidal structures through dynamic self-assembly. The novel bonding approach enables the assembly of not only discrete formations like clusters but also extended structures such as 2D and 3D crystals. This system offers immense flexibility in adjusting the dynamics and complexity of active colloids, representing a crucial advancement towards achieving “programmable” active matter that can emulate and surpass biological systems. The project’s findings have resulted in three notable publications in peer-reviewed international journals (Part C, Research Output, 8). In the first case, we published the review paper “Engineering Shapes of Active Colloids for Tunable Dynamics” in Current Opinion in Colloid & Interface Science. In the second case, an innovative method for creating micromotors using MOFs with various polyhedral shapes that are propelled by an AC electric field is detailed. The results are in the paper “Polyhedral Micromotors of Metal−Organic Frameworks: Symmetry Breaking and Propulsion” in Journal of the American Chemical Society. Finally, the realization of reconfigurable and directionally assembled structures using particles with two patches is reported in the paper published in ACS Nano as “Directional and Reconfigurable Assembly of Metallodielectric Patchy Particles”. The work of microgears and dynamic synchronization is under preparation for publication. The project has provided valuable training opportunities for postgraduate and undergraduate students, contributing to their academic and research development (Part C, Research Output, 10). Dr. Zuochen Wang, who played a significant role in the project, has successfully graduated and has published multiple papers, winning the Outstanding Thesis Award at HKU. He is now pursing postdoctoral training in University of Illinois in the US. Another student, Dr. Zhisheng Wang, has also made notable contributions with multiple publications. Additionally, a postdoctoral fellow, Dr. Ming Wu, has a forthcoming paper on the cooperative behavior of dynamic microgears. The education of undergraduate students is also successful. With the demonstrated publication and promising results, the PI has been awarded National Natural Science Foundation of China Excellent Young Scientist Fund, 2020 and HKU Outstanding Young Researcher Award 2022 (Part C, Research Output, 12). These awards are highly competitive and reflect the significance of the research outcomes. Finally, the results of the project have been discussed in local and international meetings (Part C, Research Output, 9).

17302820.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17302820.value: In this project, the introduction of selective and directional colloidal bonds has significantly expanded the potential of colloidal structures through dynamic self-assembly. While the original objectives have been achieved, there are several areas of further exploration that merit attention. First, enhancing the synthesis of multi-patch particles to improve yield and purity is crucial for advancing the assembly of extended structures. Higher yield production would enable the assembly of complex structures like the Kagome lattice, leveraging particle activity for enhanced functionalities. Second, tailoring particles with multiple symmetrical or asymmetrical patches can lead to the realization of more complex superlattices. While 2D superlattices have been achieved, exploring higher-order particles could enable the creation of intricate 3D superlattices such as colloidal diamond structures. Finally, leveraging the cluster’s ability for hierarchical assembly of microgears holds potential for constructing advanced microrobots and nanomachines. Utilizing 3D microprinting technology to design more complex colloidal clusters can facilitate the realization of these sophisticated systems. Exploring these avenues of research may require additional projects and years of investigation but is expected to yield intriguing and valuable results in the realm of active colloids and self-assembly.

17302820.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17302820.value: The main discovery of the project is that by establishing specific and directional bonds between moving tiny particles, we can increase the variety and complexity of structures that can naturally form from these particles. This new bonding approach can help assemble not only individual structures like clusters but also larger ones like 2D and 3D crystals. These structures can change shape in response to external conditions, leading to dynamic changes. By arranging many small dynamic structures in a precise manner, we can construct miniature machines that function collectively, similar to gears in everyday objects. This concept is also applied to blending artificial particles with living organisms such as bacteria and cells, generating hybrid structures that combine synthetic and biological components, like a carousel. These active materials can perform tasks on a very small scale that are hard to reach using traditional methods. Controlling the behavior and complexity of these active materials is crucial and could lead to developing materials that can imitate or even surpass biological systems. These findings could have implications for the discovery of new medical treatments and the advancement of innovative microrobots.

17303020.value: Iceland is an extraordinary location with some of the most amazing geology on Earth. It is sometimes referred to as a “Land of Fire and Ice” because of the co-occurrence of glaciers and active volcanoes. Due to its high latitude, the island experiences cold temperatures and contains many large glaciers, including the largest glacier in Europe. In fact, the record of present day glacial ice and older glacial deposits both tell an important story of the history of environmental conditions on Earth over the last 100s, 1000s and millions of years. The reason Iceland exists in the middle of the north Atlantic is because it is a site intense volcanism along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge – the rift between two tectonic plates. In fact, all of the bedrock in Iceland is composed of volcanic rock, or sediments derived from it. It is the uncommon juxtaposition or co-location of volcanism and glacial activity that gives Iceland the unique reputation as a world of “fire and ice.” In this project, I will explore the mineralogy volcanic geology of a portion of the arid central highlands of Iceland – a desert, volcanic landscape used by the Apollo astronauts as a training ground for the Moon. This site is important for understanding many aspects of planetary volcanism, but perhaps most notably for the occurrence of world class examples of volcano-ice interaction. When volcanoes erupt within frozen ground or beneath glacial ice, they produce a number of interesting types of deposits. This proposal is focused on one major aspect of the activity: the hydrothermal alteration of volcanic glass and minerals to form new minerals. These newly formed alteration minerals are key indicators of the hydrothermal (hot-water) reactions that have occurred through volcano-ice interactions. This study will focus on the detection and characterization of clay minerals – a complex category of hydrothermal minerals known for their compositional and structural complexity. The project represents a new and sophisticated approach to investigate the occurrence, mineralogy, chemistry, structure, abundance and textural and geological context of clay minerals in subglacial and hydrovolcanic deposits in the Askja region. The project will apply new technologies to show the occurrence and distribution of clays in various rocks, and the results will lead to new insights into clay formation in these amazing environments.
