17305820.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17305820.value: The era of big data provides new opportunities for the analysis of time series, most of which in real life are nonstationary. Meanwhile, large nonstationary data bring new theoretical and methodological challenges. One such challenge is that the standard cointegration analysis, based on the assumption of the fixed small number of studied series, breaks down. Proposed in 1988, Johansen’s likelihood ratio test for cointegration rank is a very popular technique. However, many previous numerical studies demonstrate the poor performance of this classical test when the dimensionality of the data is large. Even for relatively small systems with five or six variables, the test based on the asymptotic critical values does not perform well. For large systems, the size distortions become overwhelming, leading to severe over-rejection of the null in favour of too much cointegration. A typical application of cointegration analysis is the pairs trading strategy in finance, where pairs of assets with similar price dynamics are tested for cointegration, and those cointegrated pairs are used for trading in such a way that the investor bets against large spreads in the prices. However, such strategy often fails. A possible reason is that, being limited by the small workable dimensionality of the cointegration test, only the pairwise cointegration relationship is considered, even though a cointegration relationship may exist among a much larger number of assets. Motivated by the above aspects, we propose to develop three new cointegration rank tests based on the trace statistic, the largest eigenvalue and the partial trace statistic, respectively. These proposed tests would be guaranteed to work well in a high-dimensional framework and would significantly contribute to the literature on the inference in high-dimensional nonstationary time series analysis. In addition, our tests will be applied to formulate a high-dimensional trading strategy that would outperform the traditional strategy based on pairs. 在大数据背景下，数据维数远高于传统统计方法所能胜任的维数。目前的协整分析方法在高维情形下表现很差。本项目拟提出迹，最大特征根和部分迹三个统计量来研究高维协整分析及其在资产交易策略中的应用。

17305820.label: Major findings and research outcome
17305820.value: The era of big data provides new opportunities for the analysis of time series, most of which in real life are nonstationary. Meanwhile, large nonstationary data bring new theoretical and methodological challenges. One such challenge is that the standard cointegration analysis, based on the assumption of the fixed small number of studied series, breaks down. Proposed in 1988, Johansen’s likelihood ratio test for cointegration rank is a very popular technique. However, many previous numerical studies demonstrate the poor performance of this classical test that severe over-rejects the null in favor of too much cointegration when the dimensionality of the data is large. A typical application of cointegration analysis is the pairs trading strategy in finance. However, such strategy often fails since a cointegration relationship may exist among a much larger number of assets. Motivated by the above aspects, we develop new cointegration test that work well in high dimensional framework. We show that when both cross-sectional and temporal dimension of the data go to infinity proportionally, the shifted and scaled modified trace statistic converges to a Gaussian random variable. We give explicit formulae for the shift and scale parameters, as well as for the mean and variance of the Gaussian limit. The proposed test significantly contributes to the literature on the inference in high-dimensional nonstationary time series analysis. In addition, applied to formulate a high-dimensional trading strategy, our test outperforms the traditional strategy based on pairs.

17305820.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action

17305820.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17305820.value: Motivated from the over-rejection of the classical Johansen (1988)’s test as well as the frequent failure of the pairs trading strategy, the project develops new cointegration test that is robust in high dimensions. It significantly contributes to the literature on the inference in high-dimensional nonstationary time series analysis. The trading strategy based on the new test will outperform the traditional pairs trading strategy.

17305920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17305920.value: The technique of X-ray reflection and reverberation has been very successful in help us probe accretion disks and coronae around black holes. Studies of this topic have mostly assumed a razor-thin, optically thick accretion disk model, which works well for active galactic nuclei and X-ray binaries in certain states. However, many accreting black hole systems, such as in tidal disruption events, ultra-luminous X-ray sources, and high-redshift quasars, have accretion rates beyond the Eddington accretion rate and produce disks with very different geometry. In the super-Eddington accretion regime, the disk puffs up due to large radiation pressure, and a wide-angle optically-thick wind is launched, thus fundamentally changing the geometry for X-ray reflection. We propose to extend the fruitful X-ray reflection and reverberation studies from the thin disk regime to the super-Eddington accretion regime. A pilot study has been conducted by the PI's group and collaborators on studying the X-ray fluorescent Fe Kalpha lines produced from super-Eddington accretion flow. Our study has shown that the Fe line profiles produced from super-Eddington disks are distinctly more blueshifted and more symmetric in shape with respect to the line center when compared to Fe line profiles from thin disks. Therefore, the Fe line profiles can be used to effectively search for black holes undergoing super-Eddington accretion, as well as constrain the funnel geometry and wind speed. Along this line, we further propose to carry out more accurate general-relativistic (GR) ray-tracing calculations, calculate the X-ray reverberation lags, investigate how to use the observed characteristics to probe various parameters of the black hole and accretion flow, etc. Our study will be aided by the GR ray-tracing package that the PI developed, as well as the simulations of super-Eddington accretion disks conducted by the PI using a GR-radiation-magnetohydrodynamic code. In the upcoming decade, various telescopes such the JWST, LSST, SKA and Athena will allow us to detect and investigate many super-Eddington accreting black hole systems. The results from this study will be much needed for extracting information from these systems, such as the parameters of the black holes and their disk /wind structures. This study will also be beneficiary for understanding how early massive black holes provide kinetic and radiative feedback to their host galaxies. 近年來X射线的反射及反响映射的技術已經成功的幫助我們探測了不少黑洞的吸積盤及冕區。這方面的研究都集中在几何薄、光学厚的吸積盤模型上。這種模型可以應用在活動星系核和X射线双星系統上。但是，也有很多黑洞吸積天體系統，比如潮汐引力瓦解現象，超亮X射线双星，以及一些大紅移的活動星系核，有超愛丁頓的吸積率，所以它們的吸積盤有不同的幾何形態。這種情況下的吸積盤會因為很大的輻射壓力而變厚，並且大角度發射出光學厚的風。因此，這種盤對X射線的反射面幾何也隨之不同。 我們提議將非常成功的X射线反射及反响映射的技術延伸到超愛丁頓吸積的領域。我們已經做了一個先導的案例研究，模擬這種情況下發射出的Kalpha鐵線。我們的研究顯示比起標準的薄盤，超愛丁頓的吸積盤所反射的鐵線明顯更加藍移，而且形狀更加對稱。因此可以利用這些鐵線來搜尋超愛丁頓系統並量度漏斗的幾何形狀和風速。按照這一思路，我們進一步建議進行更準確的相對論射線追踪計算，計算X射線混響滯後，研究如何使用觀察到的特徵來探查各種黑洞和吸積流參數等等。 此計畫的PI研發的GR射線追踪軟件包以及使用广义相对论框架下磁流体輻射数值模拟進行的超級愛丁頓吸積盤的模擬，將為我們的研究提供幫助。即將到來的十年中，各種望遠鏡如JWST，LSST，SKA和Athena將使我們能夠發現和調查許多超愛丁頓黑洞系統。 這項研究的結果將非常有幫助與從這些系統中提取信息，例如黑洞的參數，及其吸積盤/風的結構。 這項研究也將有助於理解宇宙早期大質量黑洞如何向宿主星系提供動力學和輻射反饋。

17305920.label: Realisation of objectives
17305920.value: For this project, we have been mainly developing a X-ray reflection and reverberation package to study accretion flows around black holes with super-Eddington accretion rates. This topic is very understudied previously and our study has greatly pushed the frontier of its theoretical understanding. A pilot study was already conducted at the phase of the proposal writing, which showed that under the context of super-Eddington accretion the X-rays emitted by the black hole corona should be mostly reflected in super-Eddington winds instead of the disk mid-plane. Therefore, the X-ray reflection and reverberation properties from super-Eddington accretion disks are expected to be fundamentally different from thin accretion disks. Since the project launched, we first further developed our general relativistic ray-tracing (GRRT) code to follow the photons emitted the corona until they reach the accretion flows (Objective 1). This allowed us to accurately calculate the disk emissivity as well as the photon propagation time. The latter is needed for modelling the X-ray reverberation lags. We then extended the technique of lag calculation into geometry of super-Eddington accretion disks (Objective 2). We also examined the structure of super-Eddington flows from numerical simulations, and then conducted thousands of simulations to study the X-ray reflection and reverberation signals from such flows with different geometry and kinematics (Objective 3). Very importantly, we added multiple reflections of the coronal X-ray photons into our calculations and found that this physics can play a important role in determining some of the key X-ray reflection and reverberation features. We will discuss these findings in detail in Section 6.1. In summary, all the objectives set out in this proposal have been successfully achieved.

17305920.label: Major findings and research outcome
17305920.value: The main goal of this project is to develop a new package to probe super-Eddington accretion around black holes using the technique of X-ray reflection and reverberation. We list the major findings below. In total 6 journal papers and 1 book chapter / invited review have been published/accepted. Research Output 1 and 5 are both published on The Astrophysical Journal, a top journal in Astronomy and Astrophysics. In Research Output 1 (Thomsen et al. 2022), PI Dai and PhD student Thomsen extended X-ray reverberation studies into the regime of super-Eddington accretion with a focus on investigating the lags in the fluorescent Fe Kalpha line region. We demonstrated that the funnel-like reflection geometry in such accretion flows produces lag-frequency and lag-energy spectra with unique observable characteristics. Not only can these features be used to distinguish super-Eddington accretion systems from sub-Eddington systems, but they are also key for constraining the reflection geometry and extracting parameters from the observed lags. In Research Output 5 (Zhang et al. 2024), PI Dai and PhD students Zhang and Thomsen further allowed the photons emitted by a lamppost corona to be reflected multiple times in a cone-like funnel surrounded by fast super-Eddington winds. Very interestingly, we found that the Fe Kalpha line can have a prominent double-peak profile in certain parameter spaces even with a face-on orientation. Moreover, we compared the Fe Kalpha line profiles produced from super-Eddington and thin disks and show that such lines can provide important insights into the understanding of black hole systems undergoing super-Eddington accretion. As the structure of the super-Eddington accretion flows greatly affects the X-ray reflection and reverberation signals, we also investigated the geometry and kinematics of such flows in Research Output 2, 3 and 6. In Research Output 2, PI Dai, PhD student Kwan and collaborators systematically analysed the properties of the super-Eddington winds and jets, and demonstrated that the winds can carry more mass and energy than the jet. In Research Output 3, PI Dai, postdoc Kar Chowdhury and collaborators studied how super-Eddington winds can lead to AGN feedback effects which can be observed using X-ray telescopes. In Research Output 6, PI Dai, PhD student Kwan and collaborators examined the X-ray signals from a precessing super-Eddington accretion flows and proposed a simple model to explain a new type of astrophysical phenomenon called quasi-periodic eruptions. It is worth mentioning that our X-ray modelling results have been applied to explain observed super-Eddington systems such as tidal disruption events (Research Output 4). Furthermore, some of the major findings described above have also been included in a book chapter / invited review that PI Dai wrote together with collaborator Jiang (Research Output 7). Conference talks: The PI has given a few invited review talks at the international conferences including the European Astronomical Society Annual Meeting (online 2021), 15th Asia Pacific Physics Conference (online 2022), The 60th Anniversary of X-Ray Astronomy: X-ray Astronomy in the Time-domain & Multi-messenger Era (online 2022), The Restless Nature of AGN: 10 years later (Italy 2023), The 32nd Texas Symposium on Relativistic Astrophysics (China 2023), Anticipating the Rising Tide of Tidal Disruption Events: Theory and Observations (USA 2024), COSPAR 45th Science Assembly (Korea 2024). Some of the results obtained from this project so far have been broadcasted in these talks. Student training: 3 students have been trained through this project, including Thomsen (PhD graduated), Zhang (PhD on-going), and Kwan (MPhil graduated and PhD on-going). All students have published papers on top astronomy journals and delivered talks at international conferences based on the results obtained through this project.

17305920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17305920.value: We propose to further develop a XSPEC package based on our modelling results, which can be directly applied to fit X-ray reflection spectrum and constrain the geometry and kinematics of black hole super-Eddington winds. We expect that such efforts will be very useful for observers and therefore make a large impact in the community.

17305920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17305920.value: X-ray reflection and reflection is a very useful technique for studying black holes and their accretion disks. However, theoretical studies of such topic in the context of extreme, super-Eddington accretion has been lacking. In this project, we have developed a sophisticated modelling package for studying this topic. We have obtained significant results and demonstrated that one can use X-ray reflection and reflection to probe the structure and kinematics of these accretion flows and disclose important physics around black holes.

17306220.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17306220.value: 絕對破產下的最佳再保險

17306220.label: Project Objectives
17306220.value: In the context of optimal reinsurance, most of the research concerns about quota-share reinsurance (sometimes called proportional reinsurance), or excess-of-loss reinsurance, or a combination of the two. In the first project objective, an insurance company can purchase per-loss reinsurance. That is, there is no restriction on the form of reinsurance. It is assumed that the reinsurance premium is computed according to the mean-variance premium principle which combines the expected-value and variance premium principles. Also, the company can invest its surplus in a financial market consisting of one risky asset and one risk-free asset. There is an investment constraint that the amount invested in the risky asset cannot exceed a priori given amount. Furthermore, short-selling is prohibited but borrowing is allowed. In this setup, several insurance risk models with investment and reinsurance can be considered. Without restricting the form of reinsurance, we study the optimal reinsurance-investment problem for an insurer who wishes to minimize the probability of absolute ruin. By the technique of stochastic dynamic programming, we derive the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation and the corresponding optimal results. We then compare the results with those obtained under the objective of minimizing the probability of traditional ruin. We also investigate some properties of the optimal strategy, and carry out some numerical study to examine how the model parameters affect the optimal strategy. To make the optimization more interesting, we would like to remove the investment constraint so that the amount of risky asset is uncapped. We then re-examine the same optimal problem but without the constraint on investment. In the second project objective, we incorporate model uncertainty into an insurer's controlled surplus, and solve a novel optimal robust reinsurance problem under the objective of minimizing the probability of absolute ruin. Similar to the setup of the first project objective, the insurer can purchase per-loss reinsurance with the premium computed according to the mean-variance premium principle. The risk models of study only take reinsurance into consideration. We assume that the insurer does not have perfect confidence in the drift term of the insurance surplus. In other words, the insurer suspects that the drift of the insurance risk may be misspecified. To handle the issue of misspecification, we use the idea of model ambiguity to describe this phenomenon. Similar to the robust-value approach, we consider the reference probability measure (benchmark) and a set of equivalent measures which have absolute continuous Radon-Nikodym derivatives with respect to the benchmark. To capture the insurer's ambiguity aversion, we penalize the absolute ruin probability with a term based on relative entropy, and thus a new robust value is defined by employing the criterion of minimizing the penalized probability of absolute ruin. To tackle this optimization problem, we apply the technique of stochastic dynamic programming and solve the corresponding boundary-value problem. It is expected that the corresponding optimal reinsurance strategy and the optimal drift distortion of the equivalent measure can be obtained in explicit feedback form. Finally, we provide numerical examples to illustrate the effects of ambiguity aversion on the optimal solutions and discuss their economic implications therein. In recent years, the study of correlated classes of business has been one of the main topics in the actuarial literature. In view of its importance, we incorporate the so-called thinning dependence into the risk model of study, and then revisit the optimization problem stated in the first project objective. In the thinning risk model, an insurance company has several dependent classes of business; stochastic sources that may cause a claim in at least one of the dependent classes of business are classified into a number of groups; and each event occurred in anyone of the groups may cause a claim in each class of business with certain probability. It is worth noting that a special case of the thinning risk model is the frequently-used common shock risk model. Here the thinning risk model is assumed to follow a compound Poisson risk model. Together with reinsurance and investment, the resulting surplus process is a kind of jump-diffusion process. Although the thinning dependence has nice mathematical properties, the technique used in the first project objective cannot be applied directly to tackle the present optimization problem. The incorporation of the thinning dependence and the presence of the jump process definitely introduce a great deal of difficulty in the derivations of main results. In addition to the optimization problem, we would like to investigate the impact of dependence on the optimal results. Due to the complex nature of the resulting surplus process, it is expected that expressions for the optimal results are very complicated, and thus one can hardly work out the impact of dependence analytically. In view of this, we plan to examine how the dependence parameters affect the optimal strategy by means of a large scale of numerical study.
rows: In the context of optimal reinsurance, most of the research concerns about quota-share reinsurance (sometimes called proportional reinsurance), or excess-of-loss reinsurance, or a combination of the two. In the first project objective, an insurance company can purchase per-loss reinsurance. That is, there is no restriction on the form of reinsurance. It is assumed that the reinsurance premium is computed according to the mean-variance premium principle which combines the expected-value and variance premium principles. Also, the company can invest its surplus in a financial market consisting of one risky asset and one risk-free asset. There is an investment constraint that the amount invested in the risky asset cannot exceed a priori given amount. Furthermore, short-selling is prohibited but borrowing is allowed. In this setup, several insurance risk models with investment and reinsurance can be considered. Without restricting the form of reinsurance, we study the optimal reinsurance-investment problem for an insurer who wishes to minimize the probability of absolute ruin. By the technique of stochastic dynamic programming, we derive the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation and the corresponding optimal results. We then compare the results with those obtained under the objective of minimizing the probability of traditional ruin. We also investigate some properties of the optimal strategy, and carry out some numerical study to examine how the model parameters affect the optimal strategy. To make the optimization more interesting, we would like to remove the investment constraint so that the amount of risky asset is uncapped. We then re-examine the same optimal problem but without the constraint on investment.

Similar to the setup of the first project objective, the insurer can purchase per-loss reinsurance with the premium computed according to the mean-variance premium principle. The risk models of study only take reinsurance into consideration. We assume that the insurer does not have perfect confidence in the drift term of the insurance surplus. In other words, the insurer suspects that the drift of the insurance risk may be misspecified. To handle the issue of misspecification, we use the idea of model ambiguity to describe this phenomenon. Similar to the robust-value approach, we consider the reference probability measure (benchmark) and a set of equivalent measures which have absolute continuous Radon-Nikodym derivatives with respect to the benchmark. To capture the insurer's ambiguity aversion, we penalize the absolute ruin probability with a term based on relative entropy, and thus a new robust value is defined by employing the criterion of minimizing the penalized probability of absolute ruin. To tackle this optimization problem, we apply the technique of stochastic dynamic programming and solve the corresponding boundary-value problem. It is expected that the corresponding optimal reinsurance strategy and the optimal drift distortion of the equivalent measure can be obtained in explicit feedback form. Finally, we provide numerical examples to illustrate the effects of ambiguity aversion on the optimal solutions and discuss their economic implications therein.

In recent years, the study of correlated classes of business has been one of the main topics in the actuarial literature. In view of its importance, we incorporate the so-called thinning dependence into the risk model of study, and then revisit the optimization problem stated in the first project objective. In the thinning risk model, an insurance company has several dependent classes of business; stochastic sources that may cause a claim in at least one of the dependent classes of business are classified into a number of groups; and each event occurred in anyone of the groups may cause a claim in each class of business with certain probability. It is worth noting that a special case of the thinning risk model is the frequently-used common shock risk model. Here the thinning risk model is assumed to follow a compound Poisson risk model. 17306220.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306220.value: In the first project objective, the insurer can purchase per-loss reinsurance and invest its surplus in a financial market consisting of a risk-free asset and a risky asset. Also, the insurer can borrow to continue its business when the surplus goes below zero. Our goal is to minimize the probability of absolute ruin under the mean-variance premium principle. By solving the corresponding Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, we derive explicit expressions for the S-shaped minimum absolute ruin function and its associated optimal reinsurance-investment strategy. We further investigate the reason for the S-shaped value function and discover that the constraint on investment control can result in the kink of minimum absolute ruin function. In the second project objective, we consider an optimal robust reinsurance problem in a diffusion model for an ambiguity-averse insurer, who worries about ambiguity and aims to minimize the robust value involving the probability of absolute ruin and a penalization of model ambiguity. The insurer is allowed to purchase per-claim reinsurance to transfer its risk exposure. Under the mean-variance premium principle, we obtain the optimal reinsurance strategy and the associated value function are derived explicitly by applying stochastic dynamic programming and by solving the corresponding boundary-value problem. We prove that there exists a unique point of inflection which relies on the penalty parameter greatly such that the robust value function is strictly concave up to the unique point of inflection and is strictly convex afterwards. It is also interesting to observe that the expression for the optimal robust reinsurance strategy is independent of the penalty parameter and coincides with the one in the benchmark case without ambiguity. In the third project objective, we consider a robust optimal reinsurance problem with dependent risks for an ambiguity-averse/loving insurer to minimize the probability of absolute ruin involving the penalization of model ambiguity. By the method of stochastic control and corresponding Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, we derive not only the closed-form reinsurance-investment strategy but also the corresponding value function. For the ambiguity-averse case, our results show that the insurer becomes more conservative with the underlying retention and adopts a more aggressive investment strategy if the insurance liability is more ambiguous. Meanwhile, the insurer is likely to retain more insurance business and decrease the investment amount if the insurer becomes more ambiguity averse on the return of stock. By contrast, the insurer adopts an opposite strategy in the extremely ambiguity-loving case.

17306220.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306220.value: For further research, we may investigate the robust reinsurance contract with belief heterogeneity from joint interests of the insurer and the reinsurer in the framework of Stackelberg differential game. Specifically, the reinsurer plays the role of leader, deciding on the optimal reinsurance premium, while the insurer acts as the follower to determine the optimal retention level in a proportional arrangement. Assume that the insurer and the reinsurer have heterogeneous beliefs and adopt different claim distributions for the aggregate risk, and that the reinsurer's expected aggregate claims is unknown. It is confident that the unknown expected value falls within an interval centered around its estimate. In this setup, the optimal reinsurance problem for both ambiguity-averse and ambiguity-loving reinsurers under the time-consistent mean-variance criterion can be studied. Another possible research is to consider insurer's ambiguity towards an external source based on which the insurance and financial markets are correlated through thinning dependence. Specifically, the intensity of claim arrivals from the external stochastic source cannot be estimated accurately, and is described by the insurer's prior distribution. Within this framework, we can investigate the mean-variance optimization problem under the so-called smooth ambiguity, which aims to search for the optimal strategies in average case.

17306220.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306220.value: The study of absolute ruin has been around for many years. Specifically, under the concept of absolute ruin, whenever the surplus of an insurance company falls below zero, the company can borrow money at a debit interest rate in order to keep running its insurance business. Unlike the study of traditional ruin probability with zero level of ruin, the study of absolute ruin probability allows us to investigate the behavior of a company when it is in deficit. Although many authors have studied various problems with absolute ruin in the literature, not much has been done in the context of optimal reinsurance. We first derive the optimal reinsurance strategies that minimize the probability of absolute ruin. In practice, it is difficult to model the insurance risk process accurately. This leads us to extend our study to the case with model uncertainty. Finally, to make the problem more realistic, we further investigate the optimal reinsurance problem for a risk model with thinning dependence. It is believed that the expected outcomes of the three project objectives should at least provide the insurance profession with some useful insights. They should also be very useful for further research on the topic.

17306320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17306320.value: Marine heatwaves (MHW) are extreme climatic events that have recently been recognized as an emerging threat to marine ecosystems globally. Driven by climate change, heatwaves are already causing deleterious ecosystem and socio-economic impacts. While the global frequency and intensity of MHWs are predicted to increase, there is currently no understanding of the regional trends of MHWs or how they are modified by regional weather conditions. South-east Asia is a climate change hotspot, but the historical and current trajectories of MHWs are yet to be identified. Consequently, the impact of MHWs on coastal organisms and ecosystems in SE Asia are largely unknown. With MHWs predicted to become both more frequent and intense under climate change, developing an understanding of the regionally specific characteristics of heatwaves and the impacts they will have on the survival and adaptation of marine communities has become an imperative. Here, we will complete the first analysis of the trends of MHWs in SE Asia using historical sea surface temperature data and model future trajectories to develop regional forecasts. We will then link this new understanding of the physical conditions associated with MHWs to biological functioning by using marine plankton from Hong Kong to experimentally test the genetic and physiological mechanisms underlying adaptation to MHWs. Ultimately, we will use model organisms to experimentally unveil the effects of increasing heatwave intensity, frequency and duration on populations of coastal marine species. The outcomes of this project will provide in-depth knowledge of the trajectory of marine heatwaves in SE Asia, inform our understanding of the potential effects of future extreme events on coastal systems, and form a baseline from which to predict how organisms and systems may adapt to future change. 海洋熱浪是極端的反常氣候現象，也是對全球海洋生態系統一個新的威脅。氣候變化效驅使的海洋熱浪已經開始負面影響生態系統以及社會經濟的打擊。雖然海洋熱浪在全球發生的頻率以及幅度預計會逐漸加劇，但是我們現時對海洋熱浪局部地區的趨勢和對當地的影響所知甚少。東南亞雖然是氣候變化的重點地區，但科學家卻未有確認歷史及近代的熱浪走勢，所以這些反常的氣候現對沿岸生物及生態的影響大多是不為人知。由於全球海洋熱浪的頻率及幅度都有上升趨勢，徹底理解及建立關於海洋熱浪特性及其對海洋生態生存及適應能力的影響的框架是刻不容緩。 我們將會利用過往海洋水的面溫度進行東南亞的海洋熱浪趨勢分析及模擬其未來走勢來建立局部地區預告，然後將得到有關海洋熱浪的環境因素資料作為浮游生物實驗的非生物變數來取得生物基因層面及生理層面適應環境變化的機制。最後我們會將環境因素的頻率，幅度，以及持續時間提高來探討這些變化其他沿岸海洋生物的影響。實驗結果會提供關於東南亞海洋熱浪詳盡走勢的數據和知識，剖析這種氣候現象在未來對沿岸系統潛在的影響，以及建立判斷生物及生態適應於未來發生的現象的知識基礎。

17306320.label: Realisation of objectives
17306320.value: Goal 1: Characterize the historical trends in marine heatwave frequency and intensity from the past 40 years in SE Asian coastal waters. The data analysis and modelling for Goal 1 have been successfully completed and the outcomes in two papers (one in review, one to be submitted by end of January 2025). The results have also been presented at 3 international conferences). Issues encountered in this Goal: The climate models that were used by the IPCC to project climate change, and therefore MHWs, during the early phase of this project were the RCP suite of models. However, after we had finished the model projections for this Goal, the new IPCC report was released - in this report the new, updated suite of models, the SSP models, were released. This model release made all of our initial work on the models in Goal 1 outdated. To overcome this setback, we re-ran all of our analyses using the new SSP suite of models (taking several months of high computing power) to ensure the data were publishable. The first step in the project was to use historical sea surface temperature (SST) data to categorize historical trends in marine heatwaves in Southeast Asia. We successfully completed these analyses for the Western Pacific Ocean across the entire latitudinal gradient from the equator to 70 degrees North, a larger geographical scope than outlined in the proposal. We found that while maximum MHW intensity and number of MHW days (per year) have increased across the entire western Pacific, these increases were over 5 times greater in some temperate regions than tropical waters. Interestingly, while the overall focus of MHW research (and concern) is focused on summer MHWs, we found that the percentage of ocean area with increasing summer AND winter MHWs was increasing across the western Pacific, but that this increase was greatest in the mid-latitude temperate waters (publication 7, part C). Importantly, while winter MHWs tend to increase growth performance in most species, the combined effect of winter and summer MHWs drives declines in annual growth across all species studied, from tropics to temperate regions (publication 7, part C). The second step was to use IPCC models to project the MHWs in the region and use the characteristics of the MHWs for Goals 2 and 3. This step was initially completed using the IPCC RCP models, but with the release of the new IPCC SSP models we re-ran all the analyses – taking several months because of the size of the models – to ensure that the outputs were at the cutting edge of this research. Once finished, we took an extra step to develop thermal performance models of over 40 species of marine organisms for which the data were published and available. This extra step meant that we are able to assess the physiological effects of MHWs in addition to the intergenerational effects (Goals 2 & 3). We found that increased thermal variability in marine waters decreases the growth performance of marine species but, as with MHWs in part 1 (above), this effect was greatest in the mid-latitude temperate waters, not in the tropics as is generally thought. Critically, the increased variability associated with MHWs also reduces the thermal safety margin of species in the temperate latitudes to the point that they are pushed beyond thermal growth limits, reducing thermal resilience and potentially contributing to population decline (publication 4, part C + 2 x international conference presentations by Evans). Goal 2: Use model species to investigate the ability of populations of planktonic crustaceans to recover from, and adapt to, increased intensity of marine heatwaves through multiple generations The experiments for Goal 2 have been successfully completed and the results presented in one paper (to be submitted by end of February 2025). In addition, as part of this work, a meta-analysis was done to understand the global patterns in basis for multigenerational adaptation in planktonic crustaceans (published in 2021 in OMBAR). The experiments using a model species of marine crustacean (copepods) supported out proposed hypothesis that rapid-onset temperature rise with MHWs would cause thermal stress leading to metabolic effects. Surprisingly though, the copepods exposed to the harshest MHW scenario seemed to recover faster than those exposed to moderate MHWs, suggesting that this higher thermal stress invokes an “active” biological response to recover function rather than a “sit and wait” strategy when stress is not extreme. Importantly, while there is less energy expenditure with the slower recovery of the “sit and wait” strategy, these individuals are more susceptible to the onset of subsequent MHW events because they potentially aren’t fully recovered before onset of the next MHW. Therefore, while it seems more adaptively advantageous to reduce energy expenditure, in situations where MHWs are becoming more frequent, this biological strategy may be maladaptive at a population level (publication 5, part C). Indeed, this theory is borne out in our findings of the global meta-analysis, where species which inhabit more variable environments seem to have more active and rapid recovery to stressful conditions and are therefore able to persist in these harsher environments (publication 1, part C). Goal 3: Unveil the functional responses of populations of planktonic crustaceans to increased frequency and duration of marine heatwaves The experiment for Goal 3 has been successfully completed and the results presented in one paper (currently in review in Nature Ecology & Evolution). Issues encountered in this Goal: There were initially issues with this experiment with the populations of copepods failing. Even though we maintained these populations for experiments in Goal 1, we encountered issues with maintaining the populations and exposing them to MHWs over multiple generations, meaning that we could not get the multiple-generation responses to MHWs. To overcome this setback, we expanded on our findings in the global meta-analysis (publication 1, part C) and subsequently successfully ran a 10-generation experiment on how populations responded to ocean acidification. While a different stressor than planned in the proposal, the successful outcomes of this experiment incorporate the planned physiology, transcriptomic, and population-level responses as planned. The resulting paper is currently in review in Nature Ecology & Evolution (publication 6, part C). The key novel findings of this component of the project is that more abrupt onset of stressful environmental conditions may induce more active responses in organisms and lead to intergenerational adaptive responses within populations. In contrast, when environmental conditions were altered slowly over multiple generations, the populations demonstrated a more plastic acclimatization response which was variable between generations. Ultimately, however, this meant that the end population after 10 generations was not as well adapted to the future conditions under climate change than the population that was initially shocked by the rapid onset of change (publication 6, part C). This finding is contrary to the current thinking that populations may have time to acclimate to future conditions if the change is slow enough, but that they will go extinct if there is rapid change. Therefore, we advance the theory on understanding the population and species-level responses to climate change and what may alternatively drive adaptation versus extinction of populations.

17306320.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306320.value: The overarching goal of this project was to assess the future effects of marine heatwaves on marine species and whether (and how) they will adapt to future conditions. One key was that the biological responses would be dependent on species functional traits. For example, faster-generation species (as used as a model species in this project) will be more dependent on adaptation through selection than longer-lived species which may show more plastic physiological or behavioural responses. Therefore, as a direct result of this project we developed a new framework to predict the effects of MHWs on biological communities (publication 2, part C). Our analysis of historical trends in MHWs shows for the first time that not only are heatwaves increasing in duration and intensity, but that they are increasing in both winter and summer. While the current research is on the effects of summer MHWs (particularly in driving mortality) the effects of combined winter and summer MHWs has gone unexplored. We demonstrate that the physiological effects will be detrimental to full-year growth performance even in regions where mortality may not occur (publication 7). We extend this to show that, contrary to prevailing theory, these effects will be worse in temperate waters where temperature variation is higher, than tropical waters (publication 4). In preparing for the experiments in this project, we realised that there was no consistent experimental protocol being used for MHW experiments; therefore, we analysed the problems with the current approaches and developed recommendations for researchers (publication 3). Then, in addition to using model species in an experimental approach (below), we did a global meta-analysis of the effects of climate change on copepods, demonstrating that the effects of environmental stress are population and species specific, but also that some species demonstrate the potential to adapt over generations (publication 1). Our experiments demonstrate the mechanism for this adaptation. More abrupt onset of stressful environmental conditions seems to induce more acute stress and active responses in organisms (publication 5) and lead to intergenerational adaptive responses. In contrast, when environmental conditions change slowly over generations, populations demonstrate a more plastic acclimatization response which varied between generations (publication 6). This finding is contrary to the current thinking that populations may have time to acclimate to future conditions if the change is slow enough, but that they will go extinct if there is rapid change.

17306320.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306320.value: This project led to insights in how populations of marine organisms may respond and adapt to marine heatwaves. However, it was limited by the laboratory experiments on model species. We have extended the project to a new project (PI Russell: GRF17307723) on populations of a key planktonic krill species which is broadly distributed through the temperate regions that are this current project found will be more susceptible to MHWs. These krill are a key set of species which form the base of globally important fisheries and so the findings will have large-scale implications.

17306320.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306320.value: Marine heatwaves are projected to be devastating to populations of marine species, yet we have little understanding of if, or how, species may adapt to the effects of heatwaves. By using planktonic marine crustaceans as model species, we show that rapid onset of temperature stress may cause populations to respond physiologically and genetically to enable adaptation. While we must show caution in extrapolating from the responses of the small, short generational species, our findings that some species may adapt provides some hope that we can come up with methods to help mitigate the worst effects of climate change, at least in the near future.

17306420.label: Project Objectives
17306420.value: To formulate the forward-backward stochastic differential equations of McKean-Vlasov type for generic mean field type control problems, and study their local-in-time well-posedness. In order to solve mean field problems, such as mean field type control problems (MFTCPs) (that we will study in this project) or the mean field games (MFGs), one standard approach is to study the stochastic optimal control problems via the forward-backward system of partial differential equations (PDEs), namely the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) and Fokker-Planck (FP) equations. In general, due to the strong coupling, the forward-backward systems are hard to be mathematically analyzed, so researchers make use of the master equation, which encapsulates all the information into a single forward equation, to study the underlying problems. Since the master equation carries so much information, the master equation is highly nonlinear in general. Another standard approach is to study the forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) of McKean-Vlasov type for the MFTCPs. Due to the complexity, results in both approaches are usually for cases with special structures, such as the linear-quadratic (LQ) setting. In our first objective, we will follow the second approach, and establish the local-in-time well-posedness by applying the lifting procedure proposed by P.-L. Lions, and adapting the classical proofs (for FBSDEs in Euclidean spaces) to the Hilbert space setting. The main novelty here is to use the algebraic structure of the lifted FBSDEs, which allow us to adapt the classical proofs/arguments in the lifted variables. The PI and Co-I are very familiar with these arguments, since they have already established a similar result in a recent joint work for MFGs. To show the global-in-time existence to the forward-backward stochastic differential equations of McKean-Vlasov type for generic mean field type control problems. Even though the local-in-time existence can be established by adapting the classical proofs/arguments to the Hilbert space setting, the global-in-time existence cannot be easily obtained via adapting the classical arguments. Even for the case of Euclidean spaces, the global-in-time existence is usually required some structural conditions, such as the monotonicity condition. Indeed, the generalization of these classical structural conditions is yet to be clear in the Hilbert space setting. Our novel idea here is to extend the concept of positivity of Schur complement to the Hilbert space setting. This new extension is highly non-trivial, since the Schur complement in the Hilbert space setting will involve the inverse of a second-order Gateaux derivatives. To define this inverse, we will make use of the duality argument and Riesz representation theorem. Using the positivity of Schur complement, we anticipate that uniform estimates on the Jacobian flows for the FBSDEs will be able to be derived. Finally, we will apply these uniform estimates and the continuous induction argument to obtain the global-in-time existence of adapted solutions. Again, the PI and Co-I are very familiar with these arguments, due to their experience in a recent joint for MFGs. To verify the regularity of the value function for the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation associated with the underlying mean field type control problems. It follows from the standard argument that the existence of adapted solutions to FBSDEs of McKean-Vlasov type implies that the corresponding value function will be the HJB equation associated with the MFTCP. In a certain sense, the fact that the value function of a stochastic control problem is also a viscosity solution to the associated HJB equation follows directly from the principle of dynamic programming and the definition of viscosity solutions. In order to show the verification theorem, the value function is needed to be a classical solution to the HJB equation, which is indeed a uniformly parabolic equation. To show the regularity of the value function, we will apply PDE techniques to obtain appropriate a priori estimates for parabolic problems, of which the PI has already studied a lot in other contexts. To perform numerical simulations to verify the optimal strategies obtained in the project numerically. These numerical studies will provide a better idea on the exact values of the optimal strategies, as well as the value function of the underlying control problems. The exact values will be important for real-world applications. The numerical investigations will be implemented by a combination of cubature methods, finite-difference schemes, and Fourier-cosine techniques. To extend the Objective Number 1 to Number 4 above to the extended mean field problems. MFTCPs have a lot of real-world applications, such as the optimization problems in power grids. In applications for power grids, the dynamics depends on both the state and probability law for the feedback control. This is the extended MFTCPs. The extra law-dependence of the feedback control will create technical difficulties for applying the arguments stated in Objective Number 1 to 3 above. Therefore, we anticipate that we will impose some minor assumptions on the problems, so that the mathematical difficulties can be overcome.

17306420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17306420.value: Mean field theory has a long history and was originated from the statistical physics, in which the collective behavior of a huge number of physical particles is studied by using both partial differential equations (PDEs) and stochastic analysis. In this project we will study mean field type control problems (MFTCPs) that arise from economic and engineering contexts. Unlike mean field games, MFTCPs provide an effective approximation to the stochastic optimization problems that involve a centralized control, and perhaps a personal agent historical performance. To tackle MFTCPs, there are two standard approaches: (i) to study the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) and Fokker-Planck (FP) equations, which are a forward-backward system of PDEs; and (ii) to study the forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) of McKean-Vlasov type first, and then the HJB equation. The systems obtained in both approaches are indeed infinite-dimensional because they actually depend on the measures. As a result, classical analytic tricks in finite-dimensional spaces, such as Sobolev embeddings, Rellich’s and Friedrichs lemmas, do not directly apply. Hence, the problems are hard to be mathematically analyzed, and most of the existing results are for cases with special structures, such as the linear-quadratic setting. The aim of this project is to solve MFTCPs in a generic setting via the second approach (i.e., (ii) in the last paragraph). Compared to the first approach, the FBSDEs in the second approach are less nonlinear, but still an infinite-dimensional system with measure-valued coefficients. To solve these FBSDEs in a generic setting, we will make use of the lifting procedure introduced by P.-L. Lions, generalize the concept of Schur complement from Euclidean spaces to the Hilbert space setting, and study the corresponding Jacobian flows. After showing the existence of adapted solutions to these FBSDEs, we will also study the regularity of the value functions that satisfy the HJB equations, by using PDE techniques. In other words, in order to solve the underlying MFTCPs, we propose to use a hybrid approach that combines the techniques in and takes advantages of both the partial differential equations and stochastic analysis, so that the mathematical difficulty can be reduced. Numerical approximations for solutions will also be investigated by using a combination of cubature methods, finite-difference schemes, and Fourier-cosine techniques. 歷史悠久的平均場理論起源於統計物理學，在統計物理學中學者利用偏微分方程（PDE）和隨機分析方法來研究大量物理粒子的集體行為。在本項目，我們將研究與經濟學和工程學相關的平均場類型控制問題（MFTCP）。與平均場博弈論不同，MFTCP為涉及中央控制以及代理人歷史表現的隨機優化問題提供了有效的近似值。解決MFTCP的標準方法一般有兩種：（i）研究哈密頓-雅可比-貝爾曼（HJB）和福克-普朗克（FP）方程所組成的正倒向PDE系統； （ii）首先研究McKean-Vlasov類型的正倒向隨機微分方程（FBSDE），然後再研究HJB方程。在兩種方法中，因所獲得的系統實際上都與測度有關，故都是無限維的。是故，諸如索博列夫嵌入定理，Rellich和Friedrichs引理等在有限維空間中的經典分析技巧就不能被直接應用。因此，要利用數學方法來分析這些問題是非常困難的，並且大多數現有的結果都只針對具有特殊結構（例如線性二次控制問題）的情況。 本項目的目的是通過第二種方法（即，上文中的方法（ii））去解決一般的MFTCP。與第一種方法相比，雖然第二種方法中的FBSDE非線性程度較低，但仍是具有以測度為係數的無限維系統。為了在一般情況下對這些FBSDE求解，我們將運用由P.-L. Lions所提出的提升程序，將舒爾補的概念從歐幾里得空間推廣到希爾伯特空間，及研究相應的雅可比流。證明了這些FBSDE適應解的存在性之後，我們將利用PDE技術去研究HJB方程的解的正則性。換句話說，為了降低數學難度，我們將採用一種結合了偏微分方程和隨機分析中技術及優點的方法來解決MFTCP。數值解也將通過求容积法、有限差分法和傅里葉餘弦技術來進行研究。

17306420.label: Realisation of objectives
17306420.value: The objectives of this project have been fully addressed. The main difficulty of the first objective is the existence of the mean field term, which is a measure-valued quantity representing the status of all agents. As a result, when one applies the standard argument in the classical version of Pontryagin's maximum principle, this measure-valued mean field term is also affected when one perturbs the control variable, making the computations extremely complicated. To overcome this issue, for example, in our study of the first-order mean field type control problems, we first applied the principle of dynamic programming to derive the Bellman equation for the value function v and then applied the method of characteristics to derive the forward-backward stochastic differential equations (FBSDEs) of McKean-Vlasov type for generic mean field type control problems; see Eq. (6.6) and Theorem 6.4 in Research Output No. 3 in Part C Section 8, for instance. We also showed the local-in-time existence of these FBSDEs by using a modified version of Picard’s iteration argument. These results can also be extended to the second-order mean field problems, as we demonstrated in Research Output No. 5 in Part C Section 8. This addressed Objective 1. The global-in-time existence (namely Objective 2) of these FBSDEs is the most challenging task in this project. One of the major challenges is that the existence of the optimal control, which is equivalent to the well-definedness of the Hamiltonian, may not be guaranteed by solving the first-order condition while considering the forward dynamics subject to a generic nonlinear drift function. Our main novelty for overcoming this issue is to introduce the cone condition, which is a newly proposed condition in the literature. Technically speaking, when we derive the a priori estimates, only the state and co-state within the cone appear in the mathematical analysis; in other words, to derive the estimates, one does not need to consider the state and co-state beyond the cone. Imposing such a cone condition allows us to show the unique existence of the optimal control subject to appropriate non-linear drift rates and convex cost functions. To ensure this cone condition is satisfied globally in time, we derive a set of new crucial estimates for solutions to the FBSDEs obtained in Objective 1. These crucial estimates indeed include the sensitivity of the co-state with respect to the initial data, which turns out to be sufficient to guarantee the global-in-time well-posedness of the FBSDEs by using the standard continuous induction argument. This addressed Objective 2. For the regularity of the value function, we first show the global-in-time well-posedness of classical solutions to the Jacobian flows of the state and co-state, which are systems of FBSDEs that the derivatives of the state and co-state satisfy. As a result, by using these sufficiently regular solutions to FBSDEs, we expressed the value function as an integral formula and proved its regularity by using the regularity of these solutions. This is our approach for completing Objective 3. After obtaining the global-in-time unique solvability of the mean field optimal control problems arising from the generic setting (which includes all the small nonlinear perturbations of linear-quadratic (LQ) problems) mentioned above, our next target is to numerically investigate whether the solutions to these perturbed problems are close to the solutions to the corresponding LQ problems. The solutions to the LQ problems are well-known and can be numerically simulated by using the standard ansatz; on the other hand, the solutions of the perturbed LQ problems are generated by using the finite-difference scheme for the forward Fokker-Planck and backward Hamiltonian-Jacobi-Bellman equations. Besides the robustness of the LQ setting, another important issue in our numerical studies is the lifespan of the solutions to the FBSDEs when the costs are not convex in the state variable or the mean field effect is not small. We investigated this issue by using both mathematical analysis and numerical simulations; for the numerical simulations, see Section 3.4 of Research Output No. 5 in Part C Section 8, for instance. This addressed Objective 4. Using similar techniques to those used in our major result stated in Research Output No. 3 in Part C Section 8, we further extend our results to other settings. This addressed Objective 5.

17306420.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306420.value: The research output in this project consists of five research papers, an MPhil thesis, a capstone course report by an undergraduate student, and the establishment of collaborations with researchers in China, Hong Kong, Macau, the United Kingdom, and the United States; see Part C for more details. The main focus of this project was to solve mean-field optimal control problems within a general framework, which includes small perturbations of linear-quadratic (LQ) problems. The project encountered two main challenges: (i) The generic nonlinear drift function makes the unique existence of the optimal control highly non-trivial. (ii) Describing the connection of mean-field/measure terms between later and initial times was not straightforward. To overcome these challenges, the project newly introduced the cone condition, derived a new set of a priori estimates, and used the push-forward techniques to describe the measure-valued term. Using these new techniques, we obtained the global-in-time unique solvability of first-order mean-field type control problems, as well as their associated Bellman and master equations; see Item No. 3 of Section 8. Furthermore, the mathematical results were extended to address first and second-order optimal control problems arising from mean field games; see Items No. 4 and 5 of Section 8. As a by-product, the project also discovered that the push-forward techniques introduced for solving mean-field problems were beneficial in describing non-local behaviors in certain physical systems. To showcase this observation, we also wrote two papers (Items No. 1 and 2 of Section 8) demonstrating the application of these techniques in solving integrable systems, like the Hunter-Saxton equation. Apart from the mathematical analysis results, numerical investigations were also conducted to verify the stability of solutions to LQ problems concerning nonlinear perturbations of drift and cost functions. These experiments, as planned in the Education Plan in the proposal, were carried out by an undergraduate student as part of his research training, and details can be found in his undergraduate capstone report (Item No. 2 of Section 10). Furthermore, the maximum life-span of solutions to the FBSDEs obtained in Item No. 5 of Section 8 was numerically demonstrated as almost optimal; see the numerical example in Section 3.4 of that paper. Finally, a MPhil student was trained, and in his MPhil thesis he derived a generalized version of Ito's lemma involving both the mean-field and delay effects that are useful in this project; see Item No. 1 of Section 10 for details.

17306420.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306420.value: To solve the challenging optimal control problems subject to generic nonlinear drift functions, as well as their associated partial differential equations, the principal investigator (PI) and his research team have already introduced innovative mathematical concepts (such as cone condition, using the push-forward measure to represent the mean-field term at later times) and new techniques (like new crucial estimates for solutions to forward-backward stochastic differential equations). While the current research project effectively tackles a significant class of optimal control problems from a mathematical theory perspective, specifically nonlinear perturbations of linear-quadratic problems, there remain numerous practical applications in fields like economics and engineering that fall outside this scope. Nevertheless, the methodologies developed in this study provides a solid mathematical foundation for the PI to further study real-world applications. For instance, the parameter training in deep residual neural networks (ResNet) with batch normalization can be seen as first-order mean-field type optimal control problems, and the existence of classical solutions to these control problems will imply the convergence some parameters training procedures (e.g., Extended Method of Successive Approximations). The PI plans to further extend the framework developed in this project to also address this and other practical mean-field optimal control problems in the future.

17306420.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306420.value: Mean field theory, which has a long history and was originated from statistical physics, is a branch of mathematical theory that deals with systems involving a large number of interacting agents. By examining the behavior of these systems as the number of agents tends to infinity, this theory simplifies complex interactions into a mean-field approximation. This approach provides a framework for analyzing and understanding complicated systems with a large population of interacting agents. This project investigated a large class of mean-field problems arising from economic and engineering contexts, including small perturbations of linear-quadratic (LQ) problems. The LQ problems have been extensively studied, but our theoretical understanding of nonlinear perturbations of these LQ problems is very limited. The mathematical results obtained in this project, including the long-time unique solvability of generic first-order mean-field type control problems, provide a solid mathematical foundation for investigating mean-field problems arising from many practical applications. The new mathematical concepts and techniques introduced in this project will also be applicable to the study of other real-world optimal control problems with a large number of interacting agents. In summary, this project has significantly advanced both the theoretical understanding and practical applications of mean-field problems.

17306520.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17306520.value: Spin-orbit coupling is a relativistic effect and is now becoming the forefront of modern quantum condensed matter physics in recently years. Spin-orbit coupling is widely present in various quantum materials and especially important in the systems with heavy atoms. We are particularly interested in the spin-orbit-coupled Mott insulators where the spin-orbit coupling directly impacts on the localized electrons. The spin-orbit coupling entangles the spin and orbital degrees of freedom and leads to the formation of a spin-orbital-entangled local moment. This new type of degrees of freedom generates a rather rich physics in quantum condensed matter physics. New types of degrees of freedom bring new types of physical interactions and new types of experimental phenomena as well as distinct experimental probes. The connection between the microscopics and the new phenomena requires a detailed theoretical understanding. This is an exciting field with a lot of opportunities. In this proposal, we are interested in both the realization of Kitaev physics and the hidden multipolar orders in the spin-orbit-coupled Mott insulators. We will extend to the Kitaev physics from the popular 4d/5d electron systems to the 4f electron systems. We will establish the physical Hamiltonian and calculate or predict the fundamental physical properties of the candidate materials. We will emphasize more on the physical origin of the Kitaev interaction in these spin-orbit-entangled J=1/2 magnets. For the hidden multipolar orders, we will focus on the 4d/5d Mott insulators and clarify the spin-orbital reconstruction in these materials. We will show that, in this context, how the spin-orbital entanglements bring a large multipolar interaction. We will clarify a concept called “multipolar frustration” and predict the resulting experimental phenomena. Since recent experiments on some of the materials were about thermal transport, we will spend part of our efforts to clarify the physical origin of the thermal transports in these materials, especially in the ones without obvious magnetic orders. 自旋軌道耦合是一種相對論效應，現在正成為現代的前沿，也是近年來的量子凝聚態物理學的中心課題之一。自旋軌道耦合廣泛存在於各種量子材料中，特別是在具有 重原子的體系。我們對自旋軌道耦合的莫特絕緣體特別感興趣自旋軌道耦合直接影響局域的電子。自旋軌道耦合糾纏了自旋和軌道的自由度，並導致形成自旋軌道糾纏的局部磁矩。這種新型的自由度產生量子凝聚態物理學中相當豐富的物理學新型度 自由帶來了新型的相互作用和新型的實驗現象以及不同的實驗探測手段，它們之間的譜學和新現象需要詳細的理論理解。這個是一個充滿機遇的令人興奮的領域。在這項提案中，我們討論Kitaev物理學的實現以及自旋軌道耦合的莫特絕緣子中隱藏的多極階，我們把相關物理擴展到從當下流行的4d / 5d電子系統到4f電子系統的基塔耶夫物理學。我們將建立物理哈密頓量，併計算或預測基本哈密頓量候選材料的物理性質。我們將在這些體系中更多地強調這些自旋軌道糾纏的J = 1/2磁體中Kitaev相互作用的起源。為了探測隱藏的多極磁矩，我們將重點關注4d / 5d 莫特絕緣體，並闡明這些材料的自旋軌道重建。在這種情況下，我們將展示如何自旋軌道的糾纏帶來了巨大的多極相互作用。我們將澄清一個這個概念稱為“多極阻挫”，並預測實驗結果現象。由於最近對某些材料進行的實驗是關於熱的在輸運過程中，我們將竭盡全力弄清這些材料（尤其是沒有明顯磁序的材料）中熱傳遞的物理起源。

17306520.label: Realisation of objectives
17306520.value: In a series of works, we have made a significant progress in the understanding of thermal Hall effects in strongly correlated electronics systems. The thermal Hall transport has risen as an important diagnosis of the physical properties of the elementary excitations in various quantum materials, especially among the Mott insulating systems where the electronic transports are often featureless. We have explained the physical origins of the thermal Hall effects in quantum magnets where all the relevant excitations are charge-neutral. In addition to understanding the existing experiments, we pay a special attention to the underlying mechanisms of the thermal Hall effects in various magnetic systems, and clarify the connection between the microscopic physical variables and the emergent degrees of freedom in different quantum phases. The external magnetic field is shown to modify the intrinsic Berry curvature properties of various emergent and/or exotic quasiparticle excitations in distinct fashions for different quantum systems and quantum phases, contributing to the thermal Hall transports. These include but are not limited to, for example, the conventional ones like the magnons in ordered magnets, the triplons in dimerized magnets and generalized triplons, the exotic and fractionalized quasiparticles such as the spinons and the magnetic monopoles in quantum spin liquids. We have carefully explained their contribution and discussed their presence in the thermal Hall conductivity in different physical contexts. We expect our results to provide a useful guidance for the physical mechanism of the thermal Hall transports in quantum magnets. We have established the universal presence of the excitonic superexchange in the spin-orbit-coupled Mott insulators. We have observed that the restriction to the lowest spin-orbit-entangled "J" states may sometimes be insufficient to characterize the microscopic physics, and the virtual excitonic processes via the upper "J" states provide an important correction to the superexchange. We illustrate this excitonic-like superexchange process from a two-dimensional 5d iridate Sr2IrO4 and explain its physical consequences such as the orbital-like coupling to the external magnetic flux and the nonlinear magnetic susceptibility. The universal presence of the excitonic superexchange in other spin-orbit-coupled Mott insulators such as 3d Co-based Kitaev magnets and even f electron rare-earth magnets is further discussed. The rare-earth triangular-lattice chalcogenide is a great platform for exploring both spin liquids and novel magnetic orders with anisotropic spin interactions and magnetic frustrations. In fact, it can contain a large Kitaev interaction in the spin model and thus may be considered as new classes of Kitaev materials. Together with experimentalists, we report the thermodynamic and neutron-scattering measurements of rare-earth triangular-lattice chalcogenide KErSe2, using single-crystal samples. Our experiments revealed a long-range stripe order below 0.2 K. Although the magnetic order was three dimensional, magnetic excitations exhibited negligible modulation along the 𝑧 direction, indicating very weak interlayer coupling. Furthermore, magnetic excitation developed a well-defined spin-wave dispersion with a gap at 𝑀 points. Both the stripe order and spin-wave excitations could be quantitatively understood from the anisotropic spin interactions of the Er3+ Kramers doublets. The experimental results were quantitatively explained by our theoretical modeling that includes a strong Kitaev term. These results represent the direct application of Kitaev like interaction in quantum materials. Quantum spin liquid (QSL) is a disordered state of quantum-mechanically entangled spins commonly arising from frustrated magnetic dipolar interactions. However, QSL in some pyrochlore magnets can also come from frustrated magnetic octupolar interactions. Although the key signature for both dipolar and octupolar interaction-driven QSL is the presence of a spin excitation continuum (spinons) arising from the spin quantum number fractionalization, an external magnetic field-induced ferromagnetic order will transform the spinons into conventional spin waves in a dipolar QSL. By contrast, in an octupole QSL (where the hidden multipole moments play an important role), the spin waves carry octupole moments that do not couple, in the leading order, to an external magnetic field or to neutron moments but will contribute to the field dependence of the heat capacity. Here we use neutron scattering to show that the application of a large external magnetic field to Ce2⁢Zr2⁢O7, an octupolar QSL candidate, induces an Anderson-Higgs transition by condensing the spinons into a static ferromagnetic ordered state with octupolar spin waves invisible to neutrons but contributing to the heat capacity. Our theoretical calculations also provide a microscopic, qualitative understanding for the presence of octupole scattering at large wave vectors in Ce2⁢Sn2⁢O7 pyrochlore, and its absence in Ce2⁢Zr2⁢O7. Therefore, our results identify Ce2⁢Zr2⁢O7 as a strong candidate for an octupolar 𝑈⁡(1) QSL, establishing that frustrated magnetic octupolar interactions are responsible for the QSL properties in Ce-based pyrochlore magnets.

17306520.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306520.value: Surface fractionalization and Kondo detection: We point out that the type-II terminated 1T-TaS2 surface of a three-dimensional 1T-TaS2 bulk material realizes the effective spin-1/2 degree of freedom on each David star cluster with T^2 = −1 such that the time-reversal symmetry is realized anomalously, despite the fact that bulk three-dimensional 1T-TaS2 material has an even number of electrons per unit cell with T^2 = 1. This surface is effectively viewed as a spin-1/2 triangular lattice magnet, except with a fully gapped topological bulk. We propose this surface termination realizes a spinon Fermi surface spin liquid with the surface fractionalization but with a non-exotic three-dimensional bulk. Infinite critical boson non-Fermi liquid: We explored a distinct type of non-Fermi liquid where there exists an infinite number of critical bosonic modes instead of finite number of bosonic modes. We consider itinerant magnets with both conduction electrons and fluctuating magnetic moments in three dimensions. With Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, the moments fluctuate near a boson surface in the reciprocal space at low energies when the system approaches an ordering transition. The infinite critical modes on the boson surface strongly scatter the gapless electrons on the Fermi surface and convert the metallic sector into a non-Fermi liquid. On the ordered side, a conventional non-Fermi liquid emerges due to the scattering by the gapless Goldstone mode from the spontaneous breaking of the global rotational symmetry. Spin-orbit-coupled Mott insulator We point out the universal presence of the excitonic superexchange in spin-orbit-coupled Mott insulators. We observed that, the restriction to the lowest spin-orbit-entangled states may sometimes be insufficient to characterize the microscopic physics, and the virtual excitonic processes via the upper states provide an important correction. The universal presence of the excitonic superexchange in spin-orbit-coupled Mott insulators such as 3d Co-based Kitaev magnets and even 4f electron rare-earth magnets is discussed. SU(N) Mott insulator Large symmetry in quantum many-body systems could strongly enhance quantum fluctuations and thereby stabilize exotic quantum phases. Frustrated interactions were long known to have similar effects. Here we intertwine the large SU(N) symmetry and the frustration in a J1-J2 SU(N) Heisenberg model on a honeycomb lattice, where J1 is the nearest-neighbor coupling and J2 is the next-nearest-neighbor coupling. With a large-N analysis, we obtain a rich phase diagram by varying both N and the ratio J2/J1. The ground states include Dirac spin liquid, chiral spin liquid, valence cluster solids, flux ordered state, and stripe states.

17306520.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306520.value: Our study about the interplay between the local moments and the Dirac electrons on the surface of topological insulator could be generalized to the large topic of exploring the interplay between the real-space topology and the momentum space topology. In last two decades, we have experienced a great advance in the understanding of the band structure topology. The real-space topology is more well-understood. The interplay between these two topologies is not much explored. We plan to put some efforts into this direction of research in the future. The idea of Hund’s metal is an important one in the study of the strong correlation physics. Its role in the strong spin-orbit-coupled materials is not fully understood at all. The impact on Mott transition and the electron band structure, as well as the Mott regime should be carefully examined. The interplay between the multipolar moments and geometric frustration has led to rich phenomena, but the quantum effects on top of this interplay have not been understood. This may require the intertwined gauge structures.

17306520.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306520.value: Strong correlation physics is challenging and exciting. Often we do not even know where to begin with. It requires strong physical intuition and imagination to make progress. Once the connection is understood, the rest is calculation. In this research, we have demonstrated the power of the physical intuition by connecting the down-to-earth quantum materials to the frontier fundamental theories. These research bridges the ongoing experiments with the fast-evolving theoretical efforts. This type of research belongs to a different type of scientific styles. It is not based on the formulation of the problem from the abstract and fundamental structures in mathematics. It is also not based on the down-to-earth density functional type of calculation. It is more about establishing the connection by careful modeling, calculation, and understanding of the hidden fundamental structures inside the experiments and quantum materials. This style is challenging but highly valuable. It requires the knowledge and understanding of both sides. In the long run, the outcome of this research has both impact in the understanding of the physical nature, and also creates an interesting style for junior research to follow.
