17306620.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17306620.value: Sub-Saharan Africa will be home to 20% of the world’s population by 2050. Combined with climate and other environmental changes, rapid population growth will mark the future of the continent. Both environmental and societal changes in the future will influence the landscapes that humans rely upon as economic, cultural and ecological resources. Understanding the way environmental and societal change both affect the land, and how changes on the land in turn feedback and affect people and the resources upon which they depend is therefore of critical importance. One of the most important ways in which agriculture and pastoralism affect the land system, particularly in seasonally arid regions, is by facilitating wind-driven soil erosion and emissions of mineral dust aerosol to the atmosphere. Erosion and dust emissions thus may affect both soil fertility and human health. Understanding the relationship between climate, society, dust emissions, and health is the subject of the REDWIND project. Drawing on our team’s experience in climate and land cover modeling, dust emission and transport, and environmental data synthesis, we will couple vegetation and dust emissions models with an atmospheric chemistry-climate model. In order to quantify impacts and feedbacks it is instructive to examine both the present and periods in the past when we know that important changes in both society and environment occurred. We focus on two periods when large-scale land use change in sub-Saharan Africa was and will be important: the century centered on AD 2000 (1950-2050), and the African Iron Age transition (4.5-0.5 ka; 2500 BC – AD 1500). The latter period marks the widespread adoption of agriculture and pastoralism across sub- Saharan Africa, and the first large-scale land cover changes as a result of anthropogenic activities. Driven by novel scenarios of land use change in these contrasting periods, we will simulate dust emission impacts on soil productivity and human health, and quantify the feedbacks of dust emissions to regional climate and land use. We will evaluate the model output using a synthesis of terrestrial and marine sedimentary dust archives. Choosing the most likely scenarios, we will provide a valuable baseline for understanding the future of climate and coupled human and natural systems in sub-Saharan Africa. 到2050年，撒哈拉以南的非洲地區將擁有全球20％的人口。人口的快速增長加上氣候和其他環境變化，將對非洲大陸帶來標誌性的影響。未來環境和社會變化都會大幅改變具有經濟，文化和生態價值的土地景觀。因此，了解環境和社會變遷對土地用途所帶來的變化，以致如何影響人類和其依賴的資源均是十分重要的議題。 風蝕性土壤侵蝕所導致的粉塵及氣溶膠排放，是農業和畜牧業對土地系統其中最重要的影響之一（特別是在季節性乾旱的地區）。因此而成的水土流失和粉塵排放更可能會嚴重影響土壤肥力和人類健康。REDWIND項目的主旨是要了解氣候，社會，粉塵排放與健康之間的關係。利用我們團隊在建立氣候和土地覆蓋電腦模型的經驗，再配合粉塵排放的輸送及環境數據，我們希望將粉塵排放模型與大氣化學氣候模型結合。為了量化影響和反饋的幅度，我們必須考慮現在和過去發生的重大環境變化。本項目著重於研究撒哈拉以南非洲過去和將來兩個時期發生的大規模土地利用變遷，包括：以公元2000年（公元1950 - 2050年）為中心的世紀，和非洲鐵器時代的過渡期（公元前2500年 - 公元1500年）。 非洲鐵器時代的過渡期標誌著撒哈拉以南非洲地區農業和畜牧業的廣泛採用，並且導致了第一次因人為活動所致的大規模土地覆蓋變化。在這兩個大規模土地利用變化的時期，我們將會以電腦模擬粉塵排放對土壤生產力和人類健康的影響，並量化粉塵排放對區域氣候和土地利用的反饋。我們將使用陸地和海洋沉積塵埃數據評估模型的輸出，在篩擇最可能的方案後，為理解撒哈拉以南非洲的氣候以及人類與自然系統的關係提供有參考價值的基線。

17306620.label: Realisation of objectives
17306620.value: Major delays to this project were caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Afterward, the original PI (Prof. Jed Kaplan) left Hong Kong, and the project was transferred to a new PI with revised objectives. The revised objectives are in the spirit of the original project but were designed to be feasible given the new PI's expertise and the amount of time left in the project. Despite these challenges, all project objectives were successfully achieved: Objective 1: The first objective was successfully achieved by compiling published records of dust deposition from lacustrine and marine sediment cores across West Africa. The study focused on key locations, including the Senegal River Valley, Tilemsi Valley, Mema region, Inland Niger Delta, Bandiagara Plateau, Seno Plain, Lake Chad Basin, and Mandara Mountains. These records were filtered to ensure coverage of the late Holocene period (4–0ka), with a refined temporal sampling resolution (one sample per millennia) to improve the spatial coverage of data. Objective 2: The second objective was successfully achieved by recalibrating radiocarbon depth-age models for selected sediment records using the Bayesian age-depth modeling framework implemented in Bacon. The recalibration utilized the latest IntCal20 radiocarbon calibration curve, ensuring consistency and accuracy across datasets. The recalibrated records were aligned on a common timescale, enabling synchronized comparisons of dust deposition trends across West Africa. This process also accounted for uncertainties in the original radiocarbon dates and incorporated prior information about sedimentation rates to improve the robustness of the models. Objective 3: The third objective was achieved by performing detailed local and region-wide analyses of the calibrated dust deposition records. Local trends were assessed through individual sediment cores, while regional trends were synthesized by aggregating data from multiple sites across West Africa. The analyses revealed a general increase in dust deposition rates throughout the late Holocene, with significant spatial and temporal variability. The results also highlighted periods, such as 3500–2500 BP and the Medieval Climate Anomaly (1150–650 BP), where dust deposition trends were decoupled from climate conditions, suggesting additional forcing mechanisms. Objective 4: The fourth objective was achieved by developing a Dust Mobilization Potential Index (DMPI), which translated the land use categories defined in Kay et al. (2019) into relative importance for dust emissions. The DMPI integrated archaeological evidence and contemporary observations to quantify the relationship between land use practices - such as agricultural intensification, grazing, and vegetation clearance - and their potential to enhance dust mobilization. This framework accounted for spatial and temporal variability in land use practices across West Africa and assigned relative weights to different activities based on their contribution to dust generation. Objective 5: The fifth objective was achieved by synthesizing polygon-based land use maps into regional time series using area weighting and generating a scenario of expected relative dust emissions caused by land use. The analysis revealed substantial spatial and temporal variability in land use changes across West Africa during the late Holocene. Early agricultural and pastoral activities began in the southern Sahara and Sahel regions (~3500 BP) and gradually expanded southward into more humid regions. The Dust Mobilization Potential Index (DMPI) developed in Objective 4 was applied to classify and model relative dust emissions associated with these land use changes. Regions with intensive agricultural and grazing activities, such as the Sahel and savanna zones, exhibited higher relative dust emissions over time. The southward expansion of dust-prone land use practices correlated with increasing DMPI values, particularly during periods of relative climate stability (e.g., 3500–2500 BP and the Medieval Climate Anomaly). Objective 6: The sixth objective was addressed by comparing the modeled scenario of relative dust emissions caused by land use with regional dust deposition records. The comparison revealed a strong alignment between the modeled dust emissions and observed dust deposition trends, particularly during periods of high anthropogenic activity, such as 3500–2500 BP and the Medieval Climate Anomaly (1150–650 BP). The results highlighted the role of land use changes in amplifying dust emissions, with peaks in the modeled dust emissions coinciding with increased dust deposition rates, even during relatively humid climatic conditions. Regional differences in the relationship between modeled dust emissions and observed dust deposition were evident. The Sahel and savanna regions exhibited stronger correlations due to earlier and more intensive land use activities, while more humid regions showed delayed but increasing contributions as land use expanded southward. Objective 7: This objective was achieved through the preparation and publication of the manuscript titled "Increasing late Holocene dust deposition in West Africa is amplified by land use change" (Gao et al., 2026) in the journal Global and Planetary Change. The manuscript presents findings from Objectives 1–6, including the compilation and analysis of dust deposition records, the development of the Dust Mobilization Potential Index (DMPI), and the comparison of modeled dust emissions with observed trends.

17306620.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306620.value: This project explored the relationship between human-driven land use changes and dust deposition in West Africa during the late Holocene, culminating in the publication of the manuscript "Increasing late Holocene dust deposition in West Africa is amplified by land use change" (Gao et al., 2026) in Global and Planetary Change (DOI: 10.1016/j.gloplacha.2025.105175). The manuscript presents the key findings of the study, including the development of the Dust Mobilization Potential Index (DMPI), the synthesis of land use maps, and the comparison of modeled dust emissions with observed deposition trends. A significant outcome of this project was its contribution to training and capacity building. The project supported a diverse group of students, including PhD, MPhil, and undergraduate researchers, who were trained in understanding sediment entrainment and deposition in relation to human-driven mechanisms. These students gained hands-on experience with advanced techniques such as Bayesian age-depth modeling, the integration of archaeological and sedimentological data, and the development of models to quantify the impact of land use on dust mobilization. This training provided them with valuable skills in interdisciplinary research, combining climate science, archaeology, and geomorphology. The project also fostered international collaboration, strengthening ties with institutions such as the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology (Germany), the University of Texas at Arlington (USA), and the University of Calgary (Canada). These collaborations provided students with opportunities to engage with global experts, share their research, and expand their academic networks. Overall, this project not only advanced scientific understanding of the interplay between human activities and environmental change but also contributed to the development of the next generation of researchers in this field. Through student training, international collaboration, and the dissemination of findings in a high-impact journal, the project has left a lasting impact on both the academic community and the participating researchers.

17306620.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306620.value: This research highlights the significant role of human activities in amplifying dust emissions in late Holocene West Africa. Future studies could further develop this work by: -Expanding Geographic Scope: Extending the analysis to other regions affected by land use changes and dust deposition, such as North Africa and the Middle East, to identify broader patterns and interactions. -Refining the Dust Mobilization Index: Incorporating additional datasets, such as high-resolution paleoenvironmental records and advanced modeling techniques, to enhance the accuracy of the dust mobilization potential index. -Exploring Feedback Mechanisms: Investigating the feedback loops between land use changes, dust emissions, and climate systems, particularly their impact on monsoon dynamics and regional aridification trends. -Policy Implications: Collaborating with policymakers to translate findings into actionable strategies for mitigating the impacts of land use changes on dust emissions and climate. These developments would provide a more detailed understanding of human-environment interactions and strengthen the predictive capacity of models for future environmental and climate scenarios.

17306620.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306620.value: This research explores how human activities, such as farming and herding, have contributed to increasing dust emissions in West Africa over the past 4,000 years. While climate change has long been considered the primary driver of dust deposition in the region, this study shows that human land use changes also played a significant role. By analyzing historical land use patterns and their effects on erosion, the researchers developed a new tool, called the dust mobilization potential index, to measure the impact of human activities on dust generation. They found that as farming and herding practices expanded and intensified, the landscape became more vulnerable to erosion, leading to increased dust emissions. This trend was particularly evident during periods of relative climate stability, suggesting that human activities, rather than natural climate changes, were the main cause of the dust increases during these times. The findings provide new insights into how humans have shaped environmental changes throughout history. They also highlight the importance of considering human impacts when studying past climates and predicting future environmental changes. This research is crucial for understanding the long-term effects of land use on climate systems and for developing sustainable land management practices.

17306720.label: Project Objectives
17306720.value: We will analyze high-resolution adaptive optics image of the giant star nu Octantis to show that its binary companion is most likely a white dwarf. We will also analyze high-precision radial velocity measurements to show that the planet orbiting nu Octantis is likely a giant planet on a retrograde orbit. We will investigate how the unusual nu Octantis system formed and evolved. The options that we will consider include (i) formation of the planet in a retrograde disk around nu Octantis and survival through the evolution of the companion star; (ii) a circumbinary planet that become circumstellar through planet-planet scattering and tidal capture; and (iii) a second-generation planet that formed when the companion evolved into a white dwarf. We will examine whether the orbits of the two Saturn-mass planets around the low-mass M dwarf star GJ 1148, which are widely separated and show large eccentricity variations, are due to planet-planet scattering and the ejection of another giant planet. We will also analyze the spin evolution of the inner planet due to the tidal interactions between the planet and the star. We will perform numerical simulations to investigate whether massive giant planets could be formed around low-mass M dwarfs in the pebble accretion model where solid cores large enough to accrete gas to become giant planets are formed by the accretion of cm-to-meter sized pebbles by planetary embryos.

17306720.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17306720.value: The search for planets around non-solar-type stars is one of the frontiers in extrasolar planet research. We propose to investigate several problems related to the dynamics and origins of giant planets around giant stars, which are more massive than the Sun, and M-dwarf stars, which are less massive than the Sun. (1) We will analyze high-resolution adaptive optics image of the giant star nu Octantis to show that its binary companion is most likely a white dwarf - a type of stellar remnant. We will also analyze high-precision radial velocity measurements to show that the planet orbiting nu Octantis is a giant planet on a retrograde orbit, revolving in the opposite direction as the binary. (2) We will investigate how the unusual nu Octantis system formed and evolved. Did the planet form in a retrograde disk around nu Octantis and survive the evolution of the companion star? Did the planet originally orbit the binary and become a planet orbiting the primary star through planet-planet scattering and tidal capture? The most intriguing possibility is that the planet is a second-generation planet that formed when the companion evolved into a white dwarf. (3) We will examine whether the orbits of the two Saturn-mass planets around the low-mass M dwarf star GJ 1148, which are widely separated and show large eccentricity variations, are due to planet-planet scattering and the ejection of another giant planet. We will also analyze the spin evolution of the inner planet due to the tidal interactions between the planet and the star. (4) We will perform numerical simulations to investigate whether massive giant planets could be formed around low-mass M dwarfs in the popular pebble accretion model where solid cores large enough to accrete gas to become giant planets are formed by the accretion of cm-to-meter sized pebbles by planetary embryos. 尋找圍繞非太陽類型恆星的行星是系外行星研究的前沿之一。我們提議研究幾個與圍繞非太陽類型恆星的巨行星的動力和起源有關的問題，這些恆星包括比太陽重的巨星和比太陽輕的M型矮星。（1）我們將分析巨星nu Octantis的高分辨率自適應光學圖像，以顯示其雙星伴星很可能是一顆白矮星，一種恆星演化的最終產物。我們還將分析高精度的視向速度數據，以顯示圍繞nu Octantis的行星是一顆逆行的巨行星，其軌道旋轉方向與雙星相反。（2）我們將研究這個異常的nu Octantis系統是如何形成和演化的。行星是否在一個圍繞nu Octantis的逆行原行星盤中形成，並在伴星演化中生存了下來？行星最初是否圍繞雙星運行，並通過行星散射和潮汐效應而成為繞主恆星運行的行星？最有趣的的可能性是該行星是在伴星演化成白矮星時形成的第二代行星。（3）圍繞低質量M矮星GJ 1148的兩個土星質量行星的軌道相距很遠並且顯示大的偏心率變化，我們將研究這個軌道結構是否由於行星散射和拋射所致。我們還將分析由於行星和恆星之間的潮汐相互作用而引起的內行星的自旋演化。（4）我們將進行數值模擬，以研究在流行的卵石積聚模型中，是否可以在低質量M矮星周圍形成大質量的巨行星。

17306720.label: Realisation of objectives
17306720.value: (1) We have completed our analysis of the images of nu Octantis obtained with the high-resolution adaptive optics system SPHERE. The secondary star nu Oct B was not detected, which means that it must be a very faint white dwarf (i.e., a stellar remnant) and not a low-mass main-sequence star. An MPhil student Cheng under the PI's supervision has performed a detailed analysis of the complete radial velocity data set, which includes the high-precision HARPS data obtained by CoI Trifonov. It confirmed that, in addition to the binary signal with a period of 1050 days, there is a signal with a period of about 400 days due to a circumprimary planet. We have performed inclined and coplanar dynamical fits, using the nested sampling technique to determine the posterior distribution of the orbital parameters. Stability analysis of the fits showed that the planetary orbit must be retrograde and nearly coplanar to be stable. (2) The MPhil student Cheng has also used the binary star evolution code BSE coupled with the nested sampling technique implemented in the package DYNESTY to examine the distribution of initial binary configuration that could evolve into the present-day configuration of nu Octantis. We found that the tidally enhanced stellar wind parameter and, hence, the initial period and eccentricity of the binary orbit are poorly constrained but that the initial minimum separation between the stars is well constrained to about 1.3 au, which overlaps the current planetary orbit and makes any scenarios in which the circumprimary planetary orbit formed coevally with the stars inconceivable. We have proposed and analyzed a scenario in which the planet was captured from a prograde circumbinary orbit as a result of planet-planet scattering triggered by the binary evolution. Another plausible scenario is that the planet formed in a retrograde disc of material around nu Oct A accreted from the mass ejected by nu Oct B when it evolved into a white dwarf. (3) Another MPhil student Yuan under the PI's supervision has performed numerical experiments using the N-body code SyMBA to study the planet-planet scattering scenario for the origin of the planetary system around the M dwarf star GJ 1148, which has two Saturn-mass planets on widely separated orbits showing large eccentricity variations. We consider a third planet of 0.1 Jupiter-mass in the initial GJ 1148 system with initial orbital separations of 3.5-4.5 mutual Hill radii and initial semimajor axis of the innermost planet in the range of 0.10-0.50 au. The majority of scattering results in planet-planet collisions, followed by planet ejections, and planet-star close approaches. Among them, only planet ejections produce eccentric and widely separated two-planet systems, with some having similar orbital properties to the GJ 1148 system. We have also implemented general relativistic precession in the N-body code SyMBA and examined the effects of general relativistic apsidal precession. We have additionally performed simulations of the general problem of the origin of warm Jupiters by planet-planet scattering. A non-trivial number of stable two-planet systems are produced by ejection, which disagrees with the result by Anderson et al. (2020) showing that two-planet systems arise exclusively through planet-planet collisions. The MPhil student Yuan has also studied the spin evolution of GJ 1148 b, using two different tidal models. We found that the spin evolution of GJ 1148 b is not significantly altered by the secular variation of eccentricity induced by GJ 1148 c, because the secular timescale is much smaller than the spin-down timescale. To explore the influence of the ratio between the secular timescale and the spin-down timescale, we systematically moved both planets closer to the star by multiplying the semimajor axes by a factor beta. We found that as beta decreases, the spin evolution becomes more affected by the eccentricity variation. An exciting new development in astrophysics is the discovery of free-floating planets by microlensing observations. The above work on GJ 1148 led to a collaboration with Mao and his student Zhai at Tsinghua University to perform N-body simulations to study the ejection of planets by the instability of multi-planet systems. For systems with only super-Earth planets, we found that the time for the first close encounter between two planets and the time for the system to lose the first planet have different dependence on the semimajor axis of the innermost planet and on the orbital spacing between the planets. Most systems with only super-Earths do not have planets ejected. In systems with super-Earths and a cold Jupiter, we discovered that a cold Jupiter significantly increases the probability of ejection of the super-Earths and that the velocities of the ejected planets relative to their parent stars are mostly < 6 km/s. Most super-Earths in the remaining two-planet systems are on highly elliptical but stable orbits and have migrated inwards compared with their initial states. (4) An MPhil student Lau under the PI's supervision has successfully developed a parallelized version of SyMBA with OpenMP. Good scaling with the number of threads on multi-core CPUs is achieved by parallelizing the force calculation as well as incorporating a close encounter pair grouping strategy. This parallelized version of SyMBA was incorporated in the pebble accretion code, along with implementation of improved pebble accretion models and improved formulae for migration and eccentricity damping by planet-disc interactions by CoIs Matsumura and Brasser. With these improvements, it became necessary for us to redo our simulations of giant planet formation in the Solar System. We simulated a population of 1000-5000 planetesimals in a smooth protoplanetary disc, which is evolved under the effects of their mutual gravity, pebble accretion, gas accretion and planet migration. We found that the dynamical interactions among growing planetesimals are vigorous and can halt pebble accretion for excited bodies. While a set of simulations without planet migration produces one to two gas giants and one to two ice giants beyond 6 au, massive planetary cores readily move to the inner Solar System once planet migration is in effect. Dynamical heating is important in a planetesimal disc and the reduced pebble encounter time should be considered in similar models. We found that planet migration remains a challenge to form cold giant planets in a smooth protoplanetary disc. This work was continued in a collaboration with a student Raorane in India. We explored through N-body simulations the implications of an assumed ring structure in the disc at 5 au. A systematic study of the effects of the initial planetesimal disc mass, the number of planetesimals and their size-frequency distribution slope, pebble accretion prescription and sticking efficiency revealed that the accretion sticking efficiency is the most sensitive parameter to control the final masses and number of giant planets. We were unable to replicate the formation of all three types of giant planets in the Solar System in a single simulation. We computed the average formation time for proto-Jupiter to reach 10 Earth masses to be 1.1 Myr and for proto-Saturn 3.3 Myr, while for the ice giants this increases to 4.9 Myr. The formation timescales of the cores of the gas giants are distinct at > 95% confidence, suggesting that they formed sequentially.

17306720.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306720.value: (1) and (2) We have used new radial velocity measurements to consolidate the circumprimary planet in the nu Octantis binary star system. Stable fits to all radial velocity data require the planetary orbit to be retrograde. We have also discovered through imaging that the companion star is a white dwarf. Our exploration of primordial binary configurations showed that the initial minimum separation between the stars makes any scenarios in which the circumprimary planet formed coevally with the stars inconceivable. The retrograde planet must have originated from a circumbinary orbit or a second-generation protoplanetary disc, revealing the role of binary stellar evolution in the formation and evolution of planetary systems. A paper in the journal Nature and a conference proceedings paper have been published. (3) We have used N-body simulations to show that the architecture of the two-planet system around the star GJ 1148 could be produced by planet-planet scattering and that this system may have lost a giant planet. We have also studied the tidal evolution of the spin rate of GJ 1148 b and found that it is not significantly altered by the secular variation of eccentricity induced by GJ 1148 c. A journal paper has been published. We have performed simulations of multi-planet systems to study the production of free-floating planets by dynamical instability. Most systems with only super-Earths do not have planets ejected. The presence of a cold Jupiter can significantly increase the probability of ejection of super-Earths, with most ejected planets having velocities < 6 km/s. A journal paper has been submitted. (4) We have simulated the evolution of planetesimals in a smooth protoplanetary disc, under the effects of their mutual gravity, pebble accretion, gas accretion and planet migration. While a set of results without planet migration produces one to two gas giants and one to two ice giants beyond 6 au, massive planetary cores readily move to the inner Solar System once planet migration is in effect. We then studied the effects of an assumed ring structure in the disc at 5 au. We were unable to replicate the formation of all three types of giant planets in the Solar System in a single simulation. However, we found that the formation timescales of the cores of Jupiter and Saturn and the ice giants are distinct at > 95% confidence, suggesting that they formed sequentially. Three journal papers have been published.

17306720.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306720.value: We will continue our analysis of the nu Octantis system by examining the viability of the scenario in which the planet was captured from a prograde circumbinary orbit as a result of planet-planet scattering triggered by binary evolution. We have already coupled the binary star evolution code BSE to the N-body code. The next step will be to implement tidal interactions between the star and the planet to simulate tidal capture and evolution. We are also revisiting another binary star system with a circumprimary planet: HD 82943. We have successfully applied for time to observe HD 82943 with SPHERE to determine whether the secondary star is a white dwarf or a low-mass main-sequence star. We are also collecting new radial velocity measurements that will allow us to determine whether the planetary orbit is retrograde. We will continue our work on giant planet formation to study formation around low-mass stars. We have analyzed the observed mass accretion rate of protostars to determine empirically how the properties of protoplanetary discs depend on the mass and age of the star. We have also improved various aspects of the model near the disc inner edge. We will be able to perform new simulations soon.

17306720.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306720.value: We have investigated the dynamics and origins of giant planets in different environments. We have confirmed the existence of a two-Jupiter-mass planet in an unprecedented retrograde orbit (moving in the opposite direction to the binary’s orbit) in the nu Octantis binary star system and discovered that the secondary star is a white dwarf, thereby revealing the role of binary star evolution in the origin of this planet. We have shown that the orbital configuration of the two Saturn-mass planets in the GJ 1148 system could be explained by the ejection of a third giant planet. We have also shown that the recently discovered free-floating planets could be ejected by the instability of planetary systems with multiple super-Earths and a cold Jupiter. We have simulated the formation of giant planets in our Solar System and found that the formation of cold giant planets remains a challenge. In a smooth protoplanetary disc, massive planetary cores readily move to the inner Solar System due to planet migration. In a disc with a ring structure at 5 au, we were unable to replicate the formation of all three types of giant planets in the Solar System in a single simulation.

17306820.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17306820.value: In nature, hierarchical structures such as organelles exhibit coordinated dynamics and responses dominantly based on aqueous systems. One characteristic of aqueous systems is the ability to direct the transport and assembly of molecules through the flow of water. This process, known as osmosis, requires a selective semipermeable membrane that allows passage of water but not other solute molecules. Despite significant advances in materials science and interfacial phenomena, synthetic systems such as microfluidic channels have not taken advantage of osmosis to fabricate structures with the same level of dynamics and responsiveness as their counterparts in nature. The proposed project is motivated by two observations. First, two aqueous solutions containing high concentrations of multiple water-soluble additives can be immiscible and form an aqueous-aqueous interface. Second, the resultant aqueous-aqueous interface can behave as a semipermeable membrane where osmosis can occur. Synthetic liquid-based printing approaches for fabricating complex biomimetic structures have focused on modifying the bulk liquid inks. The poor accessibility of common interfaces and the lack of understanding of molecular assembly at such interfaces have limited the design of interfacial structures. We propose to use aqueous-aqueous interfaces for fabricating designer membrane structures. Recently, we discovered that two oppositely charged polyelectrolytes added to two immiscible aqueous phases could interact at the interface between the solutions to form a membrane with strong bonding between polyelectrolytes, and with adjustable layer thickness. This opens entirely new avenues for the use of all-aqueous systems as biocompatible templates for hierarchical membrane structures. The ability to control the aqueous phase separation osmotically affords unprecedented functions to the resultant interfacial membranes. However, a comprehensive understanding of the dynamics of molecules and functional components at aqueous-aqueous interfaces is needed, as well as precise control of the responsiveness of the resultant membranes. The aims of the proposed project are to (1) elucidate the physics of all-aqueous interfacial dynamics induced by osmotic flow, (2) develop an interfacial engineering approach to fabricate dynamic responsive all-aqueous interfacial membranes (DRAIMs), and (3) demonstrate fabrication of all-liquid microfluidics by DRAIM-based dynamic interfacial printing. In the short term, the project will provide fundamental understanding of the interactions between different molecules and the osmotic effects on their assembly at aqueous-aqueous interfaces, and accordingly suggests a physico-chemical strategy for achieving new dynamic biomimetic membrane-bound materials and systems. The proposed studies form the foundation for fabricating and bioprinting bioinspired devices and microvascular tissue models by engineering liquid-liquid interfaces. 在自然界中，諸如細胞器之類的分層結構會表現出主要基於水相體系的協同動態過程與響應。水相體系的其中一個特點是能夠通過水流來引導分子的運輸和組裝。該過程稱為滲透。滲透過程需要有一種具有選擇性的半透膜，只允許水而不允許其他溶質分子通過。雖然材料科學和界面現象的相關研究在不斷進步，但在諸如微流體通道之類的合成體系的結構中，仍未能利用滲透技術來實現與自然界中相同的動態過程與響應能力。因此，本項目的設計基於兩項實驗觀察：首先，含有多種高濃度水溶性添加劑的兩水相溶液可以是不互溶的，並能形成水-水界面；其次，所得的水-水界麵類似半滲透膜，能用於實現滲透作用。目前，用來製造複雜仿生結構的合成液基打印方法主要用於改良宏觀的液態“油墨”。常見微觀界面上的可及性差以及對在界面上的分子組裝缺乏了解限制了界面結構的設計。為此我們提議，利用水-水界面工程來設計專屬的膜結構。近期，我們通過研究發現，分別在兩不混溶的水相體系中添加帶相反電荷的聚電解質，這兩種聚電解質會在溶液界面上相互作用並形成聚電解質膜，該膜具有牢固的鍵合和可調的膜厚度。這為將全水相體系用作生物相容性模板來實現分層膜結構開闢了全新的途徑。滲透控制水相分離的能力，為所得的界面膜提供了前所未有的功能。然而，我們還需要更加全面地了解水-水界面上分子和功能成分的動力學過程，以及精準地調控膜的響應性。基於此，所擬項目的主要目標為：（1）闡明由滲透流引起的全水界面動力學的物理原理；（2）開發一種界h面工程方法來製造具有動態響應性的全水界面膜（DRAIM）；（3）展示通過基於DRAIM動態界面打印技術所製造的全液態微流控體系。短期內，該項目將提供對水-水界面上分子間相互作用以及滲透對分子組裝影響的基本了解，並由此提出一種物理化學策略來實現新型的動態仿生膜結合材料與體系。本研究項目將通過對液-液界面的工程設計，為製造和打印生物啟發性裝置和微血管組織模型奠定堅實的基礎。

17306820.label: Realisation of objectives
17306820.value: The 3 objectives have been achieved: 1. We have demonstrated osmolality differences across all-aqueous interfaces can drive water flow along specific directions. As formulating polymer concentrations in two immiscible aqueous phases, such directional water flow can be engineered to (a) trigger interfacial phase separation to induce droplet generation at interface, (b) force rapid accumulation of nanoparticles at the interface, (c) facilitate interfacial self-assembly of membranes comprised of endothelial-cell like colloidosomes, and finally (d) contribute to the fabrication of ultrasoft liquid robot featuring hierarchical membranous shells. 2. We have successfully fabricated a dynamic responsive all-aqueous interfacial membrane (DRAIM). We endow DRAIM with sensitive magnetic responsiveness via embedding magnetic nanoparticles within membranes. Liquid robots produced with such DRAIM shells can be guided by magnetic field toward target position. Besides, we design DRAIM that can respond to temperature and light, by exploiting thermo-responsive polymer or photothermal-responsive nanoparticles as membrane components. Liquid robots built with such DRAIM can shrink into smaller sizes under thermal or light stimuli, passing through narrow microchannels, such as microvessels in tissues. 3. We have fabricated all-liquid microfluidics by DRAIM-based dynamic interfacial printing. The microfluidic system, which we coined the name, VasFluidics, exhibits structural and functional similarities with blood vascular tissues. The VasFluidics is featured with a DRAIM channel wall, which is ultrasoft, ultrathin, semi-permeable, and more importantly, can respond to variations in environmental pH and salt concentration. Under a high pH value or a high salt concentration, the permeability of the channel walls can increase, allowing substances passing through at a faster speed to vary liquid compositions within channels. The responsive VasFluidics is considered a biomimetic platform that can be applied to biological fluid mechanics, biomolecule synthesis, and drug screening.

17306820.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306820.value: - Investigate the influence of osmolality difference across all-aqueous interface to the dynamics of interfacial self-assembly, and further build the understanding required for microfabrication of DRAIM. - Develop different-typed DRAIMs that can respond to environmental changes in temperature, light, pH, and salt concentration, paving the way for DRAIM-based biomimetic designs. - Build up DRAIM-based all-liquid microrobots that can be guided to swim towards a target location, which is readily exploited for medical micromanipulation and targeted drug delivery. - Set up DRAIM-based microfluidics that can regulate fluid compositions via the interaction between liquid and DRAIM walls, which can serve as a biomimetic platform for drug discovery and tissue engineering. Most of the results have been presented in various international conferences (e.g. Materials Research Society (MRS) Fall Meeting 2023, European Materials Research Society (E-MRS) Spring Meeting 2024, International Soft Matter Conference (ISMC) 2023, International Conference on Miniaturized Systems for Chemistry and Life Sciences (MicroTAS) 2022, etc) and published in respected international journals (e.g.Science Advances, Nature Communications, Physical Review Letters, Journal of the American Chemical Society, Advanced Materials, Angewandte Chemie International Edition, ACS Nano, Advanced Functional Materials, Advanced Science, etc), as shown in Part C. Some papers have been submitted and are under review, and some results are still being refined or heading towards biomedical applications in pursuit of greater impact. The results of this project also indirectly benefit other research programs. The DRAIM-based designs, especially the DRAIM-based microrobotics and microfluidics, still have great potential for more designs as tools for biomedical fields, and more work should be done in the future.

17306820.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306820.value: The projects have demonstrated DRAIM with responsiveness to different stimuli, and further demonstrated DRAIM-based microfluidic systems capable of responding to environmental variations to regulate fluid compositions. Beyond microfluidics, there are many more exciting DRAIM-based applications. One example is bioprinting DRAIM-based artificial blood vessels for tissue engineering. DRAIM-based vessels can vary their wall permeability to self-adapt to in-vivo environments; such vessels cannot be built with conventional membranes. Another example is to build organ-on-a-chip to stimulate the metastasis of cancer cells through blood flow. In such chip, the effect of vessel walls on cancer cell metastasis can be explored by modulating wall properties, providing theoretical foundations for cancer treatment. To advance these studies, we will seek collaborations with appropriate biomedical collaborators, such as Dr. Shrike Zhang (Harvard Medical School) and Dr. Daniele Foresti (Harvard School of Engineering and Applied Sciences), and apply for potentially relevant funding from agencies including the Research Grants Council (RGC). Moreover, we plan to collaborate with industrial partners, such as Koln 3D Medical Manufacture, to develop DRAIM-based microfluidic chips into commercial apparatus for research and clinical use. We aim to develop these areas with the support of research grants including RGC and the Innovation and Technology Fund (ITF).

17306820.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306820.value: The lipid bilayer of cells, a membrane self-assembled at a water-water interface, can dynamically rearrange in response to different stimuli. Such dynamics and responses have inspired the engineering of biomolecular assembly at all-liquid interfaces to synthesize structures that can mimic similar biological functions. However, the extensively used water-oil interfaces can reduce the activity of many biomolecules due to the existence of oil phase; the all-aqueous system is more biocompatible, but the approach to combine interfacial assembly at water-water interfaces and manipulation of its functionality remains an elusive pre-requisite. Here, we developed strategies to enrich dynamics of interfacially formed materials, and construct a dynamic responsive all-aqueous interfacial membrane (DRAIM) that is biocompatible, molecularly addressable, and can respond to external triggers. Functionality of DRAIM is further demonstrated by the dynamic interfacial printing of DRAIM-based membrane-bound structures, such as the all-liquid microrobot and all-liquid microfluidics. They can respond to external stimuli to change permeability or softness of the DRAIM shell for biomimetic molecule introduction and release. These DRAIM-based structures serve as role models for water-water interfacial engineering of biomimetic functional materials, potentially developed into smart microcargos for in-vivo drug delivery, artificial tissues for medical transplantation, and microchips for in-vitro simulation of biomolecule synthesis.

17306920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17306920.value: Oceanic anoxic events (OAEs) represent some of the most dramatic environmental and climatic perturbations over the last 500 million years. OAEs are intervals in Earth’s history when the oceans experienced large-scale losses in oxygen accompanied by major biological crises and mass extinctions. Little is known, however, of precisely how the chemical composition of seawater evolved during OAEs and this prevents us from mechanistically connecting loss of ocean oxygen to its corresponding ecological and climatic effects. New evidence suggests that the oceans developed anoxic and iron-rich conditions during many OAEs and the chemical incompatibility of iron and sulfur in seawater implies a collapse in seawater sulfate concentrations in connection with deoxygenation. Since seawater sulfate is the most abundant oxidant at Earth’s surface, such a collapse is a major upheaval in elemental cycles with strong potential to influence biology and cause climate catastrophes. New knowledge is needed to test the extent to which seawater sulfate is susceptible to collapse, and to determine its causes and consequences. The research proposed here will generate new data that informs on the evolution of seawater chemistry during OAEs and enables us to test the rapidity and extent to which seawater sulfate declined in response to ocean oxygen loss. We will also examine the biogeochemistry of sulfate in the modern oceans to determine how marine microorganisms influence seawater sulfate by assimilating it into their biomass. It has been proposed that assimilation becomes important when seawater sulfate concentrations decline. If so, then assimilation of sulfur could have played an important role in the collapse of marine sulfate during OAEs. We will combine our new data from OAEs with this information on sulfur assimilation in numerical models that test the broader causes of seawater sulfate collapse and the resulting influence on global climate. These models will provide mechanistic insight into the functioning of OAEs and, by extension, into how environmental and climatic perturbations can lead to biological crises and mass extinctions, including the time-scales over which this happens. Such new knowledge is timely given that anthropogenic activities and climate change are currently causing ocean deoxygenation, akin to what took place during OAEs, with currently unconstrained impacts that include risk to coastal marine ecosystems, fisheries, and food security. Mechanistic insight into the causes and consequences of past ocean deoxygenation associated with OAEs will go a long way towards informing on the potential impact of contemporary ocean oxygen loss. 大洋缺氧事件（OAEs）代表了过去5亿年来最剧烈的环境和气候扰动。在地球历史中，OAEs是海洋经历了大规模氧气损失，并伴有重大生物危机和大灭绝的时期。然而，人们几乎不知道在OAE期间海水的化学成分是如何演变的，这使我们无法将海洋氧气的损失与其相应的生态和气候影响从原理上联系起来。新证据表明，在许多OAEs期间，海洋形成了缺氧和富铁的条件，海水中铁和硫的化学不相容性意味着OAEs将伴随与脱氧有关的海水硫酸盐浓度下降。由于海水硫酸盐是地球表面上最充裕的氧化剂，因此这种崩溃会导致元素循环的剧变，具有很强的影响生物和引起气候灾难的潜力。我们需要新的知识来测试海水硫酸盐易于崩塌的程度，并确定其原因和后果。我们在此提出的研究将获取有关OAEs期间海水化学演化信息的新数据，并使我们能够测试海水硫酸盐因响应海洋氧气损失而下降的速度和程度。我们还将研究现代海洋中硫酸盐的生物地球化学，以确定海洋微生物如何通过同化作用来影响海水硫酸盐。前人已经提出，当海水硫酸盐浓度下降时，同化作用将变得重要。如果是这样的话，那么硫的同化可能在OAEs期间海洋硫酸盐的崩溃中发挥了重要作用。我们将把来自OAEs的新数据与有关硫同化的信息结合到数值模型中，以测试导致海水硫酸盐崩塌的更广泛原因及其对全球气候的影响。这些模型将提供有关OAEs运作的原理性见解，并进而揭露环境和气候扰动导致生物危机和大灭绝的机制，包括发生此类事件的时间尺度。鉴于人为活动和气候变化目前正在引起海洋脱氧，这与OAEs期间发生的情况类似，加之包括对沿海海洋生态系统，渔业和食品安全等风险目前没有受到限制的影响，这些新知识是十分及时的。对过去与OAEs相关的海洋脱氧的原因和结果原理性的洞悉，将大大有助于了解当代海洋氧气损失的潜在影响。

17306920.label: Major findings and research outcome
17306920.value: This work has elucidated key aspects of the linkages between climate system perturbations and ocean redox conditions across major intervals of environmental change during the Phanerozoic. For example, our work recently published in Nature (Bauer et al., 2024) used our integrative geochemical data to track the duration of deep ocean anoxia and the natural recovery period from the silicate weathering feedback. This work is particularly relevant to modern concerns for anthropogenic CO2 emissions as it demonstrates the protracted time it takes for the ocean to be come re-oxygenated following climatic warming-driven anoxia. Additional published results have proposed some oceanic anoxic events occurred under oligotrophic conditions, contrasting the classic interpretation of eutrophic (Bauer et al., 2023). This has inspire further detailed investigations on similar events. Work currently under revision has proposed a new model for ocean redox conditions during the recovery from the largest mass extinction in Earth history at the end of the Permian period.

17306920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17306920.value: We are already pursuing new research endeavors based on the findings of this study. Importantly, we are now further investigating additional ocean anoxic events in the context of oligotrophic vs eutrophic conditions, and exploring new novel approaches for this. We have also began working more on modern coastal depositional systems to better understand redox conditions in relation to other factor (e.g., sedimentation, clay mineralogy, biota present) that facilitate organic carbon burial.

17306920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17306920.value: Our research has enhanced our understanding of both long-term evolution of Earth's ocean–atmosphere system, as well as better elucidated the nuance of dynamic responses to climate-driven perturbations to Earth's carbon cycle. This includes tracking differences int the mechanisms that drive deep-ocean anoxia, and the processes that facilitate Earth's recovery and the rate at which they operate. This is important for understanding ancient mass extinction events and to forecast Earth's recovery from modern anthropogenic carbon emissions should they push Earth's climate past its tipping point.

17307420.label: Major findings and research outcome
17307420.value: Firstly, the PI and his former student Jiaxing Huang applied Nevanlinna theory to prove two Ax–Schanuel type theorems for functional transcendence when the original exponential map is replaced by other meromorphic functions. We were alo able to provide examples showing that these results are optimal. Secondly, by applying the theory of differential algebra, we obtain a two-sequence Ax-Schanuel theorem, which is a functional analog of Brownawell’s two sequence theorem. As applications, we also recover the classical Ax-Schanuel theorem and also obatin the Ax-Schanuel theorem for linear differential equations with constant coefficients. We also explained how our results can be formulated geometrically.

17307420.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17307420.value: Since we have obtained a two-sequence Ax-Schanuel theorem for the exponential map exp (which also covers the the one sequence Ax-Schanuel theorem for exp), we would like to investigate if one can have similar result for exp(P) at less for certain class of polynomials P and try to provide explicit examples of these polynomials.

17307420.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17307420.value: Schanuel conjecture (1966) on the algebraic independence of certain sequences of complex numbers is the main open problem in transcendental number theory. James Ax (1971) proved a function theoretical version of Schanuel conjecture when the complex numbers are replaced by power series or entire functions. This is now known as Ax-Schanuel theorem and the studies of various extensions of it is currenlty a very active area in number theory, complex geometry and mathematical logic. On the other hand, Brownawell (1975) proved a weaker Schanuel type result on algebraic independence of two sequences of complex numbers. It is then natural to see if one can obtain a two sequence version of Ax-Schanuel type results for entire functions. This project suggested a formulation of this result and proved that in fact such a result holds by using Ax's orginally differential algebra approach instead of using the more popular o-minimality theory (from mathematical logic).

17307520.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17307520.value: 量子通信網絡有望為我們的信息技術帶來一場革命：它提供了前所未有的安全性，並催生了分佈式量子計算和多方量子密碼學等應用。這些應用在互聯網商務、網絡身份驗證、在線數據保護等眾多領域中都具有潛在的優勢。然而，量子通信的廣泛應用目前仍面臨許多技術挑戰。其中兩個主要障礙是量子通信系統有限的運行速度和相對較高的運行成本。 一種有望增強量子通信競爭力的方法是開發用於監控和操作量子通信鏈路的量子增強型技術。現有的大多數技術都基於經典的設計原理，例如使用強參考脈衝來追蹤傳輸線中的波動。這些技術的效率受經典統計學原理限制，而其生成參考脈衝所需的功率給通信系統帶來了巨大的額外運行成本。與之相對，量子檢測技術可以突破經典統計學的局限性，因此對傳輸線路的監控可以達到更高速率。同時，相干量子控制機制可以避免使用強參考脈衝，從而降低總體功率需求。 本項目的目的是對於測量和控制量子通信信道開發一種完全量子化的理論。我們將確定量子設備能夠實現的最大統計效率，並將其用於檢測傳輸線路中的動態變化，估計量子通信鏈路的質量以及即時尋找可用於通信的量子網絡節點。此外，我們將探索如何使用相干量子控制來穩定量子傳輸線路並優化量子消息的路由。這種量子的、完全自動化的系統有望實現更高的通信速率並最終達到量子力學所允許的效率極限。 該項目將有助於開發配備量子監控系統的新一代量子通信網絡。同時，它將解決量子力學與機器學習之間的交叉領域中的一些基本問題，探索量子機器對周圍環境變化做出反應的能力，並為量子增強型人工智能提供新的設計原理。

17307520.label: Realisation of objectives
17307520.value: The project had a substantial output of 19 papers published in international journals, including 2 papers published in Nature Communications, and 5 published in Physical Review Letters. A detailed description of how the project objectives have been achieved is provided in the following. Objective 1: fast tests of quantum channels. We developed powerful methods for testing the properties of quantum channels, using advanced statistical techniques and developing AI-assisted tests. We started by developing statistical techniques for veryfying whether a given quantum channel behaves in a prescribed way. An important highight of this work is that our method does not require the assumption that the channel's behaviour is stable over time and therefore it can be used to monitor transmission lines that are subject to random fluctuation and to dynamical changes. In addition, our approach works even if subsequent uses of the channel are correlated. The corresponding paper was published in Physical Review Letters. We then continued the investigation by developing statistical techniques to test for different properties of quantum channels: (1) We developed a technique of "quantum causal unravelling," which can be used to infer the internal structure of a complex process from the observation of its input-output behaviour. This technique can be used to discover useful communication links in quantum communication networks, and can also serve as a first step to identify multipartite quantum processes for which process tomography can be performed efficiently. This work was published in npj Quantum Information. (2) We developed a technique to estimate the quantum communication capacity of unknown quantum channels, also in this case avoiding the assumption that the channel behaves in the same way over time. This work was published in Physical Review Research. Still on the analytical side, we developed further analytical tools for the characterization of multipartite quantum states and processes: in particular, (1) We developed a quantum protocol for estimating the amount of incompatibility of quantum observables. Our protocol is robust to noise and can be used to cluster quantum observables depending on their mutual compatibility. This work was published in Physical Review Letters. (2) We designed a quantum algorithm for estimating weak values of quantum observables, and to characterize a two-time generalization of quantum states. This work was published in Physical Review Research. (3) We characterized the extreme points of sets of quantum channels appearing in various applications, including covariant, energy-preserving, Gibbs-preserving channels. This work has been an invited contribution to a special issue in honor of Alexander Holevo (2016 Shannon Award.) In addition to the analytical techniques, we developed AI-assisted methods for the characterization of quantum states and processes. Our original approach is based on the use of a type of deep neural network, known as "representation network," which produces its own representation of quantum states only based on data, without any built-in knowledge of quantum mechanics. With this approach, we developed an AI-assisted approach to make predictions about the statistics of future measurements. This work was published in Nature Communications. Conbining this approach with other machine learning techniques, we then developed a complete data-driven method for the characterization of quantum channels. Furthermore, we explored a multi-tasking approach to train neural networks for the characterization of complex quantum systems. This work was published in Nature Communications. Objective 2: Coherent stabilization of quantum channels. We started by developing a method to test the similarity between a given quantum process (e.g. a noisy communication channel) and a target process (e.g. a noiseless communication channel.) Our method is based on the AI-assisted characterization of quantum states and processes developed in Objective 1. It can be used for monitoring quantum channels in quantum communication networks, as well as a toolbox for benchmarking the performances of quantum computers. This work has been publised in Physical Review Letters. Next, we developed a new approach of "shadow simulation," which can be used to transform a noisy quantum channel into an ideal target channel with the assistance of classical communication and shared randomness. Using classical post-processing, this approach allows to transmit the "classical shadow" of quantum states, that is, the expectation values for arbitrary quantum observables. Quite surprisingly, we showed that an arbitrarily small amount of quantum communication can be used to simulate the transmission of large quantum systems, at the price, however, of an increased overhead in classical post-processing, or equivalently, of an increased sample complexity. This work was published in Physical Review Letters. In addition, we showed that noise in quantum communication networks can reduced by coherent quantum control, using a control system that can be initially entangled with the a system located at the sender's end. Using this approach, we demonstrated advantages in quantum communication, entanglement distribution, and classical communication. This work was published in Physical Review Research. We also showed that coherent quantum control over the direction in which a noisy channel is traversed can reduce the overall amount of noise, giving rise to a form of noise cancellation effect similar to dynamical decoupling. We collaborated with the group of Prof. Biheng Liu at USTC for the experimental demonstration of our protocols on a photonic platform. The work was published in Physical Review Letters. Finally, we developed an AI-assisted method for the mitigation of errors in noisy quantum channels. This work is under review in npj Quantum Information. Objective 3: quantum learning of quantum channels. In addition to the classical characterization techniques studied in Objective 1, we explored fully quantum ways to learn quantum processes. In particular, we developed a quantum autoencoder for compressing an unknown quantum process into smaller tokens. Our algorithm can be applied to tasks in quantum cloud computing, where a server has to execute a computation on quantum data provided by a client. To reduce the amount of quantum communication between the client and the server, our algorithm transforms the desired computation into a compressed version that acts on a smaller number of qubits, thereby reducing the amount of data exchanged between the client and the server. A bonus of our method is it does not reveal any information about the server's computation other than the information present in the output. This work has been published in Quantum Machine Intelligence. In a subsequent work, we studied the problem of storing quantum gates into the states of a quantum memory, and we determined the minimum amount of energy that has to be contained in the memory in order to enable the accurate execution of a target gate. Our result applies to quantum gates acting on generally infinite dimensional systems, and can be used to determine the ultimate energy efficiency of continuous variable quantum processors. This work has been published in Journal of Physics A. Finally, we explored a different way of storing quantum processes into quantum states, developing a notion of "quantum states over time" that encode the quantum correlations between the input and the output of a given quantum process. Our construction of quantum states over time is based on a notion of canonical quantum broadcasting, which we developed in our work and which can be implemented using quantum operations and classical postprocessing. This work has been published in Physical Review Letters.

17307520.label: Major findings and research outcome
17307520.value: We developed statistical methods for verifying the action of quantum channels, to estimate their communication capacity, and to determine their causal structure. These methods have been presented in three papers, published in Physical Review Letters, Physical Review Research, and npj Quantum Information. Alongside, we developed AI-assisted methods for the characterization and comparison of quantum states and processes, developing a new approach based on deep neural networks that autonomously build their own data-driven representation of quantum states. These works have been presented in two papers published in Nature Communications and a paper published in Physical Review Letters. A feature articles on our work were published in Nature Computational Science and NewScientist. We introduced a new task, called "shadow simulation of quantum processes," in which a given (noisy) process is used to simulate a target (noiseless) process, using classical communication and post-processing of measurement outcomes. Our method can mimick the transmission of quantum states for the purpose of estimating expectation values of arbitrary quantum observables. This work has been published in Physical Review Letters. We showed that coherent control over noisy quantum channels can be used to reduce, and in some cases cancel, the noise and to boost the performance of quantum communication. A theoretical paper on the power of quantum control over noisy channels was published in Physical Review Research, while an experimental demonstration of coherent control over two opposite directions of a quantum channel was published in Physical Review Letters. We introduced a new type of quantum states over time that encodes the correlations between the inputs and the outputs of unknown quantum processes. Our results evade the famous no-cloning theorem by allowing for virtual quantum operations, which can be simulated with classical randomness and post-processing at the price of an overhead in terms of the number of samples needed for the simulation. This work was published in Physical Review Letters and featured in Phys.org.

17307520.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17307520.value: Our project opened up a research direction on the development of AI systems for monitoring and controlling quantum channels. We are currently exploring the extension of our results to multipartite quantum processes, such as those arising in the dynamics of many-body quantum systems. The natural next step is to combine the use of classical AI systems with quantum neural networks, whose applications are however on a longer time scale. Integrating deep neural networks with quantum neural networks is likely to bring further performance enhancements, provided that the computational hardware used to implement the quantum neural networks is sufficiently accurate. A natural way to continue this research would be to have a follow up project on the power of quantum neural networks for quantum monitoring and control. We are currently developing the initial results that will provide the foundations to such a project. Another important direction of development is on fundamental research. In particular, the notions of quantum states over time and shadow simulation of quantum processes introduced in our project have a potentially strong impact on the study of causality in quantum mechanics, which we plan to explore in the context of an ongoing senior research fellowship of the PI.

17307520.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17307520.value: Quantum communication networks have the potential to increase the security of our communications, with applications ranging from internet commerce to secure website authentication and online data protection. To achieve these applications, it is crucial to guarantee that quantum communication links are stable and that random fluctuations can be quickly identified and corrected if necessary. Alongside, it is important to explore the foundations of how quantum systems can be monitored and controlled. This project developed powerful techniques to test quantum communication links and to control quantum systems in order to keep noise at bay. We designed quantum setups that achieve maximum statistical efficiency in characterizing quantum systems, and AI-assisted techniques that can make accurate predictions using a limited amount of noisy data, without any built-in knowledge of quantum physics. Our results contribute to the development of a new generation of fast and reliable quantum communication networks that are boosted by AI combined with quantum monitoring and control.

17307620.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17307620.value: Hyporheic zone (HZ), one of the key units of river corridor, is a region where streams and rivers continuously exchange water and solutes with the underlying sediment and porewater. Hyporheic exchange is characterized by complex flow processes between river and streambed sediments at nested scales ranging from ripples/dunes to pool-riffles/gravel bars to meanders. As the sediment river water interface is an assemblage of mineral particles, organic and biogenic material, and biological community, this zone is regarded as the hotspot of transformation of many environmentally, societally, and ecologically relevant chemicals e.g. carbon, nutrients and heavy metals. In the past decades, HZ research, which began as an empirical and descriptive science, has become a physically grounded and mechanistic science ascribing to advances in modeling complex fluid dynamics and biogeochemical transformation. Physical model have indicated that hyporheic flow is highly subject to geomorphological metrics such as sinuosity, slope and streambed topography, and sediment materials; biogeochemical models suggest reactions and fluxes are the functions of hydrodynamics i.e. water residence time, and also regulated by geomorphology metrics. However, the studies have been limited by several vital aspects: 1) these HZ models adopted an over-simplified conceptualization for the surface water domain, which is highly subject to turbulence; 2) there have been few validation and calibration from laboratory observations and even few from field observations. This proposal aims to address physical mechanism on how turbulence regulates the hyporheic exchange and biogeochemical cycling, from flume to field scale. Some of the cutting edge topics will be plumbed. Firstly, fully coupled model between surface water and HZ under the influence of turbulences will be constructed, and validated by velocity fields in both surface and subsurface domains. Secondly, parameterization of turbulence influences on hyporheic flow and solute transport will be explored based on flume observational data. Then, the turbulence parameterized regression model will be deployed in the constraints of hyporheic exchange and biogeochemical cycling in the field river hyporheic systems, taking segments of a highly regulated river system as examples. Finally, field scale hyporheic flow and biogeochemical reaction models will be constructed and validated by velocity field and spatiotemporal biogeochemical data from the hyporheic transect. The findings will greatly advance the understanding of diagenesis and structure evolution of turbulence, and their regulation on water, solute and reactant exchanges, and will provide fundamental theoretical and observational contribution to the studies of hyporheic flow and the mediated biogeochemical cycling. 潛流區是河岸帶中河溪水與其下覆沉積物和孔隙集中進行水量和溶質交換的關鍵區域。而潛流交換主要是表征為河溪水與下覆含水層之間耦合的複雜嵌套流動系統。其流動系統的尺度從小到大依次包括：河底波紋/沙丘尺度，水潭-波紋尺度，礫石梁尺度和河段蜿蜒尺度。作為一個賦存礦物顆粒、有機質和生源物質以及生物群落的集合體，潛流區被廣泛的認為是碳、氮和重金屬之間生物地球化學轉化的關鍵區域，進而有著重要的環境、生態和社會效應。在過去數十年中，得益于流體複雜動力學和生物地球化學量化的快速發展。潛流區的研究逐漸從經驗和描述性科學，逐漸演變為物理上自洽的機制性的學科。物理模型揭示潛流交互受地形參數諸如河流曲度，坡度和河底地形和沉積類型的高度影響。生物地球化學模型則揭示潛流區域反應和物源輸送同時受到水的滯留時間和地形參數的控制。但是目前潛流相關的研究還是有以下幾點局限：（1）前人研究都採用了太過簡化的地表水域的模型，沒有考慮到地表水的湍流效應；（2）前人的潛流動力模型並未經過室內潛流沙箱流場的驗證和校正，更鮮見野外潛流模型對其動力模型進行校驗。 本項目擬從室內沙箱尺度到潛流區的潛流交換和生物地球化學循環的調控的物理機制。一些前沿的潛流科學問題將被集中研究。第一、建立湍流驅動的全耦合地下水地表水模型，并用沙箱實測流場數據對模型進行校驗；第二、對潛流對於流場和溶質運移的影響進行參數化；第三、參數化的湍流驅動潛流回歸模型將用來刻畫真實河流潛流體系中的潛流交換和生物地球化學循環；最後建立野外尺度的潛流動力模型和生物地球化學模型，同時用野外斷面觀測的潛流流場和時空變化的生物地球化學實測資料對野外物理模型進行校驗。本研究將很大程度的促進湍流在潛流的發生和結構演化，以及對於水量、溶質和反應物交換的調控。此研究也將從理論基礎和野外觀測的尺度大大推進潛流交互及其調控的生物地球化學循環的研究。

17307620.label: Realisation of objectives
17307620.value: Objective 1 Significant progress has been achieved on this objective, with completion nearing approximately 100%. A small-scale laboratory flume has been successfully established to facilitate observations, and the EPIV system has been operationalized, consistently generating reliable data for both current and future related studies. Additionally, a comprehensive radon monitoring system has been implemented, capable of conducting continuous measurements of radon-222 in field settings. This system will support further investigations into the interactions between groundwater and surface water, enhancing the scope and depth of the research Objective 2 Progress on this subtask is nearly complete, reaching approximately 100%. Conceptual models for groundwater flow and transport in both porous and fractured media have been developed. Two key algorithms were created: one for hydrogeological parameter optimization (Ref. 5) and another for fracture distribution inversion (Ref. 6), providing a foundation for model validation. Theoretical modeling and parameterization have been finalized, with experimental validation now underway using the operational EPIV system. Objective 3 This subtask is approximately 100% complete. Pore-scale DNS modelling was conducted to examine laminar and turbulent flow impacts in fractured media. The relationship between fracture geometry and flow/transport regimes under both conditions was upscaled, with findings published in JGR-Solid Earth (Refs. 9 and 11 in research outputs). Objective 4 Extensive fieldwork was conducted across diverse scenarios, including groundwater sampling, in-situ monitoring, UAV mapping, and 222Rn measurements to assess groundwater discharge (Ref. 3 in research outputs). Satellite-based GRACE data was used to analyze basin-scale groundwater dynamics and storage, leading to models for estimating recharge rates (Ref. 10 in research outputs). Microbial monitoring in regulated aquifers revealed climate-driven impacts on biogeochemical cycling (Ref.7 in research outputs). Objective 5 Coupled groundwater-river water interaction models were developed, accounting for rainfall fluctuations. Groundwater flow dynamics exhibited fractal behavior, a finding published in Geophysical Research Letters (Ref. 2 in research outputs). Objective 6 This subtask focused on how groundwater-surface water interaction studies modulate biogeochemical cycling and processes from pore scale to on-site scales. Investigations included nutrient and tracer (222Rn and radium) analysis (Ref. 1 in research outputs), quantification of pathogen processes and nutrient cycling (Ref. 4 in research outputs), and pathogen dynamics in sand aquifers. Pathogen cycling was linked to 222Rn, with storm events accelerating pathogen export to surface waters (Ref. 8 in research outputs).

17307620.label: Major findings and research outcome
17307620.value: This proposal leverages pore-scale DNS numerical modeling, extensive field investigations, UAV and satellite platforms, and regional coupled groundwater-river water modeling to explore how turbulence, driven by intensive groundwater-surface water interactions, modulates biogeochemical cycling and solute reactive transport. Key findings include: (1) the emergence of fractal behaviors in groundwater and river water dynamics under fluctuating rainfall conditions; (2) the ability to predict and upscale pore-scale flow and transport regimes using fracture geometric parameters; (3) the effective use of UAV and satellite platforms to quantify groundwater-surface water interactions across varying spatiotemporal scales; (4) the utility of 222Rn as a robust tracer for assessing groundwater-surface water interactions and biogeochemical cycling; and (5) the development of novel AI algorithms that enhance parameterization and optimization in groundwater-surface water modeling across diverse spatial scales.

17307620.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17307620.value: Certain aspects and future directions can be outlined based on current findings. Moving forward, priority will be given to the development of more advanced EPIV systems to enable real-time, in-situ observations of flow regimes and velocity fields at pore and fracture scales. These high-resolution laboratory datasets will be instrumental in validating numerical models, thereby advancing our understanding of turbulent flow dynamics from the pore scale perspective. Furthermore, they will provide critical insights into how subtle changes in flow regimes influence biogeochemical cycling processes. Morever, fully coupled biogeochemical reactive transpport model will be advocated to established to delineate the hotspot of reactions at the interfaces.

17307620.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17307620.value: This proposal addresses a critical and complex question: how does turbulent flow influence subsurface fluid dynamics in terms of flow, transport, and biogeochemical cycling? As is well understood, turbulent surface flow typically transitions to laminar flow upon entering porous or fractured media in the subsurface. By resolving this issue, we can achieve a comprehensive coupling of surface water and groundwater/subsurface flow, which is essential for addressing a range of environmental, hydraulic, and biogeochemical challenges in real-world systems. This study has employed extensive landscape investigations, modeling, and pore-scale DNS simulations, yielding promising insights into the intrinsic properties of both groundwater and surface water systems. Additionally, the project has developed innovative predictive models that integrate isotopic and remote sensing approaches to estimate groundwater recharge and discharge, as well as advanced algorithms for modeling and parameterizing groundwater-surface water interactions. These contributions hold significant practical value for stakeholders and the academic community alike.

17307720.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17307720.value: Homomorphic encryption is a cryptosystem that can be used for privacy-preserving outsourced manipulation such as processing in commercial cloud environments or undergoing predictive data analysis. Its main feature is that the arithmetic operations on the ciphertext (encrypted data) can be passed to the plaintext (unencrypted data). In algebra, the object ring is endowed with the two arithmetic operations of addition and multiplication. The mapping from plaintext to ciphertext can then be viewed as a function on rings preserving (ring) addition and multiplication. Such a map is a ring homomorphism, accounting for the word "homomorphic''. The first cryptosystem of homomorphic encryption was firstly developed by Gentry in 2009 and now there has been a couple of generations. In this project we consider a novel approach using modular forms. The security of the system is based on the intractability of the problem of finding a common zero of modular forms from their Fourier coefficients. We shall carry out investigations for the construction of algorithm, testing, implementation and security problem. 同態加密是一種可以進行隱私保護外判操作的密碼系統，可以應用於商業雲中的訊息處理或預測性數據分析運算。它的主要特點是密文（加密數據）的計算可以傳輸至明文（未加密數據）。代數中環具有兩個運算: 加法和乘法。明文到密文的映射可以看作是環上保持（環）加法和乘法的映射，稱為同態映射。也就是這裏"同態"一詞的意思。 Gentry在2009年首先開發了第一代同態加密系統。至今有不斷發展。在這個項目中，我們考慮一種使用模形式的新穎同態加密法。這加密系統的安全性建基於使用模形式的傅立葉系數尋找模形式公共零點的難處理性。我們將對這加密法的算法構建，測試，實施和安全問題進行研究。

17307720.label: Realisation of objectives
17307720.value: Using asymptotics of Fourier coefficients and radii of convergence for the inverse of the function, based on observations in ``K. Bringmann, B. Kane, S. Löbrich, K. Ono, and L. Rolen, On divisors of modular forms, Adv. Math. 329 (2018), 541--554'', zeros of modular forms have been numerically identified via the Fourier expansions. This concluded the first objective, and a flaw in the original algorithm design was identified by doing so. Namely, if an adversary collects enough encryptions of the number zero, then they should be able to identify the point where evaluations are made. As a result of the issues identified in the completion of the first objective, the original algorithm was modified. Two different potential cryptographic algorithms were developed, completing the main objective (objective 2 of the grant proposal). The first system follows the initial encryption algorithm, but instead of encrypting a value by f(z)=x, we encrypt it as f(z)=x modulo L for some integral lattice L. If x is congruent to zero modulo L, then 1/f(z) does not have a pole (the inverse of f(z)-x has a pole, but x runs through different points in the lattice), so the identification of zeros via the radius of convergence does not reveal the point z. One would have to identify the common lattice that subtracting from gives the zeros. The second cryptographic algorithm involves principal parts of weakly holomorphic modular forms. Namely, instead of giving the full Fourier expansion, we only give the principal part of a weakly holomorphic modular form at one cusp, expanding at the cusp at infinity. The secret information in this cryptographic system would be the group and the cusp. The Fourier expansions can be computed by using the Fourier expansions of a basis of harmonic Maass forms. Regarding the completion of objective 3, in addition to creating basic prototype code to numerically check the original algorithm, which was eventually neglected due to the conclusions from objective 1, testing was conducted by an advanced undergraduate on both of the modified algorithms, leading to training of both computational methods and modular forms theory (giving partial completion of objective 4). Detection of the point from searching for shifts and/or trying to detect the lattice by taking preimages of the function both seemed to fail, indicating that the algorithm seems to be secure. Since congruences satisfy a ring homomorphism, this algorithm satisfies homomorphic encryption. For the second algorithm, there was no discernible attack on the algorithm that was constructed, so this algorithm appears to be secure as well; since no potential attack could be identified, there is some indication that this algorithm may possibly be more secure than the first algorithm. The products and sums of principal parts are also a homomorphism, so this algorithm also satisfies the necessary properties of homomorphic encryption. The undergraduate tested the algorithms for efficiency as well, with the first algorithm appearing to be more efficient than the second algorithm, due to the possible sizes of the principal parts for cryptographically large levels. Regarding objective 4, we had tried to admit suitable candidates, but due to the research postgraduate quota and the ineffectiveness of communication and exchange during the Covid period, this objective was eventually partially achieved, as described above.
