17614820.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17614820.value: Background: Hong Kong’s aging population will continue to accelerate in the coming few years. Taking care of older adults is necessary but not enough for an ageing society. Promoting volunteering with rewards is important for older adults as well as the soceity. However, there are two competing theoretical perspectives arguing about decision of volunteer behaviors among this population: social exchange theory and socio-emotionally selectivity theory. With these two contradictory perspectives, how the presence of rewards influences their volunteer behaviors among older population remains inconclusive. Furthermore, current research provided mixed evidence on the presence of rewards and volunteer behaviors and most exclusively focused on the presence of non-transferable individual rewards. However, the presence of transferable rewards which allow individuals to donate their rewards to other individuals or organizations is even more attractive to older people. No previous studies have attempted to investigate whether transferable rewards are more attractive and effective in promoting intention to continue volunteering among older people. Objectives: This study aimed to investigate the effect of a reward-based TimeBank program on promoting volunteering behaviors among older people. To be more specific, this study aimed to investigate: (1) whether the presence of rewards influences volunteering behaviors among older people, as predicted by the exchange theory; (2) Whether the effect of reward on volunteering behavior varies across ages among older people, as predicted by the socioemotional selectivity theory; (3) whether transferable rewards are more attractive and effective in promoting intention to continue volunteering among older people than non-transferable rewards; (4) how the perceived balance between benefits and efforts mediates the relationship between different types of rewards (none, non-transferable and transferable) and volunteer behaviors among older population. Methodology: This study proposed to use the multiple-pretests quasi-experimental design to test the effectiveness of time banking system on promoting volunteering. The quasi-experiment will last for 12 months (two phases and 6 months for each phase). Two districts will be selected as reward and non-reward districts. Participants in these two districts will be openly recruited to participate the a health ambassador volunteering project. Conclusion. This is the first study to test the relative contribution of social exchange theory, the socioemotionally slectivity theory on volutneering behavior of elderly and across age trajectory. This study will test the effectiveness of time banking system in the read-world and inform governments of intersectoral collaboration for scale-up implementation.

17614820.label: Realisation of objectives
17614820.value: This project utilized a quasi-experimental design involving 116 participants from the timebank group (TBG) and 114 participants from the comparison group (CG) between 2021 and 2022. The TBG participants received time credits that could be exchanged for rewards, while the CG participants did not receive any time credits and continued volunteering as usual. The timebanking intervention lasted for one year, during which volunteering behaviors were tracked using an app. Intentions to volunteer were assessed at three points: baseline (T0), after 6 months (midpoint of the intervention, T1), and after 12 months (endpoint of the intervention, T2). The usage of rewards by TBG participants, including personal use and sharing with others, was also recorded. Objective 1: whether the presence of rewards influences volunteering behaviors among older people, as predicted by the exchange theory; Controlling for covariates, the timebank group exhibited a significantly lower volunteer participation rate at T1 than the comparison group (interaction term between group condition and timepoints = -1.12, 95%CI: -2.18 to -0.05, p = 0.041). Conversely, the timebank group showed significantly larger effects in increasing weekly volunteer hours (AMD = 1.37, 95%CI: 0.20 to 2.54, p = 0.021) at T2 than the comparison group. Meanwhile, the timebank group showed significantly larger effects in increasing the level of volunteer intention at T1 (AMD = 0.55, 95%CI: 0.25 to 0.87, p < 0.001) and T2 (AMD = 0.52, 95%CI: 0.20 to 0.83, p = 0.001). Our results indicate that timebanking does not effectively enhance volunteer participation compared to the non-reward condition. Further analysis showed that the timebank group sustained a high volunteer participation rate over time, and participants were drawn to the HA program from other voluntary activities. Volunteer participation within the timebank group may already have been high, potentially leading to ceiling effects on volunteer participation. An alternative interpretation is that prompting individuals who have never previously volunteered (whether due to lack of interest or other reasons) to start volunteering, especially in the context of COVID-19 may be challenging. Nevertheless, our study suggests that timebanking attracted older adults, outperforming other volunteer programs, implying that while timebanking may not significantly increase the overall rate of volunteer participation, it could help sustain a high level of participation. More importantly, our findings found that timebanking increases volunteer hours and intentions compared to non-reward conditions, aligned with social exchange theory. Our qualitative findings revealed that the timebank group felt recognized for their contributions, which may balance the costs and benefits of volunteering, leading to increased volunteer engagement and future intentions. To sum up, this suggests that the presence of rewards influenced volunteer weekly hours and volunteer intention among older adults, thus achieving Objective 1. Objective 2: whether the effect of reward, if any, on volunteering behavior varies across ages among older people, as predicted by the socioemotional selectivity theory; To examine the effects of timebanking with rewards on volunteering behaviors across different age groups among older individuals, we categorized participants into three age groups: 50-59 (N=46), 60-69 (N=133), and 70 and above (N=51). These age groups represent individuals near retirement age, the young-old, and the middle-old to oldest-old, respectively. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore potential differences in the effects of timebanking rewards on volunteer behaviors across the age groups. We found no significant differences in volunteer participation and volunteer hours among the age groups. However, we observed that the effects of timebanking with rewards on volunteer intention were significant specifically among the 60-69 age group, with larger magnitudes compared to the effects observed in the overall sample. Further analysis revealed significant 3-way interaction terms (Condition X Time X Age) for volunteer intention, indicating that the impact of rewards on volunteer intention may be more relevant for individuals aged 60-69. One possible explanation for these findings is that individuals in the 50-59 age group may already have other engagement commitments, such as employment, which diminishes the influence of timebanking rewards on their volunteering behaviors. On the other hand, individuals aged 70 and above might prioritize close social relationships over external rewards, making the presence of rewards less attractive to them. In summary, the results suggest that using timebanking to promote volunteerism may be more effective among individuals aged 60-69 compared to other age groups. This finding aligns with objective 2 of the study, indicating that targeting the 60-69 age group may yield better outcomes in promoting volunteerism through timebanking. Objective 3: whether transferable rewards are more attractive and effective in promoting intention to continue volunteering among older people than non-transferable rewards; To investigate the attractiveness and effectiveness of transferable rewards compared to non-transferable rewards in promoting the intention to continue volunteering among older individuals, we categorized participants in the timebank groups based on their reward claim options. In the HINCare App, participants could choose their reward-sharing intentions when claiming rewards using time credits. Three options were provided: "self-use," "sharing with family/friends," and "donating to others," with participants able to select more than one option. We recoded the responses for each category for analysis. For instance, in the "self-use" category, a participant's response was coded as "1" if they chose "self-use" at least once and "0" if this option was not selected. Similar recoding processes were applied to the "rewards sharing with family/friends" and "donating to others" categories. Our findings indicate that participants who used rewards for personal purposes (non-transferable rewards) volunteered more at T2 (β = 2.09, p = 0.014). However, sharing rewards with family and friends or donating them to others (transferable rewards) did not have the same effect on volunteering behavior. The qualitative study component provided additional insights, revealing that a sense of recognition generated by timebanking could encourage increased volunteering, and the personal use of rewards enhanced the volunteer experience for participants. Participants who shared rewards with family and friends experienced a sense of fulfillment and reinforcement of their prosociality. Objective 4. how the perceived balance between benefits and efforts mediates the relationship between different types of rewards (none, non-transferable and transferable) and volunteer behaviors among the older population. To investigate the relationship between different types of rewards (none, non-transferable, and transferable) and volunteer behaviors among older adults, we developed a scale to measure the perceived balance between benefits and efforts. The research consisted of two stages. In Stage 1, we conducted activities to create the initial item pool for perceived benefits and costs of volunteering. This involved a comprehensive review of existing theories, in-depth focus group discussions, and the formation of an advisory group. The focus groups provided valuable insights, and the advisory group helped create a final set of 23 items for the Perceived Benefits and Costs (PBC) scale. In Stage 2, we administered the PBC scale to participants in both the timebank and control groups during a follow-up survey. We performed appropriate tests to confirm the suitability of the data for factor analysis and assessed the internal consistency and goodness of fit of the model. We then examined the mediating effects of perceived benefits and costs on the associations between the timebanking intervention and volunteer participation, weekly hours, and intention. However, no significant mediating effects were found. We also explored the mediating relationship between different types of rewards usage, but no significant mediating effects were observed.

17614820.label: Major findings and research outcome
17614820.value: Our research provides compelling evidence that timebanking, a reward-based system, effectively enhances volunteerism among older adults and strengthens intentions for sustained engagement. Notably, our study uncovered the significance of recognition as a key factor in timebanking's influence. Participants who personally utilized rewards reported enhanced fulfillment in their volunteer experience, while those who shared rewards with their family and friends experienced a sense of fulfillment and satisfaction. Interestingly, our findings suggest that timebanking may be particularly effective in promoting volunteerism among individuals aged 60-69, compared to other age groups. This insight underscores the importance of tailoring interventions to specific age demographics when implementing timebanking programs. Surprisingly, our study did not find significant mediating effects of perceived benefits and costs on the relationship between timebanking interventions and volunteer behaviors in later life. These results indicate that the impact of timebanking on volunteerism is not directly mediated by individuals' perceptions of the benefits and costs associated with volunteering. Instead, other factors, such as recognition and the personal and social enrichment derived from utilizing rewards, play a more prominent role in motivating older adults to engage in volunteer activities. Based on these findings, we strongly recommend that policymakers recognize timebanking as a social innovation with the potential to provide a supportive platform that empowers older adults to contribute meaningfully to society. With the workforce dwindling and the demand for long-term care services escalating, the need for such social innovations has become increasingly urgent. Based on the encouraging findings from this GRF project, the PI presented the research findings to various fields, promoted the concept of timebanking to professionals such as social workers, and facilitated the development and the scale up of the timebanking. Please see the research outcome in Part C.

17614820.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17614820.value: Built on this project, the PI applied for a research grant in the 2023/2024 ECS exercise to gain a deeper understanding of voluntary work design and the impact of the volunteer environment on engagement among older adults. The principles of timebanking discovered in this project played a crucial role in informing the development of the ECS, including its regulation. Simultaneously, the PI, along with other researchers and professionals, recognized the vast potential of timebanking. As the next step, PI aimed to investigate the key elements necessary for sustaining the development of timebanks in Hong Kong and beyond. Additionally, they planned to incorporate the fundamental principles of timebanking, such as recognizing everyone as an asset and promoting reciprocity, into community development efforts focused on healthy aging.

17615120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17615120.value: Background. Informal Social Control (ISC) constitutes efforts by neighbors, extended family members, friends, and private citizens acting outside of any formal responsibility they may have, to prevent crime. Protective ISC aims at protecting victims rather than punishing perpetrators. Extensive research by my team shows protective ISC is robustly associated with less child maltreatment and fewer abuse induced sequelae. However, many gaps in the literature remain with respect to adolescent substance abuse/dependence and early sexual debut, high risk parents with ‘dark tetrad’ personality symptoms, and the explanatory mechanism for protective effects. Objectives. The study aims to resolve two theoretical problems by examining whether empathy, as measured by maternal empathy and adolescent self-compassion, explains the effects of protective informal social control. (1) The study replicates cross-sectional findings of an association between child maltreatment and ISC using panel data. (2) It investigates whether the mother’s capacity for empathy affects (moderates) the relationship between protective ISC and maltreatment. My hypothesis is that bystanders’ non-punitive actions to protect the child may model concern for both mother and child. Hence, protective ISC may temporarily stimulate maternal empathy for the child and cause desistance, but this will hold only for mothers with high empathy capacity. (3) The study examines whether protective effects hold for adolescents whose mothers have high risk ‘dark tetrad’ (low empathy) personality symptoms. (4) It tests whether protective ISC ameliorates maltreatment induced substance abuse/dependence and early sexual debut among adolescents. (5) Further, the study tests whether protective ISC weakens the maltreatment-substance abuse/dependence relationship via an increase in adolescent self-compassion (mediated moderation). (6) Finally, it produces for the first time national prevalence estimates for neglect and adolescent substance abuse/dependence in Nepal. Methods. During this 3 year study, a two-wave panel (longitudinal) sample of 1,100 Nepali mothers and youth (Aged 13-15 in Year 1 and 15-17 in Year 3) will be obtained from a random stratified probability proportional to size 3-stage cluster sample of Nepal households. Survey measures will be used to ask both mothers and youth about experiences of child maltreatment, substance use and abuse/dependence, early sexual debut, and informal social control of child maltreatment in year 1 and at the 24 month follow up. Impacts. The goal of this study is to inform the development of interventions and policies that prevent injury, disability, and death from maltreatment, addiction, and disease. Findings may also challenge the rational choice paradigm in criminology. 題目: 虐待兒童的保護型非形式化社會控制, 青少年健康行為及同理心: 尼泊爾母親及青少年的全國代表性兩期縱向研究 摘要 背景: 非形式化社會控制(ISC)是指由鄰居、大家庭成員、朋友及普通公民在他們可能承擔的任何形式化責任之外採取的行動，以防止犯罪。保護型非形式化社會控制的動機在於保護受害者，而不是懲罰施暴者。本研究顯示出保護型非形式化社會控制與減少虐待兒童相關。研究亦顯示當虐待事件出現時，保護型非形式化社會控制與對兒童有較好的影響是相關的。然而，我們對於保護型非形式化社會控制，仍是有很多不認識的地方。保護型非形式化社會控制是否能防止青年濫用物質? 更重要的是，保護型非形式化社會控制為何能發揮效用。 目的: (1)研究以縱向研究方式重新檢視保護型非形式化社會控制與虐待兒童的關係。(2)研究嘗試以兩種方式去回答一個理論性問題 - 「為何保護型非形式化社會控制能發揮效用?」。首先，本研究量度母親的同理心。我們假設母親的同理心或許是保護型非形式化社會控制中減少虐待兒童的重要條件。此外，本研究量度青少年對自己產生同理心的能力，我們假設這能力或許是讓保護型非形式化社會控制，能中斷虐待兒童與青年濫用物質之間關係的必要條件。具體來說，當旁觀者嘗試介入去保護兒童，此舉或可幫助施虐的母親由懲罰的心態轉移以同情的反應去面對憂慮的心態。然而，由於此情況或許只適用於有高同情心能力的母親，因此，我們去測試這個假設。同樣地，青少年對自身的同理心或許是保護型非形式化社會控制，可中斷兒童虐待與青年濫用物質之間關係的重要條件。(3)我們測試在母親是低同理心及有人格障礙徵狀的情況下，保護型非形式化社會控制能否起作用。(4)我們測試保護型非形式化社會控制是否與減低青年物質誤用和較早出現性行為有關。(5)我們測試保護型非形式化社會控制是否會因為青少年對自身的同理心而打破(4)所提及的關係。(6)這是我們第一次得到在尼泊爾，疏忽照顧及青年濫用物質的全國普遍性估計。 方法: 兩期的縱向研究樣本中，共有1,100名母親及青少年(第一年的青年年齡在13至15歲之間，第三年則在15至17歲之間)。隨機分層概率與三級整群抽樣樣本的大小成比例。母親與青年分別有不同的問卷。 影響: 對有關防止虐待及成癮所導致的傷害和死亡的政策，提供資訊。發展出新的理論解釋保護型非形式化社會控制為何能發揮效用。

17615220.label: Realisation of objectives
17615220.value: For this project, I have collected about fifty Catholic biblical texts in Chinese from the late Ming period to the late Qing period, roughly between the late 16th century and the early 20th century. I also build a database that includes digital versions of the major texts in this group. They form the core of my research by outlining a general picture of Chinese Catholic biblical literature over a period of three centuries. During my visits to the libraries and archives in the U.K, Russia, and Mainland China, I discovered a handful of rarely seen biblical manuscripts that have received little attention in previous scholarship. These manuscripts include for example a beautifully transcribed copy of Louis de Poirot’s Chinese translation of the Gospel of Matthew, now in the collection of the National Library of Russia. The copy was made by the Orthodox missionary Archimandrite Peter (Kamensky) in Beijing in the 1820s and later sent to St. Petersburg together with Kamensky’s other copies of Poirot’s Manchu translations of the Bible. I highlight this new finding in a recent article tracing the complex distribution network of the extant copies of Poirot’s biblical translations in both Manchu and Chinese. The findings in my research help me achieve a comprehensive understanding of Catholic Bible translations and biblical literature in late imperial China. When reading and examining the key biblical texts, I provide solid evidence to prove my view on the parallel development of two trends, one visible (i.e., authorized printed works with the imprimatur) and the other invisible (i.e., unauthorized manuscripts and hand-written copies), from the late Ming to the late Qing periods. The analysis of numerous examples also points to the distinctive pattern of transwriting Catholic scriptures into Chinese by the missionary translators (especially the Jesuits) in China. They took a practical approach due to the restrictions in Bible translations under the Roman Church, and at the same time, suppression of Christianity under the Qing regime. On the other hand, the transwriting pattern was clearly aligned with the mission strategy of adaptation, by which the missionaries took advantage of flexible interpretations to integrate Catholic doctrines with Chinese traditions, so as to realize better evangelical results. These main arguments are addressed both in the works that I have published and in the book manuscript that I am currently writing. Despite the interruptions in the Covid 19 pandemic, I published a series of articles in journals and edited volumes. I also actively participated in conferences, either virtual or in-person, and engaged exchanges with scholars in the field. My studies attract much attention, and they reveal the multiformity and complexity of biblical translations in late imperial China. I feel confident that my discussions on some underexplored topics, such as the mirror effects in Poirot’s Manchu and Chinese translations, the overlappings between Catholic and Protestant biblical translations, and the conjunction of marginal biblical literature and mainstream Chinese literature, will shed new lights on studies of the Bible and biblical literature in late imperial China. After the pandemic, I was invited to give public lectures in several universities in Mainland China. Non-academic people, including Catholic believers and officials in charge of religious affairs, joined the events. The lectures enriched their knowledge of the history of the Bible in China, and they could also correct the stereotyped misunderstanding that Chinese translations of the Bible only started with Protestant missionaries in the early 19th century. In addition, I invited visiting scholars to give public lectures, and I organized conference panels with other scholars to present up-to-date research on Chinese Bible translations in the 19th century. The research outputs reach a wider audience through my recent publication of an edited volume on translations and publications of Western books in Hong Kong and Shanghai in the modern era.

17615220.label: Major findings and research outcome
17615220.value: The major findings of my project include: (1) The parallel development of two trends among Catholic biblical texts; (2) The pattern of transwriting in early Catholic Bible translations; (3) The overlappings of Catholic and Protestant Chinese Bible translations; (3) The conjunction of Catholic biblical texts and Ming-Qing classical/vernacular literature. In Part C, I list three journal articles (two published and one forthcoming in 2025, all by high-ranking journals), three book chapters in edited volumes, seven presentations in international conferences, and four invited lectures in Mainland universities. The above major findings can be seen in these recent research outputs.

17615220.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17615220.value: I find Catholic images side by side with or embedded in biblical texts particularly interesting. These images were certainly intended for the evangelical purpose. The more frequent use of these images to facilitate biblical reading reached a peak in the late 19th century, a period when traditional Chinese woodblock printing was gradually replaced by advanced Western printing technologies (lithography, collotype, etc.). The role of Catholic images in modern biblical texts—whether in the original Western form or in a localized Chinese form—should be one key aspect for further exploration along with the writing of the rest parts of my book manuscript.

17615220.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17615220.value: This project tells the story of the Bible in China through a period of three centuries. It gives special attention to the efforts of Catholic missionaries in translating a number of biblical texts into Chinese, which predated the more noticeable Protestant Bible translations in the 19th century. In these early Catholic biblical texts, one may see the dynamic exchanges of religious and cultural traditions between China and Europe in the pre-modern era. Research on this subject will refresh people’s understanding of such Catholic heritage and its impacts on modern Chinese biblical literature.

17615920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17615920.value: Online encyclopedias such as Wikipedia have changed the way millions of people share and access knowledge across the world. While recent research in the emerging field of information commons has focused on the general platform design and the behaviors of individual users, a significant share of articles on these platforms are actually created by users who band together in small groups to create articles on a particular area of knowledge. How these users work together is a question about collective action and institutions. But as Schweik (2017) observes, “the governance and institutional design of open source commons is one of the least studied areas” (p. 265). This is not just a theoretical challenge; an informed understanding of these self-governing rules has policy implications for the practical task of designing and managing information commons. Our research question concerns how user groups in Wikipedia or Baidu Baike – two of the world’s largest online encyclopedias - come up with rules that help coordinate work within the group, and whether the rules they create improve the quality of their outputs. Apart from taking objective measures of rule effectiveness using publicly available data on both platforms, my team will conduct field interviews and participant observation with user groups based in Hong Kong, Taipei, and Shanghai to find out about the users’ own perception of rule effectiveness. At the end, we will bridge the two sets of findings by discussing how user perception and objective estimates of rule effectiveness may differ or converge. Theoretical insights from this comparison will help develop a “culturally informed” understanding of rule effectiveness in information commons, which in turn can be translated into lessons of practical value to users and platform designers. This project is built upon the PI’s long-term research program about the relationship between information and collective action in a variety of organizational settings and the team’s overall expertise in digital governance in the Greater China area. More specific to commons research, our study will bring practical insights into group-level collective action for developers of open source platforms. In the longer run, we see our work as part of the larger movement to prepare for a new economy fueled by new technologies for public value generation through crowdsourcing and “commoning”. 在線百科全書改變了人類獲得知識的方法。除了個體用戶的獨自貢獻外，不少用戶在這些平台上建立群組，並通過合作生產了大量優質文章。我們嘗試利用集體行動和制度分析理論去了解這些用戶群組的成員如何合作和互相協調。我們的實證研究工作涉及世界上最大的兩個在線百科全書--中文維基百科和百度百科，主要針對用戶群組如何選擇有助於協調組內工作的規則，以及他們挑選的組內制度有否提高作品質量。除了使用平台數據進行定量分析外，我的團隊還將到香港，台北和上海進行訪談和參與觀察，以了解用戶對組內制度的主觀看法。我們的研究結果可望為數字治理中一些重大而複雜的問題提供新的理論見解。

17616020.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17616020.value: In recent years, there has been a considerable amount of buzz concerning the use of gamification across various academic disciplines and industries. It has been proposed that gamified practices can play a key role in motivating people to engage with certain tasks such as improving their fitness, generating brand loyalty, or answering other people’s questions. Yet, despite the interest in gamification as an intriguing new approach to motivate individuals, evidence of its ability to increase student motivation and learning is mixed. Gamification has also received many controversial comments, such as “exploitationware, and “pointsfication”. Several researchers have argued that gamification itself does not guarantee effectiveness of learning; rather it is how gamification is implemented that determines its outcome. To ensure a greater likelihood of creating successful gamification designs, it is essential for designers to first understand the main factors affecting people’s motivation. In many prior gamification research, theory was largely neglected, and the empirical research lacked reference to theory (Sanchez, Langer, & Kaur, 2020; Seaborn & Fels, 2015). In our preliminary works, we formulated a theory-grounded framework to guide the implementation of gamification in higher education blended courses. This framework, consisting of five motivational elements: Goal-Autonomy-Feedback-Challenge-Collaboration (or GAFCC), was formulated based on several prominent theories of motivation, including goal setting theory, self-determination theory, flow theory, social comparison theory, and operant conditioning theory. Each motivational element is carefully matched to relevant game mechanics, such as trophy, leaderboards. Preliminary findings showed that gamified courses implemented using the GAFCC motivational elements demonstrated higher student completion rate of pre-class and post-class tasks, as well as higher student test scores than the non-gamified courses. Despite these encouraging findings, we observed that the effects of gamification can differ among different students. Building on these promising preliminary findings, we now propose to comprehensively investigate the mechanism of how GAFCC affects learners. This proposed study has three specific objectives. Objective 1 aims to provide in-depth qualitative insights on how different students may respond to each GAFCC motivational element, and its corresponding game elements. Objective 2 aims to propose some general design guidelines drawn from the qualitative insights. Objective 3 aims to empirically evaluate the effectiveness of the design guidelines using a design-based research approach on student participation and performance in online learning activities. In design-based research, theories and interventions evolve over time through multiple iterations of implementation, testing, and refinement. 近年來，關於在學術領域和各種行業中使用遊戲化的討論越來越多。有人提出，遊戲化在激勵人們完成某些任務方面可以發揮關鍵作用，例如，進行健康鍛煉，形成品牌忠誠度，或者積極回答其他人的問題。然而，儘管人們對游戲化很感興趣，並將其視爲一種用來提升人們動機的頗具吸引力的新方法。游戲化在增强學生的學習動機與能力方面的證據結果并不一致。遊戲化也收到了許多有爭議的評論，例如“利用工具”或者“記分機器”。 有部分研究人員提出，遊戲化本身並不能保證學習的有效。與之相反，遊戲化的實施方式才是影響其結果的關鍵原因。爲了確保游戲化設計取得成功的可能性更大，設計者們必須首先了解影響人們動機的主要因素。然而，在之前的許多研究中，動機理論常常被忽略了，很多實證研究未能參考相應的理論依據（Sanchez, Langer, & Kaur, 2020; Seaborn & Fels, 2015）。在我們初期的研究中，我們創建了一個基於理論的游戲化設計框架來指導高等教育混合課程中游戲化的設計。該框架由五個動機要素組成：目標—自主—反饋—挑戰——協作（或GAFCC）。它是基於幾種著名的動機理論而製定，這些理論包括目標設定理論（goal-setting theory），自決理論（self-determination theory），流動理論（flow theory），社會比較理論（social comparation theory），和操作制約理論（operant conditioning theory）。其中，每個動機要素都與相應的游戲化機制（例如獎杯，排行榜）進行仔細配對。初步研究結果表明，應用了GAFCC動機因素的遊戲化課程與沒有使用遊戲化的課程相比，學生的課前和課後任務完成率會更高，學生的測試成績也會更高。儘管有這些令人鼓舞的發現，但我們觀察到遊戲化對於不同的學生效果可能會有所不同。基於這些積極的初步發現，我們提出對GAFCC如何影響學習者的相關機制展開更加全面的研究。這項研究具有三個具體目標。目標一旨在對不同學生在面對GAFCC中不同的動機要素及其相應的游戲化機制時的反應提出深入的質化見解。目標二旨在依據質化見解提出相應的游戲化設計原則。目標三旨在運用教育設計研究方法對游戲化設計原則進行評估，並觀察此設計原則對學生在線學習活動中的參與和表現方面的影響。在教育設計研究中， 理論和干預的措施會在多次的實施、測試、和改進中不斷進化完善。

17616020.label: Realisation of objectives
17616020.value: Finding reliable research staff had been a challenge. Additionally, due to covid travel restrictions, I was unable to physically travel to overseas conferences. Despite these challenges, the project team was able to fully achieve the original project objectives. Specifically, the following items were realised. (1) We tested the theory-driven GAFCC (Goal, Autonomy, Feedback, Challenge, Collaboration) framework in developing gamified courses using the design-based research methodology. Overall, although a majority of students preferred the use of GAFCC-gamified courses to non-gamified courses, more than half of them gradually lost interest when the semester progressed. Students perceived a high level of engagement during the first half of the semester, especially for students who had their first taste of gamification. But when they became familiar with the gamification scheme, they gradually lost interest and participated less in the online activities. Results showed that the number of student forum posts and online quiz attempts decreased sharply after midway through the course. In other words, students became less motivated with the gamification elements as time went on. (2) We successfully improved the GAFCC framework by incorporating the gamification element of fantasy to yield an enhanced theory-driven framework – GAFCC-F (Goal, Autonomy, Feedback, Challenge, Collaboration, Fantasy). We tested the effectiveness of the enhanced GAFCC-F gamification framework on students’ learning performance, students' interaction in online discussion forums, and students' perceptions by comparing these outcomes to those of the original GAFCC framework. Please see "section 6. Research Outcome" for details. (3) To further understand the effects of fantasy, we compared the impact of two types of fantasy (exogenous fantasy versus endogenous fantasy) on student intrinsic motivation and course engagement in a fully online class. Students immersed in endogenous fantasy enjoyed doing the learning tasks significantly more than students using exogenous fantasy. (4) We identified several challenges that participants face when using gamification. Although badges and fantasy appear to promote student motivation and participation, the use of leader board did not always have the expected effect. Furthermore, not all students value the intangible rewards (e.g., gamification points) that do not contain any utilitarian benefit outside the gamified system. Students also became less motivated in the gamification elements as time went on. (5) Therefore, in order to further understand and address the challenge of using leader boards, we conducted further research on how positions on different leader boards may affect online student learning performance, intrinsic motivation, and course engagement. We specifically examined three different positions (top third, middle third, bottom third) in two different types of leader boards (absolute leader board versus relative leader board). An absolute leaderboard displays the literal positions of all users and is frequently employed in educational settings, while users in a relative leaderboard can only see their positions relative to neighbours below and above them. See "Research Outcome" for details. (6) To further understand and address the challenge of student lack of motivation, we conducted three studies. First, we compared the effects of intangible rewards versus tangible rewards on students' intrinsic motivation, behavioral engagement, cognitive engagement and learning performance. Second, we conducted an in-depth meta-analysis and systematic review to determine the overall effects of gamification on student intrinsic motivation and student basic psychological needs (competence, autonomy, relatedness). We further explored the specific challenges encountered in using gamification to enhance intrinsic motivation. Third, we developed a gamified course based on goal-setting theory and evaluated its effect on the quantity and quality of students’ online in-class participation. The results showed that gamification designed by goal-setting principles was effective in encouraging students to speak up more than students in an online synchronous class that received only grade incentives. (7) Overall, we propose the following design guidelines for the future implementation of gamification: (a) Use the GAFCC-F framework instead of the original GAFCC framework since the former is more effective in improving the students’ learning performance, enhancing online social interaction with peers across different study groups, and providing a joyful learning experience. (b) Use endogenous fantasy rather than exogenous fantasy to further increase student engagement, and intrinsic motivation. (c) Link tangible rewards to a standard of performance. (d) Set a specific and moderately challenging redemption goal. (e) Set personalised rewards and give students the autonomy to redeem. (f) Consider publicly releasing only the information of the top five students, instead of everyone, in an absolute leader board to mitigate possible of unhappiness among the bottom-ranked participants. (g) Consider using an absolute leader board and then reset all students’ points to 0 fortnightly to level the playing field. By doing so, students who ranked low on the absolute leader board are given the chance to perform better in the next run. (h) Consider using an absolute leader board and a relative leader board alternatively in a semester. 17616020.label: Major findings and research outcome
17616020.value: Although a majority of students preferred the use of GAFCC-gamified-courses to non-gamified-courses, students became less motivated with the gamification elements as time progressed. We incorporated the fantasy gamification element to yield an enhanced theory-driven framework – GAFCC-F(Fantasy). (a) Participants using GAFCC-F showed significantly better learning performance than the GAFCC. (b) Participants using GAFCC-F showed higher levels of thinking in their online posts than GAFCC. (c) Participants using GAFCC-F displayed more elaboration, reflection, and evaluation in their online comments than GAFCC. (d) Participants using GAFCC-F engaged in more online discussions with peers than those using GAFCC. Additionally, we found that endogenous fantasy significantly improves student intrinsic motivation and course engagement than exogenous fantasy. [Findings published in the International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, proceedings of the International Conference on Information Technology Based Higher Education and Training] Although badges and fantasy appear to promote student motivation and participation, the use of leader board did not always have the desired effect. Specifically, the bottom-ranked students struggled under the pressure of being identified and losing face. Furthermore, not all students value the use of intangible rewards (e.g., gamification points or badges) that do not contain any utilitarian benefit outside the gamified system. Students also became less motivated in the gamification elements as time progressed. The absolute leaderboard intensifies students’ sense of comparison and competitiveness more than the relative leader board. Students at different positions in the absolute leaderboard showed similar levels of learning performance and course engagement, but a higher position was associated with higher intrinsic motivation. Students ranked in the top third position of the relative leaderboard display better learning performance than their peers in the lower two thirds did. Students who ranked in different positions showed similar levels of course engagement and intrinsic motivation for learning. [Finding published in Computers & Education] Tangible rewards are more effective in increasing students' intrinsic motivation, encouraging students to complete class tasks and improving their exam performance. Through a meta-analysis, we found gamification overall enhances student intrinsic motivation, perceptions of autonomy and relatedness, but has minimal impact on competency. Two specific challenges encountered when using gamification to increase students’ intrinsic motivation include students’ lack of perceived competence and lack of perceived autonomy in gamified classes. [Findings published in the proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Engineering, Technology & Education, British Journal of Educational Technology, Educational Technology Research and Development]

17616020.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17616020.value: Most current gamified instructional designs use a ‘one-size-fits-all’ (OSFA) approach that assumes that users are a homogenous group, reacting similarly to game design elements. The OSFA approach is unlikely to optimise the effects of gamification over a long period of time since each user has different expectations and needs. Students’ individual differences have long been recognised as being of fundamental significance. Previous reviews on gamification have theorised that individual differences can be an important moderator in gamification’s effectiveness to improve learners’ engagement. Many empirical studies have reported that individual differences (e.g., gender, personality) significantly influenced students’ perceptions of gamification. Hence, engagement in gamified learning can differ from one student to another. Against this backdrop, I plan to further develop my research by conducting an in-depth investigation on the use of personalised gamification which takes the differences between learners into account. First, I plan to develop a validated and reliable instrument to measure various player types. This instrument will address the conceptual overlaps that currently plague existing instruments. Second, I plan to carry out field experiments to compare the use of personalized gamification and OSFA gamification on student motivational, behavioral, and cognitive outcomes.

17616020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17616020.value: This project examines the effects of the goal-access-feedback-challenge-collaboration (GAFCC) gamification framework on students' outcomes such as learning performance, and course engagement. Although a majority of students preferred the use of GAFCC-gamified-courses to non-gamified-courses, students became less engaged with the course activities as time progressed. We incorporated the fantasy gamification element to produce an enhanced theory-driven framework: GAFCC-F(Fantasy). We found that participants using GAFCC-F showed significantly better learning performance, displayed more elaboration, reflection, and evaluation in their online comments, and engaged in more online discussions with peers than those using GAFCC. Additionally, we found that endogenous fantasy significantly improves student intrinsic motivation and course engagement than exogenous fantasy. We also found that the absolute leaderboard intensifies students’ sense of comparison and competitiveness more than the relative leader board. Design guidelines for future implementation of gamification include: use GAFCC-F instead of the original GAFCC framework, use endogenous rather than exogenous fantasy to further increase student engagement, and intrinsic motivation, link tangible rewards to a standard of performance, set a specific and moderately challenging redemption goal, release only the information of the top five students in an absolute leaderboard, and use an absolute leaderboard and a relative leaderboard alternatively in a semester.

17616820.label: Project Objectives
17616820.value: Empirically, to map the circulations, encounters and processes by which religious individuals, networks and organizations associated with the following religious and spiritual traditions from China, other parts of Asia (India, Japan, Iran) and the West connected with each other and with secular movements around cosmopolitan ideals: (1) Confucian reformers; (2) liberal Christians; (3) Buddhist reformers; (4) redemptive societies; (5) Baha’is and Theosophists. Analytically, to unpack the content of cosmopolitan discourses within these networks and circulations, interrogating the different meanings of cosmopolitanism as promoted by various actors, how they emerged out of different intellectual, religious or political traditions, how their interconnections led to new formulations and interpretations, and their interface with social, religious and political transformations. Theoretically, to contribute to the sociological theory of cosmopolitanism: building a typology of different forms of religious cosmopolitanism; identifying and characterizing “religious cosmopolitan activists” who explicitly promote religious cosmopolitan utopias or ideals; developing conceptual tools for outlining parallel and intertwining histories of cosmopolitanism; understanding the historical conditions for the appearance of “cosmopolitan moments” and cosmopolitan networks at specific periods in space and time; analyzing the role of colonial modernity in creating the conditions for the emergence of both nationalism and cosmopolitanism.

17616820.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17616820.value: In the late Qing and early Republican periods, various cosmopolitan ideals were widely and continuously discussed and advocated in China. The ancient Chinese idea of Datong 大同 or Great Unity was revived and debated with renewed vigour and reference to the changes of the times, often incorporating the cosmopolitan ideals of religious, social and ideological movements from the West and elsewhere in Asia. Among the chief promoters were Late Qing Confucian reformers, liberal Christian missionaries, Chinese students abroad and intellectuals of the New Culture movement, and many groups including anarchists, Esperantists, Bahá’ís, Theosophists and redemptive society activists. This is a story that overlaps with, at times converges with and at times diverges from the rise of nationalism. Until now, there has been little research on the religious strands of this cosmopolitan wave. Our project aims to trace the networks, practices and social ideas of religious cosmopolitanism, in the period of transition between the end of the first Sino-Japanese war (1895) and the establishment of the Kuomintang regime in Nanjing (1927). Empirically, it will map the encounters and processes by which religious individuals, networks and organizations from China, other parts of Asia (India, Japan, Iran) and the West connected into an effervescent wave of transnational movements around the notion of Datong and related cosmopolitan ideals. Analytically, it will unpack the content of cosmopolitan discourses within these networks and circulations, interrogating the different meanings of cosmopolitanism as promoted by various actors, and their interface with social, religious and political transformations. Theoretically, the project will contribute to the sociological theory of cosmopolitanism, building conceptual tools for outlining parallel and intertwining histories of cosmopolitanism. Using these empirical, analytical and theoretical tools, the project will explain the reasons for the rise and decline of the influence of religious cosmopolitan ideals during the period of the study. With its Chinese, transnational, religious and historical focus, this case will help to correct the primarily Western-centred and purely secular narratives and theories of cosmopolitanism that lack historical depth and continue to influence much academic and public debate. 清末民初，各種世界主義理想在中國盛行，引發了社會廣泛而持久的討論。在動蕩的時代背景之下，人們重提中國傳統的「大同」思想，並賦予其新的活力——這一進程受到西方與亞洲各地的政治、社會與意識形態運動影響，並從中吸納了世界主義的理想。在當時，提倡世界主義的團體有許多：晚清的改革派儒生、自由派基督教傳教士、中國的海外留學生和新文化運動中的知識份子等。此外，許多無政府主義者、世界語者、巴哈伊信徒、證道學人、救世團體成員等也加入了宣揚世界主義的行列。這一思潮與中國民族主義的興起有諸多重合之處，二者時而趨同，時而相悖。然而，關於這一思潮中的宗教部分，現有的研究很少。本項目旨在追溯甲午戰爭（1895）至南京國民政府成立（1927）的這段社會轉型期間，與宗教世界主義有關的社會網絡、實踐與觀念。從實證的角度，本項目將展示中國、亞洲其他地區（例如印度、日本、伊朗）及西方的宗教人士、關係網絡和宗教組織如何相互接觸、聯結、共同構成一場活躍的跨國運動潮流，而這一潮流的核心正是「大同」思想及與之相關的世界主義理想。從分析的角度，本項目將深入剖析這些網絡與交流之中的世界主義話語，藉此審視「世界主義」在不同提倡者處的意涵，以及它們與社會、宗教與政治轉型之間的關聯。從理論的角度，本項目將對時下社會學中的世界主義理論進行補充，並為厘清這一概念錯綜複雜的歷史提供理論工具。基於以上三個角度，本項目將對1895-1927年間宗教世界主義的社會影響之興衰進行解釋。由於本項目著眼於中國，研究對象為跨國運動，且採取宗教學、歷史學的視角，因而這一案例有助於修正目前植根於西方中心主義與世俗化的世界主義敘事與理論，為之增添歷史的厚度，以期引起學界與公眾的討論。此外，本項目還有助於進一步質疑現代中國以世俗民族主義為核心的主流話語，彰顯其背後的複雜性。

17616920.label: Project Title(Chinese)
17616920.value: 香港自由化：港英時期言論自由與法治的覺醒 （1978-1997）

17616920.label: Project Objectives
17616920.value: Drawing upon newly released archival materials, this projects constitutes the first empirical and critical study of the historical processes by which Hong Kong society evolved from a colony of gelded freedoms and rule of law to a city whose freedoms and rule of law are highly praised globally today. The project seeks answer to this research question: How and why were such authoritarian law and political censorship practice phased out, and liberal notions of the rule of law and freedom of speech awakened, as a pressing political agenda in the final decades of colonial rule? The proposed study aims to verify the hypothesis that the free press, freedom of speech, judicial independence and rule of law that so many people in Hong Kong are eager to preserve today are, instead of a colonial legacy, more a legacy of the British decolonisation process that began in Hong Kong in the late 1980s as colonialism attempted to erect a kinder façade. The study will further seek archival evidence to verify the hypothesis that the rule of law in colonial Hong Kong was not so much informed by much-vaunted common-law values and doctrines as it was a legacy of the geopolitical power equation among China, Britain, the US, and their allies and enemies in various periods of history. It will also raise the provocative question of whether the colonial government would ever have granted the rule of law and freedoms so valued by the people of Hong Kong today if no agreement had been struck to decolonise Hong Kong and return it to China. Drawing upon the findings of both the proposed project and previous project, this project will result in the publication of a single-authored research monograph on the history of freedoms and rule of law in British Hong Kong (1842-1997), as well as articles in high-quality peer-reviewed journals, and the preparation of teaching materials in both Chinese and English on the historical development of the legal system and rule of law in Hong Kong for the secondary-school liberal studies curriculum. The scholarly contribution of the proposed project is twofold. First, it promises to provide an important corrective to conventional narratives on the legal development of Hong Kong by situating them in the broader historical context connecting Hong Kong, China and the British Far East. It constitutes the first archive-based study of the history of freedom and the law in this important former colony in the Far East, and will contribute to the emerging body of scholarship on the global and comparative study of law and colonialism. Its significance also lies in the richness of the unexplored archival data stored in Hong Kong, the UK, the US, mainland China and elsewhere, of which the project will make ample use.

17616920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17616920.value: The proposed legal history project is a follow-up to the PI’s previous GRF-funded project: “Freedom of Expression, Media Censorship and the Rule of Law in British Hong Kong (1850s-1980s)”. That project revealed how different types of media were monitored, politically censored and prosecuted throughout most of Hong Kong’s colonial era (1850s-1980s). Based on its findings, I contend that the common-law system practised in British Hong Kong until the 1980s was more interested in preserving the British Empire’s overseas territorial and economic possessions and managing the regional power equation than in safeguarding individual liberties in Hong Kong. There remains a critical research question to be answered: How and why were such authoritarian law and political censorship practice phased out, and liberal notions of the rule of law and freedom of speech awakened, as a pressing political agenda in the final decades of colonial rule? Answers to that question will be sought by drawing upon newly released archival materials to examine the trajectory of the renewed consciousness of the rule of law and various freedoms in the final two decades of colonial rule and unpack the geopolitical concerns and motivations of the British government in de-silencing and liberating Hong Kong before the handover in 1997. The proposed project is grounded in the hypothesis that the free press, freedom of speech, judicial independence and rule of law that so many people in Hong Kong are eager to preserve today are actually a legacy of the British decolonisation process that began in Hong Kong in the late 1980s as colonialism attempted to erect a kinder façade. Moving from the silencing to the de-silencing of Hong Kong, the study will further seek archival evidence to verify the hypothesis that the rule of law in colonial Hong Kong was not so much informed by much-vaunted common-law values and doctrines as it was a legacy of the geopolitical power equation among China, Britain, the US, and their allies and enemies in history. The proposed study will examine how Hong Kong society evolved from a colony of gelded freedoms and rule of law to a city whose freedoms and rule of law are highly praised globally today. The study will also raise the provocative question of whether the colonial government would ever have granted the freedoms so valued by the people of Hong Kong today if no agreement had been struck to decolonise Hong Kong and return it to China. 本研究計劃是本人上一個研究項目“港英年代的言論自由，媒體審查與法治 （1850-1980)”的跟進項目。該研究旨在透過檢視1850至1980年代，港英政府如何廣泛地政治審查大眾媒體，以證明香港歷史上實行的普通法制度，在絕大部分的殖民地時期打壓市民言論和政治表達自由，以鞏固殖民地政府的專制權力，和保護英國的外交與地緣政治利益。 本研究是解決該研究遺留的重要問題：為什麼在殖民地最後時期對媒體審查的專權制度漸漸被言論自由和法治取代？透過新近開放的史料檔案本研究試圖證明今日香港人相當珍惜的言論自由,司法獨立和法治實際是在1980年代因應解殖，地緣政治，和國際關係需要而建立在香港的制度。

17616920.label: Realisation of objectives
17616920.value: The PI has fully achieved Objectives 1 to 3 by uncovering the following history from declassified documents. Please refer the following paragraphs for a summary of how they were achieved. Well-rehearsed common law cases and remedies that safeguarded freedom of the press and freedom of expression were not applicable to Hong Kong in practice because they were simply watered-down or overruled by repressive colonial legislation until the late 1960s and early 1970s, when the future of Hong Kong after 1997 first appeared on London’s policy agenda. Despite the open opposition of the press and Chinese elites to restrictions on the press and freedom of expression since the early twentieth century, it is clear from the study that what happened in mainland China, in global geopolitics, and in China’s relations with Britain, the US and their allies mattered much more to the British and colonial governments than did the people of Hong Kong in determining the freedoms they enjoyed. Governor MacLehose’s liberated Hong Kong to some extent in the 1970s was part of London’s blueprint to cultivate civic pride in the people of Hong Kong as citizens of British Hong Kong to maximise Britain’s bargaining position in its negotiations with China over the potential continuation of British administration. Although his governorship featured a relaxation of government intervention in the media and free speech, he actually changed few, if any, colonial laws and regulations enabling the government to censor the media and suppress free speech whenever it saw the necessity of doing so. The governorships of Wilson and Patten, in contrast, “liberated” Hong Kong to prepare for the discontinuance of British colonial rule from July 1997. Thanks to the efforts of negotiators on both sides, the Joint Declaration signed in 1984 stated that the law and judicial system in force in Hong Kong prior to 1 July 1997 would be maintained thereafter, which means that the British side had more than a decade (1984-1997) to rectify the draconian colonial laws and “imperfections” in the judicial system that it did not wish to be “maintained” after Hong Kong’s retrocession to China. As a result, Wilson’s government swiftly repealed the most repressive of the laws and regulations used to supress the print media and film studios, lifted the restrictions on discussions of politics in schools and introduced civic education to the school curriculum to raise young people’s awareness of political affairs. Had the Tiananmen crackdown not occurred, it is doubtful whether the Bill of Rights Ordinance would have been passed, given the lukewarm attitude of both the Hong Kong and British governments towards a human rights law for Hong Kong prior to the incident. Another unexpected trigger was Margaret Thatcher’s loss of office to John Major, which brought about not only a change in Hong Kong’s governorship, but also in the China advisory team at Downing Street, which had formerly comprised Chinese-speaking sinologists. Accordingly, “convergence” was no longer the golden principle in Britain-China relations with regard to the legal and policy changes in colonial Hong Kong in the run-up to 1997. This legal cleansing and liberation exercise therefore accelerated during Patten’s era until the week before Hong Kong was decolonised on 1 July 1997 of the last-minute loosening in the censorship law might not be given effect after the handover. Would the unprecedented liberation that Hong Kong experienced in the years prior to the handover have occurred if British administration had continued beyond 1997? MacLehose’s efforts to liberalise the media and confer individual liberties were in large part a strategy to maintain a “civic gap” between Hong Kong and mainland China, a gap for defending the Chinese claim to Hong Kong. At the same time, MacLehose retained colonial laws to suppress the media and individual liberties should colonial “peace and order” require just in case British administration continued beyond 1997. Accordingly, the legal overhaul undertaken under in the 1980s that abolished most of the executive powers to tamper with the freedom of expression is probably best seen as part of Britain’s game plan to prepare for Hong Kong’s non-negotiable return to China. As the PI has has said in the book, however, only time and the availability of additional declassified documents will tell whether that view is correct. The PI has fully achieved Objectives 4 and 5 by publishing one research monograph, one Chinese edition of the monograph, one journal article and submitting one journal article for review, running more than fifteen talks to disseminate the findings and publicise the scholarly contribution of this project in renowned universities including Oxford, UCLA, UCL (London) and NUS (Singapore). The project's path-breaking contribution is attested to by the numerous accolades and highly positive book reviews in top-tier journals. Below are some examples of these praises. 'This is a penetrating and lucid account ...The more liberal and rule-of-law oriented regime they left behind in 1997 was, as Ng expertly demonstrates, largely a legacy of the final two decades of British rule, produced under the looming specter of Chinese reacquisition…This book forces us to confront this darker history and rethink common assumptions about the nature of British colonialism in Asia.' Taisu Zhang, Professor of Law, Yale Law School 'Michael Ng upends narratives of Hong Kong's rule-of-law past and its colonial nostalgia. Through his careful archival study, Ng shows that censorship and libel laws were long the tools of British colonizers in Hong Kong. By explaining Hong Kong's status as a fulcrum of British-Chinese relations, Ng situates the story of Hong Kong in the broader fields of comparative legal history, international relations, and geopolitics, telling a story that resonates powerfully for students of empire.' Matthew Erie, Associate Professor of Modern Chinese Studies, University of Oxford 'Carefully researched and well argued, this book addresses and provokes important questions of the nature of colonial rule, and how far notion of the rule of law could be marginalized in a colonial context. It will be of great interest not only to historians of Hong Kong, but also to those interested in the nature of colonial rule throughout the British Empire.' Michael Lobban, Professor of Law, University of Oxford (in Law and History Review) '[The book] is first comprehensive account of the development and application of repressive measures designed to target and limit speech and publication in [colonial] Hong Kong …[it] provides a critical corrective to narratives viewing the British Empire as synonymous with the development of rights-based rule of law… For anyone interested in the history of British colonial approaches to freedom of CUHK (in Asian Journal of Comparative Law) 'Ng's comprehensive and thought-provoking book makes a major contribution to Hong Kong's legal history and colonial history.’an 'read history backwards' out of post-2019 nostalgic feelings about the colonial past.' Chi-kwan Mark, University of London (in China Review)

17616920.label: Major findings and research outcome
17616920.value: The PI’s last project (RGC project ref 17605917) unfolded the history of how the media and schools were pervasively censored during most of the colonial period. This project shows how they were liberated at a very late stage of colonial rule. It successfully argues that the freedom of speech that so many people in Hong Kong are eager to preserve today are the result of the larger China strategy that Britain employed in preparing Hong Kong for its return to China. It reveals that Hong Kong people’s freedoms drifted along on these waves of change in global politics without much of a push from much-vaunted common-law values. Its specific findings are summarised in the following two paragraphs. 1.Preparing to negotiate with China from the 1970s: Overt loosening and covert control. The diplomat Murray MacLehose assumed Hong Kong’s governorship in 1971 with an express mandate from London to build civic pride and raise living standards in Hong Kong to maximise the British bargaining position in negotiations over Hong Kong’s future with Beijing. In addition to the well-known expansion of social services, MacLehose’s governorship also featured a hitherto understudied loosening of media control. Yet behind the overt building of a free city were the covert surveillance of political activists and unchanged draconian laws of political censorship that were used to crack down on anti-government dissents. 2. Liberating Hong Kong for China: De-silencing the city from 1984 to 1997. The conclusion in 1984 of negotiations between Britain and China on the reversion of Hong Kong’s sovereignty to the former marked the opening of an era of liberalistic rule of law and individual freedoms in Hong Kong. Laws and regulations that had been used to suppress free speech, control publication, and prosecute political protesters were loosened or repealed one after another in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Hong Kong’s first statute expressly recognising freedom of speech, assembly and association was passed only in 1991, just six years before the colonial era came to an end. Not only were laws and policies were liberalised in the last decade of British rule, but the 1980s and 1990s also witnessed unprecedented levels of public discussion of, and official and media narratives on, the importance of free speech and the rule of law to Hong Kong.

17616920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17616920.value: From what has been discovered in this study, there are at least three potential area for future research: 1.The considerable divergence in the law and legal ideas between the central imperial and peripheral colonial is an understudied yet highly significant area of research in the field of law and colonialism. 2.Comparative studies of the continuous state security concerns shared amongst former colonies promise to link British imperial history with the history of global geopolitics during the twentieth century. 3.Hong Kong’s freedoms were amongst the variables in Britain’s geopolitical risk hedging vis-à-vis China, and sometimes even the US. Small but strategically located colonies such as British Hong Kong, Singapore, Cyprus and Gibraltar offer a rich but under-explored history as part of the grand strategy of Britain in the long twentieth century. Behind the well-rehearsed commercial stories, the colonial history of Hong Kong actually has much to tell us concerning its role in international relations, military intelligence, the world’s China strategy and China’s view of the world powers, stories that are yet to be fully told.

17616920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17616920.value: Drawing on archival materials, Michael Ng challenges the widely accepted narrative that freedom of expression in Hong Kong is a legacy of British rule of law. Demonstrating that the media and schools were pervasively censored for much of the colonial period and only liberated at a very late stage of British rule, this book complicates our understanding of how Hong Kong came to be a city that championed free speech by the late 1990s. With extensive use of primary sources, the free press, freedom of speech and judicial independence are all revealed to be products of Britain's China strategy. Ng shows that, from the nineteenth to the twentieth century, Hong Kong's legal history was deeply affected by China's relations with world powers. Demonstrating that Hong Kong's freedoms drifted along waves of change in global politics, this book offers a new perspective on the British legal regime in Hong Kong.

17617120.label: Project Objectives
17617120.value: Transforming the current conceptualisation of Taiwanese literature Discussion of Taiwanese literature, particularly what is commonly called its “native soil literature” (xiangtu wenxue), is usually based on a terrestrial imagination. As “native soil” is usually used to refer to a specific geographic location, this approach risks an overly narrow definition of Taiwanese literature. My project takes the ocean as the core of Taiwan’s literary imagination, focusing on its fluidity, inclusiveness, and connectivity with other island- and ocean-based literatures. Engaging with environmental humanities and indigenous studies As oceans serve as the planet’s largest habitat, a project on ocean-related literature invites an interdisciplinary take that combines eco-criticism and conventional close reading of selected texts. This interdisciplinary approach will be particularly effective in analysing the works by eco-sensitive writers such as Liao Hongji and Syaman Rapongan. Adding a new dimension to the existing scholarship on Taiwan’s literary history Existing research on Taiwan’s literary history to date barely takes into account the practitioners of ocean literature, or tends to categorise writers of oceanic literature differently (such as under the category of indigenous literature). This project supplements existing scholarship by proposing to examine “oceanic literature” as a literary genre. Tracing different cultures’ oceanic imagery to recontextualise Taiwan’s oceanic writing This project will compare and contrast contemporary Taiwan’s more open and inclusive (and even anti-Kuomintang) oceanic cultural imagery with Meiji Japan’s conceptualization of Western civilization as the “ocean civilisation” in order to point out the complicity of the Japanese legacy and Taiwan’s cultural indigenisation. Introducing multi-genre and less studied texts to the realm of oceanic literature While individual writers’ ocean writing has received attention, scholars often concentrate on fiction by male authors. This project expands the scope of oceanic literature by including women writers, as well as less studied genres such as poetry and non-fiction prose.

17617120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
17617120.value: The ocean plays an indispensable role in the cultural imaginary of Taiwan. In early postwar Taiwan, it was associated with national defence. Oceanic writing at that time was usually an integral part of the military literature encouraged by the Nationalist Party (KMT). This not only circumscribed the development of Taiwan's oceanic literature, but also misleadingly conceptualised Taiwan as the model province of the Chinese mainland. Following the rise of environmental awareness in the 1980s, oceanic writing gained greater momentum. Ecological essays by female writers instilled fresh vitality into the genre. In the 1990s, owing to the rapid growth of Taiwanese cultural nationalism, representations of the ocean were turned into powerful tactics to articulate Taiwan’s new imaginary as an “oceanic country” vis-a-vis the KMT-imposed continental (Republic of) China. This characterisation of Taiwan, was further consolidated officially in 2004 when the ruling party advocated for “Looking at Taiwan from Another Angle”, that is, positioning Taiwan as part of the Austronesian family, connected with other island cultures, instead of as a peripheral island off the vast Chinese mainland. Although the ocean has been a recurrent theme or trope in Taiwanese literature, existing studies of Taiwan’s literary history do not deal with this topic specifically. Scholars also tend to focus on individual writers, without examining the evolution of oceanic literature in postwar Taiwan comprehensively. Employing genealogical and textual analysis and engaging with eco-criticism and indigenous studies, this naturally interdisciplinary project uses “oceanic” as a genre-defining concept to trace patterns across a number of selected multi-genre works produced in postwar Taiwan by writers both Han and indigenous, male and female. It will offer a detailed overview of Taiwan’s oceanic literature in the postwar era, providing a critical reappraisal regarding how “new” this oceanic cultural imagery is, especially in relation to the dichotomous 19th-century Japanese cultural imagery of oceanic (Western) civilisation and continental (Chinese) civilisation. In addition, it will evaluate the de-colonising potential of this imagery for Taiwan and explore alternative ways of conceptualising Taiwanese literature as world oceanic literature by investigating the indigenous and global dimensions of this imagery. This project's objectives are at least threefold--to propose an alternative way of conceptualising Taiwan, to facilitate a more profound inter-ethnic understanding in Taiwan along the Environmental Humanities approach, and to expand the current scope of Taiwan studies by inviting a transcultural comparison between Taiwan and other ocean-oriented cultures. 海洋為台灣不可或缺的文化想像。戰後初期，海洋與國防攸關，海洋書寫常是國民黨獎勵的軍事文學的一個整合部份。這不但限制了台灣海洋文學的發展，也讓台灣被誤認為（陸地）中國的唯一代表。八〇年代以降，環保意識抬頭，海洋書寫勢頭漸盛，女作家的生態散文尤其為此文類注入鮮活動力。九〇年代，因台灣文化國族主義的迅速成長，海洋轉成為抒發台灣作為「海洋國家」，有別於國民黨強加的陸地中國之新想像的有力策略。海洋台灣的思維，於1996年總統大選前後十分流行。2004年文建會在「換個角度看台灣」網站上載一系列地圖後，更使台灣作為自中國脫出的邊陲小島，搖身一變，被定位為與其他島嶼文化相連的南島民族的一員。2008年，反獨立的國民黨重新執政，此海洋文化想像降溫。然而，在台灣文壇，不少作家善用海洋想像，來表現自身的族群認同，或藉此重思台灣重層復刻的殖民史。儘管海洋在台灣文學中是常見主題或象喻，現有的台灣文學史，例如彭瑞金，葉石濤，陳芳明等所撰，並未特別處理此課題，觸及此課題的學者亦多僅聚焦單一作家，未能全面檢視戰後台灣海洋文學的衍變。本研究採系譜學和文本分析方法，援引生態批評和原住民族研究，重新勾勒戰後台灣海洋文學的整體風貌，探討作品包括漢人與原住民作家，男女作家兼顧的不同文類創作。此研究將批判性地重估，戰後台灣的海洋文化想像，較之於十九世紀日本的海洋（西方）文明/陸地（中國）文明的二分法，究竟多「新」，也將評估此想像對於台灣可啟動的去殖民潛能，並探索台灣文學作為世界海洋文學的另類思維方式，以深究此想像中，原住民族和全球面向共生的現象。

17617120.label: Realisation of objectives
17617120.value: In the second half of this project, I have mainly focusing on addressing the objectives 3 to 5 that were not fully achieved in the first half of this project. I am pleased to have achieved fully objective 3 by offering an ocean-centric and archipelago-focused perspective that supplements well the existing "continent-oriented" literary historiography in which Taiwan's subjectivity is often discussed against its big neighbour China or the post-1949 Nationalist regime in Taiwan. By exploring Taiwan's literature as a salient example of oceanic literature, it places Taiwan's literary production and reception in a much broader global, translingual, and cross-cultural context. It also pays detailed attention to Taiwan's multilayered de-colonisation, with the Indigenous people's challenge of the Han cultural hegemony being examined closely. It further connects Taiwan with other comparable island-based (Indigenous) culture for a fresh framework. For objective 4, I did not put down 100% mainly because I anticipate that I will still be able to identity more oceanic imageries that can serve as a reference point for Taiwan's oceanic writing. But I have tried to look at Japan's and some major oceanian cultures' oceanic imageries and integrated my findings into my research. As for objective 5, I plan to continue exploring other genres, such as prose or travelogues, but I have studied quite extensively the major genres (fiction and poetry) and have also done some research on the ocean-related works produced by female authors, a rarely tackled dimension as far as oceanic literature is concerned.

17617120.label: Major findings and research outcome
17617120.value: The major findings of this project can be divided into three points. 1) In Taiwan's oceanic literature, the political aspect remains fairly dominant owing to the ongoing Hoklo cultural nationalism that gained momentum in the 1990s. Nevertheless, other dimensions, such as the ecological dimension, the topological dimension, and the ethnic dimension, continue to enrich Taiwan's oceanic literature substantively. Among all the dimensions, the ecological/environmental one perhaps has the greatest global appeal. 2) Some of the above-mentioned dimensions are intimately connected to each other. For instance, the Indigenous author Syaman Rapongan makes a salient case demonstrating that the construction of a Tao ethnic identity is deeply intertwined with the larger environmental concerns. His case also reminds us that while the Hoklo nationalists are keen to construct a Taiwan-centric identity, the Han people's cultural hegemony over the ethnic minorities (such as the Indigenous peoples and the new immigrants from Southeast Asia) should also be critically examined. This intersecting of different dimensions of oceanic literature is one of the aspects in which the uniqueness of Taiwanese literature lies. As the number of ocean-related writing by female authors remains small in number, this genre is still largely male-dominated. 3) This research also identifies two seemingly very different traits—the nativist and the cosmopolitan—of Taiwan’s oceanic writing. The nativist trait refers mainly to the construction of an ethnic identity for a specific ethnic group, and the cosmopolitan trait means the fluidity and boundary-less features of the ocean provides a natural common ground connecting Taiwan with other oceanic or Indigenous cultures. In this regard, the ocean facilitates fresh and fruitful comparative literary studies between Taiwan and the Oceanic (if focusing on the oceanic cultures), as well as between Taiwan and, for example, native American writings (if focusing on the global indigenous cultures).

17617120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
17617120.value: As far as Sinophone literature is concerned, this project finds that “island” (or archipelago, peninsula etc) can also serve as a possible keyword for Taiwan’s new cultural imaginaries. This can enable Taiwan's literature to be discussed with other island-based literature such as the Chinese writings from Malaysia. It has the potential to be integrated into the Global South Studies. I will continue to explore possible comparable cases in my book project. I would also like to explore read more prose works or travelogues, and hopefully address the gender issue and the class issue more in my close reading (if applicable).

17617120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
17617120.value: This project goes beyond the common conceptualisation of the oceanic Taiwan as a politically de-Sinified or a KMT-wary effort by exploring other dimensions embedded in Taiwan's rich oceanic literature, such as the ecological, the ethnic, and the topological dimensions. Employing close reading and inspired by the approach of environmental humanities, this project not only offers insightful interpretations of the oceanic works by selected authors including Syaman Rapongan, Liao Hongji, Dong Nian, and Lü Zezhi. In addition, it foregrounds the ocean as an alternative space for thought and a critical lens to connect Taiwan with other research directions such as Indigenous Studies and intervene in current critical conversations such as Anthropocene and de-coloniality.

17617620.label: Co - Investigator(s)
