18607020.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18607020.value: Decades of research, largely from associational studies, show that the relationships of motor with cognitive and social aspects of development are particularly strong in early childhood. Children who are able to move proficiently also tend to have better cognitive skills and social behaviours. However, the mechanisms that underpin these relationships remain unclear and research that explores causation is still urgently needed. To understand how we can better facilitate effective and balanced child development, it is crucial that causal processes be examined. This proposed research, therefore, explores the antecedent role of motor development on cognitive and social domains. We seek to examine whether a targeted movement skills training programme facilitates improvements in the cognitive and social domains in young children. We are able to test this in the local Hong Kong context given the aims and scope of the current kindergarten curriculum guidelines. Using a group-randomised controlled trial design, we will implement an evidence-informed and co-designed fundamental movement skills training programme in kindergartens. It is hypothesised that cognitive and psychosocial outcomes will improve to a greater extent following the targeted motor training, compared to following the usual physical health and learning activities. Participants will consist of children aged 3-5 years (N=158). The training programme is informed by contemporary motor learning research, and is fit-for-purpose through a co-design process with teachers. Outcomes will be measured using standardised tests of cognitive (i.e., executive control, working memory), and social (i.e. Social Competence and Behavior Evaluation) skills. Measurements will be at baseline, mid-training, post-training, and follow-up (6 months after). To verify that the motor skills training was effective, fundamental movement skills proficiency will be assessed using the Test of Gross Motor Development-3 at each measurement time point. Covariate factors that will be accounted for include growth (i.e., height, weight), fine motor skills, and physical activity. Confounding factors in the kindergarten environment will be considered (e.g., space). The findings of this research will inform the design and implementation of kindergarten programmes that enable cognitive and social development through movement-based programmes. They will contribute to knowledge and understanding of child development through evidence of causal mechanisms. Impact will be achieved by enabling kindergarten teachers to more effectively help young children develop the ability and the confidence to move and engage with their physical and social environments. These are aspects that crucially need to be enabled early if we want children to have a better start in life.

18609220.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18609220.value: 閱讀理解往往是閱讀發展模型和閱讀教學計劃的最終目標。理解其所閱讀的內容是讀寫能力與投入社會的能力之間非常重要的一環。因此，我們有必要加強瞭解兒童在閱讀理解時所需的技巧。有證據顯示語法意識和句子結構對閱讀理解極為重要，但句子結構的意識具體如何增強兒童的閱讀理解能力仍未知，尤其對於學習截然不同的兩種語言的中英雙語兒童而言。 是次研究旨在探究：一、中英雙語兒童語法意識和閱讀理解（語言內和跨語言）的關係，二、L1 和L2語法結構的異同會否為閱讀理解帶來不同的影響，三、語法意識的發展/挫敗會否導致L1、L2或兩者閱讀理解的發展/挫敗。 是次研究將會招募香港中英雙語的兒童。我們將透過語序測驗和語法判斷及改正測驗評估兒童L1和L2的語法意識。兒童亦需進行一系列L1 和L2 的語音意識、詞素意識、詞彙知識、閱讀理解、邏輯推理和工作記憶的測驗。參加者將於三年內（小三至小五）分別完成以上測驗。 是次追蹤研究將釐清雙語兒童在一個語言的語法意識和另一語言的閱讀理解能力的因果關係，進而提升對雙語兒童閱讀理解的潛在機制理論的瞭解。我們的結果也能為L1和L2語法的異同如何影響語法意識和閱讀理解能力之間的關係（語言內和跨語言）提供線索。教師和教育工作者可因應我們的結果調教L2語法意識的教學模式，例如，強調L1 和L2語法上的異同，在教授不同語言時推廣相似、協調的學習策略。此外，是次研究將展示雙語兒童語法意識和閱讀理解困難的關係。透過瞭解語法能力和其他語言和認知相關的能力，我們能提高篩查出有閱讀困難的兒童的可能性，這有助於設計和實施更有效的介入方案。

18609720.value: 認知心理學現時有很多從兒童發展角度看兒童學習閱讀和關於正常成人的基本閱讀過程的研究，但關於長者閱讀理解能力的研究卻只有很少。長者的閱讀理解能力和一些跟閱讀理解能力相關的知覺-認知能力都很大機會受認知功能的衰退的影響。此外，理解能力的下降可能對他們從閱讀所獲得的滿足感或樂趣帶來負面影響。本研究目的是通過研究年齡增長對成人(25歲)至長者(65歲)閱讀理解能力和閱讀樂趣的影響，和比較不同年齡層的閱讀理解能力、閱讀樂趣與一些閱讀理解能力的重要相關(例如視力、中文認字、執行功能和口頭語言理解能力) 之間的相關，填補以上的知識缺口。閱讀理解能力和閱讀樂趣預計將隨著年齡增長而下降， 65歲以上長者特別如此。比起較年輕成年人的閱讀理解能力，視力和執行功能或對預測較年長成年人的閱讀理解能力起更重要的作用。本研究旨在以橫向研究四個年齡層(25-35歲、45-55歲、55-65歲、65歲或以上)來達到以上研究目的。本研究的重要在於現時有關長者閱讀理解能力和其相關的知覺-認知能力的資訊嚴重不足，此資訊對於完善我們對跨年齡閱讀的理解和建構一個閱讀的一般理論是不可或缺的。現實中高齡人口正急速增長，社會對長者整體福祉和生活素質的關注也隨之而增加。我們認為興趣為主的閱讀能作為低成本的途徑來推廣長者的福祉。更全面地了解理解過程和此年齡層的理解過程如何跟閱讀樂趣相關是很重要的。

18609720.label: Realisation of objectives
18609720.value: Objective 1 is 100% achieved because the data do show a strong declining trend of reading comprehension, measured as accuracy in answering multiple-choice comprehension questions after reading four Chinese passages, across the four age groups. These comprehension questions tap the participants’ text understanding at a literal level, ability to draw inferences, vocabulary, and ability to summarise texts. The youngest group (group 1) obtained a mean of 26.42 (out of 32) (SD = 3.50; N = 136), while the respective means for the 45-54-year (group 2), 55-64-year (group 3), and 65 and beyond group (group 4) were 23.98 (SD = 5.70; N = 51), 21.15 (SD = 5.01; N = 125), and 20.92 (SD = 4.66; N = 109). An omnibus Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) showed a significant overall age effect, F(3, 415) = 7.29, p < .001, eta2 = .05, after controlling for cross-group differences in family income and education level. Post-hoc pairwise contrasts showed significant differences in reading comprehension between groups 1 and 3, p = .015, groups 1 and 4, p < .001, and groups 2 and 4, p = .03. To summarise, the present comprehension results provide a positive answer to the question as to whether reading comprehension ability, measured as comprehension accuracy, declines from mid-twenties to 65 and beyond. Readers below age 55 years are overall speaking more accurate in comprehending text information than readers above 55 years. These differences are significant even after controlling for family income and level of education. Objective 2 is 100% achieved because the data do show an observable rising trend of reading satisfaction across age groups 1 to 4, although the corresponding age-related changes in reading interest and reading motivation, two additional constructs under investigation, are not statistically significant. The constructs of reading satisfaction, reading interest, and reading motivation were measured via well-validated standard questionnaires. Effects of level of education and family income were controlled in these cross-group comparisons. For reading satisfaction, the youngest group (group 1) obtained a mean of 13.57 (out of 20) (SD = 2.80; N = 136), while the respective means for the 45-54-year (group 2), 55-64-year (group 3), and 65 and beyond group (group 4) were 13.51 (SD = 2.12; N = 51), 13.77 (SD = 2.41; N = 125), and 14.06 (SD = 1.82; N = 110). An omnibus Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) showed a significant overall age effect, F(3, 416) = 2.76, p = .042, eta2 = .019. Post-hoc contrasts showed that the only significant difference arising from pairwise comparisons was that between groups 1 and 4, p = .037. For reading interest (out of 44), the means for age groups 1 to 4 were respectively 29.90 (SD = 5.82; N = 136), 29.53 (SD = 4.20; N = 51), 29.22 (SD = 5.13; N = 125), and 30.54 (SD = 4.65; N = 109). For reading motivation (out of 93), the means for age groups 1 to 4 were respectively 64.38 (SD = 9.57; N = 136), 64.45.53 (SD = 9.08; N = 51), 68.87 (SD = 12.04.13; N = 125), and 61.61 (SD = 9.80; N = 110). Omnibus ANOVAs did not show any overall age effects for reading interest and reading motivation. To summarise, satisfaction from reading, i.e., how enjoyable reading is, increases with age over a relatively long span of time; the main difference is that between readers in their twenties or thirties and readers above age 65 years. This rising trend of reading satisfaction contradicts the original hypothesis, which stipulates a declining trend, and offers an interesting contrast with the demonstrated age-related decline in reading comprehension. Objective 3 is 100% achieved; the four age groups differ in what perceptual-cognitive variables emerge as significant predictors of reading comprehension and reading satisfaction. First, reading comprehension was regressed on visual acuity (left-right average), accuracy in recognizing difficult and infrequent Chinese characters, the executive functions of working memory (measured via forward and backward digit spans), inhibitory control (measured via the Stroop effect), and cognitive flexibility (measured via perseverance errors in Wisconsin Card Sorting), and language comprehension (measured via a Cantonese listening comprehension test developed by the principal investigator). Stepwise regressions were performed for the four age groups with family income and education level entered as control variables at the first step. For the youngest age group (N = 131), the significant predictors were language comprehension, t = 6.01, p < .001, and character recognition, t = 4.65, p < .001, together explaining 39.4% of the variance in reading comprehension. For the 45-54-year age group (N = 49), the significant predictors were language comprehension, t = 6.24, p < .001, and working memory, t = 2.84, p = .007, together explaining 53.7% of the variance in reading comprehension. For the 55-64-year age group (N = 122), the significant predictors were language comprehension, t = 6.89, p < .001, and inhibitory control, t = 2.56, p = .012, together explaining 27.7% of the variance in reading comprehension. For the 65-year and beyond age group (N = 107), the significant predictors were language comprehension, t = 3.96, p < .001, working memory, t = 2.95, p = .004, and character recognition, t = 2.46, p = .015, together explaining 34.0% of the variance in reading comprehension. Second, reading satisfaction was regressed on the same predictors using the same method. For the youngest age group (N = 131), the significant predictor was character recognition, t = 4.62, p < .001, explaining 14.2% of the variance in reading satisfaction. For the 45-54-year age group (N = 49), the significant predictor was language comprehension, t = 2.36, p = .023, explaining 10.7% of the variance in reading satisfaction. For the 55-64-year (N = 122) and the 65-year and beyond age group (N = 107), none of the predictors emerged as significant. To summarise, reading comprehension is overall speaking more predictable via perceptual-cognitive factors than reading satisfaction. For reading comprehension, language comprehension measured via Cantonese listening comprehension is an important predictor for all the four age groups. While the executive functions of working memory and inhibitory control appear to play a more important role in older than younger readers, character recognition is important only in the youngest and the oldest readers. The present results provide general support for both the Simple View of Reading and the Extended Simple View of Reading, which highlight the predictive roles of language comprehension, word (character) decoding, and executive functions in reading comprehension. The relative roles of these predictors in the different age groups add a novel dimension to the application of the Simple View to explaining reading comprehension at different age ranges. While reading satisfaction may be explained by a small number of perceptual-cognitive factors in younger readers, it does not appear to be associated with any of these factors in any way in older readers.

18609720.label: Major findings and research outcome
18609720.value: In addition to the results discussed above, further findings are reported as follows. First, correlations among the study variables were computed for the two older groups. Reading comprehension correlated with language comprehension (r = .67, p < .001), working memory (r = .48, p < .001), cognitive flexibility (r = .30, p < .001), character recognition (r = .46, p < .001), vocabulary (r = .47, p < .001), reading interest (r = .13, p < .05), and reading motivation (r = .14, p < .05), but not with reading satisfaction. Second, for these two older groups, cognitive reserve, measured via CRIq, correlated with all the study variables (rs ≥ .18, ps < .01). A median split was performed on cognitive reserve; a high- (N = 112) and a low-reserve subgroup (N = 120) were created. The high-reserve subgroup (M = 22.93) outperformed the low-reserve subgroup (M = 20.28) in reading comprehension, eta2 = .028. The high-reserve subgroup also performed better than the low-reserve subgroup on language comprehension, eta2 = .072, character recognition, eta2 = .049, vocabulary, eta2 = .060), reading interest, eta2 = .083, and reading motivation, eta2 = .027. However, the two subgroups did not differ in working memory, cognitive flexibility, and reading satisfaction. Third, hierarchical regressions were performed to examine the relative roles of the different study variables in predicting reading comprehension in the high- vs. low-reserve subgroup. Age, education level, and family income were all entered in the first block as controls because they were found to be significant correlates of reading comprehension. All the main study variables were entered in the subsequent block. In both the low- and high-reserve subgroups, the main study variables collectively explained a significant amount of variance in reading comprehension beyond the control variables (low-reserve subgroup: R2 = .56; high-reserve subgroup: R2 = .52). In explaining reading comprehension among the older adults with high cognitive reserve, listening comprehension (Beta = .21, p < .05) and character recognition (Beta = .27, p < .01) emerged to be significant predictors. For the older adults with low cognitive reserve, language comprehension (Beta = .50, p < .001), vocabulary (Beta = .14, p < .05), and reading motivation (Beta = .19, p < .05) significantly predicted performances in reading comprehension. Fourth, the younger adults were less accurate in comprehending written sentences expressing “intensionality”, i.e., someone else has a belief about an object that is true but does not capture the whole truth, than “false belief”. i.e., someone else has a belief about an object that is false.

18609720.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18609720.value: The research is to be developed in two directions. First, more older participants (55+ years) need to be recruited to arrive at a larger elderly sample and then latent class analysis (LCA) will be performed to examine the cognitive profiles for the expanded sample, with reading comprehension as the main outcome variable. A variation of this is to conduct a similar profiling analysis with both reading and language (Cantonese listening) comprehension as outcome variables. We expect to generate three clusters of readers or language users with executive functions, reading motivation/satisfaction/interest, and character recognition/vocabulary as the respective critical predictors. The purpose of such profiling is to identify types of elderly readers whose reading performances can be attributed to different reading- or language-related factors. For instance, some read because find reading inherently satisfying while others read simply because they think they read efficiently. Second, new data on general well-being, loneliness, and life satisfaction will be collected and the mentioned profiling analysis will be expanded. We expect to see more clusters coming out with these non-reading-related variables as critical predictors because we believe that with advancing ages reading is not only a cognitive task but also a social activity having an impact on mental health and general well-being. A larger sample is necessary to support these profiling analyses.

18609720.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18609720.value: This research examines and compares Chinese reading comprehension in older versus younger adults. Findings are several. First, reading becomes less efficient when we get older and the change is most noticeable at around 55 years. This age-related change in reading efficiency cannot be attributed to declining visual acuity. Second, although reading efficiency may drop with increasing age, we seem to enjoy reading more with advancing years, especially after age 65. Third, reading efficiency is closely related to the reader’s listening ability in his or her native language, regardless of age. Fourth, in addition to listening ability, the ability to retain and manipulate new information temporarily in memory (i.e., working memory) and the ability to inhibit potent but inappropriate responses (i.e., inhibitory control) support efficient reading in middle and late adulthood. Fifth, being able to recognize difficult Chinese characters is important for efficient reading in early and late adulthood. The present findings support the idea that leisure reading could be an enjoyable pastime for the elderly although reading efficiency may decrease with age. Such decrease in efficiency may be mitigated by maintaining good working memory and inhibitory control, probably via leading an active live throughout one’s adulthood and old age.

18610120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18610120.value: As China urbanizes and grapples with a shrinking workforce, inter-city competition for skilled domestic migrants has intensified. Nearly all cities hammer out ambitious policies to lure migrants. Not only do they relax residency requirements, many also offer lavish financial incentives. Such intense and large-scale competition for domestic migrants is unprecedented and may provide critical information for analyzing China’s ongoing demographic and industrial transformation. Yet Chinese cities’ migration policies to attract highly-skilled individuals have not so far been systematically documented, let alone explained. This project aims to construct a comprehensive database of high-skilled migration policies of medium to mega sized Chinese cities, and based on the data collected, explain intercity policy variations. The database will allow for measurement of the magnitude of incentive, as well as comparison of inter-city differences. Our coding scheme is inspired by established international indices of high-skilled immigration policies and our prior analysis of migration policies in China. As such the database will transcend the mere application of international indices, which are generally ill-suited to measure the magnitude of incentives and preferential treatments, and make original contributions to the literature on internal migration in China. More importantly, to explain inter-city policy variations, the project will collect relevant city-level data such as demographic composition, human capital, influence of land developers, and welfare provision. Existing explanations generated in the western context tend to focus on the immigration attitudes of the natives and partisan politics. These explanations are less applicable to China, where local officials face unique dynamics in policy making. In particular, a widely shared yet untested speculation about the new policy is that it is caused by the oversupply of real estate. This hypothesis, if confirmed, would add a new dimension to the discussion of the determinants of migration policy, in which concerns over the property market have received less attention. Taken together, the data collected in this literature would allow for testing of hypotheses concerning the nature of migrant competition in China, theories of political accountability in an authoritarian context, and the relations between welfare and migration policy. 隨着中國的城市化進程和應對勞動力的萎縮，城市間對國內技術移民的競爭已經加劇。幾乎所有城市都制定了雄心勃勃的政策來吸引移民。他們不僅放寬了居住要求，許多城市還提供了豐厚的經濟獎勵。如此激烈和大規模的國內移民競爭是前所未有的，可能為分析中國正在進行的人口和產業轉型提供關鍵信息。然而，迄今為止，中國城市吸引高技能人才的移民政策還沒有被系統地記錄下來。 本項目旨在構建一個全面的中國中大型城市高技術移民政策數據庫，並根據收集到的數據解釋城市間的政策差異。該數據庫將有助於衡量激勵措施的規模，以及比較城市間的差異，並檢驗有關中國移民競爭的性質、以及福利與移民政策之間的關係等假說。

18610920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18610920.value: Teacher feedback shows one of the 10 largest effects on students’ learning outcomes, according to Hattie’s (2009) study of over 800 meta-analyses across two million students. However, existing studies show that not all students effectively use teacher feedback (Hattie & Clarke, 2019; Price, Handley, Millar, & O'donovan, 2010). Notably, the self-processes system (SfPS) model conceptualizes students’ self-determination role in making evaluative judgments of contextual factors (e.g., school climate, teacher feedback) affects engagement in learning, which subsequently affects achievements in learning. Based on the SfPS model, we theoretically propose and empirically test one set of mechanisms: students’ feedback orientations influence their engagement with teacher feedback, which in turn affect their learning outcomes. Feedback orientation consists of multiple dimensions (usefulness, competence, relatedness). Students’ perceived usefulness of feedback, competence to apply teacher feedback, and social awareness to use feedback for establishing good student-teacher relationships jointly determine a student’s receptivity to feedback and autonomy to respond to it. Our proposed study will test the relationships between these feedback orientations, learning engagement and learning outcomes with a sample of 702 Chinese secondary school students from Hong Kong, Macau and mainland China via a structural equation model. The results will shed light on the relationships between feedback orientations, learning engagement and learning outcomes based on the SPS model. This study will help determine the mechanisms underlying student use of teacher feedback. Informed by these results, teachers can design and provide effective feedback that students (a) perceive as useful and (b) use to facilitate their active engagement and improve learning outcomes. Teachers can also help students reflect on their feedback orientations to understand their perceived usefulness of teacher feedback and their responsibility to use it. Recent education reforms emphasize the importance of equipping both teachers and students with assessment for learning literacy, in which feedback is the core pillar (EDB, 2019), so the results of this study regarding students’ feedback orientations and mechanisms to engage students in learning can inform these efforts to harness the power of feedback and make it work more effectively in the classroom to enhance learning outcomes. 根據Hattie（2009）基於800多個包含200萬名學生的元分析(meta-analysis) 進行的研究資料分析，教師反饋是眾多影響學生學習成果的十大因素之壹。然而，現有研究表明，並非所有學生都能有效地利用教師反饋（Hattie & Clarke，2019；Price, Handley, Millar & O'donovan，2010）。值得註意的是，自我認知加工系統（SfPS）理論模型展示了學生在對環境因素（如學校氛圍、教師反饋）做出評價性判斷時的自主作用會影響學習投入程度，進而影響學習成績。基於SfPS模型，在本研究中我們從理論上提出並實證性地檢驗該機制也就是學生的反饋導向如何影響他們對教師反饋的投入程度，進而影響他們的學習效果。反饋導向是一個在反饋情景中產生的包括多個維度（例如：有用性、能力、關聯性）的教育心理概念。學生對反饋有用性的感知、運用教師反饋的能力以及利用反饋建立良好師生關系的社會意識會共同決定學生對反饋的接受性和回應反饋的自主性。本研究採用結構方程模型，對來自中國香港特別行政區、澳門特別行政區和中國大陸地區的702名中學生的反饋導向、學習投入與學習成績之間的關系進行驗證。 研究結果有助於揭示基於SfPS模型研究反饋導向、學習投入和學習結果之間的關系。這項研究也有助於揭示學生使用教師反饋的基本心理機制。研究結果可以幫助教師從多個方面設計並提供有效的反饋用以 (a)提升學生對回饋有用性的認知（b）使用回饋促進學生的積極學習參與度並改善學習成果。教師也可以幫助學生檢視和反思他們的反饋導向，以瞭解他們感知到的教師反饋的有用性以及他們使用反饋的自我效能與責任感。近期的教育改革也強調裝備教師和學生評估素養的重要性，其中反饋是核心支柱（香港教育局，2019）。本研究關於學生的反饋導向和參與學生學習的機制的研究結果可以為如何裝備教師和學生的評估素養提供資訊。總的來說，本研究結果將有利於幫助老師利用反饋的力量，使反饋在教學中更有效地發揮作用，從而提升學生的學習成果。

18610920.label: Realisation of objectives
18610920.value: The four research objectives have been satisfactorily and adequately addressed through the collaborative efforts of the Principal Investigator (PI) and Co-Investigators (Co-Is). Key findings to address Objective 1 The study provides valuable insights into student engagement, feedback orientation, and learning outcomes among Mainland China, Hong Kong, and Macau student groups. The Feedback Orientation Scale and the School Engagement Scale displayed high consistency across the three groups (Cronbach alpha values > 0.80). Similarly, the scale assessing learning outcomes through student self-evaluation of academic competence and interest in learning school subjects exhibited high internal consistency (Cronbach alpha values > 0.80). The analysis of correlations shows statistically significant correlations among feedback-related factors, engagement, and learning outcomes. Feedback utility (FBUT) showed a strong positive correlation with various dimensions of student engagement and learning outcomes, with consistently large effect sizes as measured by Cohen's d. Similarly, feedback self-efficacy (FBSE) displayed a strong and positive correlation with these components, suggesting that students who perceive feedback as useful and have confidence in its reception tend to exhibit higher engagement levels and achieve better learning outcomes. Moreover, feedback social awareness (FBSO) and feedback accountability (FBAT) also contributed positively to student engagement and learning outcomes, albeit with slightly smaller effect sizes. These patterns were consistent across the three student groups in mainland China, Hong Kong, and Macau. Notably, student general feedback orientation has a statistically significant association with both engagement and learning outcomes, highlighting the pivotal role of students' feedback orientation in optimizing educational outcomes. These findings emphasize the importance of fostering a positive feedback environment to nurture feedback-oriented students and enhance the effects of teacher feedback on learning outcomes. Key findings to address Objective 2 Feedback accountability refers to the extent to which students take responsibility for using feedback to improve their learning. It empowers students to actively engage with feedback, enhancing their self-agency in the learning process. The study also investigated the extent to which feedback accountability functions as a mediator in the relationships between feedback utility, feedback self-efficacy, feedback social awareness, and learning engagement among secondary students across the three regions. The findings reveal significant mediation effects, shedding light on the intricate dynamics of these relationships. Based on the Self-Processes System (SfPS) model, the results of our structure equation modelling analysis consistently confirm that learning engagement mediates the relationships between feedback factors and learning outcomes across the three regions. For example, in Mainland Secondary Students, feedback utility significantly enhances learning outcomes through engagement (Estimate = 0.319, p<.001). Similar findings apply to Hong Kong and Macau Secondary Students. Feedback self-efficacy also positively influences learning outcomes through engagement across regions. Learning engagement consistently mediates feedback accountability and outcomes. No significant mediation exists between feedback social awareness and outcomes, highlighting distinct feedback orientation dimensions in understanding learning engagement and outcomes. In the predictive model, over 70% of the variation in students' learning engagement could be explained by four dimensions of feedback orientation. Specifically, R-squared values are 72% for mainland Chinese, 80% for Hong Kong Chinese, 75% for Macau Chinese, and 75% for the total student population across the three regions. These findings highlight the potential of feedback orientation in guiding teachers to design programs that boost students' learning engagement, with significant implications given the established connection between learning engagement and academic achievement. Additionally, there's a direct predictive link between student learning engagement and self-evaluated academic competence and interest in learning school subjects, with 43% for mainland Chinese, 50% for Hong Kong Chinese, 25% for Macau Chinese, and 38% for the entire student sample. This suggests that a considerable part of the variation in students' self-evaluated academic competence and interest could be attributed to their levels of learning engagement and feedback orientation. Key findings to address Objective 3 This study advances our comprehension of feedback theory by introducing and empirically testing the Self-Processes System (SfPS) model. This model places students at the center of the feedback process, acknowledging their unique perspectives and experiences as recipients of feedback. Traditionally, feedback research has predominantly focused on the perspectives of educators and institutions, often neglecting the crucial role of students in this process. Through rigorous empirical analysis across diverse student populations in Mainland China, Hong Kong, and Macau, this study validates the SfPS model, demonstrating that students' perceptions of feedback utility, self-efficacy, social awareness, and accountability have a profound impact on their engagement levels and learning outcomes. This shift in perspective challenges the conventional, teacher-centric feedback models and underscores the necessity of considering students' feedback experiences and needs. By highlighting the pivotal role of students in the feedback loop, this study provides educators and institutions with actionable insights. It emphasizes the importance of creating a feedback environment that aligns with students' perspectives, fostering a positive feedback culture that enhances engagement with feedback. This study may reshape our understanding of feedback theory, traditionally dominated by literature on feedback provided by teachers, by recognizing students as active agents in the feedback process. This recognition offers valuable insights for educators and institutions, contributing to more effective educational practices and promoting a holistic approach to harness the power of feedback to maximize student productive learning. Key findings to address Objective 4 To optimize the effectiveness of teacher feedback in student learning enhancement, a comprehensive approach rooted in the Self-Processes System (SfPS) model with students at the centre is essential. First and foremost, educators should focus on fostering students’ perceived usefulness of feedback. This can be achieved by ensuring that feedback directly aligns with learning objectives and outcomes. When students clearly see the relevance of feedback to their learning goals, they are more likely to engage with it actively. Additionally, promoting feedback self-efficacy is crucial. Encouraging students to take an active role in self-assessment before receiving feedback can boost their confidence in handling feedback effectively. This self-regulation in the context of feedback empowers them to respond constructively to feedback, enhancing their overall engagement with the learning process. Cultivating feedback social awareness is another vital dimension. Creating an open and supportive classroom environment where students feel comfortable seeking clarification and engaging in the feedback loop of student-teacher interaction can promote positive social awareness of feedback. Encouraging students to discuss their feedback preferences and how they plan to act on feedback can further enhance their autonomy and responsiveness (i.e., feedback accountability). Furthermore, improving feedback delivery is imperative. Feedback should be timely and specific to individual student needs to maximize its perceived usefulness. Providing teachers with professional development on effective feedback practices is essential, ensuring they can deliver constructive, actionable, and timely feedback in alignment with the SfPS model. Additionally, integrating feedback literacy training into the curriculum, using educational technology, collecting student input to refine practices, acknowledging student efforts in feedback engagement, and involving teachers, peers, and others can jointly create a positive feedback environment. It is also important to tailor feedback to diverse student needs and implement these evidence-based recommendations for empowering students and enhancing learning engagement and outcomes in a student-centred feedback ecosystem.

18610920.label: Major findings and research outcome
18610920.value: This study, conducted in Mainland China, Hong Kong, and Macau, provides insights into student engagement, feedback orientation, and learning outcomes. Measurement tools for feedback orientation, student engagement, and learning outcomes measured by students' self-evaluated academic competence and interest in learning school subjects demonstrated high reliability. Positive correlations were found between feedback utility and three aspects (cognitive, behavioural and emotional) of student engagement, highlighting the importance of students' perceptions of teacher feedback usefulness in academic success. Feedback self-efficacy also correlated positively with these engagement components and learning outcomes. Feedback social awareness and feedback accountability positively correlated with the three aspects of student engagement and learning outcomes. Building on the Self-Processes System (SfPS) model, this study used structure equation modelling analysis to explore feedback accountability's mediating role in relationships between feedback utility, feedback self-efficacy, feedback social awareness, and learning engagement. Feedback accountability significantly mediated the connection between feedback utility and learning engagement, implying that perceiving feedback as useful partly relies on feedback accountability. Similar mediation was observed between feedback self-efficacy and learning engagement, emphasizing the mediating role of perceived accountability in students' self-efficacy regarding feedback. Feedback social awareness's relationship with learning engagement was also significantly mediated by feedback accountability. These findings underscore the pivotal role of feedback accountability in mediating the impact of feedback-related factors on student engagement, highlighting students' accountability perceptions in the learning process. Learning engagement consistently mediated feedback factors and learning outcomes, emphasizing its role in translating feedback into academic achievement. However, no significant mediation was found between feedback social awareness and outcomes, indicating the unique role of this feedback dimension in understanding learning engagement and outcomes. These mediating patterns are consistent across students in the three regions. This study advances feedback theory by empirically testing the SfPS model across diverse regions. It prioritizes students' feedback experiences, departing from the traditional teacher-centric approach. The results indicate that students' perceptions of feedback utility, self-efficacy, social awareness, and accountability significantly influence their engagement and learning outcomes. This shift underscores the crucial role of students’ agency in feedback processes, providing actionable insights for educators and institutions. It emphasizes the necessity of aligning the feedback environment with students' active participation in the feedback process and teachers' deliberate efforts to promote a positive feedback culture, ultimately enhancing engagement and academic success.

18610920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18610920.value: Current findings suggest promising directions for future research and actionable steps to enhance feedback effectiveness in education. First, researchers can explore the intricate mechanisms through which students' multidimensional feedback orientation (including utility, self-efficacy, social awareness, and accountability) influence their engagement and learning outcomes through multiple research methods (e.g., qualitative, longitudinal experimental designs for generating deeper insights into students' feedback experiences). Second, interventions and strategies aimed at improving students' feedback orientation could be investigated. Schools and teachers can implement targeted feedback training programs to enhance feedback self-efficacy and promote a culture of feedback accountability. This can positively impact students' engagement and academic success. Third, examining the link between students' feedback orientation, feedback behaviors (measured by concrete feedback literacy skills), and academic outcomes can inform tailored feedback practices that optimize learning engagement and results. Moreover, actively involving students in the feedback process is crucial. Schools and teachers should solicit feedback from students regarding their experiences and perceptions, co-creating a feedback environment aligned with their needs, which could guide teachers in providing feedback that matches students' feedback literacy and encourages constructive feedback practices. Future research may explore how feedback orientation's impact on learning engagement and outcomes varies across diverse educational and cultural contexts.

18610920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18610920.value: In this study involving over seven hundred students in Mainland China, Hong Kong, and Macau, we explored how students feel about the feedback they get from their teachers, how engaged they are in their studies, and how well they perform in school. To do this, we used reliable tools to assess students' learning engagement, feedback orientation, and their own evaluation of academic competence and interest in learning. We discovered that when students find the feedback they get useful, it makes them more emotionally, behaviorally, and mentally engaged in their studies. This also leads to better academic performance, as students see themselves as more competent and interested in their subjects. If students believe they can use feedback effectively and understand its social importance, it also boosts their engagement and performance. These findings were consistent among students in all three regions. We also looked at how students' responsibility in using feedback affects their engagement. We found that students who take responsibility for using teacher feedback to improve their learning tend to be more engaged. Moreover, students' engagement consistently links their feedback orientation to academic outcomes, showing that active engagement also plays a crucial role in turning teacher feedback into positive learning results.

18611120.label: Realisation of objectives
18611120.value: First, this project has validated the two international surveys in Chinese, the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (II) (COPSOQ-II) and the Assessment of Quality of Life-8D (AQoL-8D), using two samples of principals in Hong Kong in the two phases. In the quantitative study of our GRF project, the online survey was distributed to all 1093 school principals at primary and secondary principals. The project team spent many efforts on recruiting principal participants through training programs, workshops/conferences, and professional networking. A total of 346 surveys were received and 335 valid surveys were kept for further analysis. The proportion of males (68% out of 335) is higher than that of females (32%). Respondents had an average 13 years’ work experience and a mean age of 48 years. More than half of the participants (52%) had worked as principals for at least ten years. In the qualitative study of our GRF project, we filter and liaise with potential interview participants to schedule interviews. From the quantitative survey data collection, 56 candidates expressed their consent for sequential interviews. We had eventually selected and approached 49 participants’ support with 24 males and 24 females. About 16 participants had less than 10 year working experience, 20 of them has about 10-20 year working experience, and 12 of them had more than 20 year working experience. After synthesis of two surveys mentioned above with the participants’ responses, the six dimensions (e.g., physical well-being, emotional well-being, psychology well-being, cognitive well-being, social well-being, and spiritual well-being) has been included in the principal occupational well-being instrument in the Hong Kong context. Objective 2. To investigate the states of occupational well-being of different groups of principals (e.g., gender; principalship experience; school level; school type; individual, school-related, and contextual factors). The state of school principals’ well-being was investigated. Descriptive statistics of our quantitative dataset showed that the mean score of social well-being (M = 5.30 out of 6; SD = .77), spiritual well-being (M = 5.10; SD = .74); psychological well-being (M = 5.08), cognitive well-being (M = 4.56; SD = .72), emotional well-being (M = 4.12; SD = .76) and physical well-being (M = 3.01; SD = .84). The qualitative data also told that the physical and emotional well-being was startling in Hong Kong. For example, ne primary school principal said “I was really tired after the work. I even do not want to anything just lying on the sofa… you may not believe, I have two children, but I even do not have time to check their homework. But I am a teacher!” one secondary school principal told in the interview, “since I became the principal 15 year ago, I felt lonely, and this kind of feeling has become stronger and stronger.” Interestingly, school principals reported that they had enjoyed interactions with their schoolteachers and counterparts (school principals from other schools). This data may release that school principals in Hong Kong may have a health social relationship in the workplace. However, they may feel emotionally lonely as they are the “No 1” person in the school. Thes results are consistent with the international literature. Moreover, this project has also examined the impact of three-level factors (e.g., individual factors, school factors, and societal factors) on principal well-being. First, personal drivers (e.g., age, gender, principalship experience) of principal well-being have been also investigated. The results released that age, gender and principalship career stage had significant influence on their well-being. Second, school level demographic factors (e.g., school type, school level, funding type, school location, school size) has also investigated. However, only school level has significantly affected principal well-being. The secondary principals had lower occupational well-being than their primary peers in general. The significant impacts have been not detected in terms of principal well-being for other demographic school factors. Third, the contextual factors (e.g., intensive political pressure, reform implementation, social crisis, and limited professional autonomy) had been examined for the impact of principal well-being. The consistent results between quantitative and qualitative dataset have been observed. The frequent reform implementation, but no other contextual factors, had the significant influence on principal well-being in the quantitative dataset. Whilst the qualitative dataset told that the factors including intensive political pressure, reform implementation, social crisis, and limited professional autonomy may had the impact on principal well-being. Objective 3. To identify the psychosocial risk factors that particularly affect the occupational well-being of principals. Objective 4. To explore how the psychosocial risk factors affect the occupational well-being of principals. We would like to put Objective 3 & Objective 4 together to explain our strategies to respond these two objectives. The psychosocial risk factors examined in this project have adopted from the existing literature. These psychosocial risk factors include psychological demands, workload, professional autonomy, social support, work conditions, and other related job characteristics. The descriptive data showed that the participants give the highest ranking to social support (M = 4.32 out of 6.00; SD = .81), followed by leadership support (M = 4.89; SD = .70), working conditions (M= 3.01; SD = .67), and professional autonomy (M = 2.98; SD = .52). These four school related characteristics had demonstrated to significantly affect principal occupational well-being. Nevertheless, this project advances our existing knowledge on the roles of influential factors at different levels and motivation on school principals’ well-being. As many studies suggest that PhD school principals should develop strategies to reduce the well-being problems of their students and teachers, but not themselves. His project provides an interesting perspective to support principals to promote their own well-being, maintaining and enhancing the well-being of their followers. Therefore, the positive school outcomes will be enhanced and sustained.

18611120.label: Major findings and research outcome
18611120.value: We allocated the major findings from this project into three perspectives based on four project objectives. Accordingly, 4 journal articles and 5 conference presentations have been produced, which presented in Part C respectively. First, this project has produced two review journal articles which have been done during the project duration. The team has investigated great effort to systematically review the literature of principal well-being to better complete the project and four objectives. Two systematic literature reviews have been produced. One is the bibliometric review entitled “Looking back and ahead: A bibliometric review of research on principal well-being 1962– 2022” published in Educational Management Administration & Leadership. The other is a narrative review entitled “A conceptual framework of principal well-being: Evidence of a narrative research synthesis from 1978 to 2022” which is under review. Second, this project identified the situation of principal well-being and its measurement (in response to Objective 1 and Objective 2). The project validated the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire in the Hong Kong context. The six dimensions (e.g., physical well-being, emotional well-being, psychology well-being, cognitive well-being, social well-being, and spiritual well-being) has been included in the principal occupational well-being instrument. These findings have been demonstrated in the journal article entitled “Reconceptualizing principal well-being: state, measurement and consequences” published in Journal of Educational Administration. Second, this project identified the situation of principal well-being and its measurement (in response to Objective 1 and Objective 2). Based on the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire and the existing instruments of layman’s well-being and occupational well-being. The project validated the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire in the Hong Kong context. One step further, we also make the principal occupational well-being instrument more concise using the qualitative sample and quantitative sample of this project. The six dimensions (e.g., physical well-being, emotional well-being, psychology well-being, cognitive well-being, social well-being, and spiritual well-being) has been included in the principal occupational well-being instrument. A by-product, the consequences, work engagement and intention to leave, have been also explored. These findings have been demonstrated in the journal article entitled “Reconceptualizing principal well-being: state, measurement and consequences” published in Journal of Educational Administration. Third, this project has also identified organizational and personal influential factors of principal well-being measurement (in response to Objective 3 and Objective 4). These influential drivers include psychological demands, workload, professional autonomy, social support, work conditions, and Hong Kong job characteristics. The descriptive data showed that the participants give the highest ranking to social support, followed by leadership support, working conditions, and professional autonomy. Moreover, personal drivers of principal well-being have been also investigated. One journal article entitles “The network structure of principal well-being: the age effect” has been produced. This journal article is under review.

18611120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18611120.value: This project supports the research team to construct future research proposals on more specific topics for individual external grants (e.g., GRF) and collective external grants (e.g., CRF) applications. In terms of research foci, the team plan to develop research proposals on principal resilience and well-being literacy to enhance school principal well-being. Please kindly note that these two projects have been successfully granted by GRF after this reported project. In terms of research locations, the research team plan to extend the research locations into the GBA. The GBA is one of the most vibrant, innovative areas of China and a major growth driver. School principals constitute a critical human resource for the area and findings of this study could potentially inform policy-makers and educators in the GBA. It can help the GBA establish an international reputation and leadership in providing quality well-being care for school principals, thereby increasing its capacity to attract high caliber teachers and students who will contribute to building the GBA’s social, intellectual, and economic capital. The potential project will have a high potential to directly impact doctoral policy and practice and to benefit future schooling in the growing PhD market of the GBA and beyond.

18611120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18611120.value: This project is an empirical, mixed methods study in nature to examine the situation of principal well-being, and its influential antecedents in Hong Kong. This project is expected to improve the capacity of principals and their schools to serve the community, elucidate the potential drivers that seed success and wellbeing, build Hong Kong’s human capital, and enrich and advance the international research agenda in relation to theory, research, and practice. First, this project has produced two validated surveys, the COPSOQ-II and the AQoL-8D, for educational settings and enrich the understanding of principals’ well-being and potential factors using a Hong Kong sample. The findings have the potential to construct a framework on the nature of principals’ well-being and their influential antecedents for future research, which has already developed in a form of journal article. This has advanced the knowledge base of principals’ well-being. Practically, the project will generate knowledge to support the well-being of Hong Kong principals and suggest ways to improve working conditions and school functioning. The findings have informed the development of training programs and interventions for the preparation, selection, and on-going support of principals in Hong Kong, the GBA, and beyond.

18611320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18611320.value: Engaging students in art criticism and art making activities is the major work of visual arts teachers. With access to the free online resources provided by art museum websites and image-based electronic databases, teachers are now in a better position to make use of artworks in planning and delivering their curriculum. The following questions arise: Can art teachers assume the role of art museum curators and construct an online exhibition to facilitate student learning? How should teachers be prepared to adopt such a ‘teacher-curator’ pedagogy? Can the thematic approach and presentation of exhibitions broaden students’ horizons in considering artworks? Will learning through virtual exhibitions increase students’ motivation to learn and improve their skills in using online resources? What will be the effectiveness and impact of this way of conceptualising, organising and constructing visual arts learning opportunities? The aim of the proposed study is to answer the above questions using a design-based research. Three primary and three secondary school teachers and their students (about 165) will be invited to participate. The first phase of the study will focus on the training of teacher participants in the teacher-curator pedagogy. The second phase is the implementation stage. With the support of the investigator, the teacher participants will develop two virtual exhibitions and relevant face-to-face, museum visit and online learning activities. The third phase is the evaluation stage. Data on the impact and effectiveness of the teacher-curator pedagogy will be collected through student and teacher questionnaires and interviews. The study will be conducted in the particular cultural context of Hong Kong. Museum+, the new museum of visual culture, is scheduled to open in 2020, and the renovated Hong Kong Museum of Art will re-open in late 2019. Besides having state-of-the-art facilities, we would like to see members of our society become regular museum visitors and be culturally literate. By actively using artworks from museums to teach, the study will help to build up a critical audience for the cultural establishments in Hong Kong in the long term. Through the formulation of exhibition themes, the selection of connected artworks and the design of relevant learning activities, the study will enhance the autonomy and capacity of teachers. With a focus on using digital technology, the results of the study will contribute to developing an effective pedagogical practice in general and one that promotes online learning in visual arts in particular. 視覺藝術科教師的一項重要工作是讓學生評賞和創作藝術。透過利用藝術館和圖像資料庫提供的網絡資源，教師較以往可以更有效地運用藝術作品於課程設計及教學實踐。網絡科技的應用洐生以下的問題： 視藝教師能否以藝術展覽策展人的角度，為學生創造網上的虛擬展覽，促進他們學習？教師應該如何去準備這種「教師策展人」的教學？以主題展覽的模式展示藝術作品能否提升學生思考藝術的能力？虛擬展覽能否增加學生的學習動機和提升他們運用網絡資源的能力？「教師策展人」教學的概念、組織和建構方式，會對視覺藝術學習產生甚麼影響和效果？本研究計劃希望透過「設計為本」研究法探討以上的問題。三間中學和三間小學的教師和學生（約165人）將會被邀請參與本研究計劃。第一階段將會集中於訓練教師參與者運用「教師策展人」的教學策略。第二階段為教學試驗。教師參與者將會策劃兩個虛擬展覽，以及相關的面授、展覽參觀和網上學習活動。第三階段為教學評估。資料搜集將會以問卷調查和訪談的形式進行，用以分析有關教學方法的影響和效果。本研究將會於香港本地的文化情境下進行。以視覺文化為主的M＋展館已定於2020年開啟，而經過翻新的香港藝術館亦於2019年重新開放。除了具備各種完善的文化設施，我們希望社會大眾能夠具備欣賞藝術的文化素養以及成為展覽及文化活動的慣常參與者。透過積極地運用藝術館的展品進行教學，本研究將會有助培養具批判力的觀眾，長遠地促推香港的文化建設。透過策劃主題展覽、選取具連繫的藝術作品以及設計相關的學習活動，本研究將會有助提升教師的能力和自主性。透過應用數碼科技於教學，研究結果亦將會有助發展網上視覺藝術學習。

18611320.label: Realisation of objectives
18611320.value: Objective 1: To examine the ways in which visual arts teachers assume the dual role of educator and curator at primary and secondary school levels. In the 2021-22 academic year, each participating teacher implemented the teacher-curator pedagogy in two 4–6-week unit plans. Three whole-day workshops were held in June 2021 to provide training for teachers to uptake the role of teacher-curator and develop unit plans using virtual exhibitions. The principal investigator provided 28 individual consultation sessions to guide and support the teachers in developing the virtual exhibitions. After each unit, review meetings were held for teachers to present their virtual exhibition plans, engage in group discussions, and reflect on the process. A Teacher-Curator Pedagogical Framework has been successfully created. Key actionable steps of the teacher-curator strategy were identified, including formulating thematic exhibition plans, creating virtual exhibitions with immersive design and learning activities, implementing the teaching units by leveraging the virtual exhibition's updatability, and evaluating student learning through feedback collection and artwork assessment. The findings of the project highlight the ways in which the Teacher-Curator Pedagogical Framework allowed for blending online and face-to-face learning, broadening students’ perspectives in evaluating artworks, and setting visual arts education on a path to embrace digital transformations. Objective 2: To investigate the ways in which teachers develop themes and design relevant teaching and learning activities to form a virtual exhibition. The project has successfully achieved its second objective by leveraging the evolving roles of museum curators and visual arts teachers, as well as the potential for crossover learning between schools and museums. To implement the teacher-curator pedagogy, the project developed a total of 18 thematic virtual exhibition plans, each with related learning activities realized on the Kunstmatrix online platform. The proposed teacher-curator pedagogy capitalizes on the convergence of curator and teacher roles, allowing teachers to create learning opportunities through the careful selection and arrangement of artworks in virtual exhibitions. By connecting school learning with museums through virtual exhibitions, the pedagogy enables teachers to design activities that bridge the structured school curriculum with experiential learning. This "crossover learning" approach allows students to engage with contemporary Hong Kong artworks in thematic, interpretive inquiries that transcend traditional art historical categories. To effectively implement this teacher-curator pedagogy, the project has identified several key strategies for teachers to adopt: (1) Leverage online and digital resources to curate a diverse collection of artworks across various time periods, genres, and cultural contexts for the virtual exhibitions, (2) Take advantage of the pedagogical affordances of the virtual exhibition format, such as 3D immersion, updatability, and accessibility, to deepen thematic learning, (3) Design multimodal, self-directed learning activities that integrate direct instruction or museum learning with online engagement, (4) Provide students opportunities to explore the virtual exhibition at their own pace, and facilitating art criticism, independent learning, and peer-to-peer exchange using multimedia and digital tools, (5) Develop virtual exhibitions as an interactive space where students can provide comments, feedback, share creative ideas, and reflect through the ease of digital media. By embracing these strategies, the project has successfully demonstrated how teacher-curators can effectively develop thematic teaching units with learning activities and leverage virtual exhibitions to enhance student learning and engagement with contemporary art. Objective 3: To evaluate the effectiveness and impact on student learning of the teacher-curator pedagogy. To achieve this objective, a robust mixed-methods research design that triangulated multiple data sources has been implemented. The qualitative component involved 12 classroom observations and 12 in-depth interviews (1-1.5 hours) with the teacher participants. These interviews delved into the teachers' perspectives on how the virtual exhibition format and their dual roles as educators and curators influenced different dimensions of student learning including within and beyond class engagement, development of art criticism skills, and enhancement of artmaking abilities. The teachers also submitted weekly reflective journals chronicling their observations on student learning throughout the teaching cycles. Additionally, all student artworks were collected as secondary data, allowing analysis of the pedagogy's impact on tangible learning outcomes. The qualitative data, such as observation transcripts and interview responses, underwent rigorous thematic analysis to identify key patterns and themes related to the impact on students' visual arts competencies. Complementing the qualitative insights, the project also gathered quantitative data through end-of-cycle student feedback questionnaires. These questionnaires assessed the students' perceptions of the virtual exhibition-based learning experience and its effectiveness in enhancing their learning experience such as understanding and appreciation of artistic principles. By triangulating the qualitative and quantitative findings, the results demonstrated that the teacher-curator approach had a positive influence on student learning. Students exhibited increased engagement, improved art criticism skills, and enhanced artmaking abilities. The virtual exhibition format with its thematic content, facilitated deeper exploration of artworks’ visual qualities and background, independent learning, and valuable peer-to-peer exchange. Through this comprehensive method of evaluation, the project conclusively achieved its objective of thoroughly assessing the effectiveness and impact of the teacher-curator pedagogy on student learning outcomes in the visual arts domain. Objective 4: To evaluate the effectiveness and impact on student learning facilitated by blended learning. To achieve the project's fourth objective, data was collected through two rounds of field work to examine the effectiveness and impact of virtual exhibitions on student learning. The primary data collection methods employed were student interviews and surveys. The qualitative part involved 48 students participating in 12 in-depth focus group interviews, which provided rich, nuanced insights into how the virtual exhibitions affected students' motivation, attitudes, face-to-face learning, and self-directed learning in art criticism and artmaking. These hour-long interviews also sought students' suggestions for enhancing the virtual exhibition platform. Thematic analysis of the interview transcripts revealed significant patterns and themes that positively influenced student learning. On the quantitative part, 575 questionnaires, with a response rate of 86.9%, were completed on paper during class time after the conclusion of each teaching unit. The surveys sought to measure the frequency and duration of students' virtual exhibition visits, their preferences for online tasks, the aspects of the exhibitions they found most appealing, and the ways in which virtual exhibitions enhanced their learning experience in visual arts. Open-ended questions were included in the questionnaires to capture any additional opinions or perspectives regarding virtual exhibitions. The surveys revealed that most students (77.9%) visited each virtual exhibition 1 to 6 times, with 67.8% spending up to 15 minutes and 28% spending 16 to 30 minutes on average per visit. Students reported the virtual exhibitions helped them learn more about the artworks and understand the background information in depth. Additionally, the survey found that 71.7% of students preferred to learn via the virtual exhibitions than their previous ways to learn visual arts. Results also indicated that students preferred 3D virtual environment, multimedia exhibits display, and exhibit introduction than the hyperlinks and extended learning activities. Most of the students indicated that the virtual exhibitions helped them learn more about the artworks and understand the background information in depth.

18611320.label: Major findings and research outcome
18611320.value: A pedagogical framework assuming the dual roles of teacher and curator was developed and tested through 12 virtual exhibition learning units in schools. The effectiveness and impact of this pedagogy on teaching and learning were assessed through thematic analysis. The teacher-curator role was assumed in 12 virtual exhibition teaching units, which included relevant learning activities. Data collection involved 575 questionnaires completed by 331 students, 12 video-recorded class observations, 12 individual interviews with teachers, and 12 focus group interviews with students. The findings of the study demonstrated the positive pedagogical value of using teacher-curated thematic virtual exhibitions in art classrooms. The pedagogy empowered teachers to leverage free online learning resources and realize the benefits of virtual exhibitions for facilitating teaching and learning. The 3D presentation of artworks and the interaction created through blended learning were particularly beneficial, especially with sufficient training on the concept of teacher-curator and appropriate IT support. The study also revealed that students developed a stronger desire to share their learned content and actively participate in group critiques. The use of virtual exhibitions enhanced student autonomy and self-motivation in personalized and peer-to-peer learning contexts. With data collected from class observations, interviews, and surveys with the teachers and student participants, the followings were observed: Impact on student learning: 1. Motivate students towards self-directed and active learning: The virtual exhibitions promoted self-paced, autonomous learning, encouraging students to take an active role in their education. 2. Stimulate artmaking ideas and skills: Exposure to diverse artworks inspired students and helped develop transferable artmaking skills, fostering creativity and new ideas. 3. Enhance students’ confidence through peer learning: Students gained confidence in sharing their ideas and interpretations, which expanded peer learning through active discussions and exchanges. Impact on visual arts teaching: 1. Build technological capacity through creating virtual exhibitions: Creating virtual exhibitions helped teachers enhance their IT skills to meet new digital teaching needs. 2. Make use of the enhanced presentation of virtual exhibitions: The 3D virtual exhibition format provided a more engaging and proactive learning experience compared to traditional methods. 3. Engage learners with deep interaction through the blending of online and face-to-face teaching: Combining online activities and museum questioning strategies with face-to-face learning activities deepened student engagement and learning experiences. 4. Facilitate teaching in themes and context through digital content curation: Aligning digital content with relevant themes improved teachers’ pedagogical knowledge and teaching quality by leveraging digital research and curation.

18611320.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
18611320.value: The study identified technological limitations in using virtual exhibitions for teaching, primarily due to the constraints of default platform settings. These limitations restricted teachers from creating tailored exhibitions. Students expressed a desire for more dynamic visual designs and additional features like multi-player avatars, animations, and live streaming. Therefore, further investigation and experimentation are necessary to explore more complex applications of virtual exhibitions that promote higher-order and collaborative learning. Future research could include utilizing virtual exhibitions as art portfolios for senior-level students’ public examination assessments or facilitating student-curated group exhibitions. To address these limitations and expand the educational potential of virtual exhibitions, future research may focus on the ways in which students assuming the roles of virtual exhibition curators and examine its impact on technology-mediated learning and community of learning. The research should aim to delve deeper into the potential of 3D virtual exhibition platforms by transforming them into co-learning hubs, with the potentials for students to curate Group Exhibitions and Individual Galleries (Similar to Vlogs/ E-Portfolios), and solo exhibitions. By integrating advanced features, the research may create an immersive learning experience, broaden art knowledge, enhance collaboration, and inspire creativity for students.

18611320.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
18611320.value: Despite the availability of digital collections in museums and artwork image databases, visual arts teachers still face challenges in effectively utilizing these online resources and digital tools for curriculum planning and teaching. The study proposed a teacher-curator pedagogy, which sought to empower visual arts teachers by enabling them to take on the role of a "digital museum curator" and facilitate student learning through the utilization of virtual exhibitions. A design-based study was conducted to evaluate the pedagogy, involving six teachers and 331 students in Hong Kong during the 2021-22 academic year. Data were collected through interviews, observations, virtual exhibition designs, and video recordings of classroom teaching throughout the implementation phase. The findings of the study revealed improvements in visual art teaching including: (1) building technological capacity through creating virtual exhibitions, (2) making use of the enhanced presentation of virtual exhibitions, (3) engaging learners with deep interaction through the blending of online and face-to-face teaching, and (4) facilitating teaching in themes and context through digital content curation. The study also identified positive impacts on student learning, including: (1) motivating students towards self-directed and active learning, (2) stimulating artmaking ideas and skills, and (3) enhancing students’ confidence through peer learning.

18612420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
18612420.value: Hong Kong’s former status as a British colony at the doorstep of China made it a unique place, culturally, economically, and politically. Mainland Chinese politics has frequently spilled over onto Hong Kong’s territory. From the inter-war years onwards, political rivalry between the Nationalists and the Communists impacted the colony. During the Cold War, both camps continued to work on securing political support in Hong Kong as a strategic place for winning over the hearts and minds of Chinese outside of Mainland China and Taiwan. In this connection, the years immediately before and after 1970 constituted a critical conjuncture in which the configuration of Nationalist vs Communist rivalry changed as the latter re-emerged on the international stage and began manoeuvring to regain support from the people of Hong Kong. The rise of student activism in the decade (1968-1977) following the 1967 Riots signalled a new page in the story of Chinese politics in Hong Kong. Unlike their parents, who left China before and after 1949 to avoid political turmoil, young college students (expected to become future members of the elite as admission to local universities was highly restrictive) began to make their mark in the public arena. The campaign for Chinese to be an official language and the defending Diaoyutai movement were two of the most significant social movements organised by students in the so-called huohong niandai (period of student radicalism). A strong Chinese nationalist sentiment was demonstrated by many of these young college students, most of whom had been born, or grown up, locally. The aftermath was that many student activists embraced Maoism and turned to supporting Communist China, while a sizeable group of student leaders became left-wing radicals critical of the colonial regime. But both camps, although to different degrees, espoused Chinese nationalism. Contrary to the popular belief that Hong Kong’s local identity was formed and consolidated rapidly after the riots in the 1960s, it is our suggestion that Hong Kong’s unique culture and identity cannot be fully understood without unravelling why Chinese nationalism appealed to many in the 1970s. This proposed study, through archival research (e.g., declassified government documents and student publications) and interviews with key informants, is an attempt to fill the gap in existing research on Hong Kong society by analysing the rise of student activism and the spread of Chinese nationalism among student activists in the late 1960s and early 1970s. 香港以前作為英國的殖民地，而同時又身處於中國南大門的位置，令它在文化、經濟、政治上成為一處很獨特的地方。中國大陸的政治經常會溢出並且進入香港境內。從兩次世界大戰之間的年份開始，國民黨與共產黨之間的競爭時而影響香港。而在二戰後冷戰時期，它們雙方繼續活躍，在港爭取支持，並以此作為戰略部署，爭取海外華人的民心。與此相關，1970年前後是關鍵的時期，重新構造國共對立的形勢，尤其是中共重新投入國際政治舞台，並嘗試再次贏得香港民眾的支持。 學生運動在1967年暴動之後的十年（1968-1977）興起，標示中國政治在香港的一番新的發展。跟他們那批在1949年前後為了避開政治亂局而來港的父母不同，年青大專學生（由於大專學額有限，他們被視為未來的精英份子）在社會上的公共領域有所作為。爭取中文成為法定語文運動和保衛釣魚臺運動乃那個「火紅年代」（即學生激進主義時期）中的重大社會運動。他們表現出一份強烈的民族情緒，儘管個人背景是在香港出生或成長。事後很多學生擁抱毛澤東思想，轉向支持中共；同時亦有一定數量的學生領袖變為左傾，批判殖民政府。這兩派學生都－－在不同程度上－－接受中國民族主義。與認為香港的本地認同迅速地在暴動之後發展起來的看法相反，我們的想法認為要瞭解香港獨特的文化和身份認同，必須探討為何中國民族主義於七十年代有它的號召力。通過文檔研究（例如解密的政府檔案、學生刊物）和跟相關人士的訪問，本研究計劃嘗試填補上述空隙，分析學生運動在六十年代末、七十年代初興起，及中國民族主義在大專學生群中的傳播。

18612420.label: Realisation of objectives
18612420.value: For Project Objectives 1, 3 and 4, I conducted a review of the major college students’ publications in the period of 1967-1977. Such coverage allows us to identify key topics discussed on college campuses and the students’ changing perspectives of their identity, sense of belonging, and sense of responsibility, as well as their views of Hong Kong’s and China’s social and political affairs. The publications under review include: • 學苑 (1961-1977) • 中大學生報 (1969-1977) • 崇基學生雙周報 (1960-1969) • 崇基學生報 (1970-1977) • 新亞學生報 (1964-1977) Opinions and views expressed in student publications captured what college students had in mind when they first encountered the question of identity. Though the authors of those crucial pieces might have changed their minds at a later stage of those social movements, their remarks remained significant, and they reflected the emotions and opinions at the key moments in historical changes. For Project Objectives 1, 3 and 4, I also reviewed cultural magazines published in the 1950s-1970s. One of the challenges of this project is that my interviews with former activists were found not particularly productive for a good grasp of their social engagements in the 1960s and 1970s. The first two respondents refused my request to make an audio record of our interview on the ground that their comments touched on personal lives of former student leaders and notable figures in the cultural field. They were also most uncomfortable with the idea of keeping a detailed record of their responses. As a result, with their consent, only brief notes were taken. Later, the same rules were applied to the other four interviews. But this is only about the recording of the interviews. The more challenging issue was that most of the respondents’ comments on their social engagement seemed to be rationalized in the light of subsequent political development and changes in their views of developments in Hong Kong and China. In view of such limitations of the quality of interviews, I decided to reduce the number of interviews and focus on documentary materials for capturing student activists' opinions and views at the time of their participation in the major social movements. As noted earlier, I rely on student publications to analyze views expressed on college campuses. I reviewed articles published in notable cultural magazines for more general discussions and debates outside of college campuses. The key publications identified at the proposal stage were Pan Ku (盤古), 70s Bi-weekly (70年代雙周刊), The Seventies (七十年代), and Chinese Student Weekly (中國學生周報). In order to broaden the scope of my search, the coverage of cultural magazines under my review has been expanded. More attention was given to College Life (大學生活). Also, I included Yanmat (人物) in my review. Not only did such a minor revision of my research plan help to broaden and lengthen the coverage of the project (e.g., young people’s negotiation with the meanings of being Chinese before the mid-1960s), it also introduces new insights to my analysis. Particularly, I was alerted to the peculiarity of Hong Kong culture – the arrival of those former scholar-officials under the Qing Dynasty after the 1911 Revolution and then decades later, the south-bound exile intellectuals after the 1949 Revolution cultivated a unique cultural atmosphere and sentiments in Hong Kong. In addition to their role in the development of education in Hong Kong, they continued to preserve and promote what, in their mind, the authentic Chinese tradition and culture. These two groups of intellectuals were equally hostile to the ruling regime in the Mainland, and they challenged the official interpretation of Chinese history and culture. Their intellectual practice cultivated a cultural space in Hong Kong where there was a distinction between the so-called official interpretation and a more authentically traditional understanding of China’s history, culture, and values. Their love of the country was based upon a passion for its history and culture, not requiring them to accept the ruling regime as the legitimate political authority. While this separation of the country and the ruling political regime has become a feature of the local culture strongly buttressed in Hong Kong society, young people in the 1960s started questioning the aloofness of the south-bound exile intellectuals. This opened the opportunity for them to assume an active role in promoting nationalism first in the Chinese language movement and later the defending Diaoyutai movement. A more intensive reading of local cultural magazines helped me to collect materials to substantiate the point of young people’s search for a new identity and a new way to engage in social and political affairs in a colonial setting. For Project Objective 2, I consulted the files in the Public Records Office and the National Archive (London). Particularly useful are those files on ‘the New Left’ (e.g., FCO 40/364, HKRS 890-2-36, FCO 40/700), ‘liaison with students’ (HKRS 1071-1-5) and ‘radical/student publications’ (HKRS 1071-1-17), and ‘dossier on socially active group’ (HKRS 570-3-39) and ‘standing committee on pressure groups’ (HKRS 1151-1-8). These files inform me of the Hong Kong Government’s changing perspectives on emerging oppositional groups. Files on the New Left and student groups captured the government's awareness and assessments of the spread of radicalism among college students. Files on liaison with students and student publications showed how the government had kept its eyes on student activism in the 1970s. A Working Group on Liaison with Students was formed, and the government stayed well informed of the changing mood on college campuses. Furthermore, the Special Branch gave assessments of whether the Communists had directly engaged in those college student activities. Gradually, it is noted that the government’s focus had shifted from the so-called New Left to other forms of activism. Official files on socially active groups reflected the changing configuration of local politics and the government’s changing responses to pressure-group-type mobilization. These files capture the way the colonial government reacted to its opposition. What is most relevant to this project is that the colonial government took the rise of nationalism and patriotism among young people as an almost inevitable feature of the colonial setting. Also relevant is that the colonial government changed its assessments and coping strategy as the political environment evolved. Student politics gradually lost its political significance by the late 1970s. If student bodies were still active agents for collective actions, they were likely to work with emerging pressure groups. Many of those pressure group leaders were former student activists. They continued their social and political engagement with a newly articulated reformist perspective. This symbolized the decline of the nationalist fervour triggered by the two major social movements in the early 1970s. However, the push for social reform could also be seen as a continuation of the agenda initially put forward by the young generation since the mid-1960s – a sense of belonging and responsibility.
