25201620.label: Major findings and research outcome
25201620.value: The research yielded significant findings across five objectives related to solar-driven evaporative desalination technologies. We focused on the laser manufacturing of nanomaterials, achieving nearly 100% absorption across a wavelength range of 300 to 2500 nm. The study successfully printed plasmonic nanoparticles, specifically copper (Cu) and manganese dioxide (MnO2), using laser-induced forward transfer methods, leading to the development of a portable interfacial evaporator composed of a 3D-structured plasmonic-enhanced photothermal nanocomposite of Cu nanoparticles and laser-induced graphene (LIG). This evaporator demonstrated a remarkable solar absorption rate of 98% and reached surface temperatures exceeding 80 degrees C under one sun irradiation, with an evaporation rate of 2.29 kilogram per meter square per hour for pure water and high efficiency even with brine at 20 wt%. (Carbon 204, 231-237, 2023) We introduced an in-situ imaging approach using electrical impedance tomography (EIT) to visualize the water desorption process in cellulose nanocrystal-based aerogels integrated with LIG, revealing that heat concentration, geometric configurations, and temperature gradients significantly enhance water transport through the polymer network. (Chemical Engineering Journal 497, 154880, 2024) We examined superwetting properties and salt transportation mechanisms in a novel evaporator design combining nano-crystal cellulose (NCC), MnO2 nanoparticles, and LIG, which enabled effective management of salt accumulation due to their tunable superhydrophilic and superhydrophobic surfaces. We confirmed the optimized parameters achieved high solar evaporation rates of up to 1.82 kg per meter square per hour even with high salinity brine. Finally, we were involved in developing a prototype for solar evaporation that successfully produced bacteria-free condensed water, demonstrating its potential for freshwater generation applications. Collectively, these findings contribute valuable insights into enhancing the efficiency and practicality of solar-driven desalination technologies while addressing challenges related to water scarcity and salt accumulation. (The manuscript is currently under review, with the submission title of EIT monitoring of salt transportation in cellulose hydrogel for solar-driven evaporative desalination in Wiley as in the outcome 6 in part C).

25201620.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
25201620.value: By testing with E. coli, we found the water collected from solar evaporation was bacteria-free. This simple method can provide fresh water for direct drinking. We might further try to develop more practical applications of this research into actual world implementations in the future.

25201620.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
25201620.value: The research focused on developing advanced solar evaporation technologies to address water scarcity. We explored laser manufacturing of nanomaterials, achieving nearly 100% absorption of solar energy across a wide wavelength range. They created a portable evaporator using copper and manganese dioxide nanoparticles combined with laser-induced graphene, which effectively absorbed sunlight and reached high temperatures for efficient water evaporation. This system showed excellent performance, achieving high evaporation rates even with salty water. A real-time imaging technique was introduced to observe how water is released from aerogels, revealing that heat and structure significantly influence water movement. We examined how the unique properties of the materials used in the evaporator help manage salt buildup during evaporation, enhancing efficiency. The research confirmed high evaporation rates even with salty water and demonstrated that the condensed water collected was free from bacteria, making it suitable for drinking. Overall, these findings pave the way for more effective solar-powered desalination methods that could provide clean water in areas facing shortages.

25202520.label: Project Objectives
25202520.value: To facilitate the development of Ground Based Augmentation System (GBAS) from single frequency single constellation (GPS, L1) to dual-frequency multi-constellation (e.g. GPS+BDS, L1/B1+L5/B2) and provide more stringent precision approach services in civil aviation, e.g. from CAT I to CAT III. To design new ionosphere monitors to guarantee the safety of aviation users under severe ionosphere environment. Ionosphere anomaly is the most critical threat on satellite signals. The aim is to constrain the harm of ionosphere anomaly to an extremely small possibility by detecting and removing the faulty satellite in time. To derive a threat space of ionosphere anomaly specifically for Hong Kong. With ionosphere anomaly mostly severe at low latitudes, e.g. Hong Kong, the worst-case ionosphere gradient is bounded as the threat space. The newly proposed monitors should be able to protect aviation users against this threat space. To design new dual-frequency ground monitors with enhanced performance to overcome the restrictions in the single frequency system. The ionosphere monitors should be most sensitive to the ionosphere error and least sensitive to other error terms. The advantages of ground monitor with more relaxed detection time and more flexibility in designing the test statistics are taken. The frequency diversity is also explored to be able to estimate the ionosphere effect more precisely. To be able to detect an harmful ionosphere anomaly in time, the following ground monitors are proposed for 1) detecting a moving ionosphere front with reduced response time and simplified implementation; 2) detecting an absolute ionosphere gradient with reduced uncertainty caused by ambiguity; 3) detecting the ionosphere difference between ground stations to facilitate the detection of airborne monitors. To compare new monitor's performance with old ones with aspects of e.g. Probability of Missed Detection (PMD) for different fault size, time to alarm. The proposed monitor should be able to protect users under more sensitive situations. To validate if the new monitors are able to satisfy the CAT III requirements by a exhaustive simulation test considering impact factors e.g. the ionosphere gradient profile, the distance between aircraft and ground station and etc. The maximum undetectable error for each monitor and each case is calculated. This is a necessary step to be certified for operation in civil aviation.

25202520.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25202520.value: The Ground Based Augmentation System (GBAS) is used for precision approaches in civil aviation with improved accuracy and integrity of satellite navigation. With more satellite signals available from multiple constellations, e.g. GPS, Galileo and BDS, dual-frequency and multi-constellation GBAS is being investigated to provide more stringent approach services. Satellite signals are subject to various faults resulting in large position errors. Integrity monitoring is used to guarantee the safety of aviation users against signal failures, e.g. ionosphere anomaly, satellite payload failure. The most challenging threat is the ionosphere anomaly with its unpredictable perturbations and the difficulty to bound its influence, especially at low latitudes, e.g. Hong Kong. In this project, new ionosphere monitors are designed for dual-frequency GBAS in the ground subsystem with enhanced performance. The worst-case anomaly in Hong Kong is bounded as the threat space using GNSS ground stations across the region within a period of solar cycle. New ionosphere monitors are proposed in this project to cover the whole threat space of Hong Kong. In current single frequency system, ionosphere is monitored both in ground and air subsystems. The major responsibility of the ground monitors is to detect and remove faulty satellites with large anomalies before they are incorporated in the airborne solutions. The airborne monitor is used to monitor the residual effect as the difference between the ground and air. With limited monitor capabilities, current system is very complex and contain a few restrictions, e.g. siting restrictions, to constrain the ionosphere influence. With dual frequency signals available, the ionosphere effect can be estimated and monitored in a more precise and comprehensive way. Ionosphere is dispersive and the wave propagation speed depends on the frequency. It is therefore able to be estimated the first order ionosphere by dual-frequency satellite signals. New ground monitors are proposed exploring this advantage that are able to detect ionosphere anomaly with a certain velocity, a certain magnitude and a certain differential effect between ground stations. These new monitors are more powerful and efficient in safeguarding the aviation users under serious ionospheric situations. To prove that new monitors are able to satisfy the requirement for precision approaches, a simulation test is designed covering varying parameters that play a role, e.g. the transmission delay, the distance between ground station and aircraft and etc. 用于民航精密进近地基增强系统（GBAS）可提高卫星导航系统的精度和完好性。随着更多星座的卫星信号可用，如GPS、伽利略、北斗，双频多系统的GBAS可提供更精密的进近类型。卫星信号可能存在各种故障类型，导致定位误差过大，完好性监测的目的是在这种情况下依然保障民航用户的安全，如电离层异常、星钟故障等。其中，由于电离层的不确定性，最有挑战性的是电离层监测，特别是对于电离层比较活跃的低纬度地区，如香港。本项目设计了地面监测器，用于监测此类电离层异常。 首先，地面监测站的数据用于估计香港地区的电离层最坏情况，作为危害模型，本项目中提出的电离层监测器用于覆盖这个模型。在当前的单频系统中，电离层在空中和地面同时被监测，地面用于在检测到大的故障卫星时，可将其剔除出用于播发改正数的卫星，空中可继续监测剩余差分误差中的电离层异常。由于现有的电离层监测器性能有限，现有的GBAS设计十分复杂，从而对系统构成一些限制，如通过地面站选址来限制电离层。现有的双频信号可用于更好地估计电离层，从而以更有效的方式来监测电离层异常。原理是根据电离层的色散介质特性，可能过双频信号估计。本项目提出的双频电离层监测器可以更好地在各种极端情况下保护用户，并可简化系统的设计。

25202520.label: Realisation of objectives
25202520.value: The realization of Objective 1: This project achieved significant advancements in ionosphere monitoring technologies to safeguard dual-frequency multi-constellation (DFMC) Ground-Based Augmentation System (GBAS) users from ionospheric anomalies. Before investigating ionospheric anomalies, nominal ionospheric conditions in Hong Kong were analyzed. Quadratic polynomial expressions were proposed to bound the standard deviation of ionospheric spatial gradients. These serve as critical component for evaluating the navigation integrity. The project subsequently developed an ionosphere threat model tailored specifically for Hong Kong, a low-latitude region not previously studied. This model represents a pioneering step in characterizing ionospheric threats for such a region. Using the model, the impact of ionospheric anomalies on both single-frequency and dual-frequency GBAS was assessed for the first time over a full solar cycle. This is a major milestone, as it provides comprehensive insights into GBAS performance in a low-latitude region over varying solar activity levels. Furthermore, the project introduced a closed-form expression to overbound undetected differential errors caused by ionospheric anomalies. This expression is crucial for geometry screening in GBAS Approach Service Type D, which supports CAT II/III precision approaches. Alongside, an ionosphere gradient monitor utilizing dual-frequency measurements was developed. This monitor addresses limitations of single-frequency monitors, meeting stringent CAT III precision approach requirements. Machine learning techniques were also explored to enhance anomaly detection. A decision tree algorithm was applied to identify amplitude scintillations caused by ionospheric anomalies. These efforts mark the initial application of machine learning in civil aviation ionospheric monitoring, demonstrating its potential for future advancements. Data from BeiDou and GPS constellations were analyzed to understand their comparative characteristics. While GPS data were ultimately used due to higher availability and compatibility with existing infrastructure, insights from BeiDou measurements informed potential enhancements to multi-constellation GBAS systems. Collectively, these achievements provide a robust foundation for advancing DFMC GBAS to enable more reliable and precise civil aviation operations. The realization of Objective 2: This project designed a novel ionosphere gradient monitor employing dual-frequency carrier phase measurements to detect faulty satellites affected by ionospheric anomalies. The proposed monitor shows strong potential for integration into DFMC GBAS. It leverages a geometry-free combination of dual-frequency double-differenced carrier phase measurements as test statistics. This approach effectively mitigates the influence of tropospheric anomalies, which can otherwise lead to false alarms or missed detections. To ensure compliance with CAT III precision approach requirements, the monitor's design accounted for baseline length and filtering periods. These parameters were optimized to achieve the allocated probabilities of missed detection (PMD) and false alarms (PFA). Additionally, a novel strategy was developed to identify ionospheric amplitude scintillation events with high accuracy. Using geodetic GNSS receivers and machine learning algorithms, the project achieved a detection accuracy exceeding 99% even under severe ionospheric conditions. This high level of performance underscores the promise of integrating simple yet effective machine learning methods into civil aviation ionospheric monitoring systems. The realization of Objective 3: A comprehensive threat space of ionospheric anomalies was derived, and a corresponding threat model specific to Hong Kong was established. These elements are pivotal for assessing the feasibility of GBAS implementation in the region. Analysis revealed that significant ionospheric gradient events in Hong Kong are primarily caused by equatorial plasma bubbles (EPBs). Detailed characterizations of these phenomena—including their gradient magnitude, velocity, and width—were incorporated into the threat model. The model construction utilized GPS data from 18 Hong Kong Satellite Positioning Reference Station (SatRef) sites, covering Solar Cycle 24 (2008–2019) with a 30-second sampling rate. The resulting three-dimensional threat model effectively describes the spatial gradients caused by EPBs. Using this model, the project evaluated the impacts of ionospheric anomalies on single-frequency and dual-frequency GBAS. Moreover, various ionospheric monitors including the ionosphere gradient monitor, code-carrier divergence monitor, and dual-solution pseudorange ionospheric gradient monitoring were validated within the threat space. This validation confirmed their capability to protect aviation users against anomalies caused by EPBs in Hong Kong. The realization of Objective 4: A new ground ionosphere anomaly monitor using dual-frequency measurements was designed to overcome the limitations of existing single-frequency monitors. This monitor achieves improved performance by eliminating tropospheric error effects through the use of geometry-free double-differenced carrier phase measurements as test statistics. Compared to single-frequency monitors, the proposed monitor demonstrated higher sensitivity to ionospheric gradients and lower sensitivity to other error sources, such as ephemeris and tropospheric errors. It can more accurately estimate ionospheric gradients while maintaining a lower noise level in its test statistics. Extensive experiments using data collected from SatRef sites validated the monitor's superior performance compared to existing systems. These results suggest that the new monitor could serve as a reliable replacement for current monitor, enhancing the safety and efficiency of precision approach operations. The realization of Objective 5: The project proposed a simplified ground monitor capable of detecting moving ionospheric fronts using two reference stations with baselines of several hundred meters, aligned parallel to the runway. This configuration allows direct measurement of ionospheric gradients between the aircraft and the ground facility. Threatening gradients can thus be detected and timely alerts issued to aircraft. The monitor design addressed potential risks, such as incorrect ambiguity estimation, by bounding these effects and optimizing baseline length and filtering periods. These measures ensure compliance with CAT III precision approach requirements. By leveraging frequency diversity, the required filtering period was reduced, further enhancing the monitor's responsiveness. This design facilitates airborne monitor detection and provides timely alarms for threatening ionospheric gradients. Its implementation is particularly beneficial in low-latitude regions, where ionospheric anomalies are most severe. The realization of Objective 6: A new ionosphere gradient monitor was developed and compared with existing systems in terms of PMD and time-to-alarm. Theoretical and experimental results indicated that the new monitor achieves lower PMD and shorter alarm times. This monitor is particularly effective under challenging conditions, such as tropospheric anomalies, where existing systems may fail or produce missed detections. It also reduces the prolonged filtering periods typically required by current monitors. By employing the Hatch-Melbourne-Wübbena combination, the new monitor minimizes filtering time for newly acquired or reacquired satellites, enabling faster detection and alerting. The realization of Objective 7: The impact of ionospheric anomalies on GBAS, especially on ionospheric monitors, was comprehensively evaluated to confirm compliance with CAT III requirements. Simulations accounted for various factors, including ionospheric gradient magnitude, aircraft velocity, and ground station geometry. Results demonstrated that both ground-based and airborne ionospheric monitors can meet CAT III approach requirements. Additionally, the project established linear closed-form expressions to bound maximum undetected ionosphere-induced differential range errors. These expressions are instrumental for geometry screening to exclude unsafe satellites affected by ionospheric anomalies. Such screening is an essential step for implementing GBAS Approach Service Type D, supporting CAT II/III precision approaches.

To design new ionosphere monitors to guarantee the safety of aviation users under severe ionosphere environment. Ionosphere anomaly is the most critical threat on satellite signals. The aim is to constrain the harm of ionosphere anomaly to an extremely small possibility by detecting and removing the faulty satellite in time.

To derive a threat space of ionosphere anomaly specifically for Hong Kong. With ionosphere anomaly mostly severe at low latitudes, e.g. Hong Kong, the worst-case ionosphere gradient is bounded as the threat space. The newly proposed monitors should be able to protect aviation users against this threat space.

To design new dual-frequency ground monitors with enhanced performance to overcome the restrictions in the single frequency system. The ionosphere monitors should be most sensitive to the ionosphere error and least sensitive to other error terms. The advantages of ground monitor with more relaxed detection time and more flexibility in designing the test statistics are taken. The frequency diversity is also explored to be able to estimate the ionosphere effect more precisely.

To be able to detect an harmful ionosphere anomaly in time, the following ground monitors are proposed for 1) detecting a moving ionosphere front with reduced response time and simplified implementation; 2) detecting an absolute ionosphere gradient with reduced uncertainty caused by ambiguity; 3) detecting the ionosphere difference between ground stations to facilitate the detection of airborne monitors.

To compare new monitor's performance with old ones with aspects of e.g. Probability of Missed Detection (PMD) for different fault size, time to alarm. The proposed monitor should be able to protect users under more sensitive situations.

To validate if the new monitors are able to satisfy the CAT III requirements by a exhaustive simulation test considering impact factors e.g. the ionosphere gradient profile, the distance between aircraft and ground station and etc. The maximum undetectable error for each monitor and each case is calculated. This is a necessary step to be certified for operation in civil aviation.

25202520.label: Major findings and research outcome
25202520.value: Five major findings are summarized below: 1. Through analyzing data from the Hong Kong Satellite Positioning Reference Station Network, it was found that all significant ionospheric gradients in Hong Kong were caused by equatorial plasma bubbles, with their occurrence strongly influenced by solar activity [4, 5]. These gradients were most frequent during the midnight hours of spring and autumn equinoxes under high solar activity. Simulations revealed that ionospheric anomalies have the greatest impact when a satellite's ionospheric pierce point moves parallel to the magnetic equator within the equatorial ionization anomaly region. 2. By deriving a closed-form expression for the maximum undetected ionosphere-induced error, it was found that undetected errors vary significantly depending on ionospheric conditions [3]. Severe gradients caused by near-stationary ionospheric fronts can be fully mitigated by airborne ionospheric monitors, whereas slow-moving plasma bubbles can induce undetected errors of several meters. For moderate gradients, the maximum undetected error decreases linearly as the airborne monitor successfully detects anomalies. 3. The project developed a dual-frequency ionosphere gradient monitor, which addresses issues faced by single-frequency monitors [2, 8]. It was found that residual troposphere errors can trigger unnecessary false alarms and missed detections in single-frequency monitors. Furthermore, single-frequency monitors require prolonged filtering periods under such conditions. In contrast, the proposed dual-frequency monitor effectively eliminates troposphere-induced errors, enhancing detection accuracy and reducing filtering periods. 4. Analyzing nominal ionospheric conditions in Hong Kong, the project found that a quadratic polynomial expression best represents the overbounding value of the standard deviation of ionospheric spatial gradients [1]. Seasonal trends were observed, with larger gradients occurring during the spring and autumn equinoxes between 2012 and 2020. 5. By applying machine learning methods, it was demonstrated that geodetic GNSS receivers, when combined with decision tree algorithms and reduced multipath effects, can detect amplitude scintillation with accuracy exceeding 99% [6, 7]. This performance matches that of specialized scintillation monitoring receivers, highlighting the potential of machine learning for civil aviation applications.

25202520.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
25202520.value: The advancements achieved in this project lay a robust foundation for future research in ionospheric monitoring and GBAS enhancement, particularly for civil aviation applications. Moving forward, we aim to explore innovative methods for low-latitude ionosphere monitoring using both local and wide-area reference networks. A key focus will be on refining ionospheric modeling techniques. We plan to extend isotropic ordinary kriging to anisotropic kriging for ionosphere interpolation, enabling a more accurate representation of the complex and dynamic ionosphere in low-latitude regions. Following interpolation, we will develop advanced ionosphere error overbounding methods to achieve tighter bounds and improved service availability. In particular, the quantile overbounding method will be applied to account for the temporal and spatial correlations of ionospheric errors. By predicting specific quantiles at a given probability, this approach ensures model conservatism while maintaining practical effectiveness. Additionally, we propose a network-based ionosphere monitoring strategy that leverages existing GNSS monitoring receivers near GBAS facilities. This approach will enable real-time detection of ionospheric anomalies and provide early warnings to GBAS facilities, enhancing system reliability and safety. This research roadmap aims to advance ionospheric monitoring techniques, address low-latitude challenges, and further strengthen the safety and reliability of GBAS operations.

25202520.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
25202520.value: This project focuses on facilitating the development of ionosphere monitoring for dual-frequency GBAS which is used by aircraft during approach and landing. GBAS relies on signals from satellites, but disruptions caused by changes in the Earth atmosphere, particularly in a layer called the ionosphere, can interfere with their safety. To address this, the project developed advanced methods to detect and monitor these ionosphere disturbances. It analysed data from Hong Kong, a low-latitude region especially affected by these disturbances, to understand the ionosphere during nominal and anomalous conditions. It also evaluated the impact of the ionosphere gradient on GBAS and introduced tools to monitor the threatening gradients in the ionosphere. The designed methods aim to constrain the harm of ionosphere anomaly on GBAS users. By exploring the second frequency measurements, the newly designed monitor outperforms the current monitor under more sensitive situations and satisfies the CAT III requirements. The research output helps GBAS development and facilitate the GBAS employment in wider areas. In essence, this work contributes to making air travel safer for passengers and helps ensure that navigation technologies keep up with the growing demands of modern aviation.

25203420.label: Project Title(Chinese)
25203420.value: 配置超高強混凝土的FRP-混凝土-鋼組合雙壁空心梁

25203420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25203420.value: The deterioration of bridges constructed with steel and concrete is a huge global challenge, while the increasing demand for long-span bridges calls for innovations in the development of lightweight yet stiff and strong girders/beams. In recent years, a significant amount of research has explored the use of ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) in bridges because of its high strength/modulus-to-weight ratio. However, the practical application of UHPC in bridges has so far been limited, largely due to its high cost because of the use of expensive steel fibres to enhance the strength/ductility of the material in tension. Nevertheless, the use of steel fibres does not eliminate the brittleness of UHPC in compression. Furthermore, the long-term durability of steel-reinforced UHPC structures in severe environments (e.g., marine environment) is an issue that has yet to be clarified. This project aims to develop an innovative type of cost-effective beams with high strength/stiffness-to-weight ratios as well as excellent durability and ductility, for use as long-span bridge girders (up to 40 meters). These are achieved by the innovative use of UHPC without steel fibres in an emerging form of hybrid beams, namely, hybrid fibre-reinforced polymer (FRP)-concrete-steel double-skin tubular beams (DSTBs). Moreover, coarse aggregate is included in such UHPC to further reduce its cost and increase its modulus, leading to an ultra-high-strength concrete (UHSC). The resulting beam, referred to herein as a UHSC-DSTB, consists of an FRP outer tube, a steel inner tube placed towards the tension side and a UHSC layer sandwiched between the two tubes. The elimination of steel fibres from UHPC substantially reduces (typically halves) the material cost, and the consequent weaknesses of the material are overcome instead by the structural form: the FRP tube serves as a protective skin against corrosion and provides effective confinement to improve the ductility of the UHSC in compression, while the steel tube serves as ductile longitudinal reinforcement to resist tensile stresses. In this project, a study will first be conducted to develop UHSC with a compressive strength of over 150 MPa using locally available raw materials. A combined experimental and theoretical study will then be conducted to gain a comprehensive understanding of, and a design method for, the flexural behaviour of UHSC-DSTBs. The project will meet a very important socio-economic need in Hong Kong, the rest of China and beyond by providing a cost-effective solution for durable long-span beams/girders for bridges and other structures in severe environments (e.g., coastal structures). 鋼混凝土橋樑的劣化已經成為世界各國共同關注的嚴重問題。另一方面，城市基礎建設的發展對於大跨度橋樑的需求不斷增長。為此亟需在開發輕質高強的梁構件方面進行創新。超高性能混凝土（UHPC）具有超高強、高彈模、輕質等特點；近年來，針對其在橋樑結構中的應用進行了大量的研究。但是，迄今為止，UHPC在橋樑結構中的應用仍然十分有限，主要原因在於其使用了價格昂貴的鋼纖維，用以提高其拉伸強度及韌性。然而鋼纖維並不能完全消除UHPC抗壓脆性的問題。此外，鋼纖維對於處在惡劣環境（例如，海洋環境）中的UHPC結構的耐久性的影響尚不明確。 本項目旨在開發一種低成本、輕質、高強、高剛度且具有出色的耐久性及延性的新型梁構件，可用於大跨度（可達40米）橋樑結構。該新型梁構件是基於一種新型FRP-混凝土-鋼組合雙壁空心構件形式，並採用了不含鋼纖維但是含粗骨料的UHPC（稱之為超高強混凝土，即UHSC）。去除鋼纖維且添加粗骨料能夠大幅降低UHPC的成本（通常減少一半）並增加其彈性模量。該新型梁構件截面由FRP外管，鋼內管及填充于兩管之間的UHSC組成；鋼內管置於梁截面受拉側以增加梁截面的抗彎剛度。外層FRP管的約束作用能夠避免UHSC由於缺少鋼纖維而產生的脆性問題，同時FRP管作為保護層可提高構件的耐久性；內層鋼管則作為縱向延性增強材料抵抗拉伸應力。 本項目將首先研究如何使用本地原材料配製抗壓強度超過150 MPa的UHSC。然後將通過試驗與理論相結合的研究方法，全面研究新型梁構件的抗彎性能並提出設計方法。 本項目將為處於惡劣環境（例如，海洋環境）中的橋樑及其他結構對高性能大跨度梁構件的需求提供經濟有效的解決方案，從而滿足中國香港、內地及其他地區非常重要的社會經濟需求。

25210420.label: Realisation of objectives
25210420.value: In relation to Objective 1, we successfully characterized the in vitro effects of PM2.5 on oxidative stress and inflammation using human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2b). The studies covered a wide range of urban and rural environments across different cities, providing a comprehensive view of the biological impact of particulate matter under varying environmental conditions. The findings demonstrated that PM2.5 samples from different locations induced oxidative stress and proinflammatory in human lung cells in a dose-dependent manner, with urban samples generally showing higher toxic potencies than those from suburban or rural areas. This highlights the significant impact of urban pollution sources on PM2.5 toxicity, such as vehicular emissions and industrial activities, which are typically more prevalent in urban settings. These markers were crucial for assessing the cellular responses induced by PM2.5 and understanding the mechanisms behind the health effects associated with air pollution. In relation to Objective 2, we applied integrated mixture-toxicity experiments and modeling to quantify the contributions of specific components of PM2.5 to its overall toxic effects. Key components analyzed included trace metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and biological components such as endotoxin. By validating the concentration addition (CA) model for mixture effects of various components in PM2.5, we provided quantitative insights into how individual components influenced the toxicity of PM2.5. Metals were frequently identified as major contributors, responsible for a significant portion of the oxidative stress observed in cell cultures. Endotoxin, despite its low ambient concentrations, was shown to have a profound impact on inflammation and oxidative stress markers, highlighting its importance in the overall toxicity profile of PM2.5. The application of these advanced modeling techniques allowed for a nuanced understanding of the interaction between different PM2.5 components and their collective impact on health, emphasizing that the toxicity of particulate matter is not solely dependent on its mass but significantly influenced by its chemical and biological makeup. In relation to Objective 3, utilizing positive matrix factorization (PMF), we eeffectively mapped out the sources of PM2.5 and quantified their contributions to the particle's toxicity. This source apportionment was instrumental in identifying the specific activities and conditions contributing to the harmful effects of PM2.5. We differentiated between various sources such as traffic emissions, industrial activities, natural sources (e.g., dust), and secondary aerosols. In urban settings, traffic and industrial emissions were pinpointed as major contributors to PM2.5 toxicity, heavily influencing the oxidative stress and inflammatory responses observed in vitro. Conversely, in rural areas, natural sources like dust played a more significant role. This detailed source apportionment provided crucial insights into the relative toxicity of emissions from different sources, offering a clear direction for targeted pollution control measures. By understanding which sources contribute most to the harmful effects of PM2.5, policymakers and environmental agencies can better tailor their strategies to reduce specific emissions and mitigate their health impacts. The project objectives were comprehensively achieved, advancing the field of environmental health by providing a nuanced understanding of how urban-specific PM2.5 impacts human health. The integration of chemical and biological analyses with advanced modeling techniques established a new benchmark for research and policy-making in air quality management. By demonstrating the importance of both chemical and biological components of PM2.5, the research emphasized the necessity of a multifaceted approach to tackling air quality and public health challenges. This comprehensive methodology ensures that future air quality improvement strategies are based on a profound understanding of the sources and constituents of air pollution and their direct health implications. Overall, the project not only deepened scientific knowledge but also laid a robust foundation for developing effective, context-specific air quality management policies, thereby enhancing public health protection against the adverse effects of air pollution.

25210420.label: Major findings and research outcome
25210420.value: The project delivers a thorough analysis of PM2.5 toxicity, highlighting the intricate interplay between its chemical and biological components and their sources. The study reveals that despite reductions in the mass emissions of organic carbons in PM2.5 with higher combustion temperatures, the decrease in toxicity is less pronounced due to the persistence of highly toxic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). Additionally, it shows a significant contribution of endotoxin from gram-negative bacteria to the induction of interleukin-8 (IL-8), far exceeding its relative mass fraction in PM2.5. The source of endotoxin shifts from natural at coastal sites to predominantly anthropogenic in urban settings. Trace metals are identified as major contributors to oxidative stress, with their effects varying significantly between urban areas—dominated by traffic and industrial emissions—and rural areas influenced more by natural sources. These findings underscore the need for air quality management strategies that go beyond reducing overall PM2.5 concentrations to specifically target the most harmful components and manage their primary sources effectively. To address these challenges, the study introduces a novel approach that integrates the unequal toxic potencies of various industrial PMs to propose health-oriented control strategies. It particularly highlights the iron and steel industry (ISI) as emitting PM2.5 with a toxic potency significantly higher than those from the cement and power industries. By prioritizing control measures in high-potency sectors like the ISI, the strategy aims for more effective health risk reductions at lower costs. Integrating field and laboratory data with model-simulated PM mass concentration under ultralow emission scenarios, the research provides insights into the adverse effects of exposure to industry-emitted PMs. This facilitates the formulation of prioritized control strategies to effectively reduce toxic potency-adjusted PM exposure risks. The project emphasizes the necessity of shifting from traditional mass-based to health-oriented air pollution control strategies. By focusing on the most toxic PM components and considering their source-specific potencies, these strategies can more effectively mitigate public health impacts from air pollution. In summary, the research advocates for a tailored approach to air quality management that considers local environmental and urban contexts, essential for addressing the diverse and location-specific health risks associated with PM2.5 pollution. This approach underscores a paradigm shift in how we manage and mitigate air pollution to better protect public health.

25210420.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
25210420.value: The extensive findings on PM2.5 toxicity provide a robust foundation for further development in several key areas. Future research could expand on integrating advanced molecular biology techniques, such as CRISPR/Cas9, to dissect the specific cellular pathways affected by different PM2.5 components, enhancing understanding of mechanistic toxicology. There is also substantial potential in applying machine learning algorithms to predict toxicity based on PM2.5 composition, which could lead to real-time pollution risk assessments and more dynamic public health responses. Moreover, the development of more sophisticated source apportionment models that incorporate meteorological data could improve the accuracy of predicting PM2.5 behavior and its impact under changing climate conditions. Additionally, exploring cost-effective and sustainable technologies for the removal or conversion of the most harmful PM2.5 constituents directly from the air could provide practical solutions for urban environments heavily burdened by air pollution. Finally, there is a significant opportunity to develop and refine policies that specifically target the reduction of the most toxic PM2.5 components, informed by the detailed source and component-specific toxicity data provided by these studies. These advancements would not only deepen scientific understanding but also enhance the effectiveness of interventions aimed at reducing the health impacts of air pollution worldwide.

25210420.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
25210420.value: This project examined the harmful impacts of fine particulate matter (PM2.5), tiny air particles that can penetrate deep into human lungs, causing health issues. The findings revealed that PM2.5 is particularly toxic when originating from sources like traffic and industrial emissions, rather than natural sources such as dust. It was found that while modern combustion methods can reduce the overall quantity of these particles, some highly toxic components, like certain chemicals, do not diminish as significantly. The study highlighted that not all PM2.5 components are equally harmful. For instance, endotoxins from bacteria significantly trigger inflammation, despite being a minor part of these particles. The findings suggest that effective air pollution mitigation strategies should focus not just on reducing the volume of particulate matter but also on controlling its most harmful components and managing their sources. To address these challenges, we proposed a new method that prioritizes control strategies based on the toxicity of particles from various industries, identifying those from the iron and steel industry as particularly toxic. This approach advocates for a shift from traditional methods to more health-focused strategies, considering the specific needs of different areas to better protect public health.

25213320.label: Project Title(Chinese)
25213320.value: 下一代全球土地覆蓋圖: 多光譜激光掃描方法

25213320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25213320.value: The first global land cover (GLC) map has been found as early as the 2000s with 1-km resolution produced by coarse resolution satellite images, e.g. AVHRR and MODIS. During the last decade, the world’s first GLC map with 30-m resolution, i.e., GlobeLand30, was generated using Landsat images. All these GLC products not only physically record the distribution of the Earth’s resources, but also serve the purposes of sustainable development, climate modelling and land management. To provide a scientific vision toward the dynamic change of the Earth, it is foreseeable to have the next generation GLC map with resolution further improved up to 1- to 10-m resolution with 3D capability, hopefully covering more land cover classes. Nevertheless, the effects of shadowing and tilted buildings found in high resolution satellite images all prevent such a development. As a result, a turn-around solution points to the use of light detection and ranging (LiDAR) technology. The main objective of the proposal is to develop airborne LiDAR data processing algorithms to support the production of a fine-scale, large area 3D land cover map. Though traditional monochromatic LiDAR system lacks fruitful spectral information, the recently invented multispectral LiDAR system, such as Optech Titan, which is equipped with three laser channels, thus overcomes such a drawback. Also, photon-counting and Geiger-mode LiDAR systems are capable of collecting significantly denser and higher resolution of LiDAR point cloud than traditional LiDAR systems do. Therefore, the use of LiDAR techniques to aid in land cover classification seems sound and promising. To embrace the next generation GLC mapping based on multispectral LiDAR and other sensors, several research voids should be filled. Specifically, this Early Career Scheme (ECS) proposal aims to build on the Principal Investigator’s (PI) previous research by developing various LiDAR data processing algorithms to 1) improve the radiometric and geometric quality of LiDAR data products so as to support accurate classification, 2) develop a universal deep learning based classification framework and point cloud training database, 3) propose a practical framework for LiDAR-based GLC mapping. The project will first utilize Hong Kong and Toronto as testbeds to study the possible land cover classes and demonstrate the developed techniques, in which city-scale airborne LiDAR data are available. The research will be treated as a “proof-of-concept” showcase to international societies, including ISPRS, NASA and United Nations, in order to subsequently discuss the practical strategies and trigger the development of the next-generation GLC map. 早於2000年代，最初的全球土地覆蓋（Global Land Cover - GLC）地圖是利用了低解像度衛星相片，例如AVHRR和MODIS去製作。這些地圖的解像度是大約1公里。 在過去的十年，GlobeLand30產生了，它是世界上第一個由Landsat圖像生成，解像度為30米的GLC地圖。所有這些GLC地圖不僅記錄了地球資源的分佈，也用於可持續發展、氣候模擬和土地管理，為科學提供一個對地球動態變化的新角度。可以預見解像度進一步提高到1至10米，並具有3D功能的下一代GLC地圖可以涵蓋更多的土地覆蓋類別。儘管如此，在高解像度衛星圖像中出現的陰影和傾斜建築物都妨礙了更精準GLC地圖的發展。基於這技術上的缺陷，光學遙感雷達（LiDAR）技術就成為了解決方案。 該研究項目的主要目的是開發光學航空遙感雷達 (Airborne LiDAR) 數據處理的演算法及系統，以生成更精細的大面積三維土地覆蓋地圖。一般的單光譜LiDAR系統缺乏豐富的光譜信息，最近發明的多光譜光學遙感雷達系統，例如Optech Titan配備了三個激光光譜，因此克服了單光譜的缺陷。此外，具有光子計算和Geiger模式的光學遙感雷達系統能夠收集比傳統光學遙感雷達系統更密集，更高密度的雲點數據。這些新的光學遙感雷達技術有助於土地覆蓋分類的技術發展，為光學航空遙感雷達拓展一個新的發展領域。 多光譜光學遙感雷達和其他遙感技術為下一代的GLC地圖發展填補一些研究的空白。這項初入門研究計劃（ECS）是基於首席研究員之前的研究。研究主要是開發各種光學遙感雷達數據處理演算法，以1）改善雲點數據的輻射強度質量與座標質量去達致更準確的地域分類，2）基於通用深度學習的分類框架，建立雲點培訓數據庫，3）為光學遙感雷達的GLC地圖發展建立技術框架。 該項目將首先利用於香港和多倫多之雲點數據作為測試平台來研究土地覆蓋分類及其技術發展的可能性。這兩個地方具有城市規模的光學航空遙感雷達數據已經採集並可作研究用途。該研究將驗證利用光學遙感雷達發展生成下一代GLC地圖的可能性及可行性，並向國際學會及組織展示其成果，以帶動研後討論及日後發展策略。

25214420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25214420.value: Safety training is key to preventing accidents in the construction industry. Recently, immersive virtual reality (IVR) has been adopted to safety training in construction industry. However, if workers keep in mind that IVR is not real and do not take an IVR safety training seriously, the training cannot effectively prevent accidents or reduce the impact of incidents. The proposed project aims to improve the attitudes of construction workers towards safety trainings (with IVR and with traditional media such as PowerPoint slides). The project uses an innovative approach that allows trainees to experience the perspective of a victim of a construction accident via an IVR simulation before they begin safety training. Perspective taking with IVR has a long tradition in the field of media psychology and has been shown to be effective in many contexts. However, this approach has not been applied to construction safety before. Previous studies have examined the use of IVR for construction safety trainings. The innovative approach proposed in this project is about preparing trainees’ attitude for safety training, which involves using IVR to let trainees experience a victim’s perspective in an accident. Taking the victim’s perspective encourages trainees empathize with victims and therefore take the relevant safety training seriously. Therefore, the IVR perspective-taking experience occurs before the safety training. The proposed project focuses on two types of construction accidents: falling from a height and being struck by an object. The findings can be used to improve the attitudes of workers towards construction safety training and the effectiveness of safety training. They can also impact safety training protocols in other high-risk, labor-intensive industries. 安全培訓是防止建築行業發生事故的關鍵所在。近些年來，沈浸式虛擬現實技術（IVR）也已被用於建築行業的安全培訓中。然而，其中還存在壹些問題。例如，如果工人意識到自己只是置身於沈浸式虛擬現實(IVR)技術中，而並不是真實的，從而不能認真接受在沈浸式虛擬現實(IVR)技術中的安全培訓，則該培訓將無法有效地預防或減少事故所帶來的嚴重後果和影響。 本項目研究宗旨在於探索改善建築工人對於安全培訓的態度的方法和理論（應用沈浸式虛擬現實(IVR)和傳統媒體，如，PowerPoint幻燈片等）。項目的創新點在於使受訓人員在開始進行安全培訓前，以建築事故受害者的視角，根據沈浸式虛擬現實(IVR)技術中視角轉換理論，從而進行模擬體驗。然而，沈浸式虛擬現實(IVR)視角轉換理論在媒介心理學領域的應用也具有悠久的歷史，並且它已經證明在許多情況下都是有效的。但是，這種借助沈浸式虛擬現實(IVR)技術進行視角轉換的方法，尚未被應用於建築安全培訓項目中。 在以往的研究中，已經對沈浸式虛擬現實技術理論(IVR)在建築安全培訓中的應用進行過測試。而本項目的創新點在於，受訓人員在沈浸式虛擬現實技術(IVR)中，以受害者視角體驗在事故中安全培訓的重要性，並且改善受訓人員對於安全培訓的態度。通過實驗，旨在探析讓受訓人員能夠站在受害者的角度進行思考，並且鼓勵受訓人員對受害者進行“移情”，由此可以激發受訓人員認真對待相關的安全培訓的自主行為。因此，在沈浸式虛擬現實技術(IVR)中視角轉換的行為需要發生在安全培訓之前。而在此次項目研究中，將著重關註兩種建築事故，即，建築人員從高處墜落和被物體撞擊。項目研究理論及成果可用於改善工人對建築安全培訓的態度和安全培訓的有效性。乃至延伸、拓展應用於其他高風險、勞動密集型行業的安全培訓項目方案中。

25214420.label: Realisation of objectives
25214420.value: This research project aimed to investigate the effects of immersive virtual reality (IVR) simulations of experiencing accidents on attitudes, and learning outcomes in construction safety training. The three objectives were realized through a series of carefully designed IVR scenarios, iterative development, and multiple lab-based experiments. Below is a detailed account of how each objective was approached and achieved. The first objective focused on designing and evaluating IVR simulations that portray fall-from-height accidents from the victim’s perspective. The initial challenge was to create a scenario that would be perceived as an accident rather than an injury. After several design iterations/trials, the chosen approach involved simulating a situation where the accident was inadvertently caused by the participant. This required a task that split the participant’s attention between work tasks and safety hazards, such as inspecting overhead work while standing near an unguarded edge. The simulation was implemented using a IVR environment and tested in a lab-based experiment (Study 1 in this research project) involving 55 participants, including pilot cases. Participants engaged in the scenario and were later assessed on their attitudes and motivation toward safety training. The experiment revealed that perceived risk influenced motivation and intention to follow safety procedures. However, an unexpected finding was the potential for hazard desensitization—participants who experienced fatal accidents in a simulated environment showed reduced sensitivity to similar hazards afterward. This insight prompted a reconsideration of how IVR simulations should be designed to balance emotional impact and the potential issue of hazard desensitization. The design process was presented in a peer-reviewed conference paper (Ho et al., 2022). The finding of this study was turned into a manuscript for publication. Regarding objective 2, which is to investigate the effects of IVR simulations of accidents involving victims struck by objects, IVR simulations were carefully designed. Due to the potential issue of hazard desensitization mentioned above, the IVR simulation of struck-by-object accidents was designed in a manner that the trainees experience the accidents as a witness. The goal was to maintain emotional engagement while minimizing the risk of desensitization. A key design challenge was determining whether the victim should be portrayed as a stranger or a familiar co-worker (when they witness the accident in the IVR simulation) To simulate a familiar relationship, the research team developed narrative scenes that established emotional bonds between the participant and the virtual victim. The information presented in the narrative scenes become background story about the close relationships the virtual victim and the co-workers. Two lab-based experiments were conducted. The first experiment (Study 2 in this research project) involved 101 participants (including the pilot) and compared conditions with and without background stories (and a control condition where no accident occurred). The design process required careful scripting, voice acting, and environmental cues to ensure realism and emotional resonance. The experiments successfully enabled the investigation of empathy and motivational responses, with variations in narrative and perspective yielding distinct effects. Regarding objective 3 which concerns the effects of IVR-based simulation of experiencing accidents on learning outcomes of safety training, in Study 2, a piece of traditional safety training material (i.e., a safety training video) was exposed to the participants after they experienced the IVR simulation of witnessing accidents. No significant effects were found in the participants’ memory retention of the safety training video shown after the exposure to the IVR simulation. Although no significant differences were found in memory retention of safety content, the study provided valuable insights into how IVR design influences emotional and motivational engagement. These findings contribute to the understanding of how immersive technologies can be tailored to enhance attitudes and motivation regarding safety training. Study 2 and its findings were turned into a manuscript submitted to the journal Safety Science, which has reached the final stage of the publication process. An additional study was designed and conducted (Study 3 in this research project) with 185 participants (including the pilot), expanded the design to include two pre-accident scenes: a casual conversation after lunch and a work-related scene with a phone call involving the victim’s family. These scenes were used to build emotional depth and were selectively masked in control conditions using noise from the environment. In addition to the factor of presence of background story portraying the virtual victim’s close relationships with co-workers, an additional factor in Study 3 was perspective, which refers to the contrasts between experiencing the IVR-simulated accident from a first-person perspective (as a co-worker in the IVR environment) and experiencing it from a third-person perspective (as a purely observer or like a ghost in the IVR environment). A manuscript is in preparation to report Study 3 and its findings. The project period coincided with the years when COVID significantly impacted Hong Kong. Consequently, the data collection process was hindered due to the necessity of participants wearing a head-mounted display IVR device during the experiment procedure. This direct contact to the device raised concerns about the potential spread of COVID. Consequently, the data collection for three lab-based studies was delayed or rescheduled to occur during the gaps between the “waves” of COVID cases in Hong Kong.

25214420.label: Major findings and research outcome
25214420.value: Study 1 found that experiencing an IVR-simulated accident indirectly influences motivation for safety training via its effect on perceived risk. It also revealed a potential risk of desensitization - trainees who experienced fatal accidents in a safe simulated environment became less sensitive to similar hazards. This outcome raised concerns about the issue of hazard desensitization of experiencing accidents from the victim perspective. This study and findings were converted into a manuscript and submitted to journals. The publication process encountered challenges (including a 2.5-year of publication including two rounds of major revision but resulted in a rejection) in convincing reviewers to accept the potential risk of hazard desensitization associated with the use of IVR simulation in safety training. The manuscript (entitled “Simulated Hazards in Virtual Reality-Based Safety Training: Does Greater Danger Mean Greater Effectiveness?”) is still being actively revised and being targeting to suitable journals. Study 2 examined the effects of witnessing an accident in IVR simulations. While no significant differences were found in memory retention of safety training materials, the study revealed that witnessing an accident involving an unfamiliar co-worker improved attitudes toward safety, whereas witnessing an accident involving a familiar co-worker (introduced via background story) significantly increased motivation to learn about safety. These findings are documented in a manuscript titled “Effects of Witnessing Accidents in Virtual Reality on Reception of Safety Training: The Role of Empathy toward Virtual Victims”, which is in the final stage of publication at the journal Safety Science (according to the journal’s editorial team “should become acceptable for publication pending suitable minor revision”). Study 3 explored the psychological mechanisms underlying the effects of perspective and narrative. It found that using first-person perspective to witness an accident in IVR simulations indirectly enhanced motivation and attitudes through increased embodiment and social presence. Background story enhanced motivation by increasing perceived social closeness and empathy toward the virtual victim. These insights are being prepared for publication in a manuscript titled “Enhancing Safety Education through Empathic VR Experiences: Influences of First-Person Perspective and Victim’s Background Story.” PhD student Daniel Munoz, supported by the project, developed and validated a design framework for narratives in VR. He graduated in June 2025 and obtained a faculty position at the Department of Interactive Media at HKBU. The project also contributed to a collaborative manuscript on VR interventions for adolescents.

25214420.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
25214420.value: This research has demonstrated that IVR simulations can enhance safety training by fostering empathy and emotional engagement. Future development could focus on applying these findings in real-world construction training programs, particularly by integrating personalized storytelling and adaptive perspectives to suit different trainee profiles. One promising direction is the creation of scalable VR modules that adjust emotional intensity based on user responses, helping to maintain engagement while avoiding desensitization. Longitudinal studies could also be conducted to assess the lasting impact of empathic VR experiences on safety behavior and hazard awareness over time. Additionally, the narrative design framework developed during the project can be expanded to support VR training in other high-risk industries, such as manufacturing or healthcare. Collaborations with industry partners will be essential to pilot these applications and refine them based on field feedback.

25214420.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
25214420.value: This research project explored how virtual reality (VR) can be used to improve safety training for construction workers. Construction sites are dangerous places, and traditional safety training often fails to emotionally engage workers or help them fully understand the risks. The project aimed to make safety training more impactful by using VR to simulate real-life accidents in a safe, controlled environment. In one part of the study, participants experienced a fall-from-height accident in VR. While this raised awareness, it also showed that repeated exposure to simulated danger might reduce sensitivity to real risks. To address this, later simulations had participants witness accidents happening to virtual co-workers, rather than experiencing them directly. The research found that when participants saw a familiar character get hurt—especially one they had bonded with through storytelling—they were more motivated to learn about safety. Using a first-person perspective and emotional background stories helped participants feel more connected and engaged. This project shows that VR can make safety training more effective by encouraging empathy and emotional involvement. These insights can help create better training programs that not only teach safety rules but also inspire workers to care more deeply about staying safe on the job.

25215020.label: Project Title(Chinese)
25215020.value: 下一代无线网络中的巨址接入技术

25215020.label: Project Objectives
25215020.value: Promote Paradigm Shift from Human-Type Communications to Massive Machine-Type Communications: Following the remarkable success of cellular networks in connecting people all over the world in the past decades, the next wave of wireless technology is anticipated to proliferate in connecting machines for myriad new applications, e.g., sensors and robots in smart factories, vehicles in intelligent transportation systems, etc. Such a paradigm shift from human-type communications to machine-type communications is mainly driven by the dawn of Internet of Things (IoT), which will significantly benefit the way we live everyday lives. Contrary to human-type high-speed communications, the accent of IoT communications is on providing low-rate connectivity to tens of billions of devices. Consequently, the fifth-generation (5G) and beyond cellular communication technologies call for radically innovative solutions to support massive machine-type communications. Targeting such massive IoT connectivity, the proposed research aims to design the next-generation cellular technologies that can enable low-rate communications from a massive number of IoT devices. Identify Two Key Research Problems for Massive Machine-Type Communications - Device Activity Detection and Short-Packet Transmissions: One notable feature of the considered systems is the sporadic device-activity pattern arising from the fact that devices often stay in the sleep mode to reduce the energy consumption and only become active when triggered by emergent events. Therefore, only a small but random subset of the devices are active at any given time. The central questions for massive IoT connectivity thus lie in figuring out how to detect the active devices from a massive number of devices (who are transmitting) and decode a vast number of short data packets sent by active devices (what are being transmitted). Unfortunately, the legacy human-type communication technologies cannot address the above issues. First, the current random access schemes require users to frequently retransmit their preambles for accurate user detection in massively connected networks, which would increase the access latency and energy consumption for the delay-sensitive and battery-constrained IoT devices. Second, high-speed data transmission techniques are not designed to support short-packet transmissions. This motivates our research program to devise novel approaches that are both theoretically sound and practically feasible for detecting active devices and decoding short data packets in massive IoT connectivity networks. Explore Fundamental Limits of Device Detection: This research project will investigate an innovative random access solution that can detect the active devices in massively connected networks accurately and quickly. Further, we aim to justify its advantage over the legacy random access schemes by examining its fundamental scaling law between the number of detectable devices and the duration of detection time. Devise Practical Approaches for Device Detection: This research project will also consider practical issues for device detection under the new random access scheme. Along this line, we first aim to develop efficient approaches to leverage the side information (e.g., sensors deployed in proximity for detecting fire tend to become active concurrently) for device detection. Next, we would devise robust schemes to detect the low-cost devices when they transmit their preambles asynchronously due to lack of coordination. Explore Fundamental Limits of Short-Packet Transmissions: In addition to device detection, we aim to examine fundamental limits of information decoding in massive connectivity systems. Towards this end, we will investigate the scaling law between the number of decodable messages and the data transmission time duration. Devise Practical Approaches for Short-Packet Transmissions: Alongside the theoretical investigations, we also plan to design practical solutions to enable short-packet transmissions in such massively connected systems. For instance, we will propose efficient power control algorithms based on local channel state information at each device that can alleviate the considerable overhead to exchange global channel state information among a massive number of devices. We also plan to elucidate the role of non-orthogonal multiple access in such dense connectivity settings, considering that the number of devices is much larger than that of receive antennas.
rows: Promote Paradigm Shift from Human-Type Communications to Massive Machine-Type Communications: Following the remarkable success of cellular networks in connecting people all over the world in the past decades, the next wave of wireless technology is anticipated to proliferate in connecting machines for myriad new applications, e.g., sensors and robots in smart factories, vehicles in intelligent transportation systems, etc. Such a paradigm shift from human-type communications to machine-type communications is mainly driven by the dawn of Internet of Things (IoT), which will significantly benefit the way we live everyday lives. Contrary to human-type high-speed communications, the accent of IoT communications is on providing low-rate connectivity to tens of billions of devices. Consequently, the fifth-generation (5G) and beyond cellular communication technologies call for radically innovative solutions to support massive machine-type communications. Targeting such massive IoT connectivity, the proposed research aims to design the next-generation cellular technologies that can enable low-rate communications from a massive number of IoT devices.

Identify Two Key Research Problems for Massive Machine-Type Communications - Device Activity Detection and Short-Packet Transmissions: One notable feature of the considered systems is the sporadic device-activity pattern arising from the fact that devices often stay in the sleep mode to reduce the energy consumption and only become active when triggered by emergent events. Therefore, only a small but random subset of the devices are active at any given time. The central questions for massive IoT connectivity thus lie in figuring out how to detect the active devices from a massive number of devices (who are transmitting) and decode a vast number of short data packets sent by active devices (what are being transmitted). Unfortunately, the legacy human-type communication technologies cannot address the above issues. First, the current random access schemes require users to frequently retransmit their preambles for accurate user detection in massively connected networks, which would increase the access latency and energy consumption for the delay-sensitive and battery-constrained IoT devices. Second, high-speed data transmission techniques are not designed to support short-packet transmissions. This motivates our research program to devise novel approaches that are both theoretically sound and practically feasible for detecting active devices and decoding short data packets in massive IoT connectivity networks.

Explore Fundamental Limits of Device Detection: This research project will investigate an innovative random access solution that can detect the active devices in massively connected networks accurately and quickly. Further, we aim to justify its advantage over the legacy random access schemes by examining its fundamental scaling law between the number of detectable devices and the duration of detection time.

Devise Practical Approaches for Device Detection: This research project will also consider practical issues for device detection under the new random access scheme. Along this line, we first aim to develop efficient approaches to leverage the side information (e.g., sensors deployed in proximity for detecting fire tend to become active concurrently) for device detection. Next, we would devise robust schemes to detect the low-cost devices when they transmit their preambles asynchronously due to lack of coordination.

Explore Fundamental Limits of Short-Packet Transmissions: In addition to device detection, we aim to examine fundamental limits of information decoding in massive connectivity systems. Towards this end, we will investigate the scaling law between the number of decodable messages and the data transmission time duration.

Devise Practical Approaches for Short-Packet Transmissions: Alongside the theoretical investigations, we also plan to design practical solutions to enable short-packet transmissions in such massively connected systems. For instance, we will propose efficient power control algorithms based on local channel state information at each device that can alleviate the considerable overhead to exchange global channel state information among a massive number of devices. We also plan to elucidate the role of non-orthogonal multiple access in such dense connectivity settings, considering that the number of devices is much larger than that of receive antennas.

25215020.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
25215020.value: The future wireless cellular networks are envisioned to not only enhance broadband access for human-centric applications, but also offer massive connectivity across tens of billions of devices for machine-centric applications empowered by the Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, e.g., smart manufacturing and smart wearables. To embrace the forthcoming era of IoT, the fifth-generation (5G) cellular communication standard has already identified massive machine-type communications as a key use case in future networks. Motivated by this, we plan to devote our endeavour in this research project to a systematic and thorough investigation of massive machine-type communications for realizing IoT. Compared to the legacy human-type communications, many new design challenges arise in achieving massive machine-type communications in IoT networks. On one hand, a key feature of the massively connected IoT networks is the sporadic data traffic: the IoT devices, e.g., sensors, tend to stay in the sleep mode for most of the time for the sake of energy saving, and transmit some data only when triggered by external events. The first challenge of massive connectivity thus lies in dynamically detecting such an unknown set of active devices from a large number of devices. On the other hand, in contrast to the current human-type communications whose focus is on high-speed data transmissions, IoT applications chiefly require low-rate transmissions of short packets. Therefore, the second challenge of massive connectivity is understanding the governing principles of short-packet transmissions so as to decode a tremendous number of small-sized messages from active IoT devices efficiently. The proposed research program aims to devise effective solutions to the above two challenges from both theoretical and practical perspectives. In the first line of inquiry on device activity detection, our project will reveal its fundamental limits via characterizing the scaling law between the number of detectable devices and the detection time duration. Moreover, we will address several practical issues such as asynchronous device detection to approach the performance limits. For the second thread on short-packet transmissions, we will examine the fundamental limits via quantifying the scaling law between the number of decodable messages and the decoding time duration. In addition, this research project will develop innovative framework for power control based on limited channel state information and low-complexity non-orthogonal multiple access to enable short-packet transmissions in practical networks. Our overall vision is to provide both theoretical validation and practical guidance for the design of future cellular architecture and standardization suitable for the IoT roadmap. 未来的无线蜂窝网络不仅仅要为手机用户提供高带宽服务，同时还要为物联网业务（如智能制造和智能穿戴）中成千上万的机器设备提供可靠连接。为了拥抱即将到来的物联网时代，5G蜂窝通信标准已经把大规模机器类通信列为未来网络的一项重要业务。鉴于此，我们将于此项目中系统深入地研究大规模机器类通信技术，以实现物联网万物互联的目标。 和现有的手机通信业务不同，物联网业务中的大规模机器类通信技术面临很多新的挑战。一方面，物联网业务的一大特点是数据传输的突发性：为了节省能量，物联网设备（例如传感器）在大部分时间内处于休眠状态，而只有在外部突发情况触发下才会传输数据。因此，物联网巨址接入的第一项挑战是如何从超大规模设备中快速准确地检测到活跃设备。另一方面，和现有的以高带宽通信为主的手机业务不同，物联网业务往往只涉及低速率的短包传输。因此，物联网巨址接入的第二项挑战是理解短包数据传输的基本原理以实现对超大规模的小尺寸信息进行有效解码这一目标。 此项目意在从理论和工程两个角度解决物联网大规模通信技术遇到的以上两项难题。第一，在活跃设备检测方面，此项目将刻画可检测到的活跃设备数量和设备检测时间之间的对应关系，进而揭示活跃设备检测的理论性能极限。同时，我们将解决活跃设备检测在工程中会遇到的一些技术难题，例如物联网设备的非同步传输，以在实际系统中迫近理论性能极限。第二，在短包通信方面，我们将刻画可被解码的设备数量和解码时间之间的对应关系，进而揭示大规模短包通信的理论性能极限。同时，在实际网络中，我们将研究基于有限信道信息的功率分配、低复杂度的非正交多址接入等技术，已迫近理论性能极限。此项目的最终目标是为适用于物联网的未来网络框架和标准提供理论验证和实际指导。

25215020.label: Realisation of objectives
25215020.value: 1. Realization of Objective 1 Most of the current research on wireless communication is on human-type communication, e.g., how to keep increasing the data rate to satisfy the requirement of users. Supported by this project, we have conducted research on massive machine-type communication (mMTC). This is motivated by the recent advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT) technology. In this project, we have conducted a lot of investigation on how to enable low-latency and low-rate communication of a massive number of IoT devices. This is in sharp contrast to the high-speed human-type communication. Along the line of mMTC, we have published five IEEE journal papers, one IEEE letter, and several IEEE conference papers. Therefore, we have achieved all the goals listed in Objective 1. 2. Realization of Objective 2 Under this project, we have studied two problems under the mMTC – how to detect the active devices from a huge number of IoT devices, and how to facilitate the short-packet transmission from active devices with low latency. These two problems are unique to mMTC, and quite different from the research problems in human-type broadband communication. Therefore, we have achieved the goal of identifying two research problems for mMTC listed in Objective 2. 3. Realization of Objective 3 In our early work L. Liu and W. Yu, "Massive connectivity with massive MIMO-Part I: Device activity detection and channel estimation," IEEE Trans. Signal Process., vol. 66, no. 11, pp. 2933-2946, Jun. 2018. we have revealed that in the asymptotic regime where the number of antennas at the base station goes to infinity, the approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm can perfectly detect all the active IoT devices when the length of the pilot sequences is linear to the number of IoT devices. Under the support of this project, recently, we have revealed the fundamental limits of massive connectivity when the number of antennas at the base station is finite, in the following works Q. Wang, L. Liu, S. Zhang, and C. M. Lau, "Exploiting temporal side information in massive IoT connectivity," IEEE Trans. Wireless Commun., vol. 22, no. 2, pp. 1432-1447, Feb. 2023. Q. Wang, L. Liu, S. Zhang, and C. M. Lau, "On massive IoT connectivity with temporally-correlated user activity," in Proc. IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT), 2021. The key novelty lies in the observation that the device activity usually has strong temporal correlation. For example, if a device (e.g., sensor) is activated at one moment due to some abnormal events, then this device is more likely to be still activated by this event in the near future. In the above works, we have successfully shown that by properly utilizing such temporal correlation in device activity, it is possible to drive the device activity detection error probability to zero asymptotically even if the base station is equipped with one antenna. Therefore, we have achieved the goal of fundamental limit characterization in Objective 3. 4. Realization of Objective 4 We have contributed two points for the practical algorithm design for massive connectivity. First, in the above two works, besides characterization of the fundamental limits, we have also devised practical algorithms that can leverage the temporal correlation in device activity to detect the active devices. Specifically, we take the temporal correlation in device activity into consideration when we design the denoiser function of the AMP algorithm. Second, we have also studied a challenge in a practical mMTC scenario – it is hard to synchronize the low-cost IoT devices. When the preamble sent by each active device is delayed by some unknown number of symbols due to the lack of coordination, device activity detection is more challenging. In the following work L. Liu and Y.-F. Liu, "An efficient algorithm for device detection and channel estimation in asynchronous IoT systems," in Proc. IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing (ICASSP), 2021. we manage to cast the problem of detecting the active devices and estimating their delay and channels into a group LASSO problem. Then, a block coordinate descent algorithm is proposed to solve this problem globally, where the closed-form solution is available when updating each block of variables with the other blocks of variables being fixed. Therefore, we have achieved all the goals listed in Objective 4. 5. Realization of Objective 5 For short packet transmission in mMTC, we designed a novel scheme. Specifically, each device has a set of pilot sequences, while each pilot sequence represents a number of bits. When a device becomes active, it selects its pilot sequence based on which sequence of bits that need to be transmitted. We utilize the covariance-based method for joint device activity detection and short packet decoding. To acquire the covariance matrix of the received signals, a massive MIMO system is considered. Previously works assume perfect analogue-to-digital (ADC) converters for all the antennas at the base station, which is not cost-efficient. In the following work Z. Wang, Y-F. Liu, Z. Wang, L. Liu, H. Pan, and S. Cui, "Device activity detection in mMTC with low-resolution ADCs: A new protocol," IEEE Trans. Wireless Commun., vol. 23, no. 6, pp. 5847-5862, June 2024. we have rigorously shown that with low-resolution ADCs connected to the antenna, the covariance-based method can still work well when the pilot sequence length is linear to the squared root of the number of devices, similar to the fundamental results for the perfect ADC case. Therefore, the goals listed in Objective 5 have been achieved. 6. Realization of Objective 6 As to practical algorithm design, we have devised a low-complexity algorithm to estimate the number of active devices first, and a custom-designed stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm to detect the active devices and decode their messages by detecting which pilot sequences are transmitted by them second. These algorithms are presented in the above work and the following work Z. Wang, Y-F. Liu, and L. Liu, "Covariance-based joint device activity and delay detection in asynchronous mMTC," IEEE Signal Process. Lett., vol. 29, pp.538-542, 2022. Because the covariance matrix of the received signals plays a significant role in the above works, we have also considered the change detection technique such that when the covariance matrix of the received signals changes, we can detect such a change as soon as possible. The results are in the following works R. Liu, L. Liu, D. He, W. Zhang, and E. G. Larsson, "Detecting abrupt change in channel covariance matrix for MIMO communication," IEEE Trans. Wireless Commun., vol. 22, no. 11, pp. 7834-7847, Nov. 2023. R. Liu, L. Liu, D. He, W. Zhang, and E. G. Larsson, "Detection of abrupt change in channel covariance matrix for multi-antenna communication," in Proc. IEEE Global Communications Conference (Globecom), 2021. This can make the covariance-based activity detection and short packet decoding algorithm work in a dynamic scenario. Therefore, all the goals of Objective 6 have been achieved.

25215020.label: Major findings and research outcome
25215020.value: There are three major findings under this project. First, we show that when the temporal correlation in device activity is utilized, then fundamentally speaking, asymptotic device activity detection performance can be achieved by the approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm even when the base station is equipped with a finite number of antennas, as long as the pilot sequence length is linear to the number of devices. This generalizes the previous famous result that without temporal correlation information, perfect device activity detection can be only achieved with an infinite number of antennas. Second, we devise a new AMP algorithm that can utilize the temporal correlation in device activity. Specifically, based on the state evolution, we manage to update the denoiser function in the AMP algorithm by taking the temporal correlation information into account. Extensive simulation results verify that this new AMP algorithm can significantly improve the device activity detection performance. Third, we devise a novel scheme to reduce the delay for short packet transmission in massive connectivity, where the device messages are encoded via the selection of the pilot sequences. A covariance-based mechanism that works with low-resolution analogue-to-digital (ADC) converters connected to a large number of base station antennas has been designed.
