26300020.label: Major findings and research outcome
26300020.value: Inference calculations from numerical and observational data for a not directly measurable quantity (a mesoscale eddy energy dissipation time-scale) was performed, which can be used in numerical ocean models and have been demonstrated to lead to reduction in biases. The works additionally provide leading order constraints for future theoretical work investigating ocean energetic pathways. The established methodology can be applied to other problems (see potential for further development). Further developments for mesoscale eddy parameterisation was performed as part of the present work, leading to a new proposal for how to apply parameterisations to the eddy-permitting regime, which is a target for the next generation of ocean models for use in Earth System Models. The related methodology has shown substantial promise, and is already being seriously considered by ocean model developers in Europe and North America.

26300020.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
26300020.value: Related methodology and/or machinery is the basis of a funded RGC grant (16304021), a submitted GRF, one Royal Society travel grant (KTPR1231008), useful for a recently funded CRF proposal on sea level (C5013-23GF, lead by PolyU), and the project for a HKPFS student (PE22-72533) on inference in relation to coastal sea level, and is being actively pursued. Related work on developing parameterisations is currently being actively pursued in more realistic settings to investigate benefits afforded to physical and biogeochemical responses. The work is forward looking for its impact to the next generation of Earth System Models at the eddy-permitting resolution. The international collaborative links and most of the research tools are already in place, and is likely going to be focus of an upcoming GRF submission.

26300020.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
26300020.value: Inference calculations are able to "back out" quantities that are otherwise difficult to impossible to measure in practice. In this project we developed tools to infer for a quantity relating to ocean turbulence that has not previously measured before, but is of utmost importance for studies related to ocean energetics, as well as numerical model developments, with impacts on future climate change projections using such models. Indeed, our published results show that the inferred quantities lead to reduction in modelling errors, supporting its use in ocean climate models. Furthermore, the developed inference tools in this work can and have been adapted by us to other oceanographic problems, such as inferring for mixing in the South China Sea, uncertain parameters for coastal modelling in the Greater Bay Area, with views to inform on observational and coastal system designs. A tangent piece of research we carried out as part of the present project appears to have substantial promise in improving the next generation Earth System Models, and is being actively pursued by our group in collaboration with collaborators at international modelling centres.

26302320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
26302320.value: Active matter encompasses a wide range of non-equilibrium biological and synthetic systems that convert chemical or other forms of energy into local mechanical work. Active matter can give rise to hitherto dynamical phenomena that are sometimes forbidden in equilibrium systems. Examples include collective behavior, activity-induced phase transition and Brownian ratchet effect. Owing to its biological relevance and potential applications in the design of biomimetic materials, active matter is becoming an increasingly important interdisciplinary research area. Current research on active matter is, however, system specific, and a systematic or unified understanding of different active matter systems is lacking, thereby limiting our understanding of non-equilibrium systems and certain biophysical phenomena. The constituents of active matter often exhibit anisotropic shape. At sufficiently high concentration, these anisotropic constituents can form a nematic liquid crystal phase by developing a long-range orientational ordering but remain disordered in their spatial organizations. Indeed, recent experiments have found that certain biological systems, such as tissue cells and progenitor cells, exhibit nematic phase. Hydrodynamic modeling of active nematics has been successful in describing their microstructures and dynamics. However, current research efforts are focused on less practical, two-dimensional and achiral systems. Many biological and synthetic materials are essentially chiral. For example, DNA and microtubules exhibit chiral structures, and can self-assemble into a chiral (cholesteric) liquid crystalline phase. Another different type of chirality can emerge from constituents’ motions instead of their shapes. For example, E. coli may swim circularly near a boundary, and magnetic particles can spin subject to a rotating magnetic field. In contrast to the aforementioned structural chirality, this new type of chirality does not exist in passive systems, and is thus a dynamical feature. However, the connections between these two types of chirality and their physical consequences are not known. Therefore, in the proposed research, I will use a hydrodynamic approach, complemented by agent-based methods, to examine chiral active matter, aiming to better understand the physics of chirality in non-equilibrium systems. Specifically, I plan to extend the existing hydrodynamic model of liquid crystals to account for both structural and dynamical chirality. The model will be compared to Brownian dynamics method to elucidate the importance of microscopic details and hydrodynamic effects. As such, I propose to develop a generalized picture to understand distinct chiral active and driven matter, and provide experimentally testable predictions, paving the way towards guiding experimental efforts to engineer active matter for practical applications.

26302320.label: Realisation of objectives
26302320.value: 1. Conduct Brownian dynamics simulations to investigate the collective behavior of chiral active particles and their interaction with complex environments, with the aim of elucidating the new physics of chiral motion and how it can be used for practical applications, such as particle separation. My group has employed active Brownian dynamics simulations to study how chiral active particles interact with complex environments. We have worked on two directions, with one focusing on different obstacle lattices, the other one about self-generated chemical fields. We have successfully established a collaboration with an experimental group to verify our simulation results. 1.1. Active particles transport within obstacle lattices with different configurations or with defects. We used active Brownian dynamics model to simulate chiral particles in a two-dimensional space. We investigated the dynamics of these chiral particles in an obstacle lattice. We found that the effective diffusivity becomes sensitive to the lattice geometry, which is in contrast to achiral active particles which cannot distinguish square from triangular lattice. Finally, we found that the diffusivity of left-handed and right-handed particles differ in mirror symmetry broken lattice. The above findings are later confirmed by granular particle experiments performed by Prof. Yilong Han group. We also examined how active particles’ dynamics will be altered by a lattice defect. We therefore considered the presence of a single vacancy or interstitial defect in an obstacle lattice and showed that the probability distribution of particle self-propelling direction is modified when it passes by a lattice defect. We further found that certain defect configuration can give rise to better separation outcome compared to a perfect obstacle lattice. These research efforts have led to the following two manuscripts: - Chan et al, Nature Communications 15, 1406 (2024). - Chau and Zhang, in prep. 1.2. Chiral active droplets propelled by auto-chemotatic effects. Based on active Brownian dynamics, we have developed a model to include a diffusion equation to account for the chemical field generated by chiral active droplets. Our model successfully reproduced the curling and helical trajectories of nematic droplets immersed in a surfactant-rich aqueous solution. Our work reveals the difference in droplet velocities between 2D and 3D, and quantifies how droplet dynamics depend on Peclet number of the strength of auto-chemotactic effect. The research effort has led to the following paper: - Chan et al, Journal of Chemical Physics 161, 014904 (2024). 2. Use a hydrodynamic model of active nematic liquid crystals to shed light on how structural chirality and the mechanical properties of the underlying material dictate the dynamics of three-dimensional active matter. We have been working on hydrodynamic simulations of active nematic liquid crystals (LCs) with structural chirality. We also extended our efforts to low-twist or chiral nematic LCs subjected to active and driven flows. 2.1 Dynamics of topological defects in active nematics with structural chirality. Current research of active nematics are focused on achiral systems. How structural chirality influences defect dynamics and spontaneous flows in quasi-2D active nematics remains elusive. We have performed hydrodynamic simulations of chiral active nematics. We find that +1/2 line defects in a thin-film active chiral nematics can gain an angular velocity if the film is curved, a prediction awaiting for experimental realization. This research effort has led to the following paper: - Wang et al, Physical Review Letters 132, 038301 (2024). 2.2 Driven and active flows in chiral or low-twist nematics. We have considered two types of lyotropic LCs. For nematic disodium cromoglycate solutions exhibiting low twist modulus, we collaborated with Prof. Irmgard Bischofberger from MIT to understand the birefringence patterns observed in the pressure-driven channel flow. For nematic cellulose nanocrystal suspensions we collaborated with Prof. Monirosadat Sadati from University of South Carolina to explain the spatial pattern observed under pressure-driven flow. Interestingly, at a very low flow rate, the low-twist nematic disodium cromoglycate spontaneously develops a chiral stripe structure between two log-rolling domains. We have used theory and hydrodynamic simulation to successfully explain the emergence of such chiral structure. We also numerically studied the interplay between driven and active flows in low-twist nematics. We showed that activity can suppress pressure-driven flow of a flow-tumbling nematic in a planar-anchoring cell but can also promote a transition of the director field under a pressure gradient in a homeotropic-anchoring cell. Remarkably, we demonstrated that when above the threshold, a complex, periodic spatiotemporal director pattern emerges. The above research efforts have led to 4 publications: - Zhang et al, Nature Communications 15, 7 (2024). - Esmaeili et al, Langmuir 38 (7), 875882 (2022). - Zhang et al, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 118 (35) e2108361118 (2021). - Wang et al, Crystals 11, 1071 (2021). 3. Develop a hydrodynamic model of active liquid crystals with a chiral stress to examine the role of dynamical chirality in the dynamics of chiral active matter and certain driven matter. We considered a novel active matter system consisting of dense, self-spinning, elongated constituents. Experimentally, this can be realized by applying a rotating external field to a molecular or colloidal LC. To account this dynamical chirality in our work, we introduced two new physical terms to the governing equations. A rotation term is added to the governing equation of order parameter to account for the spontaneous rotation of the constituents. In the momentum equation, a chiral stress term is added. Our research is concerned with how these two chiral terms impact the spontaneous flow and defect dynamics in a two-dimensional active LCs. We have made the following discoveries: For an isolated defect, the chiral rotation can cause the rotation of the defect, and its angular velocity and the intrinsic angular velocity differ by a factor of 1 - m, with m the winding number of the defect. This relation means that defects with high winding number can rotate in an opposite direction. We further found that chiral stress can drive +1/2 defects into motion along transverse direction. Recall that linear active stress can mobilize +1/2 defects to move along its symmetry axis, this means that chiral rotation, chiral stress, and linear activity can mobilize +1/2 defects in different ways. We also studied spontaneous flows and defect dynamics in a confined nematic. Specifically, we consider a disk region with planar anchoring condition, which engenders two +1/2 defects facing towards boundary. By varying the two chiral terms and an additional linear active stress term, we obtain a rich diagram of different defect modes, many of which are not observed in linear active nematic systems. These different defect modes can give rise to the so-called edge currents (flows) of different strengths or even different handednesses. We further considered soft boundary by using a lyotropic LC model. Specifically, we considered droplets of chiral active nematic in another immiscible liquid. In contrast to the disk system, the edge flow generated inside the dispersed active droplet can propagate into the continuous phase. We further examined how two nearby active droplets interact hydrodynamically. We found an interesting phenomenon that these defect motion can be synchronized at appropriate choice of parameters. We believe such hydrodynamic synchronization of defect motion have important potential in emerging applications, such as photonics, microfluidics, soft robotics, and sensors. This leads to a manuscript: - Mou and Zhang, in prep.

26302320.label: Major findings and research outcome
26302320.value: Objective 1: We have successfully established a collaboration with Prof. Yilong Han from our department on experimental validation of our active Brownian dynamics simulation predictions. Specifically, Prof. Han has used a special grass seed particle, which can exhibit circular motion on a vibrating substrate. This experimental platform has verified the following simulation findings: (1) chiral active particle dynamics are sensitive to the obstacle lattice structure, a feature not found in achiral active particles; (2) chiral active particles of opposite handedness exhibit different effective diffusivities in mirror symmetry broken obstacle lattices. These findings imply that chiral active particles can serve as environmental sensors by sensing the geometry of the obstacle configurations. This experimental platform can be further used to study other phenomena in chiral active matter. We have also developed a particle-based model to reproduce curling and helical trajectories of auto-chemotactic chiral active droplets in quasi-2D and 3D, respectively. We have found that the interplay of intrinsic chirality of the droplet and its negative chemotactic effect is sufficient to reproduce the droplet trajectories. By comparing 2D and 3D simulation results, we have revealed the effect of 2D confinement on droplet dynamics. Objective 2: We have made a novel prediction that +1/2 defects in a curved thin-film of chiral active nematics can gain an active angular velocity. This new degree of freedom for self-propelled defects can enrich the dynamical phenomena of active nematics, and can facilitate their applications in cargo transport and dynamical self-assembly. This chiral symmetry breaking in defect motion can also be used to measure the chirality of the nematic. Beyond chiral active nematics, we have also established new collaborations, for example, with Prof. Irmgard Bischofberger from MIT on pattern formation in flowing achiral liquid crystals. Objective 3: Our efforts in developing a hydrodynamic model to study chiral active liquid crystals have clarified the different physics chiral rotation and chiral stress play. We predicted that high-winding-number defects can spontaneously rotate in opposite direction with respect to the intrinsic rotation of the units. We also pointed out that linear activity, chiral rotation, and chiral stress can give rise to different self-propulsion modes for +1/2 defects, which can greatly enhance the controllability of +1/2 or other types of defects in active liquid crystals. Our predictions of synchronization of defect dynamics between nematic droplets have potential in emerging applications, such as photonics, microfluidics, soft robotics, and sensors.

26302320.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
26302320.value: The further developments of the research and proposed course of action are the following: (1) In terms of theory, recent theoretical and simulation efforts in literature point out that odd viscosity and odd elasticity may emerge in chiral active matter consisting of self-spinning active particles. However, for active matter comprising circularly moving particles, how the co-existence of linear and chiral activity impacts its odd elasticity/viscosity has not been investigated. Moreover, odd elasticities of chiral active liquid crystals remain poorly studied. More theory and simulation efforts are needed. (2) Collective behaviors of chiral active particles or droplets involving auto-chemotactic effects and hydrodynamic interactions need further studies both numerically and experimentally. (3) Because the experimental effort in the report is focused on dry active matter comprised of granular particles. Experimental systems of wet chiral active matter can be developed, and the effects of hydrodynamic interactions between active particles can be examined. Experimental realization of chiral active liquid crystal has not been reported in literature; therefore, there is a great deal of space in experimental development.

26302320.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
26302320.value: The structures of biological materials, commonly called “living matter”, such as DNA, proteins, bacterial flagella, and flower petals to name a few, are predominately chiral. One the one hand, the origin of the prevalence of one type of handedness over the other in this part of nature remains a mystery, despite knowledge of its existence for hundreds or thousands of years. On the other hand, the physical consequence of such chirality in dynamic living matter remains elusive. This project aims to examine how chirality dictates dynamics of living matter. Our research discovers that the diffusion-like dynamics of chiral active particles is sensitive to the geometry of the environment represented by a lattice of obstacles. We also discover that an interplay between liquid crystal chirality and surface curvature can give rise to chiral motion of topological defects. Our research can facility identify and sort different cells or microorganisms according to their degree of activity and chirality, and therefore holds promise for applications such as diagnostics, omics, and drug delivery. The motion of chiral active particles or chiral active defects can help us detect the hidden geometry of the environment, thereby serving as potential environment sensors.

26304920.value: 大随机矩阵的低秩扰动

26304920.label: Project Objectives
26304920.value: Enhance our understanding of the asymptotic behaviour of outlier eigenvalues and their associated eigenvectors for random Hermitian matrices deformed by a small-rank perturbation. There exists considerable literature when the rank of the perturbation matrix is finite. However, in regards to when the rank of deformation grows with the matrix dimension while still remaining a lower order, the literature in this problem is still sparse. The key question is to establish the local law near the edge of support of the eigenvalue distribution of the non-perturbed random Hermitian matrices. More precisely, the Green function of the perturbed matrix is asymptotically deterministic; as such, we will give a precise estimate between the Green function and its approximation. These results will contain important information regarding statistical inference on multivariate data. Establish the limiting distribution of the outlier eigenvalues for a random independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) matrix perturbed by a finite-rank error in full generality. Study into the asymptotic spectral statistics of the perturbation of random i.i.d. matrices is still in its infancy. The project will, therefore, have an important impact on extending the current mathematical understanding on the subject. Explore the asymptotic spectral statistics of the finite-rank perturbation of a random matrix whose entries are weakly correlated. One particular example is the deformed random elliptic matrix, which can be viewed as an interpolation between the deformed random Hermitian matrix and the deformed random i.i.d. matrix. The project will establish interesting results on how the dependence structure of the random matrix models affects the asymptotic eigenvalue distributions. The key issue here is to prove the optimal local law for the random elliptic matrix on the spectral region of interest.

26304920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
26304920.value: Enormous progress has been made recently to establish quite a precise understanding of the spectral properties of classical random matrix models, such as the Wigner matrix, sample covariance matrix and random independent matrix. However, in many scenarios, practical problems naturally lead to a random matrix with a deterministic perturbation. For instance, many problems in signal processing, machine learning, information theory and statistical inference have a common, unifying goal: reconstruct a low-rank signal matrix observed through a noisy channel. The useful information is encoded in a low-rank deterministic matrix, usually unknown, and the random matrix represents the noise. The fundamental question is to understand how the spectrum of a signal matrix is altered by adding a random noise. It is known that adding a small-rank perturbation to a large random matrix barely changes the global behaviour of its eigenvalues. However, the spectrum of the perturbed matrix undergoes a transition, associated with the creation or annihilation of an outlier, when the absolute value of an eigenvalue of the perturbation matrix crosses a critical value. This phenomenon was first brought into focus for the eigenvalues of a special class of spiked sample covariance matrix by Baik, Ben Arous and Peche, and are usually referred to as BBP phase transition. The extreme eigenvectors of the perturbed matrix are also known to undergo the phase transition along the change in strength of the extreme eigenvalues of the perturbation matrix. The principal object of our investigation is the asymptotic statistical behaviour of the extreme eigenvalues and their associated eigenvectors of a large random matrix perturbed by a low-rank error. The perturbation is assumed to pass a theoretic threshold, and thus the extreme eigenvalues will deviate away from the spectrum of the non-perturbed random matrix and become outliers. Their associated eigenvectors are known to have a bias on the direction of their correspondence of the perturbation matrix. We consider several perturbed random matrix models. The first kind is concerned with the perturbation of random Hermitian matrices, including the deformed Wigner matrix, the spiked covariance matrix and the signal-plus-noise model. The rank of the perturbation matrix diverges but still remains a smaller order of the matrix dimension. We also study the random independent matrix and the random elliptic matrix perturbed by a finite-rank matrix. This project will investigate the limiting behaviour of outlier eigenvalues or eigenvectors in full generality. 最近几年，我们在经典随机矩阵模型（包括维格纳矩阵， 样本协方差矩阵，元素独立的随机矩阵）的谱性质的认知得到了长足的发展。其实，许多实际应用的数学模型经常可以归结成这些经典随机矩阵的扰动模型。比如，信号处理，机器学习和统计推断这些领域的一个共同的问题是重建通过噪声通道观察到的低秩信号矩阵。因为我们需要的有用信息常常蕴含在这个未知的低秩信号矩阵之中，而在实际观察或者测量中产生的误差可以用随机矩阵来表达。所以，我们需要了解低秩信号矩阵的谱是如何被随机的扰动来改变的。 向大随机矩阵添加小秩扰动几乎不会改变其特征值的全局行为。但是，当扰动矩阵的特征值的绝对值超过临界阀值时，随机矩阵的极端特征值会发生相变，从而产生离群特征值（这种现象由Baik, Ben Arous and Peche首先发现的，一般称作BBP相变）。同时，相对应的特征向量也会产生相变。 我们研究的主要对象是受低秩误差干扰的大型随机矩阵的极限特征值及其相关特征向量的渐近统计行为。假设当扰动矩阵的强度超过临界阀值，相应的随机矩阵的扰动模型会产生离群特征值和对应的特征向量。我们研究几种随机矩阵的扰动模型的谱变化，包括变形的维格纳矩阵，尖峰协方差矩阵，信号加噪声模型和变形的随机椭圆矩阵。

26304920.label: Realisation of objectives
26304920.value: The project has successfully achieved its primary objectives, significantly advancing in understanding perturbed random matrices and their applications. Below, I detail how each objective was met and extended: Objective 1: Understanding asymptotic behavior of outlier eigenvalues This objective was fully achieved and even extended beyond its original scope. While initially focusing on outlier eigenvalues, our research expanded to provide a comprehensive analysis of singular vector and singular subspace perturbations in the signal-plus-noise matrix model (C=A+E). We established a stochastic version of the Davis-Kahan-Wedin sin theorem for Gaussian random perturbations, significantly improving upon the classic deterministic bounds. This advancement provides sharper tools for statistical inference on multivariate data, directly addressing the original aim of this objective. The development of a new perturbation bound for singular values represents a particularly notable achievement, as it provides precise estimates between the Green function and its approximation - a key goal outlined in the original objective. This tool has proven valuable for both theoretical understanding and practical applications. Objective 2: Limiting distribution of outlier eigenvalues Building on the foundation of the first objective, we successfully extended the Davis-Kahan-Wedin theorem in a fully generalized manner. Our research advanced beyond the original scope by establishing results applicable to any unitarily invariant matrix norm. This generalization encompasses both the original goal of understanding i.i.d. matrices and provides a broader framework for analyzing matrix perturbations. The research yielded fine-grained results, including l_infinity analysis of singular vectors, l_{2, infinity} analysis of singular subspaces, and exploration of linear and bilinear functions related to singular vectors. These findings have direct applications in practical problems, such as the Gaussian mixture model and submatrix localization, demonstrating the project's impact beyond theoretical advances. Objective 3: Asymptotic spectral statistics of finite-rank perturbations While this objective initially focused on weakly correlated entries and random elliptic matrices, our research expanded to develop a more general methodology using the resolvent method in the non-asymptotic regime. This approach has proven particularly powerful for establishing results on perturbed singular values and singular subspaces in novel ways. The techniques developed during this project have laid a strong foundation for future research into more structured random noise matrices. This creates a pathway for studying how different dependence structures affect asymptotic eigenvalue distributions, directly addressing the original aim of this objective. The methodologies and results developed during this project have opened new research directions, particularly in studying more structured random noise matrices. This creates opportunities for future research building upon the foundations established through this grant.

26304920.label: Major findings and research outcome
26304920.value: The project has yielded several significant theoretical results in random matrix theory and its applications. The primary achievement is the development of a stochastic version of the Davis-Kahan-Wedin sin theorem for Gaussian perturbations. This result provides optimal bounds that substantially improve upon the classical deterministic results, offering a more precise understanding of how singular subspaces change under random perturbations. Our methodology introduces a novel application of the resolvent method in the non-asymptotic regime, leading to comprehensive results on perturbed singular values and singular subspaces in the signal-plus-noise matrix model. A second major outcome is the generalization of perturbation bounds to any unitarily invariant matrix norm, significantly extending previous results in the field. The research has produced fine-grained analyses of singular vectors and subspaces, including l_infinity and l_{2, infinity} bounds, with direct applications to practical problems such as Gaussian mixture models and submatrix localization. These theoretical advances have immediate implications for statistical learning and data analysis, particularly in scenarios involving noisy matrix observations.

26304920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
26304920.value: The methodologies developed in this project open several promising research directions. The immediate next step is to extend our techniques to more structured random noise matrices, moving beyond the Gaussian case to handle broader classes of random perturbations. This extension would be particularly valuable for applications where the noise follows different probability distributions or exhibits correlation structures. The project's findings also suggest potential applications in modern machine learning problems, particularly in understanding the robustness of neural networks and analyzing large-scale data matrices. We plan to explore these directions through collaborations with researchers in applied mathematics and computer science, focusing on translating our theoretical insights into practical algorithmic improvements. This work will bridge the gap between theoretical random matrix theory and its applications in contemporary data science challenges.

26304920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
26304920.value: Imagine looking at a blurry photograph - the original image (signal) is distorted by noise. Our research addresses a similar mathematical problem: how to understand and analyze data when it's mixed with random noise. We study matrices (arrays of numbers) that represent real-world data, such as images, social networks, or genetic information, when they are corrupted by random disturbances. Our main achievement is developing new mathematical tools that can better predict how this noise affects the underlying structure of the data. Traditional methods often overestimate the impact of noise, leading to overly cautious predictions. Our new approach, specifically designed for random disturbances, provides more precise and reliable results. We proved that when the noise follows common random patterns (like those found in natural phenomena), we can make much more accurate predictions about the original signal. These findings have practical implications for many fields, from image processing to financial data analysis. For example, our results can help improve facial recognition systems' accuracy in noisy environments or enhance the reliability of genetic data analysis. This research bridges the gap between theoretical mathematics and practical applications, providing better tools for handling real-world data analysis challenges.

26305120.label: Project Title(Chinese)
26305120.value: 高维Neyman-Pearson分类以及其在文本数据分析中的应用

26305120.label: Project Objectives
26305120.value: Develop high-dimensional classification methods under the Neyman-Pearson (NP) paradigm, where the two types of classification errors are of different importance. The classifiers will incorporate feature interactions and deal with dependent data (e.g., time series). Develop technical tools through which we can construct classifiers without a sample splitting scheme. These new NP classifiers will utilize all information in every estimation step; thus, increase estimation efficiency and reduce classification errors. Apply the newly proposed classifiers to textual data classification. In particular, we will provide solutions for issues in social media and educational applications. More specifically, we will investigate the feature-dependent data inflation problem on social media for sensitive posts about corruption; and in education we will study the college admission and design an innovative admission system targeting control of the dropout rate.

26305120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
26305120.value: Abstract Designing an algorithm to automatically classify a datum into mutually exclusive categories is a crucial step in many big data applications. In the setting of binary classification, the effectiveness of such an algorithm (or classifier) is determined by two types of errors: type I error, mistakenly label class 0 data as class 1, and type II error, mistakenly label class 1 data as class 0. Most existing classifiers aim to minimize the weighted average of these two types of errors, with weights being the proportions of class 0 and class 1 in the population. Despite their convenience, these classifiers may lead to misleading results or inefficient outcomes when one type of error should be prioritized over the other or when the distribution of data between the two classes is highly skewed. To overcome these challenges, statisticians recently developed a new framework of classification, namely, the Neyman-Pearson (NP) classification approach. This proposed project aims to construct innovative classifiers under the NP framework. The essence of the NP approach is changing the objective of minimizing the weighted average of the two types of errors to an objective of controlling the type I error under some pre-fixed threshold while minimizing the type II error. This enables practitioners to handle classification errors with discretion and sidestep the problem of unbalanced data. Although the NP approach has proved to be valid in some medical studies and social science research, its usefulness needs to be tested in more sophisticated settings, and its effectiveness needs to be enhanced through incorporating other statistical tools. To this end, this project will focus on four areas: 1) developing NP-sQDA to take care of interaction effects between features and to allow for unbounded feature support; 2) developing NP classifiers that target time series data; 3) developing unified NP classifiers without a data-splitting scheme to enhance estimation efficiency; and 4) applying the above developed methods to textual mining in order to solve some challenging data problems in social science and educational applications. These newly proposed NP classifiers will not only enrich the statistical literature on classification but also enhance the value of machine learning in real-world applications. 设计分类算法是大数据应用中很重要的问题。作为被使用最广的二元分类，其有效性是由两种错误率决定的，我们通常称之为第一类以及第二类错误。第一类错误是指样本真实来源于类别0，而算法将其错误地归为类别1；反之，第二类错误是指样本真实来源于类别1，而算法将其归为类别0。 现今已有的大部分方法都致力于缩小两类错误的加权平均，并用两类数据在群体中的比例作为权重。然而在一些重要的应用当中，有时两类错误造成的损失有明显不同，或者两类数据在群体中的比例是极其不平衡的；在这样的情形下，简单以加权平均的错误率作为目标函数的分类算法，可使统计结果不具备科学意义。为了攻克这一问题，统计学家近期提出了一个新的分类框架，Neyman-Pearson (简写为NP)分类。本课题致力于在此分类框架下，设计新颖有效的分类器。 NP分类相比于传统分类最大的不同，在于优化问题的目标函数。它是在将第一类错误控制在用户指定范围内的同时，缩小第二类错误；而不是缩小两类错误的加权平均。尽管NP分类已经解决了一些社会学以及医学研究当中的问题，它在其他领域中的广泛应用以及构造更有效的分类器还值得进一步深入研究。本课题主要致力于在NP框架下，研究以下几个方向： i) 构造能够处理特征交互作用的分类器 ii) 构造能够处理不独立数据的分类器 iii) 解决NP分类算法中数据分割的问题，以提高分类器的统计功效 iv) 研究NP分类在其他领域的应用

26305120.label: Realisation of objectives
26305120.value: Overview This project set out with three ambitious objectives. Over the course of the grant, significant progress has been made on all fronts, as evidenced by theoretical breakthroughs, practical tool development, and impactful publications. Below, we detail the realisation of each objective, reflect on challenges encountered, and outline how these were addressed. Objective 1: A central aim of this project was to advance the NP classification framework to high-dimensional settings, particularly where the two types of classification errors (type I and type II) carry different weights. Recognizing the complexity of modern data, we sought to design classifiers that not only handle high dimensionality but also incorporate feature interactions and accommodate dependencies such as those found in time series. Achievements: • We introduced two innovative NP classifiers - elda for high-dimensional data and felda for low-dimensional scenarios, without sample splitting. Both methods are designed to operate efficiently in complex feature spaces and can be extended to include interaction terms, enhancing their flexibility and relevance for real-world data. • The theoretical foundation of these classifiers was established through the development of a quantitative central limit theorem for functionals involving quadratic forms of inverse covariance matrices. This was achieved under minimal assumptions and could potentially be applied to situations with weakly dependent samples. These advances have been rigorously validated through extensive numerical experiments, which demonstrated that our methods outperform existing approaches. • The results have been disseminated through a publication in the Journal of Machine Learning Research, underscoring the significance and impact of our contributions within the machine learning and statistics communities. Challenges and Solutions: • Addressing feature interactions and dependencies required the development of new mathematical tools in random matrix theory, a task that proved both technically demanding and intellectually rewarding. Progress was achieved through sustained effort, collaboration, and the training of students in advanced statistical theory. • While the initial focus was on high-dimensional independent data, our framework was successfully generalized to accommodate feature interactions, setting the stage for future work in time series and other complex domains. Objective 2: A major technical barrier in NP classification is the reliance on sample splitting, which reduces estimation efficiency and limit the power of resulting classifiers. Our second objective was to develop new methodologies that fully utilize all available data. Achievements: • Both elda and felda were explicitly designed to eliminate the need for sample splitting, a key innovation that sets them apart from traditional NP classifiers. • Theoretical analysis confirmed that these methods rigorously control type I error with high probability, while also achieving the oracle type II error. • The elimination of sample splitting not only improved statistical efficiency but also simplified practical implementation, making the methods more accessible to practitioners. Challenges and Solutions: • Developing classifiers that avoid sample splitting required new technical tools, particularly in the analysis of covariance matrices. This necessitated a deep engagement with random matrix theory. • The process also involved extensive simulation studies to empirically validate the theoretical guarantees and to fine-tune the algorithms for practical use. Objective 3: The third objective was to demonstrate the practical utility of our theoretical advances by applying them to challenging real-world problems. Achievements: • We processed and cleaned a large-scale dataset of approximately 0.8 million Weibo posts, applying our NP classifiers to investigate patterns relevant to social science questions. This involved significant effort in feature engineering and data pre-processing to address the inherent noise and variability of social media data. • Although the results from the Weibo data did not yield significant new insights-primarily due to data quality issues-this work provided valuable experience and highlighted the importance of high-quality data for effective application of advanced classification methods. • On the biological side, we successfully transferred the core idea of asymmetric error control to single-cell genomics. We developed scDEED, a tool for detecting dubious embeddings in dimension reduction techniques such as t-SNE and UMAP, thereby enhancing the reliability of single-cell data interpretation. • The impact of scDEED is evidenced by its publication in Nature Communications, and its adoption by researchers in genomics and related fields. Challenges and Solutions: • The primary challenge in the social media context was the low quality of available data, which limited the ability of our methods to extract meaningful patterns. Despite extensive efforts in data cleaning and feature engineering, some limitations could not be fully overcome. • In response, we shifted focus to high-quality biological datasets, where our methods demonstrated clear value and impact. This strategic pivot ensured that the project continued to deliver significant outcomes, even as some initial application areas proved more challenging than anticipated. Overall Impact and Lessons Learned The achievements of this project extend well beyond the technical development and their publication in leading journals. The work has made substantial contributions to both the theoretical and applied landscapes of statistical learning, fostering methodological innovation and practical utility across multiple domains. First and foremost, the project has advanced the state of knowledge in high-dimensional classification under the Neyman-Pearson paradigm. By rigorously addressing the challenges associated with asymmetric error control, the research has provided the community with powerful new tools that are both flexible and robust. In addition to its theoretical contributions, the project has delivered practical solutions that are already being adopted by the broader scientific community. The development and dissemination of the scDEED tool, for example, has enabled researchers in genomics to critically assess and improve the reliability of single-cell data analyses. By making these tools publicly available and providing clear documentation, the project has lowered the barrier to entry for practitioners seeking to apply advanced statistical techniques to their own data. This democratization of cutting-edge methodology is a significant step toward broader scientific reproducibility and rigor. A further impact of the project lies in its role as a training ground for the next generation of researchers. Graduate students and early-career scientists involved in the project have gained valuable experience in both theoretical and applied research, learning to navigate the challenges of developing new mathematical tools and translating them into practical software. This hands-on training has equipped them with a versatile skill set that will serve them well in academia, industry, or government research. The interdisciplinary nature of the project has also fostered new collaborations and cross-pollination of ideas between statisticians, probabilists, and domain experts in genomics and social science. These partnerships have not only enriched the research but have also laid the groundwork for future joint initiatives, ensuring that the impact of the project will continue to grow beyond the life of the grant. Looking ahead, the foundational work completed in this project opens several promising avenues for further development. The integration of additional constraints such as fairness and privacy into the NP framework represents a natural and impactful extension. Moreover, the methodological advances made here provide a strong basis for tackling new types of data, and for developing more sophisticated analytical tools tailored to the needs of domain experts. In summary, the project has achieved its primary objectives and generated a ripple effect of benefits across theory, application, and training. Its contributions are poised to shape future research directions, inspire new collaborations, and enhance the practical impact of statistical learning in diverse scientific and societal contexts.

26305120.label: Major findings and research outcome
26305120.value: For Aims I and II, we introduced two innovative NP classifiers: elda, a high-dimensional classifier emphasizing data efficiency, and felda, a low-dimensional counterpart. Notably, both methods eliminate the need for sample splitting. The theoretical foundation of elda is built on a quantitative central limit theorem for functionals involving quadratic forms of the inverse sample and population covariance matrices, established under minimal assumptions. Importantly, we proved that elda rigorously controls the type I error with high probability, a key requirement in NP classification. To address complex covariate interactions, our methods can be extended by augmenting the feature space with interaction terms, thereby enhancing model flexibility. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrated the superiority of our non-splitting parametric approach compared to existing methods. This work culminated in a publication in the Journal of Machine Learning Research, a leading journal in the machine learning and statistics communities. For Aim III, we successfully transferred the core idea of asymmetric error control to single-cell genomics. We developed a novel tool, scDEED, designed to detect dubious embeddings in popular dimension reduction techniques such as t-SNE and UMAP. This tool enhances the reliability of single-cell data interpretation and has been published in Nature Communications. Regarding textual data, we processed and cleaned approximately 0.8 million posts from Weibo to apply NP algorithms for social science analysis. Unfortunately, the results lacked significant insights, which we attribute primarily to data quality issues inherent in the social media dataset. Despite this, we remain optimistic that with improved data quality, our NP framework will yield impactful results in social science research in the future. In summary, this grant has led to the development of theoretically sound and practically effective NP classifiers, validated through rigorous analysis and high-impact publications. While challenges remain in applying these methods to noisy social media data, our success in single-cell analysis highlights the broad potential of our approach across diverse domains.

26305120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
26305120.value: The research carried out in this proposal offers several promising directions for further development. One key area is the integration of additional constraints, such as fairness and privacy, into the Neyman-Pearson (NP) framework. By incorporating these constraints, we can design more advanced NP systems capable of addressing multiple objectives simultaneously. This will require moving beyond the traditional Neyman-Pearson Lemma to explore its generalized version, which accommodates multiple constraints. Building on this, we plan to develop classifiers based on the oracle classification boundary and rigorously analyze their theoretical properties. The techniques established in this work may enable the development of efficient classifiers that do not require sample splitting, particularly within linear discriminant analysis models, and could potentially be extended to elliptical distributions. On the applied front, we aim to enhance our research by sourcing higher-quality textual datasets from social science domains and refining our feature engineering and data pre-processing methods. Our long-term objective is to develop a comprehensive analytical tool for time-dependent censored data within the NP framework, ultimately delivering actionable insights to domain experts and advancing methodological standards in the field.

26305120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
26305120.value: Classification is a fundamental tool in machine learning, categorizing items like medical images or social media posts based on their features. It was used in diverse applications, from disease screening to content moderation. However, classification errors could have varying consequences; misdiagnosing a serious illness carried greater risk than misclassifying a healthy patient as sick. To address this, methods like Neyman-Pearson (NP) classification allowed us to prioritize minimizing the most critical errors. While abundant data became available through hardware development and generative models, data acquisition remains expensive in niche fields like advanced genetics or medicine. Therefore, developing efficient and modern classification methods tailored to the specific needs and data structures of these fields is of great importance. The research carried out in this proposal essentially solved the problem in NP classification when the sample size is very small. Our specifically designed methods efficiently estimate classification boundaries, unlike other NP classifiers in the literature which are either non-functional or less powerful. By applying a similar approach to single-cell analysis, we developed dubious cell embedding detectors, a tool highly useful for biologists. Our contributions advanced both the theoretical foundations of statistics, and the practical applications of machine learning, ultimately benefiting the general public.

26305720.label: Project Objectives
26305720.value: Develop a new machine learning (ML)-aided strategy for selective downscaling of climate model simulations at cloud-resolving resolution. Global warming is expected to lead to a significant intensification of extreme precipitation and pose challenges to our society. However, predictions of tropical and subtropical rainstorms entail considerable uncertainty because of the limited resolution of current global climate models (GCMs) and the complex dynamics of deep convection, which drives extreme rainfall in tropics and subtropics. The primary constraint in predicting future severe tropical/subtropical rainstorms is the coarse resolution of GCMs. Current supercomputers typically allow long-term climate simulations at a resolution of approximately 100 km, but resolving deep convection requires grid spacing on the order of 1 km. We will develop an ML algorithm that enables selective downscaling, which re-simulates selected large-scale patterns in coarse-resolution GCMs with refined grids in limited regions and time windows. The ML model will classify large-scale circulation patterns and identify those that are likely to generate severe rainstorms but may not do so in GCM due to the resolution limitation. We will then use a cloud-resolving model to dynamically downscale the large-scale patterns to a cloud-resolving resolution. Evaluate climate models with a focus on their capacity to simulate the correct variability of the large-scale circulation. Current climate models are mostly tuned to match the climatological means of various quantities. However, such tuning may not necessarily ensure that climate models can reproduce the realistic variability of large-scale circulation patterns. The ML algorithm developed in Objective 1 will be used to classify large-scale circulation patterns in climate models and evaluate GCM performance. The classification results of the ML model will be compared with observational statistics so that climate models can be assessed from the perspective of simulating extreme weather-related patterns. This evaluation approach provides a new angle of quantifying the performance of climate models and thus facilitates an improved understanding of climate models. Generate large ensembles of cloud-resolving simulations of tropical/subtropical extreme rain events in the current and a warmed climate. Traditional regional climate downscaling requires every time slice from a GCM. This strategy is computationally expensive but necessary when information on all types of weather is needed. The ML-aided downscaling approach here focuses on extreme precipitation, thus allowing us to use supercomputing resources differently. We will generate large ensembles of regional extreme rain events at a cloud-resolving resolution. These large ensembles are highly beneficial because capturing the natural variability of convective rainstorms within a small number of simulations is difficult due to the nonlinear dynamics of convection. Small-amplitude variation in initial conditions may lead to a significant decrease or increase in rain intensity later on. By utilizing large ensembles, we will fully explore the natural variability of convective storms and allow the strongest rainstorms to emerge in the ensemble. Achieve robust estimations of the sensitivity of convective precipitation extremes to global warming. Convective rainfall in GCMs exhibits significant uncertainty in their sensitivity to warming. We will use data from our large ensembles of cloud-resolving downscaling to obtain a robust estimation of the sensitivity of tropical/subtropical rain extremes to warming. Here, the limitations due to the coarse resolution of GCMs and their convection parameterization are eliminated by using direct cloud-resolving simulation. Thus, results with a significantly narrower range of uncertainty than before can likely be produced. We will also compare the potentially different responses in the subtropics and tropics. If the spread remains significant, it might be unavoidable due to the internal variability of the large-scale circulation. In that case, we will seek a solid understanding of the underlying dynamics and physics. Obtain a theoretical analysis and understanding of the sensitivity of extreme rainfall to global warming. The potential strengthening of rainstorms under global warming may result from thermodynamic factors, dynamic changes, or both. We will partition the contribution into the parts due to thermodynamics and those due to dynamics. Here, the “thermodynamic” factor refers to the increase in rain amount purely due to the moistening of the atmosphere as the temperature rises. However, what is more uncertain than this factor is the potential dynamic changes in rainstorms. Previous studies have suggested that the possible dynamic strengthening of convection can be due to the increase in available potential energy, moisture effect on instability, and large-scale dynamic forcing. We will analyze our large ensemble data sets to determine the contribution of each of these mechanisms. These theoretical questions are crucial not only because of their intellectual merits but also because they can potentially become useful guiding principles in the study of extreme precipitation in other regions. An in-depth understanding of the related dynamics and physics of convective rainstorms will benefit the regional climate community.

The ML model will classify large-scale circulation patterns and identify those that are likely to generate severe rainstorms but may not do so in GCM due to the resolution limitation. We will then use a cloud-resolving model to dynamically downscale the large-scale patterns to a cloud-resolving resolution.

Evaluate climate models with a focus on their capacity to simulate the correct variability of the large-scale circulation. Current climate models are mostly tuned to match the climatological means of various quantities. However, such tuning may not necessarily ensure that climate models can reproduce the realistic variability of large-scale circulation patterns. The ML algorithm developed in Objective 1 will be used to classify large-scale circulation patterns in climate models and evaluate GCM performance. The classification results of the ML model will be compared with observational statistics so that climate models can be assessed from the perspective of simulating extreme weather-related patterns. This evaluation approach provides a new angle of quantifying the performance of climate models and thus facilitates an improved understanding of climate models.

Generate large ensembles of cloud-resolving simulations of tropical/subtropical extreme rain events in the current and a warmed climate. Traditional regional climate downscaling requires every time slice from a GCM. This strategy is computationally expensive but necessary when information on all types of weather is needed. The ML-aided downscaling approach here focuses on extreme precipitation, thus allowing us to use supercomputing resources differently. We will generate large ensembles of regional extreme rain events at a cloud-resolving resolution. These large ensembles are highly beneficial because capturing the natural variability of convective rainstorms within a small number of simulations is difficult due to the nonlinear dynamics of convection. Small-amplitude variation in initial conditions may lead to a significant decrease or increase in rain intensity later on. By utilizing large ensembles, we will fully explore the natural variability of convective storms and allow the strongest rainstorms to emerge in the ensemble.

Achieve robust estimations of the sensitivity of convective precipitation extremes to global warming. Convective rainfall in GCMs exhibits significant uncertainty in their sensitivity to warming. We will use data from our large ensembles of cloud-resolving downscaling to obtain a robust estimation of the sensitivity of tropical/subtropical rain extremes to warming. Here, the limitations due to the coarse resolution of GCMs and their convection parameterization are eliminated by using direct cloud-resolving simulation. Thus, results with a significantly narrower range of uncertainty than before can likely be produced. We will also compare the potentially different responses in the subtropics and tropics. If the spread remains significant, it might be unavoidable due to the internal variability of the large-scale circulation. In that case, we will seek a solid understanding of the underlying dynamics and physics.

Obtain a theoretical analysis and understanding of the sensitivity of extreme rainfall to global warming. The potential strengthening of rainstorms under global warming may result from thermodynamic factors, dynamic changes, or both. We will partition the contribution into the parts due to thermodynamics and those due to dynamics. Here, the “thermodynamic” factor refers to the increase in rain amount purely due to the moistening of the atmosphere as the temperature rises. However, what is more uncertain than this factor is the potential dynamic changes in rainstorms. Previous studies have suggested that the possible dynamic strengthening of convection can be due to the increase in available potential energy, moisture effect on instability, and large-scale dynamic forcing. We will analyze our large ensemble data sets to determine the contribution of each of these mechanisms. These theoretical questions are crucial not only because of their intellectual merits but also because they can potentially become useful guiding principles in the study of extreme precipitation in other regions. An in-depth understanding of the related dynamics and physics of convective rainstorms will benefit the regional climate community.

26305720.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
26305720.value: Precipitation extremes, which can trigger landslides and floods, are expected to intensify under global warming and pose challenges to sustainable social development. However, reliable estimation of future tropical and subtropical precipitation extremes is beyond the capability of current climate models. This research project aims to use a machine learning-aided approach to selectively simulate extreme rainstorms in a warming climate and understand the expected changes with physical theories. Predictions of tropical and subtropical rainstorms using current climate models entail considerable uncertainty. Some models predict a 1% increase in the intensity of tropical precipitation extremes in response to 1° surface warming, whereas others suggest an increase of approximately 30%. Using observations to constrain model results can effectively reduce the range of uncertainty, but further improvement is still necessary. A direct cause of this uncertainty is the coarse resolution, which is typically 100 km horizontally, of climate models. Meanwhile, resolving tropical and subtropical rainstorms requires a resolution of approximately 1 km. Long-term global climate simulation at a kilometer-scale resolution remains impossible for today’s supercomputers. In this study, we will use support vector machines and cloud-resolving models (CRM) to enable high-resolution simulation of extreme rainfall events at climatic timescales. Current climate models with coarse grids misrepresent convective extreme rainfall events in simulations. We will use support vector machines to classify time slices from climate model simulations and identify large-scale circulation patterns that are likely to trigger severe rainfall events. Then, we will downscale the selected large-scale patterns with CRM to achieve reliable simulations of potential extreme precipitation events. We will produce an ensemble of extreme event simulations to address the uncertainty due to natural variability. Different climate models will be used to perform parent climate simulations. Various microphysics schemes, which may influence convection development, will be included for CRM simulations. The resulting ensemble of extreme rain events will allow us to quantify the uncertainty of our estimation and identify robust underlying trends. We will investigate the sensitivity of rainfall extremes to warming by partitioning precipitation change into thermodynamic and dynamic components; the latter refers to characteristics such as the intensity of vertical motions, storm structure, and occurrence frequency. Furthermore, we will evaluate the sensitivity of storm dynamics to warming from the perspectives of energetics, large-scale forcing, and moist dynamics. 26305720.label: Realisation of objectives
26305720.value: The objectives of this research project have been fully realized over the past four years. During this period, we developed cutting-edge deep learning algorithms, conducted high-resolution simulations, and explored the theoretical underpinnings of extreme precipitation under global warming. As a result of this work, five articles have been published in leading journals within the atmospheric sciences community. A key goal of this research was to create a machine-learning framework capable of downscaling global coarse-resolution simulations into regional high-resolution predictions. This objective was achieved through a detailed study led by the Principal Investigator (PI), which focused on tropical cities. Multiple machine learning methods were evaluated, ranging from simpler models like support vector machines to more sophisticated ones, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN). These methods were rigorously cross-validated using a variety of climate simulations and observational datasets. Our results demonstrated that the CNN-based framework is highly effective at identifying large-scale circulation patterns associated with extreme precipitation. Specifically, we found that CNN models can accurately reproduce extreme precipitation events observed in data that were missed by global climate models due to their lower resolution. This approach proved particularly successful in subtropical regions like Hong Kong, likely due to the greater influence of quasigeostrophic forces compared to deep tropical regions like Singapore. These findings were published in Geophysical Research Letters. In addition, we carried out convection-permitting simulations to study the critical processes involved in generating high-fidelity tropical circulation patterns. This research focused on air-sea interactions and cloud-radiative feedback. The air-sea interaction studies involved simulations of numerous convective precipitation events in large ensemble settings, while the cloud-radiative feedback investigation examined how cloud radiative effects modulate convection organization via a bifurcation mechanism. Our findings indicate that while a dynamic ocean model can be disregarded in certain situations, an accurate representation of sea surface temperature (SST) responses to developing convection is essential in cases of extreme precipitation. The interplay between radiation and SST, although subtle, significantly impacts convection sensitivity. Cloud-radiation interactions were also found to play a pivotal role in shaping large-scale tropical circulation patterns. Our cloud-resolving simulations revealed that under specific conditions, convective storms can self-organize into a single large supercluster, a phenomenon known as convective self-aggregation. However, this self-aggregation only occurs under certain equilibrium states within a bifurcation process. Small variations in cloud-radiative feedback or boundary layer turbulence can shift the system from random convection to a state where dry regions become drier and wet regions become wetter, eventually leading to the formation of a single convective cluster. These novel insights were published in Atmosphere, Geophysical Research Letters, and the Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems. With regard to future changes in extreme precipitation, our research focused on conditions relevant to South China, particularly orographic precipitation associated with tropical cyclones. Using a combination of theoretical analysis and high-resolution numerical simulations, we employed large-eddy simulations (LES) to capture the dynamic details of convective precipitation triggered by mountainous terrain near typhoons. While the most intense precipitation occurred on the windward slopes near mountain peaks, we discovered that the response to global warming was most pronounced downstream of the mountains, with sensitivity reaching up to 18% per degree of warming. This heightened sensitivity is attributed to changes in mountain wave patterns and alterations in cloud microphysics processes under global warming conditions. This work highlights the increased vulnerability of mountainous regions to climate change and emphasizes the potential risks to slope stability in a warming world. These findings were published in the Journal of Climate. In conclusion, the project has successfully met its stated objectives, yielding significant scientific advancements and practical insights. The PI mentored postgraduate and undergraduate students, who played an instrumental role in completing this complex, interdisciplinary work and have developed expertise in physical theories, numerical modeling, and data analysis. The findings of this research not only contribute to the scientific community but also offer critical insights for societal adaptation to the increasing frequency of extreme weather events driven by global warming.

26305720.label: Major findings and research outcome
26305720.value: This research focused on extreme precipitation under global warming, aiming to understand the physical mechanisms driving extreme weather systems and their response to climate change. We developed an advanced hybrid approach combining deep learning and physical models to estimate future extreme precipitation in a computationally efficient manner. The method leverages deep learning to analyze large-scale circulation patterns, which are reliably simulated by coarse-resolution global climate models, to identify those likely to trigger extreme precipitation systems—typically involving severe convection in tropical regions. Convection-permitting simulations are then selectively applied to these high-probability patterns, downscaling them to resolve precipitation extremes. This innovative framework offers a robust tool for assessing the impacts of climate change on unresolved-scale precipitation and benefits the regional climate modeling community. These findings are published in Geophysical Research Letters (Shi, 2020). The project also advanced a theoretical understanding of severe convective storms and their response to global warming. We examined the roles of physical processes that influence extreme rainfall intensity through different pathways. Air-sea interactions were found to strengthen convection by altering boundary layer flows, with a warm, moist boundary layer intensifying storm updrafts. Boundary layer processes and cloud radiative feedback were significant in modulating tropical circulation, with a bifurcation point in circulation dynamics. Below a feedback intensity threshold, the tropical atmosphere remains in random convection, but beyond that, it transitions to convective self-aggregation, with clustering of convection and expansion of dry regions. These findings are published in Atmosphere (Lestari & Shi, 2021), Geophysical Research Letters (Fan et al., 2021), and Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems (Shi & Fan, 2021). We further applied these theories to estimate the sensitivity of extreme precipitation to global warming, focusing on tropical cyclone precipitation over complex terrain in South China. We found that precipitation over mountains remains relatively unchanged due to offsetting thermodynamic and dynamic effects. However, in downstream regions, extreme precipitation sensitivity to warming increases by up to 18% per degree. This amplification results from the interaction between mountain wave responses and altered cloud microphysics under global warming, with practical implications for climate adaptation in tropical coastal regions. These results are published in the Journal of Climate (Chen & Shi, 2023).

26305720.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
26305720.value: The deep learning/physical model hybrid approach holds promise for advancing regional climate studies. It is both computationally efficient and scientifically robust. While our completed project focused on extreme precipitation in the South China region, the risks associated with extreme precipitation are expected to increase globally under climate change. A key avenue for future research involves extending our methodology to East and Southeast Asia, focusing on projecting future changes in tropical cyclones across the entire western Pacific. This expanded study would not only provide critical insights for a larger portion of the Asian population but also offer a more comprehensive understanding of climate change impacts on this region. Furthermore, translating climate risks into economic and financial risks presents another critical direction for interdisciplinary research. Collaborations with faculty from other departments, particularly in economics and finance, could facilitate a more integrated approach to addressing these complex challenges. The principal investigator has already secured funding for a follow-up project through the RGC’s General Research Fund, which will estimate tropical cyclone changes across Asia under global warming. In addition, we are actively developing interdisciplinary proposals in partnership with finance experts to explore the broader economic implications of climate risks.

26305720.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
26305720.value: This research project explored how extreme rainfall responds to global warming using theories, computer models, and machine learning. We developed new methods to estimate future rainfall intensity as global temperatures rise and atmospheric moisture increases. These methods are both efficient and accurate, helping scientists better understand how regional climates may change with global warming. Our project also examined the physical processes driving storm intensity, such as interactions between the ocean and atmosphere and the role of clouds. This deeper understanding of how severe weather forms can help meteorologists and scientists improve the accuracy and timing of extreme weather warnings. Additionally, the study revealed that extreme rainfall in coastal areas, especially during tropical cyclones, could increase significantly as temperatures rise. This intensification is linked to changes in cloud behavior and air movement near mountains. These findings will help engineers design more resilient infrastructure and assist policymakers in creating better disaster response and relief strategies.
