27107320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27107320.value: The overuse of antibiotics has led to the emergence of multi-antibiotic resistant bacteria known as “superbugs,” which pose an increasingly severe threat to global health. It is estimated up to ten million additional lives, and 3.8% of the global economy will be lost annually by 2050 if the antibiotics resistance is not controlled. Unfortunately, despite intensive efforts of drug discovery in the past decades, no new classes of antibiotics have been developed into new drugs. New effective antibiotics that can kill the antibiotic-resistant superbugs are urgently needed. Bacterial peptides represent a large family of antibiotics and have attracted interest due to their antibiotic potential for combating drug-resistant pathogens. Recently, we reported a global genome mining approach and applied this approach to mine the vast orphan biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) from 7,395 bacterial genomes, result in discovering two novel cationic peptide antibiotics that kill antibiotic-resistant superbugs. Our preliminary big data mining of 163,037 sequenced bacterial genomes indicates that the BGCs of NRP- or RIRP-derived peptides are incredibly diverse, the majority of which is still orphan and thus represents a huge untapped source for the discovery of new peptide antibiotics. However, the diversity and complexity of peptide antibiotics have made global genome mining difficult and consequently hinder their targeted discovery. New and effective genomics-guided discovery approaches for peptide antibiotics are highly desirable. In this proposal, we aim to 1) develop a big data genome mining approach with sophisticated bioinformatics tools for the systematic investigation and the prioritization of novel BGCs. The proposed method can prioritize BGCs of novel antibiotics with a desired new mode of action in a high-throughput manner, prior to knowing their chemical structures. 2) establish a genomics-guided discovery approach by integrating big data genome mining with the established LC-MS based metabolomics and antibiotics bioassay approaches in our department for the targeted discovery of novel peptide antibiotics. 3) mine the continuously increasing large-scale genomic data to discover novel peptide antibiotics that kill antibiotic-resistant superbugs including, but not limited to, Calcium-dependent antibiotics (CDA). Collectively, applying the proposed big data genomics-guided approach to the bacterial sequenced genome (163,037), our goal is to discover new peptide antibiotics with new mode of action to fight the antibiotics resistance. Besides discovering peptide antibiotics with therapeutic potential, the outcomes of this proposal may also expedite the elucidation of the mode of action underlying the diverse biological functions of peptide antibiotics. 抗生素的濫用導致了多重耐藥細菌即超級細菌的出現，嚴重危害全人類的健康。 據估計，如果抗生素抗藥性危機得不到有效控制，到2050年，全世界每年將會有一千萬人死於細菌感染，全球經濟每年亦會遭受3.8%的損失。 儘管過去幾十年裡人們為藥物開發投入了大量精力，很不幸的是，沒有任何一種新類別的抗生素真正被開發成藥物。利用傳統的研究方法從細菌中發掘抗生素已陷入僵局。 因此，我們亟需借助新方法開發對抗超級細菌的新型抗生素。 細菌產生的抗菌肽一直以來吸引著科學家的興趣，因為這類分子具有對抗超级耐藥致病菌的潛力。以往細菌基因組的大數據基因分析表明，有超過90%的編碼潛在抗菌肽的生物合成基因簇尚未被研究。我們最近開發了一種大數據基因挖掘方法，並利用該方法從7395個細菌基因組中挖掘到了大量未知的生物合成基因簇。從這些基因簇編碼的小分子中，我們發現了兩個能有效殺滅超級細菌的新型陽離子抗菌肽。這些大数据基因分析和新抗菌肽的發現共同推翻了細菌產生的抗生素已被開發殆盡的說法，表明細菌仍然是新抗生素的主要來源。然而，目前還沒有一種聯用大數據基因挖掘、代謝組學和生物活性篩選的高效發現平臺，辅助結構新穎活性顯著天然產物的導向、高效地、去重複發現。 在本計劃中，我們的目標是：1. 建立基於大數據多組學的藥物開發方法，集大數據基因挖掘、代謝組學和生物活性篩選於一身，導向且高效地發現結構新穎活性顯著的天然產物。我們對163,037個已測序的細菌基因組的初步研究顯示，細菌合成的肽類（NRPs和RIPPs）是分佈最廣結構最多樣化的次生代謝產物之一，其中大部分為未知的天然產物。2. 為了解決抗生素抗藥性危機，我們將應用我們开发的方法對163,037個已測序的細菌基因組進行深度分析，挖掘具有全新作用機理、高效低毒、低耐葯風險抗菌肽（比如鈣離子依賴抗生素）以應對抗生素抗藥性危機。

27107320.label: Realisation of objectives
27107320.value: Objective 1. Genome mining has become a powerful technology to exploit natural product diversity and to guide their discovery. However, it remains challenging to prioritize and identify the biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) of interest in a high-throughput manner. Here, we propose to develop a big data genome mining strategy capable of the systematic investigation and the high-throughput prioritization of BGCs from a large-scale genome dataset. Achievement: The emergence of multi-antibiotic-resistant bacteria known as "superbugs" is an increasingly severe threat to global health. Thus, new effective antimicrobial therapeutics are urgently needed. Microbes produce diverse secondary metabolites such as signal molecules, siderophores, and antibiotics that mediate bacteria-virus/bacteria interaction. Advancements in sequencing techniques in the 21st century have facilitated large-scale sequencing of microbial genomes. This, along with extensive secondary metabolite research, has assisted in discovering new peptide antibiotics through genome mining and developing genome mining tools. Our project established a big data multi-omics guided discovery approach for targeted natural product discovery by combining big data genome mining, metabolomics, synthetic biology, and chemical biology. To tackle these drawbacks, we recently developed several genomics-guided for the targeted discovery of peptide antibiotics and their biosynthesis study. Supported by this grant, The PI's independent research has led to 5 publications in the past three years. These studies centered on big data genomics mining, antibiotic discovery, and mode of action study, emphasizing the discovery of peptide antibiotics [publications # 1-5]. Completely achieved the objectives proposed. Objective 2. Integrating big data genome mining with the established LC-MS-based metabolomics and antibiotics bioassay in our department, we aim to fully establish a powerful genomics-guided discovery platform for the efficient and targeted discovery of new antibiotics. Achievement: Recent developments in sequencing-based methods are transforming our understanding of archaeal diversity, metabolism, and biological roles. However, the chemical structures, biosynthetic pathways, and biological functions of archaeal SMs are largely unknown. Whether archaea produce SMs other than protein-based archaeocins to mediate antagonistic interactions is of interest. The lack of chemical and genetic data on archaeal SMs obstructs the discovery of antagonistic metabolites and related research. We carried out the first extensive and systematic analysis of the biosynthetic capacity for antimicrobial peptides from the archaeal genome and metagenome data. Through robust systematization of large volumes of genetic and metabolic data, we successfully linked genomic information to metabolomic data. This facilitated the targeted discovery of antagonistic lanthipeptides from marine archaea. We discovered two new antimicrobial lanthipeptides by integrating big data genome mining with established LC-MS-based metabolomics and antibiotics bioassay. These findings, based upon an integrated discovery platform, reveal archaea as an untapped source for antimicrobial discovery, were recently published in Microbiome (2023, publication #3), effectively fulfilling our proposed objectives. Objective 3. The preliminary BGC analysis of 163,037 sequenced bacterial genomes indicated that the majority of the bacterial peptide is still uncharacterized, representing a huge untapped source for peptide antibiotic discovery. We will next apply the genomics-guided approach to the continuously growing genome datasets to discover novel peptide antibiotics with new modes of action including, but not limited to, calcium-dependent antibiotics (CDA). Objective 5. Prioritize candidate BGCs upon sophisticated genome mining and then apply synthetic biology strategies (e.g., DNA synthesis and assembly and heterologous expression) to convert the untapped genetic potential into chemical reality. Achievement: In our quest to discover antibiotics from microbial natural products, we developed an effective multi-omics-guided platform that combines genomics and metabolomics. Specifically, we formulated a networking-associated genome mining strategy to uncover hidden peptidases outside of BGCs for lanthipeptide maturation, which aided in the discovery of bacinapeptins and paenithopeptins antibiotics. We created a genome mining workflow and employed correlation and co-expression analyses to establish the first global correlation network between lanthipeptide precursor peptides and proteases from 163,037 bacterial genome sequences (objective 3). The power of the multi-omics approach was demonstrated by studying unknown lanthipeptidases. This correlation network, derived from extensive genome mining and transcriptome analysis, guides the targeted discovery of cryptic lanthipeptide proteases encoded by genes outside BGCs. To prove this approach's efficacy, we chose two representative BGCs and implemented synthetic biology techniques, such as DNA synthesis, assembly, and heterologous expression, to transform the untapped genetic potential into tangible chemical outcomes (objective 5). This led to the simultaneous discovery of novel lanthipeptides, paenithopeptins, and bacinapeptins, and their respective cryptic proteases. Particularly, a family of bacterial M16B metallopeptidases with previously unclear biological functions was identified as responsible for several novel class III lanthipeptides, representing a new maturation mode of action of peptide antibiotics (objective 4). These new antibiotic discoveries were recently published in Nature Communications (2022, publication #1), effectively fulfilling our proposed objectives 3&5. Objective 4. Study the mechanism of action and resistance of lead compounds, which can be targeted and be more straightforward by our big data genome mining. Achievement: Using an extensive omics mining approach within complex microbiota, we've gained new insights into the biosynthetic capacity of peptide antibiotics. We've linked them to antagonistic contributions to homeostasis through omics analysis and in vitro bioassay. The findings on the diversity and prevalence of antibiotic peptides suggest that microbes are untapped resources for antimicrobials with low resistance risks (Microbiome 2023, #2). Additionally, they provide fresh insights into their mode of action in mediating microbe-microbe interactions in complex human microbiota. These discoveries were recently documented in Microbiome (2023, publication #2), successfully achieving our proposed objective 4.

27107320.label: Major findings and research outcome
27107320.value: Excessive use of antibiotics has resulted in drug-resistant bacteria, a serious global health concern. This highlights the urgent need for innovative drugs to counteract these superbugs. Bacterial peptides, a large family of antibiotics, are gaining attention for their potential to fight drug-resistant pathogens. Our preliminary research using extensive data from 163,037 sequenced bacterial genomes suggests that these peptides are incredibly diverse and largely unexplored, offering a vast resource for new antibiotic discovery. However, their diversity and complexity make them difficult to study, impeding targeted discovery. In our project, we applied the genomics-guided approach to systematize very large volumes of genetic, metabolic, and bioactive data robustly into an integrated high-throughput screening platform of novel antibiotics (publications # 1-5) Using a big data omics mining approach on the complex microbiota, we have uncovered new insights into the biosynthetic capacity of peptide antibiotics, linking them to antagonistic contributions to homeostasis through omics analysis and in vitro bioassay. The findings on antibiotic peptides' diversity and prevalence suggest that microbes are untapped sources for antibiotic discovery (Microbiome 2023, # 2.) We used extensive genome mining to understand the relationship between BGCs of peptide antibiotics and associated biosynthetic enzymes. Our synthetic biology strategies helped identify several crucial proteases for peptide antibiotic maturation, aiding the discovery of new antibiotic peptides to combat superbugs (Nat. Commun. 2022, #1). Additionally, we identified the first antimicrobial peptides from Archaea, an underexplored domain of life, through integrated omics mining of Archaea. This finding is expected to stimulate research in archaeal chemical biology and highlight the potential of archaea as a novel source of antimicrobials (Microbiome 2023, # 3). We also applied synthetic biology to improve the production and purity of peptide antibiotic colistin, a critical antibiotic for fighting multidrug-resistant bacterial infections. Our pioneering study sets the groundwork for optimized colistin production and has been licensed to the industry. (Metabol. Eng., 2024, # 5) In conclusion, by using a data-driven approach to bacterial genome sequencing, we discovered new peptide antibiotics to combat antibiotic resistance. Our research not only discovers potential therapeutic peptide antibiotics but also paves the way for future studies on the diverse biological functions of peptide antibiotics and bioengineering for translational research.

27107320.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27107320.value: Our project effectively used a genomics-guided method to organize vast amounts of genetic, metabolic, and bioactive data into a unified platform for discovering new antibiotics. Our data analysis successfully uncovered several hidden enzymes essential for antibiotic peptide development, demonstrating the efficiency of our approach. Using an extensive omics mining strategy on the complex microbiome, we've uncovered key insights into the production capabilities of peptide antibiotics. This analysis links them to the maintenance of health, setting the stage for future research on discovering new antimicrobials from complex microbiomes. We've enhanced the production and purity of colistin, a key antibiotic for tackling multi-drug resistant bacterial infections, through metabolic engineering. This underscores the potential of metabolic engineering for the clinical use of peptide antibiotics, especially in non-standard strains. Our pioneering work in colistin production optimization forms a foundation for future endeavors. The patented method we developed has been commercialized through licensing to industry partners. Our future research will focus on the translational study of this peptide antibiotic, with the goal of combating the escalating issue of antibiotic resistance.

27107320.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27107320.value: The excessive use of antibiotics has given rise to bacteria that are resistant to drugs, posing a significant challenge to global health. We urgently need innovative solutions to combat these "superbugs". Bacterial peptides, a type of antibiotic, offer promising potential in this fight. Our research has revealed that these microbial peptides are incredibly varied and largely untapped, signifying a vast potential for discovering new antibiotics. We've developed a comprehensive platform that organizes a wealth of omics data, aiding in the discovery of new antibiotics. We've harnessed big data mining to study the biosynthetic potential of peptide antibiotics, leading to the identification of new antibiotics derived from microbiota. Additionally, we've used big data genome mining to uncover hidden enzymes involved in antibiotic peptide biosynthesis, aiding in discovering new antibiotic peptides that could combat superbugs. Furthermore, we've bioengineered the production of colistin, a critical antibiotic, through synthetic biology. This work lays the foundation for optimizing colistin production, and our patented method has been licensed for industry use. Our project effectively applied big data mining to integrate vast amounts of data into a single platform for discovering new antibiotics. This approach will guide our future research in uncovering new antimicrobials from microbes.

27107420.label: Project Objectives
27107420.value: The first objective of this proposal is to validate rat models for hepatitis E virus species C (HEV-C) infection using patient-derived and street rat-derived HEV-C isolates. HEV-C, also known as rat hepatitis E virus, circulates in street rat populations around the world. It is genetically highly distinct from HEV species A (HEV-A) - the predominant cause of hepatitis E among humans. The zoonotic potential of HEV-C had been discounted previously based on its failure to infect non-human primates in experimental settings. However, in our previous research findings, we have conclusively proven that HEV-C infects humans and is capable of causing severe clinical disease in immunocompromised persons. We have demonstrated that HEV-C is the most common rodent-borne infection in Hong Kong. Robust animal models to study HEV-C infection are lacking. Previous attempts at developing rat models for HEV-C have found that rats are difficult to infect and only capable of supporting transient infections. Appropriate animal models are vital to study pathogenesis and evaluate new vaccines and antivirals against HEV-C. We have strong preliminary pilot data for HEV-C rat models using immunosuppressants to damp down immune responses to mimic the immunological milieu of human transplant recipients, who appear particularly vulnerable to severe HEV-C infection. Therefore, the first objective of our study is to thoroughly validate immunocompromised and immunocompetent rat models for HEV-C infection using HEV-C strains from multiple sources. We then plan to perform vaccination experiments using these models as described below. We hypothesize that prior vaccine-induced immunity to HEV-A would not protect against HEV-C infection. We have previously demonstrated that prior immunity against HEV-A did not protect an immunosuppressed liver transplant recipient from HEV-C infection. Indeed, we found that HEV-C infection induced a non-functioning strong anamnestic response against HEV-A infection in this patient, in keeping with the hypothesis of original antigenic sin (as observed in secondary dengue infection). To test our hypothesis that HEV-A immunity cannot protect against HEV-C infection, we will investigate whether prior immunity to HEV-A (induced using a commercially available HEV-A-based vaccine: Hecolin®) is protective, neutral, or detrimental in the event of subsequent HEV-C infection in rat models. Answering this question is vital as nearly half the population is exposed to HEV-A infection in Hong Kong by late middle age. However, their susceptibility to HEV-C with this immunological background is not clear. The Hecolin® vaccine is already commercially available in China and is heading through clinical trials in the USA. The efficacy of this vaccine against HEV-C is completely unknown and we aim to evaluate this. The commercially available HEV vaccine (Hecolin®) is based on HEV-A genotype 1. However, most patients in Hong Kong are infected with HEV-A genotype 4 and not genotype 1. Protection against HEV-A infection is cross-genotypic i.e. immunity against one genotype of HEV-A is likely to be protective against other genotypes. But, it is not known if the same is true for protection against HEV-C, which is a completely different species. We hypothesize that prior immunity to any genotype of HEV-A would not protect against a HEV-C challenge. Therefore, we plan to compare protective efficacy of Hecolin® against an identically formulated HEV-A genotype 4 vaccine in rats. We hypothesize that a specific HEV-C based subunit vaccine would be more effective than HEV-A based vaccines to protect against HEV-C challenge in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised rats. The swift development of an effective vaccine is crucial to control of emerging infectious diseases. Given our preliminary clinical finding that a) HEV-C infections are frequent in Hong Kong and b) prior HEV-A infection may not be protective against HEV-C infection, we have developed a HEV-C recombinant subunit vaccine, which appears strongly immunogenic in rats. We aim to investigate the protective efficacy of this in-house developed vaccine against HEV-C challenge (using two different HEV-C virus strains) in immunocompetent and immunocompromised rats. Performance of this vaccine will be compared to the two HEV-A based vaccines described above.

27107420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27107420.value: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a major cause of acute hepatitis globally. As shown by us previously, hepatitis E in Southern China is largely due to the genotype 4 variant of hepatitis E virus species A (HEV-A), which is acquired via consumption of undercooked pork products. We have also proven that genotype 4 HEV-A can cause chronic hepatitis in immunocompromised persons, which can ultimately lead to liver cirrhosis and death. This proposal deals with another variant of hepatitis E: hepatitis E virus species C (HEV-C), also known as rat hepatitis E virus, which infects street rats all around the world. Molecular tests for HEV-A cannot detect HEV-C infection due to high level of sequence divergence. The zoonotic potential of HEV-C was considered minimal due to its inability to infect non-human primates. However, in 2018, we discovered that HEV-C caused chronic hepatitis in a liver transplant recipient even though he had background immunity against HEV-A. We followed up this path-breaking work by identifying seven more patients with HEV-C infection in Hong Kong. This constitutes the largest cohort of HEV-C cases in the world. Six patients were identified in 2019 alone, making HEV-C the most common rodent-borne infection in Hong Kong. Worryingly, we found that immunocompromised persons (such as transplant recipients or people living with HIV) are susceptible to persistent HEV-C infection. We even identified one patient who died of HEV-C meningoencephalitis. There is an urgent need to evaluate means of protection against this novel rat-borne threat to human health. In this proposal, we aim to validate immunocompetent and immunocompromised rat models for HEV-C infection, building on strong data from pilot experiments. These models offer convenient methods to study HEV-C transmission, pathogenesis, clinical course, prevention, and treatment. Immunocompromised rat models, in particular, are highly reflective of individuals at high risk of complicated HEV-C infections. We will use these models to test the hypothesis that immunity against HEV-A (induced by Hecolin®: a commercially available HEV-A based vaccine) does not protect against HEV-C infection challenge. In addition, we have also developed two recombinant subunit vaccines (against HEV-A genotype 4 and HEV-C respectively). The efficacy of these vaccines will be compared to the Hecolin® vaccine in protection against HEV-C challenge. Building on our strong track record of work on emerging infectious diseases and hepatitis E infection, we expect this work to lay the foundation of small animal and preventive therapeutic research on HEV-C infection. 在全球范圍內，戊型肝炎病毒（HEV）是引發急性肝炎的主要原因。據我們所知，之前在中國南方出現的戊型肝炎病例在很大程度上是由基因4型HEV-A病毒引起的，患者通過食用未煮熟的豬肉被感染。同時，我們還証實基因4型HEV-A能夠誘發免疫功能低下的群體患慢性肝炎，最終可導致肝硬化，甚至死亡。 本提案涉及一種全新的戊型肝炎病毒：HEV-C，也稱大鼠戊型肝炎病毒。它能感染世界各地的街頭大鼠。該病毒與HEV-A在基因序列上存在很大的差異，這導致用於HEV-A的檢測手段不能檢測到HEV-C感染。通常情況下，HEV-C的人畜共患病潛力被認為是最小的，因為它不能感染非人類靈長類動物。然而，我們於2018年首次在一名具備抗HEV-A免疫力的肝移植者體內發現了HEV-C病毒，它也能引起慢性肝炎。基於這一開創性的發現，我們展開了進一步研究，在香港又發現了七名HEV-C患者，這使得香港成為全球確診HEV-C感染病例最多的地方。接著，在2019年又發現了六名HEV-C患者。至此，HEV-C感染成為香港最常見的鼠源性感染事件。更加令人擔憂的是，我們發現免疫功能低下的群體（如器官移植者和艾滋病感染者）容易被HEV-C持續感染。此外，我們甚至還發現一名死於HEV-C感染的腦膜炎患者。基於這些事實，評估防護這種新的鼠源性感染疾病的方法是非常迫切而且有必要的。 在本提案中，我們的目的是利用免疫功能正常和免疫缺陷的大鼠模型來驗証HEV-C感染，從一系列先導試驗中獲得強有力的數據資料。這些模型將有助於為研究HEV-C的傳播，發病機制，病情演變，預防和治療提供有利的方法。免疫缺陷的大鼠模型，能很好地模擬容易被HEV-C感染的高風險群體。我們將利用這些大鼠模型來檢驗這樣一個假說：具備抗HEV-A的免疫力（由一種商業化HEV-A疫苗"Hecolin"誘導產生）不能保護HEV-C感染。對此，我們還分別構建了基因4型HEV-A和HEV-C的重組亞單位疫苗。這些疫苗的有效性將與Hecolin對HEV-C的保護效果進行比較分析。 依據我們在新發傳染病和戊型肝炎感染有豐富的經驗，期望這項研究能夠為小動物模型和預防治療HEV-C感染奠定基礎。

27107420.label: Realisation of objectives
27107420.value: Animal model of rat hepatitis E Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is an important cause of chronic hepatitis in immunocompromised persons. We aimed to develop a small animal model of chronic hepatitis E using immunocompromised rats infected with Orthohepevirus species C (HEV-C1; rat hepatitis E virus), which is an emerging cause of human hepatitis. Female 6-8 week old Sprague-Dawley rats were divided into 3 groups (6 rats per group): immunocompetent (group 1; IC), low-dose immunosuppressed (group 2; LD) and high-dose immunosuppressed (group 3; HD). Rats in groups 2 and 3 were immunosuppressed using a combination of tacrolimus (5 mg/kg vs 7.5 mg/kg respectively), mycophenolate mofetil (25 mg/kg vs 30 mg/kg respectively), and prednisolone (10 mg/kg vs 4 mg/kg respectively). Drugs were administered 10 days prior to infection and continued thereafter. Filtered stool supernatants containing 2.5×105 copies/ml of HEV-C were administered to rats intravenously. Stool supernatants were either from infected humans (CCY strain ; 3 rats per group) or rats (SRN strain; 3 rats per group). Stool and serum viral loads in infected rats were monitored. Antibody responses and liver tissue histology were assessed. A high-dose (HD) immunosuppressive regimen consistently prolonged human- and rat-derived HEV-C1 infection in rats (up to 12 weeks post infection) compared with transient infections in low-dose (LD) immunosuppressant-treated and immunocompetent (IC) rats. Mean HEV-C1 viral loads in stool, serum, and liver tissue were higher in HD regimen-treated rats than in LD or IC rats (p <0.05). Alanine aminotransferase elevation was observed in chronically infected rats, which was consistent with histological hepatitis and HEV-C1 antigen expression in liver tissue. None (0/6) of the HD regimen-treated, 5/6 LD regimen-treated, and 6/6 IC rats developed antibodies to HEV-C1 in species-specific immunoblots. Reversal of immunosuppression was associated with clearance of viraemia and restoration of HEV-C1-specific humoral and cellular immune responses in HD regimen-treated rats, mimicking patterns in treated patients with chronic hepatitis E. Viral load suppression was observed with intraperitoneal ribavirin treatment. HD regimen-treated rats remained unsusceptible to HEV-A infection. We also collaborated with Xiamen university to test antigen levels in serum of these rats using a novel immunodiagnostic antigen detection immunoassay. IC rats did not have detectable circulating antigen while persistent antigenemia was observed in all chronically infected HD rats, which coincided with viremia. We developed a scalable immunosuppressed rat model of chronic hepatitis E that closely mimics this infection phenotype in transplant recipients. Protective efficacy of hepatitis E vaccines against rat hepatitis E We were then interested in investigating the extent of protection conferred by different HEV vaccine types against rat hepatitis E. Hecolin is the commercial hepatitis E vaccine available in China, which is based on HEV-A genotype 1. We expressed two virus-like particles HEV-A4 p239 and HEV-C1 p241 that represent the homologs of Hecolin. Briefly, the Open Reading Frame 2 (ORF2) gene fragments of HEV-A4 and HEV-C1 were amplified from the stools of two transplant recipients with chronic hepatitis E. The amplified fragments were cloned into pETH expression vector with an N-terminal 6x-His tag for purification and over-expressed in E. coli. Six-week old CD1 Sprague-Dawley rats (Rattus norvegicus; 3 males, 3 females (n = 6) per group) received two 10 µ intramuscular doses of HEV-A4 p239, HEV-C1 p241, HEV-A1 p239 (Hecolin) or PBS (mixed with adjuvant aluminum hydroxide) spaced 2 weeks apart. According to an a priori estimate that a) all PBS-vaccinated rats and 30% of vaccinated rats would develop infection and b) mean fecal viral load would be at least 2 log10 copies/ml higher in the PBS-vaccinated group, this sample size yields a power >90% at an alpha level of 0.05. Serological responses in rats were monitored for 4 weeks after which they were intravenously administered 0.5 ml of a filtered fecal suspension containing 106 HEV-C1 genome equivalents of SRN250811: a HEV-C1 strain derived from a captured commensal rat. Serial blood taking for HEV-C1 viral loads, serology and liver function tests were performed. Rats were sacrificed 4 weeks after infection. Liver tissue was obtained for HEV-C1 RTPCR, H&E, and immunohistochemical (IHC) staining. Rats vaccinated with Hecolin (HEV-A1 p239), HEV-A4 p239, HEV-C1 p241, or PBS were intravenously challenged with SRN250811 4 weeks after the first dose of vaccine. On day of challenge, vaccinated rats showed strong HEV antibody responses on species-specific immunoblots. All PBS vaccinated rats had detectable virus in feces and serum; fecal viral loads peaked at day 7 and turned negative by day 28. All 6 rats in the Hecolin group and 5/6 rats in the HEV-A4 p239 group had detectable virus in feces peaking at day 7 post-infection. None of the HEV-C1 p241-vaccinated rats had detectable virus in feces or plasma by either quantitative or nested RT-PCR assays, suggesting that the HEV-C1 p241 vaccine conferred sterilizing immunity. There was a trend towards lower viral loads in serum and feces of HEV-A4 p239 and Hecolin vaccinated rats but this was not always statistically significant. At day 28, 4/6 PBS-vaccinated rats still had detectable HEV-C1 RNA in liver tissue compared to none of the HEV-C1 p241-vaccinated rats. One of the HEV-A4 p239-vaccinated and none of the Hecolin-vaccinated rats had detectable virus in liver tissue at day 28. Hecolin and HEV-A4 p239-vaccinated rats maintained strong HEV-A-specific antibody responses after infection with weak responses on the HEV-C1 p241 immunoblot. Liver function tests in all groups remained normal, which is typical of HEV-C1 infection in juvenile rats. Liver histology showed mild degrees of hepatitis in PBS and HEV-A-vaccinated rats. IHC staining of liver with anti-HEV-C1 polyclonal antisera showed positive signals in PBS vaccinated rats infected with HEV-C1. Weaker signals were noted in HEV-A4 p239 & Hecolin-vaccinated rat livers and no signals were found in livers of HEV-C1 p241-vaccinated rats infected with HEV-C1. To further evaluate the effect of a mixed vaccine regimen, we vaccinated 4 rats with Hecolin at day 0 and HEV-C1 p241 at day 14, followed by SRN250811 challenge. Only 1 (25%) rat had detectable HEV-C1 in feces at day 3 (4.75 log10 copies/ml) and day 7 (4.58 log10 copies/ml), which was lower than the peak viral load observed in HEV-A vaccinated rats. All rat sera and day 28 post-infection liver tissue tested negative for HEV-C1 RNA. Rat sera showed stronger bands on the HEV-A4 immunoblot compared to the HEV-C1 immunoblot. Taken together, these experiments demonstrate that prior HEV-A exposure is not protective against HEV-C1 infection in rats. This confirms the impact of HEV-C1 antigenic divergence on infection susceptibility. The HEV-C1 vaccine shows excellent protective efficacy in animal models and is a candidate for human vaccines against rat hepatitis E. We decided not to pursue this experiment in immunocompromised rats as we doubted whether HD or LD-rats would be able to mount sufficient immunological response against HEV vaccines due to severe immunosuppression based on preliminary results.

27107420.label: Major findings and research outcome
27107420.value: 1. We designed a versatile gradable immunocompromised rat model of chronic hepatitis E infection using immunosuppressants commonly taken by transplant recipients. This model will enable convenient investigation of pathogenicity and antivirals for HEV infections. This work establishes capacity to perform chronic HEV research without using large animal models or genetically modified rats. 2. Using the above model, we evaluated novel serological immunodiagnostic assays for rat hepatitis E. 3. Due to extreme antigenic divergence between HEV-A and HEV-C1, we established that rat hepatitis E is only preventable using a specific rat hepatitis E vaccine. Prior exposure to HEV-A or vaccination with HEV-A based vaccines is unlikely to protect against HEV-C1. This has major implications for population susceptibility to rat hepatitis E.

27107420.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27107420.value: 1. A major limitation of our animal model is that it is not susceptible to HEV-A infection. However, the chemical immunosuppression method can be applied to other small animals such as rabbits or gerbils that are known to be susceptible to HEV-A infection. Indeed, we are not developing a gerbil model of chronic HEV-A infection using an identical scheme of immunosuppression. 2. With regards to vaccines, we have shown proof of concept that specific vaccines against rat hepatitis E can confer sterilizing immunity. Our next step is to develop bivalent vaccines that can protect against both HEV-A and HEV-C. These vaccines will be evaluated in the gerbil model mentioned in the previous point. 3. Using rat models and vaccines developed in this study, we are also developing a toolkit of hybridoma-derived monoclonal antibodies that will be used for a variety of applications including therapeutics and diagnostics. We now have an active collaboration with Xiamen University on this point.

27107420.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27107420.value: Animal models are essential to study and understand novel infectious diseases. Rat hepatitis E is a new variant of hepatitis E that was first found to infect humans in Hong Kong. It is now the most common rodent-borne zoonosis reported in the city. In this study, we developed a rat model of this infection. As most cases of rat hepatitis E occur in immunocompromised persons, we induced weak immunity in rats and found that this efficiently prolonged duration of infection, closely mimicking clinical features of rat hepatitis E in transplant recipients. Vaccines are an urgent priority for emerging infectious diseases. We had previously designed a virus-like particle vaccine against rat hepatitis E. Evaluating these in our animal model, we found that they were very effective in preventing this infection compared to vaccines based on conventional hepatitis E variants.

27110120.label: Project Objectives
27110120.value: Unresolved DNA entanglements formed between sister chromatids can persist in anaphase and give rise to a special type of DNA bridge, termed “ultrafine anaphase bridges (UFBs)”. Although it has been proposed that UFBs serve as a driver of chromosomal instability (CIN), precise molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Our previous work showed that UFBs are processed in late anaphase/telophase to generate single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) bridges, which will eventually be broken at cell division to induce DNA damage and gross chromosome abnormalities in the following cell cycle. We hypothesise that the repair of DNA damage induced by UFB breakage is highly mutagenic due to the single-stranded nature of the bridge remnants. Therefore, we will determine the repair mechanisms of the UFB remnants. We propose that the DNA ends of the broken UFBs contain an extensive amount of ssDNA that possibly leads to G1 recombination. In addition, the ssDNA may be cleaved by nucleases, followed by ligation mediated by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), leading to deletions and translocations. Our work will provide the first study of the detailed molecular mechanisms of how breakage of UFBs leads to CIN. Failure to resolve UFBs by interfering with the functions of UFB-binding proteins, such as PICH (PLK1-interacting checkpoint helicase) or BLM (Bloom’s syndrome helicase) induces a significant increase in the frequency of chromatin bridges. Chromatin bridges often lead to micronuclei formation and occasionally induce a complete failure of cytokinesis. Therefore, proper resolution of UFBs is important for cells to maintain genome stability and proliferation. However, the origin of those chromatin bridges is currently unclear. We hypothesise that translocase activity of PICH cooperates with its binding partner, BLM helicase, to prevent the formation of chromatin bridges. To test our hypothesis, we will target PICH using our recently developed PICH degron cell line model, and investigate how impairing UFB resolution induces the formation of chromatin bridges and other cellular defects. UFBs can originate from catenated dsDNA, late replication intermediates and recombination intermediates. Despite different underlying DNA structures, we previously demonstrated a common mechanism for their resolution: PICH recruits BLM helicase to unwind duplex DNA present in the UFBs to generate ssDNA bridges. We hypothesise that specific proteins are involved in processing different types of UFBs before the action of BLM or other enzymes. For instance, BLM and TOP3A can be recruited independently to PICH-coated UFBs, suggesting that they may play distinct roles in resolving different types of UFBs. Therefore, we will determine the precise mechanism of UFB resolution by focusing on the study of the interaction between PICH and BLM/TOP3A. We will also identify novel UFB-processing proteins by immunoprecipitating known UFB-binding proteins and identifying their interacting partners by mass spectrometry.

27110120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27110120.value: Proper chromosome segregation is dependent on the timely removal of all physical connections between sister chromatids prior to anaphase. Chromosome segregation defects are commonly observed in cancer cells and can manifest as ultrafine anaphase bridges (UFBs), which are long fine DNA threads linking the two separating genomes. UFBs are considered to be a threat to genome integrity as they have been shown to induce chromosomal instability, which is a hallmark of cancer and is often associated with poor patient prognosis in many tumours. Our pilot data has shown that unresolved recombination intermediates give rise to UFBs, which are processed in late anaphase/telophase to generate an extensive amount of single-stranded DNA that may be highly mutagenic. Meanwhile, failure to resolve UFBs induces DNA damage, formation of chromatin bridges and micronuclei, and even cell death. These findings suggest that proper processing of UFBs is crucial for the cells to maintain genome stability and proliferation. The next step of our research program is important as we aim to understand the detailed molecular mechanisms of UFB resolution and how unresolved/broken UFBs serve as a driver of chromosomal instability. Specifically, three main milestones will be achieved: Firstly, since single-stranded UFBs will eventually be broken at cell division and it would generate DNA breaks, we will determine the repair mechanisms of the UFB remnants in the following cell cycle. We hypothesise that the repair of the broken UFBs could be highly mutagenic due to the single-stranded nature of the bridge remnants. Secondly, we will investigate the cellular consequences if UFBs fail to be resolved. In particular, we will focus on how impairing UFB resolution leads to the formation of chromatin bridges. We will target PICH (PLK1-interacting checkpoint helicase), which is the first protein recruited to UFBs, using our recently developed PICH degron cell line model. Thirdly, we previously discovered that BLM helicase is responsible for unwinding duplex DNA present in the UFBs to generate single-stranded DNA bridges. We will determine the precise mechanism of UFB resolution and identify novel factors that are involved. Overall, we expect to identify several novel UFB-binding proteins and determine precise mechanisms for UFB resolution and repair. Our research will provide new mechanistic insights into how UFBs promote genome instability in cancer cells. 正確的染色體分離依賴於在細胞分裂後期前及時去除姐妹染色單體之間的所有物理聯繫。染色體分離缺陷常見於癌細胞中，部份缺陷可表現為超細後期橋(UFB)。UFB是連接兩個分離基因組的細長的DNA線。 UFBs被認為是對基因組完整性的威脅，因為它們已經被證明會導致染色體不穩定，這是癌症的一個特徵，並且在許多腫瘤中常常與患者預後不良有關。我們的試驗數據表明，未析解的重組中間產物會產生UFBs，這些UFBs在細胞分裂後期/末期可能產生具有高度誘變性的單鏈DNA。同時，不能解決UFBs會導致DNA損傷，形成染色質橋和微核，甚至導致細胞死亡。這些發現表明，正確處理UFBs對細胞維持基因組穩定性和增殖至關重要。我們研究計劃的下一步很重要，因為我們的目標是了解UFB分解的詳細分子機制，以及未析解/破碎的UFB如何成為染色體不穩定的驅動因素。具體來說，我們將實現三個主要里程碑：首先，由於單鏈UFB最終會在細胞分裂時被破壞並產生DNA斷裂，因此我們將確定UFB殘留物在接下來的細胞週期中的修復機制。我們假設，由於橋殘餘物的單鏈性質，斷裂的UFBs的修復可能具有高度的誘變性。其次，我們將研究如果UFBs不能被解決的後果。特別是，我們將重點關注如果UFB不能被分解會如何導致染色質橋的形成。我們將以PICH（PLK1相互作用檢查點解旋酶）為目標，它是UFBs中招募的第一個蛋白質，使用我們最近開發的PICH degron細胞系模型。第三，我們早前發現BLM解旋酶負責解開UFBs中的雙鏈DNA，從而產生單鏈DNA橋。我們將確定UFB分解的精確機制，並找出涉及的新蛋白。總的來說，我們希望能識別出幾種新的UFB結合蛋白，並確定UFB分解和修復的精確機制。基因不穩定性的研究將促進我們對癌症細胞機制的新見解。

27110120.label: Realisation of objectives
27110120.value: Objective 1: To achieve our first objective about study of how ultrafine anaphase bridge (UFBs) lead to chromosomal instability in the subsequent G1 phase, we applied two approaches to induce a large number of UFBs: First, we first generated a resolvase-deficient (loss of both GEN1 and MUS81 nucleases) cell model that is known to induce a large number of homologous recombination-UFBs (HR-UFBs). Second, we treated cells with low doses of topoisomerase 2 (TOP2A) inhibitor, ICRF-193, which is known to induce centromeric-UFBs (C-UFBs). We showed that accumulation of UFBs induced large number of RPA-coated, single-stranded HR-UFBs, which will be broken during cytokinesis to generate RPA2 foci in early G1 cells. To understand the molecular repair pathways that will be employed to process the bridge remnants, during this reporting period, we investigated the co-localization of various DNA damage response (DDR) signaling and repair proteins with the RPA2 foci induced by UFB breakage in G1 cells. We found that RPA2 foci are colocalized with γH2AX and 53BP1 (markers for DNA breaks). Interestingly, we also observed RAD51, a repair protein that is involved in homologous recombination (HR), colocalizes with >50% of the RPA2 foci. These results suggest that the DNA damages induced by UFB breakage can be repaired by both non-homologous end joining-mediated by 53BP1 and homologous recombination mediated by RAD51. To further understand the consequence of unresolved UFBs, we depleted two important proteins that are known to be crucial for UFB resolution, RIF1 and PICH. We developed cell lines in which RIF1 or PICH can be induced to be depleted by tagging the endogenous genes with a mini-auxin-inducible degron (mAID). Depletion of either RIF1 or PICH induced increased levels of G1-DNA damage, micronuclei and chromosome segregation defects, consistent with our prediction that unresolved UFBs induce DNA damage due to bridge breakage. To identify structural variations in the genome induced by failed UFB resolution, we induced a transient PICH depletion, followed by analysis using whole genome sequencing (WGS). This approach enabled us to identify acute changes in the genome that appear frequently enough to be detected in the mixed population. We identified a strong increase of interchromosomal translocation and inversions caused by PICH depletion, suggesting that unresolved UFB ruptures can cause chromosome fusion and translocation, mirroring the predictions of the breakage-fusion-bridge (BFB) cycle. Our WGS analysis also revealed that PICH-depleted cells possess a higher proportion of SVs in non-centromeric regions compared to mock-depleted cells. Objective 2: To achieve our second objective about study of how loss of UFB-binding protein PICH leads to failure of UFB resolution and other cellular defects. We have previously generated an auxin-inducible degron (mAID) tagged PICH in RPE1 cells. This cell line allows rapid degradation of PICH to allow phenotypic analyses of failure of UFB resolution. Next, we employed our PICH auxin-inducible degron cell line to degrade endogenous PICH and complemented cells with the wild-type PICH or various PICH mutants. Our truncation experiments revealed that HELICs domain is essential for PICH to localize to UFBs. The 791-1000aa region in PICH was found to be essential in recruiting the downstream UFB proteins, i.e., BLM and RIF1, to the UFBs. Interestingly, PICH mutant that cannot recruit BLM and RIF1 can still partially rescue the loss of PICH, while the ATPase dead mutant of PICH (K128A) completely failed to rescue the PICH depletion. These results suggest that the translocase activity of PICH is critical for UFB resolution, while the protein recruitment function of PICH (i.e., to recruit BLM and RIF1 to UFBs) aids in this process. Furthermore, we found that PICH ATPase activity is crucial in unwinding double-stranded UFB to ssDNA and promoting the activity of TOP2A. Therefore, we propose a model illustrating how PICH promotes the resolution of catenated UFBs: double-stranded catenated UFBs can be decatenated by TOP2A, whose activity is stimulated by PICH in a translocase activity-dependent manner. Alternatively, the cooperative action of BLM helicase and PICH translocase unwinds double-stranded UFBs into single-stranded UFBs, which can then be resolved by the TOP3A-RMI1-RMI2 (TRR) complex, an efficient ssDNA decatenase. We propose that PICH translocase activity plays a dual role in UFB resolution by facilitating the generation of single-stranded UFBs and stimulating TOP2A activity. This model accounts for the inability of PICHK128A to promote UFB resolution, despite its capacity to recruit downstream UFB-binding proteins. Similarly, our model also explains the milder phenotypes observed in PICHΔ791-1000-expressing cells. Even though PICHΔ791-1000 cannot recruit other UFB proteins, it can still stimulate TOP2A to promote the resolution of catenated UFBs. How PICH promotes the action of TOP2A would be an interesting topic to be investigate in the future. Objective 3: To achieve our third objective about study of how PICH coordinates two UFB-binding proteins, BLM and TOP3A. We first study if PICH can interact with BLM and TOP3A independently. We deplete BLM or TOP3A by siRNAs and investigate if PICH-GFP can still interact with TOP3A or BLM, respectively. Importantly, we found that PICH cannot interact with BLM/TOP3A if either one of them is depleted by siRNAs. RMI1 forms a complex with TOP3A. Depletion of RMI1 also abolished the interaction between PICH and BLM/TOP3A. These results suggest that PICH forms a stable complex with BLM and TOP3A, and subcomplexes do not exist. We further identified the binding domain of PICH that interact with BLM-TOP3A, which is located at 921-1000aa. Using CLUSTAL Omega for protein alignment, we identified several highly conserved residues (D952, F953, N954, L955, S960) within this region of PICH. Mutating these residues to Ala (PICH5A) disrupted their ability to interact with the BTRR complex. Thus, we identified key residues in the C-terminus of PICH crucial for recruiting BLM and RIF1. Finally, we identified protein phosphatase I (PP1) as a novel UFB proteins by co-IP using RIF1 at the bait. We confirmed that PP1 recruitment to UFBs is dependent on RIF1. Depletion of RIF1 induced an increase in RPA-coated UFBs in a PP1-dependent manner, indicating that the major role of RIF1 in UFBs is to recruit PP1 to dephosphorylate and thus inhibit the activity of BLM helicase.

27110120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27110120.value: The findings from our research highlight several avenues for further development and investigation. Understanding the dual repair pathways activated by UFB-induced DNA damage opens up potential for targeted therapeutic interventions that manipulate these pathways to enhance genomic stability in cancer cells. Exploring the precise mechanisms by which PICH's ATPase activity facilitates UFB resolution could uncover new drug targets that mimic or inhibit this function, providing novel cancer treatment strategies. The identification of specific residues critical for PICH-BLM-TOP3A interaction offers a molecular basis for designing small molecules that can disrupt or stabilize these interactions. Additionally, the novel role of RIF1 in recruiting PP1 to dephosphorylate and inhibit BLM helicase presents an opportunity to investigate PP1's broader role in chromosome segregation and stability. Our proposed course of action includes expanding the use of whole-genome sequencing to identify structural variations caused by UFBs in various cell types and conditions, developing small molecule inhibitors targeting the PICH-BLM-TOP3A complex, and conducting high-throughput screens to identify compounds that modulate PP1 activity. These steps aim to translate our findings into therapeutic strategies that mitigate chromosomal instability and enhance the efficacy of existing cancer treatments.

27110120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27110120.value: Our research focuses on understanding how cells maintain their genetic stability during cell division, which is crucial for preventing diseases like cancer. Specifically, we study structures called ultrafine anaphase bridges (UFBs) that can cause genetic damage if not properly resolved. We discovered that a protein named PICH plays a critical role in fixing these UFBs and ensuring the cell's DNA is intact. PICH works by binding to UFBs and recruiting other proteins, like BLM and RIF1, to help resolve these structures. We also found that PICH must have a specific activity, called ATPase activity, to function correctly. Without it, the cell fails to repair UFBs, leading to genetic instability. Moreover, PICH forms a stable complex with BLM and another protein, TOP3A, which is essential for its function. Disrupting any part of this complex prevents PICH from doing its job. Additionally, we identified a new role for a protein called RIF1, which brings in another protein, PP1, to help regulate the activity of BLM. This teamwork is crucial for maintaining genetic stability. Our research could lead to new cancer treatments by targeting these proteins and pathways to enhance the cell's ability to repair genetic damage and maintain stability.

27111820.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27111820.value: Sjögren’s syndrome (SS) is an autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration and tissue destruction of salivary and lachrymal glands, leading to severe dry eyes and dry mouth symptoms. Due to the limited understanding of disease pathogenesis, SS patients have suffered from a lack of effective treatments in clinical management. Recent studies have suggested the critical role of immune regulatory cell subsets in the SS immunopathogenesis. Using our established mouse model of experimental SS (ESS), which recapitulates the key features of human SS, we have previously identified an essential role of Th17 cells in the disease development. Although Th1 and Th17 cells can be suppressed by regulatory B cells and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), our findings further reported defective functions of IL-10-producing capacity in B cells and impaired regulatory functions of MDSCs in both SS patients and ESS mice, which significantly contributed to the immune dysregulations during disease progression. However, the mechanisms underlying the functional changes of MDSCs remain largely unknown. In our pilot studies, we first revealed an indispensable role of polymorphonuclear MDSCs (PMN-MDSCs) in ESS development, as exemplified by exacerbated disease pathology upon PMN-MDSCs depletion. Further, we identified that aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), a ligand-activated transcription factor was highly expressed by human and murine PMN-MDSCs, but significantly decreased upon ESS progression in mice. Notably, Indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), a natural AhR agonist and the metabolite by commensal microbiota, markedly promoted PMN-MDSCs regulatory function and proliferation. Moreover, ESS mice treated with IPA exhibited ameliorated salivary function and decreased effector T cell response. Mechanistic studies indicated that IPA enhanced reactive oxygen species (ROS) production by PMN-MDSCs, while interferon-regulatory factor 4 (IRF4) served as a negative regulator in AhR signaling. In addition, IRF4 inhibitor simvastatin elicited synergistic effect with IPA on PMN-MDSC expansion in cultures, suggesting the therapeutic potential by targeting PMN-MDSCs in the treatment of SS. Cellular & Molecular Immunology. 2022, 19: 1361–1372 (Impact factor: 21.8, SJR Ranking 7/344 in the field of Medicine) 1. To identify the role of AhR in regulating PMN-MDSC functions in ESS development 1.1 Role of PMN-MDSCs in ESS pathogenesis We first successfully established the experimental Sjögren’s syndrome (ESS) mouse model in female mice by immunization with purified SG proteins. To investigate whether defective polymorphonuclear Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (PMN-MDSCs) contribute to the dysregulation of effector CD4+ T cells, particularly Th1, Th17, and Tfh cells, during ESS development, we first treated immunized mice with anti-Ly6G neutralizing antibodies upon ESS induction. In ESS mice with PMN-MDSC depletion, disease progression was markedly exacerbated, as shown by the accelerated reduction in salivary flow rate and elevated serum levels of autoantibodies. Moreover, phenotypic analyses revealed an enhanced splenic effector CD4+ T-cell response, including increases in the proportions of Th1, Th17, and Tfh cells, upon in vivo depletion of PMN-MDSCs, suggesting a critical involvement of PMN-MDSCs in restraining effector T cells during ESS development. Consequently, CD19+ GL-7+ Fas+ germinal center (GC) B cells, as well as CD138+ plasma cells, were also markedly increased, and this was associated with elevated autoantibody levels. Thus, these results identified a critical role of PMN-MDSCs in the development of ESS. 1.2 Role of AhR in regulating MDSCs function Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) was found to be expressed by a small fraction of human immune cells from healthy donors. Similarly, PMN-MDSCs were found to express the highest levels of AhR among various immune cell subsets in wild type (WT) mice when intracellular expression of AhR was further visualized. Thus, these results indicate that AhR may be closely involved in modulating the PMN-MDSC response. Purified splenic PMN-MDSCs and M-MDSCs were first incubated with Indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), a natural AhR ligand. In culture, IPA treatment did not affect the survival of PMN-MDSCs, M-MDSCs or neutrophils. Next, purified BMCs were cultured for MDSC differentiation in the presence of IPA. Flow cytometric analyses showed that PMN-MDSC differentiation and proliferation were significantly promoted upon AhR activation with IPA but suppressed by CH223191, a selective AhR antagonist. Moreover, IPA treatment enhanced the production of ROS, a regulatory molecule mainly produced by PMN-MDSCs and involved in mediating antigen-specific T-cell suppression. In addition, we performed the adoptive transfer of CD45.2 C57BL/6 MDSCs into congenic CD45.1 Boy/J mice. As indicated by the positions of CD169+ marginal zone metallophilic macrophages, transferred MDSCs localized to the white pulp T-cell zone and T-B borders in the spleen, potentiating their interaction with T cells in situ. To assess the function of PMN-MDSCs, we cultured differentiated PMN- MDSCs with CFSE-labeled naïve CD4 assay. As expected, IPA-treated PMN-MDSCs elicited more potent inhibitory effects on T-cell proliferation, which could be abrogated by cotreatment with the ROS scavenger Tempol. Interestingly, mice fed a tryptophan-free diet exhibited diminished splenic PMN-MDSCs with reduced ROS production and expression of CD244, a recently reported phenotypic marker expressed by PMN-MDSCs but not neutrophils. Notably, the impaired PMN-MDSC response in mice given a tryptophan-free diet could be restored by IPA supplementation. In addition, IPA treatment enhanced human PMN-MDSC differentiation from PBMCs. Together, these data demonstrated a pivotal function of AhR activation in regulating the PMN-MDSC response. 2. To elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying AhR-mediated functional changes of PMN-MDSCs 2.1 Transcriptional regulation of effector molecules by AhR in PMN-MDSCs In ESS mice, we detected significantly downregulated AhR expression at both the mRNA and protein levels in PMN-MDSCs; reduced ROS production during ESS progression was also detected in these cells. Interestingly, no obvious change in the expression levels of other regulatory molecules, such as CD73, LAG-3, and PD-L1, was detected in PMN-MDSCs from ESS mice. In contrast to the increased CD4+ T-cell responses detected in ESS mice; the cell counts of PMN-MDSCs were significantly decreased. We further assessed the suppressive function of PMN-MDSCs on the T-cell response. Consistently, PMN-MDSCs from ESS mice exhibited impaired regulatory function with downregulated AhR expression compared with naïve controls, an effect that could be abolished by treatment with ROS scavengers. Conversely, AhR antagonism CH223191 resulted in exacerbated ESS pathology and dysregulated effector T-cell responses, including increases in Th1, Th17, and Tfh cell subsets. Moreover, we confirmed this finding in ESS mice fed a tryptophan-free diet. ESS mice with dietary tryptophan deficiency also exhibited a defective PMN-MDSC response and accelerated ESS pathology, with significantly enhanced Th1, Th17, and Tfh cell responses detected by flow cytometric analysis. Together, these results demonstrated that the downregulation of AhR in PMN-MDSCs contributed to their impaired regulatory function during ESS development. 2.2 Role of IRF4 in AhR signaling-mediated PMN-MDSCs function During ESS development, interferon regulatory factor 4 (IRF4) expression was markedly increased in PMN- MDSCs and inversely correlated with AhR expression. Thus, anti-IRF4 ChIP-PCR analysis was performed in differentiated PMN- MDSCs, showing the binding sites of IRF4 in the AhR promoter. Notably, given that AhR was mainly expressed by PMN- MDSCs, with equal amounts of input, AhR immunoprecipitation by IRF4 was increased by IPA-mediated PMN-MDSC expansion and decreased by CH223191 treatment. We next purified BMCs from IRF4−/− mice and cultured them under MDSC polarization conditions in the presence of IPA. IRF4−/− MDSC proliferation and PMN-MDSC differentiation were markedly enhanced compared with those of the WT controls. IPA-mediated IRF4−/− PMN-MDSCs were significantly expanded, by 30-fold. Consistent with this observation, treatment with simvastatin, an IRF4 inhibitor, also promoted IPA-mediated PMN- MDSC differentiation. Although IRF4−/− PMN-MDSCs exhibited ROS production comparable to that of WT controls at steady state, markedly enhanced ROS generation was detected in IRF4−/− PMN-MDSCs upon AhR activation with IPA. Consequently, IRF4 deficiency further boosted the IPA-induced suppressive function of PMN-MDSCs in cocultures. Together, these results demonstrate that IRF4 is a negative regulator of AhR signaling. 3. Upon disease onset, ESS mice were treated with IPA or PBS vehicle twice a week for 8 weeks. Improved salivary function and decreased levels of serum autoantibodies were observed in IPA-treated ESS mice. 27111820.label: Major findings and research outcome
27111820.value: MDSCs comprise heterogeneous myeloid cell populations with immunosuppressive capacity that contribute to immune regulation and tolerance induction. We previously reported impaired MDSC function in patients with primary Sjogren’s Syndrome (pSS) and mice with ESS. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying MDSC dysfunction remain largely unclear. In this study, we first found that AhR was highly expressed by human and murine PMN-MDSCs. IPA, a natural AhR ligand produced from dietary tryptophan, significantly promoted PMN-MDSC differentiation and suppressive function on CD4+ T cells. In contrast, feeding a tryptophan-free diet resulted in a decreased PMN-MDSC response, a phenotype that could be reversed by IPA supplementation. The functional importance of PMN-MDSCs was demonstrated in ESS mice by using a cell-depletion approach. Notably, AhR expression was reduced in PMN-MDSCs during ESS development, while AhR antagonism (CH223191) resulted in exacerbated ESS pathology and dysregulated T effector cells, which could be phenocopied by a tryptophan-free diet. IRF4, a repressive transcription factor, was upregulated in PMN-MDSCs during ESS progression. Chromatin immunoprecipitation analysis revealed that IRF4 could bind to the promoter region of AhR, while IRF4 deficiency markedly enhanced AhR-mediated PMN-MDSC responses. Furthermore, dietary supplementation with IPA markedly ameliorated salivary glandular pathology in ESS mice with restored MDSC immunosuppressive function. Together, our results identify a novel function of AhR in modulating the PMN-MDSC response and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of targeting AhR for the treatment of pSS. 27111820.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27111820.value: Targeting the Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) emerges as a promising therapeutic approach in the management of Sjögren's syndrome (SS) among human patients. Dietary recommendations advocate for the consumption of AhR-activating foods rich in tryptophan, such as beef, tofu, and salmon, as they have shown potential in enhancing immune modulation. Simultaneously, ongoing clinical trials are actively evaluating the safety and effectiveness of pharmaceutical agents targeting the AhR pathway in individuals afflicted with various inflammatory disorders. These trials pave the way for the introduction of innovative therapeutic strategies that could revolutionize the treatment landscape for autoimmune conditions like SS. Furthermore, the exploration of AhR agonists derived from traditional Chinese medicine represents a promising avenue for future research endeavors. By integrating ancient healing practices with modern medical approaches, there exists a unique opportunity to enhance treatment outcomes and foster renewed hope for individuals navigating the complexities of SS and related autoimmune diseases.

27111820.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27111820.value: Sjögren's syndrome (SS) is a common autoimmune disease, with the clinical symptoms of dry eyes and dry mouth. The patients with SS suffered from the lack of effective treatment and low quality of life. In this study, our findings suggested that tryptophan enriched foods may be beneficial for patients with SS and may serve as dietary recommendations, such as beef, tofu, and salmon. This is because the metabolites derived from tryptophan, e.g. indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), could activate aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). In this study, we demonstrated that AhR signaling was critically involved in an anti-inflammatory immune cell subset, namely human and murine polymorphonuclear MDSCs (PMN-MDSCs). Defective PMN-MDSC numbers and function were observed in diseased mice with tryptophan-enriched diet, but attenuated by IPA supplementation. Molecular mechanism revealed that interferon regulatory factor 4 (IRF4) can modulate AhR signaling and their effector molecules in suppressing inflammatory T cell responses. Together, this study recommended tryptophan-enriched diet for patients with SS, which may help to recover immune tolerance.

27115220.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
27115220.value: Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular malignancy in the children under 4 years old. Most patients can survive from retinoblastoma after appropriate treatment, however, with the price of vision losing or eyeball enucleation. Chemotherapy by delivering anticancer drugs through intravitreal injection is widely used for the treatment of retinoblastoma in the past decade. However, this invasive treatment shows high risk of inevitably tissue damage and retinal detachment. Intravenous administration is noninvasive to the eye, but drug uptake by retinoblastoma is limited due to the blood-retinal barrier (BRB). The low drug accumulation at the tumor sites requires high drug dosage, causing systemic side effects. Therefore, a noninvasive, site-specific and controllable drug delivery system is highly desired for retinoblastoma treatment. Photoresponsive drug delivery systems can enhance drug accumulation at the sites where light is applied. Nowadays, the photocleavable groups used in the systems usually require UV or blue light irradiation, which, however, is harmful to the eye. Current strategies to increase the light wavelength are achieved by multi-photon processes. These strategies require high-power lasers or multiple components to achieve the photocleavage, limiting their clinical applications. Recently, our group developed a one-photon strategy of cleaving prodrugs with long-wavelength light (J. Am. Chem. Soc., 2019). A low-irradiance red LED light triggered the release of free drugs from the prodrugs. The light parameter is desired for applications in the eye. In the proposed project, we will apply this strategy to develop a low-irradiance red light-triggered drug release system for retinoblastoma treatment. We hypothesize that after intravenous injection of the system, light irradiation to the retina can trigger photolysis of prodrugs and accumulation of active drugs in retinoblastoma. The prodrugs without light irradiation in the blood circulation would not cause systemic side effects. We will encapsulate prodrugs and photosensitizers in FDA-approved polymeric micelles. The appropriate size of micellar nanoparticles and surface functionalization with the 8D3 antibody would benefit the BRB crossing. We will measure the stability and photo-triggered drug release profile. For in vivo study, we will construct an orthotopic mouse model of retinoblastoma. We will systematically investigate the pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, biocompatibility and therapeutic efficacy of the drug release system. The success of this original research will advance the development of photoresponsive drug delivery systems used in the treatment of eye diseases. The study would have potential clinical impact on retinoblastoma therapy.

27118520.label: Realisation of objectives
27118520.value: We have successfully achieved Objective 1, demonstrating that IFN-I induced oxidative stress and diminished the capacity of CD8+T cells to catabolize fatty acids by suppressing the expression of Hydroxyacl-Coenzyme A (HADHA). Specifically, through RNAseq analysis, we showed that IFN-Is treatment significantly downregulated genes related to mitochondrial respiration in Tex cells. We further observed that IFN-Is treatment upregulated genes associated with oxidative stress while downregulated those related to antioxidant activity, suggesting that IFN-Is signaling perturbed redox homeostasis in Tex cells. Furthermore, IFN-Is treatment also upregulated genes involved in fatty acid (FAs) uptake and elongation, while downregulated genes related to glucose metabolism. These findings suggested that IFN-Is signaling diverts CD8+T cells from utilizing glucose as the primary energy source, leading them to rely on fatty acids. We further corroborated the abovementioned transcriptomic findings with metabolic assays. To demonstrate that IFN-I treatment induced oxidative stress in CD8+T cells, we measured levels of glutathione, the major antioxidant in T cells, with flow cytometry. Our data showed that IFN-I exposure significantly reduced glutathione in activated CD8+T cells. Correspondingly, cellular as well as mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) were elevated in IFN-I-treated CD8+T cells compared with untreated counterparts. To demonstrate that IFN-Is signaling diverted the fuel choice of CD8+T cells, we first performed nutrient uptake assays by pulsing the CD8+T cells with fluorescent 2-NBD-glucose (2-NBDG) and long-chain FAs (BODIPY C16). Compared with untreated counterparts, IFN-Is-treated Tex cells preferentially took up long-chain FAs over glucose. To further demonstrate that IFN-Is instructed CD8+T cells to utilize FA as the major fuel choice, we conducted extracellular flux analysis. Consistent with the nutrient uptake result, IFN-Is-treated CD8+T cells had a lower extracellular acidification rate (ECAR), indicating reduced glycolysis. Basal oxygen consumption rate (OCR), a proxy for mitochondrial respiration, was similar in both experimental groups. However, IFN-Is-treated CD8+T cells exclusively decreased their OCR following the treatment of etomoxir (fatty acid oxidation inhibitor), but not UK5099 (mitochondrial pyruvate transporter inhibitor) or BPTES (glutaminase inhibitor); unlike their untreated counterparts whose OCR was sensitive to all three metabolic pathway-specific inhibitors. These findings indicate that IFN-Is-treated CD8+T cells underwent metabolic reprogramming towards mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) with an altered dependency on FAs. Of note, IFN-Is-treated CD8+T cells expressed less HADHA, an enzyme which catalyzes the last three steps of FA oxidation (FAO). Gene ontology (GO) enrichment analysis also revealed that IFN-Is treatment downregulated genes for FAO. In keeping with this, IFN-Is-treated CD8+T cells showed a marked reduction in palmitate-mediated spare respiratory capacity compared with untreated counterparts, suggesting a defect in their ability to oxidize exogenous long-chain FAs to fuel mitochondrial function under stress. Together, these data suggest that although IFN-Is-treated CD8+T cells increase the influx and reliance of long-chain FAs, they fail to effectively catabolize the ingested lipids to sustain mitochondrial fitness. In objective 2, we focused on the impact of targeting IFN-I-induced metabolic defects on CD8+T cell function with cells isolated from healthy donors. As outlined in our progress report, we were unable to include SLE patients in our study due to the inability to collect their blood samples amidst the COVID-19 pandemic. As they are immunocompromised, they were advised to self-isolate during our study period. However, we successfully addressed this issue by implementing an in vitro assay that mimics the generation of exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tex cells). This allowed us to explore how targeting IFN-I-induced metabolic defects can rejuvenate the functionality of these cells. We first demonstrated that our in vitro-differentiated Tex cells recapitulated the phenotypical, functional, transcriptional, and epigenetic hallmarks of bona fide exhausted T cells. The frequency of PD-1+cells increased upon the addition of IFN-Is, indicating a larger proportion with exhaustive potential. Within the PD-1+ population, IFN-Is treatment elevated the expression levels of PD-1 and enhanced the proportion of cells that co-expressed multiple inhibitory receptors (LAG3, CTLA4, TIM3 and TIGIT), suggesting that IFN-Is exposure accelerated Tex differentiation towards a terminal cell fate. IFN-Is-treated Tex cells upregulated TOX, an exhaustion-associated transcription factor, while downregulating TCF1, a transcription factor which marks progenitor-like Tex cells. Functionally, IFN-Is-treated Tex cells displayed reduced proliferation capacity and impaired ability to co-produce IFNγ and TNFα compared with their untreated counterparts. Of note, these defects were not detected when Tex cells were briefly exposed to IFN-Is for the first 48 hours of the assay. Altogether, these findings suggest that chronic, and acute, IFN-Is stimulation directly promotes terminal exhaustion of human CD8+T cells. Once again, IFN-I treated Tex cells displayed elevated oxidative stress and harboured increased nmuber of depolarized mitochondria. To target this metabolic defect, we cultured in vitro-differentiated Tex cells with a potent anti-oxidant: α-tocopherol (Toco). Although the addition of Toco reduced ROS levels in all conditions, it preferentially affected the exhaustion-related features of IFN-Is-treated Tex cells but not Tex cells. Indeed, Toco treatment normalized TOX expression, restored cytokine production, and partly reduced the percentage of cells with depolarized mitochondria in IFN-Is-treated Tex cells. In summary, we successfully demonstrated that rectifying the metabolic defects induced by IFN-Is can restore the functionality of CD8+T cells.

27118520.label: Major findings and research outcome
27118520.value: Persistent IFN-I signaling is a shared characteristic in numerous chronic conditions, including chronic viral infections, cancer, and autoimmunity. Another key commonality that influences the clinical outcomes of these conditions is the development of exhausted CD8+T cells. Our previous study demonstrated that IFN-I can induce metabolic stress in CD8+T cells. However, whether IFN-Is also contribute to T cell exhaustion through metabolic dysregulation remained unclear. In this ECS project, we demonstrated that chronic IFN-I stimulation instigates metabolic damage in activated CD8+T cells. Specifically, we discovered that IFN-Is induce oxidative stress and impair the ability of CD8+T cells to catabolize fatty acids by suppressing the expression of Hydroxyacyl-Coenzyme A (HADHA). Significantly, these adverse metabolic events dampened T cell function and drove CD8+T cell fate towards terminal exhaustion. Interestingly, scavenging the excessive ROS with α-tocopherol reduced TOX expression, restored cytokine production, and partially decreased the percentage of cells with depolarized mitochondria in IFN-I-treated Tex cells, suggesting that IFN-I promotes T cell exhaustion via excessive ROS production. In summary, our results conclusively demonstrate that sustained IFN-I signaling accelerates T cell exhaustion and that targeting IFN-I-induced metabolic changes can reverse this defect. These findings offer novel insights into how inflammation induces immune dysfunction in chronic disease conditions and propose potential new strategies to prevent T cell exhaustion and restore T cell immunity in chronic viral infections, cancer, and autoimmunity.

27118520.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
27118520.value: Exhausted CD8+ T cells (Tex) play a crucial role in cancer development and are the primary target for currently available Immune Checkpoint Blockade (ICB) therapy, which is the first-line treatment for many types of cancers. It's worth noting that IFN-I has been found to be elevated in many inflammation-driven cancers. Our findings revealed that IFN-I accelerates T cell exhaustion through metabolic dysregulation, and targeting these IFN-I-induced cellular changes can reverse the exhaustion status of T cells. These results provide a critical foundation for us to extend the analysis of IFN-I prompted T cell exhaustion in the context of cancer and resistance to immunotherapy. Indeed, we have already accumulated substantial data showing that IFN-I stimulated genes were specifically upregulated in Tex cells in cancer patients. Additionally, using a murine liver cancer model, we demonstrated that intratumoral CD8+T cells devoid of intrinsic IFN-Is signaling developed fewer exhaustion features and provided better tumor control. Hence, we propose that elevated IFN-I signaling presents a significant obstacle for ICB therapy, and that blocking IFN-I could potentially enhance the ICB response in cancer patients. We have already secured a GRF to further pursue our analysis.

27118520.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
27118520.value: Continuous signals from a protein known as IFN-I are commonly found in various chronic illnesses like chronic viral infections, cancer, and autoimmune diseases. These conditions also often result in the emergence of dysfunctional immune cells, e.g. exhausted CD8+T cells, which further exacerbate the disease severity. In this study, we showed that continuous IFN-I signals disrupted the metabolic machinery of CD8+T cells and acted as one of the root cause of their exhaustion. Remarkably, by addressing the IFN-I induced metabolic changes in these exhausted CD8+T cells, we can rejuvenate their functionality. These findings enhance our understanding of how inflammation affects the immune system in chronic diseases, and also suggest innovative strategies to bolster the performance of our immune cells in combating these conditions.
