28300220.label: Major findings and research outcome
28300220.value: Several classes of porous coordination polymers, also commonly known as metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have been successfully synthesized for the remediation of heavy metals and PPCPs from water. Three major pieces of work have been completed: (1) Using derivatives of 2,4,6-triphenylpyridine, a class of mesoporous copper(II) MOFs with distinct three-dimensional structures has been synthesized. "PTBMOF" with a cubic space group was prepared and this MOF was observed to exhibit mesopores with an aperture of 27 Å. The mesoporosity of PTBMOF has allowed it to be used for the direct removal of cationic dyes with different sizes. On the other hand, PTBMOF can catalyze the photodegradation of anionic dyes, rendering it an effective and general remover for organic contaminants from water systems. This work has been reported in Chem. Eur. J. 2021. (2) A series of alkaline earth metal-based MOFs has been successfully prepared using 2,6-naphthalenedicarboxylate (NDC) as the linker. These MOFs were found to adsorb copper(II) ions from water rapidly, with maximum adsorption capacities of 299.4 mg g−1 for the calcium-based MOF, NDCMOF(Ca), and 398.4 mg g−1 for the strontium-based MOF, NDCMOF(Sr), surpassing related MOFs and common adsorbents. Meanwhile, NDCMOF(Ca) and NDCMOF(Sr) displayed blue luminescence in the solid state at room temperature upon photoexcitation, and this emission would be readily quenched after the adsorption of copper(II). Such visible changes in the observed color and emission have rendered the MOFs multi-functional as versatile adsorbents and sensors for Cu2+ in the aqueous environment. This work has been reported in J. Solid State Chem. 2023. (3) In view of its biocompatibility, we have utilized the iron(III) MOF, MIL-126, for the removal of pharmaceuticals from water. To enhance the porosity and crystallinity of the material, controlled amounts of acid modulators were used in the MOF synthesis. The material synthesized with 1 equivalent of acetic acid, namely MIL-126-1AA, exhibits remarkable performance with maximum adsorption capacities of 209.65 mg g–1 for piroxicam and 452.49 mg g–1 for ketoprofen, respectively. Such values are higher than those of other porous materials in the literature. By combining spectroscopic studies with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, the adsorption mechanism has been elucidated. A manuscript summarizing the research findings has been accepted for publication in J. Ind. Eng. Chem. Furthermore, the ECS has also supported our exploration on other porous materials with rich photophysical properties to develop novel adsorbents and luminescence sensors. This has led to the publication of several additional research articles and reviews in journals, as well as a book chapter. Please refer to Part C for details of these publications.

28300220.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28300220.value: In this project, we have successfully developed several classes of porous coordination polymers for the removal of organic contaminants as well as the removal and luminescence sensing of heavy metal ions. The structural and physical properties of these newly-synthesized materials have been studied in detail with respect to their adsorptive properties. With these new insights, it is anticipated that design principles for the development of porous adsorbents with enhanced porous properties can be obtained. This will lead to the optimization of the adsorption and sensing performance of the porous coordination polymers, allowing them to be useful for the removal of pollutants of different concentrations. Further development of this research is expected to be directed on the applicability of these porous coordination polymers for practical applications. More in-depth research is being conducted to comprehensively evaluate the selectivity, reusability and stability of these porous adsorbents and sensors.

28300220.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28300220.value: Porous coordination polymers are crystalline materials with extended three-dimensional porous structures that can allow the penetration of different guest molecules. By making use of these porous channels, water pollutants can be trapped inside the porous coordination polymers to decontaminate water. In this project, several classes of porous coordination polymers with different types of pores have been successfully prepared by using various metal salts that are non-toxic to the biological system. Firstly, we have prepared a series of copper-based porous coordination polymers with large pores (mesopores) for the removal and degradation of organic dyes with different charges and sizes. The porosity of some iron-based porous coordination polymers has also been successfully controlled to enhance their capability to capture different organic drugs from water systems. In addition to organic pollutants in water, another series of porous coordination polymers has been prepared for the capture and detection of heavy metal ions. All these have contributed to the removal of emerging contaminants from water, and contribute to the provision of clean water and sanitation, which is in fact one of the Sustainable Development Goals adopted by the United Nations.

28604120.label: Project Title(Chinese)
28604120.value: 探討中產階級的非主流選擇：對中國兩個城市在家教育的定性研究

28604120.label: Project Objectives
28604120.value: To provide an in-depth account of the motivations, beliefs, and perspectives of Chinese parents who are homeschooling their children. To elucidate how the homeschooling choice and practice are shaped by the wider social class context. To compare the narratives of Chinese homeschooling parents within and across two different Chinese cities (Hong Kong and Taipei) and with broader transnational trends. To advance existing explanatory frameworks for trajectories of middle-class social reproduction in relation to childrearing and schooling.

28604120.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28604120.value: The proposed project aims to provide in-depth accounts of how Chinese homeschooling parents perceive and make sense of their homeschooling choice, with a particular focus on the relation to social class position. This project is set against the backdrop of recent homeschooling developments in Chinese societies, which have received very little academic and policy attention. Homeschooling in Chinese cities, including Hong Kong, appears to be largely a ‘middle-class phenomenon’ where often only those better-off families can afford to opt out of mainstream schools. As an expression of parental choice, homeschooling in this context epitomizes (i) a conspicuous exception to the prevailing discourses and norms of parenting in relation to schooling; (ii) an extreme form of parents’ time- and resource-intensive approaches to childrearing; and (iii) an outlier in Chinese society where school education is highly valued, and success at school is commonly regarded as the key to upward social mobility. Given these considerations, the growing and underestimated phenomenon of Chinese homeschooling parents constitutes a unique analytical leverage for theorizing a relatively unexplored area of middle-class reproduction processes. While there are other areas of inquiry, such as the outcomes of homeschooled children, which would also be worth exploring, the central focus of this project is clearly on parents’ homeschooling choice. By examining the motivations, beliefs, and sense-making of Chinese parents in the homeschooling choice, this project seeks to bridge a much-needed gap in understanding alternative beliefs and choices of the middle class in relation to childrearing and schooling. The project is also a rare attempt to provide a comparative perspective on alternative class choice as well as homeschooling in a transnational context. A case-study research design is used to examine the experiences and viewpoints of homeschooling parents in two different Chinese cities, namely Hong Kong and Taipei. These two cities are purposively selected as the research sites for comparison and contrast, given the commonalities and differences of these cities’ socio-cultural and institutional settings (e.g., homeschooling is legal in Taipei but not legally regulated in Hong Kong). Using data primarily derived from in-depth interviews with parents from a minimum of 30 homeschooling families and supplemented by further observations of regular homeschooling activities during the day in about six to eight families from the larger respondent pool in the two cities, this project will capture the nuance of alternative middle-class choice of childrearing in the Chinese context. 是次研究項目旨在深入探討在中國的在家教育父母如何看待和理解他們在家教育的選擇，尤其聚焦於此選擇與社會階層地位的關係。在家教育近年在中國社會發展起來，惟此現象在學術和政策上均很少受到關注。在中國城市中，包括香港，在家教育似乎可被視為一種「中產階級現象」，即往往只有那些較富裕的家庭才有能力選擇讓子女退出主流學校而在家自學。在這種背景下，在家教育作為一種父母選擇的表現，可被視為以下方面的縮影：（i）有關學校教育的主流論述和育兒規範的明顯例外； （ii）父母花費大量時間和資源的育兒方式之極致； （iii）有別於中國社會對學校教育高度重視的情況。由此看來，正在發展卻又被忽視的中國在家教育現象，構成了一種獨特的分析個案，可用於對中產階級再生產過程中尚未清晰的部分進行理論化。儘管還有其他方面的問題也值得探討，例如在家教育的孩子的成績，但本項目的重點顯然是在父母在家教育的選擇上。本項目通過研究中國父母在在家教育選擇中的動機、信念和意義建構，試圖彌合在理解中產階級與育兒和上學有關的非主流信念和選擇方面上的不足。本項目提供了關於非主流階級選擇以及跨國背景下在家教育的比較觀點，也是一個罕見的嘗試。本項目採取個案研究設計，以考察中國兩個不同城市（香港和台北）在家教育父母的經歷和觀點。選擇這兩個城市作為對比的研究地點，是基於這兩個城市的社會文化和制度背景之共同點和差異（例如在家教育在台北是合法的，但在香港卻未受法律規範）。本項目將對來自兩個城市至少30個在家教育家庭的父母進行深度訪談，並安排與其中約6至8個家庭進行有關他們日常在家教育活動的進一步觀察，從而捕捉在中國社會背景下非主流中產階級育兒選擇的細微差別。

28604120.label: Realisation of objectives
28604120.value: The research project has successfully achieved its objectives, using interview data gleaned from 31 family cases, supplemented by observations, in Taipei and Hong Kong. Specifically, the project has fully achieved its first objective by providing a comprehensive account of the motivations, beliefs, and perspectives of Chinese parents who homeschool their children. The study revealed that the parents primarily chose homeschooling due to dissatisfaction with mainstream education systems in the Chinese context (e.g., over-drilling for examinations, spoon-feeding, standardisation, inflexibility, and other oft-criticised approaches in Chinese education), opting for non-traditional educational models (e.g., Montessori, Waldorf and Sudbury models) to cater to their children's individual needs. Some parents had had a negative experience with their children's schools (e.g., perceived failure to take proper care of their children’s needs; disagreement in values and expectations regarding classroom management and discipline). A few parents’ motivation for homeschooling was triggered by their children's physical and mental health problems or special needs. All the interviewed parents shared a belief that every child is unique. They stressed the need to create a good fit between schooling and their children’s personal and developmental needs. They also emphasized holistic development beyond academic pursuits. They believed that children will not thrive only in a conventional school setting; instead, their homeschooling, which was rich in content and variety, fulfilled their children’s holistic development. In this light, these parents thought about homeschooling as an approach to diversifying and hybridizing educational processes. For example, rather than simple learner-educator dyadic relations, multiple actors across at least five broad sectors and disciplines played a role in the process of homeschooling: the family, the institutional school, homeschool support groups, peer groups, and private educational groups. The homeschooling experience involved multiple interactions among the homeschooled children, parents, instructors, peers, and the wider community. These interactions concerned the educational goals and plans, learning methods and activities, managing time, and progress in learning. Homeschooling families in the study used multiple educational resources, including conventional classroom learning, worksheets, pre-packaged curriculums, reading, virtual learning, and everyday life lessons (e.g., volunteering and learning through living). The project has also effectively met its second objective by providing valuable insights into how social class context, particularly the middle-class context, shapes the homeschooling choice and practice. All the 31 cases except one in Hong Kong were categorized as the middle class, considering their educational attainment, occupation, and income. By strategically employing economic resources, social networks, and cultural capital, these families created a holistic support system that enhances the homeschooling experience for their children and aligns with their educational goals and values. They afforded homeschooling expenses, such as purchasing educational materials, tools, and hiring tutors, that align with their children's learning needs and interests. Socially, they engage in support networks, community activities, and peer learning for a collaborative homeschooling environment. Culturally, they leverage their cultural capital to shape their children's education based on specific values and various enrichment activities. Notably, the Hong Kong homeschoolers with their middle-class resources found ways to continue homeschooling by navigating legal loopholes. This project has fully achieved its third objectives by exploring diverse homeschooling narratives in Hong Kong and Taipei, highlighting the distinctions between these two cities, and their alignment with broader transnational trends. The study uncovered a range of values and approaches to homeschooling among the participating families. While similarities were evident in the narratives of homeschooling families in Taipei and Hong Kong, several differences did exist between these two Chinese cities, given their different social, legal, and institutional contexts. The decision to homeschool was a thoughtful process for respondents in both cities, yet Hong Kong families faced heightened uncertainties due to the absence of homeschooling regulations and limited societal support. In contrast, Taipei families often had connections with mainstream schools, emphasizing civic responsibility and good citizenship alongside homeschooling. Taipei families tended to adopt a more structured approach to homeschooling, likely influenced by the institutionalized nature of homeschooling within Taipei's legal framework and educational system. In addition, homeschooling families in Hong Kong frequently collaborated with private schools and learning centers, whereas Taipei families integrated public school resources into their children's educational journeys. In general, Chinese homeschooling experiences in these two cities align with trends in other regions worldwide, except that most practices were primarily driven by educational and pedagogical purposes rather than faith-based motivations. This project has significantly achieved its four objectives by providing new insights into the diversity of middle-class values in relation to childrearing and schooling. The project highlights how Chinese middle-class parents emphasized diverse values for their children and supported their children’s identity development. For example, they embraced the value of passion and other non-traditional qualities like wellness and self-awareness, and redefined education and success for their children. While extant literature on middle-class social reproduction often focuses on narratives of status attainment through conventional mobility regimes, this project shifts the focus to the underexplored “margins” of the field - where middle-class families make unconventional educational choices for their children. This shift in focus offers new insights into the diverse identities and values within the middle class, considering the changing landscape of cultural values around achievement, parenting norms, and educational discourses in contemporary society. Beyond the Chinese contexts, the findings carry broader implications for the cultural transmission of social inequality, particularly concerning how middle-class socialization adapts to evolving meritocratic structures in education and the workplace.

28604120.label: Major findings and research outcome
28604120.value: Major findings: a) Motivations and experiences of homeschooling: Parents were dissatisfied with mainstream schools due to over-drilling, standardization, and inflexibility. Some parents chose homeschooling due to negative experiences with schools or their children's special needs. They believed in the uniqueness of each child so they tried to provide personalized education through homeschooling. Homeschooling involved learning experiences with family, institutional schools, support groups, peers, and private educational groups. Homeschoolers used diverse educational resources for holistic development and meeting children’s social, emotional and intellectual needs through varied learning environments. b) Social class and parental agency: Chinese homeschooling parents mobilized their middle-class resources to exercise their rights to homeschool their children as well as support their homeschooling journeys. Their homeschooling experiences showed a diverse range of alternative values and approaches embraced by the middle class concerning childrearing and schooling. c) Comparison across cities: Taipei families had more structured approaches to homeschooling compared to Hong Kong families. In Hong Kong cases, there was also a notable discord with mainstream schools; most parents prioritised their children’s individual pursuit of self-fulfilment. Comparatively, Taipei’s respondents often had connections with mainstream schools with more frequent mentions of civic responsibility and good citizenship. Homeschooling in Taipei is highly institutionalised within a legal framework and the educational system there. While Hong Kong homeschooling families often collaborated with private schools and learning centres, many homeschooling families in Taipei incorporated the learning opportunities of public schools into their children’s larger educational journeys in life. Research outcome: The project has yielded significant research outcomes, culminating in the publication of two articles in esteemed SSCI-indexed journals, namely Educational Review (Lee, 2023; Q1 in Education and Educational Research), and Sociology (Lee, 2024; Q1 in Sociology). These publication outcomes underline the project’s academic excellence. In addition, the research findings have been disseminated through presentations at local and international academic conferences. These include the Annual Conference of the Hong Kong Sociological Association, the Annual Conference of the British Sociological Association, and the Quality Learning Conference in Taiwan. By sharing these insights with diverse academic audiences, the project has not only contributed to the scholarly discourse in the respective fields but has also garnered recognition within the academic community for its valuable contributions.

28604120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28604120.value: One area worth further exploring is to capture the ways in which Chinese homeschooling families, including their homeschooled children, navigate and respond to challenges over time. The homeschooling parents’ beliefs and practices may become more adaptive as their children transition from childhood to adolescence and young adulthood. Notably, my present study highlighted the parents' emphasis on intrinsic values such as happiness, self-awareness, and passion. As their children grow older, some parents might increasingly feel urged to deal with external indicators of success and adopt a more instrumental approach to preparing their children for higher education and the workforce. It is also significant in incorporating children’s perspectives of homeschooling, which may vary based on age, gender, and personal and family experiences. A follow-up study is thus proposed to re-engage the original participants from the present study. The participants will be invited again for interviews. These interviews will primarily focus on the participants' reflections on their children's homeschooling experiences over time. Additionally, homeschooled children will be invited to participate in interviews that aim to explore their perceptions, experiences, and challenges related to homeschooling, as well as the impact on their personal growth, educational and life planning, and worldview.

28604120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28604120.value: This qualitative study examines the growing phenomenon of homeschooling among middle-class families in two Chinese cities, namely Hong Kong and Taipei. Through in-depth interviews and observations, the research explores the motivations and experiences of families who opted to homeschool their children instead of sending them to traditional schools. A comparative analysis is also drawn between the homeschooling approaches and practices in Hong Kong versus Taipei. The findings provide in-depth insights into the alternative educational discourses and strategies embraced by the middle class in shaping their children's educational journey through homeschooling. By shedding light on this non-traditional educational trend in urban Chinese societies, the research offers a nuanced understanding of how middle-class families perceive and navigate childrearing and schooling. The study also reveals a range of changing values and perspectives on parenting goals and priorities regarding children’s education and future prospects, indicating a growing emphasis on qualities such as passion and well-being. These findings carry significant implications for middle-class identities and the perpetuation of social inequalities.

28604320.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28604320.value: Integrated language skill is important to students’ academic learning and further career development. Integrated writing (IW) has become increasingly popular in both first (L1) and second language (L2) teaching and assessment. The IW task requires students to retrieve and organize the ideas carried by the sources of reading or listening materials, then draw upon their writing knowledge to compose the required essay. Due to its hybrid nature, it brings a huge challenge to students due to its hybrid nature that complex skills are involved, thus it is very necessary to explore the relevant factors that influence students’ performance in IW. Executive functions (EF) refers to a set of cognitive processes (i.e., working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, and planning) necessary for performing goal-directed behaviour. Whereas an increasing number of studies have found that EF is an important factor accounting for individual difference in various literacy skills (i.e., independent reading and writing), its relationship to more complicated skills such as IW has not been systematically discussed. This project aims to extend the research scope to explore the roles of EF in completing IW tasks in both L1 and L2. A total of 300 Grade 10 students from six local schools will be invited to participate in this study. They will be asked to complete a battery of research instruments repeatedly at two time points, including one IW task in Chinese, one IW task in English and four psychometric tasks measuring students’ EF. Demographic information such as age, gender, and social economic status will also be collected. In addition to descriptive statistical analyses and basic correlation, hierarchical regression and structural equation modelling will also be performed. The findings will help to identify the significant contributors of EF to IW performance in L1 and L2 concurrently and overtime, respectively; examine the relationship between individual differences in EF and the IW performance; and investigate the mechanism by which EF affect the development of IW skills across languages. The contribution of this project is multi-fold. On a theoretical level, it will deepen our theoretical understanding on the underlying factors influencing performance in complicated literacy skills; Moreover, it also taps into the knowledge on the mechanism that domain-general factors impact the learning of L1 and L2. On a practical level, it could shed light on the teaching and learning of IW skills among secondary students. 綜合寫作技能對於學生個人的學業及未來的 事業發展都十分重要。當前一語和二語的語言測試均十分重視設立綜合寫作寫的任務。在綜合寫作任務中，學生需從閱讀和聆聽材料中獲取信息，並運用寫作技能寫出指定的篇章。由於在此過程中要同時協調多種技能，不少學生對此感到困難。為此有必要探討影響學生綜合寫作表現的有關因素。 執行功能指的是人們進行特定行為時的一系列認知過程，包括工作記憶、自我抑制、認知彈性、計畫等能力。近年來學界越來越關注執行功能與各種讀寫技能的關係，惟對於其與更複雜的綜合寫作技能之間的關係，尚欠缺系統性的探討。由此本研究主要探討執行功能對學生完成一語和二語綜合寫作任務的影響。 此計畫擬從6所本地學中招收300名中四學生參與研究。他們將在兩個時間點上各完成一次測試。每次測試的任務相同，包括一個中文綜合寫作、一個英文綜合寫作以及四個執行功能的測試。此計畫亦會搜集學生的人口統計學資料，例如年齡、性別、社會經濟水平等。 研究資料主要用作量化分析，包括描述性統計、相關分析、階層回歸以及結構方程模型。通過這些分析，此計畫將分別確定哪些執行能力可顯著預測學生中英綜合寫作能力發展，對比發現執行功能與中英綜合寫作關係的異同點，以及確認執行功能影響中英綜合寫作的有關機制。 此研究具有理論和實踐的意義。理論上它可讓學者更好地認識影響複雜讀寫技能的認知因素，理解聯繫一語和二語學習的有關機制。在實踐上此計畫的研究成果可有助於改善教學，幫助中學生更好地提升綜合寫作表現。

28604320.label: Realisation of objectives
28604320.value: Summary In line with the recent research trend on executive functions (EF), this study primarily explores its role in complex reading and writing activities. Integrated writing (IW) is a complex task that requires students to read and listen to assigned materials and then write an essay that meets specific requirements. This research not only contributes to further understanding of how EF impacts students' performance in integrated writing and sheds light on the writing process and related influencing factors, but also could serve as a valuable reference for them and enhance the efficiency of instruction in IW. This research aimed to recruit a total of 300 Grade 10 students from six local schools, requiring them to complete a battery of research instruments at two different time points. Unfortunately, the research team encountered significant difficulties in recruiting participating schools and collecting data due to the Covid-19 pandemic. With face-to-face teaching suspended during the pandemic, schools were unable to arrange testing activities. As a result, the research team adjusted some research strategies. For instance, certain pilot research activities were conducted online to ensure the smooth operation of research tools such as EF tasks. Additionally, the team kept close communication with the schools and adopted flexible data collection methods. For instance, post-test timeframe was appropriately extended without compromising data quality (e.g., originally planning to complete Chinese and English tests within one week but adjusting it to two weeks). Through the team's efforts, a total of 306 secondary four students successfully completed all the pre- and post-test activities. The testing tasks included two IW tasks in Chinese and English, and five tasks measuring EF skills, including inhibition, working memory (visual and verbal working memory), shifting and planning. he two time points were arranged at an at least 8 months gap. In addition, during the project period, the research team has also completed seven research papers, including four journal papers (one published and three under review) and three conference papers. The research objectives of this study have been successfully achieved. Realisation of three objectives 1. To identify the concurrent and prospective effect of executive functions on the integrated writing (IW) task performance in Chinese (L1) The objective has been fully achieved. Students’ performance in a Chinese listening-reading-writing task was assessed with a well validated framework of IW competence, including four aspects, including (a) contextual awareness (b) citation and synthesis (c) opinion and argument, and (d) written expression and organization. Students scored an average of 18.17 at first time point and achieved 22.40 at second time point. By conducting regression analysis, it was found that the EF skills could explain around 9.0% variance of students’ IW performance in Chinese at first time point. Among them, only shifting (beta=.181, p<.01) and visual working memory (beta=.156, p<.01) could significantly predict IW performance. At the second time point, the explained variance dropped to 6.8%, and three EF skills could significantly predict IW performance: inhibition (beta=.135, p<.05), verbal working memory (beta=.120, p<.05) and planning (beta=.132, p<.05). Further regression analysis was also performed by using EF skills at first time point to predict IW performance at second time point. The result showed that EF skills could significantly explain 5% of variance, with visual working memory and planning as significant predictors (beta=.121 and 136 respectively, p<.05). Based on the above results, it could be seen that executive functions could have both concurrent and prospective effects on IW performance in Chinese. However, it could be noted that EF’s prediction has dropped as students advanced to higher grades. 2. To identify the concurrent and prospective effect of executive functions on the IW task performance in English (L2). The objective has been fully achieved. With a similar rubric as Chinese IW task, the project team completed rating for students’ IW performance in the English (L2) task. It was found that students scored a relatively low scored at first time point (Mean=10.27), which increased to 16.34 at second time point. The regression results showed that EF skills could explain a total of 12.4% variance of IW performance in L2, which was higher than that in L1 (9.0%). The verbal working memory was the only one significant predictor (beta=.30, p<.001). At the second time point, the total effect dropped to 8.9%, and inhibition (beta=.113) and planning (beta=.225) could significantly predict IW performance at second time point, p<.05. When examining the prospective effect of EF skills, it was found that EF skills at first time point could significantly explain 6.8% variance of IW performance in English at second time point. Both verbal and visual working memories’ beta values were significant (.145 and .153, respectively, p<.05). The above results indicate that executive functions shed a greater predictive effect on the student’s L2 IW performance than that in L1 setting, which might partially due to the additional workload imposed by the writing in a second language. Therefore, students may need to be more skillful in deploying their EF resources to memorize and complete the task. Moreover, it could also be noted that similar trend was found in EF’s effect as students grow older. Taking these results into consideration, it seemed that EF could have a less critical role when students’ literacy skills become more advanced. 3. To reveal the mechanisms by which EF may impact the IW performance across languages; The objective has been fully achieved. Using all EF skills as a latent variable, we performed two models of EF’s indirect effect on IW performance in L2 through their performance in L1. (1) EF(1st time point)-IW in L1 (1st time point)-IW in L2 (1st time point): EF’s direct effect was significant (beta=.433, p<.01), indirect effect was not significant; (2) EF(2nd time point)-IW in L1 (2nd time point)-IW in L2 (2nd time point): EF’s direct effect was significant (beta=.238, p<.01), indirect effect was also significant (beta=.079, p<.01); As we hypothesized previously, the L1 and L2 shared much skills in common thus L1 could possibly mediate the relationship between EF and L2 writing performance. However, based on the above results, it could be seen that EF could have both direct and indirect effects on IW performance in L2 via the mediation of L1 only at second time point. This could probably indicate that such hypothesis could be valid only when students possessed both L1 and L2 skills to some extent. 4. To determine the cross-lagged relationship between EF and IW skills in two languages. The objective has been fully achieved. Regarding to the possible reciprocal relationship between EF and IW performance, we performed the cross-lagged analysis using EF, L1 IW, L2 IW variables at two time points. The results suggested that all auto regressive effects were significant, including EF(1st) to EF(2nd), beta=.98, p<.01; L1IW(1st) to L1IW(2nd), beta=.499, p<.01; L2IW(1st) to L2IW(2nd), beta=.56, p<.01. However, for the cross-lagged effects, we could only find that IW in L1 at first time point could significantly predicted EF at time point 2 (beta=.206, p<.05). That meant that indeed there existed the reciprocal relationship between EF and IW, which might also suggest that students’ EF skills could be enhanced through the various practice of IW activities.

28604320.label: Major findings and research outcome
28604320.value: There are several key findings derived from this study. First, by exploring the longitudinal approach, we confirmed the importance of executive function to students’ integrated writing. Our preliminary results indicated that secondary students’ EF skills could significantly predict IW performance in both Chinese (L1) and English (L2) concurrently and prospectively. It should be noted that EF has a lower impact on IW performance at the second time point, implying that the importance of EF could be decreased as students develop higher level of language skills; Second, we discovered that the different roles of EF in L1 and L2 integrated writing. In general, the EF could explain more variance of IW performance in L2 rather than in L1. These subtle differences might be attributed to the different workload imposed to students’ writing process; Moreover, there might also be difference in the significant predictors of IW performance across two languages. For instance, visual working memory appeared to be more common factor in accounting for the concurrent and prospective effects in L1 context; On the contrary, the verbal working memory seemed to be more important to L2 IW performance. Third, we found that EF could have indirect effect on L2 IW performance through the mediation of L1 IW performance, although such effect might be significant only at the second time point. This mechanism suggested new evidence in explaining the connection between L1 and L2 language proficiency. Fourth, our studies have also indicated that EF could also be predicted by the IW performance in the cross-lagged model. In particular, the IW in the L1 context seemed to have bigger impact on the development of EF skills. All the above findings indicate that executive function is a set of domain-general cognitive skills that bear significance in integrated writing across different time points and linguistics contexts. These findings have not been reported in previous studies. Therefore, the results of the present investigation have further widened our understanding of executive function’s role in complicated literacy activities.

28604320.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28604320.value: Based on the results obtained, there are two lines of future research directions. The first one is to initiate more studies among different groups of students. For instance, it is less clear on how EF could affect integrated writing performance among students as a second language (CSL). As many studies have pointed out that CSL students might have difficulty in learning Chinese, therefore, it is worthwhile to extend the present study to CSL student groups; Furthermore, more studies could be done by exploring the connections between EF and sub-processes of IW through both quantitative and qualitative approaches, focusing on examining how EF could affect students’ writing process; Finally, increasing studies have argued that executive function does not only involve the “cool executive function” (e.g., inhibition, shifting, and working memory) but also the “hot executive function” (e.g., delayed satisfaction) (Kerr & Zelazo, 2004; Zelazo, & Carlson, 2012). Therefore, it could be meaningful to include more EF components in the study to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of its role played in various contexts of language learning.

28604320.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28604320.value: Executive function(EF) is a set of mental skills needed to achieve learning goals. While previous research has explored how EF impacts basic literacy skills, this study aimed to see how it impacts more advanced writing activities like integrated writing (IW) where students need to integrate information from different sources to form a coherent essay. The project invited 306 high school students complete writing tasks in both their first language (L1, Chinese) and second language (L2, English). The students also attended tests to measure their executive function skills. All tasks were conducted at two different time points.The study found that EF could concurrently and prospectively predict IW performance, in both their L1 and L2. Its effect was even stronger for L2 writing. The research also showed that EF skills could indirectly affect their L2 IW performance by influencing their L1 writing abilities. And there was a two-way relationship, where a student's writing skills could also predict their later EF performance. The results of this project have important implications for how schools design their curriculum and teach writing, by highlighting the key role of EF skills. Overall, this project provides valuable insights into the cognitive processes underlying complex literacy activities.

To investigate whether writers of traditional Chinese script and simplified Chinese script share the same mechanism of orthographic processing in handwritten word production
To investigate whether writers’ Chinese input methods in typewriting influence the mechanism of orthographic processing in handwritten word production

28604920.label: Realisation of objectives
28604920.value: The current project investigated the planning units in Chinese handwritten word production. Most Chinese characters consist of a semantic radical and a phonetic radical, which can be further decomposed into logographemes. The radicals provide a cue to the meaning (semantic radical) or pronunciation (phonetic radical) of the character, while logographemes are stroke patterns recurring in different characters independently. Objective 1 was to investigate whether radicals play a different role than ordinary logographemes in planning Chinese handwritten word production. Two experimental paradigms were used to address this fundamental issue. The form-preparation paradigm required participants to write down target characters upon seeing prompts. Participants’ response latencies were compared between a homogeneous context, with all the target items sharing a radical or a logographeme, and a heterogeneous context with unrelated target items. The picture-word interference paradigm required participants to write down the names of individually presented pictures while ignoring visually distracting characters. The picture name shared the same initial radical or the same initial logographeme with the distractor in the related conditions, and participants’ response latencies were compared between the related and unrelated control conditions. The results showed robust facilitation effects of shared radicals and significantly weaker effects of shared logographemes, suggesting a more prominent role of radicals as planning units of Chinese handwriting than that of logographemes. Hence, Objective 1 was successfully achieved. In order to examine the potential influences of Chinese scripts (Objective 2) and Chinese input methods (Objective 3) on handwritten word production, the project involved three groups of participants: Hong Kong participants who used the traditional script and orthography-based input methods, Taiwanese participants who used the traditional script and phonology-based input methods, and Mainland Chinese participants who used the simplified script and phonology-based input methods. The Taiwanese and Mainland participants both used phonology-based input methods but different types of Chinese scripts, so the comparison between their result patterns could reflect the effect of Chinese scripts on the planning units in handwritten word production. The results showed significant radical effects in both groups of participants. However, the logographeme effect was significant in the Mainland participants, but not in the Taiwanese participants, suggesting that the experience of using the simplified Chinese script might have increased the Mainland participants’ sensitivity to logographemes as planning units during Chinese handwritten production. Hence, Objective 2 was successfully achieved. The Hong Kong and Taiwanese participants both used the traditional Chinese script but different types of Chinese input methods, so the comparison between their result patterns could reflect the effect of Chinese input methods on the planning units in handwritten word production. The results showed significant radical effects and non-significant logographeme effects in both groups of participants. Additionally, the Hong Kong participants showed a significantly larger radical effect than the Taiwanese participants, suggesting that using orthography-based input methods might have increased the salience of radicals as planning units of Chinese handwriting among the Hong Kong participants, relative to using phonology-based input methods. Hence, Objective 3 was successfully achieved.

28604920.label: Major findings and research outcome
28604920.value: The current project conducted two psycholinguistic experiments to investigate the planning units in Chinese handwritten word production. We compared the effects of sharing radicals or logographemes on participants’ writing latencies among three groups of Chinese participants: Hong Kong participants who used the traditional script and orthography-based input methods, Taiwanese participants who used the traditional script and phonology-based input methods, and Mainland participants who used the simplified script and phonology-based input methods. Both the form-preparation and the picture-word interference paradigms revealed significant radical effects (Wang et al., 2023). While the Hong Kong participants showed a significantly larger radical effect than the Taiwanese participants, no significant difference was found between the Taiwanese and Mainland participants. On the other hand, the logographeme effect was significant in the Mainland participants only, but not in the other two groups. Overall, the radical effects were significantly larger than the logographeme effects (Wang et al., under review). The results suggest that both radicals and (non-radical) logographemes are planning units during Chinese handwritten production, whose salience may be influenced by the type of Chinese scripts and input methods that have been used. Radicals are highly salient and can induce robust behavioral effects among different groups of Chinese writers. In contrast, (non-radical) logographemes are less salient and sometimes fail to generate significant behavioral effects (e.g., among the current Hong Kong and Taiwanese participants). Moreover, the experience of using the simplified Chinese script might increase Mainland participants’ sensitivity to logographemes, and using orthography-based input methods might increase the salience of radicals as planning units of Chinese handwriting among Hong Kong participants, relative to using phonology-based input methods.

28604920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28604920.value: The current project investigated the planning units of handwritten word production among literate Chinese adults. Future studies may adopt similar experimental paradigms to investigate the development of the planning units in Chinese handwriting among typically developing children, children with dyslexia, and second-language learners ranging from young children to older adults. Identifying potential deficits of the dyslexic population in planning Chinese handwriting and potential differences of second-language learners could help develop intervention programs to facilitate Chinese handwriting acquisition.

28604920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28604920.value: To produce a handwritten word, one must construct the written word form in the planning stage. The written forms of Chinese words can be decomposed into different levels of word-form units (e.g., radicals, logographemes). The current project investigated the role of radicals and logographemes in planning Chinese handwritten production. Chinese participants from three regions (i.e., Hong Kong, Taiwan, Mainland China) were involved to examine the potential influences of Chinese scripts (the traditional and the simplified scripts) and input methods (e.g., Sucheng, Cangjie, Zhuyin, Pinyin) on handwritten word production. The current results suggest that radicals are more prominent planning units than logographemes during Chinese handwritten production. Additionally, the experience of using the simplified Chinese script might increase Mainland participants’ sensitivity to logographemes, and using orthography-based input methods (e.g., Sucheng, Cangjie) might increase the salience of radicals as planning units of Chinese handwriting among Hong Kong participants, relative to using phonology-based input methods (e.g., Zhuyin, Pinyin). These findings provide original evidence to help lay the foundation for models of Chinese handwritten word production. Future studies may use the current methods and results as a reference to investigate the development of the planning units in Chinese handwriting among children and second-language learners.

28605120.label: Realisation of objectives
28605120.value: The project commenced in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic, posing significant challenges in recruiting and testing participants. Despite these obstacles, my team worked tirelessly to ensure the proposal objectives were met. Following a reviewer’s suggestion, we sought approval to change one participant group from Mandarin speakers to French speakers, resulting in a more cohesive line-up of L1 backgrounds compared to our original plan. Overall, the project objectives were achieved, and some unexpected findings may contribute to a more sophisticated understanding of our overarching research question: the “category vs. feature” debate. For the first objective, although numerous empirical studies have examined the acquisition of L2 phonemic quantity distinctions, most only compared (i) two languages at a time and (ii) participants of varying proficiency levels (e.g., ‘beginner’ is a relative term). In this project, we lined up four L1 groups (i.e. French, English, Cantonese, Japanese) that use duration to mark quantity distinctions to varying extents. This broader comparison provided a fuller picture for understanding the category vs. feature problem. For (ii), we tested naïve listeners of the target languages (i.e. Japanese and Estonian, except when the Japanese group listened to Japanese stimuli), to enable direct comparisons among these groups. This careful selection of participants was necessary to test the “category vs. feature” debate, as McAllister et al’s (2002 [JPhon]) study had remained the only multi-group comparison on this topic. This project is thus the first to compare as many as four L1 groups with equal proficiency levels (i.e. naïve). For the second objective, we compared the performance of Cantonese and English speakers in the production and perception tasks. Both languages exhibit partial quantity contrasts but in different ways. Our results showed that English participants outperformed Cantonese participants in most tasks. For the third objective, we collected perception data using stimuli contrasting in multiple acoustic cues, as well as audio recordings that would allow us the analyse primary and secondary cues in production. Therefore, the original objective was achieved. In addition, our findings may have revealed an interesting role of pitch in quantity distinction. Unexpectedly, Cantonese participants performed the worst in both production and perception among all L1 groups, when pitch was held constant and duration was the only varying cue. Since Cantonese was the only language analysed in this project with lexical tone, this new finding may have implications for the role of pitch as a secondary cue for non-native quantity distinctions.

28605120.label: Major findings and research outcome
28605120.value: In the perception task, we found that only Japanese listeners unambiguously outperformed the others. Meanwhile, the relative performance of Cantonese and English (partial quantity distinctions) as well as French (‘quantity-insensitive’) in different tasks does not seem to be easily attributable to their respective use of duration as a quantity cue (contra McAllister et al., 2002 [JPhon]). A similar pattern was observed in the production task, although the differences among L1 groups were less pronounced. Interestingly, the Cantonese group unexpectedly performed the worst. This puzzling observation prompted us to conduct a new analysis on an old dataset, leading to new insights and a deeper understanding of L2 quantity acquisition (Lee et al., 2023 [SLR]). Overall, through a direct comparison of four L1 backgrounds, our findings suggest that using phonemic quantity as a test case for addressing the 'category vs. feature' problem is more complex than initially anticipated.

28605120.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28605120.value: In this project, we tested naïve participants using synthesized stimuli created with VocalTractLab 2.0, where acoustic cues were controlled. Future researchers could verify our findings using natural speech stimuli and test learners of different proficiency levels. If such a setup yields the same findings as the present project (including the Cantonese group being the worst-performing), we could conclude that L1 duration use may play a much smaller role in L2 quantity acquisition than previously assumed.

28605120.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28605120.value: Mastering the pronunciation of a new language is challenging, and success depends on the similarity between the sound system of one's native language and that of the new language. Researchers believe that if one's native language already includes short vs. long sounds, mastering the same contrast in a new language should be manageable. In this project, we were particularly interested in how well people distinguish unfamiliar length contrasts if their native language only partially contrasts short vs. long sounds. We found that Japanese speakers consistently distinguished short vs. long sounds better, but the other groups (i.e., English and French) were not very different. This is surprising because many believe that French does not have short vs. long sounds. Unexpectedly, we found that Cantonese speakers performed the worst, even though Cantonese partially features short vs. long vowels (e.g., gai1 'chicken' vs. gaai1 'street').

28607420.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28607420.value: This project studies the Chinese oral communicative competence of Non-Chinese Speaking (NCS) students by investigating the influences of task characteristics and intersubjectivity on students’ negotiation of meaning. Developing oral communicative competence can enable second language (L2) learners to engage in class discussions, integrate into the local community, and more importantly increase their well-being. However, oral communicative competence of NCS students is under-researched in Hong Kong. Research has demonstrated that task characteristics affect how students negotiated for ambiguous meaning in interaction. This issue is seldom examined in young L2 learners, and little is known about how intersubjectivity affects the relationship between task characteristics and negotiation of meaning. Intersubjectivity refers to children’s ability to use embodied oral discourse and paralinguistic skills to engage in interaction based on their interpretations of the interlocutor’s intentions and beliefs. Therefore, intersubjectivity has been treated as the premise for children’s interaction. This study hypothesises that intersubjectivity moderates the relationship between task characteristics and negotiation of meaning. Contributing to the literature, this study aims to investigate this issue in two participation structures: NCS-NCS students’ interaction and NCS students-Native Speakers’ (NS) interaction for the reason that it is a common practice that NCS students and NS students are learning in the same class in Hong Kong. This study has three objectives:1) to examine the effects of task characteristics on negotiation of meaning; 2) to investigate the interaction effects of task characteristics and intersubjectivity on negotiation of meaning; 3) to investigate the interaction effects of task characteristics and participation structure on negotiation of meaning. This study will recruit 10-year-old NCS students and their native counter partners in Hong Kong to form two groups of dyads: NCS-NCS group and NCS-NS group. With a repeated measure design, all the dyads will be required to perform a total of four tasks that differ in interactional demands and cognitive complexity. The intersubjectivity and negotiation of meaning will be analysed by coding the oral discourse and physical gestures. The results can advance our understanding of the relationship between task characteristics and students’ negotiation of meaning by considering the effects of intersubjectivity. From a practical perspective, the results can generate recommendations for teachers and policy makers concerning principles for designing tasks to develop NCS students’ oral communicative competence. The comparison between NCS-NCS students’ interaction and NCS-NS students’ interaction can provide insights into classroom practice for helping NCS students bridging over to mainstream Chinese language classes. 本研究探索了任務特徵和主體間性對香港非華語小學生口語互動中意義協商的影響。口語交際能力的提升不僅能夠幫助二語學習者參與課堂討論、融入本地社區，而且能夠提升他們的歸屬感與幸福感。以往的研究表明任務特徵會影響二語學習者口語互動中的意義協商，但是這些研究多以成年學習者為研究對象，很少以低齡二語學習者為研究對象。另外，主體間性如何影響任務特徵和意義協商之間的關係，也較少被探究。主體間性指的是兒童基於對對話者意圖和想法的理解，運用口語語篇和副語言技能參與到口語互動中的能力。因此，主體間性是兒童口語互動的前提。本研究將選擇非華語小學生與本地小學生作為被試，設計兩種互動模式：非華語小學生與本地小學生之間的互動以及非華語小學生之間的互動。所有被試將通過口語互動完成難度不同的任務。基於數據分析，研究將探索任務特徵、主體間性和意義協商之間的關係。本研究有三個目的：1）探索任務特徵對意義協商的影響；2）探索任務特徵與主體間性的互作效應對意義協商的影響；3）探索任務特徵與互動模式的互作效應對意義協商的影響。從理論上，研究能夠幫我們進一步認識三者之間的關係。從實踐上，研究能夠幫助我們了解非華語小學生口語互動的特徵，從而為設計有效的教學活動提供參考。

28608920.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
28608920.value: Due to technological advancement and its growing affordances, English language learning and teaching beyond the classroom with technology has received recent research attention in the fields of Computer Assisted Language Learning (CALL) and Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (TESOL) (Lai, 2017; Reinders & Benson, 2017). The PI calls this emerging phenomenon Informal Digital Learning of English (IDLE), which is defined as “self-directed, naturalistic, digital learning of English in unstructured, out-of-class environments” (Lee, 2019a, p. 116). Concurrently, it has become increasingly common for ESL/EFL learners to communicate with English speakers from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Against this backdrop, Matsuda (2017) underscores the functional dimension of English from the English as an International Language (EIL) perspective, which broadly encompasses two constructs—namely, perceptions of varieties of English and strategic competence for cross-cultural communication. Although contemporary ESL/EFL students, as authentic EIL users, are increasingly engaging in cross-cultural communication in a range of IDLE environments (e.g., talking with diverse English speakers via social media or through digital gameplay), to date there is scant research on this topic. Building upon the PI’s previous studies (Lee, 2019a; Lee & Drajati, in press; Lee & Lee, 2019a, 2019b), this proposed research aims to fill the current gap by investigating the relationship between IDLE and two dimensions of EIL among Hong Kong university students, who are increasingly experiencing diverse accents among users of English through IDLE activities (Yung, 2019). Drawing on a sequential explanatory mixed-methods research design, data will be collected from 20 ESL/EFL classes at two universities by means of questionnaires (N = 400), open-ended questions (N = 400), semi-structured interviews (n = 40), and stimulated recalls (n = 40). With an interdisciplinary approach drawing from CALL, sociolinguistics, and TESOL, theoretically this study can help us better understand and further theorize the way in which informal language practice using technology is related to contemporary students’ perceptions of EIL. From a research perspective, the triangulated data gives us detailed insights into how students’ engagement in IDLE activities is conducive to developing their perceptions of EIL. Pedagogically, the findings will offer practical insights into how English language teachers can better prepare contemporary English learners for cross-cultural interactions in digital or face-to-face milieus. Additionally, since conventional EIL pedagogy seems to be limited within a classroom setting, the findings will broaden the current scope of the EIL pedagogical model beyond a classroom setting. 由於技術的進步及其日益增長的可供性，利用科技進行課堂以外的英語學習和教學在電腦輔助語言學習(CALL)和向其他語言使用者教授英語(TESOL)在近期有很多研究 (Lai, 2017; Reinders & Benson, 2017)。PI將這一新興現象稱為非正式數碼英語學習(IDLE)，它被定義為在非結構化的課外環境中進行自主的、自然主義的數碼英語學習(Lee, 2019a, 第116頁)。與此同時，英文作為第二語言或外國語言(ESL/EFL)的學習者與來自不同語言和文化背景的英語使用者交流已變得越來越普遍。在此背景下，Matsuda(2017)從英語作為國際語言(EIL)的角度強調了英語的功能維度，它大致包括兩個構念，即對英語種類的認知和跨文化交際的策略能力。雖然當代的ESL/EFL學生作為真實的EIL使用者，越來越多地參與到一系列的跨文化交流中(例如，通過社交媒體或數碼遊戲與不同的英語使用者交談)，但迄今為止，這方面的研究還很少。在PI先前研究的基礎上(Lee, 2019a; Lee & Drajati, in press; Lee & Lee, 2019a, 2019b)，這項研究旨在通過調查香港大學生中IDLE和EIL兩個維度之間的關係來填補目前的空白，香港大學生通過IDLE活動越來越多地體驗到英語使用者不同的口音(Yung, 2019)。採用順序解釋混合方法的研究設計，通過問卷調查(N = 400)、開放式問題(N = 400)、半結構式訪談(N = 40)和刺激回憶(N = 40)的方式，從兩所大學的20個ESL/EFL班級收集資料。本研究運用CALL、社會語言學、TESOL等跨學科研究方法。在理論上，本研究幫助我們更好地理解和進一步理論化使用技術的非正式語言實踐與當代學生對EIL的認知之間的關係。從研究的角度來看，三角式資料會為我們提供詳細的見解，讓我們瞭解學生參與IDLE活動是如何有助於發展他們對EIL的看法。在教學方面，這些發現將為英語教師如何更好地為當代英語學習者線上或面對面環境中的跨文化互動做好準備提供實用的見解。此外，由於傳統的EIL教學法似乎局限於課堂環境，研究結果將擴大目前的EIL教學法模式的範圍，使其超越課堂環境。

28608920.label: Realisation of objectives
28608920.value: Engaging in passive IDLE activities, such as watching YouTube videos in English, had a significant and positive effect on students' perceptions of different varieties of English. Additionally, both the total amount of IDLE activities and active IDLE activities, such as writing comments on Facebook in English, were significantly and positively associated with students' strategic competence in cross-cultural communication. The way students perceive different varieties of English (or their thoughts about the different accents and types of English spoken by English users) plays a mediating role in the relationship between practicing IDLE activities and their use of cross-cultural communication strategies (or their self-perceived ability to effectively communicate across cultures). The findings from the structural equation model analysis supported the hypothesis, indicating that EFL students are more likely to employ effective strategies for cross-cultural communication when their perception of different varieties of English becomes more positive through regular IDLE practice. The interview data revealed the process through which practicing IDLE activities positively impacts two aspects of English as an International Language (EIL) for students. 28608920.label: Major findings and research outcome
28608920.value: The main objective of this study was to explore the relationship between engaging in IDLE activities and two aspects of English as an International Language (EIL): perceptions of different varieties of English and strategic competence in cross-cultural communication. The study also aimed to investigate how students' perceptions of varieties of English mediate the relationship between IDLE practice and strategic competence in cross-cultural communication. Additionally, the study examined the processes through which IDLE practice can positively impact these two aspects of EIL. The findings of the study revealed that participating in passive IDLE activities, such as watching YouTube videos in English, had a significant and positive influence on students' perceptions of various forms of English. Moreover, both the overall amount of IDLE activities and active IDLE activities, like writing comments on Facebook in English, were significantly and positively linked to students' strategic competence in cross-cultural communication. Furthermore, students' perceptions of different varieties of English played a mediating role in the connection between engaging in IDLE activities and their use of strategies for cross-cultural communication, which refers to their self-perceived ability to effectively communicate across cultures. In terms of research outcomes, the ECS project assisted the PI in achieving the research objectives, leading to the publication of a book and the expansion of the results to encompass other psychological, emotional, and linguistic aspects of learning English as a second language. The target groups were broadened to include primary and secondary students in Hong Kong, allowing the PI to collaborate with frontline teachers. For example, the findings were disseminated through a monograph (Lee, 2022). Building on these findings, the PI extended their research to investigate the role of IDLE in speaking proficiency, enjoyment of learning a foreign language, and willingness to communicate among primary and secondary EFL students in Hong Kong, which was presented in a public lecture (Lee et al., 2021) and published in journal articles (Lee et al., 2022; Lee & Taylor, 2022). The findings were also utilized to write a systematic review of IDLE from an ecological systems theory perspective (Guo & Lee, 2023).

28608920.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
28608920.value: The research funded by ECS has successfully achieved its intended objectives and laid the groundwork for IDLE research. It has also facilitated the expansion of research to encompass additional aspects of learning English as a foreign language, including psychological factors (e.g., willingness to communicate), emotional factors (e.g., foreign language enjoyment), and linguistic factors (e.g., speaking skills). The target audience has been broadened to include primary and secondary students in Hong Kong, allowing the PI to collaborate with frontline teachers. Moving forward, the PI plans to develop a more comprehensive model of IDLE that incorporates its various antecedents and consequences. This will involve working closely with teachers in K-12 and university settings not only in Hong Kong but also in Mainland China and similar EFL contexts. As part of these efforts, the PI has recently published a teacher guidebook on incorporating IDLE into classroom activities (Dressman, Lee, and Perrot, 2023). Additionally, the PI has applied for the GRF 2024/25 to conduct intervention research focusing on the efficacy of IDLE in improving speaking skills, considering factors such as enjoyment, anxiety, and willingness to communicate. Leveraging the research findings and the teacher guidebook, the PI plans to continue sharing best practices and lesson plans with educators, teachers, and students through public lectures and workshops in both Hong Kong and similar contexts. The aim is to extend the influence of these findings beyond academic circles.

28608920.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
28608920.value: This study aimed to investigate the relationship between engaging in informal digital learning of English (IDLE) activities (e.g., watching English videos online) and two important aspects of English as an International Language (EIL): a) how people perceive different forms of English and b) how well they can communicate across cultures. The researchers also wanted to understand how students' perceptions of English varieties affect the link between IDLE activities and cross-cultural communication skills. The study found that participating in IDLE activities can have a positive impact on these aspects of EIL. To help students develop these critical skills in today’s digitalized, multilingual, and multicultural world, teachers and educators can create opportunities for students to engage in IDLE outside the classroom. This exposure to diverse English speakers, their language varieties, and intercultural communication in digital platforms can greatly benefit students.
